Well, ok, Heroes III is da best TBS, yeah I know but I do not agree and if you lost interest in my review you should not continue reading this. ;)
Well, Age of Wonders was not a big hit back in the days in Hungary. Most guys already played HoMM II or III, so they were kinda occupied. I was not as I was a fresh gamer myself with my first PC. In addition I loved fantasy, read a lot of books and had fun discovering LotR. And one day I got a demo of this game with a magazine. In the demo there was only 2 maps: First Conflict and the tutorial. I was playing this game of hours, over and over again. Playing the same map with the 4 different factions again, and again. Saying to myself: look, orcs, halflings, elves...just in LotR, and the magic happened! :)
When I finally got the full version I did not stop playing this game for months. Imagine a fantasy TBS game with 12 different factions, some are friends, some are not, some just does no care about the others, while others are keeping the possibilities to change sides, if.... Each of these factions had at least 8-10 unique units to unlock and to play with in a beautiful fantasy environment. The whole story is so fascinating that I would still buy if someone would have the time to write a book from it. The music there was not recorded by a big orchestra but it is so pulling you in to the world of AoW that you loose reality and suddenly you fight for Julia on Keepers side, or for Meandor on the side of the Cult of Storm...
Clearly an exciting story telling, beautiful fantasy world, lots of factions and units and one of the best TBS experience ever made. One of my favourite games of all time...:)

I've only made two purchases in Steam that I didn't like. This game is one of them.
Really, this review puts it better than I could:
To echo the main points of his review that I most agree with...this game is too pretentious, too obvious, too "convinced of its own profound meaning." Wrapping up a story of human frailty in depression, that then turns into
depression, that then turns into an unresolved musing on self-worth...it all gives the APPEARANCE of wisdom literature. But then you try to find meaning in it. So you begin to peel back the layers of artsiness, of story-without-plot, of game-not-game. And at the end of it all, it's hard to get anything more concrete out of this than "I laughed, I cried, it moved me Bob."
At it's core, you're left with a pile of pretentiousness that must be True Art because we all know that True Art is Angsty, and BOY does this game crank up the Depression-o-Meter!
To put it another way...it has no conclusion, just raw emotion. It was designed that way on purpose, I know. But a story that has no conclusion, has no profound meaning. You're simply whisked away on the narrator's journey of thoughts on his friend, on emotions, on his own insecurity--the end. You're supposed to experience these feelings by proxy. All feeling, no real concrete thoughts.
This game is NOT like the Stanely Parable...except in one way. The Stanely Parable's narrator is like the player in a lot of ways. The same can be said of this game. The narrator doesn't have a clue WHAT to conclude. You, the player, will also be denied any conclusion.
Well, here's MY conlcusion on the whole thing.
If you want to simply experience an author's stream-of-consciousness and his own expression of human frailty, buy this game. But if you want an actual STORY--or even something with any MEANING--this game isn't worth your $10, it's not worth your 1.5 hours.
...
Still don't believe me?
Go read the most highly rated positive reviews of this game. You'll notice they all talk about FEEEEELLLLLLIIIIINNNNNGGGG. But I challenge you to find even five that actually draw concrete, expressible meaning out of it.

- Good permadeath system (that you'l curse).

Current Cons:
- Initially a basic multiplayer set up
- No NPC's yet
- Vehicals will be welcome
- Maybe a little bit more variety in the current/future maps
Overall very happy with supporting this game in early access and if you're a survival horror fan you probably will be too.

I have about an hour into this game, which I purchased because of the beautiful visuals. I am not great at run-and-gun gameplay like this but I was hoping I could soldier through it to enjoy the great artstyle, fitting music, and overall feel of the characters design.
There is one point I wish to stress overall: You cannot ever relax during a level. There are no lulls in combat where you can appreciate the scenery.
Its undeniably a "good game" but I did have some small points that added greatly to my frustration.
-The Parry mechanic seems slightly unresponsive. I worry this might be my (middling) PC acting up, but with the rest of the controls being so tight and responsive it seems out of place. I took more damage from missing parry attempts than from any other source while playing.
-The second greatest source of damage was, what seemed to me, unpredictable damage. Certain attacks do not have any tell for you to react to. The worst of these for me was the Twins during the plane SHMUP level. The ball they summon can go either clockwise or counterclockwise and can start above or below. It seemed I always got hit at least once during that section of the fight. I am not much of a completionist but part of your score is based on your health at the end of the level, and if you like to aim for 100% completion I can see these attacks being even more frustrating.
-If you only have one charm its impossible to remove it. Considering the early charms all have downsides this seems like a weird oversight.
I may restart my game over that last point, as I can't afford a second charm to remove the first, and TBH even if I could I think having no charm might be better. I think its more likely I will find a Let's Play of this game so I can sit back and enjoy the visuals and music.
Overall I am glad I purchased the game, and I will give it a recommendation. You can tell the devs are committed to both the style and gameplay.

90% of the reviews on here have nothing to do with the game it's self but rather the prices and the DLC content. It's a good game, and the content that is included is very well put together. It may not be worth $80.00, but the standard edition which is at $60.00 (The normal price that almost every AAA title is released at) is perfectly reasonable. The gameplay is pretty solid, the best thing I can compare it to is Monster Hunter, if it were in space. The 4 hunter roles all have their own play style, and each character unlocked for the hunter categories gives some good variety. As far as the monsters go, the Kraken and Wraith seem quite powerful, while the Goliath seems a little weak in comparrison. I suppose that makes sense as it's the starting monster though. Otherwise, each monster has a pretty unique playstyle and strategy behind it.
The game has a few minor annoyances, such as graphical glitches. The most common I am aware of is your mouse pointer getting suck on screen while you play. It doesn't hinder your gameplay, but it can definitely become annoying, especially as it seems to manifest any time you use the Steam Overlay.
All in all, I'd have to say Evolve is a pretty good multiplayer game where teamwork and strategy definitely decide who wins each match.

You're numb from the cold. Hungry. Last time you had a drink was two days ago. The wind is howling, you've no idea where you are, and worse - you can't see a thing for the thick mist that's just descended. For fear of falling down a slope that you might not see, or getting even more lost and wasting precious energy, you decide that the wise thing to do is to stay put. Makes sense, right? You do your best to stoke up a fire with your remaining wood scraps, hunker down on your torn bedroll and try to sleep for a few hours. Hopefully stave off hypothermia.
Praying that the mist has lifted, you open your eyes. Damn; still can't see much. The wind has died down though, and you were able to warm yourself a little, despite dehydration now beginning to set in. You also desperately need food, and so - tentatively - you start to walk.
Then you hear it. A WOLF.
You freeze. This is bad. You can't see it, but it's close. The snarls are getting louder. Is it behind? In front? You're too weak to run, out of flares, and frankly, out of options. Looking around frantically, you pull out your old rifle and start wildly pointing it all around you in sheer panic, ready to pull the trigger.
Hoping that you won't miss.

Sometimes an old game shouldn't be revived and brought to a new audience.
You run the risk of... Well it's not really so much a risk as it is a certainty but... You run the risk of having the new audience take one look or play an hour or two of the game and discard it for being inferior to what is out now.
Inferior in terms of graphics, of gameplay, balance.. Loads of things.
But, back when this game came out, it was incredible. It really was.
It's not looking back with rose-tinted glasses, no chance. I still play it today and it holds up. I suppose it's enhanced by the memories I have of growing up and playing it but I don't think you can seperate personal experiences with games..
That said, if I had not played it then would I enjoy it today? That's an impossible question to answer.. Perhaps this influenced my taste in genres?
All I know is that this game is amazing and I return year after year to play it. It's a classic.
The artwork is beautiful. Really nice fantasy stuff. The portraits of your Avatars are amazing and varied, really adding a sense of uniqueness to your game.
The gameplay is simple, very easy to pick up, yet it has some elements that may surprise you such as migrating towns to your own race to produce units of your own faction or dividing mana income between the researching of spells and accumulating mana points.
You can even automate your battles for instant results... Something I never even considered of being possible and only on very rare occasions do I use it. I never want to skip taking control of the battlefield and utilising my units to the best of their ability. Never. Even in battles that I know I will lose.. For example my three Human archers versus a Black Drake... I'll take control of the battle and retreat my archers, one by one while the furthest one shoots before having to flee past his Brothers who have now taken up shooting positions... All just to whittle down the Drake's health so should I encounter it again it will be that much weaker.
You can really help yourself by taking control of battles, but the option is always there for a instant result should you so desire.
And who wouldn't want to use your Avatar to their upmost ability. AI control when automating battles really does no justice to any of your units and can have really unfortunate outcomes... Such as every single catapult ever built exclusively firing at your Avatar, when surely you would be moving him out of harms way in a battle you are controlling...
The story is, in its own right, perfectly acceptable. I find the factions throughout the main story to be extremely varied and offer a distinct feel when allying with/waging war on.
Personally I absolutely despise the Azracs for reasons long forgotten. I'm sure at one point one of my Champions accompanying my Avatar was slaughtered by their hands... Oh and I feel so terribly sad for Lizardmen... What an utterly useless race that give off the most satisfying noises when killed.
Speaking of noises, the sound in this game is great. Unit voices/noises are superb and some are downright terrifying... Like the Goblin Karagh. I will never forget seeing them for the first time as they sprinted out of the fog of war in a crypt, screaming.
But I think, for me at least, the best aspect of the game, is one that ties it all together and elevates it to legendary status... Again, in my eyes...
It's the soundtrack. The music. All composed by Michiel van den Bos.
I cannot describe how good the music is. It is simply spellbinding.
Certain tracks are linked to certain factions, and you only hear them when playing those factions. That is a great way to keep the music fresh. Other tracks are universal.
All in all, the music brings back my sense of nostalgia the strongest, more so than any other aspect of the game.
If you don't fancy buying the game, just listen to the music on YouTube and try to guess which track fits which faction. Or just chill out to it. Don't forget the secret track only found in the Demo version "In the Company of Elves".
I don't want to spoil all the surprises you'll find in this game. I think what makes a game great is discovering things all by yourself. It's new and unexpected that way.
I would recommend watching the Steam Trailer for this on the store page, it think it touches on a lot of aspects of the game which should give you an indication what is on offer while keeping enough secret to amaze you when you uncover it.
I don't personally think anything in this game can be considered a negative, but if you were to force my hand I would say that having the maximum level of defense & resistance on your Avatar takes the edge off the fear of him/her dying to such an extent that you will simply send him/her into battles solo or with mimimal backup.
That said... A stack of eight archers, regardless of race (Elves are better than Humans you see..), will most likely counter that. It's just a shame that the AI doesn't really take advantage of these tactics.
And that would be another negative. The limited AI. Once you are playing against the hardest level CPU, something I do not think will take you much time, you will be left feeling the game cannot offer you any more.
But, I am sure that there are mods out there to negate this...
All in all, this game is fantastic and I would highly recommend it if you are into this type of game. If you are not, wait for it to go on sale and give it a try, claiming a refund if it's not for you.
I give this game a maximum 10/10 [Defense... Better get those archers ready...]

TL;DR Unique limited gameplay (walkind sim) that's narration-driven story, very "meta" game dev/creative process, varied stylistic environments, emotionally impactful. Themes of the 'game' may come true - what you project/put into the experience may dictate what you get out of it.
Graphics - Quite varied. Takes you on a journey from simplests & familiar to rather polished settings.
Sounds - Sounds, narration, music all fit the tone & 'story' that unfolds.
Gameplay - Truly a "walking simulator", not a traditional game. Follow where visual cues/narrator takes you. Not much to do besides walk, listen & take in the visuals.
If you enjoyed Stanley Parable, Dr Langeskov (?), or other quirky story driven & *meta* games - definitely give this a try.
It had more emotional impact that I'd expected - but I believe that this comes down to one of the thematic elements of game, you get what you put into it (the experience is yours & not rigidly determined by the creator).

I had heard a lot about this game on Reddit, and it eventuallly sparked enough of my interest to make this the very first early-access/alpha/beta game I have purchased on steam. I have stayed up until 6am playing this.
If you like isometric, survival/crafting, zombie, adventure, rpg games, then you will absolutely love Project Zomboid!
For an isometric game, the aesthetics are fantastic! The detail put into the environment is great, and the building/wall camera vision style will switch automatically, allowing you to always see your character (think Sims style) - unless, of course, you are being swarmed by zombies. There is also a great field of vision mechanic where you can only see in a cone radius in front of your character - so you can turn around to see a zombie standing right next to you (this game has prompted many screams from me lol). The music is perfect for the inensity of the game, of every single moment where it can be your last.
The controls can take a little bit of getting used to, especially considering that you have multiple menus to deal with (ex: inventory, character stats). You have the option of keeping the menus locked open, making looting much faster if you can handle the space each menu takes up on the screen.
There is a lot you can do in PZ, and it is highly recommended that you keep the unofficial map handy for quick reference. The game allows you to choose your profession, which will grant skills like higher resistance to zombie bites and scratches. You can also balance perks and negative skills, making the game more interesting. The custom mode provides a way to test out the game, allowing you to select the frequency of encountering zombies, their overall stats, how long until the electricity and water supply run out (yes, this is a critical element of the game), etc. If you want to get a good feel of the game, I recommend you start of here, just so you can better understand what you need to do without the pressure of dying at a moment's notice.
The learning curve and difficulty of this game is moderate, however, I would consider survival mode (how the game is meant to be played) to be fairly hard.
You will start off at in a random house, with only the clothes on your back. From here, you can loot supplies, hopefully finding some sort of bag item - which you can wear on your back, increasing your carrying capacity. Securing food and water is essential. Any container objects like bowls or bottles can be used to hold water from the sink, and this is critical to remember because the water supply will eventually run out. Perishable food will rot when not refrigerated.
You increase in proficiencies as you do certain things - for example, whever you sneak around zombies you will gain points in nimblness, sneaking, etc. When you attain enough xp points, you will be able to "master" the first level of a "completed" skill. So, if I have cooked enough meals to fill my first block on the skill menu (level 1), and have a level up point, I can select the skill, mastering it and improving the quality of things that I cook. You will not be able to fill higher level skill blocks until you first master the lowest tier - this prevents you from just cooking for the entire game since you have to be mastering each level as you progress. Reading specialty books also provides a bonus multiplier to the respective skill, and there are different books for both skills, and their respective levels (ex: carpentry for begineers vs. advanced carpentry).
While you play, you will have to balance your needs, eating, sleeping, and staying hydrated. You can also get bored if you are inactive, and becoming unhappy is also a possibility (leads to depression). There are items you can take to help with these needs (like beta pills, antidepressants, reading newspapers, etc), and you can also take sleeping pills to allow you to go to bed (you cannot keep sleeping unless your character is actually tired) - this is very useful for trying to settle sleeping patterns into a rhythm where you are sleeping during night time and awake in time to maximize the daylight visibility.
The crafting is not too complex, you will need to find an axe and chop down trees for logs, then convert them into wood. Crafting a rain collector is a priority - with successfully finding an area to plant/farm as a close second.
I have played this game a lot, and there was one time when I had spent 3 hours securing a base and building nice walls around it. I even had set up a farm and rain barrel, with pretty decent skills leveled up already. While looting a nearby house, I opened a window, but the alarm went off. Being overconfident in my abilities, I went in anyway, thinking I would be able to loot and leave before the house was stormed by zombies. While looting the upstairs rooms, I heard the door break open. I quickly run down and spot zombies rushing in through the front door. I try the back door, but zombies are piling in from a broken window next to the fridge. Panicking, I run upstairs, loot a shirt, tear it into sheet rope, and fashion a climbable rope on the second-level window. I slide down, but zombies are surrounding the house, and I have no way out. I hop over a broken window on the first floor and attempt to juke through the zombie horde. I take a scratch, and immediately see that I am about to die. I try to drop my bag, but it is too late. I have joined the dead.
I stare at the screen for a good 2 minutes, sigh sadly, then load up a new game.
I love this game.
If you load a save where you have died, everything you have done will remain intact, so securing and transforming a safehouse will not be wasted. You can even find your corpse walking around if you are lucky.
The mod support is not as extensive as say, Space Engineers or Starbound, however, there is a lot of potential for great user-made content. The developers, unlock Starbound, are also very active, releasing builds at good intervals. Be warned, however, not to invest to much in your saves, as you may not be able to transfer over your saves to newer builds when they are released.
If you are interested at all, give this game a try. For an early-access game, it is quite impressive and very well-done.
Highly recommend!

Please note: Currently, at the time of this review, Project Zomboid is in Alpha. For those of you who are unaware, Alpha is the  state of program/game testing in which key features are being implemented. This is typically followed by Beta, which is still in testing. You can expect there to be some bugs and issues as the game is being developed. However, as far as I have seen with alpha games, this one is very stable.
Project Zomboid is a top-down, third person survival game currently set in Kentucky with two spawn point options. You start literally with nothing with the clothes on your back and build a better means of survival as you traverse this virus-stricken world. Before spawning, you get a little bit of character customization between body type, hair style, and hair color with both male and female player models. There are a range of character traits and in-game effects called "moodles" which are situation-specific. For instance, if you are in the rain for too long, you can become wet and increase your risk of sickness. Stand near a stove too long, and you will become overheated.
There is also a wide variety of items in the game. There are two firearms currently: a pistol and a shotgun. Aside from this are  hundreds of clothing items, other weapons, food goods, materials, and the like. Items that seem mundane in reality can be very useful to help you survive in Project Zomboid.
Online gameplay was added to the alpha in February and it is still very solid. However, the one major issue I have found is that if there is too much lag, zombies will phase in and out and disappear for a short time, before reappearing randomly. Sometimes, they don't reappear at all. Of course, being that the game is still in alpha, I look for this issue to be resolved before the game's official release.
If you enjoyed Day Z or Rust, you might want to try this game. I found out about this game from gameplay on YouTube, and I can't say I regret the purchase at all to support its development. I do recommend looking into survival tips before jumping headfirst into the game. There is a short in-game guide upon startup, but the game can be far more complex than its style suggests.

When it comes to Survival / zombie games I have to give this one a 10/10 because of the level of Realism of this game.
Lets start with you, You need to eat, sleep, drink water, have fun/not become borde (only if you spend too much time in your safe house organizing your shelves/crates, If you become hurt you need to apply medical attention, wear proper clothing based on the weather, stay outa the rain, and over all protection. The combat is Stright forward, shooting has been improved and since recent changes nerffed for Realism (Blessing and a curse) you learn how to Cook, Farm and build. you gain the ability to level up your Weapon skills, sneaking abilitys and other such stats. the world (as Huge as it is it is not endless) is your Oyster. you can set up shop any where you wish by either boarding up windows, fortifying existing structures or Building completely new ones. One more thing to add is your Line of sight, just because the game is issometric doesnt mean your able to ALWAYS see behind you, you have to physical turn your character around to see behind you, same with zombies Line of sight, which I feel is a really good touch of realism.
Zombies (or zomboids lol) are not made to be one type only. Based on if you play Survival, sandbox or what ever the servers settings are set to, you can make them Fast, slow, dumb, intelligent, weak or resilient. If you running from a Horde on your tail and you stay on the same road and dont lose them, they will likely follow. the will shamble around the area and wonder into and up to buildings trying to enter for what ever reason. out smarting them is tricky but can be accomplished by cutting through Trees, Homes or allyways. They respond to smells, sights and sounds (One trick ive figured out is if I fire off a round or two and get as many as i can to follow me I would lead them in a direction i know i wont need to travel, mostly away from my Objective or Safehouse, once they lose your scent/trail they will start to stray from the pack and break up wandering around the area)
This is my first REAL review for any steam game, Overall this game is Amazingly good and should be looked at being in the same league as games like Day Z. the Fact it being Issometric doesnt change the horror or the fun of the game. If your intersted in this game I suggest Watching lets plays first and or play the Demo and Give it a shot.

Alright so I had to delete my last review because a lot of people apparently can't seem to get past the beautiful artwork and music in order to see that there are some issues with the game, as expected since it was just released the other day. Overall I DO recommend getting the game, it is a reasonable price for what it is and if you ever played difficult platformers back in the day like I did, I think you will enjoy the game even if it is the "Dark Souls" of platformers. However, music and artwork aside I do think there are some kinks to work out. For one, there are some parry objects that DON'T get destroyed when you parry them, such as the balloons in that one side scrolling level at the circus, which I think makes it really difficult to keep your hp intact if you are trying to get it from the side or bottom of it. The other issue I have is with the super move and the regular single card moves. There should be no hitbox on you during those points and if you are on a cloud level you should not be pushed backwards off of it into whatever horrors lie below you. I have died too many times trying to use either of these special moves simply because I had a hitbox I shouldn't have had or because I got pushed off a cloud to my death. I've found this renders the dragon level completely broken unless you have certain things from the shop that not all of us bought.
Overall recommend and hope people have a fun time playing as I have after figuring out how to f*cking parry finally...

A fun little point-and-click in the vein of
. You're a space merchant by the name of Powell who has crash-landed on the desert planet Deadrock. Since your captain, Novak, is injured, you must find a way to heal him and fix the ship on your own by braving the desert landscape in search for the necessary parts. However, there's more to Deadrock than meets the eye, as you soon come across another ship that has met the same fate as yours and slowly begin to uncover the fate that befell it and its crew. Will you share that same fate?
Like
, the mystery is what keeps you going in this game. The puzzles themselves are not that difficult to solve and there's the usual amount of backtracking. Unlike
however, this game is short (it took me less than 2 hours to complete), probably shorter than it should be to thoroughly explore the mystery surrounding Deadrock and get the full picture of what happened to the crew of the Armstrong (the other ship you come across). In particular, as you get closer to the ending of the game an event occurs that suggests one of them might have (recently) uncovered the secret of Deadrock but nothing comes of it; it's another mystery that will probably never be solved.
Voiceover in this game ranges from bad to acceptable but the humor makes it tolerable. If there was a soundtrack to this game, it wasn't particularly memorable as I don't recall it. From the technical standpoint, I was fearful at first by the barebones main menu that featured no settings to adjust (no display/graphics options, no keybindings) and my fears were later justified as I played: the keyboard is useless in this game; I couldn't even use the Esc key to switch between the ingame menu and the game itself. Even the mouse felt a little underconfigured for my tastes, as gameplay comes down to using the left-click at all times (can't even right-click to backtrack).
In short, if you have a couple of hours of free time and are looking for a point-and-click space adventure,
fits the bill. However, I would recommend you wait for a discount in order to get it. I myself bought it during Steam's 2016 Winter Sale at 75% off. Doubtless it will be discounted again.

For instance, you sometimes can't see a white wall 2 lanes to the side of you because there's another wall one lane to the same side blocking it from your view, so you dodge the first one and smash against the second one without knowing it.  The fact that it takes a bit too long to move when moving through multiple lanes (as opposed to moving one) only makes this worse. The immediate solution (which isn't a good one tbh) is to look at the ground most of the time and rush to the closest blue lane, but on some levels there's a red hue in the background that will confuse the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you. You'll also get control taken away from you sometimes when you hit the speed up mark, so if you happen to be switching multiple lanes you can get caught in a red one and die without being able to do anything. You'll also die because you try to switch to a green lane and get caught by a wall between the green lane and your lane, or you'll try to wait for the wall to pass and then safely switch to the green lane, but it will be too late and you'll die because you lost control over your ship. Blue lanes are a pain too. The enemies were actually fine.
Overall, even with these annoying problems aside, it doesn't have much more to offer. You'll play through it once, if you can muster the patience, and unless you're crazy about leaderboards and don't know any other competitive game more compelling, you won't touch it again. Definitely not worth 3 bucks, in my opinion, but hey, right now it's free, so if you've got time to burn and you don't mind dying to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t a tad too often, give it a whirl.

Nostalgia hit me very hard when I saw it on Steam!
What can I say - it's a classic turn based fantasy game with some RPG elements. The RPG elements are stronger in the first part and in my opinion the balance between the races is better too (halflings and frostlings are a playable choice in multiplayer, which they are definitely not in part 2). It has suprisingly great tactical depth, the terrain for ex. strongly effects the way the units move, some have advantages in certain areas like greater sight, movement range and so on. Hell yes: a quick dwarfen ambush over a mountain chain or a bunch of wall-climbing halfling rouges that are concealed in the forrest capture your sight tower out of nowhere - it can really make a difference.
The only thing that I didn't like in the first part compared to the second is the hero system: they don't play such a big role in multiplayer (which can end quite soon in case your hero dies after 15 rounds on level 6... yes, and even against critters) as they hardly gather enough experience. The "classes" are useless too as you need your heros to be able to cast mighty spells, especialy in the mid/late game. A "fighter" hero has no chance against a sorccer. On the other hand, in single player the heros are soon way to overpowerd. I remember my wizzard elf had maxed sorcery skills, was able to swim, climb walls, did holy and fire damage and some other stuff that I basically choose because I had to when I was leveling. And the fact that you need a unit to have the ability "wall crushing" to attack a fortified city was annoying too.
Anyways, I can highly recomend the game if you like turn based games! Don't fall for the olde graphics, gameplay and tactics are still thrilling.

The Park is a superbly-crafted, gloomy, dark, atmospheric "short story" historically set in
universe (if you haven't checked it out, be sure to try it out, a 7 day free trial is included in the Extras menu of the game or you can get a 3-5 day trial key from a thread in
). It's full of frights, general creepiness, intriguing lore and the frenetic search for a lost loved one all woven into an effectively told AND experienced dark tale.
- The graphics are well done overall. Nice details, shadows/lighting, especially in the world around you. In comparison to other games on the market, I'd have to say it's an 8. The character models feel/look odd at times.
But in comparison to it's parent TSW, it's definitely a 9. It is awesome to see the "historical" versions/interpretations of a familiar sight in the TSW world.
- The audio/bgm is appropriate, quietly brooding and dark. The voiceover work is well done and the voice actor cast for Lorraine was compelling and appropriately cast (the voice fits the game character).
- It's simple and basic enough to make it non-obtrusive and keep the immersion intact. (which can be a double-edged sword) My only complaint isn't about the gameplay mechanics, or the length of the game, it's about the fact that I could not change my key or controller bindings. It's a subtle thing, but important for some folks that might have handicaps or are very preferential when it comes to keys (I'm VERY left-handed and prefer to use my numeric keypad for most things when using kb/m combinations). Also, it would've been nice to have a Zoom in/out feature for the lore items (notes, pamphlets, etc.) that you can pick up or interact with. Some of those fonts were just hard to read on my 52" TV and my 27" LED monitor.
- It was a well-told, immersively dark tale worthy of the TSW universe. I have no complaints. I thoroughly enjoyed the ride (figuratively and literally.. since there are some in the game. hehe)
- This is MY personal opinion. The amount of money paid for the amount/duration of entertainment I experienced made it worth it. Some people don't like the length of play time. Alot of those folks are A->B people, the kinds of people that don't stop to enjoy the world around them, to look through and embrace the lore presented. There's nothing wrong with it. I'm not one to judge. But neither should you. You are the ones that miss out, though, when you "don't stop to smell the roses". I enjoyed myself. It was worth the price tag. Like a good horror movie at the theatre.

Would you kindly Become genetically mutated with super powers and destroy all that oppose you?
Would you kindly Rescue all of the little sisters or harvest them all for your evil deeds?

Not a bad game, allot of cool innovations I hope they improve on in later installments.  The era changes are interesting and have you thinking and planning ahead for the future.  The family and traits are also a very cool addition that adds more to the game.
The things I think need attention and are the source of many of the negative scores...
The game speed has to be the biggest.  You get your choice from paused to fast to UBER fast.  I was used to playing about every other Tropico game and enjoyed keeping the game in "slow" mode for a relaxed pace where I rarely if ever paused the game.  I know there are even more complaints you cannot adjust the speed in multi player mode but I have yet to venture into that realm.  But, I quickly learned with Tropico 5 I had to either play the majority of my time with the game in paused mode and occasionally unause it to let some time pass because time goes by so quickly you are literally flooded with events that you have no time to react to, let allone look around your island to pick a build plan and prime spots for your farms.  But if you don't mind pausing this game a TON, it is doable .. just wish they would give us the option to slow it down... I want to build a nice looking and efficient city for my islanders, not throw his here and enact that edict just to respond as fast to all the crisis that can stream at you 2 and 3 at a time.
The other thing that definatly needs work is the resource "routing".  You may build a car plant that needs a resource not available on the island... you think "no problem" import it... but you import it and it sits in your dock while you plant has none until every dock has like 3k to sell and THEN the next delivery you get before you happen to sell some in one of your docks might actually be shipped to where it is actually desperately needed.  Another thing with the routing is the "intelligence" of your delivery drivers (or lack thereof).  IF you happen to have a mine to get that resource you need for that same car plant there is a major chance your delivery driver will deliver it to the dock to be sold instead of KNOWING your car plant should have 1st priority.  Shouldn't be too hard to fix for the coders but still not done.  The only way I've found to increase your chance of proper delivery is manipulating the road system in rediculously inefficient ways.  IE build only 1 road that goes to ALL your docks and force your delivery drivers to pass by every factory on their way to the docks..... Can you say Traffic Jam??
With all this being said, I wanted to point out the couple of major flaws I found that if fixed would make this possibly the best Tropico game so far, but instead I see TONS of DLC for more money instead of listening to the masses asking for these improvements.  I think at this rate they are going to loose allot of fans for any future releases because they simply will not put fixing the 2 major flaws in the game ahead of asking for more money for additional content.
I have had fun with the game once I learned to play it mostly on pause and just not bothering to build factories requiring any resource not allready on the island, so I would recomend giving it a try but possibly waiting for a price reflective of the expected fun in the game.

A lot of zombie games share a common flaw. Zombies serve only as target practice. The aspect of prolonged survival in a post apocalyptic world is pretty much ignored, other than the occassional reference or scene. The concept of rebuilding in this new world is also forgotten. You just go from point A to B and shoot some zombies, that's it. And then there's Project Zomboid. You get to shoot zombies (bad idea!), but you also get the chance to rebuild. Find a good spot, build a wall and before you know it, you've got your own base to defend.
Of course, it's not that easy, but it should give a good idea. The game has carpentry, farming and most recently even hunting was added (to an extent). Which brings me to the second point. The company constantly adds more content. It's a good habit, one I hope to keep seeing for a long time.
So I definitely recommend this game.

Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock is a very good point and click adventure where you must explore areas of an alien planet in order to repair your crashed ship and save yourself and your captain.
The immersion factor is high, despite the static screens. It is refreshing to play a P&C game where the puzzles are logical for the most part, requiring thought as opposed to madly trying every inventory object on everything. The game world feels realistic within the realm of intelligent science fiction. For the most part, the voiceovers (the player character and the injured captain) are solid with only the occassional odd line reading.
One caveat for prospective buyers is that the game is relatively short; I achieved 100% in three hours, and I don't believe any achievements are missable. However, I feel that this is actually a good thing; the game doesn't feel bloated with ridiculous puzzles and there's hardly any backtracking. The MSRP of ten dollars is definitely worth it for the experience, especially compared to the price of a movie ticket and the length of a typical movie.
There is a demo available (and a free Flash version of the original), so if the premise and trailer appeal to you, there's no risk to try before you buy.

What I like the most about this game is the feel of realism. No monsters, no zombies, no extreme technology. It really is simply you vs the wild. Finally a real-time, first-person survival game for me!
If you are thinking about picking up this title, I will share a few things I would have liked to know up front: First, there is no in-game help or hints on how stuff work. While I enjoy having to figure out how stuff work, I can imagine that not everyone does. This is not an interface issue, though. Unless this is your first computer game ever, you will immediatly get the hang of the interface. And if not, take a look at the keybindings.)
Second, after having played for a few hours and finally made it past the first few nights, I needed to take a break. But because I hadn't seen anything about a save game function og "Game saved"-notices, I simply paused the game (press ESC). After looking around the forums I learned that the game saves at certain safe, in-game events. Like when entering a house and sleeping in a bed (as far as I understand). But when you die, you die. The save game is erased. Brutal, simple and yet another thing I really like about the game.
Third, while the videos here on Steam gives a fairly good impression about how the game looks, I have, for instance, so far not encountered other living people. Only corpses. And there is only one camera view. The feeling that the videos convey, however, are very accurate. And maybe we'll see more camera views when the game comes out of alpha/beta?

Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock is a decent, enjoyable first person adventure.
Morningstar is the sort of game that most people (or most point-and-click adventure fans) should be able to agree upon, at least broadly.  I doubt many would claim that it's one of the top tier adventure games, but it's certainly a good one.  It has an enjoyable story, appealing graphics, and nice music.  Every achievement is easily attainable.  The gameplay generally isn't difficult and there is a built-in hint system, but there are a few illogical puzzles that might trip you up for a bit.
The quick pace is generally to the game's advantage, but the most negative aspect of the game is it's pricing.  Ten USD is a steep price for any 2~ hour game, and Morningstar is solid rather than a masterpiece.  As a game without a lot of replayability (there are very few unnecessary diversions or exploration to be had), I would wait for a sale to buy this one.

Age of Wonders is a fairly old game, but I still very much enjoy its simple yet complex gameplay. While its sequels improved vastly on some aspects of the game, I still feel that combat was the most entertaining in the original.
The story is fairly straightforward, and unlike the later titles, allows you to play as the "Good" faction or the "Evil" faction for the story. At several segments, you'll be presented with a decision to make, but only the second and third decisions will influence the Campaign any. These two decisions will also alter the ending sequence.
The combat is one thing I enjoy the most in the original Age of Wonders. There's only a few voices for when units take damage (Most use a halfling-esque gasp or wail, even the orcs and dark elves!) but after a bit of fighting the battlefields truly begin to look like a battlefield  -  blood splatters onto the ground every time a successful attack is landed, and spills out when a unit is killed. These remain until the battle's ended, and really make a long difficult battle with several large stacks look so much more 'epic' to me personally.
The map editor isn't much to look at - every piece of decoration and every tile has to be placed manually, and there's no Random Map feature. However, it's still capable of making extra maps to enjoy after the built in scenarios are exhausted, but some effort will have to be put into that. The sequels refined the editors quite a bit, making detailing and carving out a map much more efficient.
Power Nodes and Altars and Dungeons... I really enjoyed the dungeon maps when you explore a location, even if they were a bit tedious at times to explore. The sequels replace these with simplified terrain maps, which are much quicker to engage in at the cost of being less aesthetically pleasing in most cases - the same with city sieges. As most of those expansive detailed maps went unused in most cases, this isn't really all that bad gameplay wise.
Power Nodes in the original only provided Magic Income if your leader wielded a sphere of magic of that element. Thus, a leader using just Death and Fire magic would receive no income from owning an Earth, Air, or Life node. In the sequels, you recieve reduced income from opposing nodes.
Altars are a feature that were removed from the sequels. They were map locations that allowed you to cast powerful AoE spells onto the world map, just like the Divine Storm and other similar magics.  Either for free after a long charge period, or immediaely for a cost - and a very steep one if you're impatient.
There are a few minor tidbits I fount interesting that don't really affect the gameplay or rating any. First, in the flavor text for the Elementals (Fire Elemental, etc) they are stated they can be called at Gates - but no such locations exist. In fact, it's not until the sequels that you could hire troops from On-Map locations.  The Sea Serpent monster also states that they can be coerced into serving via powerful Water Magic, but no spells of this sort exist. In the sequel however, the "Great Wyrm" is indeed a Level 4 Water spell.  Finally, some units claim that they will only serve 'Good' leaders, but they themselves are of a Neutral or Creature alignment,  the latter meaning they'll get along even with Evil and Pure Evil leaders!
I also very much loved the portraits that map locations and many creatures had.  Some of these were re-used in the sequel (Like the generic Human Soldier portrait) but others weren't.
I really loved this game and the series as a whole, hopefully others may also find enjoyment in this title.

Carmageddon: Reincarnation was a fairly meh game that was released for early access FAR too early, went through lengthy time-consuming overhauls and ended up being a rather bland game. Absolutely heartbreaking, a videogame tragic we've all heard a million times before.
Thankfully, Stainless actually cares for their intellectual properties and customers, they made a promise that they would deliver unto us a brand new Carmageddon game that would sing of the gorey 15-year-old boners of yore (...eww); and though the road was rockier than Boston's More Than A Feeling, Stainless have Finally created the epitome of modern day Carmageddon.
They were years late in what they told us, they kept telling us "it'll be done a little later, it'll be done a little later" but they never stopped trying.
THAT'S what seperates this from all the other horrible Kickstarter empty nostalgia cash-ins we've seen over the years; Stainless Never Stopped Trying.
They worked to make amends with their hurt fans and I believe they did just that.
Buy this game if you want a Momumental Carmageddon game. It's just as crude and cheese-filled as the original.

I rested a night on the chair, read a magazine, smoked a cigarette, ate some chocolate and chips, drank some soda, and finally unpacked the container of bleach I carried around in case this type of scenario ever happened.
I gulp down the bleach while the zombies are still pounding on the door. My character is terrified, severely depressed and in agony. A few seconds later he falls to the floor, 30 seconds later the zombies burst through the door, but it's too late, my character already lies dead.

However, for how short it is, it's still solid and didn't drag on for longer than it needed to. The devs had an idea in mind and only made it as long as needed, which I can respect. That DOES make it, however, the shortest of all three original Half-Life games, but does tht make it bad? No, I don't think so. It just comes as a surprise. I would say, if you liked the original Half-Life, then play this one out of respect for th franchise, if nothing else. The Park is an immersive game with an interesting setting and good story telling.
You play as a mother who goes into an amusement park after her kid runs off. The place is filled dark corners, creepy faces and eerie notes. The game is similar to Dear Esther and Gone Home in the sense that there is no action or combat. It's simply a story-telling game.
The notes you find shed some light on some events that might have happened in the park. As you play through the game, you uncover more of the interesting story. Luckily, the voice acting is good, because there's quiet a lot of it. Your character will talk to herself when she sees certain objects, or describe a memory when you walk somewhere. It's interesting to listen to it all because it's nicely written.
Apart from having basic interaction with stuff like notes, you can also right click to call out to your son, which will also give a visual representation of where you can go next incase you are feeling a bit lost.
The environment itself is pretty spooky. Plastic faces of mascots, and a few shadowy figures. There are jumpscares, but they're didn't manage to annoy me like most games do. The game isn't filled with them, and they only really happen because you're on edge from other stuff.
Keep in mind, the game can be beaten in around 2 hours if you fully explore and read everything, so it is a short experience, however I found it an enjoyable one. Overall, a well sculpted game with good story telling!

The Park is a short, 90-minute FPX (first person experience) horror-adventure game. You are a mother who has "lost" her child, and you enter into an eerie park to look for him. You start off by taking a ride on a few attractions - the Tunnel of Tales, where you hear the story of Hansel and Gratel, with one twist in the end. Then there's the Ferris Wheel, a spinning ride and the Roller Coaster, before culminating in the House of Horrors.
In between you read notes and letters, and there will be some strange occurrences and possibly jump scares.
I would say that the atmosphere of the game is great. I really liked how we can "ride" the rides. Nothing particularly out of the world, but well done regardless. There are some themes and monologues about motherhood as well.
There are no puzzles to solve really, nor are there any other major traditional gameplay elements. You can use the right mouse button to call out for your son, and also to find objects of interest, but I didn't think it was an essential mechanic at all.
Overall, I thought the game was pretty decent. Spot on atmosphere in particular. The graphics are fine as well.
The only big issue I had was that the ending was just too drawn out. You keep replaying that same segment like 5 or 6 times. Could have been done more briskly that. Aside from that, the optimization seems to be a tad lacking. Had to cap the game at 30fps to get a smooth framerate.
So yeah, I'd say I liked it more than Gone Home. The setting is interesting. The horror is pretty fair as well I'd say. It's not an essential game for sure, but if this kind of a genre floats your boat, then surely give The Park a go.

Where to begin? The base game is terrible. It does not feel very thought-out, and covers up its lack of content with an incredibly annoying "survival" aspect. I understand in retrospect that's what the game advertised, but I just don't like it. It might not even be how they implemented it, I just don't like that aspect of these kinds of games. I bought this because I wanted to build cities. However, when you build all the buildings in the base game you realize there really is no endgame. You survived, but there pretty much all the buildings are about "surviving". There is not much greater purpose for you or your citizens. The most grandiose building you can build is a simple chapel.
The review could end here, of course, but there is one aspect of this game that changes everything - mods. This game has a surprisingly decent modding community. It fixes (for me) the annoying aspects of the gameplay elements (many of which should have been included in the game to begin with because of logic). Now these are relatively minor quality of life mods, but what I was really looking for was an endgame. What can I say, other than, I've found it. There is a very in-depth medieval mod that pretty much changes the gameplay and design, and it is incredibly well-implemented. Not only are there new buildings, but there are more new buildings than there are buildings in the base game. These new buildings interact well with both the base game and with each other. As well, now you can build vertically (up to 3 stories). No longer are you confined to little huts. You can build a real medieval town! It's incredible, really, and the effort that went into this mod alone puts the base game to shame.
In the end, I don't know if this is a review for the game or for mods, but the end product here is a pleasant experience. If you like modifying your game, check this out. If you like city building, definitely check this out. If for some ungodly reason you like watching all your citizens starve to death every 10 minutes, stick to the base game.

A version of sword and sandals very much true to the original. Somethings have become a little more streamlined. For example you no longer have to buy spell scrolls, and you earn a skill level up at each level next to the normal attributes. Enchanting has been changes as well, which in my opinion I have mixed feelings about. Its true that each enchantment in the original basicly did the samething, but it was cool to have a choice. Now all the enchantments do is give your weapon a new skin, and up the damage a bit. A bit lackluster.
Also not a fan of weapons being locked by levels rather then your abbilities and the weight of your purse. All be it, that lvling up has become a lot easier in this version.
I would say the major pros of the games are that if you played the original that you will most certainly enjoy it. The price is great, it's not very expensive. So for the price id say its a great nostalgia trip.
Some of the things that could be improved however is that it feels very padded. There are too many fights leading up to the bosses in my opinion. It quickly becomes tedious to grind through all the trash gladiators to fight the boss. I love the addition of the dungeon fights, were your character can die against regular gladiators. And after defeating a boss you can go there to fight him again. And have a pick at his loot for a second time.
Its one of those games almost everyone played when they were a kid, and had some fun with. I always wanted to see something similar come out at a later date which expanded on this idea, but no one ever really did.
My main issues with the game are the previously mentioned padding. And the bosses aren't very threatening. And that a lot of skill paths arent viable, charisma characters have recieved a huge nerf. I hope to see a return of the bard in S&S 5.
For my character I went for the, strength and vitality route. Wanting to make him as big as possible. And he towered over everyone which was nice to see. I would recommend this strategy for new players.
TLDR: Worth a pick up for the price, for a couple hours of fun. And to revisit old memories.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is the successor to the original Red orchestra which took players into a realistic war torn world war 2 europe (Rising storm taking place in the pacific campaign).
Right off the bat i will say this game is not for the feint of heart. It is extremely realistic, 1 bullet from any gun assuming it hit in the chest or head will surely kill you. If you manage to survive 1 hit you will need to take cover to bandage yourself or you will bleed out and die, though some shots even if you survive the first mortally wound you so you bleed out anyway.
Unlike ArmA the game does not consider itself a Military Simulator, and it isnt. It is definitely made more for action and gameplay than simulating real world conditions like ArmA does. With that said though, it is most definitely more of a simulator than an arcade game.
The level of realism in this game is best described as ArmA but without crossing that threshold that makes it no longer fun. The game is extremely team oriented, you can not be a rambo in this game. You must work with your team to succeed, like older FPS games (such as BF2) RO2 still uses a "commander" system, calling in devistating air strikes and recon on points squad leaders mark via a radio.
The learning curve of this game is extremely steep, and i promise that you will die more times than you can possibly count before you get the hang of how combat works. But if you have the patience to get past this initial frustration you will find one of the funnest tactical realism shooters on the market.
No other game captures death like red orchestra does, when you shoot some one with a bolt action and see the enemy get hit you can feel it, It makes kills much more satisfying. If you have an SMG and manage to clear out a room of enemies without dying, IE a killstreak, you will feel like a god wondering how you managed to do it without being killed.
Overall it is a fantastic game, it is very dark and gritty as war always is and it manages to capture that feeling better than anyone else. If you have the patience to play an FPS that has to be played like a real war (crawling camping etc) where you have to move up methodically and carefully to succeed and dont mind realism i would definitely pick it up.
If however you are more of a fan of games such as Call of Duty i would steer clear of this game with a 10 mile pole, it will do nothing but frustrate the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.

Banished is an RTS/resource management type game set in a somewhat historical time frame. The game looks great on the cover and it was very fun for a while when I was just getting to know it. However, the point comes very soon when you've pretty much seen everything the game as to offer, and you end up just playing the same things in different arrangements. In my opinion, not worth the $20 I spent on it.
-Good design. The game allows for near-complete hud customization depending on your gaming style. The graphics and models are quite good as long as you don't zoom all the way in on them, and some buildings have mutiple potential models so you don't end up staring at a grid of the same mundane shack for an hour.
-Phenominal music. There weren't many songs, but all were beautifully composed and fit the game well.
-Mods for just about every functionality in the game.
-It's slow. Even at 5x fast forward, it takes an eternity to build or harvest or gather supplies, meaning you just have to sit and watch tiny people walk around that whole time before you get to build another building and wait for its completion.
-Limited development options for your city. There are no unlockable structures or even upgrades, so your city will always look the same.
Long story short, I do not reccomend this game. As pretty as the finish may be, the content is just too shallow to be enjoyable. I had high hopes going in, and I was sorely dissapointed.

The Long Dark. It can and will catch you unawares, even if you consider yourself one of the most prepared.
It was on my 79th day that things started to go horribly wrong. I wandered off from the gas station I had for the past 40 days considered safe haven. I had a gallon of water, a rifle with plenty of ammo, and enough food to last me a night should I get stranded. It wasn't enough.
I always thought it would be the wolves that would get me. They had been traveling in packs of 2-3 lately; if all of them came at me, surely I would take down one, maybe two, but I knew if a pack came at me I would be wolf bait. I was wrong. As I wandered up the coast, it started to get cold, as night drew closer. I heard an eerie baying close by - a wolf. I prepared myself, searching in all directions. It came charging, snarling and snapping its jaws. I took it down, but then I heard more growling - its pack. I knew standing my ground was a death sentence, so I ran, and I ran. To my luck, I came across a sea side cottage, to which I quickly escaped the snapping jaws of death in its enclosure.
I thought to myself "I'll just stay the night here, let the wolf pack wander off." I foraged around for food - there wasn't much. Some salty crackers, a soda, and some frozen cooked rabbit. I drank half of my water, and ate some of my cooked wolf jerky that I had in my pack and began to kip for the night.
I awoke to the screaming howl of the wind the next morning. I poked my head out and surely enough pure white out conditions. It had to have been at least -40, and going out would be just as surely a death sentence as the wolf pack was. I hunkered down, sipped my water and gnawed the last bits of the jerky as I drifted off to sleep to the symphony of cracking trees and ice falling. I woke a few hours later. The wind had died down! It was time. I drank the last of my water, and ate the cooked rabbit I had retrieved from the freezer previously.
This was a mistake. Not long after I finished the rabbit, there was the gut wrenching pain. I knew instantly: Food poisoning. I forced down some antibiotics I kept in my med kit, laid down praying for it to go away, or the release of a quick death. The wolves didn't sound so bad, now. I drifted off to darkness...
I awoke several hours later, the sun was just rising. I was starving, thirsty, and the howling wind was louder than ever. I had no choice. I steeled myself, eating the last few saltines in my pack, greedily drinking the soda I had found before leaving the house.
I immediately bolted. I knew with this cold, I had very little time to get to safety. I ran and ran, only stopping mere moments to catch my breath. I was soon freezing, and I had no idea how much further I had to go. Soon, numbness set in, I stopped shivering, my body was giving up. I knew I had to keep pressing on. Finally there was a familiar car in the road. I was almost there!
I was exhausted, I stumbled past the car. I could see the feint outline of the gas station through the wind and snow. There was hope! A few steps from the door I heard a growl; I turned around but it was too late. I couldn't fight  the wolf. I was too tired, too cold, too numb. On my 82nd day, I faded out, into the long dark.
The wolves got me after all.

It sort of just becomes a shoot and pray method which I don't particularly like. Another small gripe is the perry system where you press the jump button in midair shield against pink projectiles. It's a cool idea, but requiring to be in midair to perry limits your options, and there are a lot of jump through platforms in the game that will make you land on the ground before you can perry a projectile thus getting hit by it instead. just having the perry button assigned to another button would fix this issue, but I guess the developers wanted to keep the button use count to a minimum. Luckily, besides these issues, I find this game really fun, and think it's a solid game to have in your inventory, it just suffers really small hickups.

I woke on a small ice island in the middle of what was once the sea. I looked around looking at the sheer artistic beauty of this Canadian wasteland and saw in the distance a small green hut and ventured forth across the ice to it and upon arrival was met by great luck with a hunting rifle and a bullet being inside this small hut. upon exiting i see a large cabin on top of a large island and move towards it cautiosly, luck doesn't last forever. To my suprise i enter the house with no problems and inside find several days worth of supplies, a lantern, 5 more bullets, some better clothes and some food and drinks. I spent the night in this homely cabin and spent the next day exploring other green ice fishing cabins returning to my house at night. Knowing I would have to leave I cooked my raw food and kept my tinned produce for the days walking.
After a short walk collecting a few bits of food and drink from a gas station I venture up a snow track lane and walk off to get to a small ranger station to see my surroundings. I reach the station and look out spotting a new place to discover, but I here footsteps behind me and a bear begins to charge me! I ran from the killer bear and when there is some distance between us I start to fire my gun at it's face striking 4 times before being mauled and thrown about by the bear like Leonardo Di Caprio in the Revenant. After a minute of being maulled in a brutal and beautiful animation i accept my death when the black screen comes only to discover that my clothing may have saved me. I'm bleeding and have just 30 seconds to heal myself. Frantically, through blurred vision, I grab my rifle off the floor and my peaches, the bear just 15 metres away, and sprint to a nearby rock so i can bandage myself. A moments respite.
The bear begins charging again and I sprint down some rocks spraining my ankle, thankfully I see a trailer to dive into for safety the bear right behind me. I get in and rest for a few hours to heal. Upon leaving the trailer I begin to celebrate, my fight with the bear was won! The bear led on the ground dead from blood loss and i begin my newest chapter.
A day later a wolf attempts to attack me but i quickly light a flare and throw it at the wolf scaring it, feeling like Liam Neeson I Crouch down and put a bullet in the wolf's face. The same evening another experience with a bear went much better the last of my bullets in the bear I run into a building and sleep.
Day 10 now I have become a survivor and I now wear the pelts of the bears as my clothing.

Don't be turned off by the Early Access--if you told me this was the full game, I wouldn't be surprised!
Pros:
-Atmosphere.  The sound of the wind alone will follow you after you quit the game, and the changing weather, beautiful areas, and stark, lonely areas of once-lived-in buildings are haunting and immersive.  There's just enough voice work to give it color (and give you vital survival information) without being too immersion-breaking.
-Challenging.  The lowest difficulty setting is almost relaxing and meditative, but the higher two will give you a serious fight.  Death constantly seems inevitable, especially outside in unfamiliar territory when the wind might change at any time.
-Mechanically sound.  The mechanics work, and what's more, they work to make the experience seem almost real.  If I wrote more about this we'd be here all night.
Cons:
-Strange wildlife behavior.  The behavior of the wildlife is tied to the survival difficulty, with the lowest difficulty setting having bears running from you in terror and both of the higher difficulties having rabid, angry wolves who charge like a freight train the moment they think you might be there.  I'd prefer the wildlife difficulty be separate and more granular, since I don't enjoy dealing with the wildlife (and it's kind of immersion-breaking for me that wolves are playing seek-and-destroy with me, or that bears are so damned terrified) but I DO enjoy dealing with harder survival conditions.
TL;DR: Just buy it!

Fantastic ravioli
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Featuring a healthy mix of 4X and RPG, I find this, the original game in the series to be my favourite to this day. Perhaps it's because this game was a part of my youth growing up. I remember playing hotseat multiplayer games with 4 or 5 friends and being captivated for hours on end. To this day; albeit relegated to single player matches only, does still prove quite the enjoyable experience.
From an era before DLC, this game is jampacked with tons of lore, and a large number of factions to choose from outright. Featuring two lengthy campaigns and a multitude of scenarios, Age of Wonders is sure to keep you sated for hours on end. This truly was the first game I felt that "just one more turn" feeling that many people yearn for.  Both the campaigns and the scenarios offer a lot of replayability, due to the choices you make in the campaigns, as well, via the numerous factions avaliable in the scenarios. Last thing to note is the beautiful music, one of the few PC games to my mind that features many memorable tunes.
Age of Wonders seems to run very well in 1920x1080 16:9 resolution on Windows 8.1. However, the game seems to crash if I Alt-tab.
If you are a fan of either 4X or RPG games I would definetely give this game a serious look.

Oh boy...
I had confidence in this game.  A friend as pond I discovered it when browsing Steam and when we saw it had "Terraria" content in it (even to the point of Terraria having a window message saying "Also try Edge of Space"), and we were such big fans of that, we just had to get it.  I bought this game in a "buy one get one free" deal so we could do co-op together.  I tried to play this game I really tried, but there's just not enough redeeming qualities I could find to make this review positive.
First, I'd like to say I have been playing in early access rather than the full release, as I got bored during early access and couldn't even bring myself to boot it up again.  This game expects far too much from it's players.  You're practically playing a sandbox game stuck in hard mode, and forced to play with horrible controls.  There are way too many sub-menus to navigate, and the crafting system is so weird and doesn't make enough sense.
In games like this (i.e. Minecraft, Terraria, Starbound), we as players tend to remember the best crafting recipes, but Edge of Space takes the fun of that away and makes things over-complicated by having blocks fall into particular groups and letting you do the rest from there.
Every aspect of what makes this a "sandbox" game is terrible.  Placing blocks isn't satisfying as the one planet you're stuck on only offers you so many that you really might as well go to dirt to construct a "house" to stay the night.  Mining is extremely boring, and not engaging in the slightest.  I don't know if it was just me, but all ores in the game (which look far too identical to regular stone) took far too long to mine, and the steam icons that show your progress on obtaining the ore really don't change a lot so you'll be wondering how long it'll take to get anything from a vein.  Combat is also dumb.  Right when they drop you into this game, you have limited respawns, granted you can collect more.  But fighting in this game is just boring, it has no depth to it like in Terraria or Starbound and the enemies deal far too much damage that you basically fire at them from a distance the entire fight.  Not to mention these creeps spawn in caves and will interrupt your mining ALL THE TIME!
After coming back to this game and seeing the negative reviews it's getting and seeing how the Devs apparently abandoned it entirely, I'm honestly just disappointed.  There WAS hope for Edge of Space at one point, but when you release your game completely and it has a bunch of the bugs that already existed in EA, then you're basically just making an incomplete game to get a quick buck.
Don't buy this game.  If you want a thrilling space-themed sandbox game buy Starbound.  You'll get a lot more enjoyment out of it than whatever you can call this.
(Oh and co-op doesn't work at all.  You'll give up when you reach a point where you keep disconnecting from your friend's server.)

If you like ambiance, artistic and atmospheric games, and can handle puzzle platforming challenges, you'll almost certainly like this. I almost never care about stuff like that - other games that people enjoy because of their "atmosphere" don't end up appealing to me if they don't have gameplay that I'm really interested in, but this game pulls it off so well that I have to say the atmosphere is one of the main reasons I like it. The puzzle platformer aspect is perfectly fine as well. It's nothing very complex, but it manages to avoid being repetitive and is constantly introducing new mechanics for you to work with. It has highs and lows of intensity, with more action-oriented segments and other more sit-and-think type segments, and it ends up having a nice flow of stimulation because of that. I've played plenty of puzzle platformers in my time and all I can say about the puzzles in this game is that they are decent and don't detract from the atmosphere.
All of that said, unless it looks really appealing to you, it's not 10 dollars worth of entertainment. I got this for free during a sale, and that's probably the only way I would've played this game. You're paying 10 dollars for about 2-3 hours of entertainment, probably. I'm not saying that every game is only as valuable as its cost per hours ratio; this game certainly packs a lot of aesthetic and gameplay entertainment into that short time, but I just could never justify spending 10 dollars on it. If you're really into artistic games, though, you may find it to be worth it. Other than that, I would just recommend waiting for a really heavy discount. Definitely consider giving this a try at some point, though. I've played lots of games and this one is certainly unique.
