*Thunder*
Was it all a dream? All the talk of a new plague hit the streets of my hometown? Surely such a thing wouldn't happen in Kentucky!
I shoot up out of bed, looking around cautiously. Still dark, the curtains were closed, but I could still hear the irregular booming of yesterdays' storm. Being a carpenter, I know for sure that the storm would not damage my well-maintained home. I also love to sleep without a shirt, to let my hairy chest breath the nights air. I flip the lights on, grab a candle from the drawer and move towards the other bedroom. I arrive and soon remember that he was moving out, after hearing yesterdays news. Suitcases and messing drawers littered his room. Before leaving, I grab his beloved baseball bat. Surely I will need this more than he, even though it has been signed by many of his favorite players. I make my way down the stairs, quiet as a mouse.
Then - I hear it. Moaning. Grunting. What the ♥♥♥♥ is that?!? Tearing at the siding on my freshly painted house. Tapping on my front deck, slams against my windows. Clutching my bat tight, I realize this was not a joke. This was the real deal. All those zombie films my brother and I watched when we were children... was finally becoming a reality. I quickly shut all the curtains and keep the lights on low - just enough to make my way to the kitchen. If I'm going to survive through the morning and beyond, I need some food. Amidst the tapping and groaning, both of the horrors outside and of my stomache, I search the refridgerator and the cupboards. Milk, cheese, meatloaf, squash, bread, butter, eggs, mustard... this was certainly not the moment to be eating cereal. Instead I pull all the ingredients onto the table to decide what to start my day with. I find a dead rat laying besides the mustard... never liked mustard much anyway... I reach for the frying pan, the bread, butter and cheese, and I grill myself a mother♥♥♥♥ing Grilled Cheese, right there on the spot. Delicious.
This is the♥♥♥♥♥♥that we need in games like these, ♥♥♥♥ing grilled cheese sandwiches. 10/10 Would eat again.

I think the best thing about this game is how realistic it is (or seems to be; I've never actually been in a zombie apocalypse). Most of the game involves you trying to find enough supplies just to survive, which sounds like it might be boring and tedious but is actually quite tense. Also, the fact that dying is easy gives you a sense of suspense every time you emerge from the relative safety of whatever safe house you've set up. It's sort of like the Walking Dead, but with an actual fear of the main character (you) dying at any time. Oh, and it is entirely possible to spend several hours risking your life to find booze, but unlike in the Walking Dead no sane person trying to survive would actually do that because it's really stupid (someone tell Beth). Overall it's a great game, but the only drawback right now is that there are no NPC survivors in single-player mode, which can make the game feel a bit lonely. Once that changes later, I image this will be one of my all-time favorite games. But even as it stands, I heartily recommend that you give this game a try if you are into zombie games or just survival games in general.

I really want to love this game, but I can't. It is definitely the best zombie survival sandbox game I have played, but it just can't keep my attention for very long.
There's not much to say for the gameplay: you move from house to house looting food and weapons. You might kill a zombie here and there. Other than that, it is just wash, rinse, and repeat. Loot during the day, sleep during the night, loot during the day, sleep during the night. I guess I can't really argue with that though since that it probably what most people would be doing in a real zombie apocalypse.
The enviroments are pretty boring. All the houses look the same and have no character at all. There are certain buildings that do stand out, such as the lumber yard, but these locations are very few and far between. All of the houses are in near perfect condition with the exception to broken windows. I really want to see maybe some buildings on fire or reduced to rubble, anything really that makes it more exciting.
I feel like this game has a ton of potential and will be great after a few more patches, but for the time being, I do not feel like it is worth the money.

This (and to an even greater degree, its DLC, Whistleblower) is an exercise in pants-ruining terror.  To be honest, I couldn't play for more than thirty or forty minutes at a time because I would get so tense and scared.  I lost track of the number of times I almost ruined my headphone cable by leaping back in my chair.  The graphics (while not terribly fancy) certainly do the trick, and the music and sound effects are always superb.  Everything about the game (peering around corners, laboured breathing when scared, etc) is designed to immerse you in the experiences of the character.  If you like horror games, then you MUST have this in your Steam library.
There are some downsides to make note of; the climax of the main game (not the DLC) suffers from WTF syndrome and also simply goes on too long, plus thematically and atmospherically the game does begin to repeat itself (not too much, mind you).  As well, if you don't like jump-scares you should note that there are more than a few, although in my opinion they were rather well done, and certainly not cheap at all.
Long story short, I really loved this game, and cannot recommend it heartily enough.

This is a great proof-of-concept for a completely different game. It's... it's fine, I guess, for what it is... but 'what it is' isn't much.
It's billed as a city planning and resource management game... which is fair enough, and it is in a sense, but your greatest enemy isn't the size of the map or the management of resources; it's the pants-on-head guano-grade idiocy of the AI.
A hungry peasant will walk past a barn full of food, past their own house which is also full of food, into a field where he'll start harvesting more food, and then die of starvation.
I played this game for a few weekends, and, aside from figuring out when to build which food sources, understanding and compensating for the stupid AI is pretty much the only challenge the game had
I'm sure if I followed a city to the point where I need to build satellite communities and marketplace networks, I would eventually be at least somewhat engaged again... but there are no technology trees, no significant upgrades, no exploration, no real elemental danger (aside from an occasional tornado that will usually whip through the far side of the map and take out maybe two buildings and six people).. the only conflict in the game comes from wrestling with your imbecile robo-peasants' complete lack for self-preservation.
I suppose I should've been tipped off from the reviews noting the lack of real conflict, and I'm down for the occasional 'zen out and build in peace' game, but the garbotron AI just pushed this one over the edge for me.
Download this game if you want--just know that it's as much a "figure out what the hell is wrong with this AI and doctor your town so they don't starve to death" puzzle game as it is a village planning sim.

1. Cut ribs into small portions of 2 or 3 bones each. Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Season water a pinch each of salt,
black pepper, and crushed red pepper to the water. Boil ribs in seasoned water for 20 minutes. Drain, and let the ribs sit
for about a half an hour.
2. Meanwhile, preheat an outdoor grill for high heat.
3. Lightly coat the ribs with barbecue sauce. Cook the ribs over high heat for a 5 to 10 minutes on each side to get a nice
grilled look to them.
4. Place grilled ribs in a slow cooker. Pour remaining barbecue sauce and one bottle of beer over the ribs; this should
cover at least half of the ribs. Cover, and cook on High for 3 hours. Check ribs every hour or so, and add more beer if
needed to dilute sauce. Stir to get the ribs on top into the sauce. The ribs are done when the meat is falling off the bone.
The ribs were cooked completely in the first process, the rest is about flavor and texture.

The Long Dark. It can and will catch you unawares, even if you consider yourself one of the most prepared.
It was on my 79th day that things started to go horribly wrong. I wandered off from the gas station I had for the past 40 days considered safe haven. I had a gallon of water, a rifle with plenty of ammo, and enough food to last me a night should I get stranded. It wasn't enough.
I always thought it would be the wolves that would get me. They had been traveling in packs of 2-3 lately; if all of them came at me, surely I would take down one, maybe two, but I knew if a pack came at me I would be wolf bait. I was wrong. As I wandered up the coast, it started to get cold, as night drew closer. I heard an eerie baying close by - a wolf. I prepared myself, searching in all directions. It came charging, snarling and snapping its jaws. I took it down, but then I heard more growling - its pack. I knew standing my ground was a death sentence, so I ran, and I ran. To my luck, I came across a sea side cottage, to which I quickly escaped the snapping jaws of death in its enclosure.
I thought to myself "I'll just stay the night here, let the wolf pack wander off." I foraged around for food - there wasn't much. Some salty crackers, a soda, and some frozen cooked rabbit. I drank half of my water, and ate some of my cooked wolf jerky that I had in my pack and began to kip for the night.
I awoke to the screaming howl of the wind the next morning. I poked my head out and surely enough pure white out conditions. It had to have been at least -40, and going out would be just as surely a death sentence as the wolf pack was. I hunkered down, sipped my water and gnawed the last bits of the jerky as I drifted off to sleep to the symphony of cracking trees and ice falling. I woke a few hours later. The wind had died down! It was time. I drank the last of my water, and ate the cooked rabbit I had retrieved from the freezer previously.
This was a mistake. Not long after I finished the rabbit, there was the gut wrenching pain. I knew instantly: Food poisoning. I forced down some antibiotics I kept in my med kit, laid down praying for it to go away, or the release of a quick death. The wolves didn't sound so bad, now. I drifted off to darkness...
I awoke several hours later, the sun was just rising. I was starving, thirsty, and the howling wind was louder than ever. I had no choice. I steeled myself, eating the last few saltines in my pack, greedily drinking the soda I had found before leaving the house.
I immediately bolted. I knew with this cold, I had very little time to get to safety. I ran and ran, only stopping mere moments to catch my breath. I was soon freezing, and I had no idea how much further I had to go. Soon, numbness set in, I stopped shivering, my body was giving up. I knew I had to keep pressing on. Finally there was a familiar car in the road. I was almost there!
I was exhausted, I stumbled past the car. I could see the feint outline of the gas station through the wind and snow. There was hope! A few steps from the door I heard a growl; I turned around but it was too late. I couldn't fight  the wolf. I was too tired, too cold, too numb. On my 82nd day, I faded out, into the long dark.
The wolves got me after all.

Fantastic ravioli
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I woke on a small ice island in the middle of what was once the sea. I looked around looking at the sheer artistic beauty of this Canadian wasteland and saw in the distance a small green hut and ventured forth across the ice to it and upon arrival was met by great luck with a hunting rifle and a bullet being inside this small hut. upon exiting i see a large cabin on top of a large island and move towards it cautiosly, luck doesn't last forever. To my suprise i enter the house with no problems and inside find several days worth of supplies, a lantern, 5 more bullets, some better clothes and some food and drinks. I spent the night in this homely cabin and spent the next day exploring other green ice fishing cabins returning to my house at night. Knowing I would have to leave I cooked my raw food and kept my tinned produce for the days walking.
After a short walk collecting a few bits of food and drink from a gas station I venture up a snow track lane and walk off to get to a small ranger station to see my surroundings. I reach the station and look out spotting a new place to discover, but I here footsteps behind me and a bear begins to charge me! I ran from the killer bear and when there is some distance between us I start to fire my gun at it's face striking 4 times before being mauled and thrown about by the bear like Leonardo Di Caprio in the Revenant. After a minute of being maulled in a brutal and beautiful animation i accept my death when the black screen comes only to discover that my clothing may have saved me. I'm bleeding and have just 30 seconds to heal myself. Frantically, through blurred vision, I grab my rifle off the floor and my peaches, the bear just 15 metres away, and sprint to a nearby rock so i can bandage myself. A moments respite.
The bear begins charging again and I sprint down some rocks spraining my ankle, thankfully I see a trailer to dive into for safety the bear right behind me. I get in and rest for a few hours to heal. Upon leaving the trailer I begin to celebrate, my fight with the bear was won! The bear led on the ground dead from blood loss and i begin my newest chapter.
A day later a wolf attempts to attack me but i quickly light a flare and throw it at the wolf scaring it, feeling like Liam Neeson I Crouch down and put a bullet in the wolf's face. Day 10 now I have become a survivor and I now wear the pelts of the bears as my clothing.

Don't be turned off by the Early Access--if you told me this was the full game, I wouldn't be surprised!
Pros:
-Atmosphere.  The sound of the wind alone will follow you after you quit the game, and the changing weather, beautiful areas, and stark, lonely areas of once-lived-in buildings are haunting and immersive.  There's just enough voice work to give it color (and give you vital survival information) without being too immersion-breaking.
-Challenging.  The lowest difficulty setting is almost relaxing and meditative, but the higher two will give you a serious fight.  Death constantly seems inevitable, especially outside in unfamiliar territory when the wind might change at any time.
-Mechanically sound.  The mechanics work, and what's more, they work to make the experience seem almost real.  If I wrote more about this we'd be here all night.
Cons:
-Strange wildlife behavior.  The behavior of the wildlife is tied to the survival difficulty, with the lowest difficulty setting having bears running from you in terror and both of the higher difficulties having rabid, angry wolves who charge like a freight train the moment they think you might be there.  I'd prefer the wildlife difficulty be separate and more granular, since I don't enjoy dealing with the wildlife (and it's kind of immersion-breaking for me that wolves are playing seek-and-destroy with me, or that bears are so damned terrified) but I DO enjoy dealing with harder survival conditions.
TL;DR: Just buy it!

What I like:
-Nice looking cars, they are based on real life models suitably. Though the models are somewhat low-poly strangely, Flatout 1 has more detailed models..
-Pretty okay graphics still overall although NFS Most Wanted from 2004 for example already had more advanced things regarding textures, shaders and lighting system..I mean, FO2 doesn't have bump mapping, not all shadows in FO2 are realtime shadows and no realtime reflections either..yet FO2 has sharp textures in comparison for one.
-Good sound design, the cars..although they kinda lack volume and intensity..FO1 had more intense engine noises. Ultimate carnage corrected the problem by having a clipping distortion effect for the player's engine noise, it made the fo2 sounds more aggressive suitably. The sound of small rocks in gravel roads pinging and ricocheting in the wheel wells is remarkably awesome and lovely to hear, makes the countryside tracks all the better to race in. Good crash sfx, when you crash subtly versus hard the difference is plenty audible :) although there could have been more crunching metal and stressing metal type sounds.
-Handling physics, there is clearly difference between all the drive types. Though there could have been some handling nuances for some cars..aside of their grippiness rating, there is no other differentiation for the handling between cars.
-The gameplay. Cathartic. You race with cars of 3 different type, derby cars which are beat up, slow yet durable old cars. Then race cars, something alike to scuffed and worn rally cars, they are 80's-00's era cars with moderate top speeds and acceleration, and mid range toughness. And lastly the street class with import tuners and muscle cars, these sleds are devilishly fast but lack in durability overall, made worse by crashes in that class being usually on high speeds :d There is the usual circuit races and to complement those there are the derbies where the one with most collective score from damaging opponents wins..not necessarily last man standing wins, the special event races such as a oval gravel track, figure of eight and some others. Lastly there is the silly stunts, where you throw your driver out of the windshield, for example to stick to a wall in high jump to score the best height. In all races but stunts, there will be crashing..often indirect crashing too, from pushing your opponent to an obstacle.
What I don't like..
No choice to have the bloom off yet the other post processing effects on. The bloom doesn't help to make an upbeat atmosphere, rather it is obtrusive and blinding..no idea how I back then played FO2 with the post processing on.

Potential, but at this current time the game is not developed enough to be user friendly.
The campaign as such is very generic without any kind of story too it. I know car games don't usually have much in the way of story, but these are just a collection of races back to back. I played a couple of the earlier carmaggeddon games and felt an enjoyable level of progression, however I didnt feel it here.
The driving itself is, as many have described, like mario cart. It's not all that bad, but its really heavy. You turn right and the car will swing right. It reminds me a lot of the driving in Arma. It does make sense to some extent due to the cars increased weight, with all the armour etc attached, but every turn results in some form of powerslide. Feathering the wheel with corrections isn't really a thing here.
You unlock upgrades as races go on and upgrade choices. The problem with this is that they funnel you down a path that gives you the illusion of choice, except... well you only have one choice. The upgrades are also as mundane as it gets. Fill this bar up here and there, for increased performance in that area. After researching this it doesnt appear that much in the way of visual effects take place.
The multiplayer at this point in time is sadly in a worse off place. The user interface doesnt tell you much of anything bar how many people are in each game. When trying to join a game you will be met with "can't join because game is in session" error messages. The problem with this is that theres no way to tell when they are in the lobby waiting and games  can take up to 30+ mins a piece. Alternatively I tried to host a game, and was met with a network error message over and over again. I tried testing a couple of other games out at the time to see if it was the connection and they all worked fine. Maybe a select port blockage, but I'm not spending my time trying to find out which ones.
The next problem was the lack of people understably playing the game. Each time I looked there were 4 - 5 games, none of which I could join after attempting to for 10 or so minutes.
After all of this I went directly to steams help > refund request function and got my money back.
Don't get me wrong, theres plenty of potential here, but I doubt it will every be properly realised.

The tutorial doesn't give you enough info to really play the game. I spent a lot of game confused about why my happiness was high but my approval low or why approval was high but civil unrest was growing. In that regard a lot of the details of the gameplay fall a little flat. That aside the problem solving political aspect is at least enjoyable if nothing else. Whyever revolutions keep continually popping up on my island dealing with them is always an exciting element.

The Long Dark. It can and will catch you unawares, even if you consider yourself one of the most prepared.
It was on my 79th day that things started to go horribly wrong. I wandered off from the gas station I had for the past 40 days considered safe haven. I had a gallon of water, a rifle with plenty of ammo, and enough food to last me a night should I get stranded. It wasn't enough.
I always thought it would be the wolves that would get me. They had been traveling in packs of 2-3 lately; if all of them came at me, surely I would take down one, maybe two, but I knew if a pack came at me I would be wolf bait. I was wrong. As I wandered up the coast, it started to get cold, as night drew closer. I heard an eerie baying close by - a wolf. I prepared myself, searching in all directions. It came charging, snarling and snapping its jaws. I took it down, but then I heard more growling - its pack. I knew standing my ground was a death sentence, so I ran, and I ran. To my luck, I came across a sea side cottage, to which I quickly escaped the snapping jaws of death in its enclosure.
I thought to myself "I'll just stay the night here, let the wolf pack wander off." I foraged around for food - there wasn't much. Some salty crackers, a soda, and some frozen cooked rabbit. I drank half of my water, and ate some of my cooked wolf jerky that I had in my pack and began to kip for the night.
I awoke to the screaming howl of the wind the next morning. I poked my head out and surely enough pure white out conditions. It had to have been at least -40, and going out would be just as surely a death sentence as the wolf pack was. I hunkered down, sipped my water and gnawed the last bits of the jerky as I drifted off to sleep to the symphony of cracking trees and ice falling. I woke a few hours later. The wind had died down! It was time. I drank the last of my water, and ate the cooked rabbit I had retrieved from the freezer previously.
This was a mistake. Not long after I finished the rabbit, there was the gut wrenching pain. I knew instantly: Food poisoning. I forced down some antibiotics I kept in my med kit, laid down praying for it to go away, or the release of a quick death. The wolves didn't sound so bad, now. I drifted off to darkness...
I awoke several hours later, the sun was just rising. I was starving, thirsty, and the howling wind was louder than ever. I had no choice. I steeled myself, eating the last few saltines in my pack, greedily drinking the soda I had found before leaving the house.
I immediately bolted. I knew with this cold, I had very little time to get to safety. I ran and ran, only stopping mere moments to catch my breath. I was soon freezing, and I had no idea how much further I had to go. Soon, numbness set in, I stopped shivering, my body was giving up. I knew I had to keep pressing on. Finally there was a familiar car in the road. I was almost there!
I was exhausted, I stumbled past the car. I could see the feint outline of the gas station through the wind and snow. There was hope! A few steps from the door I heard a growl; I turned around but it was too late. I couldn't fight  the wolf. I was too tired, too cold, too numb. On my 82nd day, I faded out, into the long dark.
The wolves got me after all.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews.
One Hour Reviews - Game 3
Age of Wonders
Purchase Date: 5/22/2014
I'd never played any of the Age of Wonders series.  This one I picked up as part of a Humble Bundle last year.    Humble is one of the reasons I ended up with as many games as I have, as they are a great excuse to donate a few dollars to a good cause and pick up a bundle of games while you are at it.  I get a lot of of games I wouldn't otherwise try this way.
As soon as I got into the game, I was immediately reminded of Heroes of Might and Magic.  Anyone who has ever played any of those games will be familar here.  I saw a lot of the same concepts here, with an emphasis on tactical turn based combat, along with exploration and town management.
Even though it's an older game, it ran absolutely fine on my system, and I could run at my native 1920x1080 resolution.  The text is a little small to read at that resolution, but otherwise I had no issues.    I had recently played Age of Empires II, and like that game, I found myself wanting to use the scrollwheel on my mouse to zoom in and out of the map, forgetting that scrollwheels weren't used in games back then.  Graphically speaking, the maps looked good, but I wasn't as impressed with the units, particularly the animation.
I started by going through the tutorial, which is pretty basic.  It covers the basics of getting around and how to issue commands to your party, but when it comes to actual strategy you are on your own.  It doesn't give you any sense for what you are about to get yourself into.  And I say this because this is not an easy game for someone just starting out.  In fact, I actually managed to die during the tutorial and had to start over.  It was my own fault, I sent my party leader to the front lines and he got himself killed, which immediately ended the game.
Once you finish the campaign, Age of Wonders offers you a campaign mode, which you can play from one of 2 sides, either the elves or the goblins.  The game also comes with a number of scenarios that you can play as well.  Since this is only an hour review, I did not look at any of the multiplayer, but I did find it interesting that the game has a play by email option.  I'm not used to seeing that in a lot of games.
I played a quick game though each side of the campaign.  I say quick game because Age of Wonders is not a kind game, and you can get yourself killed very quickly.  I did a little better when I played a scenario, but even then it wasn't terribly long before I was wiped out.  This is a game that expects you to learn from your mistakes, like any strategy game.
Ultimately I don't think this is really a game for me.    I didn't really see anything about this game to make it stand out.   Playing this just made me think back to playing the old Heroes of Might and Magic games.
Overall Recommendation:  Pass

If anyone is on the fence with this game, Jump off and buy it immediately, this wil be a semi lengthly but detailed review as this is my all time favorite WWII game ever made in the history of mankind.
Ive played the campaign here and there but from my experiences, your going to be challenged. Its a fight for ground game working torwards each point until your team wins pretty simple. The AI is pretty smart for both sides, although there are times im just staring at a guy like seriously wtf are you doing. I play on the hardest difficulty as I play online so im pretty decent. Summary if you like a good campaign, i had fun in what little i did. not really a story as so much battles with objectives.
Now for the Golden Nugget hidden deep inside steam that very few people have ever experienced first hand and should before Christ Himself returns. RO2/Rising Storm multiplayer.
There are quiet a few options for online play, you can have you vs bots, *really recommend for your first couple experiences* bots very sometimes there dumb as nails but seem to get smarter if you start to wreck them. Pretty basic gameplay cap the points to win, you still earn weapon and level xp in this mode so its good for people looking to boost weapons which at this point is almost necessarry to even compete as most players have been playing forever. Highly recommend the Apartments map for this.
The online PvP comes with multiple modes of play, you have your basic dumbed down mode not suppressed by bullets as hard or long ect. and a few other modes inbetween. the style i want to focus on is what most servers run and is the sole reason you should buy this game. Realism.
This games is pretty much the only way to get wartime nightmares without actually going to war. Its not a run and gun game mode, you will die, you will lose. If done right, with people who talk and a commander with a brain, this game is awesome you have to use some military thinking and the minimap a lot. Tactically RO2 nails it, you can run into a building crouch at a window to take cover then sight in to pop up over the window, a feature ive yet to find in any other game in my library, you can spot enemy locations for your team which is pretty handy since most times you get shot at you have no idea where its coming from. Which brings me to the suppression feature, battlefield has a neat one, but this game, pop a corner at the wrong second and get an mg burst right by your head and it will take your guy a few seconds to snap out of it, the damage systems pretty dope as well. shoot someone in the leg they get slowed drastically, you can heal yourself if your smart and quick. The realism mode forces you to move tacitally, talk to you teammates, work as a squad move as a squad and cap as a squad. if your the commander your job is to pound them with artillery, send in supplys and recon. force spawn troops if your guys take heavy losses at the top of a spawn clock.
I should mention the rising storm campaign has american troops and weapons, the RO2 campaign is the Red army vs Germany incase you missed it in the game discription on the store page.
Basically if you have ever wanted to play a really good realistic game that will never disappoint, and you can fight through the steep learning curve, which in 88.6 hours i feel i did. this is the game for you it will punish you at every error, tear your ego to shreads for just 10 more feet of ground.
I also feel i should add ive never at least that i can remember come across a cheater yet. or maybe its just impossible to tell because you never can tell where your getting shot from anyway

Potential, but at this current time the game is not developed enough to be user friendly.
The campaign as such is very generic without any kind of story too it. I know car games don't usually have much in the way of story, but these are just a collection of races back to back. I played a couple of the earlier carmaggeddon games and felt an enjoyable level of progression, however I didnt feel it here.
The driving itself is, as many have described, like mario cart. It's not all that bad, but its really heavy. You turn right and the car will swing right. It reminds me a lot of the driving in Arma. It does make sense to some extent due to the cars increased weight, with all the armour etc attached, but every turn results in some form of powerslide. Feathering the wheel with corrections isn't really a thing here.
You unlock upgrades as races go on and upgrade choices. The problem with this is that they funnel you down a path that gives you the illusion of choice, except... well you only have one choice. The upgrades are also as mundane as it gets. Fill this bar up here and there, for increased performance in that area. After researching this it doesnt appear that much in the way of visual effects take place.
The multiplayer at this point in time is sadly in a worse off place. The user interface doesnt tell you much of anything bar how many people are in each game. When trying to join a game you will be met with "can't join because game is in session" error messages. The problem with this is that theres no way to tell when they are in the lobby waiting and games  can take up to 30+ mins a piece. Alternatively I tried to host a game, and was met with a network error message over and over again. I tried testing a couple of other games out at the time to see if it was the connection and they all worked fine. Maybe a select port blockage, but I'm not spending my time trying to find out which ones.
The next problem was the lack of people understably playing the game. Each time I looked there were 4 - 5 games, none of which I could join after attempting to for 10 or so minutes.
After all of this I went directly to steams help > refund request function and got my money back.
Don't get me wrong, theres plenty of potential here, but I doubt it will every be properly realised.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second expansion episode for Half Life 1. Similarly to Half Life: Opposing Force, the story occurs parallel to the original Half Life. The player takes control of a new character, Barney Calhoun, a security guard. The same Barney that you meet again in Half Life 2.
This episode is very bare bones compared to the original game and the first expansion. It has less weapons than both previous entries, and can be beaten in 2.5 hours if you're good. The story is not quite as interesting as before, but it has its moments. The game is still Half Life, though; all the things that make the original good, such as great gunplay, are still here.
If you're a casual fan of the series then you don't need to play this, but if you really enjoy the series then I would definitely recommend it.

I played Tropico 3 before, and this is a great improvement:
The spirit is the same, but the graphics are better (you bet...) and the Eras are a nice addition. The radio shut up a little bit, but Penultimo is still funny. You have to gather research points too to unlock new buildings, constitution options, edicts, etc. All these additions make the game more fun to play.
On the bad side, the limo is gone!! :'(
Regarding campaign mode:
The campaign mode is not boring, i.e. from one mission to the next you do completely different things. You play on a few different islands, but you will "reuse" these islands in coming missions which makes the missions more look like a sandbox game while you can get straight to the point of the mission more easily since you already know the island. It's really good to bend the learning curve a bit: just play campaign!
If you're completely new to Tropico the tutorial goes through the very basics (at some point it explains what the pause/play/fast forward icons do when you click on them...!!)
I still have to try multiplayer, that might extend the life of the game.

This (and to an even greater degree, its DLC, Whistleblower) is an exercise in pants-ruining terror.  To be honest, I couldn't play for more than thirty or forty minutes at a time because I would get so tense and scared.  I lost track of the number of times I almost ruined my headphone cable by leaping back in my chair.  The graphics (while not terribly fancy) certainly do the trick, and the music and sound effects are always superb.  Everything about the game (peering around corners, laboured breathing when scared, etc) is designed to immerse you in the experiences of the character.  If you like horror games, then you MUST have this in your Steam library.
There are some downsides to make note of; the climax of the main game (not the DLC) suffers from WTF syndrome and also simply goes on too long, plus thematically and atmospherically the game does begin to repeat itself (not too much, mind you).  As well, if you don't like jump-scares you should note that there are more than a few, although in my opinion they were rather well done, and certainly not cheap at all.
Long story short, I really loved this game, and cannot recommend it heartily enough.

At first glance the game isn’t bad honestly. Its straightforward and nice if you like planning out cities and handing out jobs. Its even neat that a Tornado can touch down outside of town and either run a sway of destruction through the town, or just pass through the cemetery and clear some space…..and trust me you’re going to need it.
Now I don’t mind a game where nature is out to get you, and people can die in droves. So long as it makes sense; but in Banished even the sensible reasons to die defy logic.
Let me start with the simplest one. Starvation. Pretty standard in a game like this, and not unreasonable. If you don’t supply enough food to feed the masses, or keep your stores stocked for winter, you’re going to have a difficult time of it. HOWEVER. In Banished people will die of Starvation even when you have an excess of food (For example 7000 units, which is well above what’s necessary for a group of say 20 people). Now I looked into this and apparently there’s something about the AI and the townfolk “hording” food in their homes. That doesn’t really fit though cause even when it was in the barn, people died. They starved to death with essentially a buffet of various foods at their disposal. Now I can’t be the only one to think that’s poorly done.
Now another common way for people to die is Freezing to Death. Again that’s pretty reasonable. There’s no electric or gas heaters. No cotton stuffed jackets. All you have is firewood and wool coats. However here is where things once again go sideways. Even when you have more than enough firewood, to the extent of being at capacity, and you have enough warm coats even have a couple extra in storage, people will freeze to death. In -8C. This….honestly isn’t that bad. Certainly not something which should kill you when you’re surrounded by properly heated buildings. Yet still they die. In droves.
Next on the list….isn’t something that causes very many deaths on it’s own, and I support it’s existence because fires are going to happen. The problem is the townsfolk are the worst firefighters of all time. So much so people who have played the game aren’t even completely agreed on how they go about fighting fires. First I’ll explained. In certain types of buildings, say a house, a fire may occasionally start. that one building will start to burn. If other buildings are sitting in too close a proximity they will also start on fire. Now you’ve got a few ways to deal with this….well actually only one, gather water, but you’ve got a few ways to do this. You can get it from the nearest river, lake, or a well if you installed one nearby. Here’s the problem from there. Though I’ve heard from argument against this, visibly only “laborers” the sort of default job for a settler when they reach adulthood, can put out fires. So say your Tailor is standing right in front of the burning house….hell it may even be their house….and there’s a well across the street? He’ll just stand there and watch it burn and spread. Worse yet, “firefighting” is apparently not a high priority task. This means that if your laborers are doing anything else, they’re not going to do jack about that fire. Even RAIN does not visibly put the fire out. So before you know it a good chunk of your town, usually the houses, have burned to the ground. This leaves you with a bunch of people abruptly homeless, and due to the need for Builders to demolish the building, which gives only a few resources (though this is reasonable, it was just on fire), its going to take you quite awhile, probably years in game, to rebuild all these homes. In the mean time a lot of people are going to starve or freeze to death and die.
Next we’ll talk about the Citizens themselves. There’s a few issues here. The most glaring of which is getting more Citizens. See for all the runs of the game I did there was only two ways to get more people into the town. For the details of the first of these please turn to your local highschool’s Sex Ed Class. The point is the people have kids, the kids grow up, and eventually they become workers. They become workers faster if you don’t send them to school. Honestly the benefits of educating the masses are outweighed massively by the need to fill jobs an entire seven years sooner. Anyway the primary issue is that the only way to reliably get more Citizens is to have them born in your town. This is a problem because occasionally you will run out of woman young enough to conceive, eventually everyone dies, and suddenly you’re looking at a ghost town.
It's possible to take in "Nomads" but this is gated behind building City Hall, which is locked behind the large amount of resources the thing takes to build in the first place. Worse yet the City Hall is basically the single most important building in the game, because it's the only way to get a bevy of useful information such as how much food you're producing vs how much is being consumed. Additionally Nomads often tip the scales for the population in a negative way. Everyone starves. Again.
Now the second issue is the aging factor. It seems like the adults age WAY faster than the children, reaching the age of 70 before some kids have even hit 10. That means when someone dies of old age it can be difficult to fill their spot. A lot of old people die at once, and you’re suddenly in very real trouble. Plus as mentioned above children become workers at Age 10 normally, or age 17 if you build a school, and while this makes them a better worker, I’ve found time and again I’d rather have them several years sooner so that fewer people die for stupid reasons. (Which they proceed to anyway).
My last issue with Citizens is actually only the smallest issue. The game gives some windows to provide “general” information, but there’s no SINGLE window that can tell you what job a person has, and if they’re actually doing it right now. Even in the job window which can take you to to Citizens with that job, you have to scroll through all of them, and their window FOLLOWS THEM so you have to either pause the game or click around wildly to catch their window so you can take a clear look at it. Its a simple thing and more of a “quality of life” issue I feel, but it still annoys me.
My last major complaint about Banished is a matter of resources. Now reasonably Trees grow back over time (you can even have your people working in Forestry plant more), while stone and iron deposits do not. The solution to this is to make a Quarry and/or a Mine. The problem here is that, both the Quarry and the Mine both take a significant amount of resources, and 15 workers each. Ignoring the fact it’s doubtful you’ll have 15 to 30 workers to spare if you don’t want people to starve (which they’ll do anyway), even when a Quarry or Mine is fully staffed their resource collection is PAINFULLY slow. In 1 ‘season’ (this refers to the work season, so basically 1 year) they will produce, even fully manned, a mere 30 or so Stone or Iron. To put this in perspective, 1 house, 1 WOODEN house costs 8 stone (along with other materials). Want to build something like a Town Hall or Trading Post? You’re looking at 60-80 Stone. That means to build just one building it will take you 2-3 YEARS and that’s if nothing goes wrong. If half the town burned down and you’re looking to rebuild, this is an even bigger issue. Obviously this is more than a little bit broken, and becomes almost painful if you decided to use a smaller sized map.
So yes there is my rant. I honestly didn’t mind the people who would one off randomly die from a rockslide or a wildboar attack. That made sense. Suddenly spread of the Mumps? Totally reasonable. Infestation in the Pasture or Crops? Over all not something to ruin my day.
I like the idea/setting of Banished. I just feel they dropped the ball a bit mechanically. With a few tweaks it could be a pretty neat game to spend days at a time on. That ends my long♥♥♥♥♥rant. I hope you got some amusement out of it.

Barrier X is a very fast-paced obstacle-avoidance game in the vein of an endless runner, except spread across seven levels and portrayed from the vantage point of a vehicle speeding toward the horizon, periodically moving left or right out of lanes as they glow red-hot, meaning you're about to crash into a barrier.  Despite the bright rails on the sides of the screen, there's theoretically an infinite number of lanes for you to change between.  Last for thirty seconds (some achievements require sixty) on a level, and you unlock the next.  Do this on the seventh and last level, and you get to see the credits and a congratulatory message--in the middle of gameplay instead of waiting until you're done, which is an awkward transition.
Levels progressively add more obstacles, such as bright blue lanes intended to shunt you toward one direction or another and bright green lanes that demand you actively stay on them for a certain length of time.  If you miss either of these instructions, your steering becomes locked, prompting you to quickly press a button to escape.  Later stages also add enemies, who after a certain length of time can lock onto and destroy your ship, but thankfully you're armed with homing fire-and-forget missiles of your own (you don't have to be in the same lane as they are), which is relatively handy when you're trying to focus more on dodging barriers than on mashing an attack button.
The most optimal strategy of protecting your ship (when enemies aren't around) is really to look at the color of the ground directly beneath you--dark blue is safe, red means escape, green means get here ASAP, and light blue means you need to look up to see which direction you're expected to go.  Movement is closer to Audiosurf than to Super Hexagon, as this game doesn't really ask for pixel-exact positioning: you "change lanes" almost immediately instead of having to worry about being caught halfway between two of them because you went too far or not far enough.  The developer suggests (
in comments) to move between one or two lanes at a time, and while trigger discipline does come in handy in later stages, it also becomes less viable because you'll end up in stretches of at least four or five red lanes at once before finding another safe zone.  Enemies feel like a nuisance when flying around since your best chance of survival usually involves focusing on the bottom of the screen, which is a shame because, despite the simplistic graphics, the game really does look amazing when everything is going well at super-high speeds.  Most of the game's important visual information is directly near your ship, however, making for a game that would be more fun to watch (so you can focus on enjoying the whole scene at once) than to play.
There's little to say about the core mechanics or replay value unless the leaderboards interest you, and the game's main feature is its really high and potentially alienating degree of difficulty.  I'm glad at some level that I finished the game, but I found myself wanting to complete later stages not because I was enjoying myself but so I could have them behind me.  The soundtrack was very hit-or-miss, with some tracks being much more notable than others, even as none of the songs got on my nerves enough to distract from the gameplay.  I did appreciate the menu having a freely selectable jukebox, and I especially enjoyed Arctic Spaceman/Wagner Koop's contributions, "Chiptune" and "YYY," both of which are freely downloadable from his Bandcamp and Soundcloud pages.

Multifaros' "The Boss" is also catchy and memorable.
Do I recommend Barrier X?  I didn't really find the core gameplay addictive or compelling for its own sake after the first two or three levels, so this is really only useful for players who absolutely crave games whose sole interesting trait is a really high difficulty that often mandates pass-or-fail decisions several times a second--otherwise, it's basically just a bland and small dish slathered with hot sauce.

This game is a marvel to look at, without a doubt. The music is nice fun and very catchy. The run and gun levels can be fun, but have some issues, which I'll explain in a moment. I do feel the run and gun levels are a little forced, which might be because of how the game was orginally just a boss rush game. Though it adds more content, it kinda feels shoehorned in.
So the game's gunning mechanic is great, the lock-on mechanic is a great feature to have. This allows aiming without having to run, games like Contra or Metal Slug could do with this feature. Now the part I had the most issues with. The parry. The game controls fine, the character is nice and responsive, but the parry feels kinda off. Which with a game that demands perfection, to have a mechanic feel off is a bad thing, killing the player with deaths that feel like "Oh come on! I hit them though!". I also have to admit the super second fire feels too weak. It refills fast... but it doesn't do a whole lot. Making something that looks like a lot of power, which should make the player feel great, feels like it was a waste of time. I've even died because of the super water blast which makes you freeze in the spot (on the ground or in air) and forces you to blast them, then drops you with no invulnerability frames, thus you get hit. So the game just feels like you need to run, dash, and shoot. The parry and super abilities just feel kinda broken.
Now the bosses, the bosses are fun to play... after you've played them a few times. Now I will say I have beaten a couple bosses first try, one of which I did a perfect on the first try. The bosses have many phases and are a blast to fight. Though I did have some moments that I said "Wow, really!? They can do that, where's the warning!?". So it's a trial and error kinda thing, which is fine especially since the bosses are just there own thing, and you don't need to do a level before the fight. The rating system after each level is kinda nice, it doesn't seem too necessary, but is still nice to have for replay value.
In conclusion the game is a challenge and is a wonderful looking game. I do feel like it still needs some polish, but I think that otherwise it is a great game. I wouldn't recommend this for people who can't handle a challenge, because it really needs perfection to beat. So if I were to score it, with some score. I would call it an 8/10. Though not perfect, it has a lot of great features and a lot of fun to have.

We arrive at the problems. The Gameplay is great..but depends on your car. The AI is fair on the start and there you can really have fun: driving, crashing around and feel like a badass. fantastic. but then the AI is so fast and drives like on rails (while you drive like on ice) and acheives 300kmh easily. and scripted enemies....we all hate them. you can crash someone into a wall and he gets last, 1 round later he is 2cond again.
The game is unfair, really damn unfair. your respawn sets you almost 4 places back (and you respawn often, trust me) and enemies drive like on drugs. now the main problem of the game: EVERYTHING ELSE THAN THE GAMEPLAY
Im serious, this game feels like the makers didnt had any time to make anything else than the cars and races, and not even them are good made.
we have about 20tracks or a bit more/less, so repeats are pretty often and nothing was planned. you cant see which races exactly or how many laps a cup will have (and the game only has cups!) neither we can play a single race in the career mode. you are foced to take a cup. they much probably forgot to add many functions. because the cups are based on points like normal (first gets 10 points, second gets 8 and so on) but you can repeat ever race as often as you want in a row, that takes both away. the challenge of cups and the fun of a single track.
Cars..oh damn that point is sad. there are quite many cars and they drive different from car to car, but mostly in 3 areas: understerring as hell, drifting as hell, or like on ice. with tuning they will drift a lot but in a good controlable way (never take a full muscle car without tuning, even with max tuning some of them wont ever make a corner with more than 100kmh) but even here everything lacks. you cant tune any visual except the colour (on some only), but the worst..you can only choose it once! you bought it in black but want it blue? well sucks to be you, buy it again. and the tuning..theres no way to test tuning and once you bought a tuning, you cant uninstall it! nitro makes your car 3 points better in nitro but 3 worse in power (about) want to unisntall the nitro? not possible. The cars wont give you a good speed feel in 80% of the game, only full tuned cars feel fast and reach 250kmh or more.
Music: Music is pretty okay, all rock songs (the sound designer was a extrem rock fan it seems) from back then very famous bands (fall out boy, nickelback, wolfsmother) that are nice to hear but if you dont like rock..you are fu**ed. and even every rock lover will hate the songs soon. why? there are only about 20songs! and since they all sound similiar you soon get annoyed by them, especially because..NO MUSIC PLAYER. seriously not even a single bit. You cant skip a song, cant play the last one, restart it, manage songs that can play or anything. heres a song, deal with it. sad when you restart a race 5 times only to have a song you like. songs skip everytime you join or leave a race, so you can control is a bit XD but yeah horrible.
The game really lacks on all else than the basic stuff. you got no proper replay function, so if you had an awesome moment like a super crash round where you killed 4 cars..well no one will believe you because you cant replay it! (i recommend recording while playing because the game will give you great moments) I killed 6 enemies once and it was a photfinish with 2 broken cars but i will forever be the only one who saw it.
the game really feels super small and repeating , the few things there are fun (and unfair) but it feels like the game was made either without love, money, or time (or all of them). If the game is in sale, i recommend, and if you love crashing in games and dont mind lack of content, try it out! no game I ever played gave me such a good feel in rampages and demolition, also it isnt so damn slow. But yeah, for fans of normal race games like nfs todays, I recommend you to not get this game, its fun, feels fun to play and is always great for a 15minutes playing, even till today, but you will wish yourself the makers added more. The concept and ideas are great and has potential they sadly never ever used.I love this game till today but even a hardcore fan like me hates many parts of this game.

The story mode finally came out, and it's completely boring trash, the title of this game is what you can expect, long boring treks through the dark with nothing happening.
As soon as you get a coat on that keeps you from instantly dropping to -50 below zero the game's just a boring trek to harvest cat tails.
You take the role of a albino Fatts Mcgee, trying to find his retard three. Enjoy the breathtaking experience of running out of energy and having to sleep 10 hours every three minutes, meanwhile, you go from fully fed to starving within 20 minutes.
Part one of the storymode is the least boring of the two. The back tracking is less tedious because there's places to enter and scavenge for the daily 20,000 calories you need as a 600 pound obese man. However, part two of the storymode is absolute forced trash, I couldn't get through it without falling asleep at the keyboard. You're first tasked with walking from one end of the map, to another, then back for a short cutscene.
Your next task is walking for a grueling 1 hour real time along railroad tracks with absolutely nothing intresting happening, to get something almost cool to happen and your first weapon of the game, a hunting rifle. Your character, no matter his status, seems to have a severe case of parkinsons, and can not hold the rifle steady, instead deciding to swing it wildly as if it were a rattle.
Now here is where my boredom became unbearable... Once you make the arduous journey back across the railroad tracks, another boring backtracking sequence, you're tasked with learning how to survive. Your first survival learning experience is.... repairing clothing. Something you already know how to do, and the game gives you 5000 unneeded sewing kits, so you should already have max quality trump tier woolen coats covered in flames. How they thought this would be mindblowing new techniques, I don't know.
At this point I realized I would need to complete at least three to four boring, long, fetch quest missions, and make the long, boring, journey back, while stopping to eat fifteen deer carcasses on the way, instead of just killing the bear with the rifle and perfectly good gear I had and continue the story, instead of drawing out the boring uneventful story in hopes of decieving people that it was worth the years waiting, and I had a major brain anyuersm and went into a coma.
Combine this with the heavy censoring of negativity and reviews the devs did in the beta stage (that lasted for years) and the incredibly boring, backtrack fest of the incompleted story that took them 3 years to create, and the dialogue isn't even fully voice acted, and I will reccomend you stay far, far away from this trash.

=== Age of Wonders - Game Review, Turn-based Strategy - 10/10 ===
If you like turn-based strategy, whether it's in a table top game or a video game, Age of Wonders is at the top of the list.
Age of Wonders was released back in 1999, so we're getting pretty close to the grand 20-year mark in age. For such an old game, you might think it would look pretty aged and unable to hold up to present-day gaming. In my opinion, this game is a classic that is still plenty of fun to play and has a great art-style that still looks great even to this day. If you go back to the original pictures of this game before it was released, the art is so simple and would easily have gotten old pretty quick. Thankfully they decided to go in a bit of a different direction which I think looks like someone painted it by hand; this sort of painted-looking art-style is definitely my favourite. Of course the visuals are important when deciding whether or not to play a game, but there's so much more to talk about.
The gameplay is turn-based; if you're really into board games, this will feel just like playing a board game where everybody takes a turn one at a time to plan out their strategy and execute their plan of action to the best of their ability. There are some options such as having the map already explored, whether or not to have your leader as a playable character in the game, and whether the turns are taken simultaneously or one at a time. Personally, I prefer to have to explore everything on my own, have a leader, and have turns played one at a time; though every once in a while I change it up for fun.
Games can be a little as 2-players all the way up to 12 with each player playing a different race; each of which have different advantages and disadvantages. Each game revolves around capturing cities and other landmarks, then using the income from those sources to create the right mixture of units to eliminate your opponents. If you've ever played a turn-based combat game, you may already understand how each attack has a chance to hit or miss. If you really enjoy the strategy of combat, you can choose to control each battle yourself, or have the game automatically generate an outcome for you. Obviously this speeds up the game to have it decide on an outcome for you, but the system has a certain way of doing its calculations which can sometimes give you a completely different outcome from controlling the battle on your own. One example is if you're trying to protect a unit that is low on health, you can choose to have that unit run away on your own, but the computer-generated outcome will run that unit headlong into battle even on 1 health point.
Throughout the game you also have to choose what spells to research to help tip the scales in your favour. Your leader and additional heroes which join you during the course of the game may or may not have the ability to cast spells. These leaders and heroes have an amount of spell points which get refreshed at the beginning of each new turn and from this they can cast spells which each cost a number of spell points. Choices of spells can change the state of the overworld map, enchant units to make them stronger, or can be used in battle to turn the tides in an otherwise unwinnable situation.
I you can't tell, I absolutely love this game and could go on and on about all the great qualities forever, but unfortunately at some point I have to aknowledge the grit of the game. There are some points which can be a little bit painful either due to the age of the game or due to design. Depending on how much time you have, you may enjoy watching all the animations. Some days I like having a relaxing time watching the animations go on, but they can be a little bit slow sometimes which makes an already long game take even longer to play. You can be playing just one map for an entire month without proceeding to the next scenario. This is why I tend to play while running a program which speeds up the game. My only other real gripe about Age of Wonders is that it has a habit of crashing while playing in any kind of windowed mode. This usually isn't a bad thing as I prefer to play on true fullscreen anyways, but there is another problem where if you tab out of the game and tab back in, it likes to either crash or not open back up... which can make it difficult if you have other things going on while you want to play some Age of Wonders. This makes you have to plan sessions to play rather than just opening it up whenever for a bit while doing other things.
Overall, even with the negatives of this game, I have to give Age of Wonders 10 / 10 because it's just so amazing for me. I highly recommend getting this game and playing through it if you're into strategy. The Age of Wonders games are my favourite turn-based strategy series so far (though I haven't managed to start playing the new Age of wonders III yet).
If you're interested in seeing some gameplay, you can head over to my Age of Wonders Gameplay page or you can watch my videos directly on my YouTube channel TheDaemonVirus.
~ Kyle Welykholowa

I discovered this game quite by chance while browsing YouTube for some new game recommendations.
I've always believed that I handled jump-scares (occurring at live haunted attractions and such) fairly well.  However, I am absolutely terrified of the concept of statues, mannequins, dolls and the like moving on their own accord.  It took me five days (pun intended) to buckle down and try FNAF experience personally rather than vicariously through someone else's gameplay.  They do say it's better to face your fears head-on, so...sure, why not?
I'm writing this review after my first attempt and I can honestly say that, for me, this game delivered.
It pretty much reinforced every deep-rooted anxiety and primal fear that I could possibly imagine (and some that I couldn't) leaving me in a serious, full-on panic wherein every light in the house had to be turned on and every lock double-checked.  It was probably a very bad decision on my part to start this so late at night.  So will I be sleeping tonight?  Nope.
FNAF is a different sort of horror game than I've every played.  The graphics aren't fancy but, in the end, they don't need to be.  For a game like this, it's all about atmosphere, and I feel FNAF has that in abundance.
In my opinion, the simplistic and limited mechanics of gameplay, coinciding with its dark ambiance and subtle alterations in sound only serve to increase the level of stress and the feeling that you are powerless.  Jump-scares are a pretty basic, yet effective, way to get a reaction and in FNAF they are executed well.  The static-filled screens and flickering lights strain your eyes and wreck havoc with your imagination.  Limited resources and a specific time-frame provide the foundation for nerve-wracking, split-second decision making and clock-watching.  Add in the that fact that your stalkers are a bunch of man-sized, animatronic stuffed animals (with eerie frozen smiles and staring eyes) who will never move when you're looking at them - this game can become pure nightmare fodder for some.
As you progress, the tension becomes greater; the mood more sinister. The urgency to react faster becomes more prevalent - testing your awareness.  You're challenged to manage your resources and time against a menace that defies logic and with each night, it draws you further in.  Underlying it all is the question: why and how is it happening?  And, for that matter, how in the world is this place considered child-friendly?!  With little information to go on, the back-story is left to mystery and further adds to the suspense.
At it's core, FNAF touches on the primal fear of being trapped alone, in the dark, facing a horror that wants nothing more than to happily chew your face off.
All in all, FNAF is engaging and proves a game doesn't necessarily have to be gory and violent to be scary.  Is it for everyone?  Probably not.  If your reaction to jump-scares and minimal mechanics is 'meh' - this probably won't do anything for you.
I recommend this game for any enthusiast of survival/psychological horror-themed games looking for something a little different.

This was just ok. I purchased this in the hopes of finding a spacey adventure game with an intense atmosphere like that of
(both involve mostly solitary exploration of strange, desolate alien environments), but was left distinctly underwhelmed by the game in general.
It's diverting enough, with sufficient mileage to absorb somewhat for a few hours, but the plot and characters are basic and lacklustre. There's also no real climax/resolution to the game--while there's a confrontation, it's expected and occurs as a cut scene that is over quite quickly, so there's no real sense of being in actual danger at any point or discovery of anything truly shocking. The voice acting is rather poor, with some lines read as though the actor doesn't fully understand their context.
On the plus side, the environments are nice to look at (although largely static--the only other character in the game doesn't move) and the puzzles are generally logical and don't require very large leaps of logic, presenting some challenges, although they're not particularly sophisticated or imaginative, either.
Overall, an easygoing, but ultimately forgettable, few hours.

I don't like pre-rendered graphics with a single point of view for each scene. Makes me feel trapped.
I don't like disappearing intrest markers in point-and-click games. It has me sweeping the screen looking for points when I'm stuck, and that's just frustrating.
I don't like dodgy voice acting. It makes the whole game feel fake and ruins immersion.
I don't like short games, as they tend to leave me wanting more.
So, why am I recommending short a 2D pre-rendered point-and-click game with disappearing intrest markers and dodgy voice acting?
Because it's worth it. The puzzles are logical, the graphics are good, the animations servicable and the atmosphere great.
The fact that it's short is a good thing, actually. It makes it so the voice acting never gets on my nerves, and the game doesn't outstay it's welcome.
At the end, I was satisfied. I'd love to explore more, but then I'd need a free-moving camera, and voice actors that aren't simply reading. I need actors to act.
Maybe not the 9,99€ asking price, but as part of a bundle it was certainly worth my time.

TL;DR I don't like some choices the devs made, but it's still a well-made game.

At first glance the game isn’t bad honestly. Its straightforward and nice if you like planning out cities and handing out jobs. Its even neat that a Tornado can touch down outside of town and either run a sway of destruction through the town, or just pass through the cemetery and clear some space…..and trust me you’re going to need it.
Now I don’t mind a game where nature is out to get you, and people can die in droves. So long as it makes sense; but in Banished even the sensible reasons to die defy logic.
Let me start with the simplest one. Starvation. Pretty standard in a game like this, and not unreasonable. If you don’t supply enough food to feed the masses, or keep your stores stocked for winter, you’re going to have a difficult time of it. HOWEVER. In Banished people will die of Starvation even when you have an excess of food (For example 7000 units, which is well above what’s necessary for a group of say 20 people). Now I looked into this and apparently there’s something about the AI and the townfolk “hording” food in their homes. That doesn’t really fit though cause even when it was in the barn, people died. They starved to death with essentially a buffet of various foods at their disposal. Now I can’t be the only one to think that’s poorly done.
Now another common way for people to die is Freezing to Death. Again that’s pretty reasonable. There’s no electric or gas heaters. No cotton stuffed jackets. All you have is firewood and wool coats. However here is where things once again go sideways. Even when you have more than enough firewood, to the extent of being at capacity, and you have enough warm coats even have a couple extra in storage, people will freeze to death. In -8C. This….honestly isn’t that bad. Certainly not something which should kill you when you’re surrounded by properly heated buildings. Yet still they die. In droves.
Next on the list….isn’t something that causes very many deaths on it’s own, and I support it’s existence because fires are going to happen. The problem is the townsfolk are the worst firefighters of all time. So much so people who have played the game aren’t even completely agreed on how they go about fighting fires. First I’ll explained. In certain types of buildings, say a house, a fire may occasionally start. that one building will start to burn. If other buildings are sitting in too close a proximity they will also start on fire. Now you’ve got a few ways to deal with this….well actually only one, gather water, but you’ve got a few ways to do this. You can get it from the nearest river, lake, or a well if you installed one nearby. Here’s the problem from there. Though I’ve heard from argument against this, visibly only “laborers” the sort of default job for a settler when they reach adulthood, can put out fires. So say your Tailor is standing right in front of the burning house….hell it may even be their house….and there’s a well across the street? He’ll just stand there and watch it burn and spread. Worse yet, “firefighting” is apparently not a high priority task. This means that if your laborers are doing anything else, they’re not going to do jack about that fire. Even RAIN does not visibly put the fire out. So before you know it a good chunk of your town, usually the houses, have burned to the ground. This leaves you with a bunch of people abruptly homeless, and due to the need for Builders to demolish the building, which gives only a few resources (though this is reasonable, it was just on fire), its going to take you quite awhile, probably years in game, to rebuild all these homes. In the mean time a lot of people are going to starve or freeze to death and die.
Next we’ll talk about the Citizens themselves. There’s a few issues here. The most glaring of which is getting more Citizens. See for all the runs of the game I did there was only two ways to get more people into the town. For the details of the first of these please turn to your local highschool’s Sex Ed Class. The point is the people have kids, the kids grow up, and eventually they become workers. They become workers faster if you don’t send them to school. Honestly the benefits of educating the masses are outweighed massively by the need to fill jobs an entire seven years sooner. Anyway the primary issue is that the only way to reliably get more Citizens is to have them born in your town. This is a problem because occasionally you will run out of woman young enough to conceive, eventually everyone dies, and suddenly you’re looking at a ghost town.
It's possible to take in "Nomads" but this is gated behind building City Hall, which is locked behind the large amount of resources the thing takes to build in the first place. Worse yet the City Hall is basically the single most important building in the game, because it's the only way to get a bevy of useful information such as how much food you're producing vs how much is being consumed. Additionally Nomads often tip the scales for the population in a negative way. Everyone starves. Again.
Now the second issue is the aging factor. It seems like the adults age WAY faster than the children, reaching the age of 70 before some kids have even hit 10. That means when someone dies of old age it can be difficult to fill their spot. A lot of old people die at once, and you’re suddenly in very real trouble. Plus as mentioned above children become workers at Age 10 normally, or age 17 if you build a school, and while this makes them a better worker, I’ve found time and again I’d rather have them several years sooner so that fewer people die for stupid reasons. (Which they proceed to anyway).
My last issue with Citizens is actually only the smallest issue. The game gives some windows to provide “general” information, but there’s no SINGLE window that can tell you what job a person has, and if they’re actually doing it right now. Even in the job window which can take you to to Citizens with that job, you have to scroll through all of them, and their window FOLLOWS THEM so you have to either pause the game or click around wildly to catch their window so you can take a clear look at it. Its a simple thing and more of a “quality of life” issue I feel, but it still annoys me.
My last major complaint about Banished is a matter of resources. Now reasonably Trees grow back over time (you can even have your people working in Forestry plant more), while stone and iron deposits do not. The solution to this is to make a Quarry and/or a Mine. The problem here is that, both the Quarry and the Mine both take a significant amount of resources, and 15 workers each. Ignoring the fact it’s doubtful you’ll have 15 to 30 workers to spare if you don’t want people to starve (which they’ll do anyway), even when a Quarry or Mine is fully staffed their resource collection is PAINFULLY slow. In 1 ‘season’ (this refers to the work season, so basically 1 year) they will produce, even fully manned, a mere 30 or so Stone or Iron. To put this in perspective, 1 house, 1 WOODEN house costs 8 stone (along with other materials). Want to build something like a Town Hall or Trading Post? You’re looking at 60-80 Stone. That means to build just one building it will take you 2-3 YEARS and that’s if nothing goes wrong. If half the town burned down and you’re looking to rebuild, this is an even bigger issue. Obviously this is more than a little bit broken, and becomes almost painful if you decided to use a smaller sized map.
So yes there is my rant. I honestly didn’t mind the people who would one off randomly die from a rockslide or a wildboar attack. That made sense. Suddenly spread of the Mumps? Totally reasonable. Infestation in the Pasture or Crops? Over all not something to ruin my day.
I like the idea/setting of Banished. I just feel they dropped the ball a bit mechanically. With a few tweaks it could be a pretty neat game to spend days at a time on. That ends my long♥♥♥♥♥rant. I hope you got some amusement out of it.
