The core gameplay in Evolve is very well done.
The problem is that you only experience that gameplay 10% of the time. The rest of the time you're just chasing the monster as hunters or running away from hunters as the monster.
This isn't fun or intuitive to me. You spend most of your time tracking monster footsteps and avoiding or fighting npc's. Also, if you're going up against a smart monster player, you won't see many trackable footsteps because he will avoid it with the game's "stealth" mechanic.
Now, playing as the monster, it's even more boring to run (or stealth) away from the hunters. Unfortunately this is a must, because you need to consistently kill npc's and feed on them to eventually evolve into a stronger tiered monster. You could engage the hunters earlier on for more action, but you're just dooming yourself because you'll be too weak to defeat them at stage 1. So the game forces you to run away and kill bots. Not what I find to be fun in a multiplayer video game.
The average game in evolve lasts, what, 10-12 minutes? Well you spend maybe a total of 3 minutes actually fighting the monster. The rest...well...you guessed it. Just running. Cat and mouse. Over and over again. I really want to enjoy the game but it becomes so tedious to chase and chase, or flee and flee all game long. You could argue that you fight the monster longer than what I mentioned, but that just means you're going up against an inexperienced player who doesn't know how to evade you properly.
I love that it takes good teamwork to defeat the monster, but at the same time it kind of sucks because one horrible random on your team can ruin everything. I don't want to chase a monster for 10 minutes just to lose in the end because my medic or support has no idea what they're doing.
Evolve offers other game modes besides the traditional "Hunt" but they all end up playing out the same way. I don't see a game focusing on 4v1 gameplay lasting very long. It'll build a small community of die hard fans over the next month but after that I see it dying, hard. Wordplay bruh, I'm sort of a rapper in my local neighborhood.

tl;dr Yes, but with a warning below.
Age of Wonders, despite the age, is still a worthwhile game. It can appear deceptively simple at first, but as you begin to chip away at the abilities and magic system, you realise just how important deeper knowledge of the game mechanics can be.
A lot of the game has been covered by other reviewers. Essentially: turn based fantasy strategy game with empire management. Unlike the sequels - and many other games of its type - in Age of Wonders if your leader dies, you lose the game. This adds an extra layer of risk - your leader is powerful and can take down many basic units, but one wrong move and the game's over. It can sound cheap, but it really puts the stress on in major battles, something other strategy games miss out on. There is an option to remove this for the skirmishes, if you're not keen on it.
THE WARNING: this game, as it sits on Steam, is faulty. It crashes a lot - A LOT. Some people are fine, but looking at the reviews and the forums, it's wide spread enough for it to be an issue. You can fix this with a Hex editor. Now, I know some basic fixes are acceptable, but having to use a hex editor to fix the game is not. I imagine a lot of people out there don't know what a hex editor is, or how to even use one. Furthermore, I don't see any reason why this can't be done on the developers end - it took me two minutes, and would save everyone else a lot of headache.
Anyway, if you know what you're doing, this thread has the instructions:
I very nearly put this as a thumbs down, but the cheap price, brilliant gameplay, and the fact that a fix is available - courtesy of the fan base (which, by the way, provide more maps and content than you'll ever manage to get through), I really can't bring myself to do it.
Thumbs up, only just, though.

When this game came out, there probably weren't a whole lot of quality original indie games to choose from, or so it seems, as critics basically creamed their pants and showered endless praise over this one. However, the game is severely overrated.
The visuals are quite good and the atmosphere is by far the game's strongest suit. It's actually very immersive and unsettling, especially when wearing a decent pair of headphones, but that's where my praise ends.
The gameplay, the most important part of any indie game, falls flat on its face here. Instead of ingenious level design that constantly thrills you and keeps you glued to your controller like true indie masterpieces such as Shovel Knight and Freedom Planet, the game shoves moronic trial-and-error gameplay in your face at every moment. It tries too hard to be the Demon's Souls of platformers and just ends up being a complete bore full of cheap, unavoidable deaths, and a lackluster sense of progression. After a strong opening, everything starts to feel the same relatively fast and you're then left with a very unfulfilling experience. That is, if you're able to force yourself all the way to the abrupt ending like I did, and saying I had to force myself to complete it is really an understatement, but since the game was recently given away for free and I always finish everything I start, I figured why not.
If you like gorgeous looking indie games with cheap, artificial difficulty, lack of story, and mundane puzzles, this is the game for you. For everyone else, check out an overlooked indie gem like Shadow Blade: Reload instead that actually respects your time as a gamer. I guarantee you'll have a lot more fun.

excellent tutorial and opening levels. most should be able to pick this game up right away. there is plenty of content here in the form of boss fights (which is what the game focuses on). the vast majority of these encounters are well-designed and very fun to learn and play through. a scoring system exists for people that want to push themselves for an extra challenge. these boss fights can be quite challenging to beat on the regular difficulty, but they is also an easy mode
there are also a handful of traditional run n gun levels, which are solid and do add a bit to the game. it's nice to break up the boss rush a bit, but it's just not where this game shines. i still enjoyed playing through them though. these levels arent required to progress through the game, but it is the main source of coins, which allow you to unlock new weapons and perks from the shop. you can also get these coins from moving around the overworld and interacting with some of the games colorful NPC's, which also sometimes provide you with hints. the unlocakable items add a lot of fun and depth to the game, especially the various weapons, which are quite varied and each have a unique special moves. you are able to swap between two weapons during a level. your loadout consists of those two weapons, a perk and one of three super moves. the super moves are acquired through special levels and while these levels are well-designed, some of the supers themselves really needed to be retuned slightly

This is not a city builder. This is a village builder, and it is the absolute best village builder there has been and ever will be. If you want a game where the goal is to make the biggest and the greatest city of all time, by all means get Cities: Skylines, but if you want to experience the struggles of keeping people alive rather than happy, then this is the game for you.
Other people might complain that this game doesn't really support expansion, and they're right, except they don't really realize that this game doesn't even care about expansion at all. This game is about growing slowly, keeping your citizens alive, and maintaining order in an incredibly disorderly world. Since the game focuses so much on the citizens rather than the economics and the scope, it is BRUTALLY difficult. Even on easy, this game will take a bite out of you and spit you out. But personally, that's why I come back every now and again to see if I'm any better (I'm not).
This game isn't really a game, it's more of a hobby. It's a means to build a village just because you want to and it gives you every single tool you could need which brings me to the best part of this game. The UI is quite literally second to none. This is the best, most customizable, most intuitive, easiest to use UI ever created period. This is pretty much the reason that the game makes it feel like it's YOUR fault for failing. It gives you all the information that you could possibly need, yet you still can't manage it.
And on top of all of this, there's the modding community. Sure, it isn't as big as other games in this genre, but the game is more than happy to run mods. It was built to be expanded on by the community.
In all, this game does what it sets out to do perfectly. It might not click with everyone that plays it, but for those that understand what it is, there is no replacement for Banished.

Let's get what everyone online is talking about out of the way first: The difficulty. Is it really as infuriating hard and broken as people been saying? In my opinion, no it isn't. The game is broken up into two main sections: Boss stages and platforming levels. The boss stages do take up the bulk of the adventure and It IS a bit harder than what you usually find in mainstream games but it's not by any means impossible like a lot of people claim it is. It's definitely not for everyone though. And that's ok.
You'd think that a game which basically consist of boss fight after boss fight would get old after the first few fights, but you'd be wrong. Each boss stage plays completely different than the next. And each one has multiple transformations and gimmicks you must overcome. Not one fight felt similar to another one. Monotony isn't an issue here.
Speaking of difficulty. For those of you wondering. The game controls like a dream. Every move you can do with cuphead feels buttery smooth. I played the whole game with a Dualshock 4 and every single death i had was due to my own fault not the game's. A final note: playing Cuphead with a friend DOES make the game easier. If you are having problems with the game, just call a friend over and split the workload.
Visually. Just looking at a screenshot would tell you how absolutely beautiful the game is, but seeing it in motion just takes the whole thing to another level. From what i understand, every single frame of animation was made by hand trying to emulate the look of old 40s cartoons. And they 100% nailed it. Everything from the silky smooth animation to the dirty film grain and color bleed used makes it look lovingly authentic. It really did blow my mind.
The same can be said about the music and sounds. It only took me a few days playing the game to make me run out and buy the OST. If you are into Jazzy pieces, you'll be in aural heaven here.
Cuphead has quickly become one of my favorite games of 2017. Cuphead is both beautiful and brutal. It's definitely not for everyone. But for those that stick with it and have the patience to learn the game and get better at it. I'm sure you'll be remembering this one for a long time to come.

**** EARLY ACCESS REVIEW ****
Let me start off by saying that the concept behind Project Zomboid is a very very promising one. If the developers take the proper route in configuring the UI, Multiplayer, and Gameplay aspects of the game, then Zomboid has the potential to be the most challenging and deepest zombie survival game out there. Overall, I do not regret buying this game even in Early Alpha.
The Good:
-Great soundtrack and tone selection.
-Focuses on survival (while combat is necessary, the game encourages you to avoid it)
-Deep crafting mechanics
-Insanely good AI. (fire a gun and zombies will hear it and will come after you)
The Bad: (note that if these are fixed, the game is going to be so awesome)
-Clunky UI (especially when it comes to switching bags and weapons)
-Crafting mechanics though deep, are still raw
-Tutorials are not that informative
-Skills are not yet clear to their corresponding benefits.
The Potential:
-The game can be a very fun multiplayer survival game if they add saved progression and alternating difficulty levels
-The game can offer an even better multiplayer experience if they introduce community and community vs community mechanics (like walking dead)
-The game can be a very fun survival or sandbox single player experience if they fix the UI, improve crafting and polish gameplay.
-I would suggest putting random events on the game just to spice it up.
Overall, great game and I'm very hopeful. Looking forward to the finished product.

Red Orchestra 2... What is there to say? It is a hidden gem, I'll tell you that much now, but let's get into the actual review though, shall we?
First off, let me say one thing. This game is not a casual experience. You don't simply turn it on and do well your first time, nor your second time, or a hundred times after. You will, in the beginning, die a lot. Often times, you will not even know who killed you! Sometimes, you will spend more time waiting to be respawned than in the actual game itself! But do not be discouraged, this is only a very temporary state, as you will, over time, learn which places to avoid, how to control your gun, and memorize popular enemy hangout spots.
If you are used to games like Battlefield or Call of Duty, you will hit a vertical wall. This isn't just a learning curve, this is a 90 degree vertical brick wall. Don't expect to do well, probably not even if you are a hardcore fan of ArmA, instead, expect to die very often, and expect to be at the bottom of the scoreboard.
The gameplay consists of your classic FPS features, you get to crouch down, aim down sights, go prone, switch fire modes on certain firearms, and of course, you get to shoot your gun. However, there is a feature that isn't common in the FPS market, there is a full cover system for most objects on the map, though I strongly recommend NOT using the cover system, and instead crouching behind high cover when necessary.
There are multiple gamemodes, by now, only one is being played by the majority of remaining players, and that is territory control. Those familiar with Battlefield's "conquest" will know exactly what this is, just add the fact that one team is attacking while the other is defending. The team which has more people in one point captures it.
You will spend most of your time sitting behind cover, or slowly creeping around tight hallways with your teammates, and that there is an EXTREMELY crucial note, with your teammates. A team is extremely important, you simply CANNOT rush through enemy lines like John Rambo anymore. In this game, you are a pawn, listen to your squad leader/commander, and stick close to your team, that's it.
Guns behave very differently from weapons you find in Battlefield, and even more differently than Call of Duty weaponry. These weapons have recoil, and that recoil must be managed. No more full-auto spraying accross the whole map, no, burst fire, semi-automatic, and bolt-action rule this game.
Rifles are, by far, some of the strongest weapons in the game. Each has a five round magazine and must be manually bolted. These rifles are very accurate, but they severely lack in rate of fire. Most people will be seen with bolt-action rifles, just like in WW2.
Sub-machineguns (SMGs) are, by far, the best weapons in the game. If you can manage the recoil of the Russian PPsH-41, or the kick of the Mkb 42, you can kill just about anybody at any range with a precise hit to the chest. SMGs are, however, limited in this game, as only a few lucky individuals can claim the assault class, and be blessed with these gems. SMGs are NOT intended for fully automatic fire unless you are in a tight, small hallway. Always fire in bursts, or even better, use them like you would a semi-automatic rifle.
Semi-automatic rifles are the weapons of Elite Riflemen, once again, they are limited to a few players per-team. In the hands of a marksman, these weapons are devastating from a long range.
LMGs are surprisingly good weapons for long ranges, if they are in a stationary position, that is. Use them wisely, and always let more experienced players take the machinegunner position, as it is a great responsibility.
Remember, all of us die, even the best of players can have bad days. Stick to high cover, never run accross open fields, stick close to your team, move from cover-to-cover, and use your weapons wisely... In Red Orchestra 2, every rifleman counts. In the hands of a good commander, even a team of inexperienced players can achieve victory!

"Half-Life: Blue Shift" is the second expansion pack for the acclaimed "Half-Life". Offering little new content, it is usually considered a lesser expansion pack than "Half-Life: Opposing Force" - and I've gotta say I understand this. There are no new weapons in "Blue Shift", and no new enemies. Still, it is a fun little game (it has a mere 8 chapters) with quite a lot of interesting easter eggs, a Gordon Freeman sighting near the very beginning and some interesting maps. And let's not forget that it is the first game in the Half-Life series to feature consistent interaction with a single non-player character. This character, as you may know, is Dr. Rosenberg. "Blue Shift" might not be the most exciting Half-Life game, but it sure is a fun and interesting experience, perhaps mostly for Half-Life geeks like myself.

TLDR; Nothing like the Stanley Parable, If you're looking for a goofy game to make you smile, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a game you can burn through in around an hour that will just make you think about the nature of people, give it a shot.
This is a difficult game to descibe. Most of the negative reviews I've seen can be summed up with "bought it cause I liked The Stanley Parable, nothing like Stanley Parable, I hate it." So yes, if you're looking for another Stanley Parable, look elsewhere. This is an entirely different experience that is trying to convey an entirely different thing.
That is not to say that it is bad, no it's just very different. SP was a narrative driven goofy game. You were given instructions, and you obeyed or disobeyed. You made choices and listened to the narrator react to said choices. You always had junctions, forks in the road, choices to make. The fun was making a new one and seeing where it takes you, standing in a closet doing nothing for 5 minutes so you can listen to the narrator get frustrated. There is nothing like that here.
This game has an experience it wants to convey and you're along for the ride. When I finished the game, I just sat in my chair. Listening to the credit music and reading the names. I wasnt clicking or pressing enter or trying to find some way to skip the credits. I just waited, just thought. I dont regret buying this, and I could probably get it refunded considering how short it was. But i'm not.
I just want this game to be here, in my Steam library. The name just occationally catching my eye and making me remember what I experienced. Maybe driving me to reinstall it and play it again in a few weeks or months.
This is barely a review because this is barely a game. It's a story, a book, a movie that you can move in a bit. You dont have choices to make, you follow the narrative, and that's okay. Because at the end, you're left with your thoughts, how you feel about those involved and that's it.
I dont know if Coda is real or not. Since the game isnt free, I cant imagine he is. That does not mean, however, "Coda" didnt have some form of influence.
Is this game just Davey poking at our heads? Being a bit pretentious? A cry for help or big laugh to see how people react?  I dont know. So give it a shot. Take from it what you will and just think about it.

I got this game in a bundle and was excited to try it around Halloween time following the hype around all the cheap jump scares found within.
If you like jump scares, very simple gameplay, and animatronic robots, then you will probably like this game. Note that there have been 2 sequels released, each adding more mechanics to enjoy.
The aesthetics are mediocre - the amount of detail is not very high, however, the nature of the game balances this somewhat (much of the visuals are muddled, dark, and seen through a camera feed). The ambient sounds are decent and add to the tension provoked by the gameplay. There is some voice acting in the beginning of each level, which is well-done and convincingly portrays a co-worker who seems to be oblivious to what actually happens during closing hours. The rationale for the animatronics coming alive and tormenting you is explained nicely.
Controls are super simple and just involve clicking on different areas. The tutorial is provided with the beginning voicemail, which explains everything you need to know. The learning curve is mostly minimal, however, the jump scares seem to be something that deters people from actually progressing.
Gameplay consists of you switching through different camera feeds to keep track of where the animatronics are moving to. You cannot actually watch the robots move, however, you will eventually see them teleport from area to another. There is one room that only has an audio feed. Your character stays in the security office, and you must survive until the morning - if an animatronic makes it inside your room, you will lose. When robots are outside the room, you can close your doors (left and/or right) to prevent entry. A light switch for both sides also allows you to check whether someone is camping outside - using the switch when the door is closed will give off a light at the bottom of the door if no one is there. As time passes, you will lose electricity/energy - every action (cameras, doors, and lights) uses energy, preventing you from simply keeping both security doors closed.
As you progress through the game, more robots will start moving around and the chances of you experiencing a hallucination will increase (these can occur any time the moment you begin playing). The game will try to scare you in numerous ways, primarily through jump scares. One example is a robot appearing right in front of a camera feed when you switch to a random room.
Overall, the game is fun for some cheap jump scares, and if you are into that type of gameplay, then you should definitely give it a try. I try not to mention price if I feel it is unnecessary, but for a few dollars more, you could pick up Five Nights at Freddy's 2 or 3, which I would recommend over this one. Also, I suggest you wait until this game is bundled or discounted, unless you are dying to try it.

Quite good a strategy game. The game description tells pretty much what you get, for once. Definitely a work of art, but not perfect. Nowhere near perfect.
The game introduces little challenge due to the slow rate of operation. At the beginning of the game it can take several hours in real time to build a single building if you have even one problem in your community. (You will have more than one in the beginning) During that time you don't do anything and therefore you don't have any challenge. You do however, later, have a plenty of challenge since you have zero control over reproduction. Sometimes people just won't reproduce, which means extinction of course. Sometimes, the opposite happens and you don't manage to feed even half of them. And since the food isn't distributed evenly, like in real life, way more than half of them will always die. You lose.
You will also have cougghhhhh*some*coughhhhh challenge with the resource production since lacking just a little bit of a single resource will cause your civilization to fall like a house of cards. No iron, no blacksmith. No blacksmith, no tools. No tools, all work seizes. Also, iron production requires tools, so you have a deadlock. You lose again. If you get the iron production up, again, the resources aren't split evenly. Not the iron producers nor the blacksmith will get the first resources but whoever first grabs them. That will be some fatass. And the production seizes, again and again and again. It never gets up again.
Another downside relates to that all building games are graphics based. The view is the game. This is a building game. The animations are Gameboy Color -level. You cannot tell apart whether a character is jacking off or harvesting crop. The visuals are a disaster. The overall graphics look like the game was published in the 1990's.
And, there's little content. After the beginning, when you have built houses and food production, there's almost nothing more to be done. You can have schools and a hospital, but it's pretty much over right after the beginning.
Certainly many people like this. But this is not what I expect from a game. Therefore, I do not recommend.

The Long Dark is beautiful and the sound and atmosphere is great. And for once in a survival game, no zombies in sight! I really wanted to like The Long Dark, but to be honest, it's a bit boring. Your character moves frustratingly slow even when at full health/rest, and after a while you tire of walking for 7 minutes just to get over a lake.The need to constantly use matches and lanterns the second you move inside buildings dont really add to the experience and only works as an distraction from the exploration. The exploration in question is good, the vast landscape and harsh winds look and souds legit and all buildings are  interesting places that tells little stories of their own.
In terms of gameplay, the main objective is to stay alive as long as possible. The survival mechanics, gathering food, staying warm and rested etc works ok but there is nothing really exceptional about it, if you have played a survival game before you know the drill. Most mechanics are bland at best but some are downright annoying, like the extremely slow walking speed, or the fact that you break your legs from even looking at a cliff. Wolfs are the only real threat (if you don't count in the environment itself) and pose little challenge overall. Combat rarely occurs and that would be a good thing since it feels so clunky.
There is simply a big feeling of something missing in this game, the gameplay is just too boring to motivate more than a few hours of exploration, when you have the area mapped out and all cottages have been scavanged interest soon starts to fade.

**** EARLY ACCESS REVIEW ****
Let me start off by saying that the concept behind Project Zomboid is a very very promising one. If the developers take the proper route in configuring the UI, Multiplayer, and Gameplay aspects of the game, then Zomboid has the potential to be the most challenging and deepest zombie survival game out there. Overall, I do not regret buying this game even in Early Alpha.
The Good:
-Great soundtrack and tone selection.
-Focuses on survival (while combat is necessary, the game encourages you to avoid it)
-Deep crafting mechanics
-Insanely good AI. (fire a gun and zombies will hear it and will come after you)
The Bad: (note that if these are fixed, the game is going to be so awesome)
-Clunky UI (especially when it comes to switching bags and weapons)
-Crafting mechanics though deep, are still raw
-Tutorials are not that informative
-Skills are not yet clear to their corresponding benefits.
The Potential:
-The game can be a very fun multiplayer survival game if they add saved progression and alternating difficulty levels
-The game can offer an even better multiplayer experience if they introduce community and community vs community mechanics (like walking dead)
-The game can be a very fun survival or sandbox single player experience if they fix the UI, improve crafting and polish gameplay.
-I would suggest putting random events on the game just to spice it up.
Overall, great game and I'm very hopeful. Looking forward to the finished product.

Carmageddon: Max Damage is the true reincarnation of Carmageddon and even more: all the performance issues are now gone, the mediocre graphics are polished up and additional content is available resulting in a great Carmageddon game.
The levels are grand, full of exploration and filled with all kinds of funky pedestrains and animals for you to squash. The opponents are racing and fighting all over the place. Depending on the way you play races can be over in about 2 mintues or take more than 30 minutes.
There are several distinct game modes, a ton of different levels and even more vehicles of which each has a unique feel. In my opinion the handling of the vehicles is fine but don't expect a racing game type of grip and be prepared to get used to the different cars. The vehicles need to be stolen during races and their capabilities upgraded (via a very simple system). Upgrading requires the collection of upgrade tokens which are scattered throughout the maps. New stages are unlocked once enough points are obtained. The varied powerups and funny puns make completing the stages a great and very addicting experience.
Now that the performance and graphical issues are finally addressed I can only name a few minor gripes: the camera can sometimes be annoying, depending on the game mode and the stage the AI can be a little bit too stupid (sometimes it is very easy to win Fox and Hounds) and the menu interface help stuff sometimes gets in the way (why does it need to repeatedly show me new stages resulting in me starting the wrong race with the wrong and underpowered car?). An ETA for the Linux and Mac versions would also be nice.
Considering its price this game is a steal. Since it is part of gaming history and the numerous educational purposes I will use my government ties to make the game part of the elementary school curriculum.

I had just finished raiding the lower dam. My rucksack full of loot, I opened a door that led outside from the depths of the dam. I took a glance down and around the ravine, didn't see anything useful, and returned to the door... but it wouldn't open from this side. I was then presented with two options. Attempt to cross a narrow ridge and risk a near certain fall to get across the ravine to an entrance to reenter the dam that may or may not even be there, or descend down into the ravine and follow the frozen river. I chose the later. What followed was a disoriented drudge through tall ravine walls and finally a labyrinthian cave that sent shivers up my spine every time I stepped into the dark. I finally emerged from the caves into a moonlit forest being ravaged by a blizzard. To my dread I could hear the yips and howls of wolves in the distance.
This is what I enjoy about the Long Dark. It will throw you curve balls and it requires you to think on your feet and weigh desicions one of which may be life (at least for a while) and the other may be death. You don't really know what's coming next.
Say you're looking for shelter. Do you stay in the dam and risk dealing with any threats that may dwell within to access all those glorious resources? Or maybe the Trapper's Homestead near replenishable natural resources, but far from anything else? Perhaps Signal Hill with a fence to keep out ravenous predators, but beaing secluded on a lonely peak?
Say you're confronted with a wolf. Do you fire your one remaining .303 round and risk a miss? Throw a flare and lose your only remaining light source? Spare a chunk of meat for a decoy and go hungry yourself? Run and hope for the best?
I highly recommed the twisting, turning journey toward inevitable death that is The Long Dark.

Red Orchestra 2... What is there to say? It is a hidden gem, I'll tell you that much now, but let's get into the actual review though, shall we?
First off, let me say one thing. This game is not a casual experience. You don't simply turn it on and do well your first time, nor your second time, or a hundred times after. You will, in the beginning, die a lot. Often times, you will not even know who killed you! Sometimes, you will spend more time waiting to be respawned than in the actual game itself! But do not be discouraged, this is only a very temporary state, as you will, over time, learn which places to avoid, how to control your gun, and memorize popular enemy hangout spots.
If you are used to games like Battlefield or Call of Duty, you will hit a vertical wall. This isn't just a learning curve, this is a 90 degree vertical brick wall. Don't expect to do well, probably not even if you are a hardcore fan of ArmA, instead, expect to die very often, and expect to be at the bottom of the scoreboard.
The gameplay consists of your classic FPS features, you get to crouch down, aim down sights, go prone, switch fire modes on certain firearms, and of course, you get to shoot your gun. However, there is a feature that isn't common in the FPS market, there is a full cover system for most objects on the map, though I strongly recommend NOT using the cover system, and instead crouching behind high cover when necessary.
There are multiple gamemodes, by now, only one is being played by the majority of remaining players, and that is territory control. Those familiar with Battlefield's "conquest" will know exactly what this is, just add the fact that one team is attacking while the other is defending. The team which has more people in one point captures it.
You will spend most of your time sitting behind cover, or slowly creeping around tight hallways with your teammates, and that there is an EXTREMELY crucial note, with your teammates. A team is extremely important, you simply CANNOT rush through enemy lines like John Rambo anymore. In this game, you are a pawn, listen to your squad leader/commander, and stick close to your team, that's it.
Guns behave very differently from weapons you find in Battlefield, and even more differently than Call of Duty weaponry. These weapons have recoil, and that recoil must be managed. No more full-auto spraying accross the whole map, no, burst fire, semi-automatic, and bolt-action rule this game.
Rifles are, by far, some of the strongest weapons in the game. Each has a five round magazine and must be manually bolted. These rifles are very accurate, but they severely lack in rate of fire. Most people will be seen with bolt-action rifles, just like in WW2.
Sub-machineguns (SMGs) are, by far, the best weapons in the game. If you can manage the recoil of the Russian PPsH-41, or the kick of the Mkb 42, you can kill just about anybody at any range with a precise hit to the chest. SMGs are, however, limited in this game, as only a few lucky individuals can claim the assault class, and be blessed with these gems. SMGs are NOT intended for fully automatic fire unless you are in a tight, small hallway. Always fire in bursts, or even better, use them like you would a semi-automatic rifle.
Semi-automatic rifles are the weapons of Elite Riflemen, once again, they are limited to a few players per-team. In the hands of a marksman, these weapons are devastating from a long range.
LMGs are surprisingly good weapons for long ranges, if they are in a stationary position, that is. Use them wisely, and always let more experienced players take the machinegunner position, as it is a great responsibility.
Remember, all of us die, even the best of players can have bad days. Stick to high cover, never run accross open fields, stick close to your team, move from cover-to-cover, and use your weapons wisely... In Red Orchestra 2, every rifleman counts. In the hands of a good commander, even a team of inexperienced players can achieve victory!

Barrier X is raw arcade twitch at it's very essence. If you are looking for a game to absorb your attention and require you think of nothing but using your skill to win, this game is perfect. Buy this if you live for Super Hexagon or AAAAaaaaaAAAAAaaaaa's frantic dodging.
Unlike a number of other cheap avoidance racing games, Barrier X avoids the major pitfalls of the genre. Whilst the learning curve is rough, it's rough in the style of a tough arcade game, not rough in the sense of a bad game. The relative shortness of the levels is made up for by focusing on mastering just a few skills, and the reliance on replay to, as the kids put it, 'git gud'. The obstacles to avoid are big and clear, and the action required to avoid them works consistently. There is adequate forewarning of obstacles, including on the horizon, so planning (albeit autonomous twitch flow planning) is possible. The addition of Blue and Green arrows actually works well, as the recovery mechanic they introduce actually extends your play options.  The soundtrack is minimalist, but works well, and more importantly, it feels appropriately paced for the levels.
There are two flaws with Barrier X. The first is an occasional pop-up between runs asking players to check out their next game. Indie devs have it extremely rough, so I can forgive that, especially since it vanished after I clicked on the Call To Action. The second flaw is the shooting the opponent mechanic, which I never quite figured out (beyond occasionally pressing the button).
All in all, I am very happy with this purchase, and it has received a significant amount of playtime. If there were more challenges and more background music options, I would easily play it for much longer still.

Plasmids are your "magic powers" and use EVE with every use. Tonics are upgrades to your body that change certain attributes, but have limited slots, and at times need to be swapped out. You can add more slots for tonics and plasmids, as well as upgrade and buy them with ADAM. The guns in the game have multiple ammo types for different enemies, and can be upgraded at certain stations that will shut down after one use.

To all the negative review due to launch-issues: This game is being made by two people. Just two young people trying to create something. And it is their first project. So give them some slack. Especially since this is an early access.
Was it mistake to not consider the option of more people buying than expecting? Yes, yes, it was. But I have been a tester of the alpha for over a month and if I can say anything about the developers is that they are definitely trying hard to constantly improve. Unlike in other titles where the developers eventually stop doing that. So I recommend you to just be patient. Another one or two days and it's gonna run smoothly. the game really is worth it.
.
Now to the game itself. As someone who grew up with Warcraft 3 and essentially bought it for the custom maps when a friend recommendet it to me, I have to say this game is a LOT of fun. The 100 hours of playtime within a month should tell you the whole story of how addicting it is. It works, it's constantly being balanced, the gameplay is fun, the graphics are ok (obviously not some mindblowing stuff, but they do it's job), the reconnect feature works perfect (unlike for the Blizzard title Hearthstone) and the creators are wanting to keep improving the game. And the bots are pretty decent as well to play against at the beginning and get used to the game.
The criticism I have on this game is purely based on small things such as an improvement of the menus, a pause feature would be nice and other such smaller things that are more for the level of comfort rather than the actual gameplay.
To give it an actual rating with numbers.
Gameplay: 9,5/10
The gameplay is still as addicting as it was during the times this was a custom map in Warcraft 3. It is fun, unique and creative. It is teambased. It is easy to learn and hard to master. And it will become even better if more content is added to the game eventually.
General features, complexity and extent of the game: 6,5/10
This is still just the very core of the game. Thus there are no additional gamemodes and other such features to give the game more complexity. Still this is an early access-title, so we will see and hope those new features and gamemodes will eventually be added.
Graphics: 7/10
This naturally does not have the graphics of a millions-of-dollars game. It is ridiculous to expect that. The graphics in comparision look outdated. But they are smooth, pleasant to watch at and do it's job to give the great gameplay a platform. Additionally the game provides a wide variety of settings for the graphics which is always a plus that you can costumize your needs and adjust to your computers performance.
Sound: 7,5/10
The ingame sound loop is pretty good and that alone definitely deserves a higher rating. It is quite difficult to create a loop that is pleasant and not annoying you after a few minutes (or hours) of gameplay. The developers managed to do that.
Unfortunately the other sounds of the game can't fully keep up with that quality. They aren't bad, they are clear, but they are simply generic. They do their job and what they are intended to do, but they don't stand out.
Overall Score: 8/10
I give it 8 of 10 points, because I value the gameplay rating twice as much as the others. At the end a game is meant to entertain you and be fun. The graphics, sound and feature-list are just meant to build up on given gameplay fun already, but not to create it. Thus 8/10 is a reasonable rating with a good chance of improving by 0,5 to 1 points if the developers keep improving the game at the pace they did previously.
That being said, they need to fix the servers-issues within a reasonable time for the gameplay to be as fun as it is. I am confident about it, but for people interested in buying the game I will recommend you to wait another day or two until it runs smoothly. From my personal experience of playing this game the wait is absolutely worth it.

I wasn't sure what to expect going into Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock, but I will say, I was very pleasantly surprised by this title.
I'm a fan of the Point & Click genre in general.  If you've played a few games in the genre, you know what to expect; you'll wander around, collect some items, try to combine them in logical ways, and when that doesn't work, try to combine them with anything interactable.  You might encounter some logical leaps, or other mini-puzzles along the way.  If that's not for you, stay away from this title.
There's lots of this type of game available on Steam, though, so how does this one in particular stack up?
In my opinion?  Very well!
First, the atmosphere is spot on.  A sand-covered world filled with scraps of twisted metal, weird alien structures, and the corpses of the unfortunate, Deadrock gives just the right amount of sci-fi macabre I'd expect from the title.  Add in a handful of really great-looking cinematics, and you've got yourself a nice little experience.
Another major plus is the banter between your hero, and Novak, an injured smart-alec captain who serves as your point-of-contact during your exploration.  Major props to his voice actor, who got a lot more chuckles out of me than I'd expect from a game like this.
The adventure is a short one, and falls a bit on the easy side.  However, one of the reasons the game feels easy is because all of the puzzles feel like they make perfect sense, which is SO refreshing.
There's no BS acheivement hunting in this game; what you see is what you get, and completing the title will earn you 100%.  And that 100% will be all the sweeter because the ending of this game is without a doubt extremely satisfying.  This is definitely worth a playthrough.

Sunless Sea has a nice atmosphere and a good soundtrack, It's basically an exploration and trade game, with a very very slow pace. Someone would say 'relaxing' and I agree only in part.
I'm 16 hours in, but at this point I don't know if I'm going to finish it, here's why:
1- the trading mechanic could have been much better.
What you need to do to obtain stuff, or lose terror, or follow the objectives can be very confusing most of the time, unless you can spend hours and hours in the game to better understand and map the logic of all the trades. IMHO most of the problems could have been solved at UI level with a better color codes, categorizations and grouping of the stuff and stats etc.
2- it really has too much text in it, at least for my tastes. At some point I just skip all the text just to see what's my gain and lose stat of the quest, So I miss all the story and the involvement, which is a shame for a game like this.
3- And this is a big one for me: slow pace = no fast travel or faster speed or faster boat. This is the one I read about and I wanted to try it in person, and I agree with others, this is a big problem.
Don't get me wrong, It is awesome to have a big map, but at some point in the game you spend so much time just watching the small boat doing nothing that you start doing other stuff while gaming or just asking yourself 'what am I doing with my life?'.
It's ridiculous and it gets worst if you lose some of the crew to go at max speed, it's just not challenging, not entertaining or engaging anymore, just plain boring.
I can think of dozen ways this problem could have been sorted out, so I guess it's a design choice, but a bad one if you ask me.
In the end, I still recommend this game because it can be enjoyable for the first 10-15 hours, and because of the effort, just be aware of this problems.

Then again, story mode has not been released yet and I've been wondering the woods helplessly trying not to get killed by wolves and the occasional bear.
Besides the lack of spark and backstory, the game's originality is amazing. For that, Hinderland Studio's The Long Dark get's an 5/5. How many other survival games are out there? Okay a lot. But nobody has done it like Hinderland Studios.
I will be updating this review when the story mode is released. Until then, I will still recommend you purchase this game. You will keep yourself entertained, and at $20, it's not that much of a gamble.

I had left a review here long ago, while the game was still in early access. That review is of course outdated and no longer reflected my opinions on the game, or the game itself, as it has evolved since then.
A survival game. It's not like Rust or Ark or the like. You're not pitted against zombies or other players or the week's wipe. Instead, its just you, the cold, and what wildlife remains. There's two modes: Wintermute, which is story built narrative, and Survivor mode, which is just pure survival sandbox.
Sandbox is complete in the sense that there is nothing missing, per se. That is to say it is 100% fun and playable in its current state. The game may have hit 1.0 release, but updates are still slated to come. As of this writing, the moose is on the way in the next update, slated for December 2017. The sandbox is fully functional and will provide you with countless hours of fun and butt clenching moments. The world is at your fingertips. Four difficulty modes provide a range of playstyles to appeal to both casual gamers and hardcore masochists alike. Each mode tunes such variables as weather conditions, ambient temperature, wildlife hostility and ubiquity, and loot tables. Crafting is available for you in case you can't find the right item. Just make it instead.
Despite the original premise for the game being story mode, and its long awaited arrival, it has left a bad taste in many people's mouths. Why? For most players, me included, the first episode is basically a walking tutorial of everything you've mastered in the myriad of hours you've invested in sandbox. Granted, it does set up the narrative for the rest of the story, which will be important as each episode is played, but its quite... boring really. The second episode tries to spice it up some, but still has you running basic fetch quests to learn about the game systems. This is good for players who have never played before, but for veterans like me it is simply busy work as we want to advance the narrative.
The studio is small. This is both good and bad, in a way. But this is the bad section, so we'll cover the bad. Their size hinders their progress because they have two babies: Story Mode and Sandbox: Each one cries loudly for attention. It can be argued that most players here want more sandbox updates and don't give a hoot about story. But equally so, the game was funded in the hopes of story mode, and it must see its course through. Thus, the studio must invest time in both modes until the point in time story mode is completed.
This is where each person's opinion comes in. There are certain mechanics about the game that some love, and others hate with a passion. Ages ago, Hinterland had a leaderboard to showcase those who survived the longest. Abusing in game mechanics, it was possible to 'hibernate' in order to use a minimal ammount of supplies in order to skate by weeks, if not months, of in game time. Hinterland's solution? Cabin Fever. This affliction is tuned a tad bit different for each mode but stays the same more or less. Stay inside too long, and the walls make you go crazy. So crazy you're willing to freeze to death in the tundra because you can't rest indoors.
Interior lighting. This bloody thing has been adjusted about 10000 times, and there are countless forum posts praising or bemoaning it. Hinterland has attempted to create a lighting engine that fits each interior location, but for reasons of some sort, the original system left interiors far too dark during full daytime hours. This has been adjusted time and again, and as of this writing, we haven't seen the last adjustment yet. You'd think it wouldn't be too hard to hammer this down, but then again, crafting such a game and engine from scratch is difficult water. The lighting in its current state is indeed passable, although sometimes annoying.
Again, this will ultimately come down to personal opinion. I for one would say BUY!!! But I encourage you to do your research first. If you want some idea of gameplay, both sandbox and story mode, check out my channel here:
(Shameless plug. I know.) I for one find the game's atmosphere the most compelling thing. It evokes emotions I cannot lay words on. The unique graphic style, the setting, and the audio and music all make for something impressive. If you enjoy a survival experience where its just you versus nature, this is certainly for you. While I can't say everyone will enjoy it, those who appreciate forging their own path and admiring the journey while smashing wolves with a hammer will find no greater joy than The Long Dark.

I really don't understand all the hype with Carmageddon and why so many people have nostalgia for it after all this time. I vaguely remember playing the really old ones when I was a kid, and looking back at videos/screenshots of it, it doesn't seem that great. Any newer attempt at a Carmageddon game just seems... weak.
The idea behind these games are good, but they are always executed so badly. The handling of cars in this game is absolutely AWFUL. They don't feel even remotely driveable. Honestly, it feels like there are a lot of other companies that could make this game much better.
Bugbear for example would be able to do wonders if they made a game like Flatout: Ultimate Carnage, and then added all the Carmageddon parts into it.
The tracks in this game are awfully designed, the environments suck and just feel like everything has been plastered anywhere they felt like. I get that a city would have people in it, but a person just standing in the middle of the street is stupid. Cows and penguins walking around those city streets? Even more stupid.
This game really would work so much better if they toned down all the gimics and tried to make a race that was actually like a death race. A massive A to B race with multiple routes, WAAAAAY more cars (seriously? 6?), had multiple people in places that seemed logical and mostly FIX THE HANDLING!
Don't recommend for now. This feels too half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
That said, I am still going to continue playing as frankly I'm not one to give up on a game.
EDIT: After playing more, I recommend this game even less. AI is AWFUL! They will get practically attached to you, constantly ramming you and ignoring everything else. Won't back up, won't give you any space to get away. They just constantly try and push you around and it complete stops you doing anything unless you waste points doing a reset.
Also the game won't re-pick up Xbox 360 controls once it loses them for whatever reason. If you have to alt-tab to desktop (full screened or windowed mode) and then you return using the mouse, it will change the control type to mouse/keyboard and can't get the controller controls back.
Lastly, the game keeps crashing every 30 mintues or so. Very badly done. REALLY don't recommend.
Lastly, at time of writing this, the game advertises trading cards but actually DOES NOT have any.

Out of all of the vehicles I have unlocked (missing only 1), about 2/3 are plagued with 'bacon grease on the wheels' in that the creators relied too heavily on simplified physics from their physics engine to dictate how cars move.
Try turning a corner at 5MPH and watch your car slide forward as though your front wheels didnt exist. Drive on a 5% angle and watch your car slide down as though friction didnt exist.
Take the 'Subpressor' for instance. Its a large vehicle with significant acceleration, which would likely mean it has great traction right? I mean, if it can accelerate quickly without just spinning tires it should have great traction. Start it off at a slow crawl, then apply the handbrake. hold it down, in fact and you will continue to roll as if there are no brakes at all. try turning at this low speed and you'll see your front wheels turning sharply but your vehicle keeps right on crawling forward.
There is a tracked vehicle in game with 3 sets of very wide tracks. On concrete it does poorly, which might be due to steel tracks on concrete or something. On dirt you'd think it'd do great, being tracked and all, large surface area on the ground. Nope, you fishtail out of control even at the slowest speeds.
Oh, and it has some bizarre mariokart-esque steering wobble. Imagine youre in mariokart and hit a banana. Remember how your cart would wobble side to side? This game forces you to ride out the wobble or stop. No steering correction for you! Nope, you just gotta let the car finish its wobbling.
Upgrades are collected throughout gameplay and can be spent on any car, but if you spend it on a car, you cannot downgrade that car and use it elsewhere. So if there are 4 additional ranks to each of the 3 upgradable trees for each vehicle and there are 32 vehicles, you need to collect *384* upgrades. Of which you can only find 3 or so per race and they do not reappear for subsequent runs of the same race. You will never be able to upgrade your vehicles fully and the upgrades that you have bought in early levels are likely completely wasted and later awesome vehicles you unlock will not have nearly any upgrades left to use on them.
Only one type of race will allow you the time to look for and collect the upgrades as needed. The others all require you to drive from A-B as quickly as possible or to destroy the opponents' vehicles. So you had better hope you can collect the 3 or so upgrades in that one racemode per track.
Police will target you and you alone. If you♥♥♥♥♥♥one off, it will pursue you relentlessly across the map, even if you 'recover' yourself back across teh entire track, the police will get to you without even seeing where you went and will continue to attack.
In A-B race modes, some of the lower level vehicles are dedicated to targetting you and have a lesser goal of going after the objective. Each vehicle has a specific 'role' to play whether it is an antagonizer or a goal-getter.
Edit:
The camera is also quite nauseating. Either it doesnt turn around when you are trying to back up OR it spins around to face the rear when you put on brakes BUT ARE STILL GOING FORWARD. There are some lockets or something that are collectable ingame but nothing is reflected in gameplay menus as to what they are or where they are used

Please note that I have not yet had a chanse to play the upcoming story mode. This review only deals with the sanbox mode.
The Long Dark is beautiful and the sound and atmosphere is great. And for once in a survival game, no zombies in sight! I really wanted to like The Long Dark, but to be honest, it's a bit boring. Your character moves frustratingly slow even when at full health/rest, and after a while you tire of walking for 7 minutes just to get over a lake.The need to constantly use matches and lanterns the second you move inside buildings dont really add to the experience and only works as an distraction from the exploration. The exploration in question is good, the vast landscape and harsh winds look and souds legit and all buildings are  interesting places that tells little stories of their own.
In terms of gameplay, the main objective is to stay alive as long as possible. The survival mechanics, gathering food, staying warm and rested etc works ok but there is nothing really exceptional about it, if you have played a survival game before you know the drill. Most mechanics are bland at best but some are downright annoying, like the extremely slow walking speed, or the fact that you break your legs from even looking at a cliff. Wolfs are the only real threat (if you don't count in the environment itself) and pose little challenge overall. Combat rarely occurs and that would be a good thing since it feels so clunky.
There is simply a big feeling of something missing in this game, the gameplay is just too boring to motivate more than a few hours of exploration, when you have the area mapped out and all cottages have been scavanged interest soon starts to fade.
Dont buy this if you hate good games.

Game: Limbo
Developer and publisher: Playdead
Released: 3 August, 2011
Genre: Side-Scrolling Platformer Puzzler
Setting: Limbo
Spoiler-free plot summary: "Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters Limbo".
Full review: Limbo is a very simple puzzle game in a few ways; simple story premise, simple art style, and simple environments. The "puzzles" however... oh dear...
Many praise Limbo for its very simplistic art-style, which, considering where Limbo is set, is very suitable. It's also easy on the eyes, and doesn't distract from playing the game.
However, what they don't tell you is that the puzzles are excruciatingly hard. And I say "puzzles" when in fact 3/4 of them are time-based events, which, if you're NANOSECONDS off, you'll fail and die and have to retry the puzzle over and over and over again until RNGesus bestows luck on your reflexes.
Another puzzle actually requires you to discover a secret area quite a while before it too, so you'd never be able to solve the puzzle if you never thought of backtracking or didn't expect to explore in a non-exploring, linear game.
After you beat the game and have collected all ten secret eggs, a secret level unlocks, and if you're deaf or hard of hearing like I am, then you can wave good-bye to your chances of unlocking all achievements, because the secret level requires good hearing and guess work because 95% of the level is pitch black! Luckily for me I eventually found a pattern in one area I had trouble with and ran on through without dying for the seventh time.
Do I recommend buying Limbo? Hell no (no pun intended). Limbo has got to be one of the worst experiences with a video-game I've ever had, along with Daikatana, Deus Ex: Invisible War, Duke Nukem Forever, and
.
For a calmer, more specific review, you can read Steam user Kryyss's review
.

Bioshock has an absolutley riveting storyline. The backstory of the protagonist, the city and its inhabitants were very well developed. The soundtrack and voice-acting was also spot on, lending a industrial american dystopia atmosphere to the city. This combined with the fact that the protagonist discovers the secrets of the city alongside you, results in a very immersive gaming experience which further accentuate the plots and back stories. However, the most brilliant part of the entire story and the entire game, was the plot twist (or twists). When all is revealed, you will finally witness the full glory that is this masterpiece of a storyline. The only let-down was at the very end, when all has been divulged and you just had to go through the motions to a cliche happy ending.
As for actual gameplay, it was pretty scary and fun in the beggining when you still don't know what to do. During this time, I truly felt that I was fighting for my life, perpetually being on the verge of death with limited ammo, money and health kits. Choices also had to be made, like should I fight that big daddy to buy more upgrades, or should I enter that room where I may be ambushed or there might be more ammo. New types of guns and "spells" are also slowly introduced throughout the game, keeping gameplay relatively fresh.  However, in the later parts of the game, you can become virtually invincible with the right upgrades, and gameplay starts to get stale. As a result, the final boss fight was a little anti-climatic with it being just hard instead of epicly hard.

This game definltey leans back to the days of the old point-and-click games, and that's a good thing. You can get a few hours out of this game, and none of it is particularly difficult. Showing a lot of love from the old-school point-and-click days, all of the backgrounds appear to be hand-painted, which only adds charm as far as I'm concerned. The inventory system is easy to use and you'll need to drag some items onto another item to create a new item. Not all of these combinations are obvious, so you might end up trying a few things; but none of it leads to frustration.
The story itself isn't bad, but it feels like a lot of disjointed ideas that are thrown together. For example, one area shows an alien that's been stabbed to death in a hidden room and supposedly the body is still warm, meaning that it's a very recent murder. Nothing of this situation is ever resolved. The alien is never identified, the murderer is never revealed, the reason for the murder is never established, and there is nothing to link it with the rest of the story anyway. So, why bother introducing them in the first place? Also, human technology just so happens to be compatible with alien technology. That's quite a coincidence.
What made this game difficult to get through was the voice acting. Oh, dear God! It's by no means the worst I've ever heard, but that's not saying much. It's bad! "Reading lines while utterly bored" might be more appropriate.
Still, the artwork, the semblance of a story, and the throwback to the days of classic point-and-click gaming made this worth playing. You might want to turn the speech off, though.

FlatOut 2 takes me back to the days of playing the scaled-down version on the PSP. It's the same fun game, but with beefed-up graphics and an insanely smooth frame-rate. Like with just about every old game I own, I search for ways to increase the graphics past what's available in the game settings. The game looks great on its own (My goodness.. has it stood the test of time!) but with some added ambient occlusion (HBAO+ via Nvidia Inspector, flag: 0x0000001F) and brute-force anti-aliasing (SGSSAA via Nvidia Inspector, no flag needed), FlatOut 2's age is significantly less noticeable. I'm aware of the better graphics in Ultimate Carnage, but there's something in FlatOut 2's gameplay that I like better. The gameplay feels identical to Head On on the PSP which is what I'm used to. Just one flaw I can think of (not a big one) is the lack of buttons you can map to a gamepad. I used Xpadder to map the last few buttons to my DualShock 4 such as Esc, Enter and arrows keys (to navigate the menu and pause the game). Awesome, fast-paced game. I recommend. Ignore my play time on Steam. I used to play a pirated copy when built my first PC in 2010. I just decided to buy it today because... 2 bucks.
EDIT: Idk if this applies for everyone, but for G-Sync users, there is noticeable motion jittering when the frame-rate isn't locked at 50 or at the default limit, 100. Any frame-rate that isn't a steady 50 or steady 100 will make motion look ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Ehh.. most people probably don't notice. I notice, but that's because I'm a smooth gameplay junkie. I had some fun playing Sunless Sea. That said, there's definitely a few issues that crop up if you're not prepared. Essentially, you can't really make money on trade routes. You'll basically only make money from storylines. This is something of an issue to a lot of people, because there's a lot of storylines/quests that require a significant monetary investment.
As far as I can tell, the idea here is that it's possible to make more money by being a bad person. Because there's a somewhat limited total amount of easily accessible money to earn, trying to be a good person involves making real sacrifices on which storylines you can complete in what manner (or at all), or committing to a large amount of fairly tedious work. In contrast, being an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will get you enough resources to do most of the things you want/unlock some really interesting storylines very quickly, but it comes at the cost of being evil.

Pros:
Cons:
The game has this awesome concept of exploring this underworld ocean as a ZEE(sea) faring captain. You trade, explore, advance the personal stories and adventures of people you meet/hire.
It sounds really good but the tedious trading system, will eventually exhaust any interest you had in this game world. After a lot of grinding, I finally completed the game under the "retire to a life of luxuary condition".
The game is not about combat. If you keep fighting pirates or ZEE monsters, you will lose money and waste time. So I almost always avoided fights, until I got better weapons about 30+ hours into the game. And even then, it was just for the fun of it. So combat can be just about entirely avoided.
As for the story, you basically unravel this by choosing dialogue options at the port.
They are not narrated and consists of texts of dialogue you have with the locals or special someone at the respective ports. You usually do errands for them. It's funny and interesting but not that great. Much of the world is left unexplained so a bit disappointing there.
And finally we have the trade system. You basically buy one resource from one port,
and sell it at another port for a measley profit. It's here that the game is ultimately let down.
The game simply doesn't have all too many trading options for you.
So you are left repeating a very few trades over and over again to make money.
You do get some compensations at your home base(Fallen London) for your travel expenses,
for exploring the world and gathering information for the empire, but it's not enough to
reduce the grind.
There are however two special trade routes you can make that give you a ton of cash, but
it feels cheap and are limited(can repeat them about 4-5 times).
It really seems like the designers themselves were aware that the trade system is weak
so they gave you a few secret ways of making much more money to compensate.
It's such a shame because the world here is really intriguing and the artwork is amazing as well.
In conclusion, I would give this a 2/5.
I could just about recommened this because I don't know of any other game like this.
And because the world concept here is really awesome and all, but really you are just going to find yourself feeling really annoyed by how much grinding you have to do.
So I say avoid it. Hope this review helped :)

I bought this as part of a bundle...I checked out the individual bits and thought "this looks OK", because it reminded me of playing something similar called "Locomotion" on the 8-bit ZX Spectrum 48k.
The music is simple, the graphics are nicely done, but the gameplay is solid.  This is definitely a game that - if you like your puzzles, especially those with a time pressure element to them - you'll enjoy this.
What starts off simple with just one train and two stations to drive between and make money, rapidly becomes more stations (and more trains), but you can always dial up the risk and earning potential by scheduling more trains, expanding between stations and seeing just how far you can push things with multiple trains on the tracks.
All the while, the clock ticks along and you see buildings and factories pop up around your stations as you get more money coming in, leading to more valuable cargoes to carry.
The beauty of it is, you don't automatically lose just because you crashed a train (or ten), you can just as easily go bust because you overextended youself by building too much and blew through too much cash.  Therefore, you need to balance your train schedules (earning money) against burning it.
For anyone who ever played with train sets as a kid (esp. Hornby) or still does, you'll most likely love it.  For anyone who wants a good, solid 'build, maintain and expand' sort of game, it gets my vote.
10/10 makes me want to go back in time to get a job at British Rail and show them how to really run things properly.

Game: Limbo
Developer and publisher: Playdead
Released: 3 August, 2011
Genre: Side-Scrolling Platformer Puzzler
Setting: Limbo
Spoiler-free plot summary: "Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters Limbo".
Full review: Limbo is a very simple puzzle game in a few ways; simple story premise, simple art style, and simple environments. The "puzzles" however... oh dear...
Many praise Limbo for its very simplistic art-style, which, considering where Limbo is set, is very suitable. It's also easy on the eyes, and doesn't distract from playing the game.
However, what they don't tell you is that the puzzles are excruciatingly hard. And I say "puzzles" when in fact 3/4 of them are time-based events, which, if you're NANOSECONDS off, you'll fail and die and have to retry the puzzle over and over and over again until RNGesus bestows luck on your reflexes.
Another puzzle actually requires you to discover a secret area quite a while before it too, so you'd never be able to solve the puzzle if you never thought of backtracking or didn't expect to explore in a non-exploring, linear game.
After you beat the game and have collected all ten secret eggs, a secret level unlocks, and if you're deaf or hard of hearing like I am, then you can wave good-bye to your chances of unlocking all achievements, because the secret level requires good hearing and guess work because 95% of the level is pitch black! Luckily for me I eventually found a pattern in one area I had trouble with and ran on through without dying for the seventh time.
Do I recommend buying Limbo? Hell no (no pun intended). Limbo has got to be one of the worst experiences with a video-game I've ever had, along with Daikatana, Deus Ex: Invisible War, Duke Nukem Forever, and
.

Quick Description: Legion TD 2 is a team-based tower defense (TD) game. As in any TD game, you place units in a fixed formation to defend against waves of monsters. What units you have available depends on your selected "legion", and tend to follow a visual and strategic theme.
Thoughts: The core mechanics of Legion TD 2 are solid, but the game is currently unpolished. Little details sometimes make this game frustrating to play, like the fact that you can't view a unit's upgrade path during a wave. That being said, I find great satisfaction in clearing a wave before your comrades, or in finding the enemy defenders insufficient to hold back the tide of monsters.
Recommendations for developers:
- Training and information: it's difficult right now to learn the subtle mechanics of the game, or the strengths/weaknessesof a legion. Videos and tutorials would be awesome when you have time.
- Allow players to see the upgrade paths for a selected unit outside of the night phase.

I've had this game in my library for a while.  I bought it back when I was looking for a Terraria-esque game, and either Starbound wasn't out yet, or I hadn't discovered it.
It seemed VERY promising at first.  So, I decided to put it on hold and come back once a few updates had been released for it.  Unfortunately, by the time I did come back...the developers had pretty much abandoned the game.
Now, that's not the only problem - the other problem is that you gather resources too slowly; now, you could make that argument about Terraria or Starbound, but there's a difference: in those game, it's it was slow at first because you needed to update your tools; and over time, you upgraded your tools, reducing the time it takes to gather resources.  Not to mention that they gave you other stuff to do in the meantime, like quests, boss battles, or exploring dungeons.  Here, it's because the things you need to upgrade are too hard to find.  It takes WAY too long to make something like a house - in Terraria, you can have a simple house up by nightfall; in Starbound, it's a bit longer if you decide to build a base on a planet instead of your ship, but it's still completable in a reasonable amount of time; in this game? ...You'll be lucky if you're even done with a quarter of the house by that time.
Even then, the other problem is that...well, once you get past the tutorial, it's empty.  There's nothing obvious for you to do.  This is because of the lack of an NPC to give you hints like in Terraria or a quest system like in Stardew Valley.  At that point, it feels like a 2D Version of No Man's Sky, minus the ability to go to other planets (to be fair though, at least this game doesn't cost nearly as much as NMS).
It's a pity that this game is now abandonware, since it does have some good ideas - I like the power system idea, since it makes you plan out your base; also, the research system is a good idea in theory (although in execution, it fails).
If the developers ever decide to pick this game back up and start updating it again, I might give it a second shot, but at the moment, I cannot recommend this game.
If you're contemplating buying this game, I would suggest passing on it and instead picking up Terraria, which does the idea of a 2d Sandbox game a lot better (not to mention it's cheaper); but if the sci-fi element is a must for you, go for Starbound instead, since while the worlds in that game aren't as big as the worlds in this game, the rest of the content more than makes up for that.

Probably my favourite of the original Half Life games, Blue Shift does a lot more than present a solid first-person shooter experience. Unlike HL1 and Opposing Force, Blue Shift shows more of the crappy underbelly of Black Mesa. You're a security guard and it shows that the company doesn't care about you like they fawn over their scientists. Door scanners are broken, you live in demountable accomadation with shared laundry facilities and don't even think about private showers in the facilities staff bathroom.
This wry humour is played out directly at the start when you're locked out and someone has to manually override a door for you, but it's written everywhere in the setting and treatment of your character by others.
A brilliant, classic shooter bolstered by witty worldbuilding and setting.

Despite being a pretty slow burn, this is a delightfully spooky and well-written survival game. Accept death, for the zee is unforgiving, and you'll want to try playing as different specialties anyway.
PROS:
* Death is frequent, but re-making your character doesn't feel like you've lost *too* much progress. You learned from your last voyage, now fix what you messed up.
* Great survival atmosphere. The music befits a somber hopelessness, and everything just looks like it belongs in this universe that's been so lovingly written out.
* Speaking of, that deserves a bullet point to itself, the story and writing is great, and to top it off, totally original. Remember this isn't the sea, this is the zee--the sea beneath the sea.
* Mostly procedurally-generated. All the coastal towns/elements and several points near London seem to be the same every play-through, but everything else seems to be randomized, at least within their own vertical segments. You can keep your previous play-through's chart if you choose that as one of your relations to your recently-deceased captain.
* Doesn't get stale easily.
CONS:
* -Can- get stale at times.
* Really wish you could increase the game's speed. As much as I enjoy the atmosphere, when you're on captain #5 it gets a little tedious.
Not much else to say, it's just a damn good survival horror game, largely carried by its unique story and excellent writing.
A classic and a gem, emanating a traditional fantasy vibe that hits the spot.

Train Valley is a railroad simulator where you play as a train operator trying to make trains arrive at their preordained destination. To do so, you lay tracks to connect stations and ensure that trains arrive at the correct location as fast as possible. The faster you get train A to station A, the more money you will make. The game's objective is simply to make coloured trains arrive at the stations of the matching colour to earn money without going bankrupt. Each game year, you will get taxed and lose money. If you crash a train, demolish important structures or send a train too late you will lose money. If you lose all your money, you lose the game. If you finish launching all the trains without going bankrupt, you complete the stage.
Gameplay-wise, it's a mouse click game where you lay tracks, change the direction of the tracks, pause the game, stop a train, reverse the direction of a train and launch trains from stations. It's very important how you lay the tracks as once you lay the track, future tracks may not be able to pass through i.e. tracks can only cross each other at 90 degree angles or join at 45 degrees. There are certain objectives that will increase the difficulty such as not demolishing tracks, not have a train arrive at the wrong station, not stopping a train
Conclusion, do try Train Valley. The puzzles are fun to do and there are some interesting effects like a rocket firing off. You can see the world slowly buildup the more trains you send.
Note : The developers are Alexey Davydov, Sergey Dvoynikov, Timofey Shargorodskiy.
1. Train Simulator
That's the main draw of this game.
1. Similar Coloured Train Stations
Light blue, white and teal are so similar that it's hard to tell them apart. The only clear colours are blue, red, yellow, orange, green, purple.
2. Game is Short
Less than 10 hours and everything is over. You would think that for a simple puzzle game, it would be able to generate more interesting stages.
1. More Effects, Please
I want to see even more effects. The best one would be to have a Rube Goldberg styled domino effect with the trains. I'm talking about the rocket lifting off.
2. Pick Up and Deliver
Could you add goods that need to be picked up? Currently, trains just move from station A to station B. How about picking up goods along the way for mission or bonus points? Or pick up and deliver? E.g. Picking up the mail, picking up grain from the grain elevator?
3. Goods
You have to create goods like corn, steel, coal, oil, liquid helium, cars. Depending on what goods the trains are carrying, the crash will be different.
4. Underground Trains
There's no metro map. All your trains are above ground. You need a map that deals with the underground as well. It can't be standalone. You have to make it above ground + under ground.
5. Player Mods
You need to create a workshop so that fans can make their own maps for you and each other. Let the community make maps that they can share and play with/challenge each other.
6. Multiplayer
Imagine the chaos that ensues when your train crashes into my train. ^&$#&$%^$
