I’ve put about an hour into Blood and Bacon. Time flies when you’re gone pigg’n.  Its 99 cents. I honestly thought about refunding it because I know at some point the joke will wear thin.  Then I remember the time I bought Dinosaur Hunt for 99 cents.
Only to swiftly refund Dinosaur hunt in less than an hour. When compared to Dinosaur Hunt, Blood and Bacon is a masterpiece. It’s rare that I delve into the 99 cent bargain bin,  this would be my third dip in the pool. Behind Dinosaur Hunt and Street Racing Syndicate.
I picked up Street Racing Syndicate on sale for 99 cents and I kept it. It’s likely I’m going to keep Blood and Bacon as well.  Because it’s fun and unlike other games in its price bracket it actually delivers everything it promises by the bucket load.
It looks like a Left 4 Dead clone at surface level. It plays like an odd mix of Killing Floor and Serious Sam with lots of blood and lots of bacon.  It’s the whole hog and it more than lives up to its title of the goriest indie game ever.
It runs smooth, and I’m confident it could even run on a toaster with no lag.  The option of multiple camera angles to suit multiple styles of play is quite a neat little feature though I couldn’t see myself playing B&B in anything but first person.
If I had 5 other people to play with I’d gift them 10 copies. It’s just that good. B&B is the real haram.  The game was released in 2016 but it looks more like a 2008 game.  It’s got multiplayer, online multiplayer and co-op which is awesome.
Getting the resolution to fit the screen right was a bit fiddly but after some optimization the game runs smoothly at a crispy 60FPS without any lag.  Makes me weirdly reminiscent about that movie “Razorback’ and if you’ve seen it you’ll understand why.
I don’t know… there’s something about blasting the **** out of a razorback that brightens up my whole day. Godless **** eating vermin.  B&B only fails insofar as it doesn’t appear to have a steam workshop or any mods, which is a massive albeit liveable shame.
On some level I can’t help but feel the game would have been better suited to lambs, goats, emus, walruses… the possibilities for mods are endless.  The day/night cycle is a nice touch and damn am I glad they gave you a way to heal in single player.
The choice of playable characters is pretty hilarious, stereotypical and borders on the edges of racist and absurd.  Johnny Blood in particular. There’s no conceivable way I will get to the 100th way by myself, even on the easiest difficulty and I’m fine with that.
The meat grinder is an interesting mechanic though if I’m supposed to kick meat into the grinder and the developer of the game forget to even map a kick button then that’s not my problem and it honestly should’ve been patched by now.
Weapon variety is basic although perfectly serviceable, even if I still haven’t gotten the hang of the electric fence.
There are a variety of 13 enemies, 12 bosses and 1 secret boss scattered throughout 100+ levels and the game accommodates between 2-6 players I’m told.
It’s a fun weekend distraction for you and a few friends for less than the combined total of a cup of coffee with serviceable weapons, a variety of enemies with zero lag and maximum challenge.  From where I’m sitting, its hog heaven!

Early Access Review:
For a game that's premise is over-saturated, Project Zomboid stands unique and fresh compared to it's peers. Project Zomboid isn't your typical zombie game nor your typical survival horror game. Project Zomboid is more of a simulator than an RPG. When playing, you'll get frustrated so many times before actually getting the hang of everything as for PZ is a roguelike, once your survivor dies, he/she is dead forever. No matter how far your progress or big your fortress. Many of which mistakes you'll make is mostly because you got too over your head, or just plain stupidity. But once you get how the game goes, you'll surely live to see another day, maybe months.
To fully enjoy the game, one must stop looking at this game as a survival RPG, and more of a survival sim. With the word simulator being said, this means managing, scheduling and farming. Think of it as a mash-up of The Sims + Farmville + Old-School Zombies. You gather supplies and build a base of operations where you can store your supplies and gear or maybe start a farm for food supplies. You can also choose to be a nomad and move from place to place.
Moreover on being a simulator, you have to take care of your survivors needs, hunger, boredom and health should be taken care of and maintained well regularly. You can't just sit all day and wait. As you build your base, the game adds a Farmville + Tower Defense vibe to it. Make sure though you don't go gathering supplies at night as it gets pretty dark and dangerous. With this scheduling is also important, make sure you make a to-do list for the day, patience pays in this game, some areas are so infested that you have to postpone your scheduled scanveging trip. Everything is important in this game, make sure to gather everything for maybe in the future you may need it.
For an Early Access Game, Project Zomboid is already filled with hours and hours of fun gameplay, as everything in the main gameplay is there, surviving, scavenging, building. It is announced and on paper though that NPC's will be added to give the game a more immersive feel and dynamic events. I personally am looking forward for the NPC's, imagine with the amount of different kinds of gameplay all mashed together in one added with NPC's and dynamic events all together can put this game into another way crazier level.
I totally recommend this game for everyone, especially for people who are up for a challenge.

Limbo is a prime example of video games as an art from.
At it's core, Limbo is a 2D puzzle/platforming game, with an emphasis on the puzzling rather than the platforming. There are a few puzzles that require precise timing, but for the most part the game is more of a mental exercise.
Limbo's execution and presentation is where the real magic happens. The game is presented in black and white, and the tone is stark, oppressive, and creepy. There is a distinct lack of music, and all other sound is few and far between, thus further establishing the game's bleak atmosphere. This style definitely isn't for everybody, and although I found myself put off at first, I slowly began to realize that the game would be missing a huge chunk of its character without its dark, depressing art direction.
Puzzle design is another of the game's strong points. Puzzles are presented in series, where the first puzzle introduces a mechanic and the next few build on that same mechanic. This is game design 101, but in Limbo it is masterfully done. I got stuck on one or two puzzles, but for the most part the puzzles are tough enough to make you smile when you solve them, but not so tough that you have to crowdsource the solution. Almost all puzzles strike a perfect balance in difficulty and are incredibly rewarding to discover and to solve.
Limbo is a game that needs to be experienced rather than described. If a 2D puzzler with a uniquely oppressive atmosphere is what you've been searching for, then worry not, you have arrived.
As a side note, the platforming doesn't hold up as well these days. The game is by no means unplayable, but it takes a little while to get used to the game's movement.
I give it a 6 out of 7.

I haven't played the older Tropico games, so I don't really have any preconceived notions about how this game should be. The game is beautiful. Lovely graphics, and the user interface if fairly intuitive and easy to use. And it runs on Linux, which is a HUGE plus.
My biggest grief is what appears to be inconsistencies in the economics. I have homeless and unemployed citizens. I build a library, I build houses, and the library sits there empty because no one will work there. The houses sit empty while the peasants build shacks round it. I build a ranch so my idle workers have a job and are producing something that you can consume and/or sell, and now I'm loosing money hand over fist. I demolish the ranch, my citizen homeless rate goes up, content goes down, but now I'm making money again. I've watched my treasury bleed away into the negative, I'm loosing money fast, and nothing I do stops it. I build docks, ranches, mines, farms. I build housing. I increase budget on buildings and ranches and farms. I give them a bar, churches, libraries, clinics, etc. Nothing I do stops the money loss.
I finally discovered two secrets to making money:
1) Don't build anything. Just sit there with the bare basic town, only build what you are told to as part of a task, add a few docs, and you make money. You start expanding with ranches, plantations, industry, etc., and no matter what you do you start loosing money.
2) Set economic difficulty to the lowest setting. NOW you can play and enjoy the game without going bankrupt in 30 minutes or less!
And you might as well get used to your people hating you. I finally figure out how to get my approval rating up to 50% so I can declare independence and not loose elections, but what you have to do to get there is not always obvious.
I don't recommend this game because of the frustration level involved with  just trying to survive. There comes a point where it just isn't fun anymore.

Tropico has always been a favorite of mine since the initial release but the trend of this series is becoming a money grab and they are starting to mess with the game mechanics too (they release more game mechanics through DLC)
So the core game itself is pretty streamlined with basic buildings, not too many options in each category. You cannot see the building upgrades make an impact on the appearance anymore. Its very stripped down, prepped for DLC unfortunately. The limited options you have with buildings make "less" impact than they used to. You no longer see people visit entertainment locations. Previously, you built more entertainment buildings if they were becoming overcrowded but thats not the case anymore, less control or micro managing which takes away from an economy style game.
After reading some of the bigger DLC packs, many players have complained that some of the game mechanics should have been in the core game and the DLCs offer more player strategic options.
Why am I rating this down? Its because it costs $120 for everything this game has to offer. If your a fan, pick up an older title on sale with all the DLC, it will be much more rewarding than buying just the core copy.
Its a great game but their model needs to change.

Gameplay wise it's a solid piece of work. You combine various objects which each other and find new and unconventional solutions to otherwise unsolvable problems

Overall I would recommend it to all of you adventure gamers looking for something new for a decent price.

I know I dont have many hours of play on this game and I dont usually review games if I have not played them for long but I have played AoW it when it first came out in 1999 and many years afterwards until my copy was lost. I think it's safe for me to review this version.
There is a bug that causes the game to freeze every 40 turns but frequent saving at the start of your turns makes this a minor issue. Simply restart your game and you're set. With that addressed this steam version is worth your money if multi unit turn-based strategy is your thing. You can find items in dungeons, caves, and castle ruins and level your heroes. Upon leveling you can pick new talents making this game rather customizable. You can play up to 12 different racial leaders in an effort to conquer the map. Each race is uniquely different than the others. You simply recruit your army through the cities you capture and upgrade the cities for more capable units. Great fun with friends either pvp or coop. The computer players have several difficulty settings. I cannot begin to tell you how much time I've spent playing this game. It has a high level of replay value due to the number of maps available. And I forgot to tell you that you can MAKE your own maps. Also there are a few fan-based sites that are STILL making downloadable maps. After 15 years fans are still releasing maps for this game.
Anyhow it's worth the five bucks. Also a caution: It can really suck you in and soak up your time. I catch myself saying 'just one more turn. Just one more battle. One more dungeon.' ... I said that an hour ago. Have Fun!

+ The setting is quirky and can be fun to explore.
+ Most events are engaging and mysterious.
+ It's a genuine struggle to start out from scratch.
- Travelling in this game is painfully slow and not at all fun.
- Combat is not very deep and can become tedious.
- It's incredibly slow to start out from scratch.
- There aren't enough events for several playthroughs to feel unique.
- Missions vary from "fun" to "terrible".
Game has an interesting setting and fun events but gets bogged down by its extremely slow pacing. Maybe get it on sale if you're patient.
This game has a lot of potential that's ultimately stifled by two major problems:
The rogue-like nature of the game will have you playing over the same events over and over and over again if you die with any frequency whatsoever. Worse yet, you'll quickly run out of different choices to make on these events, meaning you'll eventually figure out the optimal path and the events thus get boiled down to memory tests. The game needed more events or it needed not to be rogue-like.
The incredible tedium of travel is what really kills this game for me. I understand the theme the travel is trying to set: you're puttering along through a terrifying and hostile sea. The problem is that there's next to no engagement during the travel and so it actually has the opposite of the intended effect. Instead of getting engrossed in my perilous little voyage I instead found myself unable to play without having something else to distract me, i.e. watching YouTube.
Now, to make this clear, I am not at all opposed to slow paced travel in a game. It's just that it needs to be engaging on some level during what most normal people would identify as the "tedius" parts. A good way to get across what's wrong with this game is to compare it to another game with slow, slogging travel:
In The Long Dark I find myself engaged during travel because I have to worry about getting attacked by wolves, I need to look for opportunities to get food, I can pick up firewood during my travel, and I can sometimes find a tiny bit of extra loot I might have missed even when I'm travelling down a well beaten path. The weather might change and if I wasn't paying attention I'm now lost in a snow storm. If I'm injured I might decide it's better to camp out in a safe spot for a night instead of risking trying to get home while half dead.
In Sunless Sea I kind of just point the boat in the right direction and wait for an event to pop up or for the boat to hit something. Maybe some sea monster will attack me. If I can kill it I'll probably shoot at it (the combat's pretty dull, unfortunately). If I can't I'll just run away. If my crew is going insane or starving I guess I just get to hope for the best because I'm already going towards whatever place will fix the problem.
At the end of the day I'm disappointed by this because there are two obvious solutions: either have a fast forward button that lets you increase the simulation speed (i.e. x2, x3, x4) to keep travel from sucking the fun out of the game, or have random events appear as actual entities during your travel, i.e. maybe little beacons on the water, that you can drive to (or ignore). Maybe add things like currents so you can speed up your journies once you learn where they are and how to exploit them. Not sure.
Anyway, at the end of the day, if you're patient and like the premise of this game, you might want to buy it on sale. It's definitely fun at first when everything is fresh and ripe to be explored, you just might find it hard to keep going beyond that.

A weird, wonderful story-oriented strategy and exploration game. Despite a few repetitive tasks, the game is enthralling as you sail your ship around a Lovecraftian underground ocean with great artwork and a map that differs every time you play. Choose your game-winning objective and struggle to meet it. Manage your resources; don't run out of food or fuel unless you want your crew to resort to cannibalism or mutiny. Read eldritch descriptions of unimaginable creatures. Buy and sell. Avoid or destroy pirates and monsters. Transport passengers. Improve your vessel. Work for a smuggler. Or not. Have an affair with a crew member. Or not. Every choice you make will affect your game, sometimes in unpredictable ways. Buy the Zubmariner DLC and add an entire ocean-bottom world to explore while avoiding a new set of subterranean monsters.
The best way to describe the world of this game is steampunk Victoriana with strong horror elements. (If you've played the developers' free browser game
, you'll already know something about it, though it won't help you much in the game.) Gameplay is challenging but gets easier as you learn about the world, and even losing can be satisfying if you die in the right way. Each time you die, you become your own heir, and you can decide what to leave to yourself when starting the next playthrough. Absorbing enough for long play sessions, but also playable in short bursts. There is a lot of reading, which is a negative for some people.

Update,
So the game is still awesome. New changes have introduced new charecter generation traits and changes to the skill advancement and injury side of things, you can now stitch wounds and use antiseptic and such spoiler, find a needle and thread asap! the injurys while interesting can be a bit commicle such as getting scratched on the foot through your shoes, plus it seems to me that the most popular place to be bitten is the groin( had 4 out of 6 chrs died from groing bites last few run throughs) So buy a jock-strap and find a bat then go looking for that friggen ax so you can build a new water barrel!
Where to start... This is by far one of the best survival games out there. Even in its early access form the game feels complete. The crafting and farming system's are wonderfull, allowing you to build safe houses or entire compounds if you feel up to it. Farming is well thought out and the cooking side is constantly being expanded. the new systems, fishing and trapping seem to be right on track and make survival not purely based on any one food source. Combat is a bit stagnant at this point, no real aiming mechanics and some weapons are way over powerd, but this is still a work in progress. NPC's are still out of the game but the devs update weekly on progress and seems to working away at it. Multyplayer is still in its infancy, public servers are either barren or populated by people that just kill you on site. I have a private server i play with a few friends on and we have a blast. Depending on loot levels certain key items can be very hard to find, i.e trowls axes and sledgehammers, which are all required for certain tasks, making it very hard to get a good base going. Everything taken into consideration I would most definately say that this is a great game as is, and keeps getting better with every new build. There is nothing like the feeling of opening a closet looking for something to let you live just one more day and finding it filled with zed that eat you alive. The question is how are you going to die?

First an explanaiton about calling this an "Alpha".
In my book "beta" means a piece of software that is ready but needs some furnishing, fixing and an extra hand of paint.
"Aplha" means an incomplete piece of software that is under development and not complete.
The way Project Zomboid is being implemented is simillar to many Indies currently, they put out a stable "aplha" and call it "beta", but I insist that those are "stable alpha" versions.
About the game...
This could be the ultimate zombie survival strategy game, but I can not tell for sure because:
- It's incomplete and under development.
- It's too dificult to learn. Surviving is so challenging, and you have so many limitations that it's hard to even learn the crafting and farming systems.
- Even if you manage to be a super horder and live for weeks from your stash, if you die you start all over again, so you don't want to take changes.
The pro and the against of this game is the same, it is a survival challenge... to the point to be really rewarding and frustrating a the same time.
If you like the style and Don't Starve is too easy and simple for you, then this is your game.
If you want to relax and have a good time, stay away.

If you played Carmageddon before, and liked it, you will like this. If you had trouble with Carmageddon Reincarnation, this is a good update. Honestly it's just a patch with a few new cars and maps that they could have just as easily added into Reincarnation though...I can't notice any "real" differences aside from cars, more pedestrians (bikes! wheelchairs! awesome!) and better grass. Supposedly the physics are different but it's hard to tell... Supposedly it's more stable but I never had problems with Reincarnation so I can't see a difference. The new cars are nice. I get the impression grip on the street has improved causing the vehicles to be better controllable.
And in case you don't know Carmageddon : Drive around recognizable environments with people casually strolling about, ignoring all traffic rules and safety regulations. Just hit the gas and try to hit as many things as you can. The more you hit, the more the game rewards you. The gorier you can do it, the more bonusses you get. Arcade controls mean you can play this using a keyboard (and mouse for the menu's), a gamepad, a steeringwheel (didn't test this) and probably more.
Try to wreck one of the other racers for the biggest rewards. Unlock more and more cars, paint jobs, rims, game modes and imrove armor levels, speed and damage for your car as you go along. After about 20 hours you will probably have unlocked most or all cars, environments, etc... and you can go hunting for achievements or just set up freestyle games as you like. There's also multiplayer, it's a lot of fun but there's a limited amount of players so you need to ask friends or people here on Steam to join you or you will have trouble finding a match.

Disclaimer: This game was automatically added to my library probably because I bought into the Early Access of Carmageddon: Reincarnation.
Alright, my PC is less than stellar and I will be upgrading soon. Still, it was able to run this game at an acceptable level. Previously on Reincarnation I could barely even touch 25 FPS. Now I am able to go upto 40. This was on med-high settings.
The game play is the same as Reincarnation which, if you have not played, is basically the exact same take on the original (1997 Carmageddon) with a slight twist regarding powerups. Powerups now have charges instead of being activated automatically. Some powerups have a charge which depletes when you hold down the Power up button. Environmental modifier powerups remain the same as original.
Car handling is exactly the same as it was in the original game. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and thats the way it was meant to be. God forbid they ever change handling. Theres also a new car control feature while in mid-air, a somewhat similar take on GTA V's subtle car control feature.
Overall I should really hand it to the devs for taking it upon themselves for fixing bugs and performance issues with the game rather than abandoning it. Carmageddon is an inseparable part of Stainless Steel games and it would have been a travesty had it been left to stagnate by those who created it.

I actually wasn't really into super hexagon when I played it, and in my opinion this game actually surpasses super hexagon, especially in visuals and learning curve.
For the gameplay, you control a little airplane and press arrow keys to instantly switch lanes, similar to audiosurf IIRC. You have to do things like avoid white tiles rushing at you, hit green tiles, and shoot enemies. The gameplay feels quite smooth, and the animations are juicy and responsive so after a bit of playing you kind of feel like you have become the plane. Some elements are slightly frustrating and unintuitive, like there being a delay between switching lanes multiple times which can be problematic when you really need to get to a lane quickly. That said, usually when I die I feel like it's my fault and not the game's, which is a good sign.
Visuals wise, this game looks damn nice in my opinion. it's a $3 game and it's well polished, with an electric neon vibe that makes everything in the game stand out. the only minor complaint I have with it is when you reach the levels where there are enemies the enemies can be a tad hard to see, and I sometimes get so busy looking for them that I forget to watch what's in front of me.
Curve wise, I think this game does a good job at keeping you at least mildly frustrated most of the time, giving it that sought after tough as nails feel, however unlike super hexagon (for me at least) it also helps you feel like you are always at least getting somewhat better by awarding you new levels that provide extra complications which are more deep than the game simply getting faster. The curve was also gentle enough that someone pretty bad at these types of games like myself actually managed to play for like 40 minutes on end without having to take a break from frustration which certainly didn't happen with super hexagon.
Sound wise it's at the very least adequate. I think the music is about on par with that of super hexagon, and the tracks are so similar I wouldn't be surprised if I actually saw some of these tracks in super hexagon. It wasn't too memorable for me personally but it certainly wasn't bad or irritating.
Overall, I think this game is a great buy if you're into titles in this vein, and even if not, if its on sale I might reccomend picking it up anyway because I'm not into this genre either and I still had some fun with it and I expect to come back to it again in the future.

I picked up this game months ago after seeing some gameplay footage on Youtube. The survival gameplay really interested me, and before I knew it I was impulse buying as soon as I saw it on Steam. It was incredibly fun (and frustrating) figuring out where to get a good weapon, foraging (and later growing) food, crafting walls or rain barrels, memorizing the town and planning my safehouse. The zombies were a serious threat, and I wasn't some action star with unlimited ammo and life.
The game takes a lot of variables into consideration, like temperature, boredom, sickness ... It becomes a personal challenge to see how long I can last in my next life.
Obviously, it's still Early Access, but I forget that as I play. The updates that have been released since I started playing are signifigant. I'm basically pushing all my friends to play so I can hear all their funny survivor stories. I'm definately looking forward to co-op multiplayer, trapping, more crafting and NPCs.
TL;DR - An awesome zombie survival simulator with graphics that remind me a lot of Fallout 2 (which I love). Still Early Access, but with enough content to make the price worth it, imo.

Controls are very awkward on the keyboard and you can’t change them (Arrow keys based instead of WASD based). The jump key dynamically changes with the “Up” direction of your character—instead of a static Jump key like SPACE. This makes the dexterity challenges requiring rapid climbing and jumping frustrating.
Level design is unforgiving, to put it politely. Usually games show you a new mechanic/concept and teach you how to use it under simple conditions, not LIMBO. You’ll be running along and then you’re dead before you know what killed you (the death animations are rather gruesome btw) or you’ll get stuck on an environmental puzzle because you have no idea what’s environmental vs ambient. I wouldn’t’ve been able to complete this game without following the walkthrough YouTube video from the community; the puzzles are not at all intuitive.
There’s something at the end resembling a plot point, but, there is no storyline—just you running along and dying in a nightmarish Hellscape.
TL;DR: If you’re in it for the punishing platformer like those impossible Mario Maker levels, grab this game. If your games need to have a story or be mindless fun, don’t give this game a second thought.

Let's get what everyone online is talking about out of the way first: The difficulty. Is it really as infuriating hard and broken as people been saying? In my opinion, no it isn't. The game is broken up into two main sections: Boss stages and platforming levels. The boss stages do take up the bulk of the adventure and It IS a bit harder than what you usually find in mainstream games but it's not by any means impossible like a lot of people claim it is. It's definitely not for everyone though. And that's ok.
You'd think that a game which basically consist of boss fight after boss fight would get old after the first few fights, but you'd be wrong. Each boss stage plays completely different than the next. And each one has multiple transformations and gimmicks you must overcome. Not one fight felt similar to another one. Monotony isn't an issue here.
Speaking of difficulty. For those of you wondering. The game controls like a dream. Every move you can do with cuphead feels buttery smooth. I played the whole game with a Dualshock 4 and every single death i had was due to my own fault not the game's. A final note: playing Cuphead with a friend DOES make the game easier. If you are having problems with the game, just call a friend over and split the workload.
Visually. Just looking at a screenshot would tell you how absolutely beautiful the game is, but seeing it in motion just takes the whole thing to another level. From what i understand, every single frame of animation was made by hand trying to emulate the look of old 40s cartoons. And they 100% nailed it. Everything from the silky smooth animation to the dirty film grain and color bleed used makes it look lovingly authentic. It really did blow my mind.
The same can be said about the music and sounds. It only took me a few days playing the game to make me run out and buy the OST. If you are into Jazzy pieces, you'll be in aural heaven here.
Cuphead has quickly become one of my favorite games of 2017. Cuphead is both beautiful and brutal. It's definitely not for everyone. But for those that stick with it and have the patience to learn the game and get better at it. I'm sure you'll be remembering this one for a long time to come.

I really liked the Stanley Principle and thought this would be similar.  It is not.  This is more of a video that you walk through at your own pace.  As you hit certain points, the narrator will give you more insight into what he is doing and what he is trying to accomplish.  At no point is there any real choice on our part.  So, there is a lot of using the mouse and the WASD keys to walk the character through each part of the play.  Throughout the whole 30 minutes of walking and narration, I kept thinking that there must be more to it than just walking through a story.  I kept looking for the "catch" and even explored the areas to find the secret...I never found any.
After 30 minutes I started to feel nauseous (it happens on some games).   The nausea started during the scene with the "notes" from other "users" (another person noted they felt nauseous after a bit also).  I decided to log off after that point and proceeeded to look up the reviews.  After reading many reviews, the negative reviews verified that there was nothing more to the "game", that there was no "catch" and this really was all there was to it.  I deleted it from my computer.
Graphics were okay but not anything like other story games I have played (some comments said they were great...hmmm).  I believe this was all part of the set up of the play, though, so it fit.  The narration was fine and spoken as a normal person trying to talk through his decisions for doing this, which was also appropriate for what the writers were trying to accomplish.
It is an interesting piece of visual writing/exploration, but it should not be listed as a game, it is not.  It is more of a philosophical play...not sure what category that goes under!  I keep quoting "As You Like It" by Shakespeare..."All the world's a stage and the men and women merely players..." as I think about this "game".
To get a good sense of what it is, I actually recommend that you read both the positive and negative comments.  I have found that I generally agree with what those who leave rational(!) negative comments state, even if I do not agree with their overall rating.
This time, I do agree with their overall rating as I believed this was a game and not a philosophical play and so my expectations were different from what was presented.

The first thing I did before I played this game was look at all the reviews.
I thought that they might shed some light on the emotional wreckage I was about to undertake, the full experience that only a game that brings out so much sorrow and pain and self-uncertainty that a person could barely begin to comprehend, could make so much sense out of. I thought, "hey, it's the sad version of the Stanley Parable! Nbd, maybe some emotional parts here and there, but nothing that'll really stick to me like the other game did. Let's face it, The Narrator is iconic as all hell."
And I was *seriously* wrong. Like, wrong on a MASSIVE level (well, wrong about the game-not-sticking-to-me part, at any rate).
This game will stay with you. It doesn't even matter if you'll like it or not- it'll stay with you. You'll think about something one minute and then think about the lampost the next. It'll stick to your mind, and to be honest, that's the best kind of game. The one that stays with you, and the one that you can see yourself in as clearly as you see a mirror.
I just finished playing. But I truly believe that this is just one of those games that I'll keep on coming back to for years. I didn't cry when I finished playing this, unfortunately enough. Like many others, I assume that tears are the only right way to pay your respects to brilliant games like these. But, like I've said, I was wrong. This game went way beyond tears.
10/10, would stare at my screen not comprehending the emotional wreckage inside of me for a full hour again.

My first IBM-PC game ever was Monkey Island. The original, good, old (MS-DOS days), humorous Lucas Arts point-and-click adventure game. My first CD-ROM game was "Star Trek TNG: A Final Unity". Another point-and-click adventure. While these kind of adventure games are not my favorite genre, they are part of what computers games were and still are. They are a part of history, and when a great game of this kind comes along, like Morningstar, then it has to be played.
This one is really a good one. People are complaining about the price tag, and that it should technically be free, because it exists as flash game. I strongly disagree. This is a beautifully crafted game, that works similar to one of the popular interactive movies from the 1990s, with stronger puzzle elements. You definitely have to think about how to solve a problem, and having some basic understanding of technology certainly helps. It's never too difficult, and usually the provided hints, if at all necessary, are more than sufficient.
In particular the part of the game towards the end is very well done, and even if the story is not your thing, and even if you don't like adventure games at all, you should give this shot, purely for the visuals. It's a short game, but quality definitely trumps over quantity here.

-Excellent, expansive storytelling written with great presentation and atmosphere. As more than one other reviewer has said, throw HP Lovecraft, Terry Pratchett, and a dash of surrealism in a mixer and you might end up with this.
-Generally low system requirements supports running it on weaker systems. This is a good title to load on a portable computer and take with you on a trip where you will need to kill some time while waiting or in transit. The slower pace of the game also supports being able to play this while leaving some attention free to wait on standby for other obligations.
Bad:
-The excellent writing is partly locked behind a degree of timegating and a horrible amount of trade grinding, with a pretty slow paced travel system layered over top of both. For some people, all of this is a plus. For me, it is not. For the purposes of my review still being a recommend, the excesses of this negative are solely mitigated by the availability of a few cheat / Quality of Life mods and a file editing guide that can reduce the grinding to more acceptable levels.
Without these, most of my play effort is forced to focus on trade grinding just to economically survive, experiencing short pieces of story with incidental economic related deaths often resetting my progress. Instead, I can choose to focus on the meat of experiencing the story and if the Captain dies, it is more acceptably because of story or encounters. It is much more enjoyable for me to play this way and there is still a lot of game to be experienced. If the developers disabled the ability for these mods and file edits to work, I would be forced to switch this to a negative review.
-There is a degree of additional content available for free beyond the DLC, which in itself is good, but unlocking it requires signing up to the developer's browser based game, and in some cases completing specific events in that game or receiving gift items from other players there. While I understand this is a promotional gimmick, I personally do not like the concept of having content for a purchased game locked behind a different game that requires yet another login and password.

Story? It's a dark and stormy night. Everybody should play Age of Wonders all day every day. And all the sequels. Plus there's a new one coming out sometime this year *insert fangirl squeel!!!*
So, what's the game actually about? Well, other than half of my childhood?
It's a turn-based strategy game that's nothing like Age of Empires or Age of Mythology (though the name might con you into thinking that). Think of it more like you would Civ 3, but set in a fantasy world with magic, dragons, elves, and everything else. Oh, and with less diplomacy. And where the only way to win is to kill♥♥♥♥♥♥ In other words, Civ 3, but about 10 times more awesome.
The combat system is the best part. Sure, your guys can automatically duke it out in a boring little window where all that is displayed is their health, but that's no fun. What's great is when you select the "tactical" combat option. That allows you to control each individual infantryman/dragon/hero (who can also cast spells!) and position and manuver them however you so wish. There's even terrain on battlefields such as fortifications, pillars of rock, houses, etc. If you're clever, a hero and supporting units (cavalry usually in my experience) can outmanuver a much greater force and wipe them out.
In other words, buy this game. Do it. Do it now.
*Note, I've had some stability issues with the game because it was originally designed for Windows 95. I've found that most of them were fixed by running it in windowed mode.

Really fun! I like to play it with the speed on max and pause when I need to think about it. Good time killer train game. Sort of a real time puzzle game, with adjustable speed, and a pause button. Has extra objectives for completionists (3 extra per level). At the end of each "world" there's what seems to be a procedurally generated level you can play endlessly (more on that below).
It's about what you'd expect from the trailer and synopsis, and it's thus far bug free and well polished. I haven't completed it yet, so I may update this later, but here's a list of thoughts about it:
- The "box art" and promotional material show graphics that look stylized, like they're toys or something. This is the style I was expecting, but the game is actually sorta subtle-realism. I feel like they may have started with the cartoony look early in development and switched to the style that exists now, but I wish they had kept the cute toyish style!!
- Would be cool if you could rotate your camera. You can zoom, and pan, but no rotate. Not a big deal at all, really, but I'm just kind of surprised you can't!
- The procedurally generated levels are very cool, but there are some things I'd love to see changed a little. It's a little bit chaotic. Some trains give you a lot of time before they automatically leave the station, some leave by themselves almost immediately - which makes trains crash a LOT. Also, new train stations can appear in the middle of a track and destroy your track, obstructing a train's path, causing a train crash. And sometimes there are little geysers that appear, which destroy tracks, again causing train crashes. The natural disasters and appearing stations aren't an issue for me, but the randomized train-departing delay is kind of annoying - so if they made it so that trains all start with the same delay before leaving, the rhythm of sending out trains would be more cohesive, and a LOT of fun. In any case though, the procedurally generated levels are a cool addition, especially if you've completed the game and want more!
TLDR:
Well tuned, perfect difficulty, real time train puzzle game, good for decompressing after a long day.
Keep up the good work, devs!!

***Updated as of 31/10/2016***
*Intro*
Carmageddon 2 (C2) was both a technical triumph and and gaming revolution in terms of detruction, violence and humour, as much as 1 was the birth of it all, the sequel shone brighter. It had it's flaws sure, and unstable engine here and there, music and graphical battles with newer hardware but more over it had charm, a great atmosphere and plenty of character and humour.
**Disclaimer alert**
I am fully aware Stainless did not make TDR 2000 (TDR) however, I know it's sour note for both the dev and many original fans but in the fairness of a complete comparison i will be mentioning some of it's few strengths in the regard to how Max Damage fails.
***/end***
*Discussion*
Starting with the positives, the developers are very active, informative and talkative, this is always a good sign. Shane, Nobby and the gang speak out and speak up a lot on the forums both here and official site, good signs. Another good point is they at least support mods, even if that at times feels like it's not fully open to us yet, it's there. They put a lot of time into at least trying, so I can commend that, a lot of features are fun (powerups especially) but sometimes they hit and miss at no fault of the design, just in terms of application. Vehicles designs are good, some are very fun to look at, fun to smash apart, and to drive some of the much larger vehicles suits this game a lot more than the paper weight of some of the lesser cars. Final good points is they want to support this game into the future, that's always a plus, but it won't change my review to a thumbs up.
Carmaggedon Max Damage, for me, feels soulless. The atmosphere that made C2 and yes, even from TDR, so good has gone, especially in the sound department (there is now a cartoon style "stunned" sound that plays when you do heavy damage which looks stupid and sounds annoying as hell) but also graphically. It's muddied, low quality cell shaded cartoon-esq graphics make it look dated, with poor texture quality, average model quality (worse on peds), mediocre draw distances (the dreaded fog is strong in this game) and wishy washy physics engine make it feel like a lot of good ideas all smashed together and resulted in a rather, series suitable, mutation. It runs solid 60fps and so it should running on a 1070! But at what cost?
It's just boring and mostly grindy. From driving and the driving physics, from the lack of speed, the lack of "weight" in vehicles, but also how brittle, glass like vehicles feel, being able to waste a car from behind at a rather low speed makes every similar kill feel cheap, the game is SO EASY even on "hard". You feel like you are riding around in tin hollow boxes on wheels that crumple at just a wiff of an impact. Gone is the immense battles between car and truck...between truck and bigger truck, between bigger truck and "holy sh- what is that". Gone is that tense moment from C2 of first encountering Abba Cab...looming over your car and just how brutal that thing hit, and how much damage it took to finally destroy it. Gone is the feeling of personal effort, of triumph over great odds, those superb battles between machine and monster machine and that look on your face when you see the price tag on that truck...but also at the glee of "saving up" to buy that shiny new ride...none of this C1 style "stealing" of cars which i think is a boring mechanic which makes it feel more pot luck than "I earned this".
This is not a carmageddon game IMO, it's a shadow of sorts, that has suffered over the years with design change after design change, from the moment it left KS to this very moment now. Very little has changed. it performs a hell of lot better but at the cost of what? Shady LOD "phasing" issues with disappearing objects/wheels and sharp "pop in". The lack of detail in it's sounds design, or it's ambiant effects (a single whooshy wind sound is all we get on city maps, why?) No clinks and clanks, rumbles and rattles, physical object sounds, dent and crashes a nullified and sound effects lack oomph, at least there are different ones in some levels but they are very linear sounding, for a current gen game sound design should of been very high on the list. A terrible (imo) sound track overly filled with dubstep...and thrash rock that even then still doesn't "fit" the game IMO. TDR 2000 had a superb, probably the BEST fitting soundtrack for any carma game, Utah Saints and the In-house artist who provided songs for TDR was fantastic, the gloomy worlds that only looked dead but brimmed with personality, the mission structure that was both harsh and at times confusing, but still fun in a strange way. TDR did a lot right but fell down on what made Carma 2 the go to game, THE carmageddon game.
Overall, everything from the number of vehicles, the types of environments (some which are not bad at all in fairness), the size of the maps, the timid "tin box" physics, the paper light vehicles, the poor sounds, the average graphics, the "structurre" of the campaign, the "stealing" vehicles mechanic, the level of difficulty which it pathetically easy even on hard, the underwhelming a times humour and the "must try to stay relevant!" atmosphere that beams off C:MD is all in all a bit of shame.
I may not have 100s of hours, but played enough so far of C:R to know/feel that C:MD is not up to par, it needs so much more work, it needs an entirely new, up to date engine (Unreal 4 would of been PERFECT for this game, seriously, especially with the destruction engine) and a whole host more.
Credit to them, they at least "semi" support modding...but not properly, they will not let us use modded cars in career mode for fear of "breaking leaderboards" or ruining the "experience" of career
Ever heard of simple checks to disable this online related stuff? Who really cares about leaderboards when you could career through the career mode (intended) in a Dump Truck mod, or a Train on wheels style car, or C1 imports? Sure you get freeplay mode...but playing the career with mods is what Carma 2 was all about with thanks to some amazing mods, setting up greater threats, new maps, harder AI and all sorts.
*Conclusion*
I am surprised at the number of postivie reviews, reviews that do not do well to mention issues about it still loading slowly on SSD, issues with currently, the sound effects being way too quiet (compared to C:R they were too loud...lol), the dull graphics, the mediocre car list, the career structure. I see raving reviews about performance and "yay it's fixed" and "best carma ever" when it looks like non of these people understand what C1/C2 showed us. I mean that cartoon stun sound effect when you do heavy damage to cars which has spinning stars over it like in mario cart is just annoying and it ruins the atmosphere a little more by making it badly jokey.
3+ years of waiting for this game that is virtuall a shadow, with some sparks of light. This game  is NOT carmageddon to me. Unless with future changes, I can not recommend this game...unless...somehow, modders add in a C2 style career, buy system, better graphics, sounds, more environments and vehicles, heavier more weighty physics but that's a long shot. Sorry stainless, more time focusing efforts on the franchise that made you would be great, and please support the modders more so in the time to come.
-Edit 3-: When you get wasted now, it's not game over...you just repair with credits and carry on, like i said, this game is TOO EASY and is NOT a proper carmageddon game. I was just hit at low speed in a car by countslash in his lambi at maybe 40mph and it wasted me in 1 hit and made my car looks like it been hit by semi-truck at 100mph. What on earth...this was perhaps a series of powerups put together stacked against me, but it felt like an issue.

I love this game, and the feel of playing with a train set.
Each level, you will have a new map with stations spawning in semi-random location. You'll have a series of objectives, and will be laying all the tracks in place and then managing the schedules of the multiple trains. The scenarios start out simple, and get much more complex later on. For example, you might have a take of making a certain amount of profit, but later you might have to avoid stopping any trains. If you had the money to build multiple options, you can loop a train out of the way, but when you have many trains moving at once it can be challenging to avoid crashes, send them to the right station, and avoid pausing the game.
Levels are beautiful, and varied, and you have the ability to request additional deliveries if you are feeling brave.
If you enjoy realtime puzzle games, and playing with trains, this is a gem of a game that I highly recommend at full price. Worth every penny.

Well, Carmageddon Max Damage is an improvement over Reincarnation. For one, it's finally been optimized and runs pretty smoothly even on my 8 year old rig on medium settings in 1280x720. The load times are vastly improved and the overall performance is smoother. The cockpit cam is a welcome addition but it shows it was added at the last minute, as the cockpit is very blurry and low poly, no animated dash, no anything.
They haven't changed the somewhat boring singleplayer, however. The campaign is pretty formulaic, no missions like in Carma 2 and left the inferior way of getting new cars, i.e. stealing instead of buying wrecks. The gameplay is there, for the most part but it gets old very fast with the same modes you find in Carmageddon. I do enjoy the fact that driving feels less floaty and you can actually damage your opponents instead of bending like paper. I got it for free because I was a Reincarnation Kickstarter backer but I still have to give it a 6/10 because of the very formulaic singleplayer. It is a bit sad I had to wait 4 years for a semi decent experience after the kickstarter.
I haven't played the multiplayer and probably won't, so my review ends at that.

I totally recommend this game! It captures the essence of surviving a zombie apocalypse, namely surviving. There are way too many games where you're some stupidly immortal guy with guns bigger than himself running around killing a million zombies in a city with a population of 3000 or so.
In this game you're just an Average Joe and the game certainly lets you know it. You have needs to fulfill and there's no room for mistakes (maybe a few small ones, but they do have an impact most of the time, some are just downright fatal). You also have to be wary of every zombie out there, even 1! Why? Because one scratch can kill you. Even if you have 20 water items and a lot of food, you can still die easily.
On my first run, I got scratched twice and bitten in the head on day 21, so I decided to go out like a badass. So I went outside in my underpants with a sweater on, take my trusty nailball bat and just kill some walking corpses. I died a hero that day. A bit like Superman, since he also shows his underpants.
In short: if you like zombie games but get tired of all those same generic zombie games out there, get this one, you won't regret it!

Alright, let me start my review by stating that I'm going to cover each game that is within the Casino by bracket.  I'm going to be starting with Jacks or Better Video Poker as it will lay the foundation as to why nobody should waste the ten minutes it takes to install this game.
Jacks or Better, Video Poker:
First, if you get a Jack or better... It's not a push and you do not get your bet back.  Second, if you get a pair below Jack, you do not get credit for the pair.  Third and most importantly, it seems you only get a winning hand on average, once in every ten or so plays and usually that's just a pair or three of a kind.
Slots:
Okay, first of all the buy ins to play slots are insainly inflated.  You're talking 88-3,000 chips per spin.  When you play any of these brackets, the "big wins" or "jackpots" are squed.  I got a big win with a 3k buy in and the pot was 9,000 chips.  You would have to be insain to play slots in this game for an extended period of time.
Video Blackjack:
This is the only game that doesn't seem to be calibrated to destroy you.  The only game inside this casino I do not have  a poor review for... Yet..
Keno:
My only complaint about this game is that it seems as though your win ratio turns from 1 out of every 9 plays to 1 out of every 3 whenever this game becomes the daily.
Big Wheel 6:
This game seems to be working in the opposit fassion than it normally should.  Obviously, you should have a statistically higher chance of seeing a 1 or a 2 over any other number correct?  Yet, if you were to sit down and bet 5, 10, 20, J, and $ you would magically come out ahead almost every single time.  Isn't that curious?
War:
War is supposed to be a game that is literally 50% win ratio.  You're lucky to win 1 out of every 5 hands.  Unless of course, War happens to be the daily.  Then, you are magically coming out ahead always.  Outside of the daily, going to war is supposed to be a stistical 1/8 or so chance.  Yet, in this game.. I've averaged it with about 1/14 or so.  Isn't that curious?  What's crious is it seems to be almost exactly 1/7 when War is the daily. Huh??
Baccarat:
Just like war, a tie bet should be about 1 out of every 8 chances.  Yet, i've hand counted time and again that 90% of ties seem to occur between 12 and 16 times.  Maybe it's because they don't want someone who's rich enough to spam bet come out ahead?  Hmm?  Curious!
Bingo:
It seems you have a 25% chance every time you sit down for the table, your mouse, or something involved with the game in general to be buggy.  Outside of this, there seems to be all kinds of kinks and issues with the game that make it unplayable or slacking on a fun scale.  Lets not forget the insain buy ins to play a round of bingo however!  The progressive bingo games which have the biggest pots are 5 grand to buy in.  Most of the time, 20 people are playing.  You're going to lose that money.  Of course, the free buy ins only have about 3 grand for the pot.  True, you can argue that's because nobody is buying in.  But, can we expect the casino to fetch in some chips towards the pot? NOPE!!!
Regular blackjack and single deck:
Blackjack is one of those games that you should have the statistical advantage over the house simply because the dealer is forced against their will to hit until they reach 17 or higher or bust.  Yet, magically...  It is a mirricle to see the dealer bust in this game.  As a matter of fact, i've clocked blackjack busts to average for me one in every 12 hands.  Usually, some witchcraft occurs where the dealer will hit 7 times and get a perfect 21 more often than not.
Roulette:
Finally, we are now starting to talk about a Casino game I enjoy to play.  Why do I enjoy this?  Well, I believe myself to be keen with math and statistics.  I also enjoy the game in general and know many play styles.  However, the first thing to point out is that the dimonds on the table are backwords which automatically means more randomization for predictions.  Curious?  Then, there is what I like to call the conservative betting system.  You know?  The system where if you sat there 10 hours straight you'd come out ahead?  Bet on red, closest row, center row leaving you know? 4 blacks, 0-00, and the 8 reds minor loss?  I promise you if you did this system or its mirror, you will go bankrupt and FAST.  Isn't that curious?  Or when you happen to just spam the 50/50 bets and lose far more often than not.  Or you know, betting on seemingly anything and its seemingly elsewhere the ball finds itself no matter what you do?  You could say I'm a conspiricy therist with regards to roulette in this game but maybe some of my comments coming up will change your opinion.
Poker:
Oh yes, Poker...  There are 52 cards in a deck and four of each card with a different suit.  Nobody will argue this.  What I will however argue, is how I manage to get Queen with an off suit 2 through 7 twice at the same table, every single table I've ever played since I've installed this game.  Curious how that keeps happening, huh?  It's almost statistically impossible.  Yet, it keeps happening.
Craps:
Ah yes, save the best and favorite for last.  The game that the house doesn't have the advantage of.  This also just happens to be the one game that is the reason that I'm now out of chips entirely for the fourth time in a row.  Curious as to how it happened? So am I...  One of my favorite and also simplest bets to do is to simply min bet the come out roll like you should.  When it rolls and you are On, you simply bet three times the come out roll or more on the Don't come Bar, then you bet some chump change on craps, any 7, and 12. M:DtD is a story driven point&click game, starting from the moment the ship crash lands, and it's up to the player to fix it and get the hell out of that evil ridden planet.

Morningstar; Descent to Dearock is a sci-fi point and click adventure where you play as the survivor of a ship that has crashed onto a planet.  While there is no time limit to the game, the atmosphere conveys a need to progress through in order to escape as soon as possible.  The voice acting is pretty bad, making it hard to push through, but as you play through the game, there is less dialogue making it easier to stomach the farther you get in the game.
The story is decent, and does a good job of connecting you to the character that you pay as, but it is the gameplay that makes this game worth playing. You need to find items as you progress through the world and combine these items in different ways in order to progress forward. It doesn't feel like a scavenger hunt, as so many adventure games do.  The game didn't hold my hand as I went through, but it did use  puzzles and items in such a way that I had to use my brain, and work to solve the problems (even through the hint system is tied well into the story and doesn't make you feel like a cheater). This made me feel more like the character that was portrayed rather than some 3rd party player, thus why it may of added to the difficulty at times, but this also help set a stronger atmosphere.
The game was solid and sensible, and I enjoyed playing this game despite its few flaws.

I've always had a soft spot for Point and Click adventure games, they take me back to an earlier time in my gaming career when I could sit down in front of the latest Lucasarts game and lose myself with Loom, Full Throttle or Monkey Island.
My rose tinted view of these old classics tends to forget the ridiculously convoluted inventory puzzles that made up a large part of the problem solving mechanic in these games.
You remember those frustrating puzzles where you'd find yourself spending hours combining items  in your inventory at random to try and figure out what on earth you're supposed to do next.
This isn't a problem you're likely to encounter in Morningstar, A point and click sci-fi adventure developed by Red Herring Labs.
The puzzles here are entertaining and logical,  if you put a little thought into each problem you encounter here (which are mostly about finding parts and fixing machinery) then you're unlikely to find yourself stuck for too long without having to resort to the "I don't know why I'm trying to combine these items" tactic that was required in the old school titles.
There aren't  really any hidden object puzzles to  worry about  either, everything item you'll need should be fairly apparent to you as you move your mouse around the screen. There are no frustrating pixel hunts to stress you out.
This simplistic approach is  quite refreshing and  allows you to focus on the titles main selling point, the story.
Descent to Deadrock tells a compelling and mysterious tale.
The game opens with your ship crashing onto a seemingly barren desert planet. There are only two survivors, the ships captain  "Novak" and You!
Novak, like the ship itself, is in a bad  way following the crash, so it's  going to be down to you to find the items you'll need to try and repair the ship and hopefully escape the planet.
Along the way you'll scratch the surface of some of the mysteries Deadrock keeps.
Don't expect full disclosure though, Deadrock holds its secrets tightly and your main goal here is to escape the planet, there will be unanswered questions after you complete this game.
And complete it you will...
It's the strong intriguing story that'll keep  you playing though the couple of hours required to complete Morning Star.
You'll probably finish it in one sitting, which isn't necessarily a  bad thing.
There's a lot to be said for a bite sized, focused tale that completes its story arc in two hours.
A movie gives us a couple of hours entertainment and that is exactly what you'll get here, two hours of sci-fi mystery interspersed with some exploration and problem solving.
Based on an old flash game, this outing of Morningstar presents itself mostly as static screens where you'll be searching for and using items to either fix machinery or get past obstacles.
These static visuals are nothing if not atmospheric, the stillness in each location creates a sense of tension and isolation as you explore your crashed ship and later the surrounding area of Deadrock.
Due to all this stillness, when animation is used, it has a much greater impact than you'd imagine.
There are also some cut scenes, not many, but they are very effective in pulling you into the moment, I just wish there were more of them.
The game is fully voiced, and whilst the voice acting isn't going to win any awards, it is competent enough to keep the story moving forward without breaking the immersion.
Should you get Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock?
That depends on what you're looking for in a point and click adventure game.
If you're looking for an epic, sweeping tale to lose yourself in for weeks, challenging puzzles and state of the art cut scenes, then no, Morningstar isn't that game.
However, if you're looking to invest a couple of hours in an enigmatic sci-fi setting, enjoy some thoughtful but not too challenging puzzles and be entertained in an encapsulated narrative experience, then you could do a lot worse than spend an evening with Morningstar.

I can honestly say I was thinking about playing the original Morningstar game, when the title of the tituar game came accross my screen.

Sure enough, you play as 'Powell' a crew-member of the Morningstar space-ship, which hits (literrally) a bit of a problem in the shape of crash-landing on a forbidden and mysterious planet (also nicknamed 'Deadrock).
As the only guy who's either alive or not impaled, it's up to Powell's job to fix the ship and explore this seemingly dead planet......which may not be so dead afterall!
I'm not sure whether the game's creators employed the same voice-artists from the original game, but they've done a fairly satisfying job.
The graphics are nice and so is the interface, though admittedly i did have to consult the walkthrough on a few occassions....but most of the time, the slightly impaled Captain Novak can offer words of assistance and encouragement via the radio.
Overall, Morningstar-DTD is a fine remake and makes me long for a sequel or at least more explaination about the mysterious the 'Deadrock' holds, but for almost 3 hours of gameplay for a small price, I was quite delighted.

I picked up Sunless Sea on a steam sale. This little hidden gem may not look too amazing but the game itself is one of my favorites.
If you are a fan of HP Lovecraft, as I am, this is probably the game for you. The world in which the game exists is incredibly detailed and full of ancient myths and lore, most of which are alien and terrifying. It's based on a browser game called Fallen London, however I never played it and still could pretty quickly understand what was going on. The gameplay itself is that of a roguelike with many survival elements too. It is very slow paced game, though tension as you wander dangerous unexplored oceans can still get the adrenaline going.
Knowledge is key and I don't think I would've been able to play it as far as I did without referencing the Sunless Sea wiki for many encounters. Decisions are sometimes made blind and luck can play a role too. That may put some people off the game as you either follow online guides or have something horrible happen because you didn't know ahead of time what sort of decision you were facing.
Towards the end of the game (and depending on the victory condition you select for yourself on your character creation) the game does get tedious. I've got tons of hours in the game and I still haven't bothered to beat it because of the grind. I still had a lot of fun getting to that point and if I really cared to sit down and grind for the finish I could easily. A game worth checking out, though probably best to catch on sale.

Story? It's a dark and stormy night. You play a journalist investigating goings-on at a mental hospital called Cliche Asylum (at night, for some reason) and after committing a felony by breaking and entering you are shocked to discover the place has been taken over by Horror Cliches. Mad scientists, crazed patients, religious fanatics, ghosts, hillbillies... And that's really as far as I got before throwing in the towel. I got tired of dying over and over because some patroling psycho was apparently psychic and I didn't care enough about the "plot" to duke it out. There's frustrating fun and then there's frustrating annoying, and Outlast falls into the later category.

Imagine...
You are the captain of a small ship, sailing through the dark subterranean sea, darkness surrounds you and only a small beam of light from the bow lights your way ahead. Your crew is restless, the endless dark and the haunting screeches of zeebats faintly echo from somewhere far away.
Your charts are incomplete, only showing you where you've already been, and outside of the routes you've traveled there is only unknowable darkness filled with unknowable terrors. Your fuel and supplies are running low. Its been a long voyage, and you had to take a longer route than you anticipated to avoid running afoul of a deep-sea horror twice the size of your vessel. You slowly start to realize that you don't have enough fuel to make it back to port via the rout that you took. You look again at your charts, and fixate on the enormous black void that lies between you and the most direct line to safety, to home.
There is no other option. Its either a slow death at sea, trapped aboard your fuel-starved vessel, or braving that abyss. You put away your maps, and order fuel to be added to the boiler; you set your sights towards the unknown.
A few days into the voyage, the uninhabited islands that dotted the sea around you slowly start to grow less and less frequent. The shining coral and bio-luminescent seaweed beneath the waves vanishes as well. For the first time ever, there is nothing. No monsters, no islands, not even the chatter and screech of bats. Your crew goes silent, and the only sound to pierce the void is the lonely patter of your aging boiler as it pushes you farther into the black.
Your palms sweat, yet your mouth is dry. It feels wrong, it all feels so very wrong. You should not have come, you should not have sailed here. But its too late, you cannot turn back now, not enough fuel, not enough food, not enough time.
Then you feel it, a tremor passes through you, faint and distant. There is something out there, and it knows you're here...
And it the middle of the darkness, dead ahead, something opens its eye from beneath the water. And SEES YOU.

I highly recommend this classic fantasy strategy gem. For anyone that grew up playing the Heroes series, Age of Empires, Civ, etc. they will find a lot to like here. It has a nice mix of light empire building, strategy, deep combat, and a branching quest for both the heroes (Keepers) and villains (Cult of Storms). It also offers a plethora of non campaign missions which are great once you've beaten the main game. There is also a custom mapmaker for those who want to craft their own quests. Well worth a try, and if you factor in all of the content, it's a great deal for the money! If you like this one, I also recommend picking up the trilogy pack (Age of Wonders II and the Shadow Magic add-on) as the sequels expand on the solid gameplay mechanics. Recently, the highly anticipated Age of Wonders III finally released so if you have played that title and like what you see, try out the original games which inspired it.
UPDATE: With the Steam awards being announced, I decided to nominate this fantastic game for the "Test of Time" game award. Hope it wins!

Survival has such incredible depth; leaving the planning and resource management up to you, that I'm amazed there is still such a rich environment to explore beneath the core mechanics. The many different zones are home to painstakingly detailed houses, mobile homes, gas stations, watchtowers, caves and many more, all with their own stories to tell through inference. Supplies and tools have a multitude of different uses; matches to light fires and light your way around a pitch black house, hatchets to harvest animals, break down limbs and furniture or clear an ice fishing hole, cloth for repairs, cured entrails for bows, snares and fishing line and many more. Resources are carefully structured in a way to perpetuate your inevitable journey onward from home to home, but with enough ingenuity, a relatively long stay in one area is certainly achievable. It is really nice to become attached to one's shelter, each room becoming a place to store goods or cure gut, your bed will become a good friend.
The game manages to continually astound me with its beauty, sound, environment and features. A must for anyone interested in a semi-nomadic survival game.

You can pause the game while you decide how to spend your credits or how to best develop your tracks. That gives you a better sense of control over how the game plays out and allows you to adjust when something unexpected happens.
If you're looking for a deep game just avoid it, while just go for it if what I said resonates well with what you like in gaming. It is not for everyone, but it works well and shines within its niche.

I can say I really liked the story of the game, even if the ending cinematic should have been longer, in my opinion. The soudtrack, which contains jazz and soul music of the 40s/50s and also some creepy parts like in horror movies, contributes to the great atmosphere of Rapture.
About the gameplay I can say I was really satisfied with it. Fighting Big Daddies was really challenging, especially in the beginning of the game when you didn't have so many weapons and plasmids like the late part of the game. The enemies that I encountered throughout the game are also quite varied. Some of them will shoot from range with a weapon, while some will prefer to do melee attacks from behind or even from the ceiling. There are also turrets, drones and cameras which will trigger alarms (they can be hacked to shoot enemies instead of you) . Also, you can do some nice combos using plasmids and weapons.
One thing that bothered me a little was that the key binds for the plasmids always changed after you found a new plasmid, and it was a bit frustrating when pressing the key you thought it was a certain plasmid to find that it was another one.
The most annoying thing for me were the crashes to desktop. There weren't too many of them, but when it happened, all my settings were reset, including screen resolution and the gameplay settings, which I had to change back again. This usually didn't take more than 30 seconds, though.
If I had to give this game a mark, it would be 9.5/10.

Immensely fun mindless violence. It is in every dimension an improvement on previous games in the series.
Be aware that handling is very similar to the original game, and very different from most modern racing games: In Carmageddon, they make it super easy to powerslide sideways into a milling crowd of pedestrians, which is extremely satisfying.
But it does mean that you can't take precision racing seriously. You will be drifting and using walls to help you steer around corners. This is a very out-of-control, chaotic game. Embrace it. Afterwards you will be frustrated with other racing games that make it difficult to powerslide around corners.
This is a good game to just unwind with at the end of a long day to let off some steam. Don't take anything too seriously (the game doesn't). Just marvel at the havoc.
The music is perfect for this game. The graphics are shiny. The gameplay is cathartic and addictive. Some of the crude humour falls flat for me, but that's not a big deal. I am very satisfied with this game.
Common Criticisms:
-	Car Handling: Ultimately this is a matter of preference and you can’t please everyone. If you go in expecting precision, realism, or similar handling to modern racing games, then you will be disappointed. If you played the original Carmageddon games then you should be able to slip right into the groove. It can vary dramatically depending on the car. For example, I found The Twister to be the easiest and most forgiving car to drive. Vlad’s Impaler is basically impossible to drive. Try out different ones.
-	Graphics: This game does have a tinge of cartoon stylisation, particularly with the powerups and the pedestrians. Running them over isn’t so much brutal as goofy as they try to hop away with only one leg left. This is a game of cartoon slapstick violence. Effects like blood and explosions are a bit simplified and stylised, and while I personally would prefer a realistic brutal feel to the gore, it certainly doesn’t stop me enjoying the game. Everything else, especially the vehicles and the vehicle damage system, is visually stunning.
-	Carmageddon Reincarnation: There is a lot of confusion about this. You can think of Carmageddon Max Damage, as being Carmageddon Reincarnation Redux/Remastered/Definitive Edition. It improves on every aspect of Reincarnation (especially optimisation, bug fixes and graphical fidelity) and adds a whole bunch of new content (new cars, new map, new peds). And if you own Reincarnation, then you already have received Max Damage for free (If you haven’t then maybe contact their support team). So yes, it is basically Reincarnation Remastered. That isn’t really a criticism since, like I said, you got this game for free if you owned the original.
-	Bugs/Crashes: I haven’t encountered any yet.
-	Too Hard: I imagine this is probably due to frustration with the handling not being what you expect from a racing game, making you feel like you have little control. Another reason can be that your car can feel very fragile. This depends a lot on the car (they come in tiers, so the cars at the early stages of the game are much weaker in terms of offence and defence than those at the end). You might need to unlock or choose a tougher car or upgrade its armour. But once again, I have to say, if this is bothering you then you are probably taking failure too seriously. Just go nuts and have fun smashing things (including yourself)!
-	Too Easy: This mostly comes down to the fact that you can repair your car (the AI opponents cannot). When you do get smashed to bits, there isn’t that much of a penalty except cash for repairs. This is why I say it really doesn’t matter and just have fun. The other source of easiness is that the AI is a bit dumb. It does act stupid at times, but the game’s attitude is so silly it is hard to tell if that is on purpose. I would say to both the “too hard” and “too easy” people: You are taking this game too seriously. This game is great for just unwinding, mucking around smashing stuff, exploring, finding a massive ramp, launching yourself off the edge and laughing as you land with a crash, upside-down and on fire.

THIS is the new Carmageddon everyone has been waiting for, with much better optimisation running at 60 FPS and more cars and levels compared to Reincarnation, there is nothing not to love for fans of the original game.
If you have played Reincarnation before and didn't like it or were put off by the lack of optimisation, then play this and it should change your mind. Carmageddon: Max Damage is basically the same game as Reincarnation, but with many improvements, fixes and content added to make it a much better and enjoyable experience.
For people who haven't played a Carmageddon game before, then this is a car combat game that has no guns or launchers attached to the car, oh no, you have to be more up close and personal instead. The focus on winning matches is "wasting" all other enemy cars by crashing into them until you turn them into a crumpled broken mess, or by using an assortment of random and fun powerups, such as an anvil launcher, a giant flail, mines or something like a super turbo boost.
The damage modelling is great, crashing into a specific part of a car will crush and bend that area of the car, with bodywork also coming off and possibly wheels to if you try hard enough. Just like in Carmageddon 2, you can also split cars by crashing them into a corner of a building or static object.
Multiplayer is also very fun with a variety of gamemodes and levels to play on, nothing is more fun than launching your friend far into the sky by using an opponent repulsificator (or massive spring if you don't know).
Overall, this game is worth a try even if you aren't a fan of these type of games, Carmageddon 1 and 2 has had a very strong and loyal modding community and this game will have as well, so you can enjoy even mroe cars, level or powerups made by modders of the community! There is no Steam Workshop support currently, but you can look at the Carmageddon forums online for mods.
Oh, and you can also win matches by killing every ped, or finishing the race. Except if you play this game to win by racing, you're doing it wrong!
