I'd say this game is like Contra, with more customization. It's a lot of fun, and the unique bosses keep things interesting. My only gripe is that all the bosses have no health meter display, so you never know what weapon is making the most headway in a fight, and you also never know when the boss is going to change to their next tier. It sort of just becomes a shoot and pray method which I don't particularly like. Another small gripe is the perry system where you press the jump button in midair shield against pink projectiles. It's a cool idea, but requiring to be in midair to perry limits your options, and there are a lot of jump through platforms in the game that will make you land on the ground before you can perry a projectile thus getting hit by it instead. just having the perry button assigned to another button would fix this issue, but I guess the developers wanted to keep the button use count to a minimum. Luckily, besides these issues, I find this game really fun, and think it's a solid game to have in your inventory, it just suffers really small hickups.

There will be times where this game will get your heart beating. This game does capture the same atmosphere as Half-Life 1 and keeps it fairly similar to the original game as far as other game developers go. The company behind this game 'Gearbox Software' did a good job of developing this game and expanding on it.
Cons:
This game is not very long me personally only getting about 2-3 hours of gameplay. Also I feel like the story should have been a bit more engaging and more weaponry. This game was made by a different company to the first game thus not being fully as amazing and fantastic as Half Life 1.

A good game to play after finished with Half Life 1. It is very short thus you wont get too much value for money (If you do that thing where you follow the 1£/1 hour rule). I recommend getting this game in the anthology bundle or on sale to get true value.

is one of the latest point-and-click adventures to hit the PC/Steam marketplace. However, this independent title is one that may very well sneak under many a fan of the genre's radar. It was developed by the relatively new studio Red Herring Labs (
), which was then picked up for distribution through Phoenix Online Studios. The game itself is touted as being in the category of "Atmospheric First Person", placing you in a nightmarish struggle to escape an alien planet in one piece. It also happens to be a remastered version of the older PC title
. But does this updated entry stand as a good modern take on the style, or is it nothing more than recycled cliche's that are far from enjoyable?
This story follows one of the ship's crew mates named Powell. He and the captain are the only survivors of a simple mission, having crashed on the alien planet referred to as Deadrock. You are tasked to not only help your superior officer, but also repair the engines in order to escape. Of course, you don't have everything you need on board, and soon you are forced to explore the planet, as well as the remains of another downed ship and deceased crew. However, the more you explore, the more the mysterious stone heads scattered about become an ominous sign that you are not alone.
The game mechanics are just about as traditional as the story itself. Other than fantastically developed and rendered cut scenes for the opening and closing, much of visuals are images that only move when you interact in a way that would affect them, such as removing or opening a door, causing a device to explode, or simply picking an item up to keep in your inventory. The puzzles require you to find the right item, often in order for you to progress like going outside or to replace necessary fluids to help you survive the long trip back home, as well as require a number of things you will need to put together in order to solve said puzzle or create some crude replacement part when necesary. Sometimes these combinations are a bit cryptic, but you can always call your injured higher up on the radio and get a hint as to what to do next.
On top of that, it's nearly impossible to miss investigating every little object you can interact with. Much like calling for assistance, this does detract from some of the difficulty in the game, which only comes in one mode: Casual. But, by the time you finish, you'll realize this wasn't meant to be that perplexing. There are some times, however, when you can overlook things like codes or patterns later on thanks to clues that don't really point you in the right direction. This is a major issue later on (one that made me spend an hour running between three different rooms cursing up a storm as to why the planetary sequences wouldn't do anything to the main device in the ship), though it has been kind of fixed thanks to updates that hit around the time of launch. These improvements mostly factor into the keyboard you enter the sequences in, making it a little easier to do so, as well as removing the coding on the left side of the screen during the aforementioned cinematics (something that appeared in the game prior to release).
And then there's the voice acting, which is as standard as everything else in this game. The cast literally sounds like they are just reading off cue cards, rarely adding an emotion outside of sarcasm, especially when insulting one another in a manner that seems only jovial due to the dire circumstances at hand. Powell will narrate basically every move you make, so the hum drum approach does grow tiring after a while, especially when you end up a bit stumped as to what to to do next. This is, sadly, the only real punishment for abusing the easy item system. You can try combining items or placing them anywhere at any time, as long as you're willing to hear the same bland dialogue over and over if it doesn't work. Other than that, there seems to be no major repercussions that I have experienced.
But, what it all comes down is if the game itself is fun, and, yes, it is. A lot of the charm from the original is still captured here, even with the new shine the modern darker visuals bring to the table.
doesn't set out to be anything but an enjoyable, casual point-and-click Adventure game that you don't need to put a lot of effort into, or worry about forgetting something important other than certain sequences later on. The only major gripe is that the mystery of those stone heads aren't really explored outside of logs you discover. A few more cinematic scenes also would have been nice to have, though their absence doesn't really impact the title negatively. But, everything functions just as it should, and there's just enough going on to keep the player engaged for the roughly two hours that this little quest ends up being.

For the seasoned fan of point-and-click graphical adventures, this game could provide a reasonable morsel to tide you over between other releases. It was entertaining enough to play for the time it lasted, but it's short (about two hours), the voice acting is abysmal, and the story is not particularly gripping or compelling. The great mysteries of the planet never really get plumbed, many of the puzzles have solutions that strain plausibility, there's an awful lot of pixel hunting (the only part I finally looked up in a walkthrough turned out to hinge just on me having not seen a hot spot on the screen -- once I was alerted to that, it was fine), and not LOTS of try-this-with-that, but not none either. All of these design issues will be familiar to, and probably reasonably okay with the seasoned fan as mentioned above, but likely frustrating to anyone who isn't used to dealing with such things regularly. I did enjoy playing it for the evening it took, but I suspect within a couple of months I won't remember that it existed.

"Zombie Survival Game." These words have been thrown around a lot, in recent years. Sadly, most of these games are about superhuman freaks, surviving wave after wave of cannibalistic creatures, and being unable to become one of them due to either excess weaponry, ridiculously weak enemies, or just simple immunity. This game takes that idea, and flips it on its head.
Project Zomboid is the best zombie survival game on the market. The Indie Stone has taken almost everything into account, and has taken suggestions from the community to fill in any gaps. Imagine for a moment, if a zombie apocalypse were to happen right now. Think about how you would react. It's do or die time. The zombies are here, right outside your front door, and all you have to survive with are the objects inside your house. You aren't a specially trained soldier, or a secret ninja trained in the art of silent kills, you're just a normal, ordinary, Average Joe. You had a common occupation, be it carpenter, nurse, farmer, or even unemployed.
Interested, yet?
You have to think about your decisions very carefully, or else death will come much sooner than you'd want it to. You wake up in your house, and the end is here. What's your first move? Do you search through your house for anything useful before heading out? Or do you take your chances and run to the place with the best weapons? Either choice could end with you dying. Think about it this way: You're screwed no matter what. The only thing you're trying to do is see how long you can make it. Can you survive more than 1 day in Knox County? Most people can't.
How about now?
Let's say you were smart and looted your house and the surrounding houses for anything useful. You have yet to run into any zombies. Lucky break! Your supplies currently consist of half a fridge of foodstuffs, a baseball bat, your clothes, and some sheets. You're organizing your storage upstairs when you hear the telltale sign of glass shattering. Oh, no! You forgot to close the curtains and the zombies have broken into your safehouse! You're on the top floor, and now that the undead are downstairs you have to choose between going downstairs and confronting them, or jumping out of the second-story window.
Suspenseful enough for you?
You don't much like the idea of being bitten and subsequently dying of infection, so you choose to jump. Not very smart, since you don't have any nails and didn't craft a sheet rope to use as a ladder. Now your femur is sticking out of your shin. It hurts, but the zombies have spotted you and are quickly closing in on you! You try to run, but with only one good leg and the smell of blood giving away your position, you only make it so far before being completely surrounded and eaten.
Womp womp womp.~
Well... You died. That certainly sucks. There weren't really that many zombies downstairs, either. You probably could have taken them out with that butter knife you had in your kitchen, once you evaded their slow-moving grasp. Now that you think about it, you had plenty of sheets, and probably could have just put those up on the windows to use as curtains. That way they wouldn't have seen you rummaging around. Every choice counts. Make the wrong one, like you did, and you'll end up hurt, dead, or undead.
Do you dare try again? I would.
1/10 would jump again. 9/10 would make better decisions. All would play again.

*Updated with Pros and Cons after 15 hours of gameplay.*
If you are an old-school Carmageddon fan then I can definitely recommend this game.
Pros:
- significantly improved perfromance
- more variety and stability in car handling (make no mistake, this is still an unforgiving, crazy, skill-based Carmageddon style handling - just more polished, predictable and playable compared to Reincarnation)
- improved visuals
- new ability to stun opponents by hitting them hard
- more content (peds, maps, cars)
- lots of rebalancing
- lots of small details and polishing touches
Cons:
- peds are still not very satisfying to run over, although new sound effects made a slightly better impression than in C:R
- overall audio design and mixing aren't very good and would deserve an overhaul (no, this is not something you can fix by messing with audio settings options)
- I am not really a fan of the singleplayer experience of death race modes as AI does not seem very capable at competing in it (luckily the main classic carma mode works very well)
If you enjoy crazy sandbox gameplay to let out some steam and if you liked Reincarnation but wasn't satisfied with it's performance or you had minor car-handling/balancing issues then definitely try Max Damage.
Also don't forget that the game is fully modable and have a truly dedicated community that makes amazing cars and gameplay mods for the game (check out the forums as there is no workshop so far).
Also, to see a true gameplay and competitive-multiplayer potential of this game, check out YT videos by Fr0nt and Sa1cor. Those guys are crazy skilled and can really demonstrate the game's gameplay possibilities (masterful combination of great handling, map knowledge and power-ups usage).
Even though I have an old notebook I enjoy playing the game (btw I played 191 hours in Carmageddon: Reincarnation if my gameplay experience matters to you).

I played this game for a while and even if I enjoyed it, I would not recommend for full game price. Maybe at 80% discount, perhaps. Major thingies regarding to the game, both good and bad.
- Lackluster singple player campaign, the only fun part is to play together with friends and laugh at random stuff. It's kind of fun, IF you can make your peace with certain issues.
- The price is a huge ripoff, the standard Tropico 5 game has barely any content. Lack of industry buildings, lack of certain military buildings and so on. However, the developer and/or the publisher decided to scatter the content across ridiculously priced DLCs. Waterborne includes many essential buildings for 20 euros. WTF #1... It really applies the worst Paradox and Firaxis business schemes. Release a barebone game for full price, then release rest of the game as DLCs and basically you have to pay like the double or triple. How about ♥♥♥♥ you developer/publisher?
- Overall mood and tone of the game is fun, but the random generated missions are just crappily scripted and designed. I have drones flying around in my city and all the modern age improvements, then I get a mission which gives me the technology to exploit oil. WTF #2
- Combat system is broken, units frequently stuck and you can only define a single high priority building to defend, that's all. It's kind of annoying, when attack can come from multiple directions. Assigning units to groups and give them orders? Developer says no. WTF #3
- The game mechanics is poorly or not even documented, it takes a while to figure out the inner workings, even then you have to go with your gut feeling.
- Multiplayer is abysmal, desynchronization happens frequently even with top-notch PC and internet connection (I'm talking about fibre connection with 50/50Mbit) and the game can slow down considerably in later stages of the game. WTF #4 (obviously no dedicated servers, I guess the ~80-100 euros full price of the standard game+DLC doesn't allow Kalypso to maintain a couple of)
- Road building is a nightmare. You made an accidental turn or curve due to the lack of vision of trees and other stuff? Too bad, you can't delete. Maybe you can. But based on what it depends if you can or cannot, you will never know. WTF #5
- The game just abruptly ends after a few hours of multiplayer gameplay, nothing to research, nothing to progress toward.
...and many, many more. The game is fun, yet ultimately flawed and the developers seem to care only about churning out overpriced DLCs. For 30, or MAYBE 40 euros (standard game + DLCs) it's a pretty good fun, enjoyable with friends. Otherwise, avoid as plague.
PS: If even a single player from a 4 players multiplayer doesn't have a given DLC, it's disabled for all players. Talk about ripoff...

The Expendabros...Where to begin...
Story: Conrad Stonebanks, yahdayahdayahda...Story isn't a big part of this game. That's a good thing, but I still need to give it a fair rating overall...2/5.
Graphics: For a pixelated game, these graphics are spot on. The massive amount of blood and flying limbs from enemies are great, and fire and explosions look really good. Furthermore, the character's faces will change when you use their weapons, which is a nice touch. If that isn't enough, I experienced no lag while running the game. 4.7/5.
Sound: The music and backround noises within the game fit perfectly. Each enemy lets out a satisfying "BLEH" upon death, and I never got tired of the deep-voiced narrator shouting "NOOOOOO!" At my imminent death. 5/5.
Gameplay: It might be a fairly short game, but it that time period, Expendabros gives you a lot to choose from. There are seven unlockable characters, which you gain by "rescuing" them from cages scattered aroud the levels. Each of them use a different weapon, including flamethrowers, dual-pistols, miniguns, and throwing knives. If you approach natives, you can make them your personal allies by handing them AK-47s. Also, by pressing 'T,' you can have another friend join in on the fun. 5/5.
My conclusion? Download this game immediately. For a game based off of a movie (Expendables 3), this is awesome. 9.75/10.

This game is freaking amazingly perfefct.
By far one of the best side-scroll platformers/puzzle games I have ever played.
Puzzle mechanics and controls (5 buttons!) are simple and self-explanatory; the complexity doesn't come through confusing mechanics but through the necessity for application of real-life physics like momentum and gravity. While the gameplay starts slow, it quickly ramps up in difficulty and excitement.
The atmosphere and world-building is beautiful. Sound design and visual aesthetic are haunting and minimalistic; in intense sections of gameplay surrounded by buzzsaws and spiders I would almost consider it a horror game. Unlike conventional games that forcefeed a cliched narrative into the player. LIMBO subtly builds up intricacy and detail in every level, revealing a wonderfully rendered post-apocalyptic world where the remnants of inhumane technology meet the barbaric remnants of nature. Small details like the way an automatic gun creates indents in a wall, or the way that flaming tyres hurled down a slope have accumulated in a crevasse over time, are what gives this game the added realism and immediacy that makes it so so good. Ultimately a simple but incredibly haunting tale about love and death, and an endless life in limbo. :)

Your starship gets caught in some sort of magnetic disturbance, and your ship is pulled down onto the surface of a planet that has a reputation of being 100% dead. Funny thing is that perhaps that's not completely true, but you are going to have to find your way through this point click adventure to find out what this planet has to hide, and are you going to be able to get off this planet in one piece.
Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock is by Red Herring Labs and will take you on an hour and a half ride where you will get to explore this "Dead Rock" and try to find anything and everything you need to potentially get off of the planet. You will have to combine items, find items, and fix issues in order to advance the game.
The one thing that I can honestly say that ended up bugging me about the game was the EXTREMELY deadpan voice of the lead actor in the game. He definitely had the almost monotone approach of not getting a damn about anything as well as never being shocked or excited about anything. That's not to say that the other voice actor was that much better, but at least they gave a little bit of feeling to the game.
I liked the look of the game, and it was pretty straightforward in how you navigated around. You are going to see almost always 1 single view of a room or an area, there might be deeper parts of the area/room that you can explore and get a new vantage point on, but this is definitely not a game where you are going to have to search every nook and cranny to find what you are looking for.
Once again, perhaps its my time away from point and clicks until recently, but there is a hint system in place, and it was good to see that it was actually useful with out making me feel dumb. There were a couple of times where I struggled to find out what to do next, but thanks to the hint system I was able to easily get back on track.
I can honestly say the further I got into the game, the more I actually got into the game. What I mean to say is that it took me a little bit of time to find the pace, but when I finally found the pace of the game I was ready to move. It was unfortunate that once I got up to speed I found the end of the game, but hey it says something that I had no issue of playing the game straight through.
So I guess the question now is should you get this game... Well I think if you are looking for something light, has a futuristic space theme, is a point click adventure built around survival, you are going to enjoy this game. As I mentioned before the only big issue I had with it was the voice acting of the main character, and before anyone asks, there are really only 2 voice actors, so that sort of didn't do it for me, but then again it wasn't like he talked the entire time. This game gets a 7.5 out of 10.

Blue Shift is a very short expansion pack for Half Life 1 for a reason, and it is the fact that, unlike Opposing Force, it doesn't add anything too new to the game. The same weapons present in Half Life 1 are seen here, but the weapons that were in Opposing Force not being in this expansion pack is a mystery to me. I mean, at least the .357 pistol could be here since Otis uses it. Anyhow, it is short because Gearbox knew there was no point in trying to make it as long as Opposing Force since there wasn't much new content aside from yet another view of the Black Mesa incident from a security guard's eyes and a new scientist character that never appeared in any HL game after this one.
Still, Blue Shift still feels like how a Half Life game should feel like. The feeling of loneliness is much more present here and I have to say the atmosphere is very immersive, just like in the original Half Life and Opposing Force. If you enjoyed Half Life 1, go ahead and play this one too for some extra 2 or 3 hours of Half Life experience as Barney Calhoun.

I just recently played this for the first time:
I would definately recommend this game to anyone, even the scardey cats like me! Although I am a huge sucker for jump scares, and that's the whole point of this game, I really enjoyed playing it.
Here's the breakdown!
1. It was easy to understand. There isn't much to tell you what to do, but to be honest the first night kinda plays out like a tutorial. There is still some risk to losing, I assume, but that in itself would be a hard thing to accomplish (unless you left the doors closed and the lights on the whole time). In my opinion even people who don't play games too often would quickly understand that the main objective is not to run out of power!
2. It's very immersive. I find that this point is one we often take for granted. How many games can you honestly say you have been completely sucked in to? So much so that you forget that the time is in fact not 2am, and you are not sitting in a creepy office blubbering and praying that the adorably creepy animatronics don't pop to stuff your body into a metal suit, counting the seconds until 6am, or machoing it up and pretending like you don't care that your power is on 1% and it's only just hit 5am!
3. The sounds are creepy AF! Having worked on a few mobile games with an indie company I know first hand that sounds play a key role in any game. They can literally make or break a game. This point is also something I think a lot of people take for granted, but I have really got to hand it to the developer here! The ambience is spot on for this game, and I can't decide if I hate that fact or love it.
4. It's actually scary. I don't know why, I don't know how, but I was on the edge of my seat while playing this. Sure, I've seen one or two videos on YouTube of people playing this game, but it is NOTHING compared to actually playing it. The difference between watching it and playing it is astounding.
For all the positives there are, there isn't much that really brings the game down. Keeping in mind that this is an indie developed game, and there was probably no budget going into it, I can see why it has taken off and developed into a thriving series. The only thing I would do to improve this game is maybe add in a pause menu, or at least change the fact that the esc key completely terminates the game. I accidentally pressed it in an attempt to close the in game monitor before I realised you just hover the mouse over the [VVVVV].

The differences aren't worth the price tag, but if you've got the cash, I'd recommend the buy. The game's solid and I'd love to see the developers get some support and make a new game. All in all, I'm quite happy with my purchase and would suggest it, though for obvious reasons it's not for everbody.

A man named Powell awakens from the hibernation chamber and learns that one of his crew mates didn't survive. He heads to the cockpit to find the Captain of the ship impaled through the stomach by a random piece of debris. He takes a seat and reins in the damaged vehicle as it cascades to the planet below. Powell must now explore the planet and find a way to repair his broken ship.
High Points
Engineering puzzles – The puzzles are sound from an engineering perspective. You’ll find materials and parts to fix broken equipment and structures around the planet. Powell and the Captain will give us hints on how to use the parts, and from those hints we will craft makeshift sensors and explosives.
Creepy Atmosphere – Descent to Deadrock has a truly creepy feel to it. Stone statues of unknown origin watch over a sandy wasteland. Wrecked ships and dead bodies are strewn about the desolate planet leaving only the mystery of how they died. It creates a tense sensation while you search for a means to escape.
Average Points
Dem Graphics – The visuals are very 1998, and that would be acceptable if not for the stillness of the game play. It reminds me of older games like Shadowgate or Déjà Vu. You are mostly watching a still image that only reacts when you interact with a puzzle piece. I wouldn't say it’s bad, but it could use a touch of life to the environments. Wind blowing the sand, the Captain struggling to breathe in his suit, anything that makes the world feel alive.
Low Points
Voice Acting – The voice acting for the main character isn't awful, but it’s not very effectual or interesting. It’s clear that this person is just reading his lines off a sheet of paper, and not trying to inject emotion to the situation at hand. The Captain of the ship provides hints and information and he’s actually worse than the main character. I found it difficult to care about the situation when the characters themselves don’t seem to give a damn.
Clickity Click – Morningstar is an adventure game that’s a bit too far in the past. You will swirl around the cursor on the screen looking for places to interact with. The game gives you some reasonable tells to solve most puzzles and even a nice hint system. However, there are still places where you’ll have to just randomly click on items to solve a puzzle.
Short game – You can beat this game in 3 to 4 hours even after all the random clicking. You can just plow right on through to the ending sequence without much of a problem. The ending is anti-climactic as well, and it never really solves a few of the mysteries on the planet.
Conclusion
Morningstar: Descent to Deadrock hearkens back to the olden days of adventure gaming. It is light on animation and the voice acting is only tolerable. I recommend that only fans of the adventure genre invest in the short but eventful game play. If you’re not a fan of the adventure genre it isn't going to convince you to join the genre, and the bad voice work and older design might just scare you off.

In depth look at Porject Zomboid Build 27 and Review
Okay folks, yes, another zombie game but don't pass this one by just yet! As it stand this is early access which means things may or may not change, things may be added, bugs fixed, buffing or nerfing things and so on. Now if you are scared thinking early access games are "meh" I'll wait for full release fine do that but you'll miss out on a discount and see an amazing game grow and change. For an early access game there is a lot to do and enjoy. The Standard map and content have plenty of hours of enjoyment as well as replayable (Which trust me you'll be dieing until you get the hang of it) and aside from the standard game content there is already mod support and community made maps. As is I haven't tried anything but standard game but I'm sure if there is something you feel you want in your playthrough,  someone most likely has modded it.
Anyways down to the gameplay and graphics. Okay first graphics, yes may not look 'next gen' but it has it's style and the gameplay works with it very well. As the game gets more funds and work done on it the graphics will and have been improved and I am sure they will keep improving but do not expect this game to blow your mind or melt your GPU it's going to stick around a simple graphic style which works! Sounds and music are great and really add to the game. Sure you can turn off the music but I recommend you keep it on for a while before you go back to blaring your music. As the music changes depending on your situation or what's going on and the ambient sounds are haunting.
Gameplay which by far the most important thing for any zombie game. A lot of the times you pick up a game now a days because it's a zombie survival sandbox or something down that line and sure that may be true for the most part but I couldn't help but feel something is lacking. This brings the element of a big open world loaded with zombies (soon to be with NPCs that can be friendly or hostile) to a whole other level. Every structure is enterable as well as everything is lootable with farely real loot tables at the locations. (Some doors may be locked and alarms may go off if there is power)  On top of this you have to eat and drink to stay a live as well as watch you body temp to make sure you don't catch a cold or get a heat stroke. There is panic levels, depression levels and pain levels which effect your character big time. In the standard gamemode power and water supply will shut off after a couple months ( In game time ) which adds an element of storing water as well as eating perishables and saving non-perishables for later. Also fridges don't stop food from rotting just slows it down! A top of this one scratch can infect you with about a 25% chance and there is no cure and one bite is like a 96% chance of infection. So you surived a few months clear out an area and managed to get you character leveled up in certain skills that makes living easier. You go into a bathroom but since powers out you can't see at all and a zombie jumps you and bites you. That it's for that character his a goner sure you can try to live a few more days with medical supplies but eventually you're going to run out.
Now there is a character setup that allows you to name, select from a handful of starting jobs like a fireman or police officer as well as the sex. As well as traits that effect him/her like 'light drinker,' that gives -2 points and means you can't hold your drink that well and 'clumsy,' that gives you -1 point and makes more noise when walking around  but having negative points and traits allow you to get positive traits like 'light eater,' which is +3 points which makes you character not have to eat so much which can be helpful when food starts to run low. Mix and match to make a character that suits you! Skills and leveling is also very nice in this game. There is a list of skills each belonging to a group that reflect on what they generally do and you start out at level 0 and have to work to level 5 for each skill. As you do things like boarding up a window you gain overall EXP and once you gain enough EXP you level up and gain one point as well as your carpentry skill gets EXP into it. For the first level you go from 0/100 to 100/100 EXP at which point you spend on level point from your overall level to gain level 1 so you can start working on level 2 whcih goes from 0/300 to 300/300 which you then have to spend another point from your overall level which governs and over all allocation of EXP from all skills. There is MP which is still in it's baby stages but coming along and all settings for your game are able to be changed if you play sandbox not survival. That about sums up this very well designed game and even though it's early access I have to say it's more polished then some full release titles that make you pay $60 for.
Sidenote- Camera angles are a bit wonky but not to bad

Update 12/3/17:
This is extremely painful for me to do, surprisingly. I love Project Zomboid. My original review below was made THREE YEARS ago. I do believe the developers are good people who do care about this game and want the product to be a good one. But no matter how many justifications I come up with in my head, no matter how much I want to be able to recommend this game (which is still one of the most fun gaming experiences I have had), the sad fact is, 3 years after writing my review, there truly haven't been significant changes and only recently are cars starting to roll out and be added.
I saw videos of the "new animations" that they said they needed to release before they'd update us on NPC's. That has been over a year. Over a year for an animations update that, honestly, I have no actual hope of being released. The same for NPC's. I just don't see it happening.

Honestly, I love this game. I don't review often, but this is my perspective:
The crafting and base building are very well done. Cooking, using tools, building walls, farming, it's all there. I love the retro look, too. There are little details that make it enjoyable - while still being difficult, making it that much more rewarding when you finally gain all the tools necessary to make your impenetrable base. The game comes at you in waves, changing the gameplay.
First, you start off going house to house, gaining basic supplies, able to cook/collect food fairly easily due to electricity still being on. Eventually, you find a few useful tools, barricade a few windows and doors, and you've got a house you feel safe in with a nice little stash of emergency supplies.
Eventually, you need to run further and further from your home base. Then, the electricity goes off. That's when it gets interesting. You need to craft barrels to collect rain water. You no longer leave your house with little planning: instead of easily being able to cook raw food in ovens, or finding still fresh food in fridges, or drinking water from sinks, you need water bottles, food, weaponry, and supplies for unexpected stays. When it rains, you best stay indoors. When it gets dark, or you get tired, you need to find safety. You'll need to carry around rags to cover windows to avoid being seen, food and items to keep your character sane. Medical supplies to heal wounds.
You'll die often at first, and while it's punishing, your new character can eventually find your old base, and at times, if you're lucky, even your old re-animated corpse. Still, tip: ditch your stuff when you get infected and just go out with a blaze of glory.
The game needs more polish, but the game breaking bugs in almost EVERY other Early Access aren't there. I enjoyed the game thoroughly. I just wish there was more to do. That's what vehicles and NPCs are being created for. I am very excited to go back to this game for NPCs. The developers and extremely dedicated. But I really, really want the extra layer of NPC interaction, HOPEFULLY leading to allies that can stay in your base, do boring tasks like farming, and even go out scavenging with you.
I highly recommend this game, and I think it's worth a purchase right now. It's one of those gems in Steam.

While I'd rate the game as "okay," I really don't get the "Overwhelmingly Positive" ratings for it.  There are several negatives.  First, it's pretty short - I finished it in 24 hours, and I'm the kind of person who investigates every crate and every blind alley (I spent over 70 hours on FC3).  Second, it is pretty hard compared to similar shooter type games, and there are a lot of different-type controls.  For example, the "one-two" punch of shock then wrench works well, but you have to train your brain to use different keys to do it.  Third, the story just doesn't make much (any) sense and the game itself just strikes me as "weird" - the setting, the story, and the enemies.  Everything is just a little too weird for me to relate to.  The one positive is that it still manages to be fairly entertaining in spite of all this.  It's just entertaining enough  and just short enough for me to have the desire to finish it.  On a scale of 5, I'd give this a 2.5, not low enough to "not recommend" it but hardly a glowing recommendation.  There are far better alternatives with better stories, graphics, gameplay, and length of play.  Of similar games that are better, off the top of my head, I'm thinking of any Deus Ex title, FC2, FC3, HL1, HL2, or either of the Metro 2033 games.  The Fallout and Skyrim games are even a little similar and offer FAR better entertainment and gaming value.

I dont play very many horror games but i did play all of the resident evil and silent hill series so lets look at outlast. I will be going over the game in a pro/ con style and finish with my conclusion.
Pro:
It has a great atmosphere. Alot of people find medical buildings very scary such as asylums or even a doctors office. Here we are in some asylum where tests are made on patients. It is very dark and has alot of really messed up architecture. Also can not forget about the large ammount of blood covering walls and floor.

Your character leaves bloody footprints on the ground. A really cool thing that this game does besides showing us the players feet is when you step in blood you leave tracks. Not like the enemy AI fallow the tracks but it is a really cool estetic the game has working for it.
Interesting story. The story form my experience is hard to understand unless you get all the collectables and to a degree look at the wall writings to understand it. Then again being in an asylum one doesnt really need a story because insane asylums.
The dlc. The dlc has some really interesting moments that took me by surprise. I felt unease when i saw a specific set of scenes in the dlc that the entire outlast game couldnt make me feel. So yea that is nice.
Con:
The game is too dark. The only means to seeing in the dark is with the camera and that camera has batteries. Thats not very fun to manage your batteries not that its hard in anyway but can lead to alot of frustration fumbling around in the dark.
Chase sequences really do destroy the experience the game offers. Through both the main game and the dlc the player will have these sequences where they are chased by an enemy. Yes they can be terrifying at first but after a few times you just get annoyed. Sometimes the chase can lead you fumbing around to figure out where you must go, its worse in the dark. One chase inparticular is really dumb because the enemy is in front of you but you must run towards the enemy and go through a door to your left and then  jump into an air vent to progress the game. I dont know about anyone else but if I see the monster that has been chasing me very frequently in front of my; my main reaction isnt to run   towards it.
The music playing during the chase sequence. It is that violen noise that is sterotypical of horror games to have but here it just gets on my nerves. Yes i know it isnt that noise but it is the type of style that is annoying. It is suppose to make the game feel tense and such but it plays the same song during most if not all the chase sequences. It got to the point i had to turn off my volume because it got so annoying.
Conclusion:
I played outlast when it first came to ps4 with friends and it wasnt scary. It was an experience....not a good one but it was an experience. The game was just too dark and trying to be too fast pace for what a good horror game is. Alot of the time i look at the level design and think what were the developers thinking when they made this sequence. Some doors that i need to go through are hidden in the dark when the natural instinct of the player is to follow the light. The game it self doesnt have anything that stands out as fun when i am constantly rushed from part to part with chase sequences. I dont hate the game for reasons stated in my cons list; i am just critical about the games and when i hear "oh this game is really scary" or "Horror game of the year" it raises and eyebrow as to how did this slide? I went through the game not enjoying the game for many reasons and i really hope for the sequal that they changes things alot more. Instead of making the game like 95% dark and full of chase sequences see the devs focus on a more atmospheric horror that is unsettling but not frustrating. Maybe make the fear something that is lingering in the back of the players mind as they are playing.

I am rereviewing this game more than a year later, so this review is going to have a lot of comparisons to something that many poeple might not find interesting, but I want to give the devs their due. This is Early Access done right.
When I first started playing this game it had just hit a point where it was fully playable, but incredbily difficult. The wolves were in constant attack mode and they never let up. The game revolved around running from door to door as quickly as you could and even then there was no gaurantee the wolf wouldn't be waiting right outside the door. It was the harshest game I have ever played. Having recently picked it back up I will say that on the harder settings it is still a challenge but the game is a lot more balanced and playable now.
Even as a sandbox game there is enough challenge to keep you interested while you try to chase down a wounded bear or get caught in a serious storm at sunset. There are currently tons of craftables and the acheivements will force you to make good use of the new items. You can at this point get good enough to live outdoors almost exclusively. It is a really good game on its own and I actually enjoy the lack of anyone else in the world.
For me, on a personal level this game is the first Early Access title I had ever followed and the current state of it is hugely impressive. It is nowhere near as quirky as when I first began playing, but it is a much more polished a well-crafted game now. If you haven't bought it you should do so immediately.

Don't waste your money on this. Another early access game, full of promise , that ended up in the trash bin.
Nobody entirely understands what happened exactly.
I bought the game in it's Early Access. Was fun, despite the piles of bugs and issues all around everywhere.
Updates were consistent, and everything looked great! I always checked the news to see what wonderfull things they brought into the game, and it was fun trying out those features! Bugs were smashed, problems solved, and additional content added on the way. Everything looked pretty great!
Until it happened...
Still missing tons of content, they suddenly for no reason released the game!
One moment, there are regular updates with content and stuff and then poof, game released.
The soundtrack was amazing, perfectly fitting the environment, and better equipment was being added so that players could get to deeper biomes.
Then they decided to release it half-baked. There aren't even armor sets that would let you reach the deepest biomes!
Many biomes can't be reached at all! And tons of other stuff was missing still!
Combat was still very annoying, with enemies being extremely agile, having a very tiny hit-box, which sometimes wasn't even on the enemy! There was a crab enemy infamous of it's mis-placed hit box, because of which you could only hit it if you fire above it.
They kept releasing very tiny bug fix updates and smaller content updates, that only seemed to make them look like they were alive, when they didn't really add anything important.
Now, they have been silent for a long time.
The last post was a sort of "We are not dead but lots-a stuff going on now" post. They said in max a few months they would explain things. That post was put up in April.
Although nobody knows exactly what happened behind the curtains, but the most common idea is that the developers over time lost their determination to keep on going, and released the game early, turning it into a cash-grab.
The fact that even now, not having responded to anything for months, the game still gets put on sale, and once it was even sighted on humble bundle, only supports this cash grab idea even more. And then again, like i mentioned previously , before they went silent, they were releasing fake updates, that added nothing but thin-air to the game, only so that they make others think that the game is alive, when it is not.
TL;DR: Another early access game that had the potential and fun, but it mysteriously died out. Now it is only a carcass of a game that once was full of promise.
Once again, for a final time: Don't waste your money on this! I beg you...

Where do I start? Well, if I'm gonna be honest, I'll start right where many people start.
SUPERHOT is quite the shooter, and it certainly likes to hang up the banner of "most innovative", which at times, I'm inclined to agree with. Many times. The game really is fun all around - if you can get past some frustrations that may occur during some levels. But when you do pull off a really cool one? A really awesome one? Let me tell you just like everybody else.
It's. So. Dang. Satisfying.
To the point where, when given the option to save a replay, you don't mind sitting around for a few minutes waiting for it to finish uploading, because you can watch that badass replay over and over and over again and still foam at the mouth at how awesome it was. Even if you got lucky. Even if you weren't even trying. The experience was still well worth it.
The price tag on the other hand? Not so satisfying and well worth it.
And here we get to the part of the review where many, many others get to. Which is totally understandable. Because it's so easily agreeable.
The simple fact is: SUPERHOT is not worth the money. It's not worth the standard $25 price tag.
Do not be deceived by the endless mode layered with multiple challenges. I personally haven't played that much of it, but from I have played, I can tell you it is quite fun - for a while. Eventually, you just get bored, as with every game. And quite frankly, the repetitious gameplay of SUPERHOT, even with a good amount of variation here and there, does start to inadvertantly pester you. In some cases, you just feel that it's getting really old, really fast.
The story, particularly, and I'm afraid to say, ONLY in your first playthrough is enough to keep you intrigued with a drive to keep going and see it through. Unfortunately, it's just too short. And that's not entirely a fault of the devs, the main point of this game is to experience the new innovative game mechanic. The point is to experience time only moving when you move. The point is to make yourself feel like a professional badass action hero. At least when you pull it off. No joke, I beat the main game in 2 hours. And do not mistake me, that's with plenty of restarting levels, plenty of endless but vain attempts at being cocky, and plenty of anger induced rampages, usually unseccesful. That's on me though.
So, while it is disappointing that the story didn't have any great length, it was never the reason to play the game in the first place. Still though, if it was expanded upon, that'd be quite welcome, and pretty interesting.
Overall, I DO recommend SUPERHOT. But not for a price of $25. It simply isn't worth that. The cost for this game really does come at a cost, pun intended, for a player's experience. This is how you died.
The entirety of the game is how you died. There is a mystery as to why the zombie outbreak occurred, and you might even find some answers before you die. Ultimately though, Project Zomboid does not represent an against-all-odds struggle where you overcome the undead. Instead, after dying, every subsequent playthrough just lets you survive a little longer, do a little better, and learn a little more.
Death can come in many, many ways. You have to manage needs, similar to The Sims . You need to eat, sleep, and even need to rest your legs if you're running around too much . You aren't able to see meters that indicate your exact state, but moodlets will appear to let you know exactly what your character is thinking or feeling at any given time. Injuries are common, so if you're scratched or bitten by a zombie, you better tend to them quickly.
The town is populated by other survivors and looters, some just as desperate as you. Everyone is scared by the thousands of zombies roaming the city, and a looter just might find you and put a shotgun round in your chest as he takes your food and other supplies. Scripted events like this will keep you on your toes, but with every failure comes the chance to prepare a little better for next time.
The zombies themselves are the slow and lumbering kind. You can fairly easily outrun them, but they are legion, and don't easily forget. They are attracted by blood and noise, and all it takes is a single mistake to advertise your location to the horde. You've never had to think in so many different directions and cover your butt in so many different ways before. As a result, every moment is exciting because you never know what lurks around the corner and whether you missed that one thing that will give away your position. Getting into a routine and locking down your safehouse will be just as important as finding food and scavenging for weapons.
Crafting is also a large part of Project Zomboid. At the moment, your character already "knows" the recipes needed to create objects to help him: combining a can opener, a can of soup, and a pot results in a big pot of edible soup, for example. Cooking will eventually be part of the game as well, adding another layer of complexity to basic survival; after all, you don't want to be suffering from food poisoning due to eating undercooked meat if you're being chased down by zombies.
Overall, well worth a buy. It's easy to see that Project Zomboid has potential and lots of merits.

Long time ago, there was a game called "Locomotion". Train valley picks up the basic idea behind it, transfering trains from station A to station B avoiding collisions. It's, of course, level-up compared to Locomotion, the player can
- Build track,
- Remove track,
- Start trains,
- Halt trains,
all the things he/she couldn`t do in Locomotion. And although there still seems to be the common factor that the player has to change switches in order to direct trains correctly, it's not really the case, because in Train Valley, switches can be set back automatically according to trains to possibly let them pass.
For more additional material, the player is invited to consult the DLC, Super Train will appear and bombs will fall and destroy parts of the track. The level of challenge can be adjusted by three time configurations (1x, 2x, 4x) as one might tend to like it. Future games can be build on this idea and the genre further improved, may be a reasonable conclusion.

Positives:
* Beautiful art with really pretty hand-drawn characters and beautiful watercolour backgrounds. So many little details such as a little tire swing which wobbles a little in the back of the first boss. A lot of love and care went into this - they didn't just do the minimum effort possible, everything is constantly in motion which looks great. Keeping the animations at the classic 24fps but keeping actual objects in motion at 60 does a top job of keeping the animations looking classic without sacrificing playability. Does a good job of avoiding clutter - at no point during the bosses did things get in the way. It also acts as a good incentive to keep pushing when you may not otherwise have done so.
* The soundtrack is fantastic. Live recordings of fast jazz which consistently match the mood of the fight.
* Boss rush - I know a lot of people don't really like this, but I adore bosses in general in games so for a game to be just bosses makes me really happy. Especially wonderful is the phases, where each boss has a good set of attack patterns and forms. No boss has fewer than three phases, and quite a few have many more. No monotony is present at all too which is great. Some bosses have a fight while in a plane which breaks up gameplay more obviously, but even without that there is a lot of variety. It's not just every boss being a still-standing giant thing which shoots you. Some bosses are more mobile, some largely use melee attacks rather than range, some summon flunkies to attack you, some you have to fight while on moving platforms, and the list goes on. There is an astounding amount of variety in the style of battle gameplay-wise which will prevent any feeling of monotony. The multiphase battles also really help this too. Not to mention the visual designs of the bosses and their various phases are absolutely inspired. And goddamn, winning is so immensely satisfying. Some of the bosses in the third island had me literally shouting in triumph after winning them.
* The difficulty spends most of its time being at a good level for the vision - really difficult, but fair. Most often when you die you can look upon your death and go "yep - that was my fault", whether it be because you ♥♥♥♥ed up or weren't paying attention or haven't properly learned how to dodge an attack.
* Length - while each boss and running level is short - only 2-3 minutes usually with some even shorter - the game took me just over 10 and a half hours to complete on Regular difficulty for my first run, despite there only being 25 levels (19 bosses, 6 running levels). The reason for this is the difficulty - you will not complete these bosses first try most likely. Instead, you'll keep going at them time and time again. You learn the patterns of the bosses and improve each time, picking up how to dodge certain attacks that you struggled with before. I found myself often dying on the first phase of the boss for the first 5 minutes, yet by the time I was able to complete the fight I was rarely taking damage on the first phases. This, along with the quick and multiphase nature of the bosses, really prevents them from getting boring despite the fact you may be spending the most part of 30 minutes on each one. The phases that you can do reliably will pass quickly enough that you won't find them dull, and those that you can't pass easily you will spend your time concentrating and working hard so those don't get boring either. This also gives a really good sense of progression in the time it takes to beat the boss, and for me it never felt like I was just hitting a brick wall against the bosses, at least never for very long.
* I liked the weapon and ability upgrades and loadout switches, with each map allowing the equipping of two shot types, an ability, and a super attack. Depending on the boss or run 'n' gun level, a different loadout had different uses, and while I spent most of the game using the peashooter/spread attack combination, I did sometimes switch weapons and often switched abilities based on the fight.
* While this should really fit in with visuals or the bosses, I would really like to note just how much character every boss has. Their style and movement is wonderfully detailed, resulting in a really strongly character which you fight against.
* Quick restarts after death. A small thing but one which is always nice and prevents frustration.
Negatives:
* If you look at the above paragraphs, you'll notice a certain qualifier appearing very often - "in the bosses". Now, the run 'n' gun levels aren't bad, and are very fun at times with some really inspired mechanics and fantastic small animations and characters, but also contain a lot of issues that the bosses don't. They're a bit easier to get bored of, for some reason I can't quite place. There's certainly a bit more of randomness to the enemy generation, meaning I often found myself stuck in a situation where I had no choice but to take damage, and I often found myself just having to split second dodge to survive rather than the great pattern memorisation of the bosses. They often take a lot longer to perfect and complete than the bosses which is a pain. I often found the levels getting cluttered, with lots of enemies on screen, and in particular the massive cloud death animation for enemies - pretty as it is, for a game like this having vision obscured for such a time is a real issue.
* Occasionally (and I do mean very occasionally) a boss's attack feels a little unfair. This is very rare - maybe three or four bosses throughout the game have a single attack that feels unfair. One boss notably however has several attacks which feel unfair, including rather hard to dodge projectiles which force you into a position where you'll almost certainly be hit by different projectiles, and an unavoidable attack which freezes you in place for about a second during a section with many bullets. That boss was a real pain. However, to restate, that still means that the vast majority of bosses are amazing and feel entirely fair, and even those other bosses with one unfair attack feel incredibly fair and fun during their course.
* While I enjoyed the harsh difficulty, I can see why many didn't and find it too tough to continue. Not really a negative for me but worth highlighting in a review.
* There is a certain randomness element to multiple bosses. I don't mean "it's pure luck whether you survive or die", it's nothing that bad and constitutes a very minor complaint. It's merely random selection of attacks. While for many bosses this is fun and provides variety when replaying, a couple of bosses have one attack that they randomly select which is much, much harder than the alternatives. A minor issue but one that can be bothersome.
* A couple of minor bugs happened during my game. Nothing gamebreaking but one did require a restart. Not a huge issue but worth noting.
* Another minor one, but considering how much character the game infuses into the many bosses or even phases of bosses, it's really a shame that I came out feeling there wasn't much character to Cuphead, who's meant to be the main character.
Overall:
While I have many complaints about the run 'n' gun levels, the key issue was "sections" being frustrating -  I spent a fair amount of my time on the run 'n' guns enjoying myself with tough but fair gameplay and genuinely inspired platforming mechanics, and it's just a shame that the bothersome sections generally left me with a bad taste in my mouth after completing each run 'n' gun. While that may look like a high volume of complaints, my opinion of the game as a whole is overwhelmingly positive. I did somewhat enjoy the run 'n' guns, and I had an incredible amount of fun playing the bosses and spent almost every second of the boss fights really enjoying myself. The fantastic visuals and music act as a brilliant reward for the challenging but mostly fair battles. Fantastic.

The current state of the gaming Industry had convinced me indie and triple games alike had nothing to offer but patronizing encouragement for trivial in game achievements, watered down mechanics to appeal to the lowest common denominator and games that dread the thought of challenging their players in fear of alienating the village idiot. Top that off with microtransaction culture and day 1 dlc, and you can understand why I've drifted away from gaming for a good many years. With the exception of Dark Souls, I'd largely written off gaming. What was once an enjoyable pastime had become a monotonous, tedious chore, utterly devoid of any sense of accomplishment or originality.
Cuphead alone, managed to challenge my perception of gaming as a whole, and reminded me of how much gaming still has to offer. The game, aesthetically speaking is quite charming, a throwback to old cartoons in the 30’s. How the character express themselves, how they move, how they react, it’s all heavily stylized. Now perhaps it’s because I’m bored to tears with modern gaming’s fascination with realism and believability at the expense of creativity, but the artistic style really is quite endearing, the amount of creativity that went into the design of the bosses and enemies is really a spectacle to behold. It makes the game just as fun to watch as it is to play. You’ll find yourself up against everything from shapeshifting blimps that take the form of constellations, to evil middle eastern genies that try to knock you out with their own flaming skull.  Like most would say, it’s a 30’s cartoon come to life, everything from the character movement to the sound design lends itself to this 30’s cartoon quality. The creativity at play here is a brilliant breath of fresh air.
The mechanics of Cuphead are also remarkably well polished, running and firing feels natural and smooth, the platforming is precise and there is a respectable attention to detail. In example -holding A makes a full jump, tapping a gives a small jump. The fact that the jump distance is determined by how long you keep your finger on the jump button shows just how much thought and concern was given to the mechanics of the game.  Similarly, you can jump and fire down, jump and fire north east, northwest. Even if you never end up using these mechanical features, it sets a standard for the refinement of it’s mechanics, everything has been carefully optimized and feels as fluid and natural as possible. The game also adds parrying to the run and gun formula which adds an interesting skillful fold to the core gameplay. It’s a welcome mechanic that is carefully interwoven into the game, managing to add a new, interesting fold to encounters. The game also throws in plane missions similar to the likes of Phalanx or Life Force, you’ll find yourself having the entire screen to maneuver around in, which paves the way for elements of bullet hell. The game draws inspiration from a couple different genres and blends them together to form a nice palatable cocktail. Bullethell, space shooter, Contra. You can find small streak of each genre’s respective mechanics here.
My only gripe is that there are too few Run and Gun sections, there are 19 bosses in the game, and all are very vibrant and unique, one is hardly similar to the other. Comparatively however there are only 6 run and gun levels. Though the levels that are there are all fairly good, save for one, or possibly two. First, Funhosue Frazzle, which stats of interesting, but relies too much on the celling swap gimmick and becomes rather monotonous near the end and Funfair Fever which is the inverse situation. It starts off rather droll and becomes better as the stage progresses. The two levels aren’t even bad, just, more on the side of mediocre when compared to the rest, which is a high bars anyways.
The disproportionate amount of bosses to levels can somewhat diminish the thrill as I found myself wanting  there to be one extra level per each world to pace out the battle with the bosses. Though, it is almost a non issue, as I still greatly enjoyed fighting each boss and learning their individual attack patterns. Though, some bosses can also be quite a test of patience! There were many times where I screamed a string of nonsensical obscenities at particular bosses.  Looking at you, Dr Kahl. Dying will be a relentlessly repeating theme in your playthrough, the game is a true challenge, it’s why the game is so satisfying, finally beating that boss after losing 20 odd something times is a feat worth feeling proud of. So few games manage to tred the line between enjoyable and frustrating, but Cuphead manages to accomplish what few others could.
There are a couple of bugs here and there, not too many, but they are present. I recall an uncommon bug in TreeTop Trouble were the stump man’s base didn’t die and there are a one or two occasions were I felt like the hitboxes registered damage on my character when I did not see him get struck by the enemy. A certain end game sub boss comes to kind, but I am willing to chalk that up to me being careless. My other minor gripe is that sometimes it is hard to tell if you are damaging a boss, especially with certain weapons and super moves. There is also a moment with the final boss where his neck elongates and covers 95% of the screen save for a small safe area on the left and despite being in the safe area, I took damage still, a kind of annoying bug, but easy to work around. I also take a minor issue with some guns and abilites being much weaker than others. Particularly the lobbing gun and some of the insta parry abilities are very underpowered comapared to some others. I would go as far as saying that the multishot in way too many situations is the most powerful gun (not all, but most). Otherwise, I’ve got no other gripes. And if the worst complaint I have about a game had me complain there aren't enough run and gun levels, it really speaks well of the game. Especially since within mere days, most of these issues will probably be resolved anyways.
Cuphead teaches us an important lesson. Less is more. Cuphead might not have content that will last you months, but what it does have, will leave you immeasurably more satisfied than Call of Duty or whatever current sequelized mess is garnering unwarranted hype. Modern games take the Swiss army knife approach to gameplay of having multiple inferior iterations of mechanical play. Terribly implemented stealth, poorly realized rpg trees, bare bones dialogue system, ect. Cuphead, focuses just on running and gunning and perfects it, everything In the game revolves around the mechanics, the levels, bosses, maneuvers, abilities, they all serve to reinforce the same concept, thus they become interwoven. It’s the difference between a cut of meat from Mcdonalds and getting a premium steak from a 5 star Restaurant that specializes in steak. You can argue that Mcdonalds has more variety, but does it really matter if everything tastes like cardboard?
To sum, Cuphead is a game deserving of it’s praise, a game that remembers the merits of actually being one. Cuphead is a game I won’t soon forget, and for something as great as Cuphead going for $20, it’s a steal of a deal. If you’re like myself, and have grown apart from gaming per the utter lack of challenge or creativity, do yourself a favor and buy this. It’s a relentlessly difficult game, but immensely rewarding. No multi-million dollar game on the market can claim the same.
Oh, and people are not automatically entitled to the full content of ANY game. If you can’t beat the game on standard difficulty, it is entirely fair you will not see all the phases of a boss, the full extent of a level or even all the bosses. Content earned will always be more gratifying than content willfully given. This "consumer must be given everything no matter the consequences", mentality, is why gaming is in the sorry state that it is.

The thing about this game is that most of its content revolves around the way it tells the stories.
The gameplay seems pretty simple if you think about it, being a game of "Go to Point A then Point B" quests. But the catch of it is the economy of your travels.
The game's map changes in every playthrough (unless you sacrifice choosing one of your other perks to keep the chart of your previous captain) and that you're not really sure what your map looks like in the next playthrough.
That right there is the challenge.
You only have a very limited set of resources and you need to get rich. You need to establish a trade route and you need to make sure that all of your actions produces a profit for you. You also need to play it smart and make sure that you have a safety net in case of a SHTFan scenario (like bringing extra supplies and fuel, writing an ironclad will).
If you're playing this for the first time, you will be overwhelmed almost immediately about the whole economy thing. But you just need to pull through and understand how the game works.
Exploration is this game's main point, but you will always need some money to do that expedition.
If you've gotten that down, you'll be establishing trade routes and getting end game content. And you'll be able to appreciate the beauty of this game.

Where do I start? Well, if I'm gonna be honest, I'll start right where many people start.
SUPERHOT is quite the shooter, and it certainly likes to hang up the banner of "most innovative", which at times, I'm inclined to agree with. Many times. The game really is fun all around - if you can get past some frustrations that may occur during some levels. But when you do pull off a really cool one? A really awesome one? Let me tell you just like everybody else.
It's. So. Dang. Satisfying.
To the point where, when given the option to save a replay, you don't mind sitting around for a few minutes waiting for it to finish uploading, because you can watch that badass replay over and over and over again and still foam at the mouth at how awesome it was. Even if you got lucky. Even if you weren't even trying. The experience was still well worth it.
The price tag on the other hand? Not so satisfying and well worth it.
And here we get to the part of the review where many, many others get to. Which is totally understandable. Because it's so easily agreeable.
The simple fact is: SUPERHOT is not worth the money. It's not worth the standard $25 price tag.
Do not be deceived by the endless mode layered with multiple challenges. I personally haven't played that much of it, but from I have played, I can tell you it is quite fun - for a while. Eventually, you just get bored, as with every game. And quite frankly, the repetitious gameplay of SUPERHOT, even with a good amount of variation here and there, does start to inadvertantly pester you. In some cases, you just feel that it's getting really old, really fast.
The story, particularly, and I'm afraid to say, ONLY in your first playthrough is enough to keep you intrigued with a drive to keep going and see it through. Unfortunately, it's just too short. And that's not entirely a fault of the devs, the main point of this game is to experience the new innovative game mechanic. The point is to experience time only moving when you move. The point is to make yourself feel like a professional badass action hero. At least when you pull it off. No joke, I beat the main game in 2 hours. And do not mistake me, that's with plenty of restarting levels, plenty of endless but vain attempts at being cocky, and plenty of anger induced rampages, usually unseccesful. That's on me though.
So, while it is disappointing that the story didn't have any great length, it was never the reason to play the game in the first place. Still though, if it was expanded upon, that'd be quite welcome, and pretty interesting.
Overall, I DO recommend SUPERHOT. But not for a price of $25. It simply isn't worth that. The cost for this game really does come at a cost, pun intended, for a player's experience. All of your cool experiences and momentes of undeniable badass-ery, are entirely undermined with the knowledge of the outrageous price tag.
So, do yourself a favor, and buy this game! Buy SUPERHOT! SUPER HOT SUPER HOT SUPER HOT ...............................
....................... Just make sure you buy it on sale at a reasonable price. Don't spend anything over $20 if you can manage.

I'm by no means a professional critic, but I'm willing to bet that those who are get incredibly frustrated by games like this. Not for any flaws the game may have, but by trying to find that perfect balance of telling people about the game without telling them a thing.
Yes, this is one of those games that, to fully appreciate, you need to go into blind. It's an experience, rather than a challenge. You don't really "beat" The Beginner's Guide, you just let it happen.
And some people don't like that idea, asking why experiences like this aren't just made into films if there's no real sense of "winning" the game. Should games always be based on a challenge that has to be overcome to "beat" it? Where is the line that decides what should be a game and what should just be a video?
I feel like people like Davey Wreden are defining that line. Games like this showcase how to take a new medium and use the limitations and strengths to make something so incredible and profound, people like me have to waste time writing whole paragraphs trying to find a clever way to say nothing in particular.
Beause to give anything away about the experience he delivers is to do it injustice. And therein lies the problem. When something is based on a challenge it's easy to tell someone why that kind of challenge would appeal to them, but it's hard to convince someone to try an experience when you can't tell them the experience without ruining it. It's hard to sell someone on the idea of a game by saying "No no, just trust me. If I tell you it wont work."
The most I can say is that The Beginners Guide is a game about art. It challenges both those of us who create content and those of us who consume it. Who do we create for? What makes us become attached to someone elses works? Art, content, creation..it's the language of emotion. It's how life speaks to us. And this game makes you take a deep, deep look at that. If that resonates with you, this game will be an experience you wont forget.

Train valley certainly one of the best games I have ever played.
"Its just trains." Cry my friends when I rave about it, they are wrong. If you think along their lines, think again.
Firstly a warning, this is a puzzle game. If you love trains but despise puzzle games I would not recommend you to pick it up. However, to all of you still left, if you like puzzles or even have a passing intrest in them I would highly recommend this to you. You do not need to know the first thing about trains. All I know is what I learnt from a childhood addiction to Thomas the tank engine.
The gameplay for the whole time is exhilarating. You are tasked at directing the trains which pop up at various stations, building tracks to new stations and while doing all this trying to keep above that dreaded £0. This may not sound like much but it will keep you invested for many hours. This is beacuse this game is tuned to perfection. You start off with some money to build your initial track and you start to build up some income, however just as you start to feel comfortable the intensity is ramped up by the addition of another station. This ruins even the best layed plans and forces you to think on your feat. The intesity is layered up until you finally finish a level and can finally breath a sigh of releif after an exhilarating time.
Furthermore this game sets the difficulty just right. It never feels too easy or too hard. As I progressed through the game I found myself getting better and better, but the game was improving at the same pace. The game never felt as if it was throwing an impossible challenge at you, on the other hand it never felt it was just gifting you a free pass as I progressed throught the game. However, this style of design heavily impacted one important feature of any video game... Replayability. After I got through the game I replayed some of the earlier levels doing some achievement hunting, they were so easy. After you get all the stamps and the achievements you can't go back and retry the earlier levels as you will be able to play them at mostly 4X speed.
The DLC is also a very welcome addition, I bought the game without the DLC but when I finished the game I immediately bought it. It adds extra play time to the game, extra challenge and many new innovative features. Most importantly it doesn't feel like something the devs took out of the main game just to squeeze every last pound out of us, it adds many new innovative design features not present in the main game.
In conclusion this game is a M A S T A P E E C E and you should buy it. It is only £6.99 and while I got it on a deal I would happily buy it again at full price. I have had a great time with this game and I am looking forward to experiencing the joy of it all over again with train valley 2, which I will be preordering as soon as I am able to to.

This is my first time writing a review. Please bear with me on this one. :-)
What can I say about Bioshock? One of the best shooters that I have played in PC... Period! You will be engaged to the story behind Rapture while enjoying and shooting your way out of the underground city. Not only you can shoot, you have plasmids (powers). You can approach stealthily or just show and shoot. There are several endings in this game. Your actions determine the outcome of the game.
In my opinion, I rate the ff:
Story - 10/10.
Unique setting. Character development is very good and you will meet several characters in the game as you progress. The story is engaging that you want to keep moving to finish it.
Graphics - 10/10.
Outstanding graphics for a 2007 game. No doubt about that. You have options to increase/decrease the resolution, v-sync, etc.
Controls - 9/10.
The controls compensate with the gameplay. Although you cannot run, but it still is great to play and challenging as well.
Gameplay - 10/10.
I am choosy when it comes to gameplay. And this game does not disappoint. Outstanding musical score. The music compensates with the game. The gameplay is a bundle. You cannot just run and shoot. You have melee. You have plasmids (powers, requires EVE or mana). Buy ammos/plasmids. You can do stealth. You have choices. You have puzzles. Role-playing game. A bundle... AI is pretty responsive too.
