I have not been this happy with a game in at least a decade.
No, really. And we're not even into the story mode yet. We're still in the pre-release stage where we've been cut loose in a sandbox with some semi-random spawns, and I've enjoyed every wonderful second of this game, aside from any time I must spend in the dubiously monikered "Pleasant Valley."
Currently, there are several maps available for exploration, and the use of a few limited RNGs help to keep each new game experience fresh. I've begun a new file after spending nearly 100 in-game days doing quite well for myself, only to thoughtlessly tread upon my campfire in the middle of a blizzard. It didn't end well. Sadly, the game loves to save not only as you enter/leave buildings and/or sleep, but also the very moment you screw up bad. But hey, it keeps us all honest, I suppose.
That said, this game and its story have a way of turning even the most mundane things into something wonderful. As you fight for survival, you may find yourself leaping for joy at the sight of a candy bar or a toque. A bit of newspaper that you won't even read will still bring a smile to your face as you remember that it means you can start one more fire. You may even cackle with glee as you take aim at a local bear, only to hyperventilate as you run for the closest door because the bear felt that .308 and now DEATH IS COMING. You will jeer from the inside of the building because you were lucky enough to evolve with thumbs, but you will also sleep with one eye open and keep your head on a swivel until you've learned for sure that the bear has finally bled out, possibly after 2-3 days. Hint: don't harvest the bear all at once in Pleasant Valley. The blizzard that inevitably finds you as you do so will eat you alive.

This is truly an inspired, awesome game. Maybe not everyone's cup of tea but if you want to play a real survival game this is it. Pit yourself against the elements, scavenge, build yourself better gear, travel as you exhaust the easily lootable materials around you, then, hopefully, don't overextend yourself in the cold so that you have the ability to survive off the land rather than the stuff left behind by others. The weather is your greatest enemy, I have died lost in blizzards, died three steps from safety. Never had any performance or stability or bug issues and I've been playing it on and off for a year at least. New locations, great stable and thoughtful mechanics. If you want a fast paced action game this isn't for you. If you want to survive and manage your health, supplies and explore this is a great game to play. Another of the things I like on early access is that there are a couple of starting areas but there are also new ones you can only start from once you have found them. Longest I've survived is about 50 days near the lake. In the valley I keep pushing harvesting meat too far and dying of hypothermia. My only complaint is I don't like the art style, but that's an extremely minor concern against the fantastic game which is The Long Dark.

Great game. The first time I played through it, I didn't really enjoy it. The gameseemed very slow in the beginning. I didn't try to test my limits and simply stayed closeby, running by the same locations over and over and never encountering any of the interesting storylines that are held within the game. I decided to put it down and move on to other titles.  Something about this game drew me back, however, and I felt I was missing out on something big.
Don't be afraid to push your limits. This time around, I decided to change my strategy and am having a great time. I finally understand all the positive reviews in this game. The story is excellent and if you're a fan of inventory management games which require you to remember a vast amount of item locations and destinations, you should enjoy this game.
Take risks, risks are what make this game great. Playing it safe will lead to a dull, slow experience. A risky early-game where you're always on the edge of your seat thinking you're going to run out of gas, supplies, and money before you can reap in the payload, or that zee-beast or frigate is going to smash through what's left of your hull, or that next possible wound or crewmember will be your last is how this game was meant to be played.
Once the early game is up, your ship's speed will increase by quite a bit and you can enjoy the excellent writing while racking up that fat stack of delicious echoes and equipment. Setting up different routes to maximize profit and secrets is surprisingly fun.

After you've finished a level you will get a replay (which you can save) in real time which makes you feel even more awesome.
The game is fun and unique, but unfortunately the devs left it for dead. It's incredibly limited in terms of settings and just overpriced. I wouldn't buy this game unless it was on at least a 50% sale.
I actually got this one for free because I backed the other one. Don't know if everyone who backed it got it for free or if it's because I didn't get the "2D" version for free.
This was played on the HTC Vive using
which emulates the Oculus Rift (and Touch) so that you can play Oculus exclusive games on the Vive.
SUPERHOT VR surprised me with the quality. The price is 25€ and it's not available on Steam yet (they are working on a Vive version, no ETA yet) so they didn't go too crazy on the pricing (VR games have a tendency to be incredibly expensive for the quality, limited audience and all), that being said it's still a bit pricy given the content offered.
The VR version is a lot more polished than the 2D version. The controls are really buggy where the grip sometimes isn't registered and you drop an item too soon, but that might be a bug with ReVive since the game isn't designed for the Vive controllers. Other than that it's very stable.
This is the way SUPERHOT was meant to be played. Right there in the game (which is a game in a game, oh right there's a story in this as well) with full control of your movement. It's not as "free" as the 2D version was since VR is still in the awkward movement system where you pretty much have to use teleportation to keep the immersion, but SUPERHOT VR does this really well by having each level have small sections. The teleportation isn't as instant as most other VR games, instead it will fade the world in and out in a pace taht doesn't screw with your mind. You don't get sick from it and you still have enough room to walk around a bit (depending on your setup of course).

Train Valley is a ton of fun until you realize how some of the mechanics can betray you.
Why does it cost money to bulldoze?
Why does spending money take effect during builder mode while paused, if I've erased or changed some of it?
Why do trains automatically launch themselves if you mistakenly send it to the wrong station, can you not put it in a priority queue maybe? That♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s up all my other running trains.
Why do trains seemingly launch themselves when not sent to the wrong station sometimes? I was never taught this.
In addition, the lack of polish when it comes to player feedback can really, REALLY make things more difficult. Being a Unity game, it should be possible to have the icon for launching a train somehow change when you have your mouse over it. It should also be possible to have your icon and/or the tile change when in building mode to show what you're mousing over, but only if it can be built on (green tiles.)
Finally, and this is on a personal level. Why is it that on the 5th level of the game, seemingly everything is going so well, but you're given the option of a second bridge? This seems a little early in the game to start having the entire level be focused around having multiple trains launching toward similar destinations. Due to the lack of space, player feedback and some bad mechanics, I've played this level maybe 8 times and have not been able to progress.
Don't confuse this review with a lack of caring. I cared enough to really study what I was doing, pause and take it slow to plan out my routes. However, seemingly, every time either I would make one slip up and it wold excessively build, or a train would launch itself. I feel like, after 8 times on this level, actually caring enough to really plan it through, and dealing with odd mechanics, that I should have progressed on the first chapter. Some developers or readers might think, "Well, you just suck. That's not our fault." Honestly thoguh, think if I might be the only one in the future?
If I can refund it, I will. If I can buy it again further down the road, when some changes are made, I will. If I can play this game with some slight flixes in the future, I would love to.

Positives:
* Beautiful art with really pretty hand-drawn characters and beautiful watercolour backgrounds. So many little details such as a little tire swing which wobbles a little in the back of the first boss. A lot of love and care went into this - they didn't just do the minimum effort possible, everything is constantly in motion which looks great. Keeping the animations at the classic 24fps but keeping actual objects in motion at 60 does a top job of keeping the animations looking classic without sacrificing playability. Does a good job of avoiding clutter - at no point during the bosses did things get in the way. It also acts as a good incentive to keep pushing when you may not otherwise have done so.
* The soundtrack is fantastic. Live recordings of fast jazz which consistently match the mood of the fight.
* Boss rush - I know a lot of people don't really like this, but I adore bosses in general in games so for a game to be just bosses makes me really happy. Especially wonderful is the phases, where each boss has a good set of attack patterns and forms. No boss has fewer than three phases, and quite a few have many more. No monotony is present at all too which is great. Some bosses have a fight while in a plane which breaks up gameplay more obviously, but even without that there is a lot of variety. It's not just every boss being a still-standing giant thing which shoots you. Some bosses are more mobile, some largely use melee attacks rather than range, some summon flunkies to attack you, some you have to fight while on moving platforms, and the list goes on. There is an astounding amount of variety in the style of battle gameplay-wise which will prevent any feeling of monotony. The multiphase battles also really help this too. Not to mention the visual designs of the bosses and their various phases are absolutely inspired. And goddamn, winning is so immensely satisfying. Some of the bosses in the third island had me literally shouting in triumph after winning them.
* The difficulty spends most of its time being at a good level for the vision - really difficult, but fair. Most often when you die you can look upon your death and go "yep - that was my fault", whether it be because you ♥♥♥♥ed up or weren't paying attention or haven't properly learned how to dodge an attack.
* Length - while each boss and running level is short - only 2-3 minutes usually with some even shorter - the game took me just over 10 and a half hours to complete on Regular difficulty for my first run, despite there only being 25 levels (19 bosses, 6 running levels). The reason for this is the difficulty - you will not complete these bosses first try most likely. Instead, you'll keep going at them time and time again. You learn the patterns of the bosses and improve each time, picking up how to dodge certain attacks that you struggled with before. I found myself often dying on the first phase of the boss for the first 5 minutes, yet by the time I was able to complete the fight I was rarely taking damage on the first phases. This, along with the quick and multiphase nature of the bosses, really prevents them from getting boring despite the fact you may be spending the most part of 30 minutes on each one. The phases that you can do reliably will pass quickly enough that you won't find them dull, and those that you can't pass easily you will spend your time concentrating and working hard so those don't get boring either. This also gives a really good sense of progression in the time it takes to beat the boss, and for me it never felt like I was just hitting a brick wall against the bosses, at least never for very long.
* I liked the weapon and ability upgrades and loadout switches, with each map allowing the equipping of two shot types, an ability, and a super attack. Depending on the boss or run 'n' gun level, a different loadout had different uses, and while I spent most of the game using the peashooter/spread attack combination, I did sometimes switch weapons and often switched abilities based on the fight.
* While this should really fit in with visuals or the bosses, I would really like to note just how much character every boss has. Their style and movement is wonderfully detailed, resulting in a really strongly character which you fight against.
* Quick restarts after death. A small thing but one which is always nice and prevents frustration.
Negatives:
* If you look at the above paragraphs, you'll notice a certain qualifier appearing very often - "in the bosses". Now, the run 'n' gun levels aren't bad, and are very fun at times with some really inspired mechanics and fantastic small animations and characters, but also contain a lot of issues that the bosses don't. They're a bit easier to get bored of, for some reason I can't quite place. There's certainly a bit more of randomness to the enemy generation, meaning I often found myself stuck in a situation where I had no choice but to take damage, and I often found myself just having to split second dodge to survive rather than the great pattern memorisation of the bosses. They often take a lot longer to perfect and complete than the bosses which is a pain. I often found the levels getting cluttered, with lots of enemies on screen, and in particular the massive cloud death animation for enemies - pretty as it is, for a game like this having vision obscured for such a time is a real issue.
* Occasionally (and I do mean very occasionally) a boss's attack feels a little unfair. This is very rare - maybe three or four bosses throughout the game have a single attack that feels unfair. One boss notably however has several attacks which feel unfair, including rather hard to dodge projectiles which force you into a position where you'll almost certainly be hit by different projectiles, and an unavoidable attack which freezes you in place for about a second during a section with many bullets. That boss was a real pain. However, to restate, that still means that the vast majority of bosses are amazing and feel entirely fair, and even those other bosses with one unfair attack feel incredibly fair and fun during their course.
* While I enjoyed the harsh difficulty, I can see why many didn't and find it too tough to continue. Not really a negative for me but worth highlighting in a review.
* There is a certain randomness element to multiple bosses. I don't mean "it's pure luck whether you survive or die", it's nothing that bad and constitutes a very minor complaint. It's merely random selection of attacks. While for many bosses this is fun and provides variety when replaying, a couple of bosses have one attack that they randomly select which is much, much harder than the alternatives. A minor issue but one that can be bothersome.
* A couple of minor bugs happened during my game. Nothing gamebreaking but one did require a restart. Not a huge issue but worth noting.
* Another minor one, but considering how much character the game infuses into the many bosses or even phases of bosses, it's really a shame that I came out feeling there wasn't much character to Cuphead, who's meant to be the main character.
Overall:
While I have many complaints about the run 'n' gun levels, the key issue was "sections" being frustrating -  I spent a fair amount of my time on the run 'n' guns enjoying myself with tough but fair gameplay and genuinely inspired platforming mechanics, and it's just a shame that the bothersome sections generally left me with a bad taste in my mouth after completing each run 'n' gun. While that may look like a high volume of complaints, my opinion of the game as a whole is overwhelmingly positive. I did somewhat enjoy the run 'n' guns, and I had an incredible amount of fun playing the bosses and spent almost every second of the boss fights really enjoying myself. The fantastic visuals and music act as a brilliant reward for the challenging but mostly fair battles. Fantastic.

The current state of the gaming Industry had convinced me indie and triple games alike had nothing to offer but patronizing encouragement for trivial in game achievements, watered down mechanics to appeal to the lowest common denominator and games that dread the thought of challenging their players in fear of alienating the village idiot. Top that off with microtransaction culture and day 1 dlc, and you can understand why I've drifted away from gaming for a good many years. With the exception of Dark Souls, I'd largely written off gaming. What was once an enjoyable pastime had become a monotonous, tedious chore, utterly devoid of any sense of accomplishment or originality.
Cuphead alone, managed to challenge my perception of gaming as a whole, and reminded me of how much gaming still has to offer. The game, aesthetically speaking is quite charming, a throwback to old cartoons in the 30’s. How the character express themselves, how they move, how they react, it’s all heavily stylized. Now perhaps it’s because I’m bored to tears with modern gaming’s fascination with realism and believability at the expense of creativity, but the artistic style really is quite endearing, the amount of creativity that went into the design of the bosses and enemies is really a spectacle to behold. It makes the game just as fun to watch as it is to play. You’ll find yourself up against everything from shapeshifting blimps that take the form of constellations, to evil middle eastern genies that try to knock you out with their own flaming skull.  Like most would say, it’s a 30’s cartoon come to life, everything from the character movement to the sound design lends itself to this 30’s cartoon quality. The creativity at play here is a brilliant breath of fresh air.
The mechanics of Cuphead are also remarkably well polished, running and firing feels natural and smooth, the platforming is precise and there is a respectable attention to detail. In example -holding A makes a full jump, tapping a gives a small jump. The fact that the jump distance is determined by how long you keep your finger on the jump button shows just how much thought and concern was given to the mechanics of the game.  Similarly, you can jump and fire down, jump and fire north east, northwest. Even if you never end up using these mechanical features, it sets a standard for the refinement of it’s mechanics, everything has been carefully optimized and feels as fluid and natural as possible. The game also adds parrying to the run and gun formula which adds an interesting skillful fold to the core gameplay. It’s a welcome mechanic that is carefully interwoven into the game, managing to add a new, interesting fold to encounters. The game also throws in plane missions similar to the likes of Phalanx or Life Force, you’ll find yourself having the entire screen to maneuver around in, which paves the way for elements of bullet hell. The game draws inspiration from a couple different genres and blends them together to form a nice palatable cocktail. Bullethell, space shooter, Contra. You can find small streak of each genre’s respective mechanics here.
My only gripe is that there are too few Run and Gun sections, there are 19 bosses in the game, and all are very vibrant and unique, one is hardly similar to the other. Comparatively however there are only 6 run and gun levels. Though the levels that are there are all fairly good, save for one, or possibly two. First, Funhosue Frazzle, which stats of interesting, but relies too much on the celling swap gimmick and becomes rather monotonous near the end and Funfair Fever which is the inverse situation. It starts off rather droll and becomes better as the stage progresses. The two levels aren’t even bad, just, more on the side of mediocre when compared to the rest, which is a high bars anyways.
The disproportionate amount of bosses to levels can somewhat diminish the thrill as I found myself wanting  there to be one extra level per each world to pace out the battle with the bosses. Though, it is almost a non issue, as I still greatly enjoyed fighting each boss and learning their individual attack patterns. Though, some bosses can also be quite a test of patience! There were many times where I screamed a string of nonsensical obscenities at particular bosses.  Looking at you, Dr Kahl. Dying will be a relentlessly repeating theme in your playthrough, the game is a true challenge, it’s why the game is so satisfying, finally beating that boss after losing 20 odd something times is a feat worth feeling proud of. So few games manage to tred the line between enjoyable and frustrating, but Cuphead manages to accomplish what few others could.
There are a couple of bugs here and there, not too many, but they are present. I recall an uncommon bug in TreeTop Trouble were the stump man’s base didn’t die and there are a one or two occasions were I felt like the hitboxes registered damage on my character when I did not see him get struck by the enemy. A certain end game sub boss comes to kind, but I am willing to chalk that up to me being careless. My other minor gripe is that sometimes it is hard to tell if you are damaging a boss, especially with certain weapons and super moves. There is also a moment with the final boss where his neck elongates and covers 95% of the screen save for a small safe area on the left and despite being in the safe area, I took damage still, a kind of annoying bug, but easy to work around. I also take a minor issue with some guns and abilites being much weaker than others. Particularly the lobbing gun and some of the insta parry abilities are very underpowered comapared to some others. I would go as far as saying that the multishot in way too many situations is the most powerful gun (not all, but most). Otherwise, I’ve got no other gripes. And if the worst complaint I have about a game had me complain there aren't enough run and gun levels, it really speaks well of the game. Especially since within mere days, most of these issues will probably be resolved anyways.
Cuphead teaches us an important lesson. Less is more. Cuphead might not have content that will last you months, but what it does have, will leave you immeasurably more satisfied than Call of Duty or whatever current sequelized mess is garnering unwarranted hype. Modern games take the Swiss army knife approach to gameplay of having multiple inferior iterations of mechanical play. Terribly implemented stealth, poorly realized rpg trees, bare bones dialogue system, ect. Cuphead, focuses just on running and gunning and perfects it, everything In the game revolves around the mechanics, the levels, bosses, maneuvers, abilities, they all serve to reinforce the same concept, thus they become interwoven. It’s the difference between a cut of meat from Mcdonalds and getting a premium steak from a 5 star Restaurant that specializes in steak. You can argue that Mcdonalds has more variety, but does it really matter if everything tastes like cardboard?
To sum, Cuphead is a game deserving of it’s praise, a game that remembers the merits of actually being one. Cuphead is a game I won’t soon forget, and for something as great as Cuphead going for $20, it’s a steal of a deal. If you’re like myself, and have grown apart from gaming per the utter lack of challenge or creativity, do yourself a favor and buy this. It’s a relentlessly difficult game, but immensely rewarding. No multi-million dollar game on the market can claim the same.
Oh, and people are not automatically entitled to the full content of ANY game. If you can’t beat the game on standard difficulty, it is entirely fair you will not see all the phases of a boss, the full extent of a level or even all the bosses. Content earned will always be more gratifying than content willfully given. This "consumer must be given everything no matter the consequences", mentality, is why gaming is in the sorry state that it is.

This is my favorite zombie survival game to date. I've played PZ since pre-steam, and have followed the team pretty far with this game. First thing is first, There were alot of (NOW FIXED) bugs in this game that the team work hard to fix. There have been alot of updates since then, and the team is great with keeping the community updated on their website
.
--Gameplay--
Starting the game in survival, you're dropped of in a random house in (at the moment) one of three connected towns. No weapon, no food. You need to find all that stuff. The map is pretty large as it is, and I can imagine it will get more towns in the future. Randomly, within two months (game time) the electricity will shut off. And same goes for water pumps. This means all food that needs to be refrigerated will degrade and rot quicker. Get a house, stash some non-perishables and get farming supplies, because hopefully, you're in for the long haul.
---Pros---
~This game will kill you're character (see also in Cons)
And I love it. The game starts by literally stating you're going to die, and if you arn't careful, you will. This is what makes it my favorite zombie survival game, if you use your gun at your house, zombies will come and you might have to leave, if you eat rotten food, you'll get sick, and if you run in a room without being causious, a zombie might just bite you. You will get sick, and you will die if that happens (95% of the time).
~Huge map.
As said earlier, there are three towns to start in, but that won't stop you from taking a tent kit and making a checkpoint or two between your house and the next town over. There is a great map that you can put notes on at
. I suggest you try the game without it first though. It puts way more of an uneasyness on you when you don't know where you are, and that's half the fun.
~Resource collection
You need things. You may not know you need things, but if you saw it, and didn't make a note of where it is, you'll probably need it later. The game will do this to you: You found a gun! Great!... you still need to get the bullets that were "not necessary" earlier. You want to make a lamp for the garden? Go get that flashlight that you dropped and hour ago because it was too heavy. And more batteries!
~Crafting
Crafting is super useful and can be really fun, especially when you build a house out of the forest around you. Chop down those intrusive plants, and saw the logs for supplies to make your new home the most zombie free haven in town! Or out of town if you prefer. make some stairs, a second floor (Don't fall off!), and maybe a few windows downstairs to watch your property. Zombies migrate, you'll want to see that coming.
~The Team
The people working on this game are really cool and keep you in the know every week on their site. There are plenty of threads on their forums that help plenty too, so you won't feel like there is a lack of information about the game.
P.S. The sound guy deserves some immense praise too.
---Neutrals---
~Using items
This makes sence, but it gets me every time. If you want to use an item, you HAVE to to have it in your main inventory. That means, if it's in a bag or a backpack, you need to unpack it. This can slow. It's annoying, but it DOES make sense which frustrates the hell out of me. so pro tip, manage your inventory for things you know you'll need in your main.
~Multiplayer
I can't say anything about this since I havn't tried it yet. But I can Imagine... This lonesome game? With maybe eight people on a server? It could be great! Or it could be the worst, possible thing... If you found someone you don't know during your travels...
---Cons---
~This game will kill you're character (see also in pros)
This can mean hours of gameplay lost, so be FREAKING CAREFUL!!!
~Technically alpha
It is still being updated and technically it's still in alpha. Expect to find some things that need to be improved. There are still no NPCs or vehilcles, and I know some of the food that should probably spoil doesn't, but follow the PZ facebook page or the website and you'll know what's up with the development.
~I am super bias
I love this game, there are likely problems that I can't see with my rose colored glasses, take this with a grain or two of salt.
If I had to make a quick synopsis:
This is a zombie survival game that blew DayZ out of the water for me. It takes time and makes it as much a threat as it's zombies. It can kill you in ten (in game) hours but you can survive for as long as you're well supplied.
Hope this helps!

So apparently I have been missing out on many older gems while I was busy being horrifyingly poor and eating nothing but ramen for months on end. Orignally I thought folks were just swooning all over Bioshock back when it came out, kind of how like fanboys still fawn over Skyrim today.
I couldn't be happier to be wrong.
From the very beginning of the game you are immediately assualted with wave after wave of atmosphere building rooms, sound and story. Everything from the varnished wood railings to the old man cronning over the radio screams that I am in a steampunk 1950s horror film.
The above said, I woudn't be a games critic if there wasn't a few nits to pick like some poor OCD chimp. First thing I noticed is that the texture quality is nowhere near up to snuff compared to the water effects. Oddly enough though it doesn't detract from the atmposhere any. I kinda expect most of the walls to have a mossy, water damaged look to them and most of the walls do.
The sound design is exceptional as well, with only a few monsters having the same voice actor or repeating the same lines really getting in the way of the atmosphere. The gun sounds are a bit off in some places as well, but It's not game breaking in the least. However,  the rest of the sights and sounds still keep you firmly immersed in the world of rapture; the flaws detract very little from the experience.
The games controls take little getting used to. Switching from plasmids to weapons can be a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you're getting swarmed as the swaps are not very intuitive, but after a hour or 2 it no longer becomes a problem. The menus and interface are doen very well too, all of them having that 50s polished wood fel to them.
In terms of game options, the only problem I have is the lack of a colorblind option and a FOV slider. Both of them minor complaints.
In terms of gameplay, it does have few hiccups. Early on, enemies are plenty and due to lack of upgrades they can take a beating. However, around halfway through the game you start getting to the point where everything dies really easily. I'm sure there is a mod out there that bumps the difficulty back up though.
The other problems is the combat is well, kind of backseat. It's not the best shooting ever, but a far cry from the best I've ever played. Also, the game is kind of onthe short side, clocking in between the 9-10 hour range for most people. That said, it's on sale on steam fairly often for around 5$ and there are other outlets to get it even cheaper. Even at 10 hours 20$ is still a pretty fair deal. I mean if folks can chuck up 50$ for MGS demo, then they can toss 20 toward this.
All of the games problems just melt away; The writing is amazing, the story solid and engaging and the atmosphere very chilling. Every single problem I just stated becomes a non-issues becuase the game does such an incredible job of immersing you into rapture. So much so that the little buggy game elements go entirely unoticed (Unless you're a critic and have to nitpick everything.)
What you are left with is amazing game that few can match. If you have an extra 20$ (or 5 depending on steam) sitting around, give this game a run. You won't regret it.
ps: just a warning, the few first big daddys you come across can wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥something hard. Have fun dying a few times :p﻿

First Impression Gameplay:
When I first started up the game, I got a very "H1Z1: Survival" vibe, but that quickly wore off.  Almost immediately after logging in, I was relentlessly killed by other players.  The big glaring issue with this, is that new players start with a fully loaded AK47, but you lose it after you die.  So, players who have been there a while are farming ammo and guns off people who just spawn in, then those players are left high and dry.
There is no teaming up in this game, unless you load in with a friend. Also, the player base appears to be entirely made up of Russian speakers (not an issue, just beware if you're looking to voice chat in English).
The graphics feel old and muddy, while the sound seems pretty decent.  For the little amount of shooting I did get to do, the hit detection seemed to work okay.  Although I did unload 5 shots from a shotgun point blank into some kind of swamp monster who seemed unaffected.
For the actual meat of the game, you spend most of your time wandering around and looking for supplies to patch together weapons and survive off food you find in random locations.  The game world feels large, and fairly sparse between locations.  There are random areas that have this electric looking blue glow which will kill you if you go near.  I'm not sure if that is supposed to be a visual representation of radiation, as that is also something you are supposed to avoid.
All in all, this game is playable and the online servers were actually very responsible.  I did get bored quickly though and feel there are better options out there.  I'm going to say the game has some potential, but I can't recommend at this time.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is an expansion pack for Valve Software's first-person shooter video game Half-Life. The game was developed by Gearbox Software with Valve Corporation and published by Sierra Entertainment on June 12, 2001. Blue Shift is the second expansion for Half-Life, Opposing Force beeing the first one. As with Gearbox's previous expansion pack Opposing Force, Blue Shift returns to the setting and events of the original game, but portrays the story through the eyes of another person. The protagonist in Blue Shift is a security guard, Barney Calhoun, employed by the Black Mesa Research Facility. After a scientific mishap causes Black Mesa to be invaded by aliens, Calhoun must fight his way to safety. The gameplay and graphics are the same as the original one. There are no new and memorable characters except one scientist, that I won't spoil anything about him. The game is very short, in fact, it's even shorter than Opposing Force, taking about 5 hours to complete. Many people criticize Blue Shift because it doesn't feature almost nothing new compared to the original Half-Life but I don't mind. Barney Calhoun is the one of the very few people who managed to do their goal during the Resonance Cascade. Out of all three playable characters in Half-Life, Barney was luckier and faced less danger, but out of all of them, he faced the most headcrabs. Overall, Half-Life: Blue Shift is very simillar to Opposing Force: short and fun. It's a must get for any HL fans and recommend this one for any casual player after finishing the original HL.

Great game. The first time I played through it, I didn't really enjoy it. The gameseemed very slow in the beginning. I have not been this happy with a game in at least a decade.
No, really. And we're not even into the story mode yet. We're still in the pre-release stage where we've been cut loose in a sandbox with some semi-random spawns, and I've enjoyed every wonderful second of this game, aside from any time I must spend in the dubiously monikered "Pleasant Valley."
Currently, there are several maps available for exploration, and the use of a few limited RNGs help to keep each new game experience fresh. I've begun a new file after spending nearly 100 in-game days doing quite well for myself, only to thoughtlessly tread upon my campfire in the middle of a blizzard. It didn't end well. Sadly, the game loves to save not only as you enter/leave buildings and/or sleep, but also the very moment you screw up bad. But hey, it keeps us all honest, I suppose.
That said, this game and its story have a way of turning even the most mundane things into something wonderful. As you fight for survival, you may find yourself leaping for joy at the sight of a candy bar or a toque. A bit of newspaper that you won't even read will still bring a smile to your face as you remember that it means you can start one more fire. You may even cackle with glee as you take aim at a local bear, only to hyperventilate as you run for the closest door because the bear felt that .308 and now DEATH IS COMING. You will jeer from the inside of the building because you were lucky enough to evolve with thumbs, but you will also sleep with one eye open and keep your head on a swivel until you've learned for sure that the bear has finally bled out, possibly after 2-3 days. Hint: don't harvest the bear all at once in Pleasant Valley. The blizzard that inevitably finds you as you do so will eat you alive.
I can't wait for story mode. This is going to be great.

Five Nights at Freddy's is probably one of the games on Steam that everyone will have heard of; however I promised to review every game I finished so here goes...
The aim of Five Nights at Freddy's is to survive five consecutive nights in the security room of Freddy's Restaurant, hiding away from the horrors of the night, you have a limited amount of power to use the lights and keep the doors closed. It's very much a resource management game in that sense.
The graphics seem to be pre-rendered 2D style, which to be honest, they don't look the best, the security office where the whole game takes place is very pixelated and it doesn't look very pleasing, however the character models of the other bears etc. look quite cool.
As in all other horror games, the music and sound effects play the most critical role, they set the mood, and give you the most jump scare effects, and they are done very well here. The levels are all set in the same place; they just get progressively harder and harder, with different techniques used by the bears on each stage.  The game is pretty hard once you get to Night 3 onwards, and will probably have you cowering in fear.
The whole game took two hours to complete the Five Nights, this felt just the right length as I don't think I could any more of the jumps and suspense.
People who seek that jump scare experience will find the thrill here; and the puzzle aspect of having to look after your power management is a nice feature, so overall, I can recommend Five Nights at Freddy's.

This is truly an inspired, awesome game. Maybe not everyone's cup of tea but if you want to play a real survival game this is it. Pit yourself against the elements, scavenge, build yourself better gear, travel as you exhaust the easily lootable materials around you, then, hopefully, don't overextend yourself in the cold so that you have the ability to survive off the land rather than the stuff left behind by others. The weather is your greatest enemy, I have died lost in blizzards, died three steps from safety. Never had any performance or stability or bug issues and I've been playing it on and off for a year at least. New locations, great stable and thoughtful mechanics. If you want a fast paced action game this isn't for you. If you want to survive and manage your health, supplies and explore this is a great game to play. Another of the things I like on early access is that there are a couple of starting areas but there are also new ones you can only start from once you have found them. Longest I've survived is about 50 days near the lake. In the valley I keep pushing harvesting meat too far and dying of hypothermia. My only complaint is I don't like the art style, but that's an extremely minor concern against the fantastic game which is The Long Dark.

TL;DR Great story heavy game with simple combat and inventory managment. A must have if you favour writing and worldbuiling and while I recommend it anyway, take more careful consideration if slow and basic gameplay is a turn off.
A great game if you like stories and reading.  Lots of reading.  In fact, thats the majority of the game.
fittingly, the gameplay is simple.  It really boils down to inventory managment, as you need enough fuel to move and enough food to eat, as well as any other things needed for trade or story progression.  The combat is basic and while it is possible to kill enemies better equipped than you, most of the time you will just avoid or destroy with very little in-between.
The game will also tell you repeatedly not to be afraid to die, which is advice one should take to heart.  There are various bonuses you can get for subsequent captains, but they almost all require you to die in the process, which is a real d(r)owner if you've spent 20 hours on a single captain  and don't want to see him go.
Your time at sea can also quickly become very monotonous.  As one could imagine, Floating around a dark ocean with wide spaces between locations in an initially slow ship can be a real drag, and can really drag you out of it if you aren't invested in the world, which is likely to be the case when you first start.  There are random encounters but they only happen so often and you will see a number of them multiple times, somewhat diminishing the effect.  The zubmariner DLC helps with this a little as you can submerge to see all sorts of things like salvagable events, but you still need to work towards getting said zubmarine so the early game is largely unaffected.
I briefly mentioned that you will do a lot of reading.  I might have been inclined to mark that as a bad thing if the world they set up and writing they use to flesh it out wasn't so damn good.  The various people you meet or locations you visit and the strange things you witness/do are interesting, with enough told to paint a picture of whats happening while leaving enough unclear so it still feels like you don't know everything.  It treats you like a normal inhabitant of this world, who is seeing new things but isn't shown the whole picture.  I also appreciate that your character knows the basics of the world and doesn't need someone to explain common knowledge to you, while the writing fills in the player without coming across like a glorified tutorial or crash course on the place you're supposed to have lived in all your life.
But all that said, I really enjoyed the game, much more than I thought I would, and I hope you do too.

Disclosure: I am friends with the developer. However, I am friends with many developers on Steam, and usually do not purchase their games. But, this one is 99 cents, and it looked pretty cool, so, I went ahead.
Paradoxically, part of what makes this game easy to recommend is how little I have to convey about it. One plays as a pig, and uses the arrow buttons to dash around the screen, popping all the balloons one can. Hit a bird, lose one of the three starting balloons. Lose all three, lose the game. Hitting balloons causes the pig to bounce in the air, so, there's a bit of strategy involved in running away/dashing to or from balloons.
A typical game is around 2-3 minutes. It gets a little repetitive, but, there's enough to the gameplay to where it can be picked up again and again. If you've ever heard of or played Montaro, another 99 cent, simplistic game with small animals, it's similar to that - The Howler, too. One thing I appreciated was that one's multiplier rises as one progresses through the game, causing an almost exponential increase in points, which successfully generates excitement when late in the game, down to the last balloon.
I have a few complaints. It's one of those games where anything that changes the framerate actually changes the pace of the game, which means that background processes running can suddenly change gameplay speed. The prices for the pigs (the game has a variety to choose from) seem artificially high - reducing them would give a greater feeling of progression and accomplishment over the course of the time most people would play the game for. When hitting balloons, the birds fall to the ground, but, the pig falls faster if one doesn't hit the "up" arrow, meaning one can lose a balloon to the poor bird's corpse.
But, overall, I quite enjoy it. The backgrounds look great, the art style is bright and expressive, the theme fits - it's a great game to look at, and a great game to spend a few minutes on in between classes, during lunch breaks, etc. Again, Montaro and The Howler are what I would compare it to.
Thanks for reading!

Игрок выступает в роли журналиста Майлза Апшера, управление которым производится от первого лица. С собой Майлз носит блокнот, в который в течение игры вносит заметки, и видеокамеру. Так как Майлз обычный человек, не владеющий никаким оружием, видеокамера — единственный предмет, который можно использовать.
Камера оснащена прибором ночного видения, без которого по плохо освещенной лечебнице просто невозможно передвигаться. При использовании прибора ночного видения камера начинает быстро разряжаться, что заставляет игрока постоянно искать разбросанные повсюду батарейки.
Игровой процесс включает в себя решение несложных головоломок, скрытное перемещение, а также моменты, в которых необходимо убегать от своих преследователей, преодолевая различные препятствия, и скрываться в темноте, шкафчиках для одежды, под кроватями и в других укромных местах. В игре у главного героя нет союзников, не считая отца Мартина и одного пациента, который преследует и помогает вам в течение всей игры.

We follow the story of the narrator, which aims to understand the psyche of his friend, and motivate him in continuing developing video games. Every creation in this game being that of his friend, there is, in my mind, no point in criticizing the gameplay part.
In fact, the developer was able to make all these quite irrelevant parts relevant to each other, and from this point of view, it is a well done job.
But what blew my mind was the last level when the narrator went about crazy to tell his friend how he is sorry, very emotional sequence. Really.

When you get this game, you'll probably think "Oh, another game developer that released another rushed zombie game", but as you play further into the game, you'll see that this game was well planned by the game devs and shows effort.
For a game still in alpha, this game exhibits features and gameplay that is on level with the "popular" zombie/apocalyptic-survival games that are fully released and made by more prestigious companies.
As I played this game, I realized that things like noise, movement, and visibility were not just factors you could ignore as you progress in the game. They are key factors you have to consider before wandering off into the world, even when you have the best weapons equipped, because when you start running in the middle of the road in day time, there's a good chance that you'll attract zombies on the way which can create a horde that will lead to your untimely demise.
You'll also need to consider the environment. When it is raining, your character gets wet, and as they become more exposed to the rain, they are more likely to catch a cold, which can cause unwanted attention from your sneezing and coughing. The heat in the summer months and cold in the winter can severely hamper your character's effectiveness.
The immersion and realism of this game is also a neat feature that most games can't, or won't do. The gunshot from afar that attracts zombies, that apocalyptic feeling when the walls are stained with blood, and the occasional dead survivor you see on the ground, that hopeless feeling when the windows and doors are being banged on by the zombies, the tense moments when you try to get in a house undetected, and the fear you feel when the house alarm goes off.
All in all, it's an extremely developed game for a game still in it's alpha.

First off, let me say that The Beginner's Guide has a fantastic moral behind it, and the entire premise is actually quite touching. My problem with this 'game' however is that it is selling on steam for $10.
The following essentially spoils the entire game, but it's necessary to discuss.
Davey Wreden was trying to assess and identify who his friend 'Coda' was through the small games he made. He grew concerned for Coda, as the games seemed to be expressing someone who was suffering from mental health issues. Davey went as far as showing Coda's games to others and sharing his assumed concerns for Coda's mental health.
Coda took huge offense to this, and the last level in The Beginner's Guide has a series of rooms with messages in it from Coda stating things like "Would you stop taking my games and showing them to people against my wishes?"
This leaves us with two conclusions. Either Davey is so in the wrong here it's not funny, for commercially selling this experience after being told explicitly to not do so, or Coda is simply a fiction, and the game itself was fabricated to simply demonstrate a scenario like this to get us thinking.
I would like to believe that this is a fiction, because betraying someone you've already betrayed so badly again, doing the same thing but on a far larger scale, is no source for reconciliation (which Davey is seeking), and it's borderline pure evil for self-gain.
But then if it is a fiction, and Coda isn't real, then it kinda looses what made the game so emotionally impactful, that this is a shout from someone who is legitimately apologetic, and just wants to say sorry.
I guess you could justify that the fabrication of a story to deliver the moral is perfectly alright, and worth the experience. I wouldn't disagree with you. I'm just sitting in the park for if Coda actually does exist, that this shouldn't be on the Steam Store.

This game provides a neat simplistic simulation of a train network. There are some aspects I really like about this game, but sadly it is also plagued by several issues. Here's why this is only a
:
Don't be fooled by the "Puzzle" tag. Had I tried the demo, I'm not sure I would have bought this. The game has a small strategic component in track laying and decision-making and a rather large simulation/management/action aspect in switching the tracks. But this game does not challenge your brain in any substantial way and even within the same level there is a huge amount of randomness. The store page claims there are "story mode" and "random mode". As far as I can tell after beating the game, this is simply false advertising. All story mode levels are randomized (which stations open first, where trains appear, how long they are).
Since the stations have fixed locations, each level has an optimal track layout. This is obvious after playing the level, but since the locations are hidden at first and the stations appear one by one, you can get screwed over pretty badly (stations may even spawn on top of existing tracks). On your second play-through the strategic component is vastly diminished and the game is even more of a mindless clicker game.
Finally, all the hidden information makes it really hard to make informed decisions and plan ahead. Trains appear randomly at stations and before sending them out you only know their destination, not their length and speed. This forces you to react on the spot, which to me kills even the tiny semblance of a puzzle game this might otherwise have. You cannot optimize or plan ahead for those sweet moments of perfect timing.
There is also an eco-sim aspect where you have to make money to afford tracks and demolitions. While there are no running costs, for some crazy reason the developers decided to "tax" you regularly. This turns out to be horribly annoying as you might be 1 tile away from cashing in a train and still go bankrupt due to taxes, forcing you to limit building and keep a small stockpile of money. If you are caught up in building it's very easy to over-spend and lose the game which is incredibly frustrating. I don't see what purpose the tax serves, other than to annoy players.
Other criticisms include a lackluster tutorial and the game not auto-pausing upon entering a level. I still don't know where the active area of the button to send a train out of a station actually is or if there is a different reason why the game sometimes ignores my clicks. I've also had a few times where trains crashed randomly. Once reversing a train on a straight track even somehow made it crash into itself (which gave me an achivement). The level selection is styled as an album, but each time you enter the menu you have to sit through a short page-flipping animation, which gets old really fast. And some of the achievements are needlessly grindy.
And still I didn't hate the game. It wasn't the game I expected, but I simply had fun. Admittedly, mostly mindless fun, but still! The game looks and runs great, even on low-end systems. The technical aspects were solid (separate volume sliders, UI scaling, colour blind mode). You can tell the maps were created with a lot of love and attention for detail. They are filled with diverse custom objects and some really neat historical references that I enjoyed very much. There is some amount of replayability, but I liked figuring out a map for the first time best and there is no map generator. Each map giving you 3 extra tasks (like making X amount of money, never pausing, never crashing trains, etc.) gave an otherwise very easy and forgiving game a bit of a challenging edge, which I enjoyed greatly. Given my frustration with several aspects of the game I can't recommend spending full price on it, but picking it up on sale might be nice. If you still have doubts, maybe try the demo first?

The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these mechanics, to realise that they’re not just hard they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Cuphead truly ARE casuals- of course they wouldn’t appreciate, for instance, the humour in King Dice’s catchphrase “lets roll,” which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev’s Russian epic Fathers and Sons. I’m smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Studio MDHR’s genius wit unfolds itself on their television screens.

Just in case you live under a rock and didn't know, Bioshock is an FPS with some RPG and survival-horror elements, designed by Ken Levine(the creator of System Shock and System Shock 2) for 2k Games. It features a dystopian underwater steam-punk city called Rapture, where science was free of ethic or penal laws, morals and religion, which led to advances in genetics which gave people super-powers.  These super-powers then drove most of them bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane and made the whole city go to hell.
So let me start this review with this simple tagline: best game EVER!!! Ok, that might be stretching it a bit, since not all people love the FPS genre as much as I do. So I'll just say this: best FPS EVER.
Of course a lot of people will say I'm exaggerating, but let's just look at this objectivally:
Pros: +Story
+ Dialogue (or more correctly monologues)
+Combat
+Eploration
+RPG elements
+Graphics
+Atmosphere
Cons: What, are you crazy? NOTHING. Ok, I'm kidding...just some minor imperfections, no game is flawless.
Let's elaborate on this. (If you haven't figured it out yet, this will be a long and in-depth review. You have been warned):
First of all, we'll talk about story. You tell me a game with a better story and way that respective story is told, than this game. Can you? Of course some people(the♥♥♥♥♥♥percentage) will give some laughable answers like Half Life or Halo. I mean...come oooooon. Half Life is just the eternal alien invasion cliche. Yes, it does have some interesting elements that set it apart, but it's not particularly well told and is very ambiguous. It's more like a pretext, than true storytelling. And Halo is basically Starship Troopers - the video game...BOOOORING!!!!!! I'm sorry to all the Halo fans, but I gotta tell you the ugly truth: that game is HIGHLY OVERRATED. While Bioshock has a unique setting, plot-twists that, I have to be honest, I did not see coming, an extremely intelligent villain that could spout something other than how he'll kill the hero or how he'll achieve total world domination. Oh, and it also questions the very nature of life, mortality, humanity, morality,  business and commerce, crime, science and ethics...you know, little stuff like that. All while others make games about an invincible MI6 agent who stops cartoonishly evil villains from taking over the world by killing everyone in sight. S.T.A.L.K.E.R - Shadow of Chenrobyl and the two Metro games also have hugely interesting and deep stories, the way I thought only games from the ex-Soviet space could. They're the ones I'd put closest to this game in the storytelling department, but I just think Bioshock goes a little bit further, the proverbial extra-mile if you prefer. Yes, I do think Bioshock Infinite's story is good too. But is it great? NO!!! Why? Because it goes so far up its own♥♥♥♥♥ especially after opening the parallel dimensions can of worms, I just couldn't follow it at times, even though it does wrap things up pretty nicely. And no, I don't think Bioshock is at all similar in story with System Shock 2. And it is far superior. It has tons more imagination and creativity and tells its story much better. The only sad part it has(sort of) is that the protagonist has about as much personality as a sea sponge, which is the major flaw of ALL silent protagonists. But it's ok here (certainly a lot more acceptable than in Half Life) because the story's not about him. It's about the world. And so he's just a pair of eyes for us to witness this world and the story it has to offer, which we've already established is magnificent.
Now, let's talk about the graphics and overall atmosphere of the world. It didn't impress that much at the time, since S.T.A.L.K.E.R was already out and it had beautiful outdoor scenries and a few months later Crysis came and blew them both out of the water, but this is indeed a BEAUTIFUL game. It may be indoor only and you don't get to do any swimming, but DAAAMN, Rapture is so pretty (albeit creepy as hell at them same time) and so well rendered. I used to just stop and look at the surroundings and imagine how awesome it would have been to live there (you know, BEFORE it all went to hell). And the feel and look of the '50s is captured PERFECTLY, dystopia and all. And, like I said, the atmosphere is creepy. It's not actually a survival-horror FPS like F.E.A.R or Doom 3, but the creep-out factor is over the edge in this game. It's impossible not to be creeped out when you see everything that was once so beautiful now gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥and that these...creatures (for lack of a better word) that roam the halls (splicers, Little Sisters and Big Daddies) used to be human, but now have either lost any trace of humanity or still keep a fragment of it in their ru(a)ptured (pun intended) minds, between all the nonsense they're spouting ("Jesus loves me, this I know/ Cause the Bible told me so") and them whacking you with a pipe, thinking you're "the monster". Could it be that they're right, though? With the way you're killing them all, mercilessly? Nah, wipe those thoughts away and keep going. You're only defending yourself, after all. Creepy, heavy and encumbering. Just the way I f***ing like it. This makes every return to Rapture fill me up with dread, but also with a strange, eerie, totally unexplained joy.
But maybe you don't care about that as much as I. How's the game-play, you say? Totally f***ing awesome. This is a game that lets you play as a strange combination between Humphrey Bogart's Samuel Spade from The Maltese Falcon and Milo Ventimiglia's Peter Petrelli from Heroes (obscure nerdy reference alert), who has been muted for some strange reason. Now those are a couple of names I never thought I'd ever put in the same sentence. Bioshock seems to constantly manage the impossible.  So this means that the combat is fun as hell: you shoot lightning, fire and ice from your hands, weapons are fun to use and feel powerful, the selection is unique, even if the individual weapons themselves aren't,  you have a telekinesis ability that makes Freeman's gravity gun pale in comparisson, you hack security machines and use them against enemies, you can impale enemies to the wall or leave them hanging from the ceiling, there's a surprisingly rich role-playing system of passive abilities, you can even sick killer bees on them, ffs And it's not just combat that's fun. There's also the exploration element: you find food, ammo, money, vending machines to spend that money, codes for opening doors, recordings that tell you more about the wonderful world you're in, funny posters, you hack safes, you can even get hammered (and it's freaking hilarious). Just awesome. It isn't quite the best fun I've ever had with an FPS' game-play, to be honest, but topping off Half Life 2 or the People Can Fly games (Painkiller and Bulletstorm) is pretty hard. Definitely up there, though.
So there you have it: a game that's almost perfect in all of its main areas. Does it have some flaws? Sure, like any game, but nothing that stands out like a rabitt's ears. There's the hacking mini-game which isn't very awesome(not horrible, though), it's a little bit on the easy side, especially compared to the brutal and unforgiving System Shock (although The Big Daddies will offfer quite a challenge, at least at first), some weapons and plasmids become useless and the ending is a tad bit disappointing compared to the rest of the story. All minor gripes, though.
So let's do a summary and put it all in maths:
Game-play............... 9.2
Story........................ 9.8
Graphics................... 10
Atmosphere.............. 10
Overall Feeling.......... 10
So the final score is a very solid 9.8. So yeah, most definitely the best FPS of all time. Anyone wo diagrees with me can challenge me to a boxing match. Same way Uwe Boll did with his critics :D.
P.S. He beat them all to a bloody pulp :-p.

The Expendabros is a clever little piece of promo material for The Expendables 3 movie and the original Broforce game. I haven't payed Broforce yet to know how different the gameplay is, but you essentially massacre goons in a playstyle much like Metal Slug, though without the vehicles and end of level boss fights. There are occasional miniboses and a couple true bosses, but they aren't a focus of the gameplay, and more a focus of the end plot. You start off with one character that shoots dual pistols that have limited range, but moderate fire rate. Don't worry about damage, pratically all standard goons die in one hit. Throughout the levels are cages that have other Bros which automatically change your character to the new bro, lets you play with the bro's different abilities, and gives you a free life. Lives are precious, as while it is extremely easy to kill most enemies, it's extremely easy to die. All Bros have a melee attack and a standard attack which is usually ranged, though one Bro has medium ranged melee attack, and a special that requires ammo, but usually has high damage or area of effect.
It's very fun and doesn't take itself too seriously. It can be a bit fustrating to die from an unfortunate environmental explosion or hazard. And the 3rd or 4th last level killed me way much more than I'd like to admit, but I still had fun despite the constant deaths. The pixel art is charming and the sound design is intentially over the top with hard rocking soundtracks and a 'roid raging announcer. There's not alot to this game, but it's a fun little experiment that doesn't really do anything wrong (besides a UI issue on the Configure Keypad screen) and it can be finish in around an hour. Oh, and it's free.

TL;DR: If scoring and challenges are for you, then you will love SUPERHOT, otherwise you will be sorely disappointed.
I was skeptical about this at first after seeing an abundance of negative reviews about the length of SUPERHOT, but I gave it a shot after a friend's recommendation.
This is a scoring and challenge game, which I typically find short and similar to an arcade game. The extended hours of fun come from completing the challenge levels (katana-only, fists-only, fullstop, real-time, etc.) and going for speed records (speed run challenges). You will often find games like this in the following categories: shumps/shooting games, so-called rogue likes, and indie platformers. As an aside, I saw similar negative reviews for "House of the Dying Sun," a tactics/space FPS game, criticizing the length, but neglecting the challenges.
SUPERHOT is graphically simple, which helps to make important things pop out (enemies, bullets, and weapons), but is stylish enough to be interesting to look at.
Sound is slowed down with time, which provides an indicator of enemies and bullets outside of your view. The glass shattering sounds are fairly satisfying as well.
Overall, I enjoy this simple yet challenging game.

Fun little game about managing some trains. It's not a traditional sim game focused on business and economics. Instead, the strategy in Train Valley is about how to lay down your tracks and how you manage your trains.
Laying down train tracks is pretty self-explanatory. You have a budget limiting how much track you can make. Going through obstacles costs additional money. There are many things to consider when designing your track. Distance between stations, how many trains your track can hold at one time, how often you have to switch junctions.
The player controls when trains depart and which way trains go at junctions. This is most of the "gameplay": making sure trains get to the right station as quickly as possible without accidents.
The game is pretty easy if you only send
trains. However, you have the option to effectively send as many trains as you want to earn more money (until you go bankrupt from all the collisions). The is where most of the challenge was for me: testing and pushing the limits of my track and my micro to send as many trains as possible.

-Storyline running parallel to Gordon Freeman and John Shepard's.
Cons
-Shorter storyline than both Half-Life and Opposing Force.
-No new enemies or weapons that I can think of.
So obviously more of a redo of Half-Life with little variation for those of you who've played it . I'd still recommend it because it is enjoyable and gives you the feeling of playing Half-Life without having to repeat Half-Life. That being said, given its smaller, less varied nature, it's understandable if you don't get this game.

This game most likely sets itself in the description as "Simulation", it's not.  And for that matter, I do NOT recommend it to the average player.
This being said, I did indeed like the game, but I do not recommend as it has a mislabel.
Jane's Advance Strike Fighters is completely arcade; the only physics to the game would be your thrust with minimal turning resistance based on the plane. Upon playing it, I do not feel any other force such as the pull of gravity when pushing the nose down, so divebombing is mainly an easy tactic on ground forces.
It's a great time killer, but the difficulty is pretty hard even for 'Normal'.
The one thing I'd hate about this game is that the physics also applies to missles- they are not realistic.   To dodge a missle, your plane has to be a good 80-100 degrees perpendicular to it... and a certain speed. Or else you will be spammed from all angles no matter what your manuevers are. I personally do like this as my hobby of airplanes is the A-10 Thunderbolt, which is useful at the beginning of the game, but soon gets overwhelmed and hit by missles from all angles JUST because the SPEED isn't fast enough. I have no problem handling this airplane in 'simulated' games such as Ace Combat, Hawx, or DCS Universe. This puts VERY hard aggression on difficulty and on levels you will face many deaths because of this flaw- the good thing is that every in-mission objective is its own checkpoint to restart from... but your time flying from point A to point B and repetition of in-game voice will be super annoying.
This game does feature some level with friendlies... but they mostly get killed in the first few minutes, even if you're quick to destroy the enemy fighters. And by "Some" levels, I mean about 2-3, out of a good 20 missions it has. (approximate)
You will be mostly alone listening to the dialogue of your Base Control and your Pilot... which in honest opinion Base Control is a very stupid decision maker sometimes and often contradicts himself... let alone your pilot sounds like someone who's very enthusiastic... but doesn't know anything that's going on in the world around him.  Most of the time I'd just want to fly back to base and bomb it.
Gameplay is quite fast,  as said it's arcade, but it's pretty good in non-heptic moments.  There's bugs in the game, sometimes it will crash on you in-game so expect those grudges. There was even a moment in game where a convoy I was supposed to protect was killed... I got overwhelmed. Yet a fail screen never came up: the dead convoy's dialogue continued regularly and I ended up finishing the mission with a completion.  Okies....
The game does offer some challenges, perhaps a third to half the missions require you to fly low through enemy territory
so many of of the missions are air-ground combat with missle defenses shooting at you and you looking for a radar tower nearby before continuing with whatever objective you are to destroy. What I do like is a nice double-tap boost the game offers, makes you flick your afterburners to ridiculous speeds close to the ground, the graphics is nice, and the pressure on turning changes dramatically, so make sure you want to do this where you can fly straight.
Soundtrack is repetitive, but quite calming at times.  I do like how ever engagement changes the music, so you'd know if you're being attack and you won't go crazy with the same sounds over and over.
Overall, likable game to the Arcade person. Completely disliked by those looking for simulation. For the price... I'd say get it on sale. It's not really worth a full price.

The concept game is enough for me here. The only thing truly added to make this game better was more weapons. Instead of making the game more complex via varied enemies, objectives, constraints/modifiers, etc., the game only adds more enemies. This is a huge problem at the last level of the game (there are not many levels) and instead of leaving me satisfied at the end, I was enourmously frustrated.
Not only do the last levels take place in bullet hell (the bad kind), but the AI and physics inconsistencies make each try just different enough to make you want to throw your mouse through your monitor. Instead of perfecting a path and nailing the bad dudes in perfect sucession, you end up praying that the RNG gods work in your favor. The concept game worked so well because it was tight and very controlled. The full game should not be the concept with more enemies, but that is exactly what it is.
There is one genuinely original mechanic introduced in this game, but it is only in the last few levels and is quite shallow. It seems thrown in there just because someone thought of it, not because it would actually interact well with the existing mechanics.
I would not say I am good at this game, but it only took me 3 hours to beat. At $25, I recommend this to absolutely noone. I uninstalled immediately after completing the main story.

THIS GAME IS AN EARLY ACCESS SCAM
Developers realized their game wasn't working out and had too many issues to fix.  But instead of telling their customers this, they rushed to a "Full Release" version that was hilariously unfinished in September 2015 so they could get the game featured on the Steam Store Front Page right before the holidays.
They strung it along further by releasing constant "Minor updates" up through December 2015.  These updates weren't actually intended to fix their horribly broken game, but intended to keep it showing on the Steam Store Front Page as "Recently Updated" throughout the 2015 holiday season.
In January 2016, by all appearances, this developer had stopped all development.  The community manager had left, they were inactive on Social Media and Steam, and nothing was done to fix the games issues.
In April 2016, they posted a vague "Please be patient" message on Steam via a private steam account (Which, to this day, doesn't respond to inquiries about the game).  By "Coincidence", one month later, in May 2016, the game is featured in a Humble Indie Bundle.  The April Post was done simply to make potential Humble Bundle buyers believe that the game is being actively developed and supported were they to check it's news page.  The devs apparently had no intention of continuing work on the game, they just wanted to string folks along and milk every last dime they could from sales, even from within the Humble Bundle.
Their website and forums were taken down after the domain names are currently up for sale.  None of their social media accounts (Facebook, Twitter, ect) have posted anything or responded to anything.  E-Mails are unanswered.  No new activity on Steam.
This is a classic "Take the money and run" Early-Access scam, on par with what the developers of Towns did.  This needs to stop.  DO NOT buy this game.  If you do, you support these practices.  I bought into the game in it's Early Alpha stages and regret doing so.  Spread the word about developers like this and be more discerning in the future about your Early Access Purchases.  That's the only way this kinda crap is going to stop.

This game! I got the demo because I was bored but quit halfway through the first part with the female splicer because I was scared, haha. I had heard great things about the game and its sequels though. One day I had gotten 10 dollars, and I went on Steam to look for a game to buy. "Oh, look, 2k sale." I thought. I clicked on it to see if there was anything worth picking up, and for 10 dollars, Bioshock, Bioshock 2, And Infinite all in one bundle. FOR 10 DOLLARS! It was almost perfect. After comtemplating if it would be too scary or not (Hey, I know, I'm a wuss.) I decided to be a man and get the game. After all, it was a deal that wasn't worth passing up. I would feel guilty if I didn't buy it. I mean, a bundle that was originally 60 now 10 - How COULD you pass that up? Like seriously. I started playing, and after the first part with the splicer (Which honestly wasn't that bad) I started to develop a love for the game and I started to think "This really does deserve all the hype and good ratings it gets." After a week, I'm still playing and I love it. Just buy the game. You won't regret it.
STORY - This game has a pretty neat and original story. You're just an average guy who gets in an average plane crash.
Though - Me and the other players of this game wouldn't call it "average." You land in the atlantic ocean  and you're the only survivor. There is a lighthouse close to you, and like every normal person out there, you wouldn't just float in the water waiting for something. You would go to the freakin' lighthouse. Once you get in there, you see a mini submarine thing. You get in it and after hearing a little backstory, you discover the city of Rapture. A city that was built by a man called Andrew Ryan. A huge city underneath the sea! What could go wrong? Well for starters, a lot. The city is infested with monsters called splicers, which are mutated humans, and also other monsters and threats. A man called Atlas contacts you, and says that he wants to help you. And so begins your awesome and eerie journey through Rapture. 9.5/10
CHARACTERS - All the humans (Which, there are only like 3-5 in this city mainly because its mostly populated by mutated humans) Can't really be trusted. Most of them, anyway. Not much is revealed about the protagonist - YOU - But a lot is revealed about other charecters by things called diaries, where you can find all over Rapture to hear some storytime. I recommend you read them to hear the full story of Rapture and the dark, evil things that happened in the city. 9/10
GAMEPLAY - Its pretty awesome - you get these cool super powers called "plasmids" that you can damage enemies with, with things like electricity, fire, ice, and... bees. Yes, you can attack enemies with swarms of bees. It's awesome. You can switch between those and your melee weapon/gun with the right click. It's cool to get some combos in like "ICE SHOOT! Nowwww MELEE!" And its pretty fun to let loose and kill stuff in Rapture. Except for those annoying flying things with the red lights. Ugh, I hate those things. And the noise they make. Fwa fwa! Fwa fwa! FWA FWA! But you get the idea. Besides splicers, there are other enemies like little sisters, mutated little girls (Sick, right?) roaming around Rapture to collect ADAM from splicers, which is a form of liquid that you can use to upgrade your powers and such. There are also Big Daddys, mutated adults which are designated to protect and escort little sisters around Rapture. And BOY are those things SCARY! The good thing is, They only attack if you attack first. Then there are those pesky machines. Pretty self explanatory for those things, I guess. Just turrets and flying robots. 10/10
QnA
Is it scary? - Its pretty dark but honestly, after the first 45 minutes you get used to it.
Is it hard to run?  - Not at all. I can pump out 60 frames on low settings on my crappy laptop.
Is it hard? - I only have experience with easy mode, and before you go and comment "lulz u rnt no hardcor gamer" Like this kid Vinny in my school who thinks you need to be a 'hardcore gamer' By playing on the highest difficulty, which isn't true, you just have to play a lot, In my defense its more fun when its easy. I havent died once and I'm 85% Through the game. That says a lot already.
-FINAL VERDICT-
Its a great game and definitely deserves all the good ratings. I love it. It's a classic shooter and if you're a gamer, BioShock is a must play. You NEED to play this game. I can't speak for the others, though. 9.8/10
