This is a great management/building/strategy game.  It's like a combination between Mini Metro, Subway Shuffle, and Cities in Motion.
You start with a certain amount of cash that ticks down as time passes and you use that money to build train tracks to connect the train stations that will appear over time.  Once the stations are connected, you must dispatch trains from their starting station to the correct station without crashing them into other trains.  The trains also have an amount of money that will decrease as time passes so there is an incentive to get the train to the station asap.  Getting a train to a station successfully yields you whatever money is left over from its starting money pool.
The crux of the game is balancing your money (it's easy to go bankrupt on more challenging levels), building tracks that will allow trains to reach all stations (in both directions), managing the interchange directions which are constantly changing as trains pass over them, and avoiding train collisions.
My only complaint is I want more content!

My first review of Jane's Advanced Strike Fighters, and any game for that matter.
So first things first, it's Jane's......Yes Jane's, mostly known through NATO recognition books and it's WWII simulators from the 1990's, most famous being Jane's WWII Fighters which came out in 1998. After that no one heard from Jane's again until 2011 when they released this game.
I want to point something out, I have no idea why this game got SO much hate, it's the first time that the team at Jane's ever came forward with a developed game with consoles in mind, XBOX 360 and PS3, PC was already on their cards for this game.
Onto the game itself, now, in the style of the early Acecombat games. You are flying as part of an air force of a tiny but overrun republic which is in itself, close to collapse at the hands of the Northern government and the NPAF forces. There are 16 missions overall and dare I say it they are nicely laid out! Plenty of area to fly around in and having the ability to carry more than 2 weapons on your fighters, which is something Ace Combat never did, so pat on the back to them for including this.
Another good point is the amount of aircraft you can choose from, again in Ace Combat style you have factual aircraft, prototypes that flew or mysterious/fictional Superplanes. All handle well and some are a bit overpowered than they should be. The 3D models are quite nice, however the damage model is non existent, but with what you get into it doesn't really matter.
Looking at Mission design, Yes a couple could have been tweaked a little bit but it's not really noticable, how you execute the missions are down to tactics and what logic you can utilise whilst carrying out these missions, and also it depends what type of plane you choose as well, well with the large selection of 30 fighter jets you have a nice pick and mix bag on how you want to go through your missions.
Next, the AI, now given credit where it's due the AI DO FIGHT BACK, which is a nice touch, and they often outsmart you when you're being blase towards them and they don't mess around either! from the Hedgehog AA's to the defending fighters you WILL have your hands full when the mission is at it's climax!
Onto the final points, and a bit of personal thought on the game, Yes it's not as and never will be as good as Acecombat, but give it a chance and it can be enjoyable if you love a not too hard paced flying game. Unfortunately what they DID try to do with this game, was to try and get a ''Simulaton'' feel to it, which it does feel like in SOME areas of gameplay but not all of it.
Another bit of personal thought and I have a feeling it's why Jane's got so much hate, was Acecombat Assault Horizon was released the same year...I don't think it was JASF's fault. It WAS against hard competition so I feel that the game was released when it's far superior cousin was on the shelves and it ran into the obsolete trolley instantly.
Do I like it more than Ace Combat? in the long term no. Do I respect the game for what it is? Yes a lot! Do I like it better than Assault Horizon....?....Actually Yes! It's a good throwback to the original Ace Combats on PS1 and PS2! Which I think if Jane's had come out on PS2 with these graphics...it would have had fair competition.
Overall I think this game is great and it DOES deserve to be played for what it is. I guess I am probably one of the few users that stands up for what this game is.
All the best to everyone and thanks for reading my review of Janes Advanced Strike Fighters.

Train Valley is an extraordinarily simple and yet oddly satisfying game about connecting up rail stations. The game has extremely simple controls – you have the ability to build train tracks, to send a ready train out from a train station, to cause a train to get readied up ahead of schedule, to stop a train in its tracks, or to put a train into reverse.
At it’s heart, this is a puzzle game with very simple resource management. Every time a train reaches its destination, you are rewarded with money. If a train should crash into another train, or run out of track, it will blow up, denying you any money you might have earned from the train. The longer it takes for you to deliver a train to its destination, the less money you earn – and given that deploying a train early costs you money, if you aren’t fast enough on the deployment, you can lose net money in this fashion. Each train has a specific destination, randomly assigned at generation; sending a train to the wrong station will cause it to simply turn around and re-emerge, possibly wrecking havoc with the other trains you’ve got moving around the map.
Building train tracks costs money, and demolishing obstacles so you can build train tracks costs money.
Every “year” in game (and the years go by quite fast – the game proceeds very quickly through the years, though it can be paused) you must pay a tax, which depletes your money – run out of money, and it is game over.
That’s it. There’s really nothing else here. And yet, the game manages to get 24 levels of content out of it.
The trick to this game is the limitations on rail placement. The rail can go from straight in one tile, to 45 degrees in the next tile, to 90 degrees in the tile after that. Train tracks can cross at perpendicular angles – in which case, trains cannot switch tracks between the routes – or rails can merge together at 45 degree angles, allowing multiple tracks to merge together or to split traffic on the rails apart.
Thus, the game’s placement of the train stations – 3-8 per map – combined with the obstacles on the map (some can be demolished, albeit sometimes at great expense which makes it unwise to do so, but some – like mountains and rivers – cannot be) and narrow outlets for rail traffic (such as a single bridge or tunnel) make each level a different challenge.
Simply beating the game is pretty easy; the real challenge of the game is to complete the three optional challenges on each of the levels. These vary from challenges requiring perfect play – never allowing a train to go to the wrong station, never stopping a train, and never allowing a train to crash – to challenges which restrict you in other ways, like not allowing you to demolish more than a certain value of obstacles on the map (requiring you to thread your way between them) or requiring you to earn a certain amount of money (requiring you to deploy many trains early and deliver your trains quickly and consistently to their destination).
All in all, this game was simple but somehow quite satisfying. It isn’t anything overly complicated, or extraordinarily difficult, but it felt like just the right amount of challenge to be enjoyable without being brainless. Each level takes about 20 minutes to complete, which makes for a nice little bite-sized challenge, and 100%ing the game might take somewhere in the realm of 12 hours or so, as you replay some of the levels to try and complete the more difficult challenges.
If you enjoy puzzle games with some minor resource management, this might be up your alley. If you prefer more active games, though, this might feel a bit too passive; while you do have control over what is going on, and sometimes you need to switch things up fairly fast, this is more like a management sim than an action game. And if you’re looking for a story, look elsewhere; there is nothing here but simple train puzzles.

I went into this game with the mindset, "Eh, it's a popular horror game and it really doesn't look all that scary, so what's the harm in playing it?"
Three days in and I'm looking at the walls, searching for clues to whatever grizzly tale this once-innocent pizzaria posesses.
The game centers around your character, Mike Schmidt, as you work the night shift at a pizzaria called Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. The game is rumored to take place around the early 90's due to the amount you get paid (about $125 at the end of the week) being the minimum wage for that time. Also due to the pizzaria's one defining quality; animatronics of child-friendly creatures. Foxy the Pirate Fox, Chica the Chicken, Bonnie the Bunny and Freddy Fazbear. What could go wrong?
Did I mention the whole "these guys are here to kill you so have fun surviving" bit?
In the game, you are forced to survive six hours per five nights as these four animatronics try to kill you, each night getting more challenging than the last. As the nights progress, phone messages the previous night guard left for you are played, giving you hints about what to do and posters begin to change on the walls, desribing how a once-loved restauraunt became the nightmarish hell it now exists as.
The game mainly relies on jumpscares for its horror, but the true horror shines when you start paying attention to the posters on the walls and phone calls given to you. (Also I'm about to SPOIL most of the story for you so you might want to leave if you don't want the story spoiled).
***SPOILER ALERT***
Posters of the animatronics begin to rapidly change into posters of a crying child, a poster of Freddy becomes yellow, resulting in the appearence of the ghost-like, limp Golden Freddy teleporting into your office, crashing the game as he kills you. Finally is the rules poster that changes into four different newspaper articles, describing the story of a man who killed five children and stuffed their bodies into the animatronics that now roam the halls looking for you.
Did I mention the phone messages decribing an event known as The Bite of '87, where the front of someone's skull was bit off by an animatronic?
***END OF SPOILERS***
So needless to say, the haunting tale behind why the restaurant looks so abandoned in the game is some heavily disturbing material that only gets more disturbing as the second game expands upon it.
Now, of course, the game's mechanics are simple, but in my eyes, the best thing about this game is the anticipation of the jumpscare. You know that if you get caught you will be jumpscared, but you never know when it could happen. The scares are pretty lackluster, minus Golden Freddy the first time you encounter him, but the anticipation of them helps to balence them out.
There's also the fact that, by night 4, you're only checking two places on the camera to make sure the two toughest animatronics aren't moving from their spots. This makes the entire camera gimmick much less substantial to a game based around using security cameras and can take away from the game.
Then again, not having your eyes on half the animatronics by night 4 to actually stand a chance just brings the tension up even further.
So, to summize, Five Nights at Freddys, or FNAF, does great in:
A creepy setting
Creative way of giving instructions on how the game is played
Creative, fragmented storytelling that allows for a lot of interpretation
Great tension
While it doesn't do so great in:
Jumpscares being relied on so much
Little use for the security cameras
Final Score: 7/10

We recruited armored grunts for our front line backed up by herbalists, slingers and hunters. Research is slow as we've put most of our lumber, stone and iron resources into troops and housing. The Chief Thane has decreed that some of the cucumber crops that have fed us through the hard winter must be uprooted in favor of watermelon, to aid us in battle. We huddle close in the barracks, as we hear the horn blow, signaling the order to march.
We meet the enemy on the field of battle. We can see the bloodlust on the beaks of our enemies. What can turtle's do against such hate? With a roar of vengeance in our hearts, and for our families, our ancestors, we advance into the fray. The demon owl's wings flap against our shells, and their claws scratch our faces as our front line grunts deploy a pikewall to try and stop their furious charge. Our slingers and hunters unleash a barrage of ranged death at our foes. The battle rages on, until both sides fall exhausted on the battlefield, neither gaining ground. We look to our leader, our hero. We've fought valiantly, and suffered casualties. Surely a tactical retreat is in order? CHARGE!!!!!!! He commands. Like madturtle's, we scream "FREEDOM" as we waddle towards our enemies, mad with fury. The owls fight back, only to give ground and finally flap for safety as we drive them from the field. The day is our's.
All for less than 5$.

Unlike some reviewers, I knew in advance what train valley was and what it wasn't. It is NOT a tycoon game or a simulator of any kind. If you play this with a relaxed attitude and want to sit back and build a few tracks and ponder over choices, this game isn't what you're looking for. Train valley certainly has management decisions, but time and money are pressing issues; every second counts. You'll need to think quick, act fast and plan ahead if you want to keep bankruptcy and train crashes at bay. This may not be how this game looks or even plays in the first few minutes, but believe me: get another game if you want a slow paced game.
For me personally, this is exactly the sort of game I actually wanted to play when trying out openRRT: lay down tracks, navigate the routes and have a ballet of near-misses as you estimate which train is best to set first. Granted: the money aspect can feel a bit game'y: there's an annual upkeep cost, tracks cost money, train crashes cost money, building over landmarks cost money and the cargo loses value over time. You've got to accept this all "as is", but hey...that's how this game rolls.
Controls are intuitive and easy. Up to the point where I'd almost expect this game to be a mobile game, though the visuals are still a couple notches above mobile standards. Building rails is a matter clicking and dragging (which sounds obvious, but at the end of the level you probably have a complex web of relay junctions on the board) and everything else is as intuitive as can be.
The whole gist of this game is how things go from a steady, simple pace to keeping as much trains on the correct route as possible. It's not uncommon to guide train A to location B and train C to location D, only to discover that while you were busy elsewhere, you forgot to switch the junction so C would go to D instead of to B. The game is set up so near misses are common, and since train crashes are hard (if not impossible) to recover from, you can say that this game is hard and//or frustrating. But for some reason, I don't feel it either way. Yes, I seldomly do okay, but the fact that I'm totally in control of what I build or how many extra trains I dispatch reduces that. Most of the time, I think this game is just hilarious if things go wrong (yup...those train drivers do NOT stop on their own :P ).
All in all: do I advise it? Absolutely yes. Do I advise it for everyone? Absolutely not. Read the review, guys 'n girls. If you reduce this review to a simple thumbs up, I'm not one to come crying to when your calm little train simulator expects you to take risks to not go bankrupt. :P

(TL:DR at bottom)
I have a fair few hours on this game so I thought "why not review it"
Let's go over some basic pros and cons
Pros:
-Realistic bullet drop and overall bullet physics
-Realistic weapons with realistic upgrades
-everything is mostly equal
-nothing is too overpowered
-great maps
-2 theatres (Eastern front and pacific)
-Cheap (Relative to other top ranked shooters like CoD and Battlefield)
-Great community
-Good voice acting
-Tanks
-Different Roles
Those are just a few, I probably missed some
Cons:
-Small community
Now for a more detailed review.
1.) Great weapon balance: Whether you just picked up the game or you have 200 hours, the only thing determining who will win in a fight is skill.  All the weapons in the game are balanced.  I'm not saying that in the aspect like if you are facing someone with a ppsh-41 (submachine gun) and sniper at 300 meters you will have the same chance in killing one another, the sniper would obviously win, I'm saying in terms of the same class of weapon.  For example, the ppsh and mp-40 are not similar, but are balanced.  The mp-40 has a low rate of fire while the ppsh-41 has a high one.  This means the mp-40 is better at medium range than the ppsh-41 but the ppsh-41 is better at close range than the mp-40
2.) Great class balance: You may think, "Oh, screw the rifle, I will mow people down with the machine gun".  There is one downside to this.  While using a machine gun, you must deploy it to fire accurately.  Deploying it means you have to set it up somewhere and remain stationary to fire accurately.  You can hip-fire, but this is very innacurate and there is no reticle to help you.
3.) Great variety: You may also say, "Great, another game where you aimlessly shoot the other team and that's all you do".  Well, you're just wrong.  Sure, if you pick a class like rifle and assault, you do shoot the enemy, but you also do so much more.  I won't explain what those are here, but I'm sure there is a guide on it.
One final note: Noobs-please take the rifleman class
TL:DR: Great balance, variety, maps, community and voice acting.  Semi-small community.

Flatout 2, in my opinion, is one of the best arcade raceing games you can find and I'm not just saying that because of the nostalgia I have for playing it on Playstation2.
Pros:
+Graphics: For a game that came out in 2006 on the Playstation 2, it looks amazing. I would even say it's Playstation 3 good.
+Gameplay: The controls are simple but fun and there's plenty of gamemodes to make the price well worth it, from career mode to single races, minigames to demolition. The tracks are filled with hundreds of collidable and destructable objects to smash through, windows, furniture, billboards, fences, barn walls, ECT. The minigames are one of the best parts of the game, how can you not love hurling your drivers ragdoll body into a dart board or row of bowling pins?
+Very little glitches: Ignore the hours Steam says that i have played because I've spend a good few dozen hours back on the PS2 and I hardly run into any glitches. Really the only ones I seem to find is the rare object floating or getting stuck in your car for a few seconds, nothing gamebreaking.
+Soundtrack: The choice of music in Flatout 2 is amazing and I would dare say comparable to the older Tony Hawk games. Some of the bands featured in the game are Bad Religion, Megadeth, Yellowcard, Fallout Boy and Nickleback.
Cons:
- Controller support: Although you can use an Xbox 360 controller, it's only partially compadable, but to be honest I don't find it to be that big of a deal, just a bit annoying. You can't pause with the controller or navigate the menus, because controllers only work when racing.
-No online support: Don't get this game if you're looking for a racing game to play with friend online, because it's a a port of a Playstation 2 game.
-Sofia Martinez: ♥♥♥♥ that ♥♥♥♥♥! She's always right behind you and the smallest mistake can have her to pass you up.

The good: It's a lot of fun at start. Even the campaign is good, some missions are challenging indeed. The political system, health, complex industry and mass transit gives better game experiance than its predecessors. Advancements through ages is great design and really fun to play.
The bad: When your island becomes big, and your factories become numerous, the resource flow becomes terrible. Materials get stuck at one place and teamsters are nowhere to be found. Railroad system would help a lot if material mass transport would be possible.

There are so many amazing things to love about this game.
For starters, the look of the world.  Never have I seen a survival game that fit its world with its aesthetic as much as this game.  The painted feel of the world manages to both immerse one in its beauty and remind us of the harshness of the world around us.  The animals feel real, the trees feel real, and the world feels real despite (or perhaps, because) of the Robert Bateman-esque appearance.
Second, the atmosphere.  No matter what difficulty you play on, the atmosphere is perfect.  Whether it's the calm peacefulness of the North (Canadian here) on Pilgrim, the contemplative stillness that comes with Voyager, or the terrifying cold and treacherous nights that come with Stalker, the game feels consistent throughtout.  It presents the same picture with three different feelings every time.
Finally, the gameplay.  Some survival games that throw the user into a giant sandbox with a million toys and no direction, while others put the difficulty curve so high up that the game constantly feels like chore.  The Long Dark manages to find a perfect spot in terms of difficulty, and the best place possible in terms of survival.  On Voyager, the game naturally feels hard, but in an accomplishable way that encourages exploration and rewards the player for it, while on Stalker, the game feels cruel but natural, making the player feel like a tiny insect trying to survive in a harsh reality.  Unlike games where the difficulty setting just changes how many enemies spawn and how much health they have, this one makes difficulty actually mean something.  And the survival elements are perfect, stripping the game down to the basics while still giving the player enough agency to make their actions have weight and consequence.
And on top of all of that, the development team is slowly but surely making the game better, ensuring that each update is polished to a mirror shine.
This is the best survival game to come out in YEARS.  Buy it.

Overall
By game overall design one of the best idle incremental game on the market.
For casual semi-afk gameplay fits very well. Pick your heroes, let them gain experience, collect items, upgrade items. All you need for idle-incremental game is available for you. Item stats even give you options to have some RPG perspective on your heroes.
User interface
UI is simple and clean.  Everything is easy to find and logically placed.
Well done graphics. The whole theme throughout the  game is good. Not too much details and at same time it has enough details. I specially like the choise of colors and overall simplicity in graphics.
GamePlay
For idle incremental game the game flow is good. When you are actively playing you can give small boost to your heroes by clicking. Clicking is nicely combined with keyboard shortcuts. But I would not consider this game as Clicker. Clicking is just nice addon for its idle-incremental mechanics.
For Free to Play game the ingame shop does not make $$$ players superior. It does give you option to advance faster, but that is fair bonus for investing $$$ ingame.
Nice feature I like is that PvP side is separated from your single player advancements.
Its moved into 6 day long Season. At the beginning of every season you pick you 5 heroes and during that season you will compete using only those heroes. On Season side at the beginning of the season every player starts with lvl 1 heroes (does not affect your heroes in your main storyline,).
So it will somewhat even out the balance between new and old players.
Seasons also do not have AFK grinding.
So on Seasons active players will be at the top of leaderboards.
CONS:
It has some bugs in it. The ones I have seen, are not gamebreakers.
Couple features would need some balancing.
The game cleary has great potential to be successful one. Its not as bad as most commentators have made it look.
Really yucky, clunky inventory - the game doesn't hold your hand, but there's serious enjoyment here too...

IT'S FINALLY OUT. Was very excited to start the game's story after playing the hell out of survival mode and all the challenges they released to placate the starving masses. Unfortunately I'm stuck on the damned bear after working my butt off to get through episode 2. For some reason bears are not running away when I shoot them like the game says they should and I get mauled every time I try to take on the old bear. Suffice to say my save is screwed and I have lost interest in playing through AGAIN. I played through episode 1 about 5 times and kept getting murdered by wolves (same issue of not running away when they are supposed to, which did not happen as much in early access?). I understand that the game needs to be punishing, but playing through an episode takes SEVERAL hours if you wanna get all the things, and The Long Dark's narrative experience is just not good enough for me to want to see the same cutscenes and spend hours grinding the same quests more than a few times, though few things are.
HOWEVER, The Long Dark was more than worth the current $35 price tag even during early access when it was selling for less. It's an incredibly immersive, yet simplistic experience that will keep you in your computer chair for 100 hours or more, especially if you treat the survival mode as an RPG adventure. It is very easy to play a meta-game, in which you take the random encounters and the letters found everywhere, and and create your own narrative. The excellent voicework done by Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer creates prevalent atmosphere of  lonliness because whichever PC you are playing as chatters with themselves endlessly. To bring it all home is the truly enormous, beautiful, and surprisingly diverse maps, all stylisticly painted, and designed to look good on a computer with zero budget. Sure it's annoying to wake up to your character dying of thirst after every nap because of the weird time scale, but I've paid much more for much, much worse.
BUY IT, play survival mode, don't force yourself to do the campaign unless it's patched and you'll walk away after 100 hours feeling like you played a fun as hell solo experience. (WARNING: when you play The Long Dark, you eat like you are in The Long Dark. When you eat in the game you eat for real)

One of my all time favorite games ends up being an indie developed game. If you're on the fence, do it. The artwork style is interesting, quite refreshing from the confusion of games that people complain aren't real enough even though they look plain as day. Be ready to think though, you have to work pretty hard if you want to survive. I found it hard (at first) to even survive on the normal (Voyageur) difficulty until I had played quite a few hours on the easier difficulty. There are a few grievances, though they are pretty easy to overlook considering it's still in alpha.
There are a few ideas that I think would give a little extra flavor to the game. Wasn't sure where else to post these so that it could be seen for use. It's a lot, but mostly nit-picky ideas from a huge fan who spends much of his time playing this game and paying attention to ways to possibly improve the game. To the developers, please consider some of the following:
Maybe make it possible to slip on the ice when sprinting. Just an interesting idea.
Also, maybe add a few more animals and later on. You don't need to go overboard, but a little more variety might be nice. As of now, there are only a few choices: Rabbits, Deer, Wolves, Bears, or Fish (I appreciate the few species of fish rather than just FISH) and then only a few plants: rosehips, mushrooms, lichens, maple or birch saplings, and cedar or fir trees that I have discovered. Maybe a few more would spice things up.
Another thing, I don't want to see this like Call of Duty or anything, but have you considered adding maybe a scoped weapon/scope attachment for the rifle? As well, maybe a pistol and pump action shotgun for a little variety and possibly benefits/drawbacks to each.
As well, I know you can use the hunting knife when being attacked, but maybe it could also be equipped while regularly walking around. I think that would be nice.
Related to the last one, I would REALLY like to see the boxes/books of matches be able to STAY EQUIPPED when using them for light. I tend to use the match books to walk around houses to save lantern fuel, but every time the match dies, I have to reequip them and it gets a tad old. It would be a really nice touch.
Also, I don't know if it's true, but I read somewhere that the celestial bodies or whatever wasn't accurate. I like to use the sun as a compass sometimes, and it'd be pretty cool if it rose in the East and set in the West like we see in real life.
Perhaps your character could draw a map of the places they've been in his or her journal as you travel. No marker to show where you are, but just a map of where you've been. Give you more reason to go out and explore and whatnot.
Maybe an online cooperative gameplay? No versus because obviously it would get ruined by trolls and it would no longer be about survival, it would be another Call of Duty in a different form. But you know, just like a two to four player cooperative style where you could help each other, share rations and supplies, explore the world together or apart. I would REALLY love to see something come of this, because my friends and I all play the game and we get bummed that you can only play alone. I would love to work together as a pair or team to try to brave the wilderness!
Final idea, I love being able to write in my journal and see all that happened on specific days. Nice job there. But it would be cool if you could reread old journals of your deceased characters say in the main menu. Or to add on the online play idea, maybe add an option in the settings to see other players' journals where they died when you are walking around the wilderness. See their story, that sort of thing. I think they have something like that in Dark Souls, though I may be wrong.
Alright, sorry for so much writing, I just really love this game! Please, if you have yet to play the game give it a shot! It's a great game and these guys really deserve the credit! Thanks everyone!

Positives:
* Beautiful art with really pretty hand-drawn characters and beautiful watercolour backgrounds. So many little details such as a little tire swing which wobbles a little in the back of the first boss. A lot of love and care went into this - they didn't just do the minimum effort possible, everything is constantly in motion which looks great. Keeping the animations at the classic 24fps but keeping actual objects in motion at 60 does a top job of keeping the animations looking classic without sacrificing playability. Does a good job of avoiding clutter - at no point during the bosses did things get in the way. It also acts as a good incentive to keep pushing when you may not otherwise have done so.
* The soundtrack is fantastic. Live recordings of fast jazz which consistently match the mood of the fight.
* Boss rush - I know a lot of people don't really like this, but I adore bosses in general in games so for a game to be just bosses makes me really happy. Especially wonderful is the phases, where each boss has a good set of attack patterns and forms. No boss has fewer than three phases, and quite a few have many more. No monotony is present at all too which is great. Some bosses have a fight while in a plane which breaks up gameplay more obviously, but even without that there is a lot of variety. It's not just every boss being a still-standing giant thing which shoots you. Some bosses are more mobile, some largely use melee attacks rather than range, some summon flunkies to attack you, some you have to fight while on moving platforms, and the list goes on. There is an astounding amount of variety in the style of battle gameplay-wise which will prevent any feeling of monotony. The multiphase battles also really help this too. Not to mention the visual designs of the bosses and their various phases are absolutely inspired. And goddamn, winning is so immensely satisfying. Some of the bosses in the third island had me literally shouting in triumph after winning them.
* The difficulty spends most of its time being at a good level for the vision - really difficult, but fair. Most often when you die you can look upon your death and go "yep - that was my fault", whether it be because you ♥♥♥♥ed up or weren't paying attention or haven't properly learned how to dodge an attack.
* Length - while each boss and running level is short - only 2-3 minutes usually with some even shorter - the game took me just over 10 and a half hours to complete on Regular difficulty for my first run, despite there only being 25 levels (19 bosses, 6 running levels). The reason for this is the difficulty - you will not complete these bosses first try most likely. Instead, you'll keep going at them time and time again. You learn the patterns of the bosses and improve each time, picking up how to dodge certain attacks that you struggled with before. I found myself often dying on the first phase of the boss for the first 5 minutes, yet by the time I was able to complete the fight I was rarely taking damage on the first phases. This, along with the quick and multiphase nature of the bosses, really prevents them from getting boring despite the fact you may be spending the most part of 30 minutes on each one. The phases that you can do reliably will pass quickly enough that you won't find them dull, and those that you can't pass easily you will spend your time concentrating and working hard so those don't get boring either. This also gives a really good sense of progression in the time it takes to beat the boss, and for me it never felt like I was just hitting a brick wall against the bosses, at least never for very long.
* I liked the weapon and ability upgrades and loadout switches, with each map allowing the equipping of two shot types, an ability, and a super attack. Depending on the boss or run 'n' gun level, a different loadout had different uses, and while I spent most of the game using the peashooter/spread attack combination, I did sometimes switch weapons and often switched abilities based on the fight.
* While this should really fit in with visuals or the bosses, I would really like to note just how much character every boss has. Their style and movement is wonderfully detailed, resulting in a really strongly character which you fight against.
* Quick restarts after death. A small thing but one which is always nice and prevents frustration.
Negatives:
* If you look at the above paragraphs, you'll notice a certain qualifier appearing very often - "in the bosses". Now, the run 'n' gun levels aren't bad, and are very fun at times with some really inspired mechanics and fantastic small animations and characters, but also contain a lot of issues that the bosses don't. They're a bit easier to get bored of, for some reason I can't quite place. There's certainly a bit more of randomness to the enemy generation, meaning I often found myself stuck in a situation where I had no choice but to take damage, and I often found myself just having to split second dodge to survive rather than the great pattern memorisation of the bosses. They often take a lot longer to perfect and complete than the bosses which is a pain. I often found the levels getting cluttered, with lots of enemies on screen, and in particular the massive cloud death animation for enemies - pretty as it is, for a game like this having vision obscured for such a time is a real issue.
* Occasionally (and I do mean very occasionally) a boss's attack feels a little unfair. This is very rare - maybe three or four bosses throughout the game have a single attack that feels unfair. One boss notably however has several attacks which feel unfair, including rather hard to dodge projectiles which force you into a position where you'll almost certainly be hit by different projectiles, and an unavoidable attack which freezes you in place for about a second during a section with many bullets. That boss was a real pain. However, to restate, that still means that the vast majority of bosses are amazing and feel entirely fair, and even those other bosses with one unfair attack feel incredibly fair and fun during their course.
* While I enjoyed the harsh difficulty, I can see why many didn't and find it too tough to continue. Not really a negative for me but worth highlighting in a review.
* There is a certain randomness element to multiple bosses. I don't mean "it's pure luck whether you survive or die", it's nothing that bad and constitutes a very minor complaint. It's merely random selection of attacks. While for many bosses this is fun and provides variety when replaying, a couple of bosses have one attack that they randomly select which is much, much harder than the alternatives. A minor issue but one that can be bothersome.
* A couple of minor bugs happened during my game. Nothing gamebreaking but one did require a restart. Not a huge issue but worth noting.
* Another minor one, but considering how much character the game infuses into the many bosses or even phases of bosses, it's really a shame that I came out feeling there wasn't much character to Cuphead, who's meant to be the main character.
Overall:
While I have many complaints about the run 'n' gun levels, the key issue was "sections" being frustrating -  I spent a fair amount of my time on the run 'n' guns enjoying myself with tough but fair gameplay and genuinely inspired platforming mechanics, and it's just a shame that the bothersome sections generally left me with a bad taste in my mouth after completing each run 'n' gun. While that may look like a high volume of complaints, my opinion of the game as a whole is overwhelmingly positive. I did somewhat enjoy the run 'n' guns, and I had an incredible amount of fun playing the bosses and spent almost every second of the boss fights really enjoying myself. The fantastic visuals and music act as a brilliant reward for the challenging but mostly fair battles. Fantastic.

The current state of the gaming Industry had convinced me indie and triple games alike had nothing to offer but patronizing encouragement for trivial in game achievements, watered down mechanics to appeal to the lowest common denominator and games that dread the thought of challenging their players in fear of alienating the village idiot. Top that off with microtransaction culture and day 1 dlc, and you can understand why I've drifted away from gaming for a good many years. With the exception of Dark Souls, I'd largely written off gaming. What was once an enjoyable pastime had become a monotonous, tedious chore, utterly devoid of any sense of accomplishment or originality.
Cuphead alone, managed to challenge my perception of gaming as a whole, and reminded me of how much gaming still has to offer. The game, aesthetically speaking is quite charming, a throwback to old cartoons in the 30’s. How the character express themselves, how they move, how they react, it’s all heavily stylized. Now perhaps it’s because I’m bored to tears with modern gaming’s fascination with realism and believability at the expense of creativity, but the artistic style really is quite endearing, the amount of creativity that went into the design of the bosses and enemies is really a spectacle to behold. It makes the game just as fun to watch as it is to play. You’ll find yourself up against everything from shapeshifting blimps that take the form of constellations, to evil middle eastern genies that try to knock you out with their own flaming skull.  Like most would say, it’s a 30’s cartoon come to life, everything from the character movement to the sound design lends itself to this 30’s cartoon quality. The creativity at play here is a brilliant breath of fresh air.
The mechanics of Cuphead are also remarkably well polished, running and firing feels natural and smooth, the platforming is precise and there is a respectable attention to detail. In example -holding A makes a full jump, tapping a gives a small jump. The fact that the jump distance is determined by how long you keep your finger on the jump button shows just how much thought and concern was given to the mechanics of the game.  Similarly, you can jump and fire down, jump and fire north east, northwest. Even if you never end up using these mechanical features, it sets a standard for the refinement of it’s mechanics, everything has been carefully optimized and feels as fluid and natural as possible. The game also adds parrying to the run and gun formula which adds an interesting skillful fold to the core gameplay. It’s a welcome mechanic that is carefully interwoven into the game, managing to add a new, interesting fold to encounters. The game also throws in plane missions similar to the likes of Phalanx or Life Force, you’ll find yourself having the entire screen to maneuver around in, which paves the way for elements of bullet hell. The game draws inspiration from a couple different genres and blends them together to form a nice palatable cocktail. Bullethell, space shooter, Contra. You can find small streak of each genre’s respective mechanics here.
My only gripe is that there are too few Run and Gun sections, there are 19 bosses in the game, and all are very vibrant and unique, one is hardly similar to the other. Comparatively however there are only 6 run and gun levels. Though the levels that are there are all fairly good, save for one, or possibly two. First, Funhosue Frazzle, which stats of interesting, but relies too much on the celling swap gimmick and becomes rather monotonous near the end and Funfair Fever which is the inverse situation. It starts off rather droll and becomes better as the stage progresses. The two levels aren’t even bad, just, more on the side of mediocre when compared to the rest, which is a high bars anyways.
The disproportionate amount of bosses to levels can somewhat diminish the thrill as I found myself wanting  there to be one extra level per each world to pace out the battle with the bosses. Though, it is almost a non issue, as I still greatly enjoyed fighting each boss and learning their individual attack patterns. Though, some bosses can also be quite a test of patience! There were many times where I screamed a string of nonsensical obscenities at particular bosses.  Looking at you, Dr Kahl. Dying will be a relentlessly repeating theme in your playthrough, the game is a true challenge, it’s why the game is so satisfying, finally beating that boss after losing 20 odd something times is a feat worth feeling proud of. So few games manage to tred the line between enjoyable and frustrating, but Cuphead manages to accomplish what few others could.
There are a couple of bugs here and there, not too many, but they are present. I recall an uncommon bug in TreeTop Trouble were the stump man’s base didn’t die and there are a one or two occasions were I felt like the hitboxes registered damage on my character when I did not see him get struck by the enemy. A certain end game sub boss comes to kind, but I am willing to chalk that up to me being careless. My other minor gripe is that sometimes it is hard to tell if you are damaging a boss, especially with certain weapons and super moves. There is also a moment with the final boss where his neck elongates and covers 95% of the screen save for a small safe area on the left and despite being in the safe area, I took damage still, a kind of annoying bug, but easy to work around. I also take a minor issue with some guns and abilites being much weaker than others. Particularly the lobbing gun and some of the insta parry abilities are very underpowered comapared to some others. I would go as far as saying that the multishot in way too many situations is the most powerful gun (not all, but most). Otherwise, I’ve got no other gripes. And if the worst complaint I have about a game had me complain there aren't enough run and gun levels, it really speaks well of the game. Especially since within mere days, most of these issues will probably be resolved anyways.
Cuphead teaches us an important lesson. Less is more. Cuphead might not have content that will last you months, but what it does have, will leave you immeasurably more satisfied than Call of Duty or whatever current sequelized mess is garnering unwarranted hype. Modern games take the Swiss army knife approach to gameplay of having multiple inferior iterations of mechanical play. Terribly implemented stealth, poorly realized rpg trees, bare bones dialogue system, ect. Cuphead, focuses just on running and gunning and perfects it, everything In the game revolves around the mechanics, the levels, bosses, maneuvers, abilities, they all serve to reinforce the same concept, thus they become interwoven. It’s the difference between a cut of meat from Mcdonalds and getting a premium steak from a 5 star Restaurant that specializes in steak. You can argue that Mcdonalds has more variety, but does it really matter if everything tastes like cardboard?
To sum, Cuphead is a game deserving of it’s praise, a game that remembers the merits of actually being one. Cuphead is a game I won’t soon forget, and for something as great as Cuphead going for $20, it’s a steal of a deal. If you’re like myself, and have grown apart from gaming per the utter lack of challenge or creativity, do yourself a favor and buy this. It’s a relentlessly difficult game, but immensely rewarding. No multi-million dollar game on the market can claim the same.
Oh, and people are not automatically entitled to the full content of ANY game. If you can’t beat the game on standard difficulty, it is entirely fair you will not see all the phases of a boss, the full extent of a level or even all the bosses. Content earned will always be more gratifying than content willfully given. This "consumer must be given everything no matter the consequences", mentality, is why gaming is in the sorry state that it is.

The Guide isn't a game. It's another one of those increasingly popular "walking simulator" narrative games. This one was created by the same developer of the amazingly funny "Stanley Parable", which was one of the few narrative games I actually feel is worth playing (but only once, since the magic is lost on replaying it). Unfortunately, The Beginner's Guide doesn't even offer that much.
Purportedly an exploration of an avant garde game designer's own developmental history, it is arguably an autobiography or just a tale-tale. What it isn't, is particularly enjoyable as it consists entirely of walking through poorly rendered levels of never-released test-games while the narrator drones on at you. The biggest - and only - mystery is what it all means: was the developer, as the narrator insists, a misunderstood genius whose games were his only way of expressing his insecurities? Or was the "developer" just a representation of the narrator's own struggle with maintaining his creativity? Or is it something else? It's an interesting enough tangle that - fortunately - isn't wrapped up neatly by the end of the game but left to the player's own interpretation. Unfortunately, that is all the game has going for it. The "mini-games" aren't games at all, so there isn't anything to actually DO in this game except walk continually forward. There's no point to exploration since there's nothing to find, and the game (purposely) lacks in visual polish. It's all well and good to leave the meaning of the game up to the player, but that only works if the player cares enough about the product to spare it some thought. Unfortunately, the presentation was so tiresome that I just preferred to walk away from it and find something actually INTERESTING to think about.

A Strategic Puzzle game that will have you cursing because you forgot to turn one arrow and a train crashed or went somewhere it should not have gone. This is NOT a Train Simulator but it IS a rewarding Strategic Puzzle game
This game is a fun strategic puzzle game well worth a buy, whether you are looking to fill in 20 minutes or a couple of hours.
The core concept of the game is to lay tracks for trains to go from one station to another where tracks meet each other there are arrows which will force a train to go onto one or the other track becoming more complex as you try to ensure trains don't crash and arrive at the correct station by adding less direct routs but allowing more trains on screen at a time.
This game is an extremely well made game with a good number of interesting and challenging levels. As puzzle games go, this is one of my favourite, the challenges on each level very much stretches you and adds an optional layer of difficulty to a game that on the surface is quite simple. As a strategy game this is a simple and easy going game that will have you working and reworking the track positions to find the perfect layout (I personally use the sandbox mode to plan out my level without the limits of trains and money)
If you want an interesting challenge that also allows for a fairly laidback style of gameplay then you will struggle to find better experience. Considering the price this game is very much worth it even if its not on sale. Start to finish (including DLC) your looking at a about 10-15 hours if you purposely try to complete all the challenges but its very easy for the game to last you 20+ hours

Would you kindly read this review and buy this game?
If you didn't know, BioShock is claimed to be one of the most revolutionary FPS's games of all time, and that statement has plently of truth to it. It exceeds in almost all areas, but no gem is without its flaws. Unfortunately for BioShock, these flaws can be quite noticeable when you come across to them. DO NOT let that discourage you from playing this game though; it's an experience you don't want to miss.
In terms of presentation, BioShock fails to unimpress. The view of the underwater city of Rapture will amaze you when it emerges on your screen,
and the steampunk art style is very unique, while being consistent throughout the game. Voice acting is perfect without a doubt, and characters such as Ryan Andrew and Sander Cohen will leave a lasting impression long after you finish the game. Sound design is extremly well-done as well: the whale-like moans from the hulking Big Daddies are very creepy, and the game only uses music for atmospheric reasons,

adding an extra layer of immersion that makes the game quite creepy, but never outright scary (which is not what the game is trying to do).
The story is the main highlight of BioShock, and presents themes and ideologies that are very applicable to reality, mainly the view of objectivism. Plot twists and unforgetable characters will make the experience a memorable ones, and each audio-diary will flesh out the world of Rapture, especially in events following up to the game. As for the main protagonist Jack, he's the typical silent playable character that every shooter seems to have, but his background information makes him quite interesting. Despite this, the story is damned near perfect, even if it feels ever-so rushed after the games huge revelation and twist.
BioShock is a prime example of how video games are art, and is one you should not overlook. Even where it missteps in gameplay, it's story and presentation are grand throughout, and provide a unique experience you will not forget and will come back to again and again.
There is no denying that BioShock is a game that will stand the test of time.

I simply cannot recommend the game in this state.
I was trying to wait out for updates, I was trying to wait for the developers to come back from their "logistics stuff" that they've been doing for months (it doesn't take that long for someone or even multiple people to move), and the developers have seemingly fallen off the face of the planet (maybe into the Edge of Space!? lol, couldn't resist, sorry).
Starbound did a similar thing where Chucklefish relocated their entire company, but yet here's the thing: Chucklefish at least continued to maintain their website, and actually continued communications with the playerbase. Since Handyman Studios posted that update in April (It is October as I write this), there hasn't been any communication whatsoever, except for 1 tweet that advertised the game being on sale somewhere.
So, since this appears to be abandonware, I believe I can attach my own review of this game.
Do I recommend it as it is now? NO.
Do I think it could be a good game? YES, but only if the developers actually come back.
Do I hope they would come back and make it better? YES!
The game has a nice premise going for it, but there are simply too many things wrong with it to make it an actual good purchase. If you really want a tech demo to mess around with, maybe for inspiration or ideas, go ahead. I'd wait until it's on sale, though.
So, Pros/Cons:
Pros:
-A nice recipe unlock system
-Good graphics for a sidescrolling indie game
-Lots of inventive ideas (pets, character upgrades, etc)
-A unique take on the sandbox exploration game (you progress by going down)
-You start with a jetpack
Cons:
-Control/UI Bugs (your character will shoot their weapon or use their tool while dragging items around in the UI)
-Unfinished game and obvious missing content (the last two biomes are not finished, some tech unlocks are empty)
-Blah combat (you always feel weak as bleeep because your guns all suck, and it takes 10+ shots to kill anything)
-Melee combat is useless
-Cheap enemies that can fly through solid walls to attack you
-Dungeons are buggy, some of those bugs were fixed in the last update, but some remain from what I've been told
-No Real Map System (this is the huge deal-breaker for me -- you only have a "current" minimap of what you can currently see and that's it)
-Somewhat clunky UI system (inventory management, everything freshly obtained gets dumped into the hotbar etc)
-UI LAG. Yes, the UI lags when trying to move items around.
Recap: A game that has/had a lot of potential but sadly fell way short. I tried hard to like this game, because when I first started playing it, I was like "I hope they finish this game or make it better!" But sadly.. it doesn't look like that will ever come to pass. If you're a game developer and you're looking for some inspiration, I'd suggest picking this game up on sale, maybe someone else can develop something else that is similar but way better?

Overview:
Banished is a colony management game set in Medieval times that calls to mind games like The Settlers and Imperium Romanum, only without the combat aspect.  As a result, the game is focused on micromanagement of people over city management.  You build, and if your settlement isn't wiped out through starvation (and not many people freeze), you keep gathering resources, build buildings which will hopefully sustain a higher population, and that takes you back to square one.
Repetitive?  Absolutely.  Name a city or colony management game that wasn't!  The main difference, is that all you have to go for, is achievements to proudly display on Steam.  There's no in-game rewards for increasing the size of your settlement to a certain population or buildings to unlock, because every building is unlocked at the beginning.
Graphics and sound:
You've seen the screenshots.  I personally like the look and feel of everything in-game.  My main criticism is that you don't see workers in hunter's lodges taking down game, but everything looks great.  You can do nothing except simply look at the screen, and what you see looks wonderful.  (ASSuming that you don't have any pressing needs for your colony that bring your mood down!) The music is amazing, not just because it helps with setting the mood for the game, but I went a long time actually listening to it, as opposed to other games, which I normally mute, and then play my own brand of music while I enjoy a game.
Positives:
What I like about Banished invokes the memory of US Suprme Court (Associate) Justice Potter Stewart, who was best remembered for saying "I know it when I see it."  There's something I truly enjoy about the experence of Banished, which is why I kept playing repeatedly before I decided to give up completely and seek out a refund.
The system for trading with visiting merchants is by far the best feature of Banished.  Trades is purely barter, and isn't even-steven.  It would have been better if merchants came by with more than one type of product to trade, but my only complaint, was that the time I was able to trade for chickens, I could only afford one, and that thing obviously didn't get itself pregnant!  (At least nobody can accuse the game of lacking in realism in that department.)
The tutorial was exactly the way game tutorials should be:  Broken into multiple parts, highly controlled environments, and each of them actually educating the player well, with one exception I'll cover in the negatives.
Achievements in Banished are my idea of achievements.  You're not going to get anything just because you built your first building.  These are achievements which you actually have to put in a genuine amount of work to earn.
Negatives:
FOOD!!  This is a totally broken feature of the game, and especially if you're playing at the most difficult level.  (Which I always like to do.)  The game is ambiguious about how much food hunters, gatherers, and fishermen produce.  Farmlands, orchards, and animal pens are much the same way.  Even when I assign priority to the construction of food production (and producing a minimal amount of coats, firewood, and tools), I still have a serious problem with people starving.
Edit:  Food producers have varying degrees of productivity depending on the location of their building, but the game does nothing to show the projected effectiveness of food producers at the time of building placement.
As for starvation, it really makes me sick that children can starve to death, and the game informs you that the person who died is in fact a child.  Whoever put this feature in Banished should really be ashamed of themselves.  (I play video games to escape issues like child starvation...  If Banished was any worse, it would be exposing me to mass shootings, public bombings, and news of Donald Trump's latest outrage.)
How wrong is it that once onions and mushrooms harvested in the wild are grown, they can only be consumed?  Certainly even the lowest functioning of brains would know that to sustain a community, these gathered items should be planted to produce even more of them in the future.
Resource allocation in the game's natural state is impossible.  One time I got lucky enough to have a tangible population for my settlement, and once I built me a mine to gather coal (to add to my wood and iron to make steel tools), I found myself unable to make tools because the jackwagons in my settlement took all the coal, and then burned it because they couldn't wait for more firewood?
Of course, you could download mods that Banished enjoyable enough to play, but it seems pointless, because achievements become restricted.
Conclusion:
Perhaps the idiotic tendencies of the people in Banished is why they were "banished" from their homeland in the first place, but there's a huge difference between a human being of below average intelligence and a brain damaged butt monkey.  There's also a huge difference between a game who's most difficult level is challenging, and a game who's most dificult level is sadistic and impossible to play.
I purchased Banished for 70% off (US$4.99), and I still feel like I paid too much for the game.  I gave a good faith effort to enjoy Banished.  I really wish I can enjoy Banished.  If there's any groups of people who enjoy Banished, they either feel proud of themselves playing on the easiest levels, or they're the type of person who enjoys the challenge of being in defenseless situations involving robbery and♥♥♥♥♥♥  My advice is to stick to The Settlers-series of games.  Even the very first one made in 1994 is a more enjoyable experience.

Everything, including the pause menu, is an enjoyment and feels very polished in this game, which is all the more an achievement considering the rudimentary gameplay setting as well as the visual style. The vanilla game is considered to have little replayability past 15-20h, but after checking out some of the mods and mod campaigns, personally I'll continue playing vanilla for a while.
It's not necessarily an easy-going game and you may at times feel your mistakes burning as the time flies, but at the same time it's very well fitted for people who enjoy slow-paced and casual gameplay. And despite this it can be very immersive! I rarely speeded up the time in-game, there's really enough to do and check out and just follow the villagers even.
The tutorial feels somewhat overwhelming with a lot of essential reading, but the gameplay itself is best flow I've had in a while. Now about the mods (made by Black Liquid Software): they are as official as it gets, good community and well-polished mod packs! Take note that you can't access the newest mod packs through Steam Workshop for some complex reasons, so download on Black Liquid's website. The mod overhauls themselves offer a rough start with much more complex mechanisms than vanilla, but if you like complex supply chains plus rewarding customization options, then that's certainly a route you should take.
Compared to Cities: Skylines? Completely different gerne, but just as a point of reference - Skylines is a game to lose yourself in and try and learn and try again and oh boy it's 3AM; Banished is a game to hit pause and be happy just looking at the forest. Not too much music in it, but what's there is good and fitting!

There are so many amazing things to love about this game.
For starters, the look of the world.  Never have I seen a survival game that fit its world with its aesthetic as much as this game.  The painted feel of the world manages to both immerse one in its beauty and remind us of the harshness of the world around us.  The animals feel real, the trees feel real, and the world feels real despite (or perhaps, because) of the Robert Bateman-esque appearance.
Second, the atmosphere.  No matter what difficulty you play on, the atmosphere is perfect.  Whether it's the calm peacefulness of the North (Canadian here) on Pilgrim, the contemplative stillness that comes with Voyager, or the terrifying cold and treacherous nights that come with Stalker, the game feels consistent throughtout.  It presents the same picture with three different feelings every time.
Finally, the gameplay.  Some survival games that throw the user into a giant sandbox with a million toys and no direction, while others put the difficulty curve so high up that the game constantly feels like chore.  The Long Dark manages to find a perfect spot in terms of difficulty, and the best place possible in terms of survival.  On Voyager, the game naturally feels hard, but in an accomplishable way that encourages exploration and rewards the player for it, while on Stalker, the game feels cruel but natural, making the player feel like a tiny insect trying to survive in a harsh reality.  Unlike games where the difficulty setting just changes how many enemies spawn and how much health they have, this one makes difficulty actually mean something.  And the survival elements are perfect, stripping the game down to the basics while still giving the player enough agency to make their actions have weight and consequence.
And on top of all of that, the development team is slowly but surely making the game better, ensuring that each update is polished to a mirror shine.

IT'S FINALLY OUT. Was very excited to start the game's story after playing the hell out of survival mode and all the challenges they released to placate the starving masses. Unfortunately I'm stuck on the damned bear after working my butt off to get through episode 2. For some reason bears are not running away when I shoot them like the game says they should and I get mauled every time I try to take on the old bear. Suffice to say my save is screwed and I have lost interest in playing through AGAIN. I played through episode 1 about 5 times and kept getting murdered by wolves (same issue of not running away when they are supposed to, which did not happen as much in early access?). I understand that the game needs to be punishing, but playing through an episode takes SEVERAL hours if you wanna get all the things, and The Long Dark's narrative experience is just not good enough for me to want to see the same cutscenes and spend hours grinding the same quests more than a few times, though few things are.
HOWEVER, The Long Dark was more than worth the current $35 price tag even during early access when it was selling for less. It's an incredibly immersive, yet simplistic experience that will keep you in your computer chair for 100 hours or more, especially if you treat the survival mode as an RPG adventure. It is very easy to play a meta-game, in which you take the random encounters and the letters found everywhere, and and create your own narrative. The excellent voicework done by Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer creates prevalent atmosphere of  lonliness because whichever PC you are playing as chatters with themselves endlessly. To bring it all home is the truly enormous, beautiful, and surprisingly diverse maps, all stylisticly painted, and designed to look good on a computer with zero budget. Sure it's annoying to wake up to your character dying of thirst after every nap because of the weird time scale, but I've paid much more for much, much worse.
BUY IT, play survival mode, don't force yourself to do the campaign unless it's patched and you'll walk away after 100 hours feeling like you played a fun as hell solo experience. (WARNING: when you play The Long Dark, you eat like you are in The Long Dark. When you eat in the game you eat for real)

You start this game by accepting at some point during the Victorian era, London was sold
to a group of strange otherworldly forces and moved underground.  This is the world of Fallen London, and you are a zubmariner sailing the sunless seas in the underworld.  Once you've accepted this premise, the rest of the game seems to fall into place quite naturally.  Your task, should you accept it, is to make a living travelling around the sunless seas, and survive, if you can, with your body and sanity intact.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward - you start out with a ship (try not to sink it) and a blank map of the area.  There are other cities you can visit aside from Fallen London, so trade is an option.  Exploration is an option, but costs money.  You're given a quest by your mysterious benefactor who gave you the ship, so there's that option as well - but really, it's all up to you.

One of my all time favorite games ends up being an indie developed game. If you're on the fence, do it. The artwork style is interesting, quite refreshing from the confusion of games that people complain aren't real enough even though they look plain as day. Be ready to think though, you have to work pretty hard if you want to survive. I found it hard (at first) to even survive on the normal (Voyageur) difficulty until I had played quite a few hours on the easier difficulty. There are a few grievances, though they are pretty easy to overlook considering it's still in alpha.
There are a few ideas that I think would give a little extra flavor to the game. Wasn't sure where else to post these so that it could be seen for use. It's a lot, but mostly nit-picky ideas from a huge fan who spends much of his time playing this game and paying attention to ways to possibly improve the game. To the developers, please consider some of the following:
Maybe make it possible to slip on the ice when sprinting. Just an interesting idea.
Also, maybe add a few more animals and later on. You don't need to go overboard, but a little more variety might be nice. As of now, there are only a few choices: Rabbits, Deer, Wolves, Bears, or Fish (I appreciate the few species of fish rather than just FISH) and then only a few plants: rosehips, mushrooms, lichens, maple or birch saplings, and cedar or fir trees that I have discovered. Maybe a few more would spice things up.
Another thing, I don't want to see this like Call of Duty or anything, but have you considered adding maybe a scoped weapon/scope attachment for the rifle? As well, maybe a pistol and pump action shotgun for a little variety and possibly benefits/drawbacks to each.
As well, I know you can use the hunting knife when being attacked, but maybe it could also be equipped while regularly walking around. I think that would be nice.
Related to the last one, I would REALLY like to see the boxes/books of matches be able to STAY EQUIPPED when using them for light. I tend to use the match books to walk around houses to save lantern fuel, but every time the match dies, I have to reequip them and it gets a tad old. It would be a really nice touch.
Also, I don't know if it's true, but I read somewhere that the celestial bodies or whatever wasn't accurate. I like to use the sun as a compass sometimes, and it'd be pretty cool if it rose in the East and set in the West like we see in real life.
Perhaps your character could draw a map of the places they've been in his or her journal as you travel. No marker to show where you are, but just a map of where you've been. Give you more reason to go out and explore and whatnot.
Maybe an online cooperative gameplay? No versus because obviously it would get ruined by trolls and it would no longer be about survival, it would be another Call of Duty in a different form. But you know, just like a two to four player cooperative style where you could help each other, share rations and supplies, explore the world together or apart. I would REALLY love to see something come of this, because my friends and I all play the game and we get bummed that you can only play alone. I would love to work together as a pair or team to try to brave the wilderness!
Final idea, I love being able to write in my journal and see all that happened on specific days. Nice job there. But it would be cool if you could reread old journals of your deceased characters say in the main menu. Or to add on the online play idea, maybe add an option in the settings to see other players' journals where they died when you are walking around the wilderness. See their story, that sort of thing. I think they have something like that in Dark Souls, though I may be wrong.

I don't know if the supposed two hours of gameplay that people claim this game is includes the many number of times you'll have to retry levels over and over again until the game finally lets you win, or if that's "two hours as long as you beat the levels on the first couple tries".  I do know that 30 minutes into the game, I can feel that tell that the game is set up against you.
You can only implement trial and error if you can figure out where and when enemies will spawn.  However, it's completely random except for the initial spawns, then it's a crap shoot.  I shoot and kill a guy, turn around because I know there's one coming from the other direction and I'm suddenly shot in the back.  How is that fair?

I really wanted to like this game. I'm a big fan of casino games in general. I don't gamble much in real life, but it's nice to be able to have fun with little expense. Unfortunately, this game didn't really fit the bill.  From a social aspect, it's fine. Most of the people are nice. The rest of the game though, is severely lacking.
Poker has the same problem it has anywhere else. It's free. People still make boneheaded calls and go all-in with nothing.  The bigger problem is that the only tournament you can play is with 6 people at one table. You start with $50k which would be fine if the blinds didn't go up extremely fast. It makes trying to play a realistic game of poker virtually impossible, as very soon after starting you're pretty much pot committed once you bet anything.
Blackjack is probably the best part of the game though, especially after the last update, it literally feels like the dealer is getting 20 or 21 every other hand. Still, there is money to be made if you know how to play.
That brings me to the worst part of the game, table machines. Slots, keno, video blackjack and video poker are money suckers with what seems like much lower payout percentages than even Vegas. I literally sat there for 30-45 minutes without a single bonus round. Forget trying to bet anything higher than the minimum because you will soon be out of money.  There are only three types of slot machines which gets old really fast especially when none of them pay.  Keno has a minimum bet of $100 and video blackjack has a minimum of $200. With poor payouts, again you will be out of money quickly.  The game also has war, roulette, big wheel, craps and bingo which are all pretty standard.  Again, especially with war, it seems like the more money bet, the lower percentage of times you're going to win.
You have daily tasks to do, receiving $200 for each of the 6. Unfortunately, most of the time you will be spending more than that to complete the tasks. There are weekly tasks, mostly revolving around getting a certain amount of XP. An example of the problem with this is me spending 45 minutes playing a $400 per spin slot machine, losing 40k and gaining a whopping 200xp. That would have been great if the weekly task wasn't 1,000 XP with a few thousand reward for doing so.  There is a VIP section for high rollers but I honestly don't know how people get to be high rollers unless they have spent real money or gotten extremely lucky.
Again, I really wanted to like the game. Unforunately, there is better poker to be had on any online site and the rest of the game is just no fun with the extremely low payouts.  If you're just in it for the social aspect and don't mind betting small, go for it. Otherwise, I'd stick with other products.

You win some, you lose some with Tropico 5.
There were definitely some nice features that they pulled out from Tropico 4, which was definitely a shame. The addition of multiplayer makes the game pretty fun, it's nice to be able to work alongside, or against other players. The soundtrack doesn't have nearly the oomph that Tropico 4 did, I find myself muting it and going back to the 3rd and 4th soundtracks to keep the vibe.
Thankfully, glitches aren't as abundant as they were in past games, but when they happen, they break a game you worked hours on. Mod support is okay, it's only as good as the community making the mods, and right now it's definitely not as large as other communities like Fallout and Prison Architect.
All-in-all, this is a good vanilla gaming experience. Multiplayer is fun, and if this is your first Tropico game, you won't be set up for disappointment. It's a great city-builder, with many options to keep things fun for hours.

One of my favorite games. Has a very good sense of humor and an overall good vibe. This is the first Tropico game I've played and I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys city building games.
There are a few flaws though, such as the fact that Mac user cannot use the mission editor. Or that the DLC is a little overpriced. But other then that I think this is a great game!

TL;DR at the top: Great city builder for $15 or less. Short game unless you buy overpriced DLC hence the low value of the standalone game.
Pros:
Good city building sim.
Building placement has a grid in this tropico which takes some getting used to after playing 3 and 4 but works great.
The trading is a bit more in depth with added import/export trade agreements based on foreign relations.
The graphics, sure it makes the island seem less like Havana and more like Paradise island but it looks great and really makes the island come to life if you're building tourist attractions.
Tourism is a lot simpler now that you can set building to only allow tourists which makes it easier to avoid traffic jams.
Military is actually important in this tropico. Also the varying types of military buildings/units is a plus.
The different eras were really neat.
The industry changes were also really cool. Chocolate for example, you needed a sugar plantation, a cocoa plantation and a cattle ranch to produce chocolate for export.
Space program actually has a purpose of generating research points.
Swiss bank acount is actually useful in this game.
Constitution adds a new variety to how you build your city.
Cons:
The multiplayer was a neat idea, but for city building it just doesn't work due to the length of games.
The faction leaders aren't as likeable as the ones in Tropico 4 and there are way fewer.
Penultimo's voice actor just doesn't work as well as the last.
Very few presidente costumes compared to 4.
Rebel attacks a bit too frequent even when your people are happy.
Bigges complaint: DLC DLC DLC, it seems like most of the game was delivered but then the rest was held back to sell as DLC, the game is a year old theres already two $20 "expansions" and like ten $4 DLC packages each one seems to be the same 1 outfit 1 map for $4... I'm personally not buying any DLC.

I'm most likely not going to even pay for the discounted version of Tropico 6 if they continue down this path. Buying this game on sale for $15 or less would be well worth the money.
