In the 90s, Jane's Combat Simulations was a whole series of flight simulation games published by EA (you read that right, it was EA before they became the stupid EA we all know today) with the branding of Jane's Information Group, a publishing company specializing in warfare. I have limited experience with flight simulation, and didn't discover it until way after Jane's games stopped being made, but I haven't heard anything but good things about the series.
Now ignore everything I just said because it doesn't apply here at all. That's right, just like all the other reviews said, the "Jane's" name has nothing to do with this game. It's an arcade game; think HAWX or Ace Combat, but Jane's Advanced Strike Fighters is way more like HAWX 1 (I haven't played HAWX 2 so I can't say). Which I'm okay with - HAWX 1 was actually enjoyable for what it was, especially in multiplayer co-op... but where HAWX failed to capture the essence of Ace Combat, Jane's fails to even capture the essence of HAWX. And that's just sad.
First things first,
and limited controller support. You have to go into the controls menu and rebind the keys for your controller before you can do anything, and even then you still can't control the camera nor can you use the controller for the menus - you gotta have your keyboard handy. Plus, I don't know if this was just me, but some of the graphics seemed really weird - I had some werid light flickering every now and then, and explosions didn't look like explosions at all.
On that last note, the graphics are passable. The aircraft models aren't very-well detailed, but they're not mishapen blocks that don't look like the Super Hornet or A-10 - they're passable, at the very least. Music and sound design are... poor, really. Nothing stuck with me at all, and I'm not trying to look for the soundtrack online or anything. Adding on to that, voice quality is really horrible. I mean, the writing can be okay at times, but the main character doesn't seem to give a damn about anything. He always sounds so upbeat, even when someone you're escorting is about to die. The guy voicing Control sounded like he was reused for some of the ground forces, which really confused me during one of the early missions.
The gameplay of JASF is the worst part, unfortunately. Nothing seems to be obvious enough, especially concerning incoming missiles, which you can't dodge normally unless you use countermeasures. Seriously, those things stay glued to your butt like hell, and it's not like you have an infinite amount of flares when the enemies gang up on you. You'll find yourself dying just because the missiles are magically homing on you. Not like your missiles have the same capabilities. Additionally, when using bombs, your aircraft can be destroyed by those very bombs. Of course, you have no way of knowing this (and no other arcade flight game has this feature AFAIK) until you do it yourself, and even then you'd be hard-pressed to figure it out.
Mission variety is also extremely broken. First mission is a patrol, followed by an escort. Second mission is a low-altitude attack, followed by an escort. Third mission is a low-altitude attack, followed by an escort. Am I the only one seeing a pattern here? Escort missions are the bane of some players' existence in Ace Combat games, so if you hate escort missions, stay the hell away.
For what it's worth, I spent exactly $1.00 of my Steam wallet (so, technically, free since it was from trading cards), so I don't think it was wasted - I did enjoy what I was doing until I got shot down by a swarm of MiGs in... the third mission? Hard to remember since they're so easy to forget.
In all honesty, HAWX 1 is better than this, and most Ace Combat games are better than that. Go look there. Jane's Advanced Strike Fighters isn't worth anyone's time or money.

Indie games, like everything else in gaming, is hit or miss. Some indie games attempt to bring something new to the table while others take a familiar formula and mix it up a bit. Limbo is the latter taking elements from games that veteran gamers will probably recognize, but put in a package that has not been seen before.
In Limbo, you control a boy that’s looking for his sister in Limbo. Yes that’s all you get for storyline because there will be plenty of interpretations of the plot once the gaming public gets their hands on it. There are so many nuances and details throughout the game that you feel that there’s a deeper story hidden, and the only way to learn about that story is to replay certain areas again and again to see how it all fits. A common theme you’ll find in this review that the simplistic look and gameplay of Limbo is just the surface of this complex game.
Reminiscent of an indie film, Limbo is only done in black and white. No colors or 3D, but instead a very animated 2D style. Your character has a very artistic look to him with only white eyes on a black silhouette, and the world has many instances where the objects and creatures on screen are simply mesmerizing. Again, what comes to mind when playing through this game are those movies that choose black and white rather than color to give their film a distinct yet considerably powerful look to it as Limbo has done. Keeping the game devoid of color, your mind wants to almost see the color that should be there making you pay even more attention to those object that should have some sort of color to it. Then there are scenes that are so detailed that you may overlook the lack of color because you see so much around you that color becomes not important. It’s simply an impressive sight to see a game that has no color yet provides such artistic imagery.
As the graphics of Limbo remind me of various black and white movies, the game itself brings back memories of multiple games that I’ve played throughout my time as a gamer. Essentially the game combines platforming that most gamers are familiar with, and puts you in puzzle situations that require a lot of thought. As you make your way through the level, you’ll eventually come to an obstacle of some sort. Whether it be a ledge too high to reach, a body of water to traverse, or a creature in your way, it will be your task to figure out how to get by as your character does not have any abilities aside from jumping, running, and interacting with objects.
Not only does your character not have any abilities, but the boy is frail. In the words of Until We Win host Lord Kat, you’re going to die... a lot. You can’t swim, survive long drops, defend yourself against creatures, or even take a hit to the head from a box falling from a certain height. Limbo might as well have been called "Trial andError" as you will be doing that for hours on end. Thankfully the developers Play Dead Studios (kind of fitting that they would have "dead' in their name) made dying less of a hassle. The game is split into areas where the puzzle is located. This means you’ll always find yourself right when the puzzle starts, and you can’t get any further until you pass the puzzle. The deaths in the game are particularly brutal making for this to be the bloodiest black and white game. Dying is especially painful to watch in certain situations when you realize that this is a child that has just been offed in such a callous way. It fits with the nature of the game as the seemingly simple and innocence of a child searching for his sister takes such a harsh turn making for a more dramatic experience sans the audible narrative.
Taking about 4.9 hours on average to complete, the only true reason to keep playing Limbo is for achievements. I must add the achievements are far from being conventional as well as being far from easy making for a true challenge for achievement ♥♥♥♥♥s.
Limbo is a game for a certain type of gamer. A gamer that enjoys a good challenge in a game rather than having it be overtly difficult, someone that appreciates a game that feels familiar to other games of the past, while not being a complete knock-off, and wants a taste of something new with a flavor that is still recognizable. For that reason, I can’t recommend that everyone needs to play this game, but I do feel that people should play this game. If anything, this game is one of those refreshing breaths of air that a gamer needs to take here and there to remind you that there are games that offer something different.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is the reason I bought this two game bundle, I remember playing Red Ochestra: Ostfront 41-45 by Tripwire before it even came out on steam. When I saw this game on steam, I did not even know that Red Orchestra 2 was a thing, call me a man living under a rock if you would. I bought the game with no disappointment, this game is worth $60 despite being only multiplayer. Just as COD is a game children play, this is a game men play, you may rush into battle in COD and get 85 kills with only 30 deaths (I used to get scores like this in W@W) all by yourself, but this game is different. Without your teammates, you're nothing, you won't get anything done without teamwork, capturing the flag? That isn't going to happen without your teammates.
Here's an insight on what you will experience in this game, assume the role of a Wehrmacht Soldier, you're in a firefight. You're a rifleman, armed with nothing but a Karabiner 98 Kurz and a couple of incorrectly named M24 Stielhandgranates. You all are unloaded at the same location, and you're first instinct is to march forward and prepare for battle. Bullets whiz  past you and you duck for cover, You peek out of cover and shoot a Red Soldier. He drops his weapon and falls, and starts sobbing uncontrollably in Russian. You watch in utter horror as a teammate puts a bullet in his head. The Red's Squad Leader calls in for T34's to support them, and your Squad Leader calls in for Panzer IVs and Artillery. They arrive, and the Panzer IVs immediately open fire, they wreck the T34's shoddily made armor, then they start killing everything. Artillery ruins the buildings the Red Army is hiding in. A Machine Gunner with a DP-28 blows your legs off, you start sobbing in German as a medic runs over to try and help you, but your wounds are fatal, you pull up your Karabiner and attempt to shoot the Machine Gunner to save your teammates, but to no avail, you're too shaken to be able to hold the rifle steady. You crawl to the Machine Gunner Nest which is only a few feet away while he is focused and hellbent on killing your squadmates and pull an M24 Stielhandgranate and jump on him, you kill him and die with him, but you saved your squadmates and increased the odds of winning.
There is no other series on the market that makes you work so hard to get some points, this game will work your fps skills up and you will never look at WWII the same way again, this isn't your arcade COD, this is real WWII. This is the best WWII simulator on the market, with one of the the best Tank Simulations on the market that is integrated into an fps, and no less the best FPS of the century.

This has always been my favourite of the three Half-Life games and I can't really put my finger on exactly why.
I think it's the sense of realism. On your way to work, you see the outside of Black Mesa. You see your colleagues eating breakfast and getting their laundry. The door to your working section won't open. You go to a shooting gallery and a room with security cameras. You see the security guards' locker room. All the scientists have different personalities. All the small details in everyday life is here.
Not to mention the elevator part. This is my favourite part in the whole series. It's terrifying and at the same time it feels more realistic than most things in the game, because it actually could happen in real life (except the aliens part, of course). What a way to start the game!
The High Definition Pack was a nice addition in the original release as well, which deserves high points.
The only things that bug me are the short length, the lack of new weapons and an overall grey mood that hangs over the game. It's hard to explain and I might be a minority on this, but the sense of fun in the first two games is lacking a bit. The over reliance on puzzles also makes the game seem more like hard work, rather than a pure fun action game. You really have to work for your survival, which is more realistic, but it's a little overkill here for me.
I still love the game for its realism. However, in the end, there are more small problems with it than the first two, and with its short length, they are all the more noticeable. It may not be a great game, but it's still good, and even "just good" Half-Life games are a joy.
I'd give it a 6,5/10. If you liked the first two, you should at least give it a chance. At the very least, it offers more variety.

Sunless Sea is one of those games we just don't get often enough anymore.  Creative and unique to the nth there's nothing I've played in recent memory that has had such a real world to learn, the whole game is new thoughts and ideas presented through wonderfully written prompts that know the importance of both brevity and bredth.  Jumping into Sunless Sea is certainly daunting and it really offers very little in terms of hand holding but that was part of what set the hook for me, being presented with a world I knew nothing about wanting to know everything about it.  The gameplay is easy to pick up and does have some degree of nuance to it once you reach the later stages of your captains developement but the rogue like map building and varied enemy types never let you get comfortable with what might be just off the edge of the screen.  The gameplay itself, particularly the combat does leave something to be desired, its not bad by any means but I often felt more frustrated by it then not, especially when I lost a really good run to a big shark that wouldn't get off my butt or somethign akin.
Good game overall, masterfully built world, creative ideas across the board and a combat system that, while not perfect, gets the job done.  Would recomend to anyone who likes The Binding of Isaac, spooky sea tales or whos been feeling bored with games in general.

There are so many amazing things to love about this game.
For starters, the look of the world.  Never have I seen a survival game that fit its world with its aesthetic as much as this game.  The painted feel of the world manages to both immerse one in its beauty and remind us of the harshness of the world around us.  The animals feel real, the trees feel real, and the world feels real despite (or perhaps, because) of the Robert Bateman-esque appearance.
Second, the atmosphere.  No matter what difficulty you play on, the atmosphere is perfect.  Whether it's the calm peacefulness of the North (Canadian here) on Pilgrim, the contemplative stillness that comes with Voyager, or the terrifying cold and treacherous nights that come with Stalker, the game feels consistent throughtout.  It presents the same picture with three different feelings every time.
Finally, the gameplay.  Some survival games that throw the user into a giant sandbox with a million toys and no direction, while others put the difficulty curve so high up that the game constantly feels like chore.  The Long Dark manages to find a perfect spot in terms of difficulty, and the best place possible in terms of survival.  On Voyager, the game naturally feels hard, but in an accomplishable way that encourages exploration and rewards the player for it, while on Stalker, the game feels cruel but natural, making the player feel like a tiny insect trying to survive in a harsh reality.  Unlike games where the difficulty setting just changes how many enemies spawn and how much health they have, this one makes difficulty actually mean something.  And the survival elements are perfect, stripping the game down to the basics while still giving the player enough agency to make their actions have weight and consequence.
And on top of all of that, the development team is slowly but surely making the game better, ensuring that each update is polished to a mirror shine.
This is the best survival game to come out in YEARS.  Buy it.

The first time I played I explored the city until I died.  It was fun.  After doing this a few more times I started to wonder if I was doing it wrong...  It turns out I absolutely was.  The idea is not some epic cross country journey killing zombies, it's a careful and cautious attempt to carve out a place for yourself in a zombie apolocalypse and last as long as you can.
You will die.  That it how it eventually ends.  But how long can you last?  Every day you survive is like getting closer to a "high score".  I was proud when I survived my first day, then my first week.  On my latest attempt I'm about to reach a month.  I hear power and water are cut off at 2 months.
So some tips:
1.  Find a weapon.
2.  Find a safehouse.
3.  Go loot nearby houses.
4. Take the loot back to your safehouse and organize in cubbards, fridges, medicine cabinets, etc.
5. When on a low-risk looting run, put one bag on your back, and another in your off hand to help carry the largest haul possible.  (Even a Baseball bat can be used in your primary hand alone, but with reduced effectiveness).
6.  SURVIVE!
So ya, definitely recommend.

I had been watching this game for a few... yeah, guess it must be years by now... and finally it was on such a massive sale that I had to try it out. You know if it's cheap enough anything goes - just ask a hooker with the clap. I know. From personal experience.
So this is basically a simulator of how to slowly kill a medieval township by starvation. Well, it might not be meant to be exactly that, but that's how I play it. Or at least how my games usually play out. Who needs farmers anyway?
You control af few plebs (that will eventually turn into a horde of plebs) and have to build a town they can live in (and just wait a bit... and then they will die in it as well). Make them build housing so they won't die from exposure. Make them farm crops and hunt game so they won't starve to death. Provide medical aid so they won't die from diseases. And build a huge cemetary, 'cause in the end old age or some other thing will get them. If you are lucky your dying plebs had a herd of children and you can continue plotting new ways of starving the next generation to death.
The game plays like a well balanced mix of games like Settlers (with storage and route management being the key), Caesar and any City Builder you can name off the top of your head. So yeah. The Nobel Prize for Innovative Game Design goes to... someone else obviously.
But its still kinda fun in a relaxed Sim City-esque kinda way. I can lean back, sip my wine, and enjoy how those clueless pleb minions do my bidding. That's worth the fews bucks the game costs at the moment.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is the reason I bought this two game bundle, I remember playing Red Ochestra: Ostfront 41-45 by Tripwire before it even came out on steam. When I saw this game on steam, I did not even know that Red Orchestra 2 was a thing, call me a man living under a rock if you would. I bought the game with no disappointment, this game is worth $60 despite being only multiplayer. Just as COD is a game children play, this is a game men play, you may rush into battle in COD and get 85 kills with only 30 deaths (I used to get scores like this in W@W) all by yourself, but this game is different. Without your teammates, you're nothing, you won't get anything done without teamwork, capturing the flag? That isn't going to happen without your teammates.
Here's an insight on what you will experience in this game, assume the role of a Wehrmacht Soldier, you're in a firefight. You're a rifleman, armed with nothing but a Karabiner 98 Kurz and a couple of incorrectly named M24 Stielhandgranates. You all are unloaded at the same location, and you're first instinct is to march forward and prepare for battle. Bullets whiz  past you and you duck for cover, You peek out of cover and shoot a Red Soldier. He drops his weapon and falls, and starts sobbing uncontrollably in Russian. You watch in utter horror as a teammate puts a bullet in his head. The Red's Squad Leader calls in for T34's to support them, and your Squad Leader calls in for Panzer IVs and Artillery. They arrive, and the Panzer IVs immediately open fire, they wreck the T34's shoddily made armor, then they start killing everything. Artillery ruins the buildings the Red Army is hiding in. A Machine Gunner with a DP-28 blows your legs off, you start sobbing in German as a medic runs over to try and help you, but your wounds are fatal, you pull up your Karabiner and attempt to shoot the Machine Gunner to save your teammates, but to no avail, you're too shaken to be able to hold the rifle steady. You crawl to the Machine Gunner Nest which is only a few feet away while he is focused and hellbent on killing your squadmates and pull an M24 Stielhandgranate and jump on him, you kill him and die with him, but you saved your squadmates and increased the odds of winning.
There is no other series on the market that makes you work so hard to get some points, this game will work your fps skills up and you will never look at WWII the same way again, this isn't your arcade COD, this is real WWII. This is the best WWII simulator on the market, with one of the the best Tank Simulations on the market that is integrated into an fps, and no less the best FPS of the century.

I can sort of recommend this game - if you just tend to get a kick out of arcade-style flight. The basic play experience is competent, if uninspired. (To be fair, though, these guys did "full freedom" flying better than "Air Conflicts," and it's all forgiving enough to work with the not-very-good PC controls.)
"Ace Combat" this isn't. There's very little variety, and challenge is mostly provided by swarms of opponents firing nigh-unshakeable missiles. Outmaneuvering an enemy pilot isn't a problem at all. Having only a few countermeasures to throw at things you can't really dodge is where things get tricky.
That can all be forgiveable under the right circumstances. The game's real weakness is its presentation.
To be blunt, "Jane's" feels blatantly like a cash-in title. I got the strong impression that someone figured, "If we license some fighter aircraft, and slap the name of Jane's Information Group on the thing, we can sell a few units." It's not that the game is buggy, it's just that it's so...cheap. You fly over the same terrain and landmarks all the time, and there are basically only five mission types: Air-to-air, air-to-ground, recon, a mix of the previous, and a mix of the previous with flying under radar detection altitude.
And there wasn't a single opponent that I felt was truly interesting to get into a fight with.
Alongside the above, the depiction of the fictional "Afghan-Iraq-Iranistan" is caricatured and insulting. There was a point where I couldn't be sure that the developers weren't intentionally trying to take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the whole thing. The voice acting is thoroughly unconvincing, and the characters are parodies of themselves. I can't imagine the voice-talent taking the script seriously in any real way.
Like I said, though, if you like arcade-style jet combat enough you might be able to stomach this offering. I got sufficient enjoyment out of the game to play through it twice.
But this really is a cheap knockoff of far better things.

Half-Life: Blue Shift follows the original Half-Life expansion pack formula, by telling the same story of Black Mesa through a different pair of eyes. And, to be completely honest, I like this take on the Black Mesa incident more than Opposing Force. This time it's not about aliens or taking over the facility as Gordon or Shepard. You're stuck right in the middle as a security guard who's natural impulse is to just get the f*** out of there. There's no G-man (save for a brief cameo), no high stakes, just aliens, marines, and getting the f*** out of Black Mesa. The story is tight enough for the little developments to come when they do and it's has enough investment that by the end you're on the edge of your seat waiting for what's about to happen. In that regard, I think Blue Shift is a more effective story than Opposing Force.
That being said though, Blue Shift is a bit lower on the gameplay end. Some puzzles are pretty easy, while some are very oddly designed (like pushing a barrel into a TNT line to blow up a door, even though that was never introduced as a concept in the game before), and there's no addition to the weapon line-up like Opposing Force had. You have almost all the same guns as the original Half-Life and you cover a lot less area in Black Mesa than the previous two installments.
However, everything I love about Half-Life is still here, it's just more condensed. I'd consider Blue Shift the cliffnotes version of the Half-Life story. It's short, sweet, and over in about 3 hours. Is it as grand as Half-Life? No. Is it as expansive as Opposing Force? No. But is it still enjoyable? Yeah, I think so. I enjoyed the 3 hours I spent in Blue Shift. It might not be for everyone else, but I still think it's a fine expansion pack to a fine game. I'm giving Half-Life: Blue Shift an 8/10.

IT'S FINALLY OUT. Was very excited to start the game's story after playing the hell out of survival mode and all the challenges they released to placate the starving masses. Unfortunately I'm stuck on the damned bear after working my butt off to get through episode 2. For some reason bears are not running away when I shoot them like the game says they should and I get mauled every time I try to take on the old bear. Suffice to say my save is screwed and I have lost interest in playing through AGAIN. I played through episode 1 about 5 times and kept getting murdered by wolves (same issue of not running away when they are supposed to, which did not happen as much in early access?). I understand that the game needs to be punishing, but playing through an episode takes SEVERAL hours if you wanna get all the things, and The Long Dark's narrative experience is just not good enough for me to want to see the same cutscenes and spend hours grinding the same quests more than a few times, though few things are.
HOWEVER, The Long Dark was more than worth the current $35 price tag even during early access when it was selling for less. It's an incredibly immersive, yet simplistic experience that will keep you in your computer chair for 100 hours or more, especially if you treat the survival mode as an RPG adventure. It is very easy to play a meta-game, in which you take the random encounters and the letters found everywhere, and and create your own narrative. The excellent voicework done by Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer creates prevalent atmosphere of  lonliness because whichever PC you are playing as chatters with themselves endlessly. To bring it all home is the truly enormous, beautiful, and surprisingly diverse maps, all stylisticly painted, and designed to look good on a computer with zero budget. Sure it's annoying to wake up to your character dying of thirst after every nap because of the weird time scale, but I've paid much more for much, much worse.
BUY IT, play survival mode, don't force yourself to do the campaign unless it's patched and you'll walk away after 100 hours feeling like you played a fun as hell solo experience. (WARNING: when you play The Long Dark, you eat like you are in The Long Dark. When you eat in the game you eat for real)

One of my all time favorite games ends up being an indie developed game. If you're on the fence, do it. The artwork style is interesting, quite refreshing from the confusion of games that people complain aren't real enough even though they look plain as day. Be ready to think though, you have to work pretty hard if you want to survive. I found it hard (at first) to even survive on the normal (Voyageur) difficulty until I had played quite a few hours on the easier difficulty. There are a few grievances, though they are pretty easy to overlook considering it's still in alpha.
There are a few ideas that I think would give a little extra flavor to the game. Wasn't sure where else to post these so that it could be seen for use. It's a lot, but mostly nit-picky ideas from a huge fan who spends much of his time playing this game and paying attention to ways to possibly improve the game. To the developers, please consider some of the following:
Maybe make it possible to slip on the ice when sprinting. Just an interesting idea.
Also, maybe add a few more animals and later on. You don't need to go overboard, but a little more variety might be nice. As of now, there are only a few choices: Rabbits, Deer, Wolves, Bears, or Fish (I appreciate the few species of fish rather than just FISH) and then only a few plants: rosehips, mushrooms, lichens, maple or birch saplings, and cedar or fir trees that I have discovered. Maybe a few more would spice things up.
Another thing, I don't want to see this like Call of Duty or anything, but have you considered adding maybe a scoped weapon/scope attachment for the rifle? As well, maybe a pistol and pump action shotgun for a little variety and possibly benefits/drawbacks to each.
As well, I know you can use the hunting knife when being attacked, but maybe it could also be equipped while regularly walking around. I think that would be nice.
Related to the last one, I would REALLY like to see the boxes/books of matches be able to STAY EQUIPPED when using them for light. I tend to use the match books to walk around houses to save lantern fuel, but every time the match dies, I have to reequip them and it gets a tad old. It would be a really nice touch.
Also, I don't know if it's true, but I read somewhere that the celestial bodies or whatever wasn't accurate. I like to use the sun as a compass sometimes, and it'd be pretty cool if it rose in the East and set in the West like we see in real life.
Perhaps your character could draw a map of the places they've been in his or her journal as you travel. No marker to show where you are, but just a map of where you've been. Give you more reason to go out and explore and whatnot.
Maybe an online cooperative gameplay? No versus because obviously it would get ruined by trolls and it would no longer be about survival, it would be another Call of Duty in a different form. But you know, just like a two to four player cooperative style where you could help each other, share rations and supplies, explore the world together or apart. I would REALLY love to see something come of this, because my friends and I all play the game and we get bummed that you can only play alone. I would love to work together as a pair or team to try to brave the wilderness!
Final idea, I love being able to write in my journal and see all that happened on specific days. Nice job there. But it would be cool if you could reread old journals of your deceased characters say in the main menu. Or to add on the online play idea, maybe add an option in the settings to see other players' journals where they died when you are walking around the wilderness. See their story, that sort of thing. I think they have something like that in Dark Souls, though I may be wrong.
Alright, sorry for so much writing, I just really love this game! Please, if you have yet to play the game give it a shot! It's a great game and these guys really deserve the credit! Thanks everyone!

I really really enjoyed this game, even as short as it is (6 hours?)
It's the most innovative shooter I've played in a long time, but I don't want to say too much.
If you are standing still, time doesn't stop, but it moves really slowly. If you turn or look around, it moves a bit faster. If you walk or pull a trigger on a weapon, times moves normally. It sounds weird, but the mechanic works really smoothly.
The result is some innovative gameplay, that makes you feel like you are in an old John Woo movie. For example: You're unarmed, so you punch the guy next to you three times and kill him. Run, grab a pool ball, and throw it at the guy with the gun. Grab his gun in midair, use his gun to shoot him. Waiting for another bullet to get into the chamber takes too long, so you throw that gun at a third guy to stun him. Grab a pool ball, throw it at that same third guy to keep him stunned. Run over to him, punch him, grab his shot gun, shoot him, and the guy sneaking behind you. You're out of shells, so you throw that gun at the guy with the katana. Take his katana, slice him. Watch a new guy smash a window, then throw the katana at him. Even when the game gets difficult (and I found the last level pretty challenging), I didn't care that I was doing the same level because even my failed attempts were so fun.

The joy of a good game is in learning and improving.  A good game provides clear, consistent rules and rewards you for playing better, smarter, cleaner.
Cuphead wants to test you, but more than that, it wants you to get better.  When you fail, you know why it happened,  There are no mysteries to its mechanics, and it makes no effort to slap you down with the unknown or unknowable.  And yes, proper execution is still a barrier even if your strategy is sound, but Cuphead always values cleanliness and consistency over reflexes.
This is that rarest of games where difficulty is a product of smart design rather than variables being ratcheted up to the point of punishment.  In other words, it's fun to fail, because you always know that you can succeed if you keep trying.
And I guess it's a neat bonus that Cuphead is one of the most achingly beautiful video games ever released.  Just like its play design, every stitch of its presentation is thoughtful and lush.  The amazing visual design and animation are self-evident, but just the little things: the fonts, the menus, the wonderful tap-dancing rapid fire sound of your default weapon.  Cuphead is deliberate to a degree that makes other, bigger, pricier games feel slapdash.
I think just about everyone can get something from Cuphead, even those who tend to find "hard" games intimidating.

Been waiting a long time for this game to be on Steam. The game itself can turn from a walk in the park to a nightmare in seconds as players may find themselves in situations which may compromise their own schemes to survive in the long run.♥♥♥♥♥♥can hit the fan pretty quick, a scavenging or scouting mission could end up in the player getting chased by a horde or infected after a scuffle. Zombies aren't only the greatest danger one can encounter, factors which affect the human condition can also be the cause of death. Food can run out and spoil as the electricity supply cuts off after some time. Water and drinks become scarce as the pipelines shut down. And worst of all; illnesses and injuries can spell one's doom as the zombies close in.
Survival is determined by one's own wits and luck as the player is given a plethora of options to survive. One may farm (or hunt game) and build a fortress hidden in the woods or hole up in a fortified office building or suburban home somewhere in the more civilized areas, whilst scavenging for supplies in the nearby homes, restaurants, hotels, etc.
Weapons are another thing. They all degrade and the player is forced to rely on improvising as their favorite axe or spike bat may fall or break apart at the worst possible time. Guns have become a luxury and almost impractical if one intends to lessen the attention the undead pays to him or her. Guns are to be used only as a last resort or if one has enough in stock, be trigger happy with.
To sum it all up; Project Zomboid is the best zombie survival game out there developed by an independent company. 8.5/10.

It's important that you understand that this is a puzzle game, not a train simulator.   The game has 4 'levels' with 5 maps in each level (plus an extra level of 5 maps in the Germany DLC).  When you start a new map you see two train stations that are already constructed and it's your job to build track between the two stations.  Once track is laid you will start getting alerts from the individual stations that a train is ready to depart.  You are also shown where that train's destination is (marked by an easy to understand color system).
Sounds pretty easy, right?
It's not nearly as easy as it sounds.  After you get past how to lay the track (with limited funds that vary from map to map.  You also gain funds by getting trains safely to their destination in a timely fashion, or risk reduced income) you are also given parameters to meet in order to get a "perfect" score on each map.  There are always 3 parameters you will need to satisfy to get a perfect score (anything from "Don't allow any train to arrive at the wrong station" to "Do not destroy over $20,000 of assets, like trees or buildings or even track you've previously laid).  As the levels move up, so does the challenge.
To add one more little piece of difficulty; the trains will automatically depart if you do not manually send them to their destination within an allotted amount of time).  Not much of an issue on early maps but it certainly makes things difficult later in the game.
I love building games, puzzles and trains and this one checks all three of those boxes.  For the price, it's the best game I've purchased on Steam.  If you like puzzles, building games and trains, then what are you waiting for?!

Outlast is a "found-footage" esq. horror game that takes place in Mount Massive Asylum. As Miles Upshur, a journalist called to investigate the shady practices in the Asylum, you enter to find out everything has gone to sh*t. From there on, the game delves further and further into darkness. The main gameplay has you running, hiding, and outsmarting enemies within the Asylum, which for some could be a bit repative. Overall the scares are good, with the mood and ambience adding on to the expertly crafted scenery placed around the Asylum to make the game feel even creepier. The jumpscares, while not too much as to be overused, are well made in perfect timing throughout the game, and don't feel cheesy or lame. My biggest gripe with Outlast itself (Not including the Whistleblower DLC) is the fact that the story ends in such a massive unexplained cliffhangar, it's almost a requirement to buy the DLC to undersatnd what fully happened, even though the DLC leaves certain things unanswered as well. The game also requires you to search for documents to piece together certain backstories within the game, which for some could be tedious.
Overall Outlast is an 8/10 experience by itself, but combined with the Whistleblower DLC the game is a solid 9/10.

Will it Run on My Computer? - 10/10 - Most likely, if you're computer is a new computer, it can run this, you don't need a very powerful rig to play this game. Graphics - 7/10 - Actually, the game looks pretty good, looks reminiscent of games like Counter-Strike: Source or Half-Life 2 graphically. Another cool thing I got a little smile over, the shells ejected from your gun, they stay, they don't magically disappear, love firing the AK-47 with infinite ammo enabled, only to fire 1000 rounds and look down on the ground to see a mess of shells. Another thing that is surprisingly good, is that they have full-body-presence nailed, no it's not just legs, it's the actual third-person viewmodel being viewed in first person (when you look down you see the body, and the left arm doesn't look like it's magically coming out of your neck, a small detail many $50 AAA titles like Call of Duty or Battlefield still don't get right), I wish this was something done in every game. Graphically the game isn't impressive, but the amount of detail they tried to push out of such limited graphics is impressive.
Gameplay - 11/10 - The gameplay reminds me a bit of classic arcade shooters, no objective, just pure gore and fun, I love it. EDIT: This game is so fun, I forgot to configure settings and didn't even realize I'm only running in 800x600p resolution, you know it's fun when you forget about the whole "graphics" thing. What should have been a relaxing experience immediately becomes frustrating when you're thrown into the game without any explanation whatsoever leaving you to figure out what the hell to do on your own - not an easy task on a screen overloaded with colourful hand drawn artwork - , introducing the first mode of "relaxation" this trash heap provides.
The other comes once you figured out how to play and what to do. Any semblance of movement is agonisingly slow and clunky, with no clearly visible paths. Most of the time, you will find yourself dragging the cursor over the screen at random, attempting to figure out where you can and cannot go.

The minigames themselves are standard fare: concentration, some rotation puzzles, skipping stones and even a classic jigsaw puzzle. Nothing atrociously bad, but nothing remarkable either.
To put it in a nutshell, if you like looking for small objects on a cluttered screen, backtracking, playing overused minigames and waiting for the screen to finish scrolling down everytime you cross the borders, you will absolutely love this. Buy this if you hate fun.

Tropico is a series of city builders lite where you are also a dictator (a pirate lord in 2) who has to stay in power while trying to build his little heaven (or hell) on Earth.
And whereas Tropico 4 was just a Tropico 3 with more stuff - Tropico 5 has many features changed, reworked, added (and some cut) to warrant being called a proper sequel. Oh and it also has MUCH more stuff to do.
With changes in economy and many product chains and raw resources added compared to the previous game - it may take a few failures to wrap your head around the way things work.
Your tropical dictator paradise can now also have sharper teeth with more offensive stuff to beat down rebels and invaders with (although with changes in faction system the rebellions happen a lot more often for my taste).
All other categories of things to build and create are expanded as well, coming with a lot more comfortable interface.
As usual Sandbox mode is where the real game's at. And now it doesn't have time limits, albeit the generator is unfortunately simplified.
Instead the time frame takes you through four eras starting with colonial one where you are just a mere local manager of the king - you have to use crown's cash to kickstart your playground which you also have to make independent before your term's over. Don't worry it can be extended by doing missions (later on they give you much more varied rewards).
Of course if you don't want to bother with the colonial era (with it being quite different from the rest of the game, but I personally like it) - you can pick any other era to begin your game in.
I recommend it both to newcomers and previous Tropico players alike.

If you like a good story, are no stranger to reading and can handle some frustration over losing progress, you must play Sunless Sea. Gameplay-wise it might be a little dull. It’s mostly about inventory and stat management. The quests are pretty much glorified fetch quests and in the beginning you might even avoid combat altogether. Taking on anything else than the crabs near your home port with your starting ship is a death wish. It’s a pretty unforgiving experience because death is permanent. Once you die, you must start all over with a new captain.
All this shouldn’t stop you from trying this game out though. What it lacks in gameplay it absolutely makes up in story and atmosphere. The name of H.P Lovecraft gets thrown around a lot, but Sunless Sea manages to capture that similar feeling of cosmic dread and fear of unknown that his works are known for. However, the writing in the game doesn’t just emulate his style. It’s chock full of its own quirks with a good amount of humor thrown in also. Sunless Sea feels like a fully fleshed out world teeming with lore. The sound effects and music do a superb job of building an eerie atmosphere that always makes you feel a little worried about what might be ahead.
It might take a few tries to get a hang of what you should and should not do, but the learning curve is worth it. Sometimes the game can be a little frustrating, but I don’t feel like it ever is unfair. I lost a couple of days’ worth of progress a few times, but they were always because of unnecessary risks I took. Some of these times I didn’t feel like starting a new game anytime soon, but Sunless Sea always sucked me back in. Once I learned the ropes, I found myself making detailed itineraries of my trips around the Unterzee, trying to determine what ports I should visit and in what order. Careful planning might make it less likely that you die a horrid death on your trips, but you still never know if you’re going to return home once you disembark from the docks of Fallen London. The game is at its best in these moments when you are racing against dwindling supplies and growing madness, trying not to give in to the temptation of eating your crewmates in hopes of staying alive long enough to reach next friendly port.
Sunless Sea is a slow burner. If you approach it as more of an interactive novel than a high-paced action fest, I’m sure you will enjoy it. It might not be for everyone, but once it gets under your skin it doesn’t let go.

This game has come a long way since I first bought it years ago.  The main appeal for me are the words contained within.  The exquisitely delicious words.  The prose is excellently written which is important because that is the primary way that information and story, such as it is, is conveyed to you.  Sunless Sea is an excellent game in which you start out as a near penniless Unterzee captain in which you struggle to complete various overarching quests while trying to ensure the continuity of your own lineage which each death (or more rarely, choosing to retire) allows you to start as a new captain with some small (and not so small) bonuses based on how well you did over your last career and the various legacy goals that you have accomplished.
You will die, the dark unforgiving zee will claim your body and your crew, and your heirs will carry on your legacy.  The game is difficult, especially before earning any legacy bonsuses.  But if you perservere, continuing to venture out onto the Unterzee time and again, you will forge something lasting and the satisfaction in doing so will be immense.

The Long Dark is a first-person survival game. A geomagnetic event has caused your character's plane to crash somewhere in the snowy Canadian wilderness, and armed with only a small handful of supplies, you must do what you can to stave off death for as long as possible.
Unfortunately, death comes in many forms in this game. Due to the fictional geomagnetic catastrophe in-game, the weather has gone into a permanent winter, with random snow, fog and winds which vary in intensity from "mild" to "I literally cant see 5 feet in front of me". The event has affected wildlife as well, and some- especially of the 'wolf' and 'bear' variety- will attack you on sight.
--BASICS--
The elements arent the only thing out to get you. In The Long Dark, you are basically tasked with survival, and to do so you must satisfy 4 ever-decreasing statistic bars: Warmth, Sleep, Hunger and Thirst.
"Warmth" is affected in a number of ways. First, there is 'temperature', as well as 'wind chill'. Im not 100% certain how one affects the other, but needless to say, the lower the numbers, the faster your "warmth" meter will decrease. You can add 'warmth' by means of clothing (which some can be layered for additional temperature increase bonus), standing near fire or heat sources, eating hot food/drink, or going to an interior, closed location (in a cabin, etc). Sleeping will add warmth, but if the surrounding temperature is cold enough, you will still wake up freezing if you do so outdoors.
"Sleep" stat will slowly drop as the day goes on, and can be hastened by carrying too much weight, thus making you tired earlier than usual. Sleep is possibly the stat with the least amount of worry involved with it, as you can pretty much sleep anywhere (so long as you have a sleeping bag, and you begin the game with one). It may not always be SMART to sleep, depending on circumstance, but it is about always possible. "Sleep" can be restored by... well, sleep. Hot tea can be consumed before rest to increase the effectiveness of your rest, and hot coffee can be consumed to reduce the rate at which the bar depletes.
"Hunger" stat naturally drops as time progresses. In this game, hunger is represented by "calories". At the maximum 'full' level, your character has 2,500 calories. Items which you eat will replenish calories, and depending on what the item is, the recovery value will vary from 0-1000 calories per item use. If you eat something which would put your calorie count above 2500, the number caps and the remainder of that item will stay in your inventory, so you can eat the rest later. You are not going to be able to survive forever on the junk food you find in cabins, etc, so ultimately you will have to find a way to harvest those delicious animals running around the map.....
"Thirst" depletes as time progresses, or if you eat something salty (IE, a box of crackers). Not certain if it drops faster with strenuous labor. Water in this game is a commodity that is everywhere- literally. Your character's main source is from the snow itself, and while you have a fire built you can melt snow into water, then boil it for safe consumption. Water can be found in a number of places including bottles of the stuff and from a toilet bowl...and all can be consumed, but if you do not boil non-pure sources before drinking, you can stand to catch disease and die without treatment.
Once any of the 4 stat bars reaches 1/4, an icon will appear in the corner letting you know it needs attention soon. If a bar reaches "empty", a percentage will appear next to the appropriate icon. It begins at 100%, and if it hits 0 your game is over. Multiple bars can be reduced to 'below empty' at once.
--SURVIVE!--
You dont begin with very many supplies, there is no map in the game as of yet, and the odds are stacked against you... yet you still have a fighting chance. Your first few games will find you learning the ropes, and-- due to the fact that the game is still in ALPHA and has no much-needed tutorial-- this will either involve you dying a lot, or referring to the Wiki a lot, which spoils a lot of the surprises to find.
Once you have gotten a good feel for the game and begin to remember certain details of the maps ("if I follow these train tracks it'll take me to a bunch of cabins in a lumber yard!"), things will become much more fun, and you can concentrate on exploration rather than figuring out how the game's rules work.
Find all sorts of gear to help you survive, from oil lamps, axes, knives and even a rifle, to clothes, food, firewood, medical supplies of all types and more. You can 'harvest' these items for basic materials to repair your other gear, or even to make new items altogether at a 'work bench'. No firewood, and youre indoors? Chop the tables, chairs and shelves up and burn em. Hunt for wildlife-- and then eat them, gut them and turn their skins into wearable coats, warmer sleeping bags, ETC. Loot corpses of other explorers who didnt make it. Pull a torch out of a fire and use it to swing at attacking wolves to scare em away. Find a hut on a frozen lake and do some ice fishing! Stagger blindly through a white-out blizzard with your stats all nearly bottomed-out, thinking youre about to die, when suddenly you see the shape of a house in the distance.....
--THOUGHTS--
The Long Dark could REALLY stand to use a tutorial, but seeing as how it is technically still in Alpha it can be forgiven. Other than that, the game feels very solid and is quite addicting to play. The elements against you and your meters constantly draining put an urgency on you to make progress in the game, but never to the point of it making the game obnoxious to play. Sometimes your stats may be struggling and there is tension in trying to 'beat the clock' before you die, but thats part of the fun. Will you make it?? *IS* that a house you see in the distance..??
*YES!!!* .....is exactly how you will react when you DO find one. My favorite aspect about this game so far is the act of DISCOVERY. After staggering through the harsh wilderness for hours up to days, fending off animal attacks, cold and starvation, it feels extremely rewarding to find even the smallest of cabins dotted around the maps. Every one of them is loaded with goodies, and item locations/ "drops" are random in every playthrough so you never know what youll find, but you always know itll be good stuff.
The graphics look nice, especially the skyboxes. Ive taken a number of screenshots of the game and for a title with "white snow everywhere" its amazing how much color gets packed in there. Weather effects look great- the snow will actually blow with the wind currents, spiral off rooftops and get sucked into the breeze... its nice attention to detail VS 'randomly falls from sky at various quantities'. Maps are massive and packed with things to see and discover, lots of interesting locations, and a widely-varying topography that will make you FEEL like youre standing on the top of a mountain, or at the very base looking up at one. Sound is very well done and is plenty convincing, from old panes of glass clattering in their window from howling winds hitting them, to the roar of a bear before he eats your face. Music is intermittant, but always pleasant to the ear. It sounds cool and mysterious, much like the game itself. Controls are solid, and the little bit of aiming which takes place is pretty accurate.
Overall, I'm hooked. Its a lot of fun, presents a reasonable challenge and- most importantly- is still being worked on/updated by its developers. I purchased this game for $5.00 during the Steam Holiday Sale and it was totally worth it, but with 50+ hours already into the game and Im barely beyond map 1, I'd be willing to have paid full price. If you like survival sandboxes give this one a go!!

Overall very entertaining assymetric multiplayer. Although it can be daunting at first it doesn't take too long to get the hang of the various roles and monsters. Each character comes with a video tutorial when played (alongside an interactive tutorial for monster + hunter).
Each match there are the hunters which include the 4 classes: Medic, Assault, Support, & Trapper
These players work cooperatively against the single monster player (Goliath, Kraken, or Wraith).
Players can create the standard custom match or join a quick single match. The most entertaining aspect is 'Evacuation' which combines the various modes into 5 matches where you will fight against the same hunter/monster player(s). Each match has a resulting  map specific effect for the next round depending on who won.
+ Addictive gameplay
+ Variety of characters each with different abilities/weapons add replayability
+ Good map variety
+ Solid AI that takes over players who may leave (also allows you to 'take a break' during a match)
+ Offline mode available against the AI
- Matchmacking currently appears to be level based which may cause more experienced players (i.e. Alpha/beta players) to be placed with newer players (at least initially after launch)
- Some minor bugs/issues may arise (e.g. loading screen delays)
- Initial learning curve in multiplayer can be daunting (I'd recommend playing the hunters first with something like the Assault class)
If you enjoy games for their addictive competitive multiplayer then I'd recommend this game.
NB: Every current character is unlockable through progression (12 hunters, 3 monsters).
The current DLC available as of now are some skins (colour variations)

Every time I start up the game and see those words I get chills.  Project Zomboid is an isometric view survival zombie game. It involves managing hunger/thirst, mood, physical well being, zombies, and figuring out how to live once the power and water shuts off.  You can tell by my hours spent in game I LOVE it!
A very unique game.  I have never played anything like it. Every time I play this game I want to watch The Walking Dead. Every time I watch The Walking Dead I want to play this game.  It is a custom built game engine that is THE zombie survival game I always wanted.
Updates are meaningful and consistent.  Every time an update comes out I know I am in for a treat.  You can test the update before it is part of the official steam release, but I only did that once. When they release it the update is very stable with only very minor bugs.
There is a sense of desperation. As you character gets panicked and tired and you are far from your safe house the tension goes up.  When you finally use that gun you know you will be overwhelmed by a horde because of the noise.  Scavenging has never been so fun.
Multiplayer adds a great way to play with friends or join a server for  more competitive play.
Modding is supported. Players are starting to make really cool custom maps and interesting mods.
It is just fun.
Once you clear out an area, establish you house, create a few rain barrels, and start farming, the game looses lots of tension. Zombies don't spawn after you kill so many. The engine redistributes zombies by in game events that are limited to gun fire and helicopter noises, but in practice they don't bring that many after you truly cleared your area and the surrounding area.  In one game I no longer feel I am in threat of dying.
The early history of the game has a pretty bad black eye involving loosing all their work because they didn't back it up and their laptops were stolen.  TotalBiscuit still referenced it recently when he talked about it in his breakdown of the daily summer sales.
Build 27 (the current stable build as I write this) advances the game to the point I can finally wholeheartedly recommend it.  Even if they never do another update, the game is fun enough and unique enough to establish itself as a worthy game at full price.
There is a challenge mode, multiplayer, and mods. Even if you get to the point of feeling safe (like I do now), I can always start new or jump on my online server with friends, join a public server, or try the challenge mode.   I am going to see how long my current guy can last. So far 700+ zombies killed and over 2 months alive! woot!!
BUT...it is not going to stop updating anytime soon. The most anticipated update is NPCs. They used to be in the game, but they rebuilt under the hood stuff so they can introduce them with a sadistic AI. It will open up a higher degree of tension and give modders great tools to work with.
The UI is slated to be updated, crafting and skills keep getting tweaked (as they should be), and minor bugs are getting ironed out. The map is expanding, items and recipes are increasing, and new features are still being implemented.
I believe they are even working on a system to better redistribute zombies or keep them spawning. I hope so anyway.  I thought I read that they intend to add more zombie spawning options-multiplayer servers particularly need that option as they cuurently depend on the admin manually spawning zombies.
As of now admins can also do a soft reset that respawns zombies and loot, turns back on power and water while restarting the clock to their shutdown, but the soft reset keeps player crafted buildings intact.
It will be better if automated zombie spawning is implemented or zombie spawning scripts can be utilized.
Don't be fooled by old reviews or info.
This is the golden age to get the game. Full price is still cheap. The current full price is worth it. The Indie Stone has enough of a track record and community involvement to feel confident this great game will only get better. Don't pass this one up!
NPCs, vehicles, and hunting are just around the corner, as well as the official release.

This
a sim or a builder, there's not much economy here. it's a
game. Intensive and frustrating at times, but also fun.
The concept is interesting enough: lay down tracks and guide trains from A to B (and later on from C to F and from E to B and from F to B simultaneously) while balancing both budget and time. Don't go broke or trigger any fail-criteria (most often this entails crashing trains) until the time ends and you  pass the level, with extra stamps (the game's equivalent of stars) for its bonus criteria. All while on a
space-constrained map, where terrain features will make some connections impossible, and others too expensive to build. What is there of the mentioned eras and locations is expressed purely through graphics and rolling stock, the gameplay doesn't change.
The initial levels are simple and fun, but later on it gets tough. Not for the easily frustrated, because you'll be replaying some levels over and over until you find a solution that works. The game makes that a bit harder though, because on every replay the level is slightly altered: stations activate in different order and of course the exact sequence of trains is never the same.
The frustration kicks in in the later (and longer) levels, when the trains start going off on their own because you kept them waiting too long.Then you're frantically trying to arrange the switches so that they don't get completely lost or crash, and with every next train on the tracks it gets more and more unworkable. And then you fail the level, restart and try again.
What you're actually managing here is what the "big" transport-builder games do for you automatically: start and stop trains, and toggle switches so that your trains reach the destination, leaving you to only plan and build. If you think it's fun - go for it. Otherwise stay with the transport builders you know and love.

Buy this game! Sale or not, buy this game. This is one of the first indie/early access games I've ever said this about besides Running With Rifles (look that up too). I could spend paragraphs telling you about why this game is good or my exeriences with the game but I'd rather just point out this one simple fact. The developers of this game are amazing. If you read through the list of features on the store page, every single one of them will be in this game sooner or later.
A lot of early access games have people crying that the devs "jumped ship" and took the money and ran. This is not the case for Project Zomboid at all. The developers seem to have a love for their own game which pretty much always means the game will be good. They don't cut corners to have the game be "finished" so they can charge more or get those 'early access haters' off their backs. In a recent update they've straight up told us that they don't feel the game complete enough for a 1.0 release because of the game lacking the major features on the Planned Features page. The developers are simply awesome and love their game just as much as they want us to love it.
Buy this game if you like DayZ, Nether, Rust, State of Decay or any other multiplayer/singleplayer co-op/pvp zombie survival horror game out there.
If you have the time, I'd also like to share one of my experiences from the game anyway.
If you don't have the time, I've crafted the story in such a way that you can read the last sentance of every paragraph to get a very brief summary of the story.
During a routine resource gathering trip we alerted quite a large group of zombies. Seeing no other option I pulled out my fully loaded pistol. In the craziness and panic of everything that was going on around us, I accidently shot my friend in the head. The gunshot wasn't leathal.
I'd like to imagine it was some sort of grazing shot caused by somebody moving in the way of the gun at the last second. He was badly injured though. I fought off the remaining zombies and helped him stumble home. We got all the bandages taken care of and swallowed a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of painkillers. His wound was infected.
It was dinner time, we were both starving. I'd found some raw steak in a neighboring house the day before. I thought it a good idea to cook it as a potential last meal. Zombies surround the house, I assume because they have a sense of smell (they really do) and were attracted by the cooking meat and/or blood from our wounds. I forgot about the steak.
Soon after dealing with some of the zombies outside the house I returned to the kitchen. The entire kitchen was engulfed in flames. The house was rapidley decaying. My friend was too injured to sprint. I did my best to help him to the door, but as we approched the door, it too burst into flames. We tried to find another way out but the only way was through the flames. We burst through the hole where the charred remains of a door lay. We were both on fire.
As the death credits rolled telling us our stats, it started to rain. Had we stayed in the house 30-40 seconds longer, we could have survived. A sense of dread overcame us. The dread soon gave way to awe as we realized the intense moments an indiependantly developed game made us feel. It was awesome.

Okay, so as a real game developer I have a few things to say.
First of all this is for people who are, well, serious about what they do, even if we're talking about creating a short game.
GMS2 is a great tool, it does lack in some areas, compared to other IDEs and engines, but it's more user-friendly and easy for beginners.
I made a bunch of mobile games in it and they are doing well in the App store and Google play, so GMS2 does work in the way it's intended to work.
It's also a great tool for quick prototyping, there are lots of assets in the market and of corse one of the best parts in that the community is quite active and friendly, you can ask your questions in the forum expecting to get meaningful answers, suggest new features etc. One of the features that I suggested in a forum discussion was picked up and implemented in the next GMS2 update and it didn't even took a month for the devs, so obviously I was very pleased.
Now for the minuses: you have to understand, that even though the GameMaker Studio was used to make a number of great indie titles, it requires a lot of effort to actually master its use. Also, there are some limitations that you won't see in "bigger" engines. Sometimes you have to "reainvent the bycicle", spending considerable time and effort to make an effect that would be done in few clicks in Unity (for example). One of the biggest limitations is the GameMaker Language that is used for coding here. While in the aforementioned Unity you're backed with the full pover of C#, here you're offered a much more modest number of options of what you can actually do in your code and that's sad.
It's just a big open sandbox with no campaign and no goals.

I will never forget the first time I descended in to Rapture. The city, A major character as much as it’s inhabitants, was simply fascinating. Like Bill McDonagh had said: “Who can forget their first view of the city? Amazing what a man can create once he gets  government and God off his back”. It wasn’t just because of it’s beauty(even almost destroyed, the city was stunning) or it’s creepy atmosphere. It was alive. It had a story to tell. It invite us to enter it, so we could live a journey that would be with us forever.
To me, Bioshock is, to this day, the best FPS ever made. It brought an seemly dead “genre” to life(The same from System Shock and Thief), and we probably wouldn’t have games like Deus Ex: Human Revolution, Dishonored or Thief 4 if it wasn’t for this game. It played with the player’s expectative, It gave you powers that you could combine and use for several combos and results. It has a fantastic AI(I will never forget the fist time I saw a hurt Splicer run away from me looking the first med-station available, of a burned Splicer looking for water to stop the fire). It was challenging like few action games dared to be. It was also a eerie game, both in it’s atmosphere and in it’s inhabitants(Splicers pretending to be dead just to jump at you, anyone?).  Finally, it had one of the most well written stories ever tell in a game, with tons of memorable characters, specially the unforgettable Andrew Ryan, creator of Rapture, and one of the best and more complex villains I ever faced in a game. It was a game that deserved every single praise it got. It’s a truly masterpiece, and if you haven’t played yet, there are few games I could recommend that much for you.
Welcome to Rapture.

Tropico is a series of city builders lite where you are also a dictator (a pirate lord in 2) who has to stay in power while trying to build his little heaven (or hell) on Earth.
And whereas Tropico 4 was just a Tropico 3 with more stuff - Tropico 5 has many features changed, reworked, added (and some cut) to warrant being called a proper sequel. Oh and it also has MUCH more stuff to do.
With changes in economy and many product chains and raw resources added compared to the previous game - it may take a few failures to wrap your head around the way things work.
Your tropical dictator paradise can now also have sharper teeth with more offensive stuff to beat down rebels and invaders with (although with changes in faction system the rebellions happen a lot more often for my taste).
All other categories of things to build and create are expanded as well, coming with a lot more comfortable interface.
As usual Sandbox mode is where the real game's at. And now it doesn't have time limits, albeit the generator is unfortunately simplified.
Instead the time frame takes you through four eras starting with colonial one where you are just a mere local manager of the king - you have to use crown's cash to kickstart your playground which you also have to make independent before your term's over. Don't worry it can be extended by doing missions (later on they give you much more varied rewards).
Of course if you don't want to bother with the colonial era (with it being quite different from the rest of the game, but I personally like it) - you can pick any other era to begin your game in.
I recommend it both to newcomers and previous Tropico players alike.

I am a latecomer to kalypso's Tropico titles, so my perspective is that of someone who isn't all too experienced with city-builders in general. Keep that in mind.
I always read reviews before I buy stuff, and the majority for this game said to buy Tropico 4 instead. So, that's what I did. I bought tropico 4 and played quite a bit, and then I bought tropico 5, and I've played them within days of each other.
I think Tropico 5 is the better game. The graphics upgrade is... substantial. I don't know if people say to play Tropico 4 instead because they've been long time followers of the game and weren't impressed with the new mechanics or what, but Tropico 4 is just too easy. Time consuming, but easy. Tropico 5 is hard. Much, much more challenging than Tropico 4, and it adds in some new elements and removes others. The "Faction" system seems to take less of a precedence, and foreign politics and a trade system seemed to have taken it's place. The trade system, the rebel system, the edicts, and the constitution all make Tropico 5 the more challenging and worthwhile title, in my opinion.
Now, don't get me wrong, I didn't dislike Tropico 4 even when compared to Tropico 5. I've played more hours of Tropico 4 to date, but I believe I'll play more Tropico 5 in the long run because it's just kicking my♥♥♥♥♥even on low difficulty. That's why I reccomend Tropico 5 over 4.

Here it is, the sequel to a timeless classic, but is it better or worse?
Well, a large majority will likely say the former, while looking through a pair of rose-tinted Nostalgia-brand glasses.
Me? not so much.
There are some big improvements over Flatout 1, but some problems have been made significantly worse. First, lets start with the driving.
DRIVING:
The driving feels overall pretty solid and nice, arcadey, but not to the extent of say, need for speed. Its sort of a blend of realistic behavor with physics breaking abilities. So far, its pretty good. Front-wheel drive cars tend to understeer into corners, rear-wheel drive tends to slide around more, oversteering, and 4WD is a bit of both, mostly understeer though. All well and good and as it should be.

Sometimes it can be very very unpredictable. Sometimes when landing a jump, your car will smash into the ground, either bouncing into the air or veering to the left or right, causing you to wreck, sometimes your car will completly flip upon landing a jump. THis all depends on the car, but really it can be complete luck weather you land a jump and keep going or crash and have to restart the race, which you will be doing, ALOT.
Next, the tracks
TRACKS:
Oh, dear lord did they mess this one up badly.
You know that thing i said in my Flatout 1 review?

Yeah, well imagine that, only about ten-thousand times worse.
Holy moly did they go overboard on the smashable props! It wouldnt really even be so much of a problem, if said props dissapeared or became uncollideable after being smashed into, but, no.
The props just go everywhere, all over the track at critical points before turns or after jumps, and ALL of them will cause you to wreck, every single one, even the cardboard boxes.
These props are everywhere, on every track in the game, and they are nearly impossible to avoid.
Id say, out of the hundreds of wrecks that ive had in the game so far, 98% of them have not been my fault, 78% is likely due to the props, and at least 20% are due to the bad AI, which we'll get to later.
Not to mention, the unbreakable solid objects badly placed on the edges of the track are still here, though, they are usually just boulders instead of trucks or diggers. However they are all pretty much completely hidden by grass, you wont know its there until you've hit one, and half the time you'll be saying "What the f**k did i just hit?" as you restart your race for the 17th time in a row, and no, thats not and exaggeration.
THE AI:
Im just going to be blunt here.
This game has the worst AI rubberbanding ive ever seen in a racing game, ive been playing racing games for 12 years, many have had AI rubberbanding, but this one tops them all.
To give a little explanation on this, ill use Gran Turismo 1/ Gran Turismo 2 for example, games nutorious for having AI rubberbanding.
In GT1 and GT2 The AI would speed up or slow down depending on how much you were beating them, or them beating you. THis is used in an attempt to keep the racing close and fair.
If you got 2 seconds a lap ahead, the AI would speed up a bit, usually matching your speed, your able to stay out in front, but if you make a really bad turn or crash, they will catch back up, or pass you. If your in a really fast car, you can outrun the speed boost. The same thing applies if your being beaten, the AI cars slow down by 2 seconds, giving you a chance to catch up, or pass them if you wrecked.
Thats essentially what its like here, only its done way, way worse.
Instead of your cars being equally matched, In street class, the AI cars will be almost twice as fast as your car, no matter what car it is or if its fully upgraded. The race starts and your left in the dust. then they brake a bit, allowing you to pass, only to smash you to bits or fly right past you once again.
Basically, it doesnt matter how good of a driver you are, no amount of perfect driving lines or well timed boosts is going to give you an edge. The AI is basically there to stomp you, and you have to either get out in front and drive nearly perfect to stay there, which due to the AIs speed, wont last long, Or you and try and smash everyone who gets near you to peices. Either way, its racing hell.
Finally, the multiplayer.
MULTIPLAYER:
The multiplayer is where the real fun lies. No garbage AI to ruin your day here, and usually less props get involved, due to  less people smashing into them. (though some are unaviodable and automatic, like the rock slide on Pinegrove.)
The game has, or, had real online multiplayer, which was a huge plus over Flatout 1. However in late 2012 rumors that GameSpy, the company responsible for Hosting Flatout 2's online servers, and many many other games , would be shutting down. This would sadly prove true, as on May 31st 2013, Gamespy shut its doors for good, and took all of its servers with it..
However, its not all bad, nowadays you can use many different programs to play GameSpy hosted games online, Flatout included.
The multiplayer on Flatout 2 is very fun, you can race with, or smash other real players to bits. You can host lobbies with up to 8 players. As a host, you can change what tracks will be raced, what derbies or events will take place, what cars players will be able to use, how many laps a race will have, and so on.
Theres also text, and voice chat in lobbies. Ive never seen anyone using a microphone though, so i cant really answer to the quality of voice chat.
OTHER STUFF;
The Soundtrack here is pretty great, aside from the 2 Nickelback songs that is. Theres songs from, and not limited to:
Megadeth
Papa Roach
Fall Out Boy
Rise Against
Wolfmother
Rob Zombie
There havent been any really noticable bugs in what ive seen so far, aside from one minor glitch, where you can drive through a wall on a City track, however the glitch is useless, and wont give you a competitive edge.
OVERALL;
While i do reccomend this, because it can be quite fun, its also very frustrating at times. Be prepared to restart races 10-15 times to win.

The Long Dark is an excellent survival simulation. The ability to play in "Pilgrim" mode is perhaps the most thought out variation in any survival sim I have ever played. Most other sims give you no choice in battling zombies, mutants or other worldly denizens. Having the opportunity to just survive against nature in a butal environment is an excellent idea, one I have looked for, for many years. The folks at Hinterland have made this right.
Don't get me wrong, I enjoy the added dimension of aggressive, starving wildlife. Just in reality, most wildlife really has no desire to interact with humans.
Not having a save option, may be one of my favorite parts of the game. When you do something stupid, try something a bit beyond your abilities., you either get seriously hurt or fade into "The Long Dark". This ultimately gives you a chance to reflect on how difficult it is to survive in the wilds of Canada, in the winter.
Great job, Hinterland! Keep evolving!
