Buy this game! Sale or not, buy this game. This is one of the first indie/early access games I've ever said this about besides Running With Rifles (look that up too). I could spend paragraphs telling you about why this game is good or my exeriences with the game but I'd rather just point out this one simple fact. The developers of this game are amazing. If you read through the list of features on the store page, every single one of them will be in this game sooner or later.
A lot of early access games have people crying that the devs "jumped ship" and took the money and ran. This is not the case for Project Zomboid at all. The developers seem to have a love for their own game which pretty much always means the game will be good. They don't cut corners to have the game be "finished" so they can charge more or get those 'early access haters' off their backs. In a recent update they've straight up told us that they don't feel the game complete enough for a 1.0 release because of the game lacking the major features on the Planned Features page. The developers are simply awesome and love their game just as much as they want us to love it.
Buy this game if you like DayZ, Nether, Rust, State of Decay or any other multiplayer/singleplayer co-op/pvp zombie survival horror game out there.
If you have the time, I'd also like to share one of my experiences from the game anyway.
If you don't have the time, I've crafted the story in such a way that you can read the last sentance of every paragraph to get a very brief summary of the story.
During a routine resource gathering trip we alerted quite a large group of zombies. Seeing no other option I pulled out my fully loaded pistol. In the craziness and panic of everything that was going on around us, I accidently shot my friend in the head. The gunshot wasn't leathal.
I'd like to imagine it was some sort of grazing shot caused by somebody moving in the way of the gun at the last second. He was badly injured though. I fought off the remaining zombies and helped him stumble home. We got all the bandages taken care of and swallowed a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of painkillers. His wound was infected.
It was dinner time, we were both starving. I'd found some raw steak in a neighboring house the day before. I thought it a good idea to cook it as a potential last meal. Zombies surround the house, I assume because they have a sense of smell (they really do) and were attracted by the cooking meat and/or blood from our wounds. I forgot about the steak.
Soon after dealing with some of the zombies outside the house I returned to the kitchen. The entire kitchen was engulfed in flames. The house was rapidley decaying. My friend was too injured to sprint. I did my best to help him to the door, but as we approched the door, it too burst into flames. We tried to find another way out but the only way was through the flames. We burst through the hole where the charred remains of a door lay. We were both on fire.
As the death credits rolled telling us our stats, it started to rain. Had we stayed in the house 30-40 seconds longer, we could have survived. A sense of dread overcame us. The dread soon gave way to awe as we realized the intense moments an indiependantly developed game made us feel. It was awesome.

This game right here, is one of the best survival simulators I've played in quite a while. Not only are the graphics beautiful,(which can also be played on most laptops/computers with decent fps), but the atmosphere is incredibly astounding. If you play this game with headphones on, you're in for a good time. You'll get to experience some very realistic sounding noises,(heavy breathing when you run, occasional lines your character says, and most importantly, the atmosphere around you.) Even during blizzards, you can't help but appreciate how great it sounds. Aside from graphics/atmosphere, the gameplay is great. The crafting system is creative. In terms of diffuculty, this game varies. Play on easy, you get easy. Play on normal, your experience will be a bit challenging. Play on hard, prepare to punch your computer/laptop in frustration. Aside from difficulty, you're given the chance to play in different maps, which are all conected to each other. (Each map is harder to survive in from each other.) Personally for me, my favorite part of this game, is the danger. The danger in this game is REAL. Trek on a journey to your next safe house, and you just might get burried in a blizzard. Step out in the open at the wrong time of day, you might freeze to death/run out of supplies, etc. Make one wrong step, break your ankles and tear your clothing, exposing you to more cold, and slowing you down. So many things could go terribly wrong, forcing you to really play your cards right. The replay value in this game is great, where you can waste hours upon hours trying to survive as long as you can. All in all, if you want a TRUE survival experience,(and you like the cold,) this game is definitely for you. Personally the price is certainly fair and worth it. I would rate this game a 9/10.

Oooooo slow mode bullet dodging "puzzle" game. This is a refreshing first person shooter "puzzle" game and its originality is well executed. Many people often talk about playing a game with the ability to do matrix effects (bullet dodging) yet it took this long for a studio to finally develop a game that actually does that and use it as one of its core mechanic. The game seems to be heavily inspired by The Matrix Trilogy not only from the bullet dodging, but also with the hot switch/take over mechanic (Neo going into Agent Smith in the first movie, and Agent Smith taking over other people's body). The theme is also a sci-fi dystopia like, except the player takes the side of the machine instead.
There are over 30 levels in the game, but some are tutorials and some are story levels where there is no gameplay. Though the levels that do contain gameplay are incredibly engaging, espcially near the end. It is slightly disappointing that a deep philosophical theme was set up for the narrative but was mostly ignored and overshadowed by the game play. The campaign was also a bit short, with around only 3 hours.
The longevity of the game can be seen in its endless and challenge levels after completing the campaign, where one can spend endless hours in killing enemies over and over again.
The game makes great use of the Unity Engine’s Physic Time Scale to create the game play, though on occasions, the physics seem to be a bit out of place when throwing items around.
TLDR;
Pros:
-You can become Neo
-Stylized minialistic art
-Refreshing game play with originality
-Cutting bullets in half!!!
-Endless mode with additional hours of fun
-Unique story line, which also challenges the player in real life
Cons:
-Story was cut short and not well polished despite having a great introduction to it
-Seems a bit meh for $35 CDN
Overall:
If you have the bucks to spare, this is worth a grab for its originality, especially if you grew up watching The Matrix. If you don’t have extra cash laying around, then grab it on sale, and I will strongly recommend getting it during sales.

Project Zombiod stands as the single best depiction of surviving a large scale zombie outbreak on the market today.  Period.  Sure, there are plenty of other zombie games out there (too many, one might say), but no other is so willing to forsake story for simulation than this game.  Simply put, Project Zombiod is the only zombie-themed sandbox game that matters.
Survival is the one and only concern in Project Zomboid, and the zombies aren't even the biggest danger.  Hunger, sickness, fear, blood loss, and sleep deprivation are all there waiting in this game, and your character is just as easily to succumb to these dangers than the zombies.  Now one mustn't discount the zombies and the dangers they they represent, but you are just as likely to slip up and cut yourself climbing through a broken window whilst escaping zombies as you are to die at the hands of the undead themselves.  Just as likely to starve as all of your carefully gathered food stores rot in their cupboards.  What will you do when the power goes out?  The water?  Or when a recently migrated hoard of zombies settle displace you from your bullet-stocked safehouse?
Since this game is still Early Alpha one must make some concessions.  There are still a number of features that remain to be implimented.   While the survival aspect of the game works remarkable well for an Early Alpha game, there is still no NPCs to be seen.  You will occasionally hear gunshots during the night (which will attract hordes), you will see not another character (unless they be a human on a multiplayer server).  Food gathering is limited to what you can find inside abandoned stores and houses, and what you can grow on your own (though I've never survived long enough for that).  Gamepad support is still lacking, which is a shame (though not a deal-breaker, in my opinion).
So there you are.  There is a ton of content and experiences that have been left out of this, but this is something best experienced on your own.  All I can add is if extreme zombie survival is something you are interested in experiencing, then I can think of no better game for your (at any price).  Where else can you watch in horror as all of your carefully laid survival plans come crashing down because of a scratch you got after having to crawl through a smashed window to escape a horde of zombies?

It seems that no matter how good a game series is, it's always destined to have a black sheep, so to speak. Sometimes the game isn't even bad, just not as solid as the rest and people act like by proxy it's the worst thing ever. It happened with Fallout 4 compared to Fallout 3 and New Vegas, and I feel like it happened with Half-Life: Blue Shift.
Half-Life is the second and final expansion pack that Gearbox developed for the original Half-Life, and much like Opposing Force, Blue Shift puts you behind the perspective of another Character during the Black Mesa incident. In Blue Shift, you play as Barney Calhoun, a security guard and familiar face to those who've played Half-Life 2. Much like in Half-Life, Barney is starting his day of work at Black Mesa by commuting via tram, and after arriving at his scattered workplace, he gets his gun and presses a button for some rude as hell scientists in an elevator before everything goes FUBAR. As aliens begin teleporting in from Xen, Barney's elevator crashes into the ground, killing every occupant other than himself. Upon regaining conciousness, Barney sets off on a mission to escape Black Mesa, eventually meeting up with a Dr. Rosenberg, and the two partner up to escape the facility.
One of the greatest criticisms leveled against Blue Shift is that unlike it's sister expansion, Blue Shift does not add in any new weapons or enemies, without even recycling the ones in Opposing Force. Barney also does not gain access to any of the neater weapons that Gordon Freeman was able to get his hands on like the Tau Cannon or the Hive-Hand, the biggest gun Barney is able to weild outside of console commands being the RPG. While these criticisms are certainly valid, it's not fair to say it doesn't bring anything new to the table. Blue Shift is decidedly much more story driven than Opposing Force, as Dr. Rosenberg is a very important character to Blue Shift's story and is one of the few persistant NPC's in the original trilogy. Dr. Rosenberg explains alot of exposition about his old lab in the facility wile also serving as one of the few charaters with the knowledge and equipment to actually escape the facility.
As such, the latter half of the game consists of Barney doing various errands for Rosenberg to help calibrate his antiquated teleportation machines, such as going to set up a machine in the border world and restoring the backup power deep below the lab. Even though this may not seem all that important, it really does help Blue Shift feel like it's own experience, which is also accompanied by the game's unique handling of Armor. Barney is the only protagonist of the GoldSrc games who lacks a form of powered armor, so he must use the armor of his fallen comrades to protect himself. This can make the game feel really tense as armor becomes less of a second health bar and more of a finite resource which is found few and far between the last.
That aside, I feel like the strongest point of Blue Shift is it's level design. The enemy placement and the size of the levels is pretty great, and the Xen levels are honestly really well made compared to the ones in Half-Life. While I'd say Opposing Force has the better gameplay of the two, I feel like Blue Shift's level design is much more consistant than OpFor's. Despite this, the other grave flaw with Blue Shift is it's shortness. Blue Shift seems to end just when it's beginning to get really good, and there's some puzzles in the game that don't make alot of sense initially, like the barrel and TNT puzzle.
At the end of the day, Blue Shift may not be the best Half-Life game and may arguably be the weakest of the expansions, but it's still a Half-Life game, and it's still just a solid shooter in general. The persistant NPC's in the game as well as the level design and the armor tweaks make Blue Shift still a very positive experience overall, and if you liked Opposing Force or just Half-Life in general, you really should play Blue Shift. While less isn't necessarily more here, you can't really go wrong with a bite sized Half-Life.

Firstly, I would like to emphasize that I strongly, *strongly* recommend playing this game. The immersive nature of it is gripping, and it's sure to make you feel like a seasoned wilderness survival expert and adventurer while you sit in your comfortable chair in your heated home eating cheese doodles. However, it seems like every other reviewer has already said all the good things there are to be said about it, so I would like to focus on some of the more negative aspects of the game.

As far as video games go, it's (*mostly*) highly realistic. The only survival mechanism missing from this game is the ability to poop and pee. Sleeping, eating, hydration, freezing, injury, you name it, the game probably has a mechanic for it. And don't get me wrong, this is a good thing, it serves as nice refreshment from most modern AAA titles. The negative aspects of the game come about from the noticeable juxtaposition that is created from those few aspects that are unrealistic.
I need to eat 2,500 calories a day to stay healthy. Alight. That's realistic, and fair enough. A good mechanic. Wolves attack you for no absolutely reason. Okay. While not realistic, it adds a good element of challenge to the game, which is what games are for, after all. I'm out and about for 3.5 hours, become exhausted and need a nap to prevent myself from dying of fatigue. Hold on, now wait a minute. Nobody, except for those who are extremely young or elderly,  no matter how strenuous of an activity they are doing, requires a nap after just 3.5 hours.
It's the meticulously crafted realism of almost every mechanic in the game that makes you notice and cringe at these small incongruities with the real world. They pop up where you least expect them. Like when you think "surely four shots at a bear with this massive rifle is more than enough to kill it" before it then proceeds to maul you to death. I'm no expert or gun enthusiast, but based on the size of the bullets in the game, I'm fairly certain that it would only require one, two at *most* to take down a bear in real life.
All this being said, the game is still in alpha. I'm sure that plenty of these mechanism will be tweaked before the actual release. Here's to hoping for an "Injury Inflicted: Bladder Infection from waiting too long to pee" mechanism in the future.

Like Stanley Parable, I felt that Beginner's Guide was an interesting concept with a deeply flawed delivery.
This time around you are playing through a number of game prototypes while the narrator explains the background story behind these games and their creator. The prototypes themselves are rather unfinished and not particularly enjoyable.
It is clear the game tries very hard to be a deep emotional experience. Unfortunately, for me this didn't really work. The narrator is way too heavy-handed with his message and this made the whole story fall flat pretty quickly. Without the emotional impact there's little left to enjoy as the gameplay and the graphics are very basic by design.
I can't really recommend the Beginner's Guide. It's another title that's interesting as an art experiment but failure both as a game and as an emotional narrative.
The good:
- Interesting concept
The bad:
- The narrative feels too forced and pretenteous, robbing it of any emotional impact
- The game prototypes are pretty terrible, even considering the fact that they are supposed to be unfinished
- Very short

Evolve is a somewhat original game where you play 4 (hunters) vs 1 (monster).  This concept is however not really polished into superb gameplay. Usually as a monster you start too weak to combat the hunters, so you walk around the map a bit, eat to get stronger and try to avoid the hunters, until you reach level 3. At level 3 you are usually strong enough to completely wreck the hunters. This is basically the entire game. And it feels somewhat repetitive. There are a few modifications of this gameplay in evacution (story mode), dor instance egg hunt, and save survivors, but they add very little to the gameplay, and feel more like they were created as a quick afterthought.
Personally I dont mind repetitive gameplay... I've played l4d2 scavenger only on atrium for a 1000+ hours, and play the same 3 maps in natural selection 2 all the time. But it becomes very annoying in evolve that there are a lot of unnessecary 'loading screens' some really are just loading screens, but others are there to see your stats, to see what gamemode is coming next (unskippable for 30 or so seconds!), then a seperate screen which takes a long time to load to pick your character. Then a non-skippable introduction movieclip. And I'm sure I am forgetting some screen that you cannot skip. All in all, this takes up a lot of time (especially if your teammates are on slow pc's).
Another important point is the day 0 DLC. This is an absolutely repulsive businessmodel and created a lot of anger towards both the developer and the publisher. After playing this game for 30+ hours, I can say most of the critism is somewhat correct. This already does not feel like a full 50Euro game so taking away content in order to sell as DLC is just horrible.
Finally, there are still a lot of bugs (cursors dissappearing), timers stopping, falling through the floor. And the controls feel a bit clunky.
TL;DR The game is repetitive, lets you wait a lot for no good reason, and is based on a repulsive businessmodel. Tho the concept is fun, right now I cannot recommend it for the full price. Let's just hope Valve makes Evolve 2, because with Valve's polish this game could really shine.

I think the "IDLE" in the title is a bit misleading for those of us who are used to thinking of Idle games as something that you can only do so much  as everything is on an ever-increasing timer to get things done.
In this game you can play as much as you want, where the "idle" part of the game is in the fact that your heroes keep adventuring even after you turn off the game, and only stop when your inventory is completely filled with loot.
Sure, there are real-world timers in certain campaign modes that can only be done once per day, or the traveling merchant that only replentishes his stock every 6 hours or so, but nothing that actually halts playing.
There's a micro-transaction shop like in most Free To Play games for the more impatient players, but gem and hero unlocks can be accomplished via dedicated play time.
So, all in all, this is a very solid, enjoyable game that is highly addictive like good F2P games should be and the gameplay is solid and satisfying.
My only personal quibble is that you can't sort inventory according to the level of the items, but there is a filter for rarity and equip slots, which makes it all the more baffling why they didn't include sorting by item level.
But since it is F2P and a very quick download, it's worth checking out for RPG'ers and loot [censored] who are looking for a casual, stress-free gaming moment of running characters through endless campaigns and digging through piles of loot.

This is a very powerful piece of software -IF- you are creative enough to utilize its tools.  Purchasing this is not suddenly going to make you a creative genious that cranks out moneymaking masterpieces left and right.
Pros:
- GML is a very solid language that can definitely be used for more than crappy little mobile games or Steam Greenlight early access trash.  If you are looking to learn how to code, GML is a great place to start learning the fundamentals.  Much of the knowledge will carry over to more complex languages in one way or another.
- There are hundreds of quality youtube tutorials available.  Most of the old Game Maker 8 and Game Maker Studio 1.4x vids are perfectly servicable for use with GMS2.
- You can make full blown applications as well as games.
- The built in sprite editor is excellent and can be used as is to create art resources and animations with no need for third party software.  The integration is seamless and very smooth.
- Game Maker Studio does 2D very well.
- The UI is slick looking and tries to pass itself off as a proper node based editor.
Cons:
- The UI is not a proper node based editor.
- The UI lacks much in the way of customization options.  You cant really make it your "own".  You just have to put up with its idiosyncracies.  At least for now.  Hopefully the developer will address this in time.
- While the software is not nearly as unstable as some people are hyperbolically trying to claim.  It is unstable enough to warrant very agressive backup policy while coding.  Frequent saves are a must.  Make sure you use an incremental save system.
- Game Maker Studio does not do 3D very well.  If you want 3D, use Unity or UE4.

I played this game during the Big Alpha but was unable to find time during the beta. From my Alpha experience it felt well polished as it was and very fun. Between random matches and playing with friends the game overall felt worth trying out.
This is my opinion as of launch. (if you want a quick summary head to the bottom of the review.)
So far i haven't played with friends as none are currently available to do so. The experience with random people has been fun and i got into some really fun and tight matches with the same group for a few hours and i didn't mind at all. I haven't had any disconnects aside from somebody rage quitting that we found him almost instantly stage 1 and destroyed him.
The rank up system is still the same from the Alpha but less grindy. There isnt much to comment on here.
I do have one issue with the game, i have a pretty good computer build and great internet, but the moment i open Chrome and a match starts the game hogs resources. Chrome freezes and the game stutters to the point where i have to tab out and close chrome to fix this. I had the same issue in the Alpha and hoped it would be fixed. I plan on streaming this with friends at some point and if the multiplayer will not cooperate with other programs running I can't stream it and play at the same time.
The other issue I have other people have covered too, and its not with the game itself. The amount of DLC is disgusting. I am satisfied having paid for the base game, but the DLC is not only expensive, but there is too much of it that clearly could have been part of the base game. I understand you do not need any of the DLC to play freely online, but i would like to play as these hunters and monsters. At the current price i refuse to shell out any money for the DLC as much as i would like to play them. I strongly encourage people to not buy the DLC. If you enjoyed the Alpha or Beta buy the game but under no circumstance buy the DLC. The one thing that seems like it may kill this game is the situation with the DLC driving away people buying the game, or even fully enjoying it.
Overall:
Good game. Smooth launch. Overpriced DLC that should not be DLC. Tons of fun.
Buy the game if you enjoyed the Alpha or Beta. DO NOT buy the DLC. If nobody buys the DLC they may notice something is absolutely wrong with how they handled it.

There is a lot to like about this game and after installing a few mods (expecially Colonial Charter, Creamery Diary, and Windmill & Bakery, which adds a ton of new content), I would highly recommend this game if you enjoy strategy, city building games. It's also pretty challenging, especially if you play it on a harder difficulty. The natural disasters can be absolutely devistating to your town and if you're not prepared, can easily lead to total annihilation of your townfolk.
Some reviewers are saying that it's only good for a few hours, but it took me at least 6 just get familiar with everything and get my town started. Then something like a disease can break out and wipe out your people before you can get back with your cup of coffee ;) so remember to pause, or at least slow down to real-time before you leave for any extended period of time.
There's definitely more replayablilty than the negative reviewers are leading you to believe. Lots of different types of resources (pears, apples, blueberries, wheat, etc.) that you can eventually turn into Wine, Ale, or Pies if you wish. Which your townfolk will sell in market, pubs, etc. The setting of the game is actually excellent.
It would be fantastic if this was merged with a game like AOE where you have to defend your village from other players or NPCs, but it's still pretty good game as is. Overall, it's one of the better city-building games I've played and I wouldn't hesitate to purchase it, even at full price, if you like these types of games.

Overall I'd give this game an 8.5/10. It is very solid and quite enjoyable, however has some serious problems. Fortunantly these can be fixed by the devs, I will list them below:
- Wolf respawn sucks, they respawn about every 3-5 days. If wolves are going to respawn that quickly please have ammo for the rifle respawn.
- You get hungry really quick. I understand tiredness, thirst, and body temperature. All of those have reasonable depreciation times (the time and speed at which the condition drops). However, you get hungry FASTER than you get thirsty (only slightly). In real life a full meal can keep you alive for a month. Now I'm not asking for realism, as food would now become trivial. But please have the character stay full longer, I struggle with food more than any of the other ones.
- No map. Now this might be controversial, but I run this game in windowed mode. I tab out to check my heading and pick out a destination to explore. I know not everyone likes this, some people like the challenge of not knowing where they are going but I would like this to be an option. When you go flying in real life, you always bring maps; especially of the areas you are flying to and from, and even over. So if they made it optional (a setting you could turn on) that would be great.
Still a great game, looking forward to the story mode which comes out soon! Definantly a pick up if you like survival games. If you are on the fence, wait for it to go on sale. 50% off or more is an absolute steal.
Also, the graphics are fine people, stop trashing this game for it. Frankly, I think updated graphics would take away from the experience, this games graphics are like a painting and it works well.

Very touching... I'd hesitate to call it a game, more like a walkthrough with narrative. It's not really fun, no replayability, but is very interesting to go through the first time. It's basically a collection of work with narration over it describing some of the meaning behind it. It's also an in-depth look at what happens to the artist when a work of art is being created. And, yes, a video game CAN be art without being super pretentious.
Even though it's only 90 minutes long, even though it's not really a game, this is one that'll stick with me for a very long time, a lot longer than most of those other games.
You've been warned.
Now, my question is: was this coda a real person? Is this a name he made-up for the creation of the narrative of this game? Or was it himself in the past, but he no longer feels like this person?
If it was himself, then I don't have a problem with him selling this on steam, it's his own work and he can do with it what he pleases. And I love the fact that he never reveals himself to be Coda, which would be very in-line with the works that Coda produced, you have to suss out the meaning yourself (even though he describes the meaning behind the rest of the work).
If it was made-up, then I feel kinda jipped and pleased at the same time. Jipped, because I actually felt for this character that doesn't exist, and I feel kinda silly for that, but pleased because he created it so well that it's extremely relatable.
If this was a real person, however, then basically selling someone else's work with a voice-over is an extremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing to do! Shame on the developer for this! (if this is true). I enjoy "walking simulators" because they bridge the gap of narrative storttelling between video games and literature/cinema. Most other games fail to convey meaningful themes or motifs, and a good bunch can't even create a compelling world with engaging characters or plots.
But games like "Gone Home" and "The Beginner's Guide" are given the freedom to do what other genres fail to do since the gameplay is near non existent.
However, for me personally, there is a big difference between a game like "Gone Home" and "The Beginner's Guide" and that is the story they choose to tell and how it's told.
Where "Gone Home"'s narrative is simple and it's themes universally understood, "The Beginner's Guide" tackles an unorthodox story which hits home in many ways but fails in others.
The biggest strengths of the game include the soundtrack, narration style and tone. As previously stated, the plot is unique. A programmer creates a multitude of "unfinished" games and the narrator (the creator of this and "The Stanely Parable") reveals his interpretations of said games.
However, the way the interpretations are delivered is very heavyhanded and it soon becomes obvious he is making his views clear to reincorporate them in the final act of the story. Although I didn't see the ending coming (and as a whole the ending was satisfying and thought provoking on
), it left me with a bad taste in my mouth when I realised his interpretations were only given for reincorporations sake, which would be fine if it wasn't so blatant.
The story arcs allow for tonal shifts, and the change to dark, depressing worlds created by the programmer alongside the haunting score allow the player to form their own opinion on the state of the programmer.
In conclusion, although I can't say I loved or even liked the game, I appreciate its existence and can admire the aspects it gets right. Like many movies I may not enjoy, I recommend this due to how interpretation heavy the game is. One person may find the themes more powerful than I and the game allows for that to happen. It is a shame it didn't quite click with me but I hope it does for others.

The Beginner's Guide aims to be a moving and subversive experience rather than a conventional game, even by the standards of other metanarrative titles like The Stanley Parable. I expected it to be an achingly raw story of real-life pain and uncertainty. Unfortunately, I think it fell a bit flat for me. There are a couple of reasons, which are hard to cover in full without going into spoiler territory (so
), but ultimately I think it came down to the fact that I could, as it were, see the strings.
The problem started with the game's pedigree. I was a big fan of the creator's previous work, The Stanley Parable (he was one of its two creators), so I went into The Beginner's Guide with my mind sharp and alert, looking out for the tricks, the clever little details I was expecting them to spring on me. And for most of the experience, as the narrator Davey guided me through the experimental games made by his friend Coda, I was deeply immersed. These mini-games were effective in their bizarre simplicity, with great creepy atmosphere and a haunting beauty, and the narration enhanced the experiences with its interpretations and observations. As the story went on and things began to get darker, however, I found myself beginning to question the whole narrative, and not in the way I had expected. I thought I'd seen the big twist in the story coming (for what it's worth, I was wrong), but then I started to wonder whether I was actually asking the right question. The ultimate downfall of The Beginner's Guide for me came when I first seriously asked myself one game-breaking question: "is this
a true story?"
And unfortunately, the final breaking point came during the climax, the mini-game known as "The Tower". This, unfortunately, was the point where the entire experience broke my suspension of disbelief, right at the dramatic climax of the story. It felt contrived, but at the same time the game didn't come clean and admit "this was a fictional story" even though it had already given away that it was. It was the little bald man still pretending to be the mighty wizard, saying "pay no attention to the man behind the screen" even after he's been revealed. And this dissonance undermined the whole story for me. I could see the game trying to pull my emotional strings and instinctively pulled back in resistance.
Even now after I'm done, I have no idea whether or not this game is the real expression of personal darkness for the creator that it expresses itself to be, or whether it's just a carefully-constructed facsimile of one. It's still a haunting and at times beautiful experience, and I can't in honesty give it a negative score, but it did disappoint me- it left me feeling quite hollow, but its message got so jumbled by the end that I was left quite confused rather than thoughtful. I myself suffer from social anxiety disorder, but the realisation that, as far as I can tell,
undercut everything the story had to say about the issue. I'd still recommend it to others, maybe they'd get more from it if they went in without the expectations I did, but if you've read this far in my review it's probable the things I've already pointed out will have corrupted the experience for you as well. If so then, for that, I'm sorry. It's still a potent and atmospheric visual experience and worth your time, but the narrative fell short.

This game is insanely well designed content-wise. Do not let the "Early Access" fool you; this game is so immense in features that it actually feels finished.
This game is like a storyless Fallout with its intense depth, woo-hooless Sims with its building and crafting, tacticless Jagged Alliance with its coop gameplay, and missionless Syndicate with its art style.
What is awesome:
- Well, first of all, it gave one of the best Co-Op experiences till now. The glasses breaking, zombies walking in, the sense of pitch black when it's midnight, the desperation to get to safety, the "omg the glass just broke" feeling, the "this door is locked man, we have to find another exit, I lure them into this room and close the door from behind, you find another door" type of conversations... It's fun.
- The content! So much to do. So much to craft. So many things to use as weapons. Every item you find that is lootlable is somehow usable. Every single thing can be used somewhere somehow. There is no "garbage loot" (except for a few stuff which don't have functionality attached to them yet, such as some pieces of clothing).
- The "apocalypse" feel: Yes, they nailed it. You walk into a motel, just to find some doors open, blood everywhere, with two zombies shuffling in the bathroom when you open the door. The hoard of zombies that shuffle around the streets. The hordes filling the room at midnight when accidently a gun goes off.
What the game needs:
- Currently the only things that I've seen missing are the sprites (backpacks on the back or carried as secondary), unique art for some hand-held items (rolling pin looks like and is handled like a baseball bat), some animations (water drinking animations) and character-related stuff to add variation (more hairstyles) and so forth.
- Instead of basic texturized lawns and such, the developers could go for rather more sophisticated "environment design sprites" for some locations, which would be static, hand-drawn images for backgrounds. The way it's done in the Fallout games, Wasteland 1-2 and the new Torment game (Tides of Numenera). Sure, mapmaking is dead easy right now probably using an incredibly easy-to-use tool that adds blocks, paints roads, etc., but still...
- The game could also benefit more from character creation and customization options. Sure; the trait system is fine, but somewhat lacking in content. There are only 5 pre-selectable professions, and about 12 or so traits, half of them being negative and the other positive. So it doesn't always give a unique combination for each character created.
- Better UI overall. The in-game inventory UI is fine, interactivity is good, but may need "quick switch" buttons so that we don't have to sift through the huge inventory to find the damn rolling pin.
Last thoughts:
Considering that driving, vehicles and more cities/towns will be added to the game in the future, the current level of depth in such a short period of time (despite everything the developers have gone through), I can positively believe that any promised feature will be delivered by the developers.
It will definitely not be for people who like isometric games, but if you can get past that prejudice, you can unlock the full potential of Project Zomboid.

When you double click something you want that object to_______

I have used GM/GMS for long years, created several apps and used several engines with different languages and I think GM/GMS has been the best engine among all platforms because of several reasons: 1. Easy to learn. 2. Simple to manage. 3. Entertaining to create.
However, GMS2 is far from these…
First the positive aspects:
-Layers provide a good solution for some cases.
-More DnD functions including some tapping facilities.
-A sole-code mode.
-Some nice small features such as project time measuring and removal of useless buttons at the top.
-Developments in code editor with colorful clues.
-UI seems really beautiful while GMS1 looks quite old fashioned. Most beautiful design to be honest!
But these are just make up issues and the negative aspects are extremely much:
1. Messy UI. This is against all our habits of using Windows interface. Yes, it seems as a nice idea, but in practice it is a real pain, especially if you don’t have a huge screen it is quite claustrophobic:
-Windows stay under windows. Why I have to navigate? Why I have to use the mouse middle button to focus?
-Lines everywhere...quite useless and seems like an imitation of Unreal Blueprint...
-What is the function of zooming in/out of buttons? Why they are not in proper resolution?
-What is the reason for adding everything on a single workspace including all different elements?
-Tons of elements making everywhere crowded. Waste of screen. Even the Grid Alpha value...
-It is clear for me that GMS1.X was designed by a very open minded, simple thinking, analytical, tidy person while GMS2 seems someone who wants to create something like Unity.
2. Clearly longer load time.
3. Do we have to connect to internet regularly. Why? Even Microsoft does not request it for something we already paid!
4. Clearly longer test time.
5. Clearly longer compile time.
6. Maybe they have good functions but editors are mostly useless for me. They make GM bigger, complex, slower and open for bugs... Definitely I would prefer a compact, editor-free version. I already use editing tools. This should be optional…
7. Strict combination of exporters. I just build for Android, why I have to pay for Mac exporter? What is the relation between Windows and Linux export?
8. Removal of a free full version which can be very good for educational and promotional purposes! The limitations should only stay in exporting. I should test what I produce before I buy! Many Dollars for educational copy? Come on, I want to promote GMS for education but which school will pay it while there exist free alternatives?
9. Price policy. While many other tools are getting cheaper and even free GM is getting expensive. If you are good at game making you can cover it but for a starter no... And we all know it is the best tool for starters… But, at least it is not yet membership based model!
10. More crashes, more compile errors... GMS is used to be a very stable engine. Crash is the last thing we need.
11. Probably due to this UI Engine consumes more CPU and slows down computer. Even 3D engines are not challenging my processor compared to GMS2.
12. Clearly slower help look up facility.
13. Irrelevant changes of components, changes in format...
At final, I really wonder the root of these changes. Have a research to ask opinions of users been conducted? Or are these "we just did in that way" approach. Now GMS2 consumes more energy of my computer and more energy of me. Why? It seems that new policy is about making GMS an experimental all men’s tool for making 2D games. It is OK... Lets try to be open... Maybe all things are acceptable but if the UI will not be remastered it will definitely bring the end of this product.

The graphics were good and the humour was there too (if not a bit repetative, a joke is funny once, twice, three times, four times -cringe, again, again and so on). Too little dialogue was included.
I'm sorry to say the gameplay just didn't work. What do I mean by that? Well, it was boring by comparison!
One of the features that unfortunatly dictate how the game is played, is that each scenario is played on a different island. That in itself is not a problem, but two or three scenarios later you go back to the island that you previously developed and you have to try and remember how and where all the resources are and how you developed the 'supply chain'. It was like going back into somebody elses half-played game and trying to work out what's wrong with it - even though it worked when you left it!!!
The menus are at times difficult to work with - important features, that can make or break a game, are sometimes buried deep in a menu that you hardly use or struggle to find (even though you might remember it was somewhere).
My next comment is strange, yes I agree. But it is like the rebels and armies are random. Now I know that they are not. But I felt like they were detached from what I was doing even though I do understand the mechanics.
I have saved my biggest gripe/problem until last. Groan. The price of the DLC's!!! I paid a lot of money for this game £35. Firstly, I would like to emphasize that I strongly, *strongly* recommend playing this game. The immersive nature of it is gripping, and it's sure to make you feel like a seasoned wilderness survival expert and adventurer while you sit in your comfortable chair in your heated home eating cheese doodles. However, it seems like every other reviewer has already said all the good things there are to be said about it, so I would like to focus on some of the more negative aspects of the game.

As far as video games go, it's (*mostly*) highly realistic. The only survival mechanism missing from this game is the ability to poop and pee. Sleeping, eating, hydration, freezing, injury, you name it, the game probably has a mechanic for it. And don't get me wrong, this is a good thing, it serves as nice refreshment from most modern AAA titles. The negative aspects of the game come about from the noticeable juxtaposition that is created from those few aspects that are unrealistic.
I need to eat 2,500 calories a day to stay healthy. Alight. That's realistic, and fair enough. A good mechanic. Wolves attack you for no absolutely reason. Okay. While not realistic, it adds a good element of challenge to the game, which is what games are for, after all. I'm out and about for 3.5 hours, become exhausted and need a nap to prevent myself from dying of fatigue. Hold on, now wait a minute. Nobody, except for those who are extremely young or elderly,  no matter how strenuous of an activity they are doing, requires a nap after just 3.5 hours.
It's the meticulously crafted realism of almost every mechanic in the game that makes you notice and cringe at these small incongruities with the real world. They pop up where you least expect them. Like when you think "surely four shots at a bear with this massive rifle is more than enough to kill it" before it then proceeds to maul you to death. I'm no expert or gun enthusiast, but based on the size of the bullets in the game, I'm fairly certain that it would only require one, two at *most* to take down a bear in real life.
All this being said, the game is still in alpha. I'm sure that plenty of these mechanism will be tweaked before the actual release. Here's to hoping for an "Injury Inflicted: Bladder Infection from waiting too long to pee" mechanism in the future.

STORY:
Cuphead was a cheap imitation of Mickey Mouse created in the early 20th century in order to bank on the success of Disney, he however has never reached the mainstream audience and was relegated to the radio. Needless to say no one today had ever heard of Cuphead before this reboot. The player is Elder Kettle, an anthropomorphic kettle living peacefully with his son Mugman. At the start of the story, a mysterious masked casino army kidnaps Mugman and sends Kettle off to rescue his lost son. Haunted by the death of his other son, Cuphead, and his abusive father, Kettle takes pink pills to deal with his crippling depression. These pills, which make the user feel nothing, are the only escape the denizens of Inkwell Island have from the reality of wasteland life. As Kettle ventures through the wasteland, he finds many different party members that aid him on his quest to find his son, from a scarred pig war veteran turned salesman to an entire barbership trio missing a 4th member. These party members all have in depth backstories that I do not want to spoil here.  Gaining the trust of the party members and learning their stories is likely the most interesting part of the game. Kettle finds the aftermath of the dice armyl; razed towns and corpses litter the wasteland. Their leader, Dice, constantly taunts kettle, showing up and forcing him to make long lasting decisions that will impact the rest of the game. However, as Kettle explores more of the wasteland, he finds that not all is as it seems.
Gameplay:
This game is truly the Dark Souls of Mickey Mouse. Many of the elements are lifted straight from the Souls series. For one, most of the challenges in the game come from the boss fights, of which there many and all of them unique. Trial and error will be necessary as the player learns the boss patterns and how to roll to avoid them. Another Souls aspect is that the player may be invaded by another player, who will then attempt to help or hinder the player whose game they joined. Finally, parrying from Dark Souls is prevalent in this game, however the player may only parry pink objects. This game also borrows heavily from Super Mario and the Smash Bros series. Platforming segments are prevalent and very mario-like; players will have to bounce on enemies, collect coins, and reach a flag at the end. Additionally, the player can get powerups that will allow them to shoot fireballs that allow them to kill enemies. From the Smash Bros series is lifted the "Final Smash" attack that Kettle can perform once he takes enough pink pills. This devastating attack will destroy all in the player's way and feels very satisfying to use. Additionally, RPG elements permeate the game, from the party and leveling system, to the act of finding new weapons and armor and equipping them to party members. I am happy to say that although these gameplay elements are wildly different, they all blend seamlessly into one expertly crafted gameplay experience.
Style:
The game has an old cartoon look that may turn some players away from this game. Because Cuphead is a reboot of the failed early 20th century cartoon, the developers decided to use the same lazy tactics of that day to create the visuals for this game. As such, the game has a cartoonish, unrealistic look that pales in comparison to other modern games of this era, such as Battlefield 1. While the developers wished to create a cheap artstyle in order to save budget, the end result is a cheap looking, seemingly damaged "artstyle" which is hard on the eyes. I would have preferred a modernized look more akin to, say, modern day Rick and Morty. However, the gameplay more than makes up for this blunder.
Conclusion:
This game has an incredible story and crazy good gameplay, however the art takes a hit.
I give this game a 6/10, everything is perfect but the art.

Project Zomboid is a zombie apocalypse game where players have no other objective other than to survive.
Interactivity in the game is extremely good, almost all objects have a purpose and players must use them to their advantage if they are to survive. This is complimented by a hud design which is easy to manoeuvre and is not obstructive in the slightest.
The Zombie intelligence is good, they are relatively easy to out manoeuvre, but this is purely by design. Don’t think this means you can let your guard down though. If they are given the chance to form in a group and besiege your place of residence, your chances of survival are slim at best.
Combat is relatively basic, but personally I do not mind as the game, for me at least, is more about survival opposed to hack and slash. However, if you are more attracted to games that are based upon combat and a more traditional first or third person view and style, you should maybe look elsewhere.
The graphic design of the game is nothing less than startling. When day turns to dusk it is one of the most beautiful scenes in a game of this graphic style – of any game you can find. The soundtrack too is great, it captures the mood superbly.
The player health system works well with individual statistics for every different limb. Other than the immediate physical health statistics there are separate ones for hunger, fatigue, and the amount of weight being carried. Carrying too much at once puts extra strain on your survivalist. These are just a few of the many statistics available. The system is very broad and useful.
There is also a construction system, where players are allowed to build unique structures. Anything from a small shed to a fortress is achievable. The system allows players to build with components such as walls, doors, furniture, floors, etc. This really stresses the need to collect a broad variety of materials, as they will become a necessity later on as you attempt to settle down and fortify an area.
Overall the game is extremely entertaining, all of the game mechanics work well. Project Zomboid is a must play for any true post-apocalyptic, survival, or zombie genre fan.

The joy of a good game is in learning and improving.  A good game provides clear, consistent rules and rewards you for playing better, smarter, cleaner.
Cuphead wants to test you, but more than that, it wants you to get better.  When you fail, you know why it happened,  There are no mysteries to its mechanics, and it makes no effort to slap you down with the unknown or unknowable.  And yes, proper execution is still a barrier even if your strategy is sound, but Cuphead always values cleanliness and consistency over reflexes.
This is that rarest of games where difficulty is a product of smart design rather than variables being ratcheted up to the point of punishment.  In other words, it's fun to fail, because you always know that you can succeed if you keep trying.
And I guess it's a neat bonus that Cuphead is one of the most achingly beautiful video games ever released.  Just like its play design, every stitch of its presentation is thoughtful and lush.  The amazing visual design and animation are self-evident, but just the little things: the fonts, the menus, the wonderful tap-dancing rapid fire sound of your default weapon.  Cuphead is deliberate to a degree that makes other, bigger, pricier games feel slapdash.
I think just about everyone can get something from Cuphead, even those who tend to find "hard" games intimidating.

Bioshock is a fantastic story based shooting game with some roleplaying elements. It is along the same lines as System Shock 2, and indeed I have heard that it is the spiritual successor to that great game. I highly advise playing this game, and when you do I recommend you do so alone, in a dark room, with surround sound or noise canceling headphones and the volume up to the point where it feels like you are really in Rapture.
The game is very immersive, and the story hits hard and fast if you desire. You can just wander around aimlessly, I suppose, but I think the game has more impact when you allow the story to give you a sense of being rushed.
This game has fantastic graphics for the time it was made, including av ery realistic water effect. The water looking real may not sound like much, but understand that this game takes place in an underwater location. I won't say any more, to avoid spoiling it.
On the downside, this game absolutely will not work for you if your graphics card does not support Shader 3.0. That is absolutely crucial. I obtained this game while I was running a laptop that did not have this feature. There is apparently a crack somewhere that can override this and make the game vaguely playable on some specific graphics cards that do not support Shader 3.0, but I don't recommend risking it. Plus, all the places that host this graphics hack appear to have gone down. I know; I spent about 12 hours trying to get this game to work on that laptop. Back then I did eventually find it, and it didn't work as it only works for some graphics cards! PLEASE make sure your computer meets the minimum system requirements!

I wholeheartedly recommend Morphopolis if you want to overcome your fear of bugs (the technical term is entomophobia, or insectophobia).
However, as a game, in whole conscience I cannot recommend Morphopolis to anybody. It's a short game, thank goodness, but apart from a few interesting puzzles (veeeeeeery few) it doesn't offer much on the fun front. Quite the opposite, it offers a lot on the "getting angry at the screen" front!
It is excruciatingly painful to move your bug across screens, the game doesn't do anything to make you understand what to do, and there are some puzzles which make absolutely no sense at all! There is one in which you need to rotate small pieces that connect with each other, and basically any combination is fine, but the game wants you to find the single one which is, I guess, more fine that the others. It is infuriating.
The flower of the first level is also a terrible puzzle: you need to arrange the colour in a specific way, but there is nothing telling you which is the combination which is supposed to solve it! Luckily somebody posted a walkthrough on Youtube...
To conclude, I don't suggest to buy Morphopolis even if heavily discounted. Just watch a white wall for a couple of hours and you will be better off. Unless you suffer from entomophobia, as I wrote at the beginning. Then Morphopolis can help you.

I bought this as it was an honorary mention in an online "best games of the year" set of awards. So maybe it was good on a tablet. It is just not good on a PC.
It has a unique art style which is the best feature of the game. It certainly looks good. There are no instructions, no clues on what the menu options are, how to save the game or if it autosaves. I lost my level progress several times pressing random icons hoping one was a save game option. I don't think there is a save game option. If you are mid level and something comes up and you need to go out. You lose all your progress. It is just frustrating. But what kills the game dead are the frustrating controls. They are slow to respond. The bug moves very slowly. or the bug doesn't move and just turns left-right-left-right like crazy. You can hold the mouse down to the right of the bug, and the bug will move left. The art is nice to look at, but you have no clue where the bug can go. You guess what you need to do, or where you need to go. But it just doesn't seem to work. You eventually find out it was what you guessed all along. So you seem to fight the controls to complete the level. The ambient background music was fine, nothing special, but did not seem to relate to the world itself and so did not make the world feel alive.
I expected the game to have a relaxing, fun, mysterious, exploration type feeling but I guess I was so frustrated by the controls I just wasn't enjoying the exploration at all. And it was just a feeling of "No, please don't make me go all the way up to the top and back down again, not again..". The world is just a static background, no leaf movements. There are no wind or "plant" sound effects. It just does not feel like a living world you are exploring. And when you finish the game there is no ending, you enter the temple and the screen goes dark. I was hoping to at least see the inside of the temple!
Really creative unique art, unique idea. But I just cannot recommend playing this game at all, there are just so many other indie games out there that do the mystery and exploration genre better and without the frustrating controls.

I started this game not expecting too much, and with some questions, namely: Where the heck's my two new characters that bring me back to BroForce once I'm done with the last batch!? I got a little angry seeing this had six(?) new characters, and my $15 dollar game didn't. But, being the fan that I am and needing my monthly BroForce fix, I tried it out anyways.
First Impressions: "Oh look, the eagle on the logo has a skull now, and the player screen looks different". When I played the first mission, I was dissapointed. "Okay, I have the Boondock Bro's guns (characters from the Original BroForce), THREE sticky grenades with small explosions rather than one big one, Ash Brolliam's face, and Nebro's head, I was pretty much a frankenstein of the last game. Walking around, it looked fairly samey, same enemies, same color pallet, except now there was prettier crates. Woo-hoo. Although, I noticed some mechanics I wasn't exactly opposed to. Now you can swing backon wires, instead of being forced in one direction thanks to an accidental jump, and use of a cutscene. It may not seem like much, but it told SOME story, where in the last BroForce, you could've just been waging homicide at the ski-mask-and-red-paint expo.
Second impression: I died at the first boss, "GREAT! Now I get to restart all of that progress just because I got landed o- wait, what's this?" It was a cutscene and a minigame. That's new. I honestly laughed at the minigame, and liked the villian because he was just as cocky and iggnorant of his imminent butt-whooping as every other lovable bad-guy.
When I finally found a second life, and therefore character, I wasn't impressed. "New face on Brochete, yay, but NOW the knives are smaller and fire faster! Now let's see the same, 'everything-infront-of-you-is-now-on-fire/dead' special. Well, I got what I expected, and it wasn't even as exciting as the original.
Environment: As I played along and unlocked new levels/characters, I did have fun. New enemy, new (enemy) vehicles, and one small thing that impressed me.
A circular saw.
Not a barrel, or a bigger barrel, a SAW! I was so used to the usual hazards, barrels, white propane tanks, falling blocks, that a saw took me by suprise, it even let me take time to notice the new textures, lighting, and background, which were all very welcome, mainly since they weren't the same array of bright green and orange.
Back to the saw.
I had no idea how to react, it was like somebody was playing Call Of Duty, and suddenly, a giant turtle appeared in the middle of the map, unexpected and alien. What would anybody in any game have done?
Shoot the poor thing. No reaction.
New idea: Push somebody into it. I couldn't help but giggle like a school boy as a terrorist got sawed to pieces, call me phsyco all the like. I have no idea why, but it was so cool that now I didn't just have barrels for me and my enemies to fear, and it was awesome when it broke off the wall and started carving a trail to the neared fleshy creature on the screen.
Bros: Once I unlocked them all. To best describe it, think of Super Smash Bros, if you've ever played one of the games. I felt like sure, there were familiar faces (sometimes literal copy-pastes of old abilities or models), but there were changes. When I got to Brocter Death, I thought he was just another Nebro/Captain Falcon kind of character, except I realized something new: It was HIS kind of class! Sure, there's melee-focused characters, close-range attacks, little to no ranged ones, but that's because that's the sub-class they were in, melee. One thing I've always loved about BroForce and SSB (and some other games) was how I could LOVE a character who was quick and had to get close to do damage, my friend would disloke that character, and opt for a slower character who could do damage at long/mid range. That same scenario came up in this run, where I'd want Broctor death, or, say, Marth (SSB again), while my friend would want Bro Caeser or Snake (SSB, last time, I swear). There were also some new attacks and specials that put a spin on the 'bam-bam-BAM' combat of the last game, if not by much.
Bosses: There were a total of two, the first of which was, well, unimpressive. He was pretty much another copy/paste of the GR-13 boss, but then game the second (final) boss.
First thing's first: More Nintendo comparisons (sorry!). If you, the reader (at this rate, only Free Lives staff, if I'm lucky) have played a Zelda game, you'll know that the bosses can be fairly threatening, and seemingly invincible, until you throw half of all the items you've collected at it. What I like about those bosses, and this one, is that they're a review of everything you learned in the last level set. In the original BroForce, a boss had to scurrying up a building as it was destroyed behind you by a massive helicopter. Missiles didn't affect it, bullets didn't scratch it, and plasma didn't even phase it (bah-dum-tschhhh). Eventually, when you reached the roof, you had to start running right as it dropped missiles on you. On this roof there where the white propane tanks mentioned earlier, which, if you fired your gun at any point, you would know rocket-off in the direction they're pointed at when shot. Many of them were pointed up, towards the boss. 2+2, people. There was how to defeat the boss.
With this final boss, a level or few before him, a wall of missile-launchers slid from the ceiling. Knowing I could destroy the missile launchers themselves, I started attacking them. Interesting thing was, I missed, and hit some of the paneling making up this "wall", which then broke, and allowed me to pass through it. And guess what the final boss was riding around in? Boom, solution time. I pounded on the plating on his "ship", and started attacking him, which led to another mini-game, cut scene,  and a chase sequence, which was great fun.
Final say: It's a great demo. It's much shorter than BroForce, but I can say this with a great amount of certainty: It was better-designed, and was more fun than BroForce. but that raises a question, why was this 'demo' better than a full game that's been worked on for almost a year, and that cost money? Maybe Free Lives and Devolver Digital had some help from Lion's Gate, or they just really wanted to impress, but I'd say that if BroForce's length and character roster was added to The Expendabros, I'd rather buy it than BroForce.

DISCLAIMER: I've marked this review as "Not Recommended", but a more accurate descriptor would be "Recommended with Heavy Reservations". Read on to find out why.
---
"Half Life: Blue Shift", a Gearbox Software expansion to Valve's debut title "Half Life", is the first thing I've seen in quite some time to leave me completely unsure how to feel about it.
On the one hand, it's not a bad game per sé. It's got generally the same gameplay one comes to love playing "Half Life", it's got the same gimmick of remaining in full control of the player character, this time around a security guard named Barney Calhoun rather than Dr. Freeman, throughout the entire game with no cutscenes, and it provides a unique perspective on the Black Mesa Incident we haven't seen before in "Half Life" nor in Gearbox Software's previous expansion pack "Opposing Force".
These all sound like good things, but there's a wide variety of bad things about the game as well. Firstly, it's too short. Because I'm a terrible gamer it took me about 4 hours to complete, but it only takes most people about 3 hours. None of the new weapons introduced in "Opposing Force" return, many of the weapons from the original "Half Life" don't return, including the iconic Crossbow. Throughout most of the game, the only enemies players can expect to run into are headcrabs, vortigaunts, barnacles, houndeyes, and HECU soldiers. While other enemies such as bullsquids and alien grunts will occasionally appear, at no point in his adventure will Barney Calhoun encounter zombies of any kind, Black Ops personnel, or any of the new enemies introduced in "Opposing Force". Alien controllers will appear only once, during Calhoun's brief stay on the borderworld of Xen. In a truly shocking display of pure laziness, there isn't even a final boss. Bear in mind here I'm not saying the game failed to introduce an original final boss and simply recycled one of the old ones, which would still be bad but forgivable, I'm saying there literally is no final boss; the entire grand finale is literally just pressing some buttons. In lieu of any kind of variety in enemy encounters (or even enemies themselves), players can expect at least one headcrab to be hiding behind EVERY corner and inside EVERY wooden box. I mean that, by the way; no matter how strapped for ammo you are, break wooden boxes at your own risk.
Enemies aside, the story is weak and uninteresting. Without spoiling anything (although there's hardly anything to spoil), the basic plot is that Calhoun must help the Black Mesa scientists execute a hare-brained plan to teleport outside the doomed research facility. This heavily simplistic story is relayed to the player exclusively through lengthy bouts of expository dialogue from random NPCs whom one couldn't be blamed for wanting to kill rather than listen to. Unfortunately, one of these NPCs cannot be killed as he is an essential character to the story who, at one point, must be escorted by the player to his destination, making "Blue Shift" the first "Half Life" game to feature an escort mission. Expository dialogue, even in excess, can be forgivable if the story is interesting, but here, it just isn't. Again, it's simple and boring.
All of that being said, though, is it really that bad? Sure, the story and the enemies are both overly simplified, but is this really that much of a problem in such a short game? Herein lies my dilemma in determining what I think of this game. Most of my problems with it come from how simple it is, but is simplicity itself necessarily a bad thing? I, for one, am inclined to say no, it's not.
Just to have some semblance of a conclusion, I'll say that if you've recently finished playing "Half Life" and now you just want another fun romp through the Black Mesa facility as a new character with a new perspective on the Incident, then this game won't disappoint you. However, if you'd prefer a full game and unique experience like "Half Life" or "Opposing Force", stay away, as this won't sate you.

Half-Life is a series that has become massively well known amongst gamers, and it is no wonder why when the games are just so damn fun, Blue Shift is no exception to this.
Pros
Blue Shift allows you to take the role of a security guard at the Black Mesa facility (Barney Calhoun)
Blue Shift has several easter eggs based on the other two expansions Opposing Force and Decay (Although Decay wasn't released at this point it shows one of the main characters named Gina Cross)
In true Half-Life fashion enemies are placed in such a way as to catch you off guard if you run in guns blazing through every door.
Probably some more but I can't think properly right now, far to hot where I am.
Cons
The game is very short with someone as rubbish at first person shooters as me managing to beat it in about 3 hours (I left the game running when I went for lunch resulting in it displaying more hours than I actually played), and someone who is experienced probably managing in much less time, you can't really complain though as it is very cheap.
Some aspects of the game are very vent heavy, or in Xens case, small tunnel heavy.
It feels like they were far to heavy handed with Headcrabs in the vents with one vent sticking out to me as every corner seemed to have a headcrab.
Conclusion
Honestly, though this game has its flaws, it is extremely fun to play and definitely worth checking out if you haven't already, just don't expect this to have the same play time as Half-Life 1, it is just an expansion after all.

I was lucky enough to come across shelter on my second day... a dam, ominous interior but warm. I began breaking down the crates and shelves within the dam's lower quarters so that I could get a roaring fire and stave off hypothermia. It was then that I discovered the body. In the corner just beside my fire barrel was a frozen corpse, head down in rigid repose. I could not move the fire I had already started, so I would have to deal with the body for the time being. Finally, a place to heat up these cans of soup and get a good night's rest.
I woke up in the middle of the night to snarling. A wolf had wandered into my makeshift camp; or perhaps I had wandered into his. Armed with nothing but a torch, I brandished my tool at the beast in a desperate attempt to drive it off. It worked for a while, but the creature returned. My body screamed at me to sleep, to get the desperate rest I needed to go on, but I knew I could not tear my eyes away from the shadows for a second, lest the wolf take me. Glowing green eyes pierced the shadowy veil around my fire, which I struggled to maintain. My torch was burning out, and still the pair of eyes stared - waiting, watching, growling.
There was little I could do against the animal, and my only tool for driving it back was losing fuel quickly. I instinctively backed into a corner and realized I had bumped into something - the body. The frozen man which had horrified me earlier would soon become my eternal friend, now that the wolf had me. But wait, what's this? You can search corpses in this game? A feature I had not expected could now save me! But only if the man had something on him like a rifle or...
A knife!
The wolf lunged and I fell back, stabbing wildly with my new weapon and screaming at the screen in a moment of defiance. It was him or me, and thanks to my frozen friend I had leveled the playing field. The creature shrieked in pain and fell off me, whimpering and darting back into the shadows. No longer would its eyes haunt the night. After about an hour of hovering over the fire and taking whatever medicine I had gathered prior to the encounter, I heard the beast let out a final cry of pain from the next room. My valiant defense had killed the creature. I won.
Three days later I died to a bear. This game has quickly become one of my favorites because of moments like the one listed above. Could not reccomend it more.

I am fairly new to the survival game genre, but that doesn't mean i can't recognize a great game. The Long Dark, is freaking brilliant. It is one of those games that tries to be as realistic as possible. You need to watch your hunger, hydration, body temperature, and fatigue. The hardest of the 5 is temperature because the game drops you in the middle of a post appocolyptic arctic landscape with sub zero temperatures. You start with nothing but the clothes on your back and and an old sleeping bag. As soon as you start, it is a race to find shelter, food, water, warmer clothes, medical supplies, fire making supplies, etc. With a variety of maps, some will make this easier than others. The starting map, Mystery Lake, has plenty of man made shelters and cabins scattered throughout. Even so, you always need to be planning where you will spend your next night. If you stay in one shelter too long, you will run out of supplies or not have enough for your journy to the next shelter. Your best bet is taking off at first light so you have the whole day to find supplies and shelter. The game really throw a wrench in your plan though. Often, a storm will develope and eat away your daylight. Storms force you to seek shelter from the wind. You better hope that when a storm comes, you have the necessary supplies to stay in your shelter for however long it last. That means you should always have plenty of food, water, and fire supplies on hand. Storms aren't the only thing that can trap you though. Wolves are also scattered throughout the wilderness. You may find your self trapped in a broken down car waiting for the wolves to leave. Sometimes a flare can scare them off, but don't rely to heavy on that. Basically, this is an awesome game, and a must buy for any survival game enthusiast.

STORY:
Cuphead was a cheap imitation of Mickey Mouse created in the early 20th century in order to bank on the success of Disney, he however has never reached the mainstream audience and was relegated to the radio. Needless to say no one today had ever heard of Cuphead before this reboot. The player is Elder Kettle, an anthropomorphic kettle living peacefully with his son Mugman. At the start of the story, a mysterious masked casino army kidnaps Mugman and sends Kettle off to rescue his lost son. Haunted by the death of his other son, Cuphead, and his abusive father, Kettle takes pink pills to deal with his crippling depression. These pills, which make the user feel nothing, are the only escape the denizens of Inkwell Island have from the reality of wasteland life. As Kettle ventures through the wasteland, he finds many different party members that aid him on his quest to find his son, from a scarred pig war veteran turned salesman to an entire barbership trio missing a 4th member. These party members all have in depth backstories that I do not want to spoil here.  Gaining the trust of the party members and learning their stories is likely the most interesting part of the game. Kettle finds the aftermath of the dice armyl; razed towns and corpses litter the wasteland. Their leader, Dice, constantly taunts kettle, showing up and forcing him to make long lasting decisions that will impact the rest of the game. However, as Kettle explores more of the wasteland, he finds that not all is as it seems.
Gameplay:
This game is truly the Dark Souls of Mickey Mouse. Many of the elements are lifted straight from the Souls series. For one, most of the challenges in the game come from the boss fights, of which there many and all of them unique. Trial and error will be necessary as the player learns the boss patterns and how to roll to avoid them. Another Souls aspect is that the player may be invaded by another player, who will then attempt to help or hinder the player whose game they joined. Finally, parrying from Dark Souls is prevalent in this game, however the player may only parry pink objects. This game also borrows heavily from Super Mario and the Smash Bros series. Platforming segments are prevalent and very mario-like; players will have to bounce on enemies, collect coins, and reach a flag at the end. Additionally, the player can get powerups that will allow them to shoot fireballs that allow them to kill enemies. From the Smash Bros series is lifted the "Final Smash" attack that Kettle can perform once he takes enough pink pills. This devastating attack will destroy all in the player's way and feels very satisfying to use. Additionally, RPG elements permeate the game, from the party and leveling system, to the act of finding new weapons and armor and equipping them to party members. I am happy to say that although these gameplay elements are wildly different, they all blend seamlessly into one expertly crafted gameplay experience.
Style:
The game has an old cartoon look that may turn some players away from this game. Because Cuphead is a reboot of the failed early 20th century cartoon, the developers decided to use the same lazy tactics of that day to create the visuals for this game. As such, the game has a cartoonish, unrealistic look that pales in comparison to other modern games of this era, such as Battlefield 1. While the developers wished to create a cheap artstyle in order to save budget, the end result is a cheap looking, seemingly damaged "artstyle" which is hard on the eyes. I would have preferred a modernized look more akin to, say, modern day Rick and Morty. However, the gameplay more than makes up for this blunder.
Conclusion:
This game has an incredible story and crazy good gameplay, however the art takes a hit.
I give this game a 6/10, everything is perfect but the art.

This is more a walking simulator than an actual game. Not that I'm deriding it - Walking simulators are an interesting offshoot of games that explore the rules of interactive experiences. And this is very much in that vein, as a narrator leads the player through several interactive experiences, explaining how they reflect on the creator. But there is more to it than that, and things take an interesting turn. There's a lot to decompress here, but it is a thoughtful experience, not an action one. Some of the environments  and the experiences are interesting, and some funny, and some thoughtful.  It's not as enjoyable an experience as the Stanley Parable was, but it makes for a melancholy meditation on what games are for.
