When I bought this game I thought I was in for a fun and relaxing time. Little did I know I had signed up for hell. Albeit the first few levels are pretty straight forward and easy, the steep difficulty curve that swiftly follows out of nowhere is very hard to adapt to. That however is what keeps the game interesting to me. Being a completionist makes it hard for me to leave levels without completing all three of the objectives set out for me. This in turn is both infuriating and wonderful as it makes the replay value for each level much higher for me. I'll replay until I get all 3 stamps per level.
I can see why the game may not appeal to some. It isn't really a simulator. There really isn't all that management when it comes to funding of new trains and things like upgrades. The only thing you need to pay close attention to is changing the arrows on the tracks so that trains go to their correct stations and of course making sure you don't go bankrupt while you are crazily building tracks. There really isn't much micromanaging required to play this game. Avid simulation fans will be mad, avid casual gamers who like only a little bit of management so that the game doesn't tie them down for too many hours at a time will rejoice.
I personally, although annoyed by some levels because they are so damn hard to even complete for a first time, love this game. It's a fun way to kill a bit of time, it isn't too demanding unlike other simulations where you need to focus on a lot of different little things and it is really easy to pick up thanks to the simple mechanics.
Overall, for $10 it is worthwhile adding this game to your collection. Some may beg to differ as the change in difficulty pretty early into the game can make it seem uninteresting and even make it unplayable for some; but personally for me I think it is worth it. I get lots of replay out of it. It's a simple concept with easy controls and it is at times mentally challenging, causing myself to really think out my approach to each level. I personally enjoy a little bit of a challenge when playing games like this so if you feel much the same, I recommend it 100%

Banished is made by a single person. That alone is a huge accomplishment considering the depth and quality of this game. With all colony sims, the mechanics and choices what make or break this genre, and I'm happy to say, that Banished excells in all the important aspects. The maps are random generated based on user-defined settings, which actually decides a huge chunk of the difficulty too (size of useful real-estate, arable land, access to resources, etc).
The backstory is mere background noise, but it's not really all that important anyway. A bunch of people got "banished" from a nation for one reason or other, and now have to start a new life somewhere in the wilderness. You start out with a handful of colonists, a storehouse and some basic raw materials. It's up to you to make the best of it, and survive, thrive.
The first winter is usually the biggest challenge. Can you produce enough food, shelter and firewood to last through the cold, desolate months? Or will you watch with helpless desperation, as your colonists starve and succumb to the frigid embrace of winter? As spring comes, you gather the survivors and get ready for the next winter...then the next one...and the next one, etc.
After your first year, it's basically the same things over and over, going through the motions of expanding, ramping up production, food, wood, tools, clothing, houses, amenities, and so on. Make sure to keep your population in check, because with rapid growth it's easy to underestimate the amount of stuff you need to stockpile, and running out of food, firewood, clothes, etc, in the dead of winter can decimate your colonists. Which in turn drastically decreases your workforce, wich means less people to produce stuff, which leaves you with less stuff to stockpile....and you can end up in a downward spiral of failure.
The other important aspect of Banished is juggling your workforce. Idle hands are the devil's tools, as the saying goes, and in Banished, the game punishes your dearly for not managing your colonists right. There is no real specialization for colonists, so you can freely reassign them to different tasks as needed. For example, all the farmers working the fields from spring to fall, would sit idly by in the winter months unless otherwise specified, so after a particularly bad harvest, sending them fishing, hunting or wood chopping can mean the difference between life or death sometimes.
The same goes for managing real-estate. The maps are usually fairly stingy with buildable land, so you must take a hard look at your stocks before you decide how to expand. Do you need more food? Fields, orchards and farms take up a huge amount of space, and clearcutting that forest can potentially leave you without precious firewood, herbs and raw materials that you may need later. And while having a large, untouched forest can yield lumber, leather and medicine, if you don't play your cards right, all you'll be able to do is starve in the shade. One wrong decision can lead your entire colony to ruin, so learning these subtle changes and knowing how to constantly balance your economy is one of the key aspects of Banished.
One negative point I mentioned, is that Banished has no endgame. Most city building sims have a tree of technologies and buildings you can unlock by meeting certain milestones with your colony, so there is always something to look forward to, goals to work towards. In Banished, it's a free-for-all. You can build every single building in the game from the start, given you have the resources for it. Now, this provides a huge amount of freedom in terms of what you can achieve, but you also run the danger of getting confused or being too ambitious too early. Banished is very tricky this way, since there is actually a clear progression of what you should and shouldn't build at a given stage of your colony's growth, only the game won't outright tell you about it. You can only figure it out by trial and error, which can lead to some frustration with a number of players. But once you do, the challenge basically disappears from the game entirely. Also exactly because of this, there is no real endgame, no big picture, no final goal to work towards, other than expanding to the entire map, with basically the same exact buildings your had in the beginning.
Speaking of which, the selection of buildings isn't all that great either. You have basically one building for every type of job needed, and that's it. One woodcutter, one smithy, one storehouse, merely two types of housing, etc. No scaling, no bigger or smaller versions to suit your surroundings or production plans, no real possibilites to fine tune or handle different sections of the map differently, other than the ability to increase or decrease the number of workers in some of them. This not only makes your town utterly boring to look at, but also severely restricts your options of what you can accomplish with planning your settlement other than this ham-fisted "one-size-fits-all" approach.
In conclusion, Banished is a really solid, well made colony sim, or more like a base of one. It is already a pretty fun and challenging game, but it could use TONS more additions to really open up the possibilties. Sadly, the developer declared the game finished and ceased all development on Banished a long time ago, so sadly we can't expect any more official additions. However there is a pretty good selection of mods in the workshop, so there is still a glimmer of hope. If you like  a solid colony building sim without all the fuss, definitely give Banished a try!

Coming into this game I was hoping for a more simulation style Ace Combat, unfortunately that is not the case. First thing I did, as I do in all games, was check the key layout and controls for flying with a keyboard. It was doable in writing, unfortunately, it's poorly executed in-game. The throttle up key (arrow key up) does exactly that it throttles up, however it also turns the camera  in-cockpit 90 degrees left. Slowing down (arrow key down) does the same thing, it throttles down with the expense of turning your camera 90 degrees right.
Also, before purchasing JASF, I read in multiple places that the game can be used with a joystick/gamepad/Xbox 360 controller. Nope. I restarted the game (with Xbox 360 controller connected) and was prompted with the "Enter" key as well as the arrow keys for navigating the menu. Fair enough, the menu is keyboard exclusive, I can understand that. As I went in-game I soon noticed that there were new icons. For instance, instead of an arrow key, it was the "A" button. I pick up my Xbox 360 controller and press "A" for a solid 10 seconds... Nothing. The voiceover is still going, droning about my important task at hand. I keep pressing "A", then "B" then every other button on my controller. Nothing. For a game that is ALSO on Xbox 360, there was a transition error or flawed coding to not have a smooth transition to PC.
Graphics: Not much concern. Although, I did experience some screen tears and occasional stuttering throughout my loop-de-loop camera turning spiral into the end of the runway. Nothing gamebreaking however. Planes look good, environment is minimal but effective. Cockpit perspective looks alright. Not much criticism here.

So, it's safe to say that this is no user error, this is a game with potential, but failed to properly execute the most basic of video game tasks, the controls.

Newcomers! Please, hear me out before writing this game off!!!
Through deciding to make this game a free-to-play title, which I'm all for, they've unfortunately made some negative changes that really only the veteran players would notice, so this *edited* review is more for old players hoping to maybe hop back into the game, not directed to new players who won't really notice the changes. I miss the OLD Evolve, as a veteran player since day one, having spent well over $100 on this game (unregretably), I genuinely love this game - or more accurately - the ORIGINAL version of this game.
PROS
FREE TO PLAY: Through making this game free to access for all, finally the game can start to see a new breath of life with a new and hopefully more active community of players. I'm all for the switch in the theory, and welcome new players, especially considering without them, the game would be forever dead.
EVERYTHING IS UNLOCKABLE: No longer do you need to make excuses about expensive DLC, as everything in the game that was previously locked behind paywall is now 100% accessible through simply playing the game.
MORE FREE CONTENT UPDATES: Since the new updates, the devs are hoping to add even more characters, possibly maps, emblems, and more (and already have) so there will be no shortage of things to try and unlock at least for a little while.
PLENTY OF CHARACTERS: If you seriously have to still complain about lack of characters in this game, you're pathetic and worthless. There are 6 characters (and rising) per class (5 classes) and each character is totally different from the last and take a lot of time to master, and with the amount of different possible team builds, there is definitely no shortage of unique characters to play.
GAMEPLAY: The game still FEELS great. Responsive, easy to learn hard to master, just the way it was when I first fell in love with it day 1. The shooting is chunky and has satisfying weight, the monsters are hulking yet agile, it all just feels so well built.
CONS
GONE IS CO-OP PVE: They have completely taken out literally my favorite game-mode. Why would they have any reason to do this??? There were already so few game-modes to begin with, and they take out the one that's most fun to play!? WTF!!!!!!!
LEVEL RESET FOR ALL PLAYERS: If you're like me, or any vet player, you probably spent a lot of time and energy leveling your profile and specific characters, so to now be treated with a nice COMPLETE RESET OF EVERYTHING - it's a little aggravating. Almost 50 hours of work *poof* gone.
TOTALLY CHANGED/REMOVED SKILLS: Being a huge Support class player, I of course proceed to try out my favorite character, Bucket, only to find one of the Support class's most valuable skills - invisibility - completely removed. WHAT??? I can understand giving players options to swap skills, but to just permanantly remove and replace such an integral skill and force players to learn a play style they don't want to is messed up.
PERFORMANCE DUMP: Granted some of you may still think 60fps is totally fine - and it is! - but the fact that I used to be getting easily 80-90+ fps max settings running on a GTX 780, to now be getting maybe steady 60fps if I'm lucky is absurd.
So yeah, if you are brand new to this game and hoping to try it out, PLEASE DO! I made it a "not recommended" for OLD players, not new ones. I think it's still a great game, and for new players that wouldn't notice the changes otherwise, it seriously is one of the absolute best F2P games you could ever play - considering you don't have to pay a single dime for anything people like me had to pay $100+ for! \

I genuinely can't find anything wrong with this game.
PROS:
-Combat is incredibly smooth. Every bullet has a real sense of impact, the weapons have weight, the swapping feels just right.
-Playing as ANY character including the monster is totally a blast and each have their own rewards, both in game and personally
-Great sense of balance. I really don't think anything is OVER powered or UNDER powered, it's all dictated on how well you work as a team, or in the case of the monster, how well you can work under fair pressure alone. But it isn't HARD to work well as a team either. With strangers, or with friends, the communication options really help guide the whole team.
-Insanely well optimized. I'm running on a GTX 780, 16GB RAM and i7 so maybe this isn't difinitive, but on max settings I'm easily stable at 80+ FPS and my lowest dips are in the mid 60 FPS range.
-Graphically truly a next gen game. Self explanatory, it looks so good I STILL get jaw drop moments even having played alpha and beta.
-Replay value? YES. It's a big question with a lot of people thinking they'll get bored after a few matches because it's "repetitive" or "shallow" etc etc whatever whatever. This is not true. In one game mode, you play 5 matches, all voted, all different, different maps, different monsters. You need to realize with 15 possible (just out of the box) characters to mix and match a team, there are TONS of possibilities for loadouts/team builds. Not just that, but every time you win OR lose a match, the next match changes environmentally, so say my team wins a match, in the next game we unlock portals to bring us to the center of the map for fast travel, say we lose that match, the monster has now destroyed a toxic tank area and we're at risk of poison. Each match is different every time, think of it more like maybe say Payday 2, but I would argue better!
-ALL playable in single-player. ALL playable with 1, 2, 3, 4 friends in quick, found AND custom matches.
-Mic quality is basically flawless. Haven't had any bugs or issues with screeching like in the alpha (to be expected) and you can turn push to talk on or off.
-Progession system feels fair and not grindy at all. I feel rewarded when I actually put work into the match and when I'm lazy it shows. Again, it's fair to who puts in how much work. If you sit back and do nothing you don't deserve XP.
-Full controller support, and yes, I played on both K&M and controller and both setups works super well for me. Everything vanilla is laid out well for me to memorize and access quickly.
-DLC is NOT part of the base game and if that's what keeps you from buying a game you're a pathetic loser and you should get a job. Not everything in life is free, get over it.
-The community so far is not full of over zealous $h!t monkey 10 year olds like on consoles, but it did JUST come out so we'll see.
CONS:
-I genuinely am asking what questions you might have if you haven't picked it up yet as to what concerns you may have that I didn't touch on. Again, this is my personal experience with the game, it's not absolute, but neither is the opinion of some "profesional" reviewers on some liberal sheep site.
If you're trying to decide whether or not to pick this up - look at it for a second. Are you into co-op games? Would you play a game like Left 4 Dead, Payday, Borderlands with AND without others? Do you like amazing game engines? You're PROBABLY going to enjoy this game.
Do you like Call of Duty? Do you have poor social skills? Are you an angry 9 year old brat with no concept of the value of money? Do you complain about every little thing that doesn't actually matter, just so can feel more important, even though you're probably worthless? This PROBABLY isn't for you!

#1 PROTIP for hunters, don't just follow the tracks of the monster. The monster is faster than the hunters and you will never catch him like that. Split up into 2 teams of two. One team chases the monster (monster players usually skirts the edges of the map). The other team stays central to the map, and moves in to cut off the monster once the chasing team has found him in a favorable spot. The team that cuts off should have the trapper with the mobile arena ready to go. There are a lot of variations to this tactic, so experiment! However EVERYONE on the team needs to be a good tracker. Do not rely on the trapper player to do all the heavy lifting when it comes to finding the monster. And ABSOLUTELY DO NOT rely solely on daisy (maggies trapjaw pet) to find the monster. She will always be one step behind the monster. Daisy is simply a tool to figure out general direction of the monster. Its up to the players to actually find the monster using that info. Unfortunately the game kinda trains new players to simply follow daisy and simply follow the monster tracks. And its probably why some new players might find the game "boring" at first since all they are doing is mindlessly chasing a monster they can never catch.
Also realise that most negative reviews are from people not owning the game and simply played the alpha for a few hours. Also note they are mostly Salty about the DLC. Do your own reseach on DLC. Its not that bad or different than most DLC. There is no Day 1 DLC (other than cosmetic skins, the monster-pack monster is still being made). All future maps and game modes are FREE. Wraith is not locked behind a paywall (you can unlock her through normal gameplay).  I would say the only thing that bothers me about the DLC is the price. A little too high imo. Also 2k biggest mistakes was pushing the DLC too hard and too early in a VERY anti-DLC enviroment.

The greater military focus means huge outlays for rebels that cannot seemingly be appeased or defeated, constant battles with seemingly random outcomes and incredibly important upgrades hidden in rarely-accessed menus. The campaign's focus on four islands means a nice sense of investment, but as every mission has to be playable on one of two choices, say hello to incredibly bland islands with pretty much every resource - and sod if you can guess which island would be best to play the subsequent mission in each era on, because you can't play more than one mission in each era per island.

This is an Alpha & Beta review. That means it is subject to change at the time of the official product release.
Evolve was iconic at E3. It delivered cutting-edge visuals with immersive gameplay. It also introduced a style of gameplay that has not been ventured into much by other developers.
At E3, Evolve was the next big thing. It was the successor to Valve's immensly popular Left4Dead franchise. But did it deliver its intended effect?
No.
The visuals are stunning, the physics are wicked, the concept is good and the mouse optimization (along with changing the color scheme on the mouse) when you play as different classes is the neatest thing I could ever imagine a game would have (though I was slightly confused initially, as I did not know the game could do that). Then, what went wrong?
The core gameplay. The core gameplay lacked most of the elements which make a game worth playing. Throwing in millions of dollars and thousands of hours of development to introduce nifty elements to the game failed to mask its complete failure at entertaining the player.
In my five hours in-game, I chased a raving leaping lunatic monkey relentlessly, occassionally cornering it and killing it. However, the amount of time spent in chasing the said monkey was so high, that it was not worth the kill. The hunters were disabled by the fact that the monster moved significantly faster than them and could easily elude them even at close ranges. Occasionally, we spent nearly three-quarters of an hour, searching for a monster that switched positions from corner to corner of the map, making it impossible for hunters to intercept or even reach remotely near.
Did you want to wait instead and set a trap for the monster near the power relay and kill him once he arrived there as a stage 3 beast? Too bad he had full armor at that stage, his hits dealt 3x damage and the power relay had very little health.
Trapping the monster in a portable dome didn't help either, because he'd lunge around the dome till it ran out and escape, leaving you chasing him for another half-hour. Additionally, to the monster's advantage, there was no time limit on how long each round would take, so the monster could eat and elude at his leisure and take his sweet time destroying the power relay.
Lastly, the FOV of the game felt slightly absurd and personally for me, induced mild motion sickness, so that's a disclaimer for anyone wishing to try the game.
By the end, the game made me feel as bitter as this review is.

A visually gorgeous little game with a surprising and original premise, some decent puzzles and above all else, lovely design and soundtrack. It was offered at a tiny fraction of its already low price via a gift coupon from Steam, so I gave it a go.
The developers say it was inspired by games like Machinarium and The Tiny Bang Story, but here the idea is taken to a totally different level. The "protagonist" is a little larva which gradually transforms (hence "Morpho"-polis, also a reference to the iconic film Metropolis by Fritz Lang) into a perfectly grown insect, all the while helping other creatures and plants in its environment find food or complete their own development. The pretty much repetitive process in each part of the story (five in total) is interspersed with full-screen puzzles of varied styles, not too hard to solve once you have got the hang of it, but where what you are supposed to do isn't always obvious or straightforward.
That, and some occasional difficulty in moving the main "character" around and interacting with the surrounding objects could be considered as a very small drawback to an otherwise exceptionally beautiful, relaxing and enjoyable game.
The game is shorter than the rest of the Half Life series but it is still a great game that lives up to the original Half Life.

You may see a lot of reviews slamming this game for being "dumbed down" or overly simplified compared to previous titles, and to be honest they may not be entirely incorrect. However, what these people don't seem to grasp is that sometimes less is more. I will admit that Tropico 5 is certainly not a perfect game, nor is it even the best game in the series, but it still holds it own and should be considered by anybody who is a fan of the series or the genre.
I will start with the good, which there is plenty of. Tropico 5 has the most robust campaign of any Tropico game to date, with persistent islands that carry over from mission to mission and a new dynasty system that allows you to pass your legacy on to your offspring if you choose to. While the dynasty aspect could have been fleshed out a little more, it is still fun and finally gives you something to actually do with your off-shore account money (which is used to upgrade dynasty memebers). As usual the story to the campaign is wacky and goofy, and completely unbelievable, but that is all just part of the charm to Tropico. Tropico 5 also introduces a new era system where instead of always starting during the Cold War, you can now start as early as colonial times and work your way up through 4 eras to modern times. While not game-changing per say, this does add a nice touch to the game and a fresh way to play it. The voice acting throughout is solid and charming, the music is catchy as always, and the visual are superb. The color pallete is bright and cheerful, and the level of detail on some of the buildings is rather impressive when you zoom in. It should also be noted that as with most Kalypso games technically the game is great, it runs wonderfully and I have had zero crashes.
As I mentioned though, the game is not perfect I'm afraid. There are a couple of aspects of the game that have been simplified compared to old titles. For example, when setting the salary for a building instead of a slider that allowed you to set whatever dollar amount you wanted, there are just 5 pre-set payrates to choose from. Furthermore, while you can still set the pay from every building of that kind, you can't set it for all workers of that education. A slight annoyance, but still something that may detract from some and it also points to the larger issue with this game I think many have. This game is not City:Skylines, it is not Banished, nor is it even SimCity in terms of complexity. Tropico 5 is a largely streamlined experience that is intended to let you focus on the big picture without getting too caught up in micro-managing. Some people like this, some don't, which I get, but it should be noted Tropico games have always been like this so it really shouldn't be a shock that Tropico 5 continues the pattern. Another annoyance is the lack of content in this game. While the campaign is robust and plenty of maps are included for sandbox mode, it is frustrating to see buildings and concepts introduced in previous games either omitted or held out so that they can be introduced through over-priced DLC. That said, the base game as is still provides plenty to do and can be enjoyed without spending a penny on DLC. It should be noted though that the exact same argument could be made about the last game, as without the Modern Times expansion Tropico 4 was a little lacking in endgame content, so again this really is nothing new for the series.
All-in-all Tropico 5 is a really solid game. Not great, but also really not bad, and very much worth the only $40 it costs. I will admit that you may want to start with Tropico 4 (skip 3, 4 is just an upgraded version of it), and if you want a really good game that is completely different from the rest of the series play 2, but if you already have played these and are hungry for more or you just want to play the newest game, you will not regret this purchase. Also please note while my Steam account doesn't reflect it I have played every game in the series extensively, in particular 4 on the XBox 360, and while 2 actually remains my favorite 5 is right up there as well.

Connect the stations - Send the Train - Toot toot - Connect another station - Send the next train - Toot - no wait, stop, sh*t, reverse, reverse... BOOM - Sh*t - Connect - Send train - send next train - reverse - forward - train - points - train - train - points - connect - train - train - train - 3 green ticks - hold it together - YESSSSSSSSSS!
At the time of writing this review I am 17 hours in and have almost completed the 4th 'Valley' with only the German DLC remaining. Although clearly not as quick at completing this as other gamers, it has been an intense, short, er, ride. So, is the game worth it? Well, yes, frankly. Utterly addictive, frustrating and satisfying depending on what is happening. Ultimately, the satisfaction of getting it right is what keeps me playing - even if I have to have a short break to find serenity before carrying on.
The controls and gameplay are very simple. It can be played with just the mouse. Although, I do like to keep one finger on the space bar to pause. Laying the track is simple enough and works well enough, although I would like an undo function while paused to correct a mis-layed bit of rail.
Graphics are nice, if basic and should give no problems to lower end systems. The gameplay is smooth and faultless and the sound effects are spot on.
So, IMHO, it is well worth the £6.99 (price correct at time of review) and I cant wait for some more DLC and Train Valley 2. I'd love to see where they take it next.
Cheers.

I have used GMS for a long time and finally upgraded to GMS2.  Overall it has been a very positive experience.  There have been many great new features in the workflow and specific aspects, while also staying similar enough that someone can jump right back in.  It should also be easy enough for beginners to use as well!
Pros:
-Workflow can be very useful and efficient once learned
-Nice default colors for gml code, (variables being purple, objects being red, etc.)
-Easy to "drag" objects, sprites, and everything else to connect things to eachother (seriously... it's just fun to do)
-Tilesets are a great step forward
-Layers take some time getting used to but can be helpful
-Converting from GameMaker Studios (1) is easy (And my game runs WAY better on GMS2 when i converted it)
-Quick to access helpful tabs such as the Manual
-Most code is the same as GMS allowing for ease of use
-More sprite and sound functionality
-DnD and GML are completely separate (This was very annoying in GMS)
-Blog posts which show off new features or give walkthroughs on how to do cool things like shadows
-Great documentation
-Tons of tutorials (Most tutorials for GMS will be completely applicable for GMS2)
-The Cleanup event
-Gesture events (I haven't used them much, but from what I know they seem to be very useful)
-Yoyogames is working hard to make sure that GMS2 is the best it can be, which means that most of the Cons I have here might even be fixed in due time!
Cons:
-Dark coloring theme can be hard to see
-Small bugs and colors in certain menus don't always work right
-Difficult to use on a very small screen with the way the workspace works (or if the middle mouse button does not work...)
-The old depth system was very useful but is now more difficult to use

Cute little game, and i surprised myself with how much i enjoyed the first few levels.
The basic gimmick is that you are an insect and your job is to interact with things to ... i'm not sure. Grow up i guess? Transform? Beat all five levels in total? Whatever the purpose, you spend half your time playing a sort of hidden objects game where you're hunting through the cluttered and messy backdrops for materials to help or hurt other bugs and open areas of the map. If you ever get stuck and can't find the objects you need, you can click the question mark on the topright to get a freebie. This is really good at getting your brain unstuck when you're frusterated cause you can't find all the materials you need to go forward. The insect aeshtetic gives this game a really nice vibe of just being a little guy roaming the woods. The second part of the game is the puzzles, and there are a lot of them. Mostly they pop up when you finish finding an amount of resources. They're always visually tied into the game but but the puzzles are very abstract in what they are and how they will affect the world. I really enjoyed some of the puzzles i came across, but the way to solve them is completely unexplained. A bit more direction in these would be nice, i constantly found myself going to the walkthrough to try and figure out what i should even try to do to solve the puzzle.
The main problem i had with the game was the walking speed. It's painfully slow, and in the later levels the stages get rather large making it take ages to walk from place to place. Presumably you can spend this time looking in the background for goodies but it just feels unnecessary. As a secondary problem, i found the later levels quite slow and dull, maybe the hidden object game had grinded me down because i could not find the effort to finish the game. Also menus suck.
Nice aesthertic combined with good ideas that don't last very long, but it's enjoyable when you first encounter it. If you want %100, there is a good guide that shows all the solutions as well.

Passing the game a few times will make you at times memorize where the scary enemy AI's will go and which lockers and or beds they'll check. If you get that feeling, try a bigger difficulty. Enemies become much smarter then.

LIMBO is a fantastic if slightly depressing game that's worth downloading.  I've played through on my phone once (an outside Steam purchase *gasp*), and when I found out that it was free on Steam, I had to get it.

The color scheme is a mix of black, white, and greys, and all that can be seen of the character is his black body with white eyes outlined against the 2D background.  The subtle sound effects and music are great additions to the lonely feel of the world.
The controls are straighforward, but I didn't always understand that the character was close to something he could grab.  If he can drag or push something, his arms will come forward, but often that meant putting him closer to harm than I realized at first which created some annoying deaths.
The puzzles are challenging enough to make the game fun, and new elements and variations are introduced often enough that I wasn't bored or feeling like the game got repetitive.

Evolve, the game that got way more BS than it deserves.
Yes there is DLC, but people are heavily misinformed about it.
There is no day 1 DLC. Look at the store right now (since it's day 1) the only "DLC" you can get are skins, no content at all. If day 1 skins are really such an issue for you, then this indeed is not the game for you.
Second, milking. People keep talking about milking because the game was built to support DLC. Does this mean we'll be milked? No, it means the game properly allows for extra content to be added. We'll also be getting free content like maps and gamemodes. But I bet you those journalists forgot to mention that in their DLC rants.
I agree that the DLC is too expensive though; it costs more than twice as much for the same amount of content (buying 3 monsters and 12 hunters would cost you $120, while the game costs $60 and gives way more than that). That is quite ridiculous. For those claiming the DLC isn't overpriced becuase the game features heavily discounted content: that would make the game overpriced at $120, not many people would pay that for the base game.
All DLC aside, this is a great game! After playing countless matches in the alpha and beta, I still get an adrenaline rush every time I get a close match (which are common by the way, the balance in this game is exceptional). Don't be fooled by the DLC, you can still play the game fine without. You can even fight people who did buy the DLC (so even if you don't buy that monster, you can still fight it!). Heck, if a hunter plays a character you don't have and leaves, you can take over that character even though you don't own it.
So stop being misinformed, kick your local game journalist for not informing you properly about this games DLC scheme and go buy it!

I am a bit mixed on this game to be honest. I do consider this to be a good game in the sense that it succeeds at what it sets out to accomplish. However I do not feel as though I can recommend this game to most people. The reason for this is that the game is rather frustrating in terms of gameplay and tries too hard to assault the players sense with loud noises and jumpscares, that the gameplay just becomes tedious.
The game ends up building paranoia in the fact that it is unpleasant to have to deal with a loud ear piecing scream coming from anamatronics that are lifted straight out of the uncanny valley. Yes I will give the game that it has a decent sense of atmosphere, but if it were not for these absurdly loud jump scares, it would not be nearly as scary. Technically, regardless of whether you believe jump scares are actually scary, they do work here, but that is the problem; they work to well.
This game is not enjoyable to play because of this, and it feels more like a test of endurance. The game is still admittedly well made considering its resources, and it has a lot of interesting background lore to it. However I can only really recommend this to hardcore fans of these types of games that really enjoy the adrenaline rush. However, for those that expect games to be entertaining and that want the sense of atmosphere, you'd be better off just watching a lets play.

Well... I did enjoy it... a lot, actually.  Blue Shift is an expansion taking place from the beginning of HL1 to the chapter Apprehension, where
.  But wait, that was still somewhat early in the game, right?  ...Yeah.  We'll get to that.
First, I just want to address the things it really got right.  Blue Shift feels like it should-- a complete expansion to the original.  As a security guard, you start off the game first locked out of the office as Gordon slides by looking at you slightly amused, then stopping at the firing range, and watching the Anomalous Materials experiment get prepared on CCTV's.  There's an extreme attention to detail spanning most of the game, and it feels like Gearbox always kept in mind what was happening on Gordon's side.
It also does an excellent job of tying together storylines.  While interactions are rare between the stories of Gordon (HL1), Barney (BS), and Adrian (OF), there are constant references and signs where someone who played the other games will recognize key events.  It's definitely interesting to see HL1's plot rewritten from a simple linear story to a whole universal event, now being explored by three radically different roles.
On the side, the actual game is... solid.  The levels are decent, the story is good, and overall it feels like more HL1 minus the benefits of the HEV suit, instead opting for standard body armor.  There just isn't that much different from HL1 once you get past the blue HUD and story.  Thankfully, the levels are a completely new deal and while you'll cross paths with key events, the game still stands on its own without constantly relying on you to connect it to the base game.  It's not the kind of game where not knowing the original storyline leaves you completely clueless-- Barney discovers the HECU's mission on his own, he goes through his own escape and survival, and he meets with other scientists in his escape.
Still, the biggest flaw I can point out is its time.  Three hours, total.  I'd like to say I got lost or stuck twice.  This is by no means a long game.  Yet, by the end it does start to feel like it overstays its welcome anyway.
While the pacing in the beginning is exactly as it should be, I feel like the last stage of the game simply dragged on for far longer than it should have.  Still, while not difficult in any sense of the word, the finale is definitely alright for a small expansion-- rather than a boss battle, you more or less follow your fetch quest with an interactive cutscene, which even foreshadows the "Red Letter Day" in HL2 to an extent.
Perhaps the biggest thing I can say against Blue Shift, though, is that it has no multiplayer.  This was criminal.  Absolutely unacceptable.  For shame!
So yes, I
recommend it, but rather half-heartedly.  You'll have fun with it, but HL1 and Opposing Force have much more to offer.  They're both more interesting and better executed than Gearbox's second expansion ended up being.  Not to mention, it offers much less in content than HL1, which went on for around 9-15 hours plus multiplayer deathmatch, and Opposing Force, which while also somewhat short featured an overhauled multiplayer with CTF and more weapons.  Play those first, and when you see a good sale or don't have other games you can get for this price, go for it.
==UPDATE==
As commanderox pointed out, you may experience a gamebreaking bug in the opening chapter that prevents you from equipping your body armor and helmet (which triggers an event).  I didn't run into this personally, but a restart should be enough to fix it.

This game is one of the most well executed ideas I have ever played. Even in its early stages, it sets out to provide an isometric, more realistic sort of zombie survival game, and it does so incredibly well. It has a fantastic atmosphere, amazing soundtrack, and now with the addition of multiplayer, it really can't be beat in terms of gameplay, value, or really anything. Its learning curve may seem a little steep at first, but only because "normal" zombie film tactics will never work. Firing a gun is a last resort which draws zombies to the area, and being able to take out more than 2 or 3 zombies at once with a melee weapon alone, is nigh impossible. You are tasked with starting a new settlement in the middle of nowhere. All you have are a few prebuilt shelters, some resources, and a group of families. You're faced with the annual cycle of weather, growing buildings and resources to increase your city size, and ensuring everyone has the clothing and food necessary to survive. Simple, right?
This game gets more addicting as you start to understand the tradeoffs between rotating workers to different roles and optimizing things like harvest time, distance from crops to trading centers, and other things that I will let you find out for yourself. Winters can be lonely when it's below freezing, all your crops are harvested or dead, and people are dying from exposure while mining stone. Nothing hurts more than everyone dying off in your fifth winter.
My one minor complaint is that I have to reposition windows such as the worker assignments and resource quantities every time I load the game. There is probably a mod that does that for me, but I don't do modding. And at the end of the day, that's a minor gripe--especially when your gaming hours are distributed across a few but very long sessions. Overall, this game is a 9.5 out of 10. (And when on sale, it's cheaper than a movie!) Also I'd recommend having videos playing on the other screen or music in the background to keep things interesting.

Hey guys, I just made the jump from GM 1.4 Pro to GM2 Desktop.
For anyone interested, GML is a easy to learn language, and there are a lot of tutorials online for beginners.
It also has a great built in coding manual which shows examples of how the code will work and ways to customize it.
It will autofill as you type, so you don't have to look up spelling and if you click the middle mouse button on your code, it'll open the manual and show examples and definitions.
Just now, theres not too much going on in the way of tutorials, but for the most part, coding in 1.4 and 2 aren't too different.
2 is a very clean slate right now though.
I'm still learning the layering system, but it seems a lot more beginner friendly and overall the GUI is better than in 1.4.
easy list for you
-------
Pros:
* New design and GUI!
* Option to choose drag and drop or code only when creating project
* Newbie friendly, has a built-in code manual with examples.
* Only minor coding changes from 1.4, so exporting or import 1.4 games with go easily into 2.
* You can change gameplay rate, how big the resolution is, the view of your character, etc.
* Layering system which makes map making a lot more fun and friendly
* Tileset system works a lot nicer than in previous versions, auto-tiles too!
* Layers can have parents and now theres animation editor which has layers too, and drawing while the animation is going!
Cons:
----------
* Sometimes i think it takes longer to load than the other version? may just be my pc.
* No achivements *yet*
* Gm 1 basic edition was free, and now im broke lol, i got this at a discount since i owned 1.4 pro and im *still broke* :(
but if you make a game with this, and it makes you happy, its worth it. Or if you can make something and eventually move on to being a game developer and earning your own cash from it, then its an investment and should be rewarded!
Good luck :D

I've been using GameMaker since I was 10 years old. Ahh, the good memories of building drag and drop games on the lite version. Back then I had no full time connection, so my learning resources were pretty much limited to the documentation (Which I didn't know about until I actually got internet), and the included tutorials. Eventually GameMaker 8 came out, and we had a whole 200MB worth of data to use every month! I immediately obtained GameMaker 8 Pro, and with the Pro version came the ability to code. Even though I had no sources to learn programming, the drag and drop programming gave me a good foundation, and I was soon able to write a few scripts by converting my drag and drop into code. Eventually we got full time internet, and I was able to watch tutorials and research what I needed. I was learning fast, faster than ever before. Then came GameMaker Studio, but being too attached to the interface of GM8, I ignored it. My primary reason was that my imported 3d projects didn't work, and at that point in time I was focusing solely on crappy 3d horror games. Nonetheless I really enjoyed it, and I kind of miss those carefree days where I made games for at least 6 hours a day. (Yes, I was homeschooled -_-). Long story short, I moved to GMS and started working on my first commercial title when I was 15 years old. I wasn't really planning on making it commercial since I develop for the fun of it, but I thought it would be interesting to experiment with Steam. I asked my dad for an investment to obtain a Greenlight license, and popped it on. The feedback was mixed, people calling it an asset flip, while others enjoyed the idea that Sometimes: Success Requires Sacrifice presented. Traffic was booming, well, for the first 2 weeks at least. Soon no one was visiting the page anymore, and I kinda forgot about the fact that I submitted a game. One unexpected day, I opened my email to find one from Valve that congratulated me on my game being greenlit. The rush was incredible, probably the biggest rush I've ever had in my game development career! Unfortunately, the hard work of entering into the commercial side of things began. Luckily I turned 16 while the game was floating about on the greenlight page, so I went about registering a business and opening a bank account etc. Learning how Steam worked was a bit tough for me at the time since I've never really been in CMD or any form of terminal, but it was a good learning experience. Finally, I finished uploading the game, and then I started working on trading cards and backgrounds. I feel the need to share this bit of humour, mainly as prove of how awesome the Steam staff members are! So my max level badge art got rejected because it wasn't sparkly enough, so I added more sparkly goodness, and left a comment saying that it's so sparkly even the twilight vampires are ashamed. The staff member responded to the humour by stating that the Vampires are now crying in the trees. The game was published, and although I won't consider it a commercial success, it still helped me grow a metric ton with all the feedback. Fast forward about a year, and my second game "Gal-X-E" went live on Steam. It's not selling much either, but I've learned so much once again. A few months ago I received news about GMS 2, and being me I grabbed the software as fast as I could. I've been using it for quite a while now, and it's definitely a step up from GMS 1.4.  The layout is more spacious in my opinion, and I can manage multiple windows with ease now. The sprite editor lost some features such as colorization, and rotation animations, but I don't use those anymore since I do it in code for optimization's sake anyways. The games perform better now as GMS 2 utilized DX11. The only real complaint I have at this moment is that I have to rebuy all the modules I bought for GMS 1.4 at full price, but I understand that they need to make a living too. I'm currently working on my 3rd commercial title, and with GMS 2 accompanying me, what could go wrong? (Laughs nervously)

This should not have the Jane's Name attached to it.  "Advanced Strike Fighters" would be a better name as it is an arcade like flight simulator, nothing like the in-depth realism of the other Jane's titles.  I am going to reccomend this game, but for a very specific reason, skip to the last paragraph if you want that break down.  The rest of this review will be focusing on all the problems with the game.
The game has some serious flaws.  The most jarring is the voice acting.  It's horrible.  The voice actors don't know what accent they are trying to replicate, and the end result is that 'control' (the guy giving you missions) sounds like a caricature of a middle eastern terrorist, your allies all sound either Russian (maybe) French (sometimes) or just stupid (almost always).  And then there is the main character you play, 'Razor', who has less personality then a cardboard box.  There is also the stupid decision to reveal major plot points while you are dogfighting multiple enemies.  I've screamed 'Shut up control! KIND OF BUSY!" while the middle eastern terrorist is rambling about president Karzei or Dimitriev.  Shutting the radio off is probably a good idea in this game, because it will be less frustrating.  And the plot is generic and bad anyway, make up your own story as you shoot down enemies.
Moving on, the gameplay.  It's not great.  Enemy fighter planes spawn and then go after you like a cruise missile.  The force balance is blatantly unfair as well, enemy fighters swarm you very quickly, and 10 on 1 furballs are never very fun.  Enemy missiles track rather well, and your countermeasures are basically only good for one missile.  If you have three flares, and you pop them, the game stops the tracking on three missiles (not all 12 headed at you) so again, not really realistic.  AAA fire can't shoot at you until you are within 2 miles, but can then track and hit you constantly (even through mountains) until you are 10 miles away.  Enemy SAMs always outrange ground munitions, so wild weasel can be interesting.  Now one by one, all of these enemy elements can be dealt with, but usually the game spawns 10 fighters, 4 sams, and an AAA site all at once and tells you 'GOOD LUCK!'.  This can be extremely frustrating at times.  I played one game where I died five times, but at the end, I had 94 ground kills and 138 air kills, achieveing a kill ratio that would be envied by any air force.  But to beat the level, there was no way you could do it on a single life, and this is a gameplay decision that bothers me.  Skill should be a factor here.
So that's enemies, what about your plane?  Well there is a good selection of aircraft, and they are all sort of rendered nicely.  I mean, the graphics in this game are not that great, but they get the job done.  One jarring thing for people who like planes, is that when maneuvering the planes surfaces do not move properly.  The ailerons and elevators and rudders all work, like on a Cessna, but these are Fly by wire aircraft.  Elevators work in tandem to roll planes along with elevators, flaps and ailerons should deploy to aid elevators in pitch maneuvers, rudders function as pitch and yaw assist on most aircraft as well.  This is not modeled, unlike say Ace Combat, where the planes are basically pornography.  Your weapon selection could best be described as generic.  There are no real munitions in this game, all the munitions are made up names with different capabilities.  You only really need three to win at this game, the Shrike, Eagle, and Basilisk.  The Shrike is a AA-11/sidewinder equivalent, the Eagle lets you pop enemy planes at long range (20 k in this game...) and the Basilisk is a cruise missile with submuntions.  You can't loadout your aircraft with anything other then pre-set loadouts, so I'll just tell you that the SU-35BM has this loadout in a 4/4/4 config.  Use it the moment you unlock it for every mission.  So your weapons are pretty generic and the explosions/missile traces are boring.
Ok, so why am I listing this game as recommended.  Well I am saying it is worth buying if it is on sale for only one reason.  It is fun to play Co-op.  Single player this game is dissapointing, but every mission in the game can be played on co-op mode, and you can have a lot of friends in a single session.  The enemy count doesn't change, so the game actually becomes more fair when you fly with wingman, about the only concession to reality the game makes.  If you have some friends to fly with, this game is pretty fun to play and the aircraft selection means you can all be flying your favourite modern jet.  If you don't intend to play co-op, stay away from it.

Having recently completed Half-Life Opposing Force, I cannot recommend Blue Shift. I only feel compelled to write this review because Blue Shift was so underwhelming compared to the original and the expansion. It has half as many weapons as either previous game but none of the new, charming weapons found in OF. Though it includes a few decent Half-Life style physics puzzles, boring and frustrating filler sections bury the good parts.
To start with, there is just too much exposition comprised of unnecessary Easter eggs winking at the original or the expansion. For a 2.5 hour long game, the 20-30 minute exposition adds nothing by retracing the steps of the original. The expansion further wastes time with long NPC dialogue sections that consist mostly of pointless techno-babble which does nothing to flesh out or expand the Half-Life universe. The game also contains a needlessly long NPC escort portion chock full of pathing bugs. At the end of the game, the same NPC leads the player through another pointlessly long Simon-says segment with nothing to do but press a button every minute or so.
When the action actually happens, the game frustrates by leading the player down long, maze-like corridors with headcrabs behind every box, rock, and corner. Fights with soldier-type enemies similarly become frustrating because the game throws so many at the player at once. Combined with their high ridiculously high health pool (a problem shared with the original), the player spends long stretches shooting at enemies who won't seem to die and who won't stop coming. By contrast, fights with alien enemies simply pit the player against easily dispatched pairs or triples of Vortigaunts or Houndeyes. The most difficult enemies are a few grunts. None of the new, difficult enemies introduced in OF appear.
As a whole, the expansion plays more like a fan made bonus level relying exclusively on existing game assets. It lacks the polish and clever moments of the original and the sci-fi schlock charm of the OF expansion. The player learns nothing new about the Half-Life universe that the original had not already covered. As a whole, Blue Shift adds nothing to the Half-Life experience except for a few new short, frustrating levels. It might as well be skipped even if you picked it up as part of the anthology.

Half-Life: Blue Shift was released in 2001 as the second Gearbox Half-Life expansion. In this game, you play as Barney Calhoun, a Black Mesa security guard during the time of the original Half-Life's Resonance Cascade, and the subsequent invasion of Black Mesa by the US military in attempt to cover the event up.
The game is similar to Opposing Force in that it illustrates a part of the world of Half-Life during the time of the Resonance Cascade, though from the eyes of someone other than Gordon Freeman. In Blue Shift's case, you start in a similar environment to Gordon within the depths of the Black Mesa Research Facility as an employee there, and after a casual introduction into basic mechanics and the neat environment Barney works in, you're thrown into combat quickly after the Cascade hits within 15 minutes into the game.
Most of the basic weaponry Gordon has in Half-Life can be used by Barney, from the Shotgun to the Revolver to the Crowbar, and the plot surrounds Barney's attempt to escape Black Mesa and resist against US marines who are pouring in to the facility to cover the whole Cascade up, along the way, you'll solve puzzles, fight baddies, and help scientists to find the way for yourself and others to escape the doomed facility before the impending nuclear destruction of the facility kills your chances.
The game itself is pretty great; because it was built around the same engine and built around Half-Life as an independent game, it resists many problems itself; most being attributable to those that Half-Life had itself (the flashlight that could stick to surfaces across the room). That being said, the game has a few glitches (saves breaking, certain elevator scenes near the beginning leading to game-overs, Gordon getting stuck on the tram tracks, etc) but none that were utterly game-breaking or capable of ruining the player's experience.
That being said, this game's main problem is its length and the amount of content it introduces. While Opposing Force, the previous Gearbox Half-Life expansion, had within it a fairly long plot, introduced many new weapons, aliens, and even had a boss battle, Blue Shift is fairly short and doesn't really introduce new weapons, (that being said, most of them to my knoweldge use different skins) and in my opinion, serves more as a compliment to the original game by allowing fans of Half-Life to see more of Black Mesa behind the scenes.
To summarize: In my opinion the game is great and is my personal favorite of the Half-Life expansions and vies with Half-Life 1 for the best original Half-Life title; I've always enjoyed the character of Barney Calhoun, and I find it enjoyable that there's an entire expansion detailing his own escape from the Black Mesa complex. However, I do recognize the flaws that this game has: This game doesn't introduce as much content as Opposing Force did to be considered a different title from Half-Life, and isn't as long as either Opposing Force or Half-Life to have as much of an impact on the average player post-completion. That all being said, I enjoyed what it was, the narrative and story was solid, and I enjoyed the chance to see the Resonance Cascade and the subsequent invasion of Black Mesa from the eyes of Barney. The game has a certain narrative to it that creates an interesting environment that compliments the plot, and because of its length, you spend more time with other characters and as such are able to more greatly build an understanding of their character because you spend more time together. While it's short and doesn't add much to the Half-Life universe, I myself liked it and found it enjoyable, even if it's only around 2-3 hours long in comparison to the original Half-Life being around 10-12 hours in length.
In the end, the game's narrative and plot outshine its gameplay for me; it's interesting to see the quest of a security guard escaping Black Mesa while it's under seize by Xen creatures and the military, and the ending is a complete contrast of the ending of Half-Life, and I can't help but feeling like it hit all its narrative marks in those regards.
I myself recommend it, but whether you want to pay 5 bucks for something like this is your opinion in the end. That being said, I myself got it as a part of the
Steam Bundle, which goes on sale during every major seasonal Steam sale. If you were thinking of getting this title or any of the other games in the Half-Life franchise, I'd suggest you turn to that bundle during a sale, as you get discounts for all the games if you buy it, so it's cheaper than buying each game individually.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is a very short game and can take you a maximum of 3 hours. That's how long it took for me at least, others say that it took them about 2 hours to be the game. It's as short as MGSV: Ground Zeroes, but doesn't mean that I didn't have with this game. On the contrary, I enjoyed it for what it was.
GAMEPLAY!
The game plays just like Half-Life 1 and Opposing Force (no big surprise, honestly), but instead of the HEV or PCV suit from the other games, you have your security guard helmet and vest as the armor you got. You can't use the Health or Shield regeneration station, instead you must find pick up dropped helmets and vests from dead security guards. It makes sense as in the other games, the security guards never really seem to be wearing any special suits like the HEV or PCV.
There is no new weapons in this game, all you have is the standard military weapons from the original game.
There is also no new enemies to fight, you got the Vortiguants, Marines, Headcrabs, Barnacles, and Zombies. I pretty sure there were more enemies, but those are only ones I remember.
Pretty much, this is like the original game except your a security guard.
LORE!
As I said, there are no new enemies so, you won't be seeing any new aliens or special black ops here like Opposing Force did. Instead, you will be fighting the traditional enemies from the base game. In terms of story, it answers some questions, such as how Barney got out of Black Mesa and how does the portals work. There not a lot of things here that is new here.
VERDICT!
Although, I really listed a lot of cons to the game that will turn people off. I'm still going to reccomend this for anyone who wants a little more insight on Black Mesa and the Security Team. It's definitely not a bad game, but it just lacks anything new. Still, I think people will find it pretty enjoyable.

Morphopolis is a beautiful looking and sounding game. In some ways, it reminds me of Botanicula in terms of the concept- you wander around as various insects, solving puzzles to progress through the undergrowth. Unlike Botanicula, the majority of these puzzles are in the form of finding the objects hidden in plain sight amongst the plants. This is not an overly difficult game; the objects are relatively easy to spot if you study the scenes, and the majority of the puzzles are pretty easy to solve. However, be warned that the final puzzle to complete the game may drive you completely up the wall; I found myself having lost all the calm gained from the rest of the game. Some people found it ok, I personally spent an hour fighting to work out how to solve it and, even though I looked up youtube walkthroughs and guides on steam, I still only solved it by random clicking rather than purposeful puzzle solving. There is also very little replay ability with this game, though I will be replaying one or two chapters now and again simply for the calming atmosphere.
Overall, considering the cheap price, this game gets my recommendation.
Pros:
- Beautifully designed scenes that look amazing.
- Wonderfully calming music, that compliments the beauty of the scenes.
- Creates a peaceful atmosphere while playing; a great game to relax to if you've had a bad day or are feeling tense.
- Worth it for the cheap price; especially if you grab it on sale.
Cons:
- It is a short game; it took a max of 2 hours to complete it, 1 hour of which was spent on the final puzzle.
- Limited replay ability.
- Expect to get frustrated with the final puzzle, and for it to take a lot of random clicking,
- Not good for those that have a dislike of insects.

An amazingly beautiful hidden objects/puzzle game. More similar in gameplay to The Tiny Bang Story than typical hidden objects games, you play as some insect crawling through beautifuly colored settings with a nice acoustic guitar background music.
The game is divided in 5 chapters corresponding to each stage of the insect life from larvae to adult (Lepidoptera). With the ability to use pheromones to interact with the environment, the game consists mostly of finding a given number of certain objects (leaves, seeds, bugs, bug parts...) to then feed some bigger insect or fix some plant to obtain some reward or open a pathway. The main goal from chapters 2 to 4 consists of bringing back to life some dying insect.
Morphopolis is sadly quite short( ~1hour) and can be completed in one setting. All achievements are obtained after completing the game.
The insect movements are a bit slow and how to make it move is confusing at first before figuring out you only need to hold the left mouse button in the direction you want it to move.
Most puzzles are pretty easy, there is just one puzzle that I wrongly thought bugged (the chinese checker alike puzzle with flower seeds) because controls appeared irresponsive but the answer of how it worked was on the forum:
In all, I found it was a pretty relaxing game but a bit short. The art was really beautiful. If you are not bothered by bugs (there is no spider in the game, but a lot of other things, some with lots of legs), I definitely recommend it.

This game really is the first true zombie survival simulator.
The level of detail and the amount of content you will find in this game will make you question how this must be in early access. The developer of this game is extremely dedicated to improving this game in every way, so I'm very excited to see how the final product will turn out.
What you can expect from Project Zomboid is a realistic take on the zombie apocolypse. You don't have super human health, or immunity, or unlimited ammunitions. You'll need to watch your back at every turn, keep yourself from starving, find water after all the water supply runs out, fortify a house with planks and grow food -- the possibilities of how you choose to approach any situation are seemingly endless.
I strongly recommend this game to any zombie genre fanatics who would like a realistic take on surviving the zombie outbreak.

What is Train Valley?
Genre: Top-Down Train Track Puzzle & Strategy
Setting: Establishing and improving railroad lines in different countries, completing special tasks along the way
Difficulty: 3/10 - 7/10 - depends on the selected scenario chapter
Length: 5-10 hours for a campaign walkthrough
Mode: singleplayer only
Similar games: can't name any, sorry
What's good about train valley?
- unique chapters with different artworks (e.g. Russia, Japan, Germany, USA)
- additional special tasks ("challenges") to always keep on improving the railroad network
- easy to get into
- some levels contain unique specifications you have to deal with
- more simultaneously running, longer and faster trains make up a challenge for your mind!
The negative aspects:
- balancing issues. While one mission can be easy, the next can get surprisingly tough
- trains and stations can't be chosen, they are prespecified by the game (to be fair, that's part of the game mechanics, too)
- the game's music is horrible, and pretty cliché (especially the German tracks)
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
Train Valley is a nice puzzling game, using trains as a theme. Depending on your mind skills (hopefully you got some), you will have a challenging or overcharging time fulfilling the missions and special tasks. In general, decent and colourful graphics, varying and motivating special tasks and missions sum up to present the game in a nice and friendly atmosphere. However, the soundtrack is horrible, better turn on your music library while playing - if your mind skills allow you to listen to music and concentrate on the game at the same time.
Recommended!

This game is in my top three favourite Telltale games. I've played it twice, once on PS4, and the other on PC, and loved it both times. The story is masterfully crafted, and a very original take on The Dark Knight.
A lot of characters are different than their comicbook/film counterparts, which in my opinion, is a good thing. In a game where you have to make your own choices, basing your choices off of outside knowledge on certain characters can drag the game down, which I admittedly did with certain characters. Different doesn't equate to bad.
As for the gameplay, most of the action set pieces are pretty good, some of which are even great. The detective gameplay is mostly boring, however those segments don't happen very often.
As for the choices you make, well, they're pretty good. They affect the game more than choices from other Telltale games do, but they're mostly hit or miss, with some exceptions.
If you like Batman, or just stories in general, you should definitely buy this game, as long as it's on sale. The $25 USD it's being sold at while writing this review is steep to say the least.

As someone who played Tropico 4, I was actually a bit disappointed with this. It has some features that are better than Tropico 4, and some that Tropico 4 doesn't have. However, it is also missing much of the stuff Troico 4 had. I'll do a little list:
What Tropico 5 is missing that was in Tropico 4:
1. Placeable statues of the Player Character
2. Stupidly large golden statues of the player character
3. Character customisation (to the extent it was present in Tropico 4)
4. The ability to be a brutal Dictator, and stay in power
5. Decent Political system
6. The ability to sdjust wages, and rents on residences, in the same way as was possible in Tropico 4 (Only the simplified budget mechanic is there)
7. The ability to play as famous figures from the period
8. The ability to actually choose you characters name
9. Cool DLC (As opposed to crappy cash grab DLC)
10. Good Music (In my opinion the music in this is worse than in Tropico 4)
11. A wide selection of buildings (there is a similar number of buildings, despite the fact that Tropico 4 takes place over 50 years and Tropico 5 over around 100)
What Tropico 5 has over Tropico 4
1. Multiplayer
2. Tanks, Military Aircraft and APC's (Although you need DLC to get APC's despite the fact they can be seen driving around in the main menu on the base game. This is what I mean about cash grab DLCs)
3. Ability to control soldiers (Although they are discustingly clunky to control)
4. A grid system for ease of placing buildings
5. Random Map Generator
6. Reasearch
7. Different Era's
Basically, buy Tropico 4 unless you want to play with friends, I think it's better and so do so many others.

While the first game was hard FlatOut 2 is beyond easy & hard. It is arbitrary, luck decides if you win or not and you as the player have little influence on that.
There are two main issues
You cannot predict how your car will react during a jump or hitting an obstacle. Sometimes it runs smoothly, sometimes you will lose your position or advantage. Therefore there is little space in getting better or master the game, because you don't get proper feedback which action benefits you and which one will be punished.
You will find at the bottom a video I've done about two stunts. The only thing I do is pressing throttle without pausing it, so there is no room for variation. I do this in both stunts. Two exact same actions from the player result in different outcomings.
Some of them are trolls, not interested in winning the race just ramming other cars and putting themselves at the tail end while giving you a hard time.
The other extreme are the flawless ones, usually using one of the higher level cars which you have to unlock first. Catching up with them happens rarely. They usually drive clean and boost forwards if you are getting close. Starting at the last position puts you in huge disadvantage against those.
The other thing is that the AI adapts to you. Are you driving faster or have you upgraded your car? They get better as well, so the difficulty seems to stay stable. At least to a certain point. Buying a new car with much better values makes the races easier, but not as much as I expected.
-The starting position varies, but most times I got the last place or something near that.
-Later in the game you may have to repeat races a couple times to collect the amount of money to buy a car you've just unlocked. Winning all level 1 races doesn't guarantee you having enough money for a Level 2 car.
-Strangely a Level 1 car isn't necessary good enough to compete in Level 1 races. I once had to grind for a better one and repeated the races.
-NPCs get fixed cars from the start of a class and some of them get ones from a higher tier. It would be fairer if everyone would use a car from the same level.
All in all: Driving good doesn't get rewarded, you need a certain amount of luck. Both, losses and victories, felt cheap and latter one never satisfied me. I was just relieved to be over the current race.
Now the most important point:
Does this all make the game unenjoyable? It depends.
Are you looking for a serious racing game? Is anything but 1st place not an option to you? Then skip this one. It started pretty easy and was fun, but the further I got into the game the more the races turned into bitter and teeth-gnashing hours of retries which felt more like playing roulette and waiting until the ball hits your number.
If you don't care about the mentioned issues, because just beating the game is enough for you or you just want to have a bit random wacky car physics fun, you might wanna try it. At least it won't hurt as long as you don't take it too seriously and bite your teeth into it.

I have about eighty-four hours invested into Edge of space. (with about one third of my time in pre-release, over 404 hours in Terraria in comparison). It was exhilarating  to see a game with the science-fiction setting in the genre. I wanted to like this game, but it's been a letdown overall. Exploration and expansion become quite hindered by your armor and weapons. Crafting remains over-complex and tedious. It is all too easy to sink hours looking for resources that are a little -too- scarce. Items take sometimes a half-dozen ingredients to make (which themselves take several crafting stations). In comparison to Terraria, most items take three or fewer (excluding endgame content). This game is an example of a great premise bogged down by poor development. This is one of the few games I keep trying every so often to see if they've fixed it, and so far they haven't. I'm not yet at the point where I wish I could trade or return it, but I'm not too far from that either.

This game wasnt terrible, but it wasnt very good either. The premise could be good if the mini games were clever, if it were the hallmark of great games design starting from something simple with actual promise. The problem lies in that the little games he is presenting just arent very good, they arent really games just slices of levels which are only just interesting enough to keep you going.
The notions of depth and philosophy that the narrator is trying to convey just dont exist. I think this is why it has been called pretentious, It is great in theory to subvert and challenge notions of what a game should be, but you have to replace it with something worthwhile, you have to prove to the viewer that which you are showing has validity, and this is where it fails. Its like going to a gallery and seeing an instalation of a tv playing white noise endlessly. You can buy in to the premise all you like but deep down you know its garbage.
So the whole game becomes a platform for his narration, the climax of which just made me think he was a bit pathetic and selfish over something with very low stakes. I have worked for a number of years as an artist and understand the insecurities that go with it as well as understanding mental health problems. Here he never really provides anything tangible to say about these things. he just sort of hints at things until his outburst. I guess for some the greatness of this game lies in his final revelation.

So currently I have Less than an Hour on this paid version(40Hour Update below) but rest assured I have been using GM2 for probably 100 hours since the initial beta. I also have thousands of hours on GM:S though just not on Steam.
TLDR;
Gamemaker Studio 2 is an amazing upgrade from GMS1, it does everything so well I am so happy to have finally purchased it.
[Importing Large GM:S Projects]
So I wanted to start off by addressing one major thing that I'm sure some people will want to know and is something I didn't see in any reviews and that is how well Gamemaker Studio 2 handles importing large projects and I have to say I am extremely impressed, my game I have been working on and off for about 2 years now (Mainly more done in the past year) has a tonne of objects, sprites and lines of code so I was expecting to import it and have hundreds of errors and broken bits of code, so I'm shocked that the game runs without a single error, there are a few issues I've noticed like the optimisation I had needs to be fixed and some sprites continuously play but that is easily fixed and won't take a fraction of the hours I thought I might have to spend fixing everything.
10/10 For that!
[Interface]
Wow, is the interface so much better, I hated GM:S and having the things open in actual windows as I often found that after some time of use and quite a lot of compiling led to them bugging out and being a massive pain. Gamemaker 2 Allows you to have everything in 1 or more workspaces where you can zoom in and out of different objects without having to close and re-open them which is amazing. Also GM2 is just so much better to look at in general.
[GML]
I like the new changes to some of the code to the GML, such as creating objects you now set the depth when you create it so you don't have to worry about sorting that out on the object and instead just create it how you want it.
[Room Editor,Tiles]
My God do I love the new room editor, apart from it just looking better it has a handful of new features that make it so good such as having the depths of everything on the sidebar so you can just easily drag and drop what you want ontop of things etc. Also TILES are amazing now, one thing that was a pain in a large room I found (And still seems to be apparent in GM2) is that is very slow and so tiling a map can be so annoying but thanks to the amazing Brush tool for tiles you can create things outside of the room editor and then just paste them in which is incredible.
[Conclusion]
GM2 is a phenomenal step up from GM1 and well worth the price (I owned GM1 so I got the 40% discount) and is a must have for anyone new to game development or very experienced. 10/10
[Update 18/03/17]
I've been using GM2 for 40 hours now so I feel like I should say if my opinion has changed, and yes it has, it has become better, the most noteable thing I can say is the compile times ARE SO FAST. On GM1 every few compiles I could compile in 20 or so seconds with my large project however every few attempts it'd usually freeze up and make me wait a couple minutes, this NEVER happens in GM2, it compiles in seconds without fail which is incredible.
My only complaint is that due to my project having so many objects in the room editor if I change the depth (move an object up or down the list or even add something onto it however this bit doesn't apply to that) I risk crashing GM2 and my computer as it uses 11GB's of RAM and can take 10-20 minutes to actually sort itself out which is a problem however aslong as I only move one object at a time usually it sorts itself out however 1 time crashed GM2 after about 30 minutes.
That's literally the only problem I have, GM2 has made making my game a thousand times easier. <3
