Whilst having over 600 hours using GameMaker Studio 1.4, both inside college on my game design course, and outside for personal projects, GameMaker has always been by far the most user friendly game engine I've ever used. Although I have experience in using game engines such as Unreal Engine and Unity, GameMaker is always at the top of my list for 2D game development due its user friendliness and being able to produce good results so quickly.
The major thing which is striking about GameMaker Studio 2 is its new interface, the layout of the software itself has been completely re-worked, despite having the familiarity of GameMaker: Studio 1.4. Since I use purely GML in my projects, the new workspaces feature has vastly improved my work efficiency, by being able to keep code windows open without them protruding on my screen. The new workspaces are essentially like Unreal Engine's blueprint system, however they still retain each type of object event (such as create, step and draw) like in GameMaker: Studio 1.4.
One thing which was complained about in GameMaker: Studio 1.4 was its primitive tiling system. If you have ever tried to create wall sprites in GameMaker: Studio 1.4, you will know what it is like to have the issue of manually placing each type of tile. This process is incredibly time consuming. However, with GameMaker Studio 2's auto tiling system, you can now define different types of sprites in a sequence (whether they may be corners or edges etc) and GameMaker Studio 2 will automatically detect different types of intersections between tiles.
In my humble opinion, backgrounds were a relatively useless feature of GameMaker: Studio 1.4 and these have since been removed and replaced with sprites alone. Backgrounds can still be created however in the room editor, by creating a background layer, and then selecting a specific sprite to tile with.
After having used GameMaker Studio 2 for over a day now, I have noticed subtle changes to certain features within the GML language, the first of all is that the editor now features an auto-complete feature, which detects any declared variables you have initialized (which is incredibly useful).
Some functions from GameMaker: Studio 1.4 have since been removed but there are work arounds for (pretty much) everything. The most notable thing I've found is that the
function no longer exists. This has since been replaced with
and
. These functions allow for alterations which have been made to the depth feature within GameMaker.
Another notable thing is that they have implemented a feature which I have been wanting for ages... The ability to define the game's speed using microseconds per frame, over frames per second using the function
. The disadvantage of using frames per second is that if the game speed slows down to below your room speed, the game's time system also slows down. On the other hand, defining your game speed using microseconds per frame (MPF), the game speed can constantly change, to compensate for the loss in frames. As an example, a room speed of 60 will equate to 16666 microseconds per frame. Room speed is now also defined by a setting in the game preferences, rather than being unique to every room.
One thing I am sad about though on the flip side is the removal of d3d functions. These were used to draw 3D primitives. Whilst I am aware that GameMaker is an engine primarily orientated at 2D game development, and it can be fairly limited in regards to other 3D engines, having these features was a massive benefit for the people that wanted to explore 3D within GameMaker. Since the removal of d3d functions, developers have to manually manipulate what are known as
that have an incredibly steep learning curve.
For a full list of implemented functions click this link:
ER MA GERD... The sprite editor has been improved so much, the main notable feature which has appealed to pretty much everyone is the drawing while animating feature. This has really amazed me because I haven't even seen a tool like this in Adobe Photoshop, one of the most premium image manipulation packages out there... Some real innovation by YoYo games here!
Whilst I did want to wait to purchase GameMaker Studio 2 a little longer, this was this feature which adherently tipped me over the iceberg. GameMaker Studio 2 now uses DirectX 11 as it's graphics API, in comparison with it's predecessor which used DirectX 9. Whilst the update removes the ability to compile projects for Windows XP (I know right), this is a feature which will greatly improve the performance of your project, (providing that you write efficient code).
As a whole, purchasing the upgrade for GameMaker Studio 2 has been a very viable decision for myself. It will be for you too! If you're still a bit sceptical, I'd definitely consider purchasing it. I myself am currently working on a game project called
, which is a 2D top-down tank game. This project was initially wrote in GameMaker: Studio 1.4, however my intention is to re-write the project using GameMaker 2 as there are features I want to implement such as delta timing.
More information about my game project and other things can be found on my website at:
One final recommendation for the engine which I still think it should have, is the ability to compile 64bit executables at run time, although the performance increase is marginal between 32 bit and 64, having the RAM limitation of 4GB there could potentially be a large headache for huge projects.

TL:DR This game should please Batman fans but if you're not a fan of Telltales earlier games you might not like this one either.
Full Version:
Telltales take on Batman turned out to be a nice surprise for me. I wasn't sure they'd be able to do a good Batman game with their usual formula, but they've actually done a nice job. The games beginning seems to take place early in Batmans career as in this game he meets Catwoman for the first time, Two Face is still Harvey Dent and running for mayor and Penguin is still Oswald Cobblepot.
What was most surprising is that they have taken some artistic licence with the appearance and origin of some characters, but I actually think this is a good thing as it's allowed them to create a gripping story. I mean it's not unheard of since the comics for many superheroes sometimes reboot the origins and appearance of the heroes and the villains (Alfred Pennyworth first appeared in the comics as a fat clumsy guy for example). Another thing I thought this game did really well was explore Batmans life as Bruce Wayne, something no other Batman game I've played has done. You'll often play as Bruce as he gets entangled in the politics of Gotham and sometimes you will have a choice as to whether approach characters as Bruce or Batman.
It's not all positive though. As is usual with Telltale games it sometimes feels like your choices don't matter as certain things seem to happen regardless of what you choose. I also found the game to be a bit buggy on occasion. I experienced stuttering on occasion during scenes and witnessed Bruce have a telepathic conversation with Alfred as he didnt move his mouth once in one particular scene. Luckily this sort of thing didn't happen frequently enough where it ruined my enjoyment.
Overall if you're a fan of Batman this game is worth playing as it felt like a fresh approach to a Batman game and had a very good story to go with that. However it still suffers the flaws of previous Telltale games and if you're not a fan of their games this one probably won't change you mind on that.

As someone who has used Game Maker since when it was in version 7, way back about 10 years ago, this is a gigantic step up.
GMS1 looked and functioned to me just as GM7 and GM8 did way back in the day, and that was the reason I got back into using GMS as a whole. There were gripes I had with it, I had primarially used the scripting language and some of the ways of ghettorigging code was a bit weird at times, and the documentation wasn't really the best, but that all changes with GMS2.
A fully featured documentation on their site, a really well designed interface, the ability to have multiple windows of interfaces, allowing for you to put another thing of code on another monitor and have even more room of doing stuff, great for people with multiple monitors, I can imagine using this for quite awhile.
I have about 400 hours in GMS1 and I have a feeling that I'm going to be using GMS2 for quite a bit longer than that. I've published games onto google play with GMS1 and now that I've used GMS2, I have a feeling this is going to be the next big step forward. Props to YoYo to finally making an interface upgrade that GM so desperately needed, and another round of props to them for making the interface much easier and more responsive to use.
Other added features and changes include a completely new sprite editor interface, seperating the GML side of programming and the drag and drop into completely seperate project types, only allowing one or the other, and overhauling the engine and interface as far as I can tell. Also a complete room interface overhaul, better font handling, and other great stuff.
I have not used the Drag and Drop interface as of yet, I only used GML in gms1 in the first place so I can't really say how good the DnD interface of GMS2 is, but from the screenshots it seems like they have completely redone it.
All in all, This is a fantastic upgrade to the Game Maker line of products overall, and I'm really happy that I have purchased it. I would recommend if you liked GMS1 or have used Game Maker in the past.

Would I recommend The Chemist? Sure, it's really early access at the moment, but the devs seem to be on it with the patches and community forums, and it's in a pretty stable condition.

This is one of those games that LOOKS amazing.  It has amazing graphics.  It has amazing character design.  It has an amazing concept.
Unfortunately, it's just not fun to play.  In order to win as the monster, you have to run away until you're level 3.  Since it takes quite a while to reach level 3, most of the game is spent either sneaking around and slowly growing as the monster, or searching a gigantic map for a monster that can easily get away unless the trapper sneaks up on it.  When the fight finally takes place, it's usually over before the first barrier ends, and the winner is decided by what level the monster reached.
The only time this isn't the case is when both teams are very skilled.  A VERY skilled hunter team can survive fighting a level 3 monster, and a very skilled monster can abuse line of sight to avoid combat while inside a barrier.  This means when you get better, your games change to a stalemate until level 3, and then a very long, drawn out endurance match between hunters that can split up and fly away from you and a monster that can duck around corners until it gets a chance to eat and heal.
As a result, the game is only fun while the novelty lasts, which for me was a few hours.
It would be more interesting if both teams started out even and the hunters could find equipment upgrades around the map that allow them to "level up" too, turning it into a race of who can evolve faster.  This would give the monster a reason to seek out the hunters and attack them if the monster is evolving more quickly.  It would also give a defensive purpose to the barrier, to keep a monster OUT while hunters search for gear.  At least then, both sides would have an interest in forcing engagements, so more engagements might actually happen, and the monster would actually have an opportunity to win in the first 10 minutes of a match.

Blue Shift is the second PC expansion for the Half-Life games. Originally, Blue Shift was meant to be an add-on for the Dreamcast version of Half-Life, much like Half-Life: Decay was an add-on for the PlayStation 2 version of Half-Life. (Which you can now play as a mod for the original Half-Life:
)
The fact that Blue Shift was originally just an add-on which became an expansion later on is really visible when looking at the time it takes to finish it. Opposing Force took me 6.6 hours to complete on normal, while Blue Shift took me 2.5 hours. In my opinion, Blue Shift is also too easy with too many health crates laying everywhere. What also makes visible that it was originally just an add-on is that you get no new weapons, and you only get to use the non-alien weapons of the original Half-Life. Even though this expansion of the Half-Life universe is maybe lesser in content. I still enjoyed it. It is short which makes it get to the action directly. Also, you go to the alien dimension more often in this one.
The gameplay in this expansion is mostly just shooting and not really any puzzle solving. The game also doesn't have any boss fights. Everything is mostly combat oriented. With some more parts in the alien dimension.
This expansion takes place at the same time as the previous Half-Life games with references to the previous expansion and the original game. The only difference this time is that you experience the story from the perspective of a security guard.
Throughout the story, you can really see the style of Gearbox once again with adding a lot of humor in it. What I think is funny to mention is that one of the characters is voice acted by the voice actor of Duke Nukem. Years later, Gearbox went on to create Duke Nukem Forever.
With Blue Shift I encountered some bugs. One was that every time I loaded a checkpoint the game acted as if I was  holding the mouse button. So when I spawned the weapon just kept shooting.
It was fun to play Half-Life again from a different point of view. but in my opinion the expansions like this or Opposing Force don't really add too much to the story. Still, this expansion pack has some nice action during the short time of playing.

Thus, this is why playing with friends is a good idea.
Unfortunately, the game will be plagued with negative reviews due to the whole DLC fiasco. I do agree that this indeed is an overpriced game. (Base game: $60 (thank goodness?), Deluxe: $80, Monster Race: $100). I heavily dislike DLC and the current plague it has on our generation's games. In this case, it appears the DLC includes skins, a fifth monster, ect. I wouldn't have outright called this situation out if it wasn't for the fact that the >fifth< monster is DLC, nor the preorder one. This, however, was DLC ANNOUNCED even before release or anything, so it obviously has been taken the wrong way, not including the behemoth. That was NOT a good idea to include monsters as DLC, because they are a major point of the game's core. So, a bit of mixed feelings on this whole ordeal. Another thing is, whether you like this whole DLC fiasco or not, most of today's game (including those from the past few years) will always have a DLC ordeal like this. It's not a question of taking things personal because of this, but the fact that you either purchase the game or not, simple as that. Don't grunt and mourne on your reviews like this is all a new thing, because it's not. Released maps for this game will be free.
Nevertheless, as I said, the game is fun, and I recommend it if you wish to play some serious co-op with friends. I still believe it has good replay value, and that's including the rest of the game modes, or if you wish to practice yourself against bots. Whether the game will be ongoing in the next year or so is dependent on you, the consumers. It will keep ahold for those who enjoy the game, not for those to take it personal over the DLC.
And no, I payed the regular $60, which is good enough for me. If half the game's out there somewhere else, then there's no need for me to spend any more money for a price I believe should be justifiable enough. I'm not being forced to buy it, and I have no reason to castrate a game for it, with the reasons included above.
The game appears to be properly optimized on my system. 60 frames per second is achieveable and uninterrupted at resolutions 1920x1080, 1920x1200, ect, but don't mourne over the fact that you can't achieve it on a 4k resolution, because you won't. Infact, this may actually be one of the smoothest releases of this year on my system.

The Good: This is a clever, creative, deeply atmospheric game. It is extremely well written, and the creators have come up with a fantastically surreal universe. Exploring the Undersea is a lot of fun, and you are always driven to see what's past the next patch of dark sea.
So why the downvote?
The Bad: This is a terrible game for a rougelike mechanic.
Whenever you die you have to start over with a new captain. You get to pass along some advantages, but the game itself starts over. The upshot is that you spend A LOT of time playing, then replaying, then re-replaying the same five hours or so of content. You visit the same starting islands, run the same early quests over and over again. It's like reading a really great novel, except every 50 pages you have to go back to the beginning and start over.
In a game dedicated to exploration and experiencing a vast, fascinating world, having to constantly see the same things again and again kind of kills the fun. Add to that the truly random feeling of many of your interactions, the tediously slow travel time, the enormous amount of grinding you have to do, and the sheer guesswork involved with solving quests, and what should feel like a process of discovery ends up feeling like frustratingly bumbling around until the game kicks you back to the beginning.
All in all, the people who made this game are absolutely terrific writers. They're just not very good game designers.

Steam doesn't allow neutral reviews, so I should start by saying that this game has one of the best settings I've ever seen, the writing is really good, the mood is great, and I very much like the music too. The text-based segments of the game are usually excellent.
Which makes it all the more heartbreaking that the awful, awful ship mechanics are ruining the game.
First issue: the starting ship is insufferably slow. Seriously, I can't stress how absurdly slow it is.
And you'd think that a stronger engine or lighter ship would solve that problem, but it doesn't, because stats don't mean what you'd think they mean in this game. Increasing Engine Power barely does anything for speed (it greatly increases fuel consumption, of course) and "upgrading" to the second ship, which is 70% lighter than the default one, doesn't even make any visible difference in speed and pretty much no difference in fuel consumption either, it just cripples a bunch of your other stats. Your viable options are to get a special add-on (which early ships can't get) that lets you go Full Power without your engine exploding all the time, or getting the best engine in the game, which also requires a much more expensive ship.
Once you get a faster setup and can now stand playing the game, you'll find your efforts sabotaged by a feature called "Something Awaits You", henceforth known as SAY. In this game, you can't just do things at a port. Most repeatable actions can only be done once per port visit; they take away your SAY. I actually wouldn't mind that, except... SAY isn't port-based. You can go to a port you haven't visited in forever (or ever), but if you just did something at another nearby port, your SAY won't be back yet. You'll have to go back at see and wait for SAY to reappear. And if you have supplies you can still farm any port by just standing next to it, but you'll be staring at your screen and doing nothing for a while. Basically, the content is gated behind your ability to stand boredom.
Combat also takes place during the "action" segments. It's sort of real-time, except with gauges that decide when you and the enemy can fire. There's a way to stagger enemies that sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. I once killed the strongest enemy in the game without taking any damage, just by standing in front of it and spamming attacks. Came back a bit later, did the exact same thing, and I was destroyed in less than 15 seconds. That was the only time I died in that game.
Speaking of which, permadeath works well if runs take 15 minutes to an hour. But a Sunless Sea playthrough can easily last 20 hours. Dying feels like a terrible waste of time. And you can pass on some things to your next captain, but not others. You had 25,000 cash on you? You can pass all of that on. You had 10,000 and 15,000's worth of stuff on you? You lose the 15,000's worth of stuff.
Another annoyance: almost all ships have very low cargo space. You have to bring lots of stuff everywhere on the map, and you'll have to settle for a tenth of it per trip unless you have a really big ship. Also, you'll often find yourself dumping valuable treasure overboard just because you don't have space for it. In my opinion, the Merchant Cruiser is the best ship in the game just because it has the highest hold capacity.
In summary... an exceptionally great text game, ruined by unbearable ship mechanics.

If I had to describe this game in two words it would be: missed potential
Let me just say that the mood the game sets at the beginning is bloody amazing! The colour pallet suplements and enhances the feel of mystery and danger. The titular sea (Zea in game) is massive and really gives of the feeling of desolation and helplessness. This, however, is also its first and most glaring issue... the ship in which you sail is excruciatingly SLOW. I have no idea why the developers have not increased the speed of it already because it doesnt add to the atmosphere and is just frustrating. To be fair there are speed upgrades... which are expensive and will cost more fuel.
Furthermore the gameplay itself boils down to 3 things as far as I can see: Fetchquests, Resource management, and Combat. And sadly all of them are flawed in some way. Fetchquests: Thats basicly the main part of the gameplay and that in itself is bad enough but it also doesn't tell you where to look  aside from vague sometimes none existant hints. Resource Management: First I do have to say that they did a good job making the resources balanced. Fuel and Supplies (Food) feels rare and in high demand. But then there is the insanity meter, which will f you over if you don't constantly return to the main harbour (atleast at the beginning of the game).  [Tangent: One of the main draw of the game is the exploration of the world, which is severely hindered by the insanity meter. This is effect is enhanced by the slowness of the boat.] Combat: Yawn... There are monsters which charge at you and ships which run into rocks, get stuck, with easily exploited path finding and try to shoot you. Or you flee from them.
Genre issue: Most of these things would be fine though if the game didn't have permadeath. Don't get me wrong permadeath can be an interesting concept. This game, however, failed to grasp the catching point of it. A good example is Dead Cells. When you die in Dead Cells you can jump right back into the action. No character creation or preparation or text; just gameplay. Permadeath is supposed to increase the stakes enough to make it interesting but it is also incentivises you to try once more. But this isn't possible if a another round of a game is more than half a day long which is the case for Sunless Sea.
I could say some more negatives and positives but I have seen some apt reviews for the other issues. Let me just say as some sort of conclusion that the developers shouldn't have focused on making all this text in favour of gameplay because after some time you just don't care anymore and I have found myself skipping most of the text avalanche because I knew there wouldn't be anything interesting to read. Don't get me wrong the writing wasn't bad but the game throws so many unknown words at you that they stop having any sort of meaning after a while because you don't get any explaination what they mean.
Anyway if you have read this entire review and still considere buying this game then heed this: This review is about the amount of text you will have to read on a typical new island... every time.
I hope this helped you in your decision.

I'm kind of sorry for giving this game a thumbs-down, since it is in large parts a window into the personal troubles of a developer that I feel sympathy for. The fact of the matter, though, is that I did not enjoy The Beginner's Guide as a game, nor as a narrative, and that I indeed would not recommend it. While playing the game, my feelings changed from curiosity to disappointment to severe boredom. From about half-way through onward, I just wanted it to end.
The Beginner's Guide is a sequence of about a dozen extremely short games that could be considered experimental. Most of these games are completely linear, choice usually does not exist (or does not matter). They present some original concepts, but I also found them uniformly bland and boring - they are, at least in parts, meant to be that way, and there is an omnipresent narrator who reflects on this, though he is also enthused about these games because he sees something in them that I do not.
Many of these short games are also deliberately unenjoyable - e.g. puzzles that cannot be solved, repetitive mazes, or a sequence where you would be locked in a room for one real-time hour. There is barely any freedom and no point in exploration (if the latter is even possible, in many of these games it is not). You simply repeat exactly what the game tells you to do, otherwise you cannot progress. The narrator forces you through this boring experience by making "additions" to the games that make them "playable".
The general unapproachability of the games is part of the game's narrative. This narrative, if it worked, might have been able to create a level of engagement that the gameplay was obviously never intended to have. And judging from the reviews, it seems that the narrative succeeded with this for some people. For me, it just didn't. While the premise seemed interesting, the story soon turned into a grating, drawn-out experience until the narrator, after 90 minutes of completely linear gameplay, finally arrived at a fairly obvious realization, one that I would have wanted to tell him 10 minutes into the game when he simply skipped the first maze for me. The message of the game is actually an important one, especially if you have an interest in art, its reception, and the often troubled process of its creation. But forcing players through 90 minutes of (mostly) boredom may not be the best way to present it.

I thought I'd dislike the game. No, really - when it unexpectedly popped up and I checked some of it, I decided to avoid it. I thought that it's not for me, that it talks about stuff I experienced and realised long ago, that it would be like reading your teenage diary, where you realise something and it's awkward to check today because so much stuff passed.
And then Davey contacted me again to translate some more bits of Stanley into Russian for the awesome boxed release that he's doing (I translated the game and mod into Russian) and as a thank you gave me the Steam key to The Beginner's Guide. I felt like - now I have to play it.
My opinion changed a lot during playing. There were sections that, I feel, could've been shorter or cut. And it does go from really nice and clever pseudo-documentary-like structure to being more of an observation on how not just games are made, and how people making games work, but how a person creates something and how that creative (any person who creates anything) person works. The presumptions. Understanding or lack thereof. About things that sometimes seem contradictory but can coexist in one person. About searching meanings and giving meanings. But it sometimes does it... I dunno. Not very well, as much as it does well at other times.
So I went from trying to be as neutral to it, to finding myself actually liking it, to then feeling the "get on with it" vibes. To then kind of liking it again. To then feeling like... yeah, that... I guess that was nice?
There's something about this that is good, surprisingly good, given how simple things it talks about are. Things that are probably not going to be anything new to you. Just because it talks about them in an entertaining way. And there are bits of it that feel unnecessary, overthought, not very good.
So, The Beginner's Guide is nice. It's not a witty exciting game like Stanley. It's not a life changing experience. It's just... an hour and a half well spent.

GameMaker Studio 2 is the long awaited followup to GameMaker: Studio, I personally feel I am quite experienced with this software as I have 530+ hours on GameMaker: Studio and over 100 on versions not on Steam and GameMaker Studio 2 Beta, I have to say the software has improved a lot.
- Interface much easier to navigate as a beginner than GMS 1.x
- Same programming language as GMS 1.x so an easy transition
- Much improved sprite, tileset and room editors to make your games look much better.
- Nice animations that make the engine look very polished.
- Networking that is easy to handle.
- Very expensive export modules, but at least they are cheaper such as mobile which combines iOS and Android.
- No 3D functionality, but that wasn't a surprise for me.
- No Steam Workshop functionality (so far).
- Modules are different pieces of software, not just DLC for the main one (I am not really sure what the point of that is   YoYo)
- No Demo version on Steam, GMS 1.x just had a pro dlc and the basic version was free.
GameMaker Studio 2 is a great engine thatin my opinion smashes competitors such as Clickteam: Fusion and Construct 2 and I really recommend it, don't expect to make a Triple-A game with this but a very small amount of engines enable you to even come close to that, overall I completely recommend this engine and I encourage you to at least download the demo from the YoYo Games website and give it a go.

The goal is to take contracts from various companies and then buy the chemicals to produce a product that will fill the contract while still making money. Sounds simple, right? It is and it isn't in The Chemist. Mulitple resources needed and the added pressure of the timer makes every pour important. It's not impossible but it does increase in challenge the farther you get into the game. There's also no handholding. They tell you what a product does but it's up to you to figure out how to best use it in a particular situation. Let's just say you can put sulfuric acid in a body wash but it's not recommended.
This game is heavy on the simulation aspect, too. My first few playthroughs were breaking beakers and spilling resources everywhere. It was colorful but not very productive.  Eventually I got the hang of it though and it became natural and fluid and quite a lot of fun. It's quite different in that respect from most simulation games you'll play.
It's still a work in progress and I expect much will change before it's fully finished but if I had to give a single reason to purchase The Chemist it would be to support this developer. I don't know them personally but I've had some interaction with them since the game hit Steam and it's been nothing but positive. I do know that if more developers were like alpha (the devs Steam name) then gaming would vastly improve. No attitude. No assholishness. No "it's my game so screw you and your input." Just great customer response and service. Gamers should buy the game just to keep alpha in the business of developing games. Considering what we've seen from other developers our happiness may depend on it. Thanks, and happy gaming.

I also have a good understanding of languages like Java, C# and C++ and OpenGL and use a Java framework for coding Android games at the company I work in. Well, the thing that I liked the most in GMS2 is how they are handling Tiles. It is really what they should have implemented from the very beginning. I slowly stopped using Game Maker Studio 1.4 for making large tile-based maps because the way GMS 1.4 handled tiles was pathetic and I really question the reason for including such a crappy system.
With GMS 2.0 it is different. Now they have started using a system that can be said as one of the most efficient ways of handling tiles (if they are only drawing the tiles between the camera coordinates, but that's what I suppose).
Also, the room editor is a blast with many nice features.
The included image editor now supports Drawing to multiple layers which is really nice.
--- Requests to GMS 2.0 Team ---
- However, I would request the addition of the IMAGE COLORIZATION, GRADIENT FILL and other animation related features (from GMS 1.4) back in GMS 2.0. They were truly useful.
- Also add the airbrush that was there in 1.4.
- Add a more efficient way of iterating through arrays. It is really slow.
And above all:- Please ADD MULTITHREADING SUPPORT, even though accessible by some complex pathway and NOT recommended for naive coders. (I understand concurrency issues and all, but now there are advanced users of GMS and they will get a lot of help from multithreading)
I have only used GMS 2.0 for 4 hrs, so have not touched all features yet.
UPDATE 1
The image editor is worse than I initially thought. I really feel they should make it at least as good as GMS 1.4's. When I used GMS 1.4, I felt like using a complete program and was confident that I don't have to switch to other drawing software for small thing. But I can NOT say the same thing for GMS 2.0. It feels like a very incomplete feature and I really wish they work on it, because a complete (even though complete) set of drawing tools would be very helpful for most hobbyist developers.

Once I knew what I was doing and I could get a decent spawn near a river, I could expand my ♥♥♥♥-happy society across the biggest map before the 3rd generation of my society was getting gray hair. There's no real 'research' or empire building mechanics. No ability to send caravans of people elsewhere to start new colonies. No real options other than to get your resources sustainable in line with your population. And all that said, this game is still enjoyable. It's totally fine at what it does. I just don't think that what it does is worth a full $20. Pick this one up on sale for 5 or 10 bucks.

It's surprising how research and progressing through eras makes this game feel fresh and new. There's more to do now, more to fight for, but it's also become a little bit easier in my opinion. However the series seems to have lost much of the personalities of the citizens, I rarely find the need to micro-manage citizens, and issuing edicts on them hardly seems worthwhile. They're just numbers in Tropico 5. Also, the music is more akin to the original Tropico, which is a little calmer and suits well the with colonial era.
Surprisingly, the campaign involves only two islands at first! You go back and forth between these islands as the campaign progresses, keeping progress between missions. Then, after the first chapter is complete, you get two new islands to play on, but these are somewhat more difficult. The ending was a bit abrupt, but all in all a satisfactory and somewhat challenging campaign.
The game has no official support for mods (the devs find it too troublesome to offer support on mod issues), but they still allow mods in the game. I suggest having a look at them, as there are some additions which the devs should have though of from the beginning. Also, the new multiplayer feature seems interesting, though I haven't tried it yet.
On the minus side, the game is quite lacking in buildings compared to the previous Tropico. Some people seem to think this is so they can earn more money on over-priced DLC (which I tend to agree, far too expensive for something that's little more than a fan mod), but the game is still enjoyable without the DLC.
If you like the Tropico series, this game won't let down. It's more of the same, with some imho great new flavours.

The Chemist is relaxing and chill, but at the same time does require you to think a little because you have to manage money, chemicals, contracts, deadlines, and logisitcs. Its very satisfying.

I'm really looking forward for what this game has to offer, because its really a great idea. For an early access title this game already seems polished, streamlined, and really well thought out.

Attention: Really heavy subjective review with criticism for modern horror game design. Don´t be a silly fanboy or  b  i  t  c  h   and comment before not giving it a proper thought. Let´s go on then.
Why do I not like one of the most loved Horror games?
Needing batteries and having to preserve them aren´t my cup of tea. I hate the idea of a night vision lasting 5 mins until you get to use another pair of batteries and once you are down on them too/all of them, your vision is basically just becoming an annoyance, a hinderance which disables you from exploring many dark areas thoroughly. Annoying in the sense of   s  h  i   t   t   y   depth of field, chromatic abberation or film grain  but ALSO in the sense that you have to heavily rely on that crappy filter madness and night vision itself so much that it disconnects itself from the world. All that in a game which would sell its atmopshere way better without night vision constantly on. Such a shame in game design. Just integrate a second mode into the camera with flashlight. Maybe now we can find a solution.
I want to slowly explore this game, look at every nook and granny, but it has this psychological effect of pressuring me in hurrying the  f  u c  k   up because of this unrealistic battery system while I wanna play on the hardest difficulty.... It´s   f  u  c  k  e  d   up. Afterall the battery system serves no active effect in avoiding or battling your enemies. Just give me a camera without all this battery  b u l l s h i t . Fixed. Afterall you can just take down the camera and disable the night vision, but that´s not the issue here as it doesn´t fix the issue of still not having an illumination device, it´s basically just filter madness camera view battery saver mode. If you actually want to enjoy this game without being hesitated by this game design, you can´t avoid the garbage night vision game design. And that pisses me off.
If you hide from enemies and don´t use night vision or have run out of batteries and rely on your hearing, you basically notice that it´s becoming way more fun that way, but also hard as   f  u  c  k   as the darkness hides them so very well too and none of the level design or generally speaking, element of the game balances it out well enough to not needing to rely on the night vision, meaning, the level design and general stealth design don´t support a non night vision playthrough without making it a hell for the player.
All that coupled with always being in some kinda locker or under a bed, just becomes a game of patience. When to progress is often just a lame approach of when does the f  u  c  k  ing  a  s  s  h  o  l e  go away. Not my cup of horror. I wish it was more like: How can I smartly trick him into going away? Throw a brick would be enough for me already, even the very basics such like these are missing from the game. You often just flip some switch, lure him to your vicinity, hide somewhere and he goes away. Annoying to say the least. The sheer pressure is part of the game, but for me it was just torment and fun was pushed aside for faked stresslevels. Watching over my batteries more than over my life. How  r e t a r d e d .
I just have the feeling that I play a levelforced idiot with breathing issues trying to get himself killed and I´m constantly reminded of that. I needed more logic and character development than just an silent protagonist playing down what the devs throw in front of me. In the end you just rush the game.
Due to blackscreen crashes etc, technical isssues unfixable, I waited till evening and watched an immersive Let´s Play as I didn´t want to forcelie this review, which I usually never do, and could confirm what I feared the most. The game even if I played on, had a complete lack of variety and continues its issues.
Graphics and controls are standard, nothting new. Interaction button, and run button, nightvision
button, crouch etc. Done. Graphics fit the presentation but never look really great. Pretty mediocre textures and models. Shadows look decent, shaders barely exist. Meh, graphically. Would say Thief III looks even better than this in many points except for the low poly models of 2004 of course.
If you like the hide n run patience games like this one is, you will find Outlast to be the top notchest game out there. But for me true horror starts when I have to act freely and find myself helpless by my own actions in an immersive atmopsheric world which makes me feel hopeless and depressed with good depth of gameplay, even if a gun or fighting system exists or if the gameplay just is one of stealth, true stealth. !Thief 3: Deadly Shadows The Cradle level! But hide n seek is    f   u  c  k  i  n  g   boring to me if it continues without gameplay depth like actual stealth games often provide them. And I hate this whole amnesia, soma, outlast trend. Give me chances to be witty... I´m not a brianless hipster pressing only two buttons all the time.  Not , yeah just run to the locker, hide under this and wait for the dumb  f  u  c  k  to go away. Horror starts for me where the unbelievable begins to haunt. This game is prediction after prediction too, sadly.

I can keep beat this game with every single setting on its hardest in sandbox mode. Getting to the next era (Colonial, World Wars, Cold Wars, Modern) is very difficult. Pros.
-The unique challenges of each era (colonial, world wars, cold wars, modern) basically turn each sandbox game into 4 different mini games. This extends gameplay.
-Once the trading logistics is mastered, it is very useful.
-The randomized quest force the player to react to different situations each game, ensuring no repititive gameplay.
-The ABSOLUTE BEST implementation of a xbox controller for strategy game that I am currently aware of (on pc).
-The tropico series in general, is a very unique game that has a pleasent blend of violence and simcity.
-Game length is good. 3-4+ hours.
Cons
-This game requires advanced logistics, but doesn't provide the tools or controls to micro-manage them. For example, I can't control which dock resources that are traded are delivered too. Nor can I control which farm/factory teamsters will go to. I have to basically build teamstears near buildings that are important.
-The thing that I hate the most about this game is that it desperately needs districts. I want to be able to set different policies for different parts of the island and it would be cool, if certain districts could be attacked/occupied by rebels. I am thinking like the hunger games.  You have a capital district where all the rich/military people are. Then poor-improverised districts spread out through the island.
-I don't like this single building DLC. I would rather have large expansions and higher price points on those.
-I don't like buying tropico after tropico. It is redicilous. Just stick with one and release "real" full priced expansion packs  (I am talking like game changing features like districts. I would pay $50-$60 for real expansion packs)

Initially I was very interested in Evolve. Asymmetric gameplay is a big undiscovered world with much potential and as a former dedicated L4D2 player I was hyped for this game.
Unfortunately this excitement vanished with the beta. To me the game feels empty and pointless. Arbitrary character progression is in place to give you a reason to play but the upgrades and perks you achieve do not make much of a difference. As some content is only unlocked by said progression, the system acts as a feature block, forcing you into a grind.
That would be okayish - L4D has no progression at all - the problem is, that most battles are very linear, one sided and just not as deep as one would wish, making the grind a chore.
I do not see Evolve being fun for a long time.. it's an okay game for in between.
That said I am very surprised by the insane price model the publisher is pushing here. Evolve really has not enough to offer, to justify a price point of $60 - let alone a package of DLC ramping the whole thing up to $120. This approach is not only priced without any regard to the market or the quality of your product, it's also confusing for anyone who just wants to enjoy a game.

Some people just realised that the so called Hunting Season Pass actually is not a season pass. It is a single DLC package called the "Hunting Season" Pass. This is not even cheeky anymore, this is fraud. Stay away.

This game shares the same structure and mechanical flaws that Half-Life has, being effectively the same game.  Where this game is set apart from that game though, is in the construction and flow of the game.  This one, (a much shorter game), flows much better, and other than one or two spots, it forgoes the platform game style that Half-Life has.  Only occassionally do you have to leap, duck and weave across impossible terrain and asinine engineered structures, and by the removal of this completely annoying aspect of the original game, this one has not aged as poorly....
Let's face it, games back then, especially of this genre, grew from those platform styled games, and it's what game developers knew, but it's old hat and it doesn't stack up well.  Thankfully Blue Shift doesn't fall into that old game cliche often.
The plot for Blue Shift flows better as well.  Instead of just hunting down an alien to kill it, this is a better defined story arc, requiring working towards a non-violent goal of escape (though not without a good dose of alien and military murder-mayhem along the way).  Interesting, considering in the original you're a scientist and this one you're a security guard.
For anyone that is curious about Half-Life, this is probably the game for you, since it's short and IMO, better.  (still be prepared for Crate Smashing II - Return of the Exploding Rubbish, and for clunky and clumsy game controls.

Bought this on a recommendation for a relaxing game to play after a long day at work. Wow was that a bad idea. This game annoys at almost every level.
Art: OK the art style is pretty nice.
Story: Beats me. According to the game description it's about metamorphosis. Call me crazy but I was not aware that caterpillars morph into grasshoppers, which then morph into bees. Did I miss that day in high school biology?
Hidden picture mechanic: It works. It's not annoying. That's about the highest praise I can give this game.
Music: Dear god no. Annoying. Annoying. Annoying. Annoying. Annoying. Does that constant repetition annoy you? Then you will hate the music for this game. Actually, calling it "music" is generous. It's the same 4 bars repeating over and over. And over. And over. And over. And over. And over.
Puzzles: Puzzles are completely unintuitive with no feedback whatsoever on how to complete them. I had to go to YouTube for half the puzzles just to figure out what the heck I was supposed to do in order to play the puzzle. Not how to solve the puzzle. How to PLAY the puzzle.That is terrible game design.
Movement: Oh good god please save me. I can watch an entire season of Arrested Development in the time it takes my bug to move across one screen. And that's only IF my bug doesn't get stuck somewhere rotating back and forth forever. In the very first level, within the first two minutes of the game, I would click the bottom half of the screen to try to collect an item and my damn bug would decide to walk up and transition to the screen above. EVERY SINGLE TIME. I think I read the entirety of the Shakespeare canon whilst waiting for these transition screens to finish and allow me to collect each item down there.
Ending: There is no ending. Sorry to spoil it.
Achievements: Don't work.
Verdict: I only paid $0.49 for this game, so it's hard to say that it's not worth the money. However, I'm far more upset about the time in my life that is now gone than I am about the fifty cents. The joy of a good game is in learning and improving.  A good game provides clear, consistent rules and rewards you for playing better, smarter, cleaner.
Cuphead wants to test you, but more than that, it wants you to get better.  When you fail, you know why it happened,  There are no mysteries to its mechanics, and it makes no effort to slap you down with the unknown or unknowable.  And yes, proper execution is still a barrier even if your strategy is sound, but Cuphead always values cleanliness and consistency over reflexes.
This is that rarest of games where difficulty is a product of smart design rather than variables being ratcheted up to the point of punishment.  In other words, it's fun to fail, because you always know that you can succeed if you keep trying.
And I guess it's a neat bonus that Cuphead is one of the most achingly beautiful video games ever released.  Just like its play design, every stitch of its presentation is thoughtful and lush.  The amazing visual design and animation are self-evident, but just the little things: the fonts, the menus, the wonderful tap-dancing rapid fire sound of your default weapon.  Cuphead is deliberate to a degree that makes other, bigger, pricier games feel slapdash.
I think just about everyone can get something from Cuphead, even those who tend to find "hard" games intimidating.

Starting from best to worst:
1) Fresh idea - I played as many things, but never a bug.
2) Minigames are fine - nothing I haven't seen before, but nicely done.
3) Visualy the game is no masterpiece. Hand-drawn, OK, but the shapes and colours seem random, chaotic.
4) Music is so boring and repetitive that it literally put an innocent bystander to sleep. That's what's supposed to be relaxing here, I guess.
5) Each chapter is pretty much the same. At second one you already know what to click, what will be gathered and what creature you're be biting into.
6) The controls are made in HELL ITSELF.
a) There are some random points near corners on some boards that makes the bug go in unpredicted direction (eg. you click at the bottom of last board and it goes up to the next).
b) Once you start crossing from board to board, there's no stopping or going back until it's on the other side - and that takes AGES (so does waiting for gathered items to float to inventory).
c) If you hold the mouse clicked a second too long while going to next board, you might get sent back to the previous one (again, no stopping before the action is completed).
d) There's no saying where you can pass and where not.
e) Changing direction is animated as a sudden flip that personally flips me out. The whole game is soooo sloooow and then you have those random jumps out of nowhere. Vietnam flashbacks or what?
f) You have to drag the bug every step of the way (and it's moving very slowly), each time, every time.
g) You can't stop in between boards (although they are fully drawn and animated) and you can't skip to them either.
Enough, this is getting too long.
TL;DR: the game is not relaxing, it's just extremly slow, repetitive and frustrating.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the shortest of the two expansions for Half-Life that provides the back story of Barney Calhoun as he fights to escape Black Mesa with other science personnel.  Players may recall Barney's role in Half-Life 2 and in the case of Blue Shift, it felt nice to view the events of Half-Life through a different lense, just as in Oposing Force.  That being said, the game is indeed short and does not really introduce anything new in terms of weapons or gameplay compared to Half-Life.  The only major gameplay difference is that Barney cannot use the H.E.V. charging stations and instead must collect armor vests and helmets (actually a nice throwback to older shooters).  You'll go back to Xen for a short mission but most of the time you will be working your way through Black Mesa resuing scientists.  There are a few nods to other games in the Half-Life timeline too scattered throughout Barney's journey.  For the price and length of the game, I'd recommend getting this on a sale if you enjoyed Half-Life and want more lore.

Do I recommend this game itself? Definitely, because I think its awesome and I had a great time with it. Do I recommend it for its full price? Probably not. The story mode is very short, and you'll probably be done with it in about three hours. Just for that, the price is very steep. I did get 25h out of it, but that covers doing everything the game has to offer, such as getting collectibles, playing endless arenas and doing all challenges, which is basically playing through the game many times with different rules and restrictions, drastically changing how you play and which means you use to get through the levels. Most of this isn't unique content though, so I'm sure a lot of people will not care about it. Completionists do have a bit of content to work on here, which can get very challenging as well. I did get lucky in several ways in some challenges, and if I didn't it could have taken me several more hours to 100% it. But I could have easily spent several less hours if I quit when it started getting too repetitive. All in all, it depends on how much you think you're going to get out of the game, but waiting for a discount is definitely a good idea.
A quick rundown for people unfamiliar with the game; time only moves when you do, allowing you to stand still and look around to see where enemies and bullets are coming from in order to dodge them. You can string some phenomenal combos together, which in combination with quite some freedom in how to beat each level made me love my playthrough of it. Throwing objects at enemies, punching them to death, taking their guns, jumping on top of a guy, making them shoot each other, slicing a bullet in half with a katana and then throwing the katana to impale someone are just some of the things you can pull off. I'd describe some of the combo's I've done, but words just wouldn't do it justice. Have a look at the artwork section to see some gifs instead. It just gets awesome when things work out, and after beating a level you see a replay of what you did in real time, which is a nice touch and makes you look like a god. The means of narration and menu browsing were quite refreshing, and adds to the game's already great and unique style.

Train Valley might look like a 'casual' game, but it's far from easy, and approaching it as a loose, casual game will only bring you grief! You need to make friends with the 3-step speed controls and the Pause button in order to succeed. That's because although laying your track is half the battle, the funds to build and destroy it come from the deliveries you make, and crashes and wrong destinations all impact your income. In other words, the main fight here is with scheduling your trains.
The game mechanics are fairly intuitive, and of course the more you play, the more you understand. In this way, Train Valley is both rewarding and frustrating, because there are still some things that require some time and attention to understand. One key concept here, which I'm still not entirely sure about really, is of your trains taking off of their own accord once the cargo value timer has dropped to a certain point. This appears as a set of tiny figures above each train, and if I have only one complaint with the game, it's that this essential bit of information is too small to see comfortably. There is a handy option to scale the UI up and down, although the figures don't scale with it.
The feedback between your tack layouts and the efficiency of your scheduling is pretty tight -- get one right, and the other will work so much the better too. With successive timely deliveries made, your cash reserves will be able to cope with the odd crash or mis-direction. In the end though, it's easy to over-spend, so walking that tightrope between track design and scheduling is, again, crucial.
As much as Train valley is about quickly clicking on your junctions and switches, the game definitely gives your brain a good workout, in much the same way that Bridge Constructor-type games do. I think it's well worth the 10 Euro Steam price, although I got mine for 2 Euros from Bundlestars, which is an absolute steal, frankly. Great game, and I highly recommend it.

It's a good story manifested in a game, and the game is it's downfall.
The general gist is: You are an unterzee (under sea) captain exploring the depths. You travel in your ship from place to place to interact with things and keep the story going.
The biggest issue I have with this game is EVERYTHING to do with sailing the ship from place to place. It's a very, very slow minigame of you mostly just avoiding combat to get to the next place to continue the story. In fact, my hours would be a third of what they are, had I been able to just say "Set sail for this place" and then have RNG decide if I encounter a monster or arrive there peacefully.
The next big issue is the quest log/inventory. It is disgustingly unclear, and understanding what certain things are used for is difficult. This is a big problem, because for some things, you might have fair reason to know what it is, why you have it, where you're going next, etc. For other things, you're not meant to know. So Google runs a risk of telling something you actually don't want to know.
And the final issue brings us back to sailing, and is the combat. There were only ever three enemies I bothered to fight, because the combat system is truly awful and adds nothing to the game.
Overall, I wish they'd just made this a text-adventure game. I really love the world and want to be involved in the story, but the slow sailing speed killed it for me. It's a fun mechanic to begin with, but after an hour you'll just end up thinking "I just want to get to the ♥♥♥♥ing salt lions".

The tumbs down is because I do not recommend this game, not because I didn't enjoy the game. This is my first Telltale game, there were things that I really enjoyed and some not so much. I hope this review will shed some light to some newcomers such as myself to help them make the right decision, of course everyone thinks differently so this is just my impression, ironically this game is all about decisions. Without further ado, I will start positively addressing all the things I do like about this game.
The good thing about this game and its strongest selling point is the story. I'm a big Batman fan, I enjoyed his darker stories across all media, whether throught the comics, movies or videogames, if Batman was in it, I needed to see it. In this version of Batman the writers got pretty creative with Batman background by changes some stuff around, this keeps some fan on their toes on picking who or who not to trust. This is great for me because it felt like I was learning about Batman again for the first time and made some choices difficult. The music was also great, it really gives that epic Batman vibe to everything and keeps you on edge. And finally the choices you make through out the game impacts the story, so there's good reason to come back and play again after you beat the game.
But that's the thing that also negatively affects this game, I have no desire to jump right back in and play the game again,  at least not for awhile if you have a huge backlog of games like I do. I see this as a movie, you see it once and with the story fresh in your mind you probably don't want to rewatch it for awhile, well here is the same concept. Getting to point in case this game feel more like a movie than a game, a movie that you can make some choices to alter it's path. That's why it makes it so hard to review as a game, it's as if the creators have no clue who their target audience is, it's not a game like the Arkham games, but it's not a movie either, so who is this supposed to appeal to, both or neither? I find this oversight irritating because there's alot of wasted potential here. If this is meant to be a game, it's too short, too easy, and even through multiple playthrough there's just not enough gameplay, so as a game it's lacking. As a mobile game however this might work, perhaps I was too hasty when I bought the steam version, I should've done more research. If you have the option I would pick mobile since there's not much gameplay needed and I imagine the swipe touch screen would fit perfectly here, not to mention being portable so you can take it anywhere like a book. Also another big issue I had with the game was the quality, I couldn't get a stable frame rate to save my life, I was constantly getting frame drops that killed my experience with game, even though I can easily get stable fps on more demanding games like Arkham Knight. This is another reason I don't see any reason to go with the steam version of this game, your specs are wasted here, no matter how good your computer is, you will get frame drops because of poor optimization, which probably will do better on a mobile.
Overall my score for this game is a 6/10, good story with great twists but poor gameplay probably more suited for different devices.

Yes, I will acknowledge that this radically changes some characters, but these changes are, for the most part, a breath of fresh air. This series does not take place in any established universe, this story is entirely self-contained, and as such, I believe it works to an incredible degree. The Penguin is styled much more closely to the Gotham portrayal of the character, and Two-Face's origin, while fairly rushed, is still very harsh and believable. Catwoman is an absolute standout and steals the show whenever she is on-screen. She is so much stronger and better realized character than in Artkham City or Arkham Knight. But I think this game's shining achievement is making Bruce Wayne an interesting character, which is VERY hard to do as most filmmakers and comic authors can attest to. All in all, it's not a 'classic' Batman story, it doesn't hit all the same beats as the Arkham series, or adapt any well known stories like the animated movies, but taken as it's own product, it is an amazingly well-realized, stunningly gorgeous, and incredibly well written experience. What a hell of a game.

I rememember quickly picking up and putting down Bioshock 2 on Sony (free on PS Plus) approx 5 years ago and hating it. I didn't know how to take it (was used to generic shooters back then) or take the time to appreciate the world/setting. Before you say "oh,but It's a different game",I didn't give it a chance at all and formed an opinion on Bioshock as a whole from the get go. As you can imagine,when this came in a bundle I purchased,I wasn't really that excited about it,but seeing Steam reviews convinced me to install and try it. To my suprise,I love it and would now consider it one of my favourite FPS's. A few notes from my experience:
. Runs decent for an older game on a modern system. Had a no in-game audio bug to begin with which was easily fixed with a Google search and occassionally have what appears to be a load stutter,but overall it runs pretty smooth
. The graphics still hold up strong today,they're beautiful (especially maxed out in Nvidia control panel)
. The gameplay is amazing,I love being able to swap between weapons and powers with the click of a button. Both feel satisfying and fun to use throughout. At first the controls and player movement felt really weird to use,but a quick Google search and some changes to the .ini file fixed this to be more like FPS controls,rather than optimised for console. Love the upgrade system also,heaps of different options up until the end to keep the game fresh. The world and environment is like no other you'll find in a game,and is quite an experience
. This gameplay is quite repetitive throughout,so If you do/don't enjoy it in the first hour,you're going to experience more of the same later on. That being said,everything is done so damn well,and is quite addictive If you get into it
. It's weird and I'm not sure If it's just me,but I uninitentionally didn't follow the story or dialogue,It just didn't grab me and make me pay attention. I just automatically phased out for the entire game without even realising. Seeing so many positive reviews for this crediting It's story means I may have to play it again,and this time really concentrate on the storyline. It does go to show just how captivating and enjoyable the gampelay and environment really is though
. This game contains heaps of looting throughout,theres more things to loot than not and I found it didn't get boring like most games. I didn't realise how much time I spent looting until now. While there's no Steam achievements,I found this actually took the pressure off me to find every collectible,and focus my time on enjoying the game
All in all,It's well worth the $20 asking price,let alone the small amount I paid for it. It has converted me,and I'm now looking forward to playing the others in the series

The whole point of the game is to work together with each and every member of your team/squad to achieve a goal using flanking, smoke and clearing, suppressive fire while rifleman advance, and nailing excellent shots on moving targets from 100 meters away.  This game is a tactician's dream.  If you want to be a rifleman sweating behind a rock trying to avoid certain death from a pounding MG, a squad leader leading the charge of 15 men into a successful capture, a flamethrower wiping out bunkers of fleeing Japanese, or rain artillery from above as a team leader, you can do this and even more as a soldier in Rising Storm and Red Orchestra 2 alone.  This game is a must-buy for any PC gamer who claims they love a good challenge.  Believe me, once you're looking through the eyes of a Pacific soldier down Guadalcanal or German machine gunner on a freezing but heated front, you'll be hooked for hours and hours to come.

This is one of those games that LOOKS amazing.  It has amazing graphics.  It has amazing character design.  It has an amazing concept.
Unfortunately, it's just not fun to play.  In order to win as the monster, you have to run away until you're level 3.  Since it takes quite a while to reach level 3, most of the game is spent either sneaking around and slowly growing as the monster, or searching a gigantic map for a monster that can easily get away unless the trapper sneaks up on it.  When the fight finally takes place, it's usually over before the first barrier ends, and the winner is decided by what level the monster reached.
The only time this isn't the case is when both teams are very skilled.  A VERY skilled hunter team can survive fighting a level 3 monster, and a very skilled monster can abuse line of sight to avoid combat while inside a barrier.  This means when you get better, your games change to a stalemate until level 3, and then a very long, drawn out endurance match between hunters that can split up and fly away from you and a monster that can duck around corners until it gets a chance to eat and heal.
As a result, the game is only fun while the novelty lasts, which for me was a few hours.
It would be more interesting if both teams started out even and the hunters could find equipment upgrades around the map that allow them to "level up" too, turning it into a race of who can evolve faster.  This would give the monster a reason to seek out the hunters and attack them if the monster is evolving more quickly.  It would also give a defensive purpose to the barrier, to keep a monster OUT while hunters search for gear.  At least then, both sides would have an interest in forcing engagements, so more engagements might actually happen, and the monster would actually have an opportunity to win in the first 10 minutes of a match.

Very fun, and requires a ton of team work. However, if you do manage well in a team, the game can be extreme amounts of fun. As a monster, you have to be careful and manage your strategies effectively just as much as the hunters must do so. There are four classes to decide from as hunters, and each one will have to communicate and do their part properly if you want a successful victory. Thus, this is why playing with friends is a good idea.
Unfortunately, the game will be plagued with negative reviews due to the whole DLC fiasco. I do agree that this indeed is an overpriced game. (Base game: $60 (thank goodness?), Deluxe: $80, Monster Race: $100). I heavily dislike DLC and the current plague it has on our generation's games. In this case, it appears the DLC includes skins, a fifth monster, ect. I wouldn't have outright called this situation out if it wasn't for the fact that the >fifth< monster is DLC, nor the preorder one. This, however, was DLC ANNOUNCED even before release or anything, so it obviously has been taken the wrong way, not including the behemoth. That was NOT a good idea to include monsters as DLC, because they are a major point of the game's core. So, a bit of mixed feelings on this whole ordeal. Another thing is, whether you like this whole DLC fiasco or not, most of today's game (including those from the past few years) will always have a DLC ordeal like this. It's not a question of taking things personal because of this, but the fact that you either purchase the game or not, simple as that. Don't grunt and mourne on your reviews like this is all a new thing, because it's not. Released maps for this game will be free.
Nevertheless, as I said, the game is fun, and I recommend it if you wish to play some serious co-op with friends. I still believe it has good replay value, and that's including the rest of the game modes, or if you wish to practice yourself against bots. Whether the game will be ongoing in the next year or so is dependent on you, the consumers. It will keep ahold for those who enjoy the game, not for those to take it personal over the DLC.
And no, I payed the regular $60, which is good enough for me. If half the game's out there somewhere else, then there's no need for me to spend any more money for a price I believe should be justifiable enough. I'm not being forced to buy it, and I have no reason to castrate a game for it, with the reasons included above.
The game appears to be properly optimized on my system. 60 frames per second is achieveable and uninterrupted at resolutions 1920x1080, 1920x1200, ect, but don't mourne over the fact that you can't achieve it on a 4k resolution, because you won't. Infact, this may actually be one of the smoothest releases of this year on my system.

Maybe you'll evade the wolves long enough to acquire a decent weapon.  If you can tough it out, you'll become the predator, strolling around proudly wearing the wolfskin coat, deer hide boots and pants, and rabbitskin mitts.  If you're particularly savvy with your rifle and flare gun, you'll even manage to sleep soundly in a handmade bearskin bedroll. It's a good story manifested in a game, and the game is it's downfall.
The general gist is: You are an unterzee (under sea) captain exploring the depths. You travel in your ship from place to place to interact with things and keep the story going.
The biggest issue I have with this game is EVERYTHING to do with sailing the ship from place to place. It's a very, very slow minigame of you mostly just avoiding combat to get to the next place to continue the story. In fact, my hours would be a third of what they are, had I been able to just say "Set sail for this place" and then have RNG decide if I encounter a monster or arrive there peacefully.
The next big issue is the quest log/inventory. It is disgustingly unclear, and understanding what certain things are used for is difficult. This is a big problem, because for some things, you might have fair reason to know what it is, why you have it, where you're going next, etc. For other things, you're not meant to know. So Google runs a risk of telling something you actually don't want to know.
And the final issue brings us back to sailing, and is the combat. There were only ever three enemies I bothered to fight, because the combat system is truly awful and adds nothing to the game.
Overall, I wish they'd just made this a text-adventure game. I really love the world and want to be involved in the story, but the slow sailing speed killed it for me. It's a fun mechanic to begin with, but after an hour you'll just end up thinking "I just want to get to the ♥♥♥♥ing salt lions".

That being said, they WILL reimburse any chips that you lost to bugs if you send in a ticket, contrary to what many other reviews have claimed.
But aside from the bugs, the game is really quite solid. Most of the time all the games and machines work perfectly fine, and the variety is good. They also run tournaments periodically for when you're feeling a bit more competitive.

In order to get free chips, you can do both daily and weekly tasks that reward you with chips. After that, you get one Super Slot spin per day. But beyond that the game is reasonably generous. When you win chips, you also slowly build up premium currency. You can win your way into the VIP lounge by playing enough, and many of the cosmetics can be attained by earning achievments.
The social elements of the game feel somewhat forced but that's true of most MMO-styled games.
Overall, if you like casino games, you can't go wrong giving this a try.

This one saddens me.
For singleplayer gaming, there is no reason whatsoever to play this game, as it's significantly dumbed down from Tropico 4, and the core gameplay and engine are still pretty much unchanged from Haemimont's first, Tropico 3 (beyond the DX11 minimum requirements here).
Compared to 'T4', large layers of complexity have been removed, building variety 'simplified', and so on. Where previous titles had fires break out, and a fire station to fight these, this was essentially cut from the game with few exceptions, and fire-fighting is provided by an upgrade to the police station. Where previous titles would give you a convincing degree of control over your economy & housing, here you may merely set a 'budget' slider that affects everything from quality to costs. Gone is the feeling that you can freely choose to give housing to the masses or expensive mansions to the rich -- or to go full-on far-left and build beautiful mansions for the unemployed. Gone too is the notion of having plentiful factions with their own ideals on your island, forcing you to make meaningful choices. The reduced amount of factions among your citizens never make you feel they are actual entities with their own agendas (a feeling prevalent in, say, the first Tropico).
It's truly telling that when you first start this game with a game controller connected, it makes you play with console-specific UI / menus / controls.
Like in any The Sims title, all the content you're used to from the previous ones' DLCs is again gone, to let you await the opportunity to re-buy similar stuff when it gets released for the current game.
Besides some mildly funny pop-culture references, the SP campaign is entirely forgettable and not worth playing.
For completionists, each major DLC adds 10 achievements to make it impossible to "100%" the game without buying all of the massively overpriced expansions.
The multiplayer, a first in the series, is what should make this game worth buying.
It is, however, full of bugs, glitches and design issues.
That they only added the option to save your game in multiplayer after release should be telling - the mode doesn't feel like it received any playtesting. Very often some form of desync occurs, which for whatever idiotic reasons disables the ability to save completely. If you don't manually save every 5 to 10 minutes, you will soon lose hours of progress to this (auto-saving exists only in SP).
The worst thing is that any player even just alt-tabbing from the game in borderless windowed mode, while you watch the game run normally in the background, seems to always cause an initially hidden desync. Soon you won't be able to save and then you find out that everybody has their own version of reality, with buildings complete/incomplete/destroyed, armies stuck in fields unable to move, and so on.
Speaking about armies, when playing cooperatively your armies help each other out -- but that always bugs up to get the combined Tropican Defense Force stuck at the place of their last engagement instead of letting them return to their bases, so in the mid to late game, you will have rebels in the south and all the army in the north, unable to get there before your buildings are annihilated... every single time. If you don't team up from the start, there are some diplomatic options, but they don't involve temporarily sending military aid to your friends -- you either accept the inevitable problems or can't help each other.
Inexplicably, things like removing roads just don't work properly in MP, and you will likely be stuck with any accidental constructions.
Knowing Haemimont and Kalypso, none of this is bound to get fixed -- as an example, they and the equally inept AMD managed to break water rendering in the game with the 'Omega' graphics driver release in late 2014/early 2015, and neither side has managed to do anything to solve this in over half a year.
EDIT: The AMD-specific water rendering issue was eventually largely fixed with a game update, but it still depends on the precise AMD driver you're running.

The Beginner's Guide is genuinely thought provoking.
First off, and without going into any real analysis or content, it's unfair to call this game pretentious. It never pretends to be anything it isn't, and the ideas present are all stated plainly through the game's environments and narration, that is, until they aren't, but designed ambiguity doesn't mean something is pretentious. This is one of those rare instances where it actually enriches the experience. The game does an excellent job at transitioning from a curated walking simulator where you learn about design and personal expression into a walking simulator where you feel like you're getting some bigger answers from the margins. I personally found it to be affecting in a way that kind of surprised me, and the revelations stick with me still.
