Tropico 5 is still a Tropico game through and through, although it is a slight step below Tropico 4.
There has been a lot of reviews that say that Tropico 4 is better, and it is, but Tropico 5 is still a fun game and that doesn't mean you should skip it.
In Tropico you still play as a lovable dictator leading his latin america island to glory. You have to manage the economy, population happiness, military defence and politics in order to survive.
There is flexibility in what economy you want, whether it be exporting raw materials like iron and coffee, turning them into goods like steel or canned food, or tourism.
Politics is more advanced than in Tropico 4, where you have the Constitution which affects your country in different ways, and what you choose will affect your standings with the external world powers and also the internal factions in your country.
The things that Tropico 4 did better are little things like Penultimo being voiced by a goofy hilarious voice actor, but in Tropico 5 he sounds like a monotonous person with no charisma.
Tropico 4 also had nice music with the singing, but Tropico 5 doesn't.
These little things however create the funny and fun atmosphere that Tropico is famed for, and something that is slightly missing in Tropico 5.
Overall Tropico 5 is still a good game for people who love the franchise. But if you have never played Tropico 4, that game may be more worth your money.

I rememember quickly picking up and putting down Bioshock 2 on Sony (free on PS Plus) approx 5 years ago and hating it. I didn't know how to take it (was used to generic shooters back then) or take the time to appreciate the world/setting. Before you say "oh,but It's a different game",I didn't give it a chance at all and formed an opinion on Bioshock as a whole from the get go. As you can imagine,when this came in a bundle I purchased,I wasn't really that excited about it,but seeing Steam reviews convinced me to install and try it. To my suprise,I love it and would now consider it one of my favourite FPS's. A few notes from my experience:
. Runs decent for an older game on a modern system. Had a no in-game audio bug to begin with which was easily fixed with a Google search and occassionally have what appears to be a load stutter,but overall it runs pretty smooth
. The graphics still hold up strong today,they're beautiful (especially maxed out in Nvidia control panel)
. The gameplay is amazing,I love being able to swap between weapons and powers with the click of a button. Both feel satisfying and fun to use throughout. At first the controls and player movement felt really weird to use,but a quick Google search and some changes to the .ini file fixed this to be more like FPS controls,rather than optimised for console. Love the upgrade system also,heaps of different options up until the end to keep the game fresh. The world and environment is like no other you'll find in a game,and is quite an experience
. This gameplay is quite repetitive throughout,so If you do/don't enjoy it in the first hour,you're going to experience more of the same later on. That being said,everything is done so damn well,and is quite addictive If you get into it
. It's weird and I'm not sure If it's just me,but I uninitentionally didn't follow the story or dialogue,It just didn't grab me and make me pay attention. I just automatically phased out for the entire game without even realising. Seeing so many positive reviews for this crediting It's story means I may have to play it again,and this time really concentrate on the storyline. It does go to show just how captivating and enjoyable the gampelay and environment really is though
. This game contains heaps of looting throughout,theres more things to loot than not and I found it didn't get boring like most games. I didn't realise how much time I spent looting until now. While there's no Steam achievements,I found this actually took the pressure off me to find every collectible,and focus my time on enjoying the game
All in all,It's well worth the $20 asking price,let alone the small amount I paid for it. It has converted me,and I'm now looking forward to playing the others in the series

I wanted to like this game I really did, it impressed me early on but a quick downslide made me upset. The mechanics are solid, and the way the game progresses up to a certain point is smile inducing. Then for some reason this turns into the star wars prequels, just a major let down from early expectations.
So a little lingo that I use for this real quick; the game is broken down into 4 campaigns: US Army, US Navy, Japan Army, Japan Navy. Each campaign has a number of mission arcs that require you to go through 4 battles a piece.
Through each difficulty, the AI makes modest strides in its advancement, the basic AI is not where the real problem stems. The true problem stems in the artificial difficulty that crops up in Leader and Legend Mode. This is my first major issue with the game.
My second major issue with the game is the random objective battle generation. This too is broken at higher difficulties. With both issues combined you’re forced to find the portions of the coding that are mentally impaired and exploit those to no end. This literally saps the enjoyment that the game begins with away. I found it quite upsetting, truth be told.
Let’s start at Easy difficulty. Just don’t play this I had one battle per campaign mission where the enemy fighter just crashed into the ground for no reason. Like just started the battle and nosedived straight into the sea I just laughed. I went to normal shortly after and found the game to be enjoyable for a time. Then I went to ACE and found the game to be even better.
Unfortunately, these became easy to accomplish as well. I went to Very Hard and began to see some discrepancies in the application of certain rules. The first campaign mission arc I faced off against enemies whom felt no need to follow the 2 High G maneuver restriction and began throwing out three to four of these moves, making it extremely difficult to keep pace.  Mix in their two to three ACE maneuvers and you got a hell of a fight brewing on your hands.
Now, this wouldn’t be completely terrible if it weren’t for the mission selections. In Normal and ACE you can expect to see mostly fair fights with a rare unfair one early then becoming more abundant later on. Once you go to Leader mode though this gets thrown completely out of whack. You’ll suddenly face off in 3v1 battles very early on. I hope you can begin to see how the combination leads to some frustrating mission arcs.
Finally, I began to beat missions in Leader mode, but something was suddenly missing. The fun had totally evaporated. I wasn’t devising better tactics to combat the enemy I was exploiting weaknesses in the AI and that was it. I was using the same combinations over and over again. It became instantly repetitive. I was frustrated that the game boils down to proving you’re more flexible than a computer program. Check my achievements, you can see that I can beat 3v1 missions on Leader, it’s just that it’s not fun.
With the difficulties that I enjoyed ending up becoming easy quickly this game lost its fun factor after the second campaign. You’ll try and get more satisfaction from this but you’ll end up more disappointed than before you started that quest. It’s ok to enjoy bad things though so play on.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is similar to the episodic expansions for Half-Life 2, but in this case it Blue Shift expands of the world of the first Half-Life. Blue Shift has you play as Barney Calhoun, a security gaurd at Black Mesa who gets caught up in the events of the resonance cascade. The objective is the same as in the Half-Life main game, and that is to escape the horrible mess that you are entangled in. The graphics of the game are dated, but are not hard to look at, in fact I would say they give the game a charm to it. The game plays identically to the original Half-Life with no real new gameplay changes; same weapons, and same enemies. There are however a few new textures and characters that are part of the overarching Half-Life story. Blue Shift is an overall great experience that is a must have if you are trying to learn everything about the Half-Life universe.

Tropico 5 is still a Tropico game through and through, although it is a slight step below Tropico 4.
There has been a lot of reviews that say that Tropico 4 is better, and it is, but Tropico 5 is still a fun game and that doesn't mean you should skip it.
In Tropico you still play as a lovable dictator leading his latin america island to glory. You have to manage the economy, population happiness, military defence and politics in order to survive.
There is flexibility in what economy you want, whether it be exporting raw materials like iron and coffee, turning them into goods like steel or canned food, or tourism.
Politics is more advanced than in Tropico 4, where you have the Constitution which affects your country in different ways, and what you choose will affect your standings with the external world powers and also the internal factions in your country.
The things that Tropico 4 did better are little things like Penultimo being voiced by a goofy hilarious voice actor, but in Tropico 5 he sounds like a monotonous person with no charisma.
Tropico 4 also had nice music with the singing, but Tropico 5 doesn't.
These little things however create the funny and fun atmosphere that Tropico is famed for, and something that is slightly missing in Tropico 5.
Overall Tropico 5 is still a good game for people who love the franchise. But if you have never played Tropico 4, that game may be more worth your money.

The Beginner's Guide is genuinely thought provoking.
First off, and without going into any real analysis or content, it's unfair to call this game pretentious. It never pretends to be anything it isn't, and the ideas present are all stated plainly through the game's environments and narration, that is, until they aren't, but designed ambiguity doesn't mean something is pretentious. This is one of those rare instances where it actually enriches the experience. The game does an excellent job at transitioning from a curated walking simulator where you learn about design and personal expression into a walking simulator where you feel like you're getting some bigger answers from the margins. I personally found it to be affecting in a way that kind of surprised me, and the revelations stick with me still.

Fun and simple city builder, worth getting on sale.
It might feel like it's hard at the beginning, because Banished can be very unforgiving for your mistakes and a good play can turn into disaster with a blink of an eye. However once you get a handle of it, the game becomes extremely easy. It's a good choice for someone who wants to try the genre but doesn't want to get overwhelmed with too much management.
Unfortunately, for the same reason, it feels that the content it offers is very limited. Once you get your town up and running with enough supply of all the resources you need, there isn't much anything else to do, aside from collecting steam achievements and setting up your own goals.
This is where the fan made content is a real game changer. With amazing new buildings, challenges and more features, Banished really becomes something else. If you ever dreamed of building a great, breathtaking medieval city, you will love some of these mods and what they have to offer.
Another downside is the AI of your villagers. To express it simple - It's pretty bad. You learn to work around it as you play, but still, watching your little people starving to death, or not fulfilling their job because of the absurd AI, it can really tickle your nerves.
And if you dream of having a reeeally massive population, prepare yourself for FPS drops and more issues, as the game likes to just ... fall apart at that point.
Despite all that, Banished should provide enough hours of fun gameplay to return the money you'd spend on it.

This can lead to satisfying discoveries or frustrate the hell out of you, as it did for me in one situation. I would have liked more of an optional challenge system, hints and such.
There is no save function in level, which I would've liked simply because some of the puzzles can make you rage quit. If you do, you have to do the whole level again instead of just returning to the puzzle. There are also no hint option during the puzzles, even though for the hidden object portions they are available.
Also, I hate slider puzzles. Personal opinion, but apparently shared by many. That last puzzle was probably the main thing that tipped my scale over to not recommending this.

Looking at
store page a while back, I overlooked this game as a basic train simulator, when in fact it plays more of a puzzle game with some real-time strategy elements thrown in!
uses some fairly simple but effective rules. Lay a track between stations, and deliver as many trains without incident, as quickly as possible. You can choose where to lay the track, purchased from the earnings you get from train deliveries, and trigger when the trains depart. These are colour coded to let you know where to send the train. You can also rush trains by purchasing them for bonus score & turn trains around or stop them.  Your money is always going down so the pressure is on!
Where tracks overlap, you have get a switchboard, that you can reposition between your alternative track paths. On complex track layouts, this can be quite challenging to keep every train going where they should especially when you start to juggle multiple trains enroute at a single time. Good planning is a must!
Puzzle mechanics are easy, but increase exponentially as paths multiply. As you progress through the 20 scenarios
across 4 seasons, the difficulty is increased by putting more obstacles in your way, increasing the frequency of the trains & also other level specific challenges. Each level has 3 bonus goals to achieve as well, which can be done on multiple playthroughs. When things get too hectic, you can pause the timer giving you a moment to regroup. Although the maps are small, there is ample variety in the challenges presented, they are thoughfully designed, balanced & do not become stale.
Sound design is good, providing clear audio feedback to the actions occurring on screen, but these can get repetitive
. Levels are clear to navigate and laying track is generally an easy task. Occasionally, you can lay a track as your mouse moves slightly to the adjacent square, causing issues laying things the wrong way. It would be good to be able to demolish for the same cost if the timer hasn't been resumed to recover costs
.
Likewise, the financial impact of two trains colliding plus the many squares of track loss often spells doom & essentially the end for your level. It seems a bit excessive at times, and can frustrate, as can that random train departure who has just got in the way of everything! Thankfully, most levels are pretty quick to balance this out to a degree.
Despite these stress points, it has been hard to drag myself away from
for very long. Still trying to beat some of the later levels in the German DLC. It is highly addictive once you get a few levels in and will continue to challenge your time management & coordination skills all the way to the last level.

At almost 900 hours and 5 years of playing, I'm still impressed with this realistic, fun, PTSD generator of a game, and feel that I must finally post a review. It has helped me through long hours of boredom, and bouts of aggression when I'm irritated with certain situations in my life. I will go over the reasons of why I like the game, and touch up on things I feel still need improvement.
The Pros:
-Outstanding graphics, visual effects and sound (for a game of its time, over 5 years old).
-Immersive interface and interaction with enviroment (although see Cons)
-Realistic gameplay; encumberance affects stamina, which in turn affects speed, and accuracy. and fairly realistic ballistics for weapons (again though, see Cons).
-Great expansion with the addition of Rising Storm a couple of years ago.
-A fair leveling system with stats and achievements.
-Great "soldier" feel, without all of the political ideologies of the time being drawn into battles where most soldiers cared about survival more than racial/political superiority.
-And probably more that I forgot to add.
The Cons:
-The biggest complaint I've had for years (and probably that of many other players as well), is the stupidity of the AI, combined with their impossible accuracy/shooting skills. A kill shot achieved when my (bot) killer is aiming at a 90 degree angle from me or at a dead sprint are examples of this. Also, their questionable ability to follow orders....
-As stated in the Pros, the interface with enviroment is great, however, the cover option is a little clunky at times. Maybe an improvement?
-The classes are grouped pretty well, but maybe adding new classes/abilities? Such as a medic, perhaps, with a revive system.
-The weapons are great with exception of the AT rifles.  Maybe AT launchers could be implemented, such as panzerfaust or panzershrek? And yes, I know they aren't historically accurate for the time, but then again, neither was the G41 (G43), or Mkb 42 (STG 44) used as frequently as a game battle portrayed during the Stalingrad era. And if not those, maybe "mountable" AT guns, such as a Pak, or even a commander option for anti-armor CAS support. Just suggestions.......
-Rising Storm was a great expansion, with new factions, weapons, and maps. Maybe a new official expansion, such as a Western Front expansion, British faction, new weapons, etc. Once again, just suggestions, given the age of the game.
-And probably a few others that aren't too important to mention....
Red Orchestra/Rising Storm is a GREAT game as it stands, and I won't stop playing any time soon. Additions/improvements, in my opinion, would make it even better, and expand the life of this game even more. It can only get better.......

The Beginner's Guide is an incredibly interesting and introspective look at the process of human interaction. It is, on its surface level, a narrative about game design and its struggles, but the overarching theme is so much more wholly dependant on how the player connects to all of the (two) characters. Outlast can be daunting since its first minutes. With an incredible ambience, endowed with great graphics (though less demanding in terms of hardware) and a suitable soundtrack to its climate of terror and constant tension. About the gameplay, there is no fighting, just run and hide. The protagonist is an investigative reporter who goes to a psychiatric hospital after an email with complaints against the institution. There he encounters a "strange" situation with police vehicles abandoned on the door and decides to find a way to enter the hospital. From there follow many scares, despair and terror, all under the gaze of the protagonist and especially your camera, which has the night function and helps a lot to create a scary atmosphere. As said in previous reviews, this camera and events remind us a bit of REC film, with little difference, because the enemies are internal of the institution (and it is worth remembering that not all the crazy pose threats, but some ...) .
Excellent from start to finish, a great horror game!
I did not play the expansion, but I intend to do it as soon as possible!

Where to begin with this game.  BioShock is an FPS with RPG elements.  A very fine one at that.  As you should know there was a game called System Shock then there was a game called System Shock 2.  BioShock is considered a spiritual successor to System Shock 2.  System Shock 2 is a masterpiece but is BioShock? The answer is, yes.  BioShock is a beautiful game.  It is set in an underwater city called Rapture.  The most original setting for a video game in my opinion.  In the game you are a survivor of a plane crash that landed in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.  You swim to a nearby lighthouse and discover a pod that takes you into the depths of the ocean and takes you to the city of Rature.  Now the game is not your average shooter.  It has not only guns but plasmids which you inject into your wrist and gain powers.  If you've ever played System Shock 2 this game will feel like a watered down version of it.  It actually is.  That's not an entirely bad thing but it certainly isn't a great thing.  I remember being blown away by this game when I was younger.  You can shock the water that enemies are standing in and it will kill them.  The Big Daddies are big giant scubba diving looking things that protect these creepy little girls called little sister.  If you play the game you will learn about these two really quickly.  Anyway, this is one of my favorite games of all time.  A flawed masterpiece.

The Long Dark manages to make me incredibly anxious the entire time I'm playing. I often find myself swearing profusely at my screen as I inch across the snowy wilderness, angry at myself for not having left my resource-collecting expedition just a minute earlier than I had so that I might have missed the storm that caused me to walk for ten minutes in the wrong direction. I find it incredibly easy to immerse myself in the experience of being alone in the wilderness, and that's what I like most about this game. Survival is difficult, and once you're dead, that's it. No starting from a save point, no retreiving that rifle that it took you a week to find, you have to begin again entirely. And it's by no means an "easy" game. It takes planning, and a great deal of wandering around at the brink of death to get good at this game.

This is a wonderful survival game. I am a big fan of survival games, from Minecraft to Don't Starve and most everything in between.
The Long Dark does an excellent job of creating an immersive environment, with a unique art style that is a pleasent departure from the strive of most game makers who try to make a game true to life. The style does not break the immersive qualities of the game, and you soon become lost (quite litterally at times) in the frozen wilderness that you have been stranded in.
The game in it's current state is fairly complete, and anything more that is added to the game will only add to the enjoyment of play. I have been playing the game off and on for awhile now, and have seen the changes the devs have made in the balancing of the player's stats and the resources available in the game. They have only improved over time until now I am enjoying playing the game for extended periods.
Not to mention the new areas of the world they have added which are all tied together. You can pick an area to start in, and each area is rather large and challenging on it's own, especially since you are spawned into that area in random places at random times of the day, making for better or worse odds of surviving even your first night. But then you can travel between these areas, which is great, as some resources or tools can only be found in specific areas (Like a forge that is in one area, that allows you to create metal tools and weapons.)
If you are looking for a beautifully stylized survival game, that doesn't pull any punches, and truely gives you a sense of satisfaction knowing that your actions are the reason you survived (or got eaten by wolves!), then this is the game for you.

Though this game gets a lot of praise it has some glaring flaws that you should be aware of, I'll touch on the good points first:
*The car destruction looks very realistic, and you'll notice actual changes in handing as your car accrues more damage; when your car is badly damaged for example it will lose a wheel and handling will become a nightmare.
*There are a wide variety of off and on-road environments to race on, from deserts, to cities, to forests, as well as some fun mini-games to add replay value. The named opponents and different driving styles also add some personality to the career mode.
---
However on the whole this game left me more frustrated than entralled, so now I'll get to the bad news:
The handling in this game is just bad, to the point that it feels like you're driving a hovercraft rather than a car, and a single shunt or slight oversteer can sent you off the track into a wall. This is also counter-intuitive to the design of the game since you're encouraged to drive aggressive and crash into things, but when the margin for error is so high it's usually safer to avoid taking jumps or smashing into traffic lights.
The single-player mode relies on the catch-up effect to prevent a single spinout from taking you out of the race, but in the (now-defunct) online multiplayer this is nonexistent - meaning a single oversteer or ram from an opponent in the first minute of the race can take you out, which is frustrating rather than fun in an acade racer.
Aside from that, the game's musical score feels out of place for a destruction-oriented racing game, consisting mainly of pop punk, emo, and alternative rock tracks - it seems to have taken a cue from the Burnout series here. The graphics are also a little too bright and cheerful for my taste.
The final notable flaw is the unbalanced cars. The game is divided into 3 classes of cars, and each class has 1 or 2 high-end cars which are far-and-away superior in every respect to the others in their class. In multiplayer this means that nearly everyone will just end up driving the same car in every race, while the others just go unused.
While this isn't a terrible game, on the whole I consider it overhyped and overrated; though the single-player mode may offer a casual racing diversion to some.

Batman: The Telltale Series puts you in the cape and cowl of Batman and Bruce Wayne. Live your life as Bruce Wayne, managing your company and figuring out your parents mysterious actions. Solve crimes and stop threats as Batman, using your knowledge of martial arts and gadgets to stop corrupt, evil men. You notice your childhood friend, Oswald Cobblepot come back to Gotham, and coincidentally after turns upside down as soon as he showed up. Challenge yourself with stopping terrorist organizations while at the same time managing all your relationships as Bruce Wayne.
Pros:
Telltale twist.
Lots of freedom and choice.
Fleshed out characters. You care about everyone.
Lots of tough choices that impact the game later on.
Lots of replayability with different choices.
Lots of twists and turns in the story.
Telltale went off canon with usual Batman villians and stories, and I liked it.
Each character is voiced beautifully and animated well.
Cons:
As for lots of Telltale games, not all of your choices matter and some outcomes always are supposed to happen.
Some dialogue choices are often incorrectly said than expected.
Audio glitches and bugs.
Very laggy and choppy at the beginning of new scenes.
Overall, Batman: The Telltale series is a fantastic Batman story and game. Right from the start, it hooks you into the atmoshpere with its brilliantly written characters and situations. Ending is satisfying, but still makes you want more. I'd recommend this game to Telltale fans and Batman fans.

This is not one of the best Telltale games I've played, but it's passable. The story can be a bit disjointed at times, but overall, I really felt like I was Batman. The heroes and villains really displayed a human side to their emotions and motivations for being heroes or criminals, respectively, not often seen.
Telltale may not be in the business of making fighting games but having to press buttons at certain times does make me feel like I'm part of the action. However, nearing the end of the game, even with my NVIDIA GTX 1060 graphics card, the fight scenes were a little slow and buggy. The graphics are a bit cartoonish, which I like for these games, but it shouldn't be so slow.

The art is gorgeous, but the game is truly an excercise in frustration. I have no issue with the premise, but the poor controls severly hamper the gameplay. The character only moves by holding down the left mouse button and often gets confused with the direction to move in, resulting in spinning in place or sometimes completely moving the wrong way. This can result in the character triggering a screen transition and further waste your time/patience. Click/drag/swipe is imprecise and forces you to often repeat inputs just to collect an object or make a move in a puzzle. Non-interruptable animations further amplify the cost of a buggy input system. Most of the puzzle concepts are fine although at least two I think are "unfair". Finally, the lack of any save/checkpoint system while in a chapter means you will not want to quit the game lest you're forced to deal with the aforementioned ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t all over again. Despite the vibrant art style which drew me to Morphopolis, I really can't recommend the game at any price since it has so much difficulty actually providing gameplay.

I bought this game looking for something like the old-schoold game Atrain (DOS) and when I first launched it, I was disapointed as it wasn't like that. But that's okay as it never was promised as such and I didn't read the description before purchasing it. With the amount of positive reviews it has, it was a sure buy - and it has trains.
I was instantly hooked on the game once I got the overall concept and how the game worked. It's a game like none other I have played despite having the same concepts as others. But it is unique in the method of which everything is applied.
Train Valley is a simple game as-is, but that doesn't make it easy. It can be a very challenging game and you'll spend a lot of time getting those last few stamps. With a relative small map, you have to build train tracks between given stations and change the tracks to direct your trains towards the proper station. That in itself would be easy if you had unlimited money, time, and space - but you don't - and that's where the challenge lies.
It would have been nice with a few more levels and maybe a few bigger ones, but for a sales price it's more than enough content and you can have hundreds of hours entertainment for very little money.

Sunless Sea is a beautifully crafted game. Did I win anybody over, yet?... I didn't expect to... In an observation of the complete spectrum of features that cause me to swoon over this game, I find that it is the aesthetic appeal and namely the impeccable dialog and exposition. I had no problem with the unforgiving rogue-like features to this game and found it as a source of motivation above all else to continue delving into the world of Fallen London. Yes, it can become time consuming to restart with a captain with the exact same name as my old captain but with worse equipment, but, besides the fact that I could have considered naming my captain something besides Captain Edward Smith the second time around, I found it to be the main source of my pride when I found each island and explored, surveyed, and assisted them individually. I'm an avid reader, so the content was always interesting to me, besides repetition about how the office would react to my dock reports and other info. Although, the game did eventually become repetitive to its core when I tried to replay after an eternal session. It seemed as if I had already done everything and I was backtracking. I found that the aesthetic yet grim nature of the game held its ground during the backtracking. Nothing seems to catch the human eye more in horror genres more than water: whether it is found falling from above or below, it is always the great equilizer and yet the most powerful of them all. Pardoning myself for the digression, I recommend this 'game' to readers.

Train Valley met my expectations.  I find the videos and screenshots to be misleading, as they feature zoomed in views of the map.  I play zoomed all the way out so I can always see the entire map.  I don't see any advantage to zooming in.  Each level starts with two or three stations.  You decide where the track goes.  Trains appear at random stations, and you need guide each train to its desired destination.  As the level progresses, more stations appear.  You have much more control than in Mini Metro, and consequently you do more micromanagement - mostly toggling switches to try to route trains where you want them to go.  On the plus side, this means that when things go wrong, it is almost always your fault, whereas success in Mini Metro depends more on luck and chance.  More trains + more track + more switches = more complexity.  You can also call in extra trains for extra points.  The challenge is designing and discovering track layouts that are easy to manage.  Some of the UI elements could be improved (see my comment in the Steam discussions), but I have adapted to the unfortunate UI deficiencies.

Being in Alpha doesn't stop Project Zomboid from being one of the most in depth and elaborate zombie survival games you will ever play. The game, at this time, features four game modes, Multiplayer, Survival, Sandbox and Last Stand, on two different maps.
Survival mode gives you lore friendly zombies that shuffle around the map and can infect you with just a scratch if your unlucky, where as Sandbox give you can choose how fast you want the zombies to move, from baby steps to full out sprinting, how strong they are, how much damage they can take, how the decease is spread and more. Sandbox also always you to change how many zombies spawn on the map, where the zombies are distributed, the length of a day, how much it rains and more.
Once you have made your choose of game play, you are brought to a character menu, where you choose name, gender, race and your hairstyle. After you have made your characters model, you are brought to the Occupation and Traits menu. Choose a job and various traits. Are you a clumsy overweight person with a heavy appetite, but is stout and brave, or will you be light drinker with a short tempered and brood over your moods, but be lucky and graceful so no zombie will hear you? There are many chooses to be made.
But no matter which traits you choose, you will spawn in a random house or apartment around the map and have to survive. Find weapons, which can be anything from a pencil to a frying pan, just grab something and carefully explore for some form of a backpack, even if it is a garbage bag, to hold all the ammo, weapons, food and water that you can find. Soon after you will need shelter for the night, because you can't stay up forever and you are going to need somewhere to store all these supplies you are carrying. Avoid large swarms of zombies and try not to make to much noise. Guns are effective for killing zombies, but you will run out of ammo and the sound it makes could attract a horde of zombies. If you survive enough to set up a base, make sure to stock pile water, because water and electricity are doomed to fall. But the game always ends the same way, with your death.
In Last Stand you spawn a single house and survive wave after wave of zombies. How long can you last?
Over all Project Zomboid is a fun and worth while game which I hope will continue to grow with the workshop and all the future updates. Thank you.

I suggest playing on hard difficulty or higher, because of the simple fact that the amount of equipment and hits you can take before dying is greatly diminished as compared to that of normal difficulty, and it serves to make it feel as a blessing when you do finally reach the next safe room or find a new battery to power your camera.

I guess it's on sale right now for 5.50, so at that price you'll get a probably 15 to 20 hours of interesting (sometimes boring) gameplay.  Its a great START to a city builder... but once you overcome the initial challenge of survival and grow your population, there isn't much left to do.  The game needs to expand, where you unlock new building options/services that your citizens demand, forcing the farms to the outskirts so you can expland your city with more than just houses, a tavern and a church...  The game play spans centuries, so there should be options to modernize all buildings or for citizens to develop needs/wants according to ideology.  The game does nothing of this sort, starting you out with a handful of bulding options and not adding to them the entire game.
The interesting challenge here, is adapting your labour force to suit your needs on a whim.  Bringing farmers from the mines to the field with the changing of the seasons, or starting a new fishing village and watching it grow and eventually become part of the main city.  Bulding tunnels through mountains is cool, as well as the quarries.  But once you play through say, 10 to 20 hours (an inflated amount of time due to the slow pace of gameplay.....), thats about it. you might as well restart and play through the frustrating and at times tense challenge of getting your town off the ground.
This game would be much better if it offered more, and allowed your town to grow faster.  It can be VERY boring watching the seasons change, hoping a student will enter the workforce next year so you'll have a full compliment of farmers next season, or so that you wont have to borrow fisherman to harvest this time.
I haven't tried the mods, but I think I'm done with this game anyway.

Now, first of all, I do have to say (and this shall not detract from my overall opinion of the game in the review itself), I had TONS of trouble trying to get this darn game to work. I never got it to work on Windows 7, despite following all common proceedures (running compatibility modes and certain launch parameters etc.). And after a solid three days of trying to get it to work, and it still refusing to run, I then went to try and run it on a Windows 8 laptop, and hey-ho, it worked! So just a warning, purchasing this on Windows 7 may prove to be quite a bit of a gamble, unfortunately. I hear some people work it perfectly, while others, not so. Anyhow, the game was eventually working, and so our journey begins:
-------------------------
One of my main concerns with the the first Bioshock, upon purchasing the Bioshock Triple Pack was,
It's simple. The answer is: HELL YES, GOOD SIR/MA'AM.
Rapture (now probably one of my favourite game settings
(I still must play Stalker, mind you! :3)) captures your full attention from start to finish. If you're anything like me, and you find yourself intrigued by the prospect of dystopian societies (whether that be through: 1984, Terminator, Brave New World and whatnot), you will love Bioshock. The true nature of Rapture really shines through, with the presence of audio logs, scattered around the game, which provide tons of insight into the fascinating city, all on top of the brilliant linear story Bioshock presents.
I usually hate collectibles in games, seeing that they mostly provide little incentive, other than some measly achievement, or a disappointing extra cut scene. But Bioshock somehow makes it worthwhile! It certainly helps that it all has top-notch voice acting, lots of really interesting back-story in how Rapture came to be (and then not be), and also, if you listen carefully, great links to the overall linear story of the game. At first, the audio logs have an uncomfortable overall  aroma of optimism, despite you knowing what the city ultimately becomes. And the way in which you hear the people recording the audio logs progressively lose their minds is equally sad and unsettling.
Even the enemies you gun down become somewhat sympathetic, despite Rapture essentially being a society whereby the smartest, the richest, and the cockiest are all clumped together underwater - all while forgetting any sense of moral values, that are thought to 'plague' the world above.
In terms of the linear story, I will admit that it's major purpose is to build up to one 'twist', about 2/3 of the way through the game, and this is one twist that arguably could define the entire game, in terms of its legacy. For me, this twist was spoiled approximately 2.3 billion times before I actually played the game, but, I still enjoyed it nonetheless! As although it seems rather unremarkable and unpredictable, the context is everything. Not to mention the mind-blowing way it is delivered, and one that is sure to top some of my favourite ever moments in video games. Do try very hard not to get it spoiled though, that is, please don't research the plot on Wikipedia. You won't regret it. :) That all being said, unfortunately, don't be expecting any equally revolutionary ending of the game, as it is rather underwhelming and predictable. (Especially with a slightly out of place end-boss fight) Which is a huge shame! Although I do suppose Bioshock is often cited as one of the greatest games, with the worst endings.
The combination of using plasmids (genetically modified, almost 'magic' abilities, that allow you to do various disgusting things with your hands), and weapons is quite fun. Although, it may initally appear a "step-back", for those that played Infinite first, like I did, or Bioshock 2 (although God Only Knows why you'd play that before the previous instalment), since those games allow you to use both weapons and plasmids at the same time. Whilst in Bioshock 1, you must use the right mouse button to switch between them. Do not fear, because you get quite used to it.
'Bioshock' does have one thing going for it though, and that's the sheer variety of ways you can use its combat mechanics to your advantage. I still struggle to choose what I found most satisfying to do, but I believe there's probably a playstyle for just about everyone in the game somewhere. For instance, you'll often be found in a situation whereby there's a large group of enemies, and you have a whole arsenal of plasmids and weaponry to accompany you. You could just telekinesis the explosive barrels at a group of splicers, and ignite any remnants of oil on the floor to prevent them getting to you. Or you could hack into a disabled turret to help take them out for you, and set explosive and electrical traps to keep them at a distance. Maybe you just want to silently bash them over the head and freeze them solid? You got it. It's not quite Deus Ex, or Dishonoured, but it's probably about as close enough as it gets.
One particularly interesting enemy was the highly memorable, 'Big Daddies', which I don't want to get into too much detail about. But oh boy, they're pretty tough. The Bouncer' quick reflexes, charges, and the shockwaves it unleashes make things really interesting, and it constantly keeps you on your toes. As you scurry around the surrounding area, thinking of ways you could make your life significantly easier at that very moment of time.
I have heard many complaints regarding the ammo and loot distribution being a bit unbalanced, especially further into the game, as some people believe that some of the tension is rendered a bit pointless when you're absolutely loaded with first aid kits and bullets. While I can see where those people are coming from, I personally didn't have much of a problem, as I often enough, found myself in situations where I had to conserve my ammo somewhat if I wanted to make progress. Mind you, there's probably room for improvement, but it didn't bother me that much.
Moving on, sound design: PHENOMENAL. I really do dig games which evoke incredibly bone-chilling atmopsheres (eg: Dead Space, Metro 2033, Alan Wake). But I believe Bioshock to currently be my favourite of them all (again, I'm yet to play Stalker. :P). And a huge contributor to Bioshock's amazing atmopshere is the way sound is used to really amplify moments of tension: The distant shrieks, screams and complaints of splicers, the unforgettable stomps of the 'Big Daddies', the gurgling and gushing water, the creaks of the dying architecture of Rapture, and various other things... And when it's all combined with quite effective use of lighting, and a soundtrack that pays perfect tribute to the sheer insanity of Rapture's citizens: Bioshock becomes a masterpiece.  The game is not particularly 'scary' per say, but the atmosphere is built in such a way, you'll trick yourself into constant paranoia. And I loved every minute.
I have no idea how I had not managed to get around to playing the Bioshock series sooner, but I can assure you, I've been missing out on a lot. Even if you're only remotely interested in the game/series, you should give it a good shot. The first game in particular will always stand up there with all my favourite games of all time. And in my humble opinion, masterpieces don't have to be absolutely perfect, and I am willing to forgive the few flaws I have found with Bioshock, because it is just that good. I think it's a masterpiece. And (apologies for the cliche'), a must-play.
It's so tempting to give it a 10/10 overall, so I just think I will... Just excuse the ending? :P

I LOVE this game. It's one of the best survival games I've actually played. I don't have a lot of hours on it but the hours I've played have kept me constantly entertained and wanting more. It's been a while since I've eagerly awaited the next time I'd play a game.
Rather than being a faceless no-one in first person, your character actually speaks, which I found really surprising and it brings something to the game. I'm currently playing the passive mode (where no animals attack you unless provoked), and I'm having a blast walking around and gathering what I need.
It's too bad we can't carry more than 30kgs, but it makes logical sense. I'm glad we can also go OVER that, with consequences to speed (which, when you're playing in passive, doesn't matter as long as you can find shelter before you become exhausted).
While we're on the topic of kgs, it's a shame you can't choose which temperature and weight conversion you want to go by. I like Celcius and pounds, but I have to go imperial or metric. It'd be nice if there was a specific choice, but it's not a deal breaker for me.
There are maps online on the wiki if you really need them, and they're fairly updated.
My only complaint is that the character feels very low to the ground, and it seems like you're already crouched when you're just standing. It doesn't feel like a (typically) six foot man standing. (I don't know what it's like on the women side, but I can guess it's similar)
Even with my drawback, I still give this game a 10/10 for anyone who wants to play a survival game. I hope to one day see desert maps and different season cycles! It's a GREAT game.

The game features the usual Telltale fare of unimpactful choices and goofy graphical glitches, but I found they didn't distract from the overall experience. The only glaring issue I saw with this game is a few severe performance problems. I run a mid-to-high end PC and would often encounter stuttering and freezing expecially in the earlier episodes. This definitely upset me a bit, but I managed to push through it.
Half-Life is better, but it's a nice short game that adds a different perspective to the events at Black Mesa.

There is much to say. There is so much to say, and yet only so much I can say if I don't want my review to be one massive spoiler. I will try anyway. Before I begin, though, and because the outstanding quality of this game is based on its writing, I must say that english is not my foreign language : I am good enough at it to understand everything it says, and yet not familiar enough not to find myself spellbound by some of the turns of phrase I encountered. Which will help me adress the first point of my review : although the game hasn't been translated, as long as you have some bases, you can still very well enjoy it even if english isn't your first language, and perhaps even more so than an english native speaker could, because of the exotic dimension there is in reading good writing in a foreign language you understand.
Let's be fair : Sunless Sea's success was an unlikely series of risky gambles. First of all, the gameplay is tedious : you lead your ship from island to island at an incredibly sluggish speed ; the fights lack a strategic dimension and any kind of suspense or chance for you to take on bigger opponents before your ship is armed to the teeth ; the permadeath system, while keeping you on your toes, forces you to replay through the same stories over and over again ; a single wrong choice in a storyline's development can have incredibly punishing and dramatic consequences. By Failbetter's own admission, the roguelike part of the game was a failure.
And yet the writing saves it all. Whether this was purely by luck or the result of machiavellian calculation is unclear, but the fact is that the tedious, clunky, harrowing gameplay, which often makes you feel miserable and desperate, works towards the incredible tension that comes from knowing that you will soon discover a key element of the storyline you are currently pursuing. There is something inherently british about this game : it wants failure to really hurt the player. This makes the bit of text you are to unlock next all the more desirable and precious. Sunless Sea feeds the intoxicating spell of its mysteries with your player tears. All this time you've been spending doing basically nothing while cruising the zee from port to port has secretly been used by the game to build up your expectations.
It goes deeper. I will try to keep this paragraph as spoiler-free as possible, but there is one particular storyline that openly defies one of the principles modern games are based on : gain. That particular storyline alone is worth buying and playing the game, because it is the single best thing I have experienced in a videogame since playing Pathologic and The Void (by Ice-Pick Lodge). Rather than rewarding you for pursuing it, that storyline demands more and more sacrifices from your character and yourself - because if you reach that point, it means you have been investing time and effort into that captain- to the point where said storyline ends up requiring that you destroy your character to be able to continue and finish it. You will be paid in words only, but oh what wonderful words those are. Even now that more than two years have passed since I finished that particular storyline (of which I will only say that the word "Salt" now holds a whole different meaning to me), I still find myself reciting a few lines of that text in my head, and the world around suddenly seems painted in strange colours.
The writing itself is kaleidoscopic. The main writer is Alexis Kennedy, founder and former member of Failbetter Games, and his style is incisive, concise, beautiful, and entirely aimed at freaking you out, but lots of islands' content has been written by guest writers, and thus the writing style, while always of high quality, is quite variable : sometimes it will be short and evocative, sometimes it will consist of extended, detailed descriptions, and so on.
I will try to keep this review relatively short. Sunless Sea is a game I have been playing since Early Access, when most of the islands and content weren't implemented yet. I have been fascinated and obsessed about its secrets for years now. Imagine a captivating book that requires you to cut your own right hand to be able to read the last chapters, and you will have a pretty good idea of what Sunless Sea is essentially about. If you don't enjoy reading and self-inflicted pain, keep walking. If you do, Sunless Sea is an exceptional, overwhelming experience, albeit cruelly unforgiving and gleefully unconcerned about your spare time.

Now, first of all, I do have to say (and this shall not detract from my overall opinion of the game in the review itself), I had TONS of trouble trying to get this darn game to work. I never got it to work on Windows 7, despite following all common proceedures (running compatibility modes and certain launch parameters etc.). And after a solid three days of trying to get it to work, and it still refusing to run, I then went to try and run it on a Windows 8 laptop, and hey-ho, it worked! So just a warning, purchasing this on Windows 7 may prove to be quite a bit of a gamble, unfortunately. I hear some people work it perfectly, while others, not so. Anyhow, the game was eventually working, and so our journey begins:
-------------------------
One of my main concerns with the the first Bioshock, upon purchasing the Bioshock Triple Pack was,
It's simple. The answer is: HELL YES, GOOD SIR/MA'AM.
Rapture (now probably one of my favourite game settings
(I still must play Stalker, mind you! :3)) captures your full attention from start to finish. If you're anything like me, and you find yourself intrigued by the prospect of dystopian societies (whether that be through: 1984, Terminator, Brave New World and whatnot), you will love Bioshock. The true nature of Rapture really shines through, with the presence of audio logs, scattered around the game, which provide tons of insight into the fascinating city, all on top of the brilliant linear story Bioshock presents.
I usually hate collectibles in games, seeing that they mostly provide little incentive, other than some measly achievement, or a disappointing extra cut scene. But Bioshock somehow makes it worthwhile! It certainly helps that it all has top-notch voice acting, lots of really interesting back-story in how Rapture came to be (and then not be), and also, if you listen carefully, great links to the overall linear story of the game. At first, the audio logs have an uncomfortable overall  aroma of optimism, despite you knowing what the city ultimately becomes. And the way in which you hear the people recording the audio logs progressively lose their minds is equally sad and unsettling.
Even the enemies you gun down become somewhat sympathetic, despite Rapture essentially being a society whereby the smartest, the richest, and the cockiest are all clumped together underwater - all while forgetting any sense of moral values, that are thought to 'plague' the world above.
In terms of the linear story, I will admit that it's major purpose is to build up to one 'twist', about 2/3 of the way through the game, and this is one twist that arguably could define the entire game, in terms of its legacy. For me, this twist was spoiled approximately 2.3 billion times before I actually played the game, but, I still enjoyed it nonetheless! As although it seems rather unremarkable and unpredictable, the context is everything. Not to mention the mind-blowing way it is delivered, and one that is sure to top some of my favourite ever moments in video games. Do try very hard not to get it spoiled though, that is, please don't research the plot on Wikipedia. You won't regret it. :) That all being said, unfortunately, don't be expecting any equally revolutionary ending of the game, as it is rather underwhelming and predictable. (Especially with a slightly out of place end-boss fight) Which is a huge shame! Although I do suppose Bioshock is often cited as one of the greatest games, with the worst endings.
The combination of using plasmids (genetically modified, almost 'magic' abilities, that allow you to do various disgusting things with your hands), and weapons is quite fun. Although, it may initally appear a "step-back", for those that played Infinite first, like I did, or Bioshock 2 (although God Only Knows why you'd play that before the previous instalment), since those games allow you to use both weapons and plasmids at the same time. Whilst in Bioshock 1, you must use the right mouse button to switch between them. Do not fear, because you get quite used to it.
'Bioshock' does have one thing going for it though, and that's the sheer variety of ways you can use its combat mechanics to your advantage. I still struggle to choose what I found most satisfying to do, but I believe there's probably a playstyle for just about everyone in the game somewhere. For instance, you'll often be found in a situation whereby there's a large group of enemies, and you have a whole arsenal of plasmids and weaponry to accompany you. You could just telekinesis the explosive barrels at a group of splicers, and ignite any remnants of oil on the floor to prevent them getting to you. Or you could hack into a disabled turret to help take them out for you, and set explosive and electrical traps to keep them at a distance. Maybe you just want to silently bash them over the head and freeze them solid? You got it. It's not quite Deus Ex, or Dishonoured, but it's probably about as close enough as it gets.
One particularly interesting enemy was the highly memorable, 'Big Daddies', which I don't want to get into too much detail about. But oh boy, they're pretty tough. The Bouncer' quick reflexes, charges, and the shockwaves it unleashes make things really interesting, and it constantly keeps you on your toes. As you scurry around the surrounding area, thinking of ways you could make your life significantly easier at that very moment of time.
I have heard many complaints regarding the ammo and loot distribution being a bit unbalanced, especially further into the game, as some people believe that some of the tension is rendered a bit pointless when you're absolutely loaded with first aid kits and bullets. While I can see where those people are coming from, I personally didn't have much of a problem, as I often enough, found myself in situations where I had to conserve my ammo somewhat if I wanted to make progress. Mind you, there's probably room for improvement, but it didn't bother me that much.
Moving on, sound design: PHENOMENAL. I really do dig games which evoke incredibly bone-chilling atmopsheres (eg: Dead Space, Metro 2033, Alan Wake). But I believe Bioshock to currently be my favourite of them all (again, I'm yet to play Stalker. :P). And a huge contributor to Bioshock's amazing atmopshere is the way sound is used to really amplify moments of tension: The distant shrieks, screams and complaints of splicers, the unforgettable stomps of the 'Big Daddies', the gurgling and gushing water, the creaks of the dying architecture of Rapture, and various other things... And when it's all combined with quite effective use of lighting, and a soundtrack that pays perfect tribute to the sheer insanity of Rapture's citizens: Bioshock becomes a masterpiece.  The game is not particularly 'scary' per say, but the atmosphere is built in such a way, you'll trick yourself into constant paranoia. And I loved every minute.
I have no idea how I had not managed to get around to playing the Bioshock series sooner, but I can assure you, I've been missing out on a lot. Even if you're only remotely interested in the game/series, you should give it a good shot. The first game in particular will always stand up there with all my favourite games of all time. And in my humble opinion, masterpieces don't have to be absolutely perfect, and I am willing to forgive the few flaws I have found with Bioshock, because it is just that good. I think it's a masterpiece. And (apologies for the cliche'), a must-play.
It's so tempting to give it a 10/10 overall, so I just think I will... Just excuse the ending? :P

Overall:
I think that in it's current state the game shows a ton of potential and has some very great features. I really like the Terraria/Starbound 2D worldcraft type gameplay and the controls/combat of this particular title does the style justice. If you're a fan of these, this game is a must-play as it is a bit more forgiving than Starbound or Terraria in some ways but also very challenging in it's own right.
Positives:
There is a great amount of appealing content in the game so far. The combat is a lot of fun. I like how easy it is to find and upgrade resources as well as unlocking content by simply fighting monsters and mining. Each (fighting/mining) give you exp points equally. There are also mini-dungeons you come across regularly to clear out. These in addition to deployable tower defense and other styles of mini-game dungeons adds a fun spin to the roguelike worldcraft indie style.
Negative:
The biggest issues I have with the game are stability issues and bugs. After initially binging on the game for several hours, I lost everything I had built due to a client crash. I still had my character and all the inventory, but the planet/area's safe file was corrupted so I had to start from a fresh new save. This made me lose all my storage and the structures/bases I had built.  Also it seems that about half the time the game has trouble deploying your character as playable into the world. Sometimes the screen is dark and everything responds, but you cannot move or take control of your avatar. It is easily fixed by a restart or two (if it happens sequentially).
Neutral:
This game isn't a solid world like in Terraria or Starbound. There are large open spaces inbetween land masses that you must use your jet pack to travel between while heading deeper in the map without taking damage on impact as the gravity is similar to that of earth. This I feel like has both negative and positive effects for creating elevator shafts and fast-travel between different levels. For instance, one thing I liked about terraria was creating an easily navigated mine-shaft to drop very deep very quickly, although in this you can just build a teleporter wherever you want and teleport straight to it. So it really allows you to focus on more combat if you want to.
End thoughts. Worth overall. I will update my review as it is developed.

1st attempt at survival-
Everything was going well. It was 2 days since the event, and I had collected some decent clothing, had a good supply of food, and sodas, and was surviving well. I had come across an abandoned dam, so I scavenged it for anything I might be able to use and decided to make it my "base" for a short time, to aquaint myself with the surroundings and get an idea of where I might go next. 2 days passed of me scouting the general area and my supplies ran low so I decided to head out, following a set of train tracks into the unknown. I came to a collapsed tunnel just as night descended so I built a fire with what scraps I had and decided to sleep for an hour or two. I had ran out of sodas at this point and hadn't realized that I could melt snow for hydration. My health had deteriorated quickly. I froze to death in my sleep.
2nd attempt at survival-
Day 4 since the event and I've figured out how to melt snow for a water source. I have food, water, and my clothes are in great shape. I delve into a cave and come out the other end to a forested hillside. There was a wolf right in the middle, and I thought "I'll tangle with him, take his meat and hide, and be on my way". We struggled briefly and I injured him, so he ran over a small ridge to get away, and I got up and gave chase. I get to the top of the ridge and look down the other side to see him running straight at me. I'm like "You won't get away this time!". He runs right past me, bleeding everywhere. A giant bear comes running up shortly after, chasing the wolf, then turns on me and chews my stomach to shreds. I already took a good hit from my fight with the wolf, but I managed to survive the bear attack with 6% condition. I roll over bleeding and coughing and manage to get to my feet, and by the time I stood up and attempted first aid, the last bit of life force had drained from me, and I headed straight for The Long Dark.
TL;DR
Great game, would definitely recommend to anyone.

Half Life: Life Blue Shift is one of the two standalone expansion packs for the original Half-Life. Developed by Gearbox and overseen by Valve. Blue Shift is definitely weaker than Opposing Force in terms of pretty much everything. That does not mean it is bad, the game just refuses to take risks or add anything new. You play as Black Mesa security officer Barney Calhoun, who is in the middle of his shift when the Resonance Cascade happens, he then has to find a way to escape Black Mesa. The gameplay is the same as the original Half-Life, but with no fun new enemies or weapons like in Opposing Force. But I still recommend the game because it reveals more of the story of Half-Life, and it is always fun to see a game's story line from a different perspective.
TLDR: The weaker of the two expansions for Half-Life because it does not take risks or attempt anything new. Still keeps the fun gameplay, and it is cool to see the Black Mesa Incident from a different perspective.

Sunless sea is a game set in the fallen londen universe (echo bazaar is their other title, a free browser game) and is a game world with some of the most batshit epic lore that I have ever experienced. Peeling away the layers of mystery is a big appeal of the game but I sometimes wonder if this game wouldn't be more enjoyable in book form. Its mostly text based with a topdown exploration element. The game is punishingly difficult and a big part of the game is managing sanity by sticking near coastlines and trying to keep your prow light on. There is also a trading angle but this is intended as a way to get a little extra money on the side, not as a standalone way to play the game. The storylettes are creepy as hell, which is incidentaly a place that you can go in game to do buisness.
-the writing is great and the universes lore is insane. INSANE. Look up some spoilers, because much of the lore is tied up in echo bazaar and can take a LONG time to get to, it's a big time investment
-the overall game world and concept is very cool, sailing the dark seas is pretty immersive
-the game balance is frankly out of whack. The game is super slow and very unforgiving in the early stages and the way they have balanced the game makes doing everything drag out. Get a re-balance patch, it makes the game so much more enjoyable
-lots of errand running
-modding out some of the difficulty robs the game of the sphincter clenching 90+ madness limp home moments but honestly it's an ok trade
Overall I like sunless sea, dispite it's flaws which to be honest are significant enough to warrant trying to mod out. The writing is maybe not for everyone and the game is a bit of a slow experience but the universe is very well imagined and lots of fun to explore. A very interesting game that goes it's own direction and it mostly works, reccomended for people who like reading eldritch horror

From elsewhere:
Bioshock, when first released, had a lot of buzz. I was kinda excited as previews and reviewers mentioned a somewhat RPG-styled FPS much like Deus Ex.
Playing through it several times (I've put well over 50 hours), I can easily summarize the game as just a mediocre FPS. Harsh? Compared to how nice everyone else is to this game, yeah, but I think it's a more objective view.
Before we read a laundry list of what could have been differently we should examine what this game does right: atmosphere. The maps, the lighting, the sound, the contents of the recordings, and the art design (a very retro futuristic style that made the first Fallout so memorable). Exploring the Rapture was great fun for the first time, but very linear. Yes, there are things you can miss on the sides one your first play through, but it doesn't effect the game at all. But that should be expected from a decent shooter. Of course any sense of dread is not to be found as the fear of dying in this game is non existent.
The plasmids are kinda like augments of Deus Ex, in that when applied, they may change the style in which you play the game. Not by much, and in fact, disregard the notion of it changing your play style. They're nothing special, and the only one mildly entertaining to use is telekinesis (which behaves like the gravity gun of Half-Life 2).
Combat feels kinda sloppy and not as responsive as, for example TF2 or Borderlands, as the enemies (being poorly animated) move very awkwardly in a jerky motion. It's not the worst, but the weapons don't feel as responsive as they should (aside from the shotgun and wrench).
The game overall isn't anything special; how could it have been better?
For one, more vents/alternative routes. This could do more for a stealthy play through than Decoy and Chameleon plasmids.
Make character development through plasmids a little more permanent. By this I mean, when changing your DNA, whatever is added can't be undone, and no swapping with the gene banks. Also beyond that, they should have made different paths for builds, like when choosing one plasmid you open the way for one group but close your way to other ones (and of course increase the number of plasmids as well). This would make how you spend your Adam more interesting.
One the same theme as plasmids, weapon upgrades feel bleh. It felt stupid that by the end of the game all of the weapons you found could be upgraded completely. A better solution would have been to follow the same route as the proposed plasmid upgrades: have way more options but not all of them selectable as the choices you make affect the upgrades that can be made. And since you'll almost always have 500 dollars on hand, why not make the upgrades cost something?
The amount you could carry followed the same issue with everything else in the game: you can do everything! This means, at any point in the game you could switch to any weapon and meet any situation. If there were limitations to how many weapons and ammo you could carry and with numerous weapon mods available, the game would be more interesting, have better replay ability.
I could outline more, like how the story is literally a copy and paste job from System Shock 2 (much like this review I wrote on Gamespot long ago), but really... I still don't feel expanding into it.  This game is still meh.

1st attempt at survival-
Everything was going well. It was 2 days since the event, and I had collected some decent clothing, had a good supply of food, and sodas, and was surviving well. I had come across an abandoned dam, so I scavenged it for anything I might be able to use and decided to make it my "base" for a short time, to aquaint myself with the surroundings and get an idea of where I might go next. 2 days passed of me scouting the general area and my supplies ran low so I decided to head out, following a set of train tracks into the unknown. I came to a collapsed tunnel just as night descended so I built a fire with what scraps I had and decided to sleep for an hour or two. I had ran out of sodas at this point and hadn't realized that I could melt snow for hydration. My health had deteriorated quickly. I froze to death in my sleep.
2nd attempt at survival-
Day 4 since the event and I've figured out how to melt snow for a water source. I have food, water, and my clothes are in great shape. I delve into a cave and come out the other end to a forested hillside. There was a wolf right in the middle, and I thought "I'll tangle with him, take his meat and hide, and be on my way". We struggled briefly and I injured him, so he ran over a small ridge to get away, and I got up and gave chase. I gave this game a thumb's down many months ago when it was in early access.  Today I'm revising my review with a thumbs up because almost all of the issues that made it unplayable (to me) have been fixed.  Several flaws remain, which I'll get to later, but despite these The Long Dark became an engrossing survival game.  It sets itself apart from others in the genre thanks to a story mode which gives you goals to work toward instead of settling for a never-ending grind.
The survival elements are very thorough and realistic.  Eating replenishes calories, performing actions depletes them.  Clothing can get wet.  Everything degrades and needs repairing.  Starting fires is more complex than just clicking a button.  The weather, temperature, and time of day have a huge impact on your experience.  (Fires are harder to sustain in the wind, for example.)
And now, the cons:
-Animal AI is terrible.  I've never played a hunting/survival game with convincing animal AI so maybe it's just not possible with our current level of technology, but it seems to me that programming rabbits and deer to avoid the player instead of running directly at them can't possibly be that complex... but what do I know?
-Wolves are insufferable, partly due to bad AI and partly due to spawn locations meant to maximize irritation.  Example: A wolf was feeding on a deer carcass in the road so I went to sleep in a trailer to avoid walking past it.  Ten hours later, of course the wolf is still there eating that carcass.
You're supposed to be stealthy to get past wolves I guess, but honestly it's so much easier to just sprint past them or let them attack you.  As long as you have medical supplies to heal your wounds, the meat you get from killing them is worth it.
-No tracking?  Injured animals don't leave footprints in the snow for you to follow, (although the player leaves footprints) and the blood trail isn't visible unless you are directly on top of it.  Blood should be very visible against white snow even from a distance.  This seems like a major oversight for a game of this sort.
As annoying as some of these issues are, they haven't stopped me from enjoying the game or from wanting to continue to play.

I once thought one of the hardest city sims in the world was Pharaoh by Impressions Games. Once I picked up Banished, I realized very soon after that this game was much less forgiving. Banished has made city building challenging, something most games don't really capitalize on. What accomplishes this is most city sims deal in concretes, you know exactly what your city holds and what services will give you. Banished is unpredictable and constantly sets you on edge.
A town thriving with 40 people can suddenly become only 15 due to one bad crop year. Birth and death can be very sudden, one can surge while the other is stagnant, forcing you to apply laborers from one area to the other. In my opinion the constant management is what makes this game great, because it keeps you active. Where most city sims really just require you to set up and loosely manage your population, occasionally expanding production, Banished throws you through all sorts of twists and turns, just to survive.
The sandbox appeal is nice, but I hope in future versions there could be actual missions or accomplishments with unique end goals. I also feel the addition of Crime could be a possibility, because sometimes the biggest problem is the people themselves.

I've never written a review of this game, or any game, but I have to say this as a starting point. I have never been a big fan, or really even liked any outlet that portrayed Batman, but I have always had a soft spot for Telltale Games, and their ability to make a story so fleshed out, and to allow for a player, whether casual, or more hardcore, immersed in their story. So, of course, I decided to push my bank account into an uncomfortable position for the mere expression of support of Telltale.
In this playthrough, I realized from conversations with a few of my friends, and some help of the internet, that the story of this game strays from the comic books, and media portrayal, and allows for someone who is new to the lore of Batman to understand this version quite thoroughly, and, for hardcore fans to have a refreshing take of the classic superhero vigilante, as he takes on some of the most adverse villains I, and many others have yet to face.
Bruce Wayne starts with many of his iconic movie/comic tropes, having been the inherit owner of a wealth of cash, and having access to being one of the financial pillars of the ficticious Gotham, but with a twist I shant spoil. He is well into his role of Batman in this story, so if you look for the up-and-coming hero aspect, this may disappoint slightly.
The game follows the same formula as any other game by the company, the standard point-and-click adventure with dialogue and choices to forge the story to a pretty diverse factor, oh, and did I forget? Quick time events that leave your hands bent in awkward angles that make your brain have to physically dust off the old cogs to process these prompts. Plus the addition of some really fleshed out characters, most of which can be built up, or burnt down the heavy influence Mr. Wayne possesses in his city.
(Read this only if you have beaten the game in its entirety and want to avoid spoilers.
Or, on less of a spoiler note, the association of Catwoman, AKA Selina Kyle, who is the primary romantic interest for this series. She plays a central piece to this story. She is a person who has sat on the proverbial fence for many times, with the sole interest being the best outcome in her favor and safety. She has the ability, which is shown, to switch sides on a moments notice when she notices things going downhill, in an act of self preservation. The romance felt real, as she has a backstory of betrayal, which led to distrust, and actions of deceit in an attempt to protect what she wants. She is portrayed not as a damsel in distress, but rather as a strong female who can pull her own weight, without the help of Batman, and protests letting him be her "Knight in shining armor" and at times, left me thinking of some of my ex-girlfriends, which is a sign of a character so realistic it is almost a human being.
This game takes its time to build enough suspense over a few episodes before finally picking up, into a big ball of inferno, which quite literally is Bruce Wayne's life and the entirety of Gotham. And, as any classic game reviewer, or old commercial about Smokey the Bear would say "Its up to you to fill the shoes of Batman" or "Only you can stop these fires"
I would recommend this game to anyone, and have, in many cases. The game captivated me with its story, pulled me in with its characters, and broke me with each sharp turn it took. This game was a rollercoaster that sucks you in for the whole ride. Whether you are new to the scene of Batman, or a die-hard fan, I would recommend at least putting this on your wishlist for the hope of a sale off of what already is a steal, which is a great game, for only $24.99.
