Morphopolis is an incredibly indulgent and simple game. It is plagued with downright unpleasant controls and confusing mechanics. The first level is the most enjoyable - mostly because it makes sense. You start out as a caterpillar that needs to collect some food, and make another bug move out of your way, so that the caterpillar can get into the right spot, and go into the chrysalis stage. This is not explained in any real fashion - you have to figure the objective out for yourself. I'm okay with not spoonfeeding a player with information, especially in a puzzle game, but Morphopolis does not even explain the controls well enough for you to grasp what you are doing, or are supposed to be doing. It exacerbates this issue by only using one button (the left mouse button) to do every single thing in the game.
The second level (through the fourth level) does not have you going through a real stage of metamorphosis, but instead crawling into the head of a larger (dead) insect. Now, I know that there are a couple species of parasites that do this, but not just any cricket or bee can walk into the corpse of another insect like it was the sliding door of a Walgreen's and pilot said insect like that alien from the Men In Black movie - so this idea very much catches you off guard. In practical terms it means you really are just wandering around, completing minor tasks, unsure of where all of your actions are leading until you get there. To make matters worse, the actual mechanics of getting to your new, squishy corpus are painfully slow.
For some unknown reason, no matter what form you take, you are the slowest insect to have ever lived. Perhaps it is because your former self is using some kind of Rube Goldberg lever and pulley system to move the new shell? Maybe it is because the insect from the first level is having to manually move each successive leg inside of each body like Ace Ventura inside of a matryoshka doll of rhinos? I digress - the in-game reason matters not, it is the end user experience, that matters. The game forces you to hold the left click button down for the duration of movement until you reach your destination. This mechanic is made all the more painful because, aside from the time spent actually moving, you really only need to spend about 15-20 seconds on each map before needing to switch to another one.
The reason for the minimal amount of time needed on each map is is that the bulk of what you do involves collecting objects to appease the other insects on the level so they will let you pass. They demand this of you even though completing the task seems to not actually benefit them in any way. These tasks are mostly fetchquests where the Ace Ventura player-insect shows up on the map and then stands there without interacting with the environment in any way as the player (left) clicks on each bauble. The other tasks involve bringing the baubles to some point on the map and then rearranging them until you solve the "puzzle" they constitute. Sadly, you cannot actually collect these objects as you see them. Instead must wait until you have collected all of the objects for the previous task, return to the insect that gave you the task, and then go find the next insect with the next, inconsequential task
I could honestly go on about the failings of this game - but it really boils down to this: it took me two hours to complete an entire game that easily contained less than half an hour of content. It's too slow, too inexplicable, and too unrewarding to make me feel good about the $.19 I spent on it.

Sunless sea is a game set in the fallen londen universe (echo bazaar is their other title, a free browser game) and is a game world with some of the most batshit epic lore that I have ever experienced. Peeling away the layers of mystery is a big appeal of the game but I sometimes wonder if this game wouldn't be more enjoyable in book form. Its mostly text based with a topdown exploration element. The game is punishingly difficult and a big part of the game is managing sanity by sticking near coastlines and trying to keep your prow light on. There is also a trading angle but this is intended as a way to get a little extra money on the side, not as a standalone way to play the game. The storylettes are creepy as hell, which is incidentaly a place that you can go in game to do buisness.
-the writing is great and the universes lore is insane. INSANE. Look up some spoilers, because much of the lore is tied up in echo bazaar and can take a LONG time to get to, it's a big time investment
-the overall game world and concept is very cool, sailing the dark seas is pretty immersive
-the game balance is frankly out of whack. The game is super slow and very unforgiving in the early stages and the way they have balanced the game makes doing everything drag out. Get a re-balance patch, it makes the game so much more enjoyable
-lots of errand running
-modding out some of the difficulty robs the game of the sphincter clenching 90+ madness limp home moments but honestly it's an ok trade
Overall I like sunless sea, dispite it's flaws which to be honest are significant enough to warrant trying to mod out. The writing is maybe not for everyone and the game is a bit of a slow experience but the universe is very well imagined and lots of fun to explore. A very interesting game that goes it's own direction and it mostly works, reccomended for people who like reading eldritch horror

You'll need to find gear, you'll need to make safe houses which can be overrun in an instant, you'll need strategies and multiple exit points. The Long Dark is a survival game of a unique flavor. Unlike most other survival games out there, TLD offers a solitary, pensive and evenly paced experience. As you walk slowly through the snow-covered landscape, you must reason about what you should do next -- be careful though, because a misjudgement might lead to your death. Identifying what is a threat to your survival is the main element of the gameplay, from gathering wood to start a fire and keep yourself warm to catching some fish to eat. If you don't pay attention, you might end up in a situation where you might not realize that you're practically dead. Every trip outside should involve some strategic planning to ensure that you'll make it to safety at the end of the day. The world might look beautiful and picturesque, but it's harsh and relentless -- and if you don't learn quickly, you will find yourself cold and hungry outside during a blinding blizzard, and the last thing you'll see is the whiteness before the Long Dark takes you.

Reviews and reviewers make me angry. Don't read this. Buy the game and make your own mind up. Then have a good think about how the creative industries as a whole use reviewing to part you from your cash. Theft really is not the word for it.
I like a good scare. This game is good at scaring. However it is not the immersive terrifying experience that  some (paid?) reviewers have been prone to bill it as. The best games ever produced had fantastic scripts written by very talented people balanced with superior game mechanics that match the intended experience. This feels like its a level below that. It relies on in your face frights and atmospheric noises just a little too much whilst neglecting, a little too much, a truly terrifying script/game design that will fully engage your imagination.
After a few hours the scared stiff breathing of the main protagonist gets more than a little annoying. The inablity to fight back is, to begin with, a treat to get the adrenalin running. However I'm often brought out of the game immersion to simply get annoyed at the noises he makes along with the lack of retaliation or even... I don't know! maybe effin knock something over behind you as you run or hit that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a plank in the dark as he comes through the door. DUUUUDE do something to survive you moron. I have more than once died trying to get through an open door in a hurry but then again at this point I barely care if he lives or dies. Terror has been suspended by annoyance.
One immersion breaking point is watching the characters move in the dark, sure footed and as if the room is brightly lit.
It often becomes apparent that the other characters follow a rigid script that can be exploited, until you realise that it's not exploiting, this is simply the game. AI feels like it is almost non existent. The plot feels like it too obviously advances in a number of set scenes. You intuitively know when you are safe to run around because you know that you have just 'finished' the latest scene.
This could have been the single most scary game ever released but it is unable to sustain fear due to there being so many immersion breaking points.
All of the parts are there, quality graphics, quality sound, quality programming but it misses on bringing all this together. Not by far, but enough to make this game good, not great. Once again hype and fanboy aggression trumps fact and for some ruins the expectation.
Having said this the game is very playable. Play it in a dark room, with decent sound then engage your imagination and it should give you some nice chills/scares.
Finally it should be noted that having the camcorder light as your only real tool is not very original. It is a variation on a number of games, perhaps the most obvious being Alan Wake. Its inclusion produces a wry smile to those of us who have played video games on dozens of platforms, for decades. We just keep seeing the same music, films and games coming around in shiny new packages to suit the next generation. Sad really but a lesson we all learn as we transition into grumpy old ............

I can't write a real in-depth review because I'm not sure if I want to play this for much longer - it feels rushed, really rushed, with a lot of design and gameplay problems.
You get xp from basically doing anything, and you can spend it on unlocking further tiers of sciences - but there are so, so many branches that's absurd. Melee weapon, energy weapon, projectile weapon, phase weapon - four different ones. Explorer, fighter and builder armor, utility, consumables - it's overbearing and really hard to notice what's useful. Crafting is also a mess - it's great that you can multiple materials when the recipe only asks for *metal*, but you need to pick the chosen one from a drop-down menu. There's an autofill button that uses the lowest tier? most abundant? resource of yours, but in that case I don't know why is that not the basic option. Not to mention that opening one dropdown menu doesn't closes the other, and they overlap - I can't believe this is happening in a finished, released game. And finding the actual items from the crafting menu is just a nightmare - if you check "all", there are too many options, but other than that, you can filter by type. And you know what does that mean - even more dropdown menu, trying to find out which one has a craftable, or even a useful item in it.
Graphics are vibrant coloured ones, but it's like someone smeared something opalesque on it - hard to take out silhouettes, the size of the blocks, the aim of weapons/tools.    But hey, we have a spaceshark companion who's sounds are like a girl whining in an anime... ON A SPACESHARK.... just... no.
If I should summerize the game in a world, I would say  it's  unintuitive. But to a high level.  Stay away from this one - Terraria still provides so much fun and depth, and even Windforge has more style with it's weird 2.5D graphics than this game :\  Maybe I'll come back to force some progress, but this game is a definite NOT RECOMMENDED.  Not to mention that the 15€ price is infuriatingly high.

SUPERHOT is proof of what can happen when a small, indi development team puts out what is essentially a labor of love: they create a product that easily competes with the big boys, those AAA developers with all the money and the huge offices and marketing and labor pools...
SUPERHOT has breathed life into the ailing FPS genre. It brings original mechanics, notably its "bullet time" system to freshen up a genre that has simply become: "guy get gun, go blow things up, BOOM". Its plot, like its graphics, seems simple at first, but as the player advances through the various "cracked" levels, a more far more interesting, layered, and sinister plot begins to show itself.
The graphics themselves are pretty... They're simple polygons of red, black, and white, but they are utilized extremely well . The game flows smoothly, and I don't once find myself wishing for something more "realistic."
The gameplay itself is easy to pick up, but hard to master, particularly as more and more mechanics are added, and there are even a few mechanics hidden, just waiting to be discovered by accident, or by particularly creative players (It's a me! Mario!).
If I had any gripe... it would be that the game mechanics feel almost TOO simple I love bullet time, and I love being able to pull off matrix-like moves, but let me do more of it. Let me run on walls. Let me crouch and lean to avoid bullets. Let me do what I'm accustomed to doing in an FPS, but do it with more style.
The variety of weapons could also use a bit of work. Maybe add in an explosive or two... rather than either every gun having bullets or every melee object simply being there to throw... This game is amazing, and it has TONS of room to grow. Now if you'll excuse me, I want to dig some more into this mystery.

Batman: The Telltale Series is an alternative universe for Batman where you learn some dark truths about the Wayne family. You have to guide Bruce Wayne and his alter-ego Batman (or is it the other way around?) through the story as you delve deeper and deeper into your family's past. The gameplay is a simple point-and-click adventure with QTE action sequences. If you are looking for something that's similar to the Arkham games, you're going to be disappointed. Also, if you're a Batman canon fanatic, then this game will also upset you. You have to go into it with a fresh new perspective and ready to relearn the story of Bruce Wayne and the Wayne family. You must balance the perception of Bruce Wayne and Batman in the eyes of Gotham and the other main characters in the plot. The choices have some impact on the game as who trusts you and who doesn't is determined by the choices you make. There is also a sequel out, and the choices you make in this game will invariable make their way into the second installment (although I have yet to see if they are major or minor).
If you like Telltale games, this one is an above average one (average being their Sam & Max series or their Back to the Future series, with their top being The Walking Dead Season 1, below average being Jurassic Park). There's some framerate drops in the beginning and some hilarious glitches (like when Vicki Vale makes a sad-ish face, her face literally grows as it moves down) and those things need to be addressed on Telltale's end. The game engine is also getting a little tired. The animation-style is okay since these are comic characters, but when you see the Arkham graphics and you can see how a comic can be done with great graphics, I think it's time for Telltale to start investing in a new engine.

Interesting little game, it's a turn-based tactical game, sequal to the original Sid Meier's Ace Patrol. It is very basic in its design, set in the Pacific during WW2, you can choose to play as either the Japanese Imperial Navy or the US Navy.
In terms of challenge - On easy there is very little skill involve - simply get behind your opposition, not in front of them, and continue to shoot them until you've defeated them. As you increase the difficulty the challenge really does ramp up and you will need to plan what manueveres to upgrade your pilots with and understand how and when to use them, it becomes like a chess game.
I was dissapointed by the use of famous naval battles to represent each chapter, the opening page of the chapter gives you a very basic run down of the battle, however the subsequent fights have no relationship to the so-called setting, they are literally just randomly generated engagements based off the same 4 engagement types - Combat Air Patrol, Search & Destroy, Recon or Escort. Really it either needed to be related or it could've just been called "Round 4" or something.
I prefer the original version, at the end of the day there is a bit more variation in it than this one and you get to choose the engagements which means you can choose to challenge yourself or avoid doing that one engagement type that you've become bored of.
Overall if you like turn-based tactical or even if you're just a fan of WW2 it could be and interesting way to waste a few hours.

Blue shift is a standalone mod for Half life 1, or the gold source engine so to speak, that is based around the original half life series. During the game, you play as a security guard, working yet another day at black mesa. But this day is'nt the same as any other. All of the aspects of Half life, thrown into a smaller and shorter story.
It may be short, but there are a few puzzles that make you run around a bit, even though the answer was right in front of your face the entire time. Alteast that was the case for me. As I played, I made my own way of what weapons to use against what enemies. How to take them down and so forth. If you know how to B-Hop, then the movement will go a lot quicker. If you dont? Oh, wow this game came out when?
1992. Such an odd blur of memories swims around in my head; hanging out with the kids on my street after school, playing Wolfenstein 3D with my neighbor, watching Ren and Stimpy as often as I could. It is all one big flannel coated memory with Nirvana and Criss Cross songs in the background. Now, I never had a Neo-Geo or an NES. All I had was my Dad’s 486 that could barely play Alone in the Dark. Baseball Stars 2 was completely off my radar, I even had to check the wiki page to see the history of it. Yet, here it is on Steam in all its glory. Will it still hold up after twenty-five years? I’m about to drink some pixelated kool-aid and find out.
With bright green and yellow hues predominating the screen, there is a rather nice hand drawn look to the splash screen. This extends throughout the game with what I consider well-colored pixel art even though it seems every character is smirking angrily as if they are part-time evil villains on the weekend.
It has a genuine baseball card feel to the art style along with perhaps a dated 80’s comic book look to each baseball player. There are animations throughout the game, including pitching, hitting, and the like. Don’t expect to have still graphics here, it’s entirely animated with slight movement throughout. Sometimes the graphic action moves a little too fast for me, as power-ups and player changeouts surprised me with the quick speed across my screen.
To my surprise, I can even play this in 4K. Granted, it looks the same as if I did in 1080p. I set the graphics to widescreen which squishes the players slightly but looks well enough. I’m impressed by the graphics options on a game this old. One caveat, I tried this on both my gaming PC and my laptop. Since my laptop is not 1080p, and the game uses cloud saving, it would not render properly on my laptop once I sent the graphics to 1080p on my gaming PC.
It’s loud and arcadey with the occasional “BASE..BALL.STARS..2!” thrown into the music. It really does feel like the same type of music as the other Neo Geo games I have played like Metal Slug. I don’t really mind it, but once you play in single player mode you might be turning down the volume if you didn’t lower it already from the options menu
When you start out you can play single-player or a two player local co-op. If you decide to play the single player, watch out. You have to play the entire playoff series in one full playthrough with no saves in between. Basically, you will be there to battle it out with six teams for several hours unless you decide to quit the game without saving.
There are two modes of gameplay, easy and hard. I recommend using the easy setting to start out with as it’s a whole lot easier to catch a ball in the field. From there, you get to pick your team. Take a look at the stats to see what team you prefer. This is somewhat important because those stats carry on into the game, meaning that teams that hit better, catch better, are evenly balanced and such will have those same advantages in the game. What is kind of nice is that none of these teams exist and Baseball Stars 2 has fun with that bit with such things as players named Mummy or Zombie if you pick the New York Monsters as a club. I imagine there are no license hoops to jump though because they omitted using real major league names in the game.
Right here is where the gameplay gets to the nitty gritty. It’s slightly basic in how you can hit or pitch. However, don’t think it’ won’t be hard. Pitchers throw curveballs, fastballs, slow balls, and everything in the middle. It can be exasperating to hit something. When you do, unless you are hitting a home run you will likely be out because the CPU is an expert at catching balls. I believe I only had one grounder that they missed, barely making it to first base. There are power-ups and player changeouts to play with too, so if you really need a homerun then use that power-up to knock it out of the ballpark. If your pitcher looks tired and the pitches are slowing down, change him out. Pitching was perhaps the only thing I was half decent at in this game. I could aim just towards the edge of the mound and switch up between fastballs and slowballs. Try as I might, I could not get a proper curveball to work. At best, I could shut out the opposing team for an inning. Mostly, though, they would hit a ball and I would miss the catch if I was too far from it.
Catching was perhaps the worst part of the game. The angle is super low, making it very hard to judge where to be when the ball comes crashing down. Also, if it hit to the back of the field you would have to scramble to catch it with players that felt disjointed as I controlled them all in one massive grab – usually falling flat. For the most part, they looked like foosball players all missing the mark repeatedly in unison. This went on and on as I missed those catches, making me want to cue some Benny Hill sax music. I usually lost big time in the pennant race, so if you play this I say play with a friend so that it evens your chances.
It’s kinda fun. While I doubt I would want to play the single player again against all the teams in succession and no saves, the local co-op aspect of the game it pretty neat. I can see myself loading this up with a buddy and some beers to see who could win with these fielding controls. My Xbone controller had no troubles in the setup and frankly, it’s a decent port by Dot Emu. There are some funny moments when you hit a batter with a ball and he comes over to punch you in the face. That right there is golden.
While I would not say it’s a must-buy game, it is surprisingly well designed and holds up for a nice arcade experience from 1992. Despite its age and limited controls, I think I could find some fun with a friend and trying to catch balls from backfield – while not entirely sober. That’s well enough for me anyway.
Rating: Save for Later

Despite I like the atmosphere of this game and find myself reading the stories with curiosity like I read most of H. P. Lovecraft works (Of course they not as good as HP's work, but they are quite interesting to read) I can't enjoy this game because of its tedious gameplay.
First of all, I'm not the fan of trading games like "Port Royale" or "Patrician" because I find them too grindy for my taste and I get bored too quickly. Therefore, this is my first problem with this game because you HAVE to trade goods and find profitable routes to make a profit and keep your crew well feed and your ship stocked with fuel.
Of course, you can make profit by selling other stuff that you will find during your exploration but it will be a bare minimum and if you want to buy yourself, a decent ship you have to trade.
Eventually, you have to memorize which port sells which goods, how much they cost, where you can sell them to make more profit, and do not forget about other docks that offer you other stuff to sell and buy not for money. Because for some reason there is no way to see that vital information in the game anywhere except in the dock itself, as well as information about docks like can they repair your ship and do they sell fuel and supplies.
The second thing that I did not like is slow ships sailing and slow game progress. It would be great if the game had an acceleration of time with the automatic pause feature in important situations because you will be using your start ship for a long long time before you can afford something better.
However, if you have patience, then this world is quite interesting to explore. Many different places offer a bunch of different text events that, in one way or another can affect the world and as I said earlier, they are interesting to read.
In general, I don't think that rogue like gameplay is very good chose for the story driven game because in this game when you die (and you will) you either start all over again or continue to play as successor however in both ways, all of your story progress will be reset.
When I bought this game I thought that it will be something like an exploration game with unnecessary trading and trivial surviving, but instead, I got an another trading game in the unusual world which you occasionally can explore, and surviving elements which just slow down your progress because you constantly monitoring the status of your supplies, crew, and money.
I wish that there were some story mode, which will allow you to explore the world, complete quests and do other stuff without worrying about your supplies.

A good poriton of this review will be singing the praises of the port of this game, more so than the game itself.
Baseball Stars 2 is a solid, albeit basic, 16-bit baseball game.
This version, however, is unique as it is more than a simple rom/emulator combo. The devs have taken the time to build a custom front-end menu. More importantly, they've actually changed the nature of the timer in the game.
Normally, you will see the timer counting down. As this was originally an arcade game, you only had 3 and a half-minutes of gametime. At which piont you would need to add another quarter. This behavior carried over to the home verson on the Neo Geo AES system.
With this port, thee timer starts at 0:00 and counts up. Maybe a minor rom hack, but a significant one that makes this the best possible version of the game. This minor tweak converts a game that was designed  to eat quarters and turn around players quickly, into a more relaxed home experieence.
Utlimatelly, while I like the effort  of the remade menu, I don't feel it's necessary, but the tweak to the timer is invaluable and really brings the game in line with what you'd expect from a console game.
The value proposition of spending $3-$10 for this game (regularly available in bundles and sales) is a personal call. Having lived through the days of the $200 Neo Geo games (not the console, but the actual game itself. One  cartridge. And they couild cost over $1,000. Not adjusted for inflation), I find value in picking it up at one of the lower price points.

It occurs to me that while this game deservedly possesses the Lovecraftian tag, playing Sunless Sea is very much like reading a Dickens novel.  It's set in a gloomy, alternate London (which is now located in a vast undersea cavern), atmospheric, moody, deliberately paced (that's a nice way to say slow), sometimes overly verbose, and stuffed full of memorable derelict characters.  And, just like a Dickens novel, it can take a while to get a handle on what's really going on.
The gameplay is an eclectic blend combining elements of several disparate genres: visual novel, 4X, RTS, RPG and even a bit of rogue-like influences are all to be found.  You play a zee (yes, zee; not sea) captain whose primary function is to explore the dark, vast Unterzee.  Along the way, missions are obtained, unusual characters (and terrors) are encountered, and more likely than not it ends in a watery grave.  But even doom has a certain morbid appeal to it in this game.  Taken as individuals, each of the elements listed above would be found wanting.  However, Sunless Sea does a really nice job of combining them in a way that makes the whole much better than the sum of its parts.
If you enjoy games that feel subtantive and dense (again, like a Dickens novel) you're likely to enjoy Sunless Sea.  On the other hand, if you prefer more straightforward, frenetically paced action, take a pass or wait for a deep discount.  I happen to think Sunless Sea is a very good game.  But it's simply not going to be to everyone's taste.

Summary:
Going beyond "run and gun corridors," "monster-closet AIs" and static worlds, BioShock creates a living, unique and unpredictable FPS experience. After your plane crashes into icy uncharted waters, you discover a rusted bathysphere and descend into Rapture, a city hidden beneath the sea. Constructed as an idealistic society for a hand picked group of scientists, artists and industrialists, the idealism is no more. Now the city is littered with corpses, wildly powerful guardians roam the corridors as little girls loot the dead, and genetically mutated citizens ambush you at every turn. Take control of your world by hacking mechanical devices, commandeering security turrets and crafting unique items critical to your very survival. Upgrade your weapons with ionic gels, explosives and toxins to customize them to the enemy and environment. Genetically modify your body through dozens of Plasmid Stations scattered throughout the city, empowering you with fantastic and often grotesque abilities. Explore a living world powered by Ecological A.I., where the inhabitants have interesting and consequential relationships with one another that impact your gameplay experience. Experience truly next generation graphics that vividly illustrate the forlorn art deco city, highlighted by the most detailed and realistic water effects ever developed in a video game. Make meaningful choices and mature decisions, ultimately culminating in the grand question: do you exploit the innocent survivors of Rapture...or save them?

It’s still light, but only for a moment. You check your status and see that only a few hours of daylight remain and you are already starting to freeze because of the blizzard swirling around you. After taking a few moments to analyze the amount of equipment you have, you make the decision that you have to find more, and fast. As you begin walking, you can see that your status is decreasing quickly, so even though it will make you tired faster, you make the decision to run. The light slowly starts to fade around you as you pant through the woods, desperately searching for anything that will help to keep you alive, you hear the howl. You turn quickly towards the direction of the footsteps, but the animal is already upon you, ripping at your clothes, trying to survive also.
He does, you don’t. You have faded into The Long Dark...
The Long Dark is a sandbox survival game where a massive blizzard has rocked the Canadian wilderness and trapped you, where you have to rely upon basic survival abilities and a whole lot of scavenging to survive.
The game begins with one of a multitude of canned quotes about survival, or connection to the wilderness, which is a nice way to start a difficult game. When the black quote screen fades away, you see one of the reasons that this game shines above its counterparts, which is the devastating beauty that the developers focused on in the world around you. Instead of crumbling buildings and a sharp grittiness to the environment, the art feels more like you slowly floated into a world that has descended into silence. The art style is somewhere between cell shading and being in an actual painting, which is the perfect environment to try and survive in.
The game is hard, because the world is brutally unforgiving, especially to those who are used to ‘survival’ games where you can stock up on items, or simply hunker down and wait it out. On more occasions than I like to admit, I found myself huddled next to a fire or a furnace waiting until I could muster enough strength to find a granola bar, or water bottle that would sustain me for only a few minutes more. I could certainly opt for gutting a deer and harvesting its meat, but first I would have to find one that was already dead (because you can’t even think about weapons until you are 4-5 days in, unless you are lucky enough to find a rifle). The amount of energy needed to get that meat is enormous though, and can often lead to freezing or hypothermia if you are not stocked up on your basic survival bars. The bars used to keep you in the know about your ability to survive are: Temperature, Energy, Hunger, and Thirst, or as I like to call them, Sims Bars. Basic tasks must be metered and prepared for, because once they are complete, it is imperative that you refuel your Sims Bars. This is how I imagine it would actually be in this environment, so it is a true feat of gameplay to feel it so quickly.
After getting the hang of the basics of survival though, you run into the elements of the game that prevent TLD from being everything that it could be. The items in the game world quickly become monotonous and the thrill of finding things is replaced with the recurring question of whether or not it is worth the extra inventory space for another Summit Soda, or if you should simply drink it quickly and move on. Although it certainly plays into the narrative of the game to limit the amount of interesting items that can be found quickly, though it creates a boredom that comes surprisingly fast. Add a strange injury system that causes ‘fall’ injuries while walking up hills, a stealthily hidden linear open world that rewards you for remembering each and every plot line (which never change), and almost no character progression to the list, and you have a good understanding of what you are getting into.
What is strange is that levels of fire making or crafting are shown in the relevant screens, but there is no actual progression. Additionally, although it is a nice touch to have the character you are playing to occasionally voice something specific to the situation you face, there is no back story or interaction aside from these voiceovers that makes you feel a connection.
There is no doubt that the creators of The Long Dark have something unique and special on their hands, but if fleshed out more, it could be a game that stands alone in its genre, and stands strong. I will keep playing it, and loads of others should too.

Yet another testament to the great Kickstarter/Early Access deluge of 2014.
The game has, as near as I can tell, been completely abandoned by the developers and the community manager, with one of the former regularly going on about a new project he's working on.
No one from the dev team appear to have been anywhere near the Steam forums (nor the official forums, from what little I checked) for around three months now.
The game seemed interesting enough, with an interesting (if somewhat grindy) Science XP mechanic, wherein mining and killing critters got you Science XP to unlock crafting tiers.
Sadly, attempting to load a game, or even start a new world with a saved character causes a Coherent UI crash, which the devs have never fixed. IF you are able to get your world to load then you will be stuck without a HUD. No way to manage your inventory, and no way to transfer/drop/change items. Crafting is also impossible.
tl;dr? Yet another dead, abandoned game that serves as a testament against Kickstarters and Early Access.

My feelings on this game are strange. Its lacking so many things, but its still the only survival game that centers on survival, so its really the only one I can recommend.
Pros
-Nice environments.
-Good struggle to keep health.
-Great weight system.
-SFX are pretty good.
Cons
-No compass. Some say the event in the main story disables compasses, but that's no excuse for sandbox.
-Weird animals. Wolves will attack, completely unprovoked. A single wolf wont just attack a healthy, able bodied person. I assume bears are the same way. Massive deer will run back and forth around your area, and don't get spooked until you're close.
-Lack of animal life. Five animals, and four fish. They didn't even bother to program a doe (female deer).
-Extreme lack of plant life. Other than firewood, there's one tree you can craft, a single fungus (and it isn't chaga), and cattails. Wheres my rose hips, juniper, and field garlic?
-Plants don't respawn.
-Whetstones are made of bread. Its the only way I can explain getting only twenty uses out of them. You should be able to get thousands of uses, and once worn, a second whetstone can be used to resurface the other. Also, sharpening is incremental, instead of limited by skill.
-All the food in Canada goes bad after a month. I have no idea who came up with this system, but I don't think he owns a refrigerator.
-Total lack of weapons. You get bows and a rifle, and that's it. No shotguns, atlatls, slings, or spears. You can't even defend yourself with a knife, which could work against black bear, as they don't like a challenge.
-Limited tools and skills. No axes, large knives, buck saws, folding saws, tomahawks, scaling knives, awls, flint and steel, bone tools, trap setting, bed crafting, shelter crafting etc.
I could go on, but my fingers are cramping.
I understand, full well, that this game wasn't designed around sandbox mode, but they accidentally made a proper survival game, and I will be very disappointed if they don't expand on it. Hell, at this point, I'd pay a hundred USD for an actual survival game. I'd love to see some non-winter map expansions (swimming and boats maybe?), a tool and crafting system overhaul, and a recalculating of the item condition degradation system.
Lastly, this has that really annoying Unity bug, for Linux, that locks your view directly up, and faces you to one direction, sometimes.

I played SMAP initially on iOS a couple of years ago, so when I saw both SMAP games on Steam I jumped at them.  These are turn-based dogfighting/fighter mission games.  Think of them as a lite version of the Wings of War boardgame.  These days, IMHO Sid will put his name on anything, so it is good to read the reviews and watch the previews to see if it is something you like.
For me, it was.  I think I got this game for less than USD$3 and it is worth it for that price, as you will be challenged, you will go down in flames a few times (or more) and you will get 25-30 hours of turn-based gameplay out of it.
If this kind of game is interesting to you, or the strategy around dogfighting or ground attack missions interests you, then I think you will find it interesting. So, this is a short game about the life of the insects (but not really). It's point&click puzzle game, with very chill vibe to it. The story (if one may call it) is really short and consists of 5 missions, each taking anything from 5 to 20 minutes to complete.
Controls are a bit lackluster, but absolutely nothing to worry about in such a short game. Puzzles are pretty simple, except for the very last one (took me around 15 minutes to solve).
Visual aesthetics are the main selling point of the game, I think -- hand-drawn insects look pretty unique, I don't think I've seen anything like this game before. It looks an illustration that came alive out of some some old biology book.
Overall, this game is a great way to spend an hour, if you don't have anything better to do. I would definitely recommend it to people who enjoy an occasional puzzle or two.
Extra points for not having any bugs (except for those that are, you know, actual bugs -- as in, insects)!

Train Valley nails the simple game mechanics + good execution = fun gameplay formula. There isn't much to Train Valley, you can build tracks, start or stop trains, and toggle switches between tracks. The real fun in the game lies in trying to reach the level goals and achievements. Complete the level without ever stopping a train or maximize your efficiency to make as much money as possible. It has a lot of parallels with tower defense games. You want to build you train tracks in an efficient layout, connecting all your stations in all directions, but using the minimum amonut of space. You only want to spend money on new track when you have to, using surplus cash to send extra trains for even more money.
Overall a solid recommendation. Especially if you enjoy the mazing and profit min/maxing parts of tower defense.

Sunless Sea - I pulled it out on recommendation of Extra Credits. That being said, I'm conflicted over its content.
Thematically, this game is great. The universe created is deliciously dark; monsters, madness, cannibalism, and just that right amount of creativity to add its own world-specific conflicts, like Sunlight smuggling, and the Red Honey trade. These factor into gameplay too - it's hard to make an honest living, but if you're just willing to skirt the law a little bit, things get just a little easier, adding a good reason to be a bad guy.
Also, there is a lot of writing put into this story. Tons of hidden stories, branching questlines, and choices that rely a lot on your own common sense as to whether you should go for a risk. Heck, just because a choice has a 20% success rate doesn't mean it's always bad to give it a shot if the consequences aren't bad.
However... this is supposed to be a Roguelike game. Once you die, a part of your progress is transfered over to your next character, and you may improve how much is transfered over by purchasing a house, a Will, and more. Cool in concept, except for what your expected game length is. On my third life, I have a little over 10 hours worth of progress, and will probably lose almost all of the time spent progressing storylines, making the back and forth trips in dangerous waters, never mind the levels gained (I can, at most, keep half the progress of a single skill).
The entire way this game is built is simply not in line with what a game with perma-death should have. Roguelikes have the appeal of perma-death, but that's passable because you're not expected to live very long anyways; I mean, how long do you live in Rogue Legacy or Binding of Isaac? Maybe 2-10 minutes? Maybe in One Way Heroics you could have a 2 hour long life taken away from you with a bit of bad luck if you went for one of the pure endurance objectives. In Sunless Sea, we're talking hours on hours of reset progress.
Then, on top of that, the game also fails to be entertaining beyond the first couple hours. When you start off, the world is undiscovered, full of secrets to slowly uncover, but as you progress, you find yourself running fetch quests or hunting down obscure items to finish recipes. It even turns into a farming simulator at some point, having you make back and forth trips to secure little bits of profit so you can buy the next ship and do it again.
Yeah, there's still a fair bit of stuff I haven't discovered yet, and probably won't, because as soon as I die, all those things I was so close to discovering will have their progress reset, which is going to mean hours of work just to get to where I was before. It's not even -hard- work either, it's mostly just back and forths, hoping I don't screw up.
The game's universe is astoundingly well written and I hate to give it a bad review, but it flops as an actual game. The UI is weird and makes you really dig to try and check up on your objectives, there's a lot of farming, and the Roguelike mechanics which revolve around death don't make up for how much is actually lost each time. At the end of the day, if a game is advertising itself as a game, then it has to be fun to play, and I honestly can't recommend it as such.

Sunless Sea is a fascinating, text-based, adventure game mixed in with a real-time, 2D, rogue-like, exploration and resource management game. I spend most of this review complaining about a few massive problems, but that's because I loved the game enough to care.
You create an identity as a ship captain, ready to take your chances on the open (but very dark and scary) sea, hoping to make your fortune and leave a legacy. The legacy thing is important because the game expects you to die eventually, at which point, if you have been paying attention, you will have something to leave to your successor, making their adventures a little bit more likely to succeed. These adventures typically involve setting sail for foreign ports, each of which present you with various text-based options when you arrive. This is how Sunless Sea tells its wonderful stories, and the decisions you make as captain have a way of affecting many other things, often in very unexpected ways. Each time you leave your home port of London you feel a mixture of excitement and trepidation because there is a strong possibility that this particular captain might never see home again. A lot can go wrong on the dark sea, whether from the ramifications of hasty or ill-informed decisions on foreign soil, or from the problems thrown up by the real-time juggling act of managing your food, your fuel, your light, your visibility to enemies, and the mental health of your crew, assuming you haven't had to eat them all just to stay alive.
With its graphics, its music and its language, Sunless Sea creates an amazingly evocative atmosphere, despite being a slow-paced, top-down, 2D game. Of course there are monsters out there who want to eat you, and hostile ships who will attack you on sight if you show them your prow light. It can take a long time before you are properly equipped to deal with such threats, but happily they can usually be avoided with a bit of care and patience. The real threat is not the beasties with the tentacles, it's the fact that if just one thing goes wrong while you're out at sea that one thing can have a domino effect on everything else - I never once got eaten or capsized, but I did limp back into home port countless times with 0 food, 0 fuel, and far fewer crew members than I left with. Since returning home to London and cashing in port reports (from all the other ports your visited since you last left London) is for a long time your best way of making reliable money, doing so is really the only way you have of figuratively and literally keeping your head above water, at least until ages down the line, when you can afford to buy a ship with enough cargo space to begin trading goods with other islands. This constantly pushes you to take more and more risks, visiting ports much farther afield as you try to explore the map, gambling with your food and fuel supplies - if you make it back you'll make more money, but only
you make it back.
The slow pace of Sunless Sea is something you'll just have to accept, and shouldn't be seen as a problem - it's just how the game is. However, there are some problems which really started to bother me and finally caused me to stop playing the game altogether, at least for a while.
Being a rogue-like, your captain can die and the game gives you the option of creating a new one. You can pass on the previous captain's legacy to the new one if the previous captain got that far, but (amazingly) all story progress your previous captain made is reset. This makes no sense in terms of continuity - if one captain passes something on to their successor on the same timeline, how can all the developments put in place by the previous captain on that same timeline be wiped away? This leaves you feeling like every single decision your previous captain made was completely meaningless, since all that ever had to happen for everything to be reversed was the death of that particular character. Considering the sheer amount of time it takes to move the text-based stories forward and to make any real progress, the idea that it will all be scrubbed clean if your current captain dies was enough on its own to make me determined not to lose a single captain, which in turn sidestepped the whole point of the rogue-like part of the game.
Unfortunately you can only have one captain (and one ship) at a time, and the game autosaves (no reloads if you make a mistake). This seems like such a strange contradiction to me - the game wants you to treat the death of a captain with a shrug and a 'oh well, that's the game', as though such a loss is just a minor and even intended setback, but then it punishes you so severely for losing a captain that it ensures you will find a way to bypass these terrible consequences (such as by finding out where the game's autosave file is hidden and constantly making backup versions of it). Some players have argued that this reset mechanic is the only way to learn how to play the game - no it isn't, you can just start a New Game if you want to. I had the same captain for ages and she never died, and that was fine by me.  There's a reason why games no longer send you all the way back to the start of the game and reset all your progress if you die just once - no-one wants to play games that way any more.
The text-based adventures can also bite you in the hull with similarly disastrous effects. You might find a particularly profitable trade route (involving coffee, for example) and come to believe that this is one of the best ways of making money in the game, which it is. At least until you return to the trader to find that he has packed up shop and skipped town, shutting down that trade route forever. The game requires you to make tons of money if you want the best gear (and you definitely do, unless you want to trundle around at the speed of a dead jellyfish forever), but it so heavily restricts your ability to make money that putting any cash together becomes a huge chore. The game's economy is hard to understand but appears to be terribly designed - there are so few goods that you can buy low and sell high, and having only one ship and very limited cargo space means that trading can be a huge time sink. OK, it's not a trading game, but if it isn't then why is everything so insanely expensive? The answer is that the developers want you to spend a lot of time playing the game, but if so why do they reset all progress when you die, ensuring you will immediately stop playing and possibly never return? Mad.
By far the worst offender of all the text-based adventures was the one which (without warning) results in the London admiralty no longer accepting your port reports because they consider you an anarchist. For me this represented an immediate Game Over - the port reports should have been an untouchable constant in the game, impossible to break. At some points in this game it feels like the developers were a little too in love with the idea of Sunless Sea being a rogue-like with major implications following from your decisions, forgetting that some things are just absolutely no fun. I should want to keep playing, not feel like I just got completely screwed because the game was smugly hiding information from me.
This game will fascinate and enthral you, it will take up a lot your time, it will occasionally leave you stunned as parts of its stories are revealed, and it might break your heart (in a good way). But don't set sail without realising that there are one or two game mechanics hiding under the surface which can feel cheap and even cruel. Backup your save file and stay away from the anarchists and you'll probably be alright. Ignore this advice and it's possible that you might never want to return to this game. For the record, I will go back at some point, having earned my sea legs the hard way.

On the edge.
Always a few seconds away from a uninformed decision or a simple risk and your little boat capsizes into the deep and dark fathoms of the sea.
If a bunch of story tellers and mathematicians got together to design a game - this would be it.
Question - is it any good?
Queen Victoria betrays London to an entity called Echo Bazaar to save her husband.  The mysterious creature, with the help of thousands of bats, takes the city down, deep, submerged and surrounded by the Unterzee. A subterranean cavern.
You are a ship captain. Formerly a poet or a priest. Maybe you was a street urchin years ago? You choose your background and more interestingly your final goal. First time around I chose to be a former soldier looking to find his lost father - assumed dead. Can I bring his bones back to London for a proper burial?
The art style got my attention first. Top down. The eerie glow of dark green constantly fighting back the depths of black. A strange image of a shark in chains. A little boat almost struggling, slowly, silently chugging along. Some landmarks that not quite feel familiar - was that St. Pauls?
These strange boxes of information and people, making choices and interactions. Lots of options. So many choices. Almost like one of those old choose your own adventure story books.
The game was nothing like I imagined.
Sunless Sea goes against the grain straight away by stating death is not the end - in fact it is positively encouraged. I have come to believe dying at least once is the way to go as you are able to transfer some wealth to your scion. To Lord Azlan The Second. After death the game resets itself so if you have - for example - exhausted a trade route - your second character can do it again. You can pass on a house, your best weapon and at least half your cash. Later on in the game, if you fall in love, become a parent, buy a mansion, pass on even more to your children.
It took me a while to get my head around that.
On the edge.
Fuel. Food and Terror. You need to keep an eye on each otherwise a miscalculation or risk taken in good faith can start a downward spiral that leads to certain death. On one island I took a slight risk and lost half my crew. Thinking that could not happen again I threw the dice once more expecting a better outcome - It didn't. I was a poor fool of a captain!
Another time I was barely limping back to London with one hull point of strength left. I could have turned up the engines and sped home much faster but I decided to try and conserve fuel when I had fuel in abundance. One lucky shot from a low life pirate ended my story.
Not all deaths have been due to my own incompetence. One time I invistagated a strange sea creature and my poor little ship got whacked from some sort of energy wave. Lesson learned.
So many lessons to learn. Reminds me of a phrase in a certain film that God only knows everything because He has been around for so long. Each time you play and die, you learn a little more.
I have been so stupid. But I have also been brave. Even sailing my little ship of the edge of the world to see what would happen.
On one island I found a bunch of zombie undead that wanted to go on one last sea cruise. Another island seemed to be devoted to a postman god. One had monkeys with a zeppelin. I better stop - so many spoilers. The story telling is pretty good and you should resist the urge to treat this game as a simple resource management game. Slow down and immerse yourself in the text. It is fantastic.
Improving your wealth allows you to buy a better ship and equipment and gaining experience allows you to increase your base stats which helps in the numerous chance based choices the game sends your way.
Crew members are required for sailing your ship effectively. They can also be seen as extra parcels of food if the going gets tough. Officers are another story. Each has their own unique one. Some are incredibly well written and heart breaking. Officers improve your stats and can also be used as trainers.
Trading is diabolical. Just barely profitable if you take fuel and supply costs into account. I wish there were some decent routes. Buy coffee. Sell coffee. Make 20% profit. Nothing like that. Even the few that are found end up being nerfed by the inbuilt choices and consequences in the game.
The best way to improve the life of a simple ship captain is to adventure and unfold the various stories. Rewards gained by exploring and working through adventures probably lead to mroe wealth than any trading can do.
One time I gained the courage to take on every nasty little opposing ship I met on the zee. I managed to beat opponents that had double my fire power. Combat itself is very basic but can be a good source of food supplies.
In the end I can't say if I really enjoyed my 100+ hours in the game. It's unique and challenging.
Question - are you Bill Murray or Agrajag?
In Groundhog Day Bill Murray went through a time period over and over again and each day he died. Before he came through it he went through some very rough times of despair and darkness. In Sunless Sea I would recommend you play with a note book as the in-game journal - though interesting, just can't cut it. You need to maximise your journey expenses against rewards. Your captain must optimise as far as possible. After many play throughs some things will become familiar.
In Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams wrote about a creature called Agrajag who was killed by Arthur Dent in every reincarnation. Every time he came back, as a fly or dragon, or man, Dent killed him. He went mad.
So you are kept on the edge, who will you be?
Some tips
Maybe travel around at full speed because fuel is much cheaper than supplies.
Consider waiting to haul sphinxstone until you have the larger cargo ship - as the runs are limited.
Note any time your stats are increased - note the island and the choices you made.
Note the places where fuel and supplies can be purchased - NOTE THEM
The evil looking guy with a sharp knife bearing gifts? I did my best performance when I said NO THANKS
Some negatives
Trading is deliberately - DELIBERATELY - hard. I just wish it was better by just 5%
In game hints and explanations are lacking.
The trapped in an eternal cycle, going round and round, following the same paths, can get damning.
FINAL
Lovely, complex, very difficult, strange, unique.

Baseball Stars 2 is a very fun retro baseball game.  I don't believe I played this game back then, but I am very glad the game  is on steam and I have the privilege to play it.  I highly recommend this game to sports game fans and those who play casually.
The gameplay is fairly simple, but yet at the same time has depth to it.  When pitching you can change the ball's path and/or increase the speed.  When batting you can move around in the hitters box to best position yourself to hit the ball,  You can also steal bases or prevent the player from stealing a base.  This is just some of the mechanics that you can do in-game, there is more that you can do.
One gripe I have is there is no mid/between game saving.  When you enter a game mode you have to play against quite a bit of teams and the matches go on for quite a bit.  If you exit the game, that is it and you have to start all over.  This is a bummer because if you play in short bursts like I do, it can get frustrating because you potentially can't beat the game.  I am hoping some sort of saving will be implemented in the future.
From an hours to price ratio, you will definitely get your money's worth and much more.
Overall this is a very fun game, I haven't enjoyed a baseball game in a very long time and this hits the spot.  I hope this review helps.

Reviews and reviewers make me angry. Don't read this. Buy the game and make your own mind up. Then have a good think about how the creative industries as a whole use reviewing to part you from your cash. Theft really is not the word for it.
I like a good scare. This game is good at scaring. However it is not the immersive terrifying experience that  some (paid?) reviewers have been prone to bill it as. The best games ever produced had fantastic scripts written by very talented people balanced with superior game mechanics that match the intended experience. This feels like its a level below that. It relies on in your face frights and atmospheric noises just a little too much whilst neglecting, a little too much, a truly terrifying script/game design that will fully engage your imagination.
After a few hours the scared stiff breathing of the main protagonist gets more than a little annoying. The inablity to fight back is, to begin with, a treat to get the adrenalin running. However I'm often brought out of the game immersion to simply get annoyed at the noises he makes along with the lack of retaliation or even... I don't know! maybe effin knock something over behind you as you run or hit that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a plank in the dark as he comes through the door. DUUUUDE do something to survive you moron. I have more than once died trying to get through an open door in a hurry but then again at this point I barely care if he lives or dies. Terror has been suspended by annoyance.
One immersion breaking point is watching the characters move in the dark, sure footed and as if the room is brightly lit.
It often becomes apparent that the other characters follow a rigid script that can be exploited, until you realise that it's not exploiting, this is simply the game. AI feels like it is almost non existent. The plot feels like it too obviously advances in a number of set scenes. You intuitively know when you are safe to run around because you know that you have just 'finished' the latest scene.
This could have been the single most scary game ever released but it is unable to sustain fear due to there being so many immersion breaking points.
All of the parts are there, quality graphics, quality sound, quality programming but it misses on bringing all this together. Not by far, but enough to make this game good, not great. Once again hype and fanboy aggression trumps fact and for some ruins the expectation.
Having said this the game is very playable. Play it in a dark room, with decent sound then engage your imagination and it should give you some nice chills/scares.
Finally it should be noted that having the camcorder light as your only real tool is not very original. It is a variation on a number of games, perhaps the most obvious being Alan Wake. Its inclusion produces a wry smile to those of us who have played video games on dozens of platforms, for decades. We just keep seeing the same music, films and games coming around in shiny new packages to suit the next generation. Sad really but a lesson we all learn as we transition into grumpy old ............

I think the highest praise that I can give to this game, is to say that this is the best Batman experience after Arkham City. As a Telltale game, you not only shape how the story takes place, but also what sort of a Batman Bruce Wayne ends up becoming. You could have a monster that terrifies all those who see him, or you can create a symbol that is a beacon of hope for the innocent and a source of dread for the wicked.
As far as gameplay is concerned, Telltale tried its best to incorporate an innovative combat system into its game. While the action isn't as satisfying as that in the Arkham series, it is well timed and enjoyable. The story, while not exactly cannon, is an absolute masterpiece. The graphics are stellar, and the music will remain with you long after you've finished the game.
If you are a fan of Batman, video games, or good storytelling in general, do yourself a favour and play this remarkable game.

I absolutely loved SUPERHOT from the moment I started playing this game. It will take you back to when first person shooters were less about simulating real life combat and more about destroying the nameless opposition.
The game is visually stunning with its basic black, white, and red minimalist colour scheme. The slow motion effect makes the game all that more artistically satisfying; SUPERHOT is more about the art of sniping than it is about run-and-gun chaos. Imagine a gun fight in which you can take in all the information around you before making the right move. By the end of the game, my aiming accuracy improved so dramatically that I was completing missions much more swiftly à la James Bond.
I also appreciated the metanarrative where one is playing a game as one is stuck inside a game. In that sense, SUPERHOT shares something with Pony Island. The game is also replayable since beating it only unlocks more material. You'll want to beat your personal best in these new levels, which makes SUPERHOT a great game for the highscore-obsessed gamer--it reminds me of N++ that way.
In short, buy this unique game; it's simple and complex, simultaneously. You'll be left repeating SUPERHOT! SUPERHOT! for hours once you start. Trust me on this...

I love Tropico and have done since my first experience as El Presidente in the original (i love it so much that i rebought 1-4 on steam). For a long time all I ever played were city building games, and I will say that the Tropico series are my favourites. While yes Simcity (the old ones) and even the new Cities Skylines are enjoyable, I usually get bored of the city I'm building after a while with the whole zoning, waiting for people to come to the city and build house/shops/industry build some services then repeat. The Anno series steps it up with you building each building, production chains and the occasional quest making it more engaging for me. Tropico gives me that but it also brings a fantastic humour to my megalomania experience (sorry in advance if I over use humour/funny etc, but it's true) that has me laughing out loud every time I play it and after nearly 300 hours of play I'm still not bored.
In this latest instalment the humour that has kept me endlessly amused in previous games is still fantastic (I wish we could all have a Penultimo in our lives). The building models are done with great detail, the colours and textures of my island paradise are amazing. I sometimes like to zoom the camera right in and tilt it so it's like you standing at street level and watch the occasional sunset/rise.
I used to feel that I never really had enough time lording over my adoring subjects (benevolently lording, most of the time anyway), especially in sandbox with games 3 and 4, but with the eras setup in this latest instalment I’m in El Presidente heaven. The addition of the colonial time is really nice, when declaring independence I always say 'let the redcoats come, I ain't paying the crown anything' (I'm actually British before anyone says anything). And the era specific random quests have fantastic humour in their delivery. There's one quest during the world wars era where La resistance needs messenger animals, the result of each animal tried - pigs are too tasty and become bacon before reaching their destination, still make me laugh every time.
I know there have been a lot of disagreements over the whole DLC thing, I have to admit with other games I've thought they were a bit of a rip off, but with Topico's I've been really quite please. For £2.50 the small single mission ones have kept me entertained for at least a weekend on each play, the 2 £14.99 new campaign ones at least a couple, so I see them as good value (I have played them all more than once). The new random 'side quests' that accompany the DLC's are just as funny as those in the vanilla game and playing through the main campaign again with them popping up can drastically change how things play out. I failed a mission during my 10th play through of the main campaign after the addition of the Mad World and Espionage DLC's, due to a revolt caused by my overuse of banish/kill of crime lords and enemy spies. It was hilarious. So I have bought them all and I probably will continue to buy anymore that come out - if anyone from Kalypso is reading this I loved Pirate Cove, so if you wouldn't mind doing a piratey DLC. As Lulu say's everything is better with pirates!
The one thing I will say I don't like and that's the complete reduction in advisors/representatives. I miss Miss Pineapple and her love of spanking (her little guest appearance visiting the fish people in one of the new side quests from the Waterborne DLC was a nice addition). Where's El Diablo telling me to stop letting the riffraff in. And while I love Lulu's radio show, Sunny and Penultimo's banter in 4 was just as fun (maybe they could do a guest spot). What happened to the other nations diplomats? Sometimes I could do with the 30,000 instead of the promised camel
I’ve would definitely recommend Tropico 5 to anyone who likes city building games and I hope that Kalypso will continue to bring us more life as El Presidente

I've only played the multiplayer so here's the review for the multiplayer side of Red Orchestra 2.
This is hands-down the best WW2 game you can lay your hands on right now. The graphics are superb for a game from 2011 and the environment is very detailed and immersive. Most of the maps hold a decent design and are very fun to play but you will most likely prefer some to others.
When you first start off playing you will die a lot and not only because it's so hard but also because it's a big part of the game. A lot of soldiers died on the fields in WW2 and it feels like this game tries to portray just what happened in a sense.
It is a realistic first-person-shooter game and it's quite hard to get used to with the some-what bulky controls and original game elements, so I highly suggest that the first thing you do before getting into combat is to indulge yourself in the boot camp, you will get to familiarize yourself with the controls and also learn a bit of how the game works.
I've heard rumors about bugs, but I have yet to encounter a bug so I guess there are no major bugs lingering around.
If you like the WW2 theme and realistic games where you will have to think and act fast, where you always have to be ready to get involved in some serious combat and intense battles, I highly recommend this game for you.

I backed this game more than two years ago, when the Kickstarter for it first came out. During that time, I played less than 10 hours because I couldn't figure out how to keep my captain alive and I got fed up with the slow ship speed. This summer I returned to the zee and instantly wasted days on it.
This game takes time to get used to. It starts off slow, with every port explored taking momentous effort. Almost everything is capable of killing you. But from there you can only go up.
This game is for those who love stories. If you're not a person who takes the time to read the flavor text or likes to piece together fragments of ideas until they form something coherent, you would be missing out on the Sunless Sea's greatest treasure. All of the gameplay mechanics, hunger, terror, etc. only serve to immerse the player into the world of Fallen London.
Just a note, it's absolutely possible to play Sunless Sea without knowing anything about the source game it came from, Fallen London. In fact you might come across lore relatively early on which FL doesn't cover until much later.
But as for my personal impression of the game, all I can say is I love it. I love the stories it weaves together and the concepts it takes from FL and build upon. I love running into new islands and ports which I never knew existed and the excitement of uncovering a whole new secret. It makes me tense and almost scared whenever I'm on the verge of dying, only one zee monster collision away from sinking below and losing all the quest progress I've built up. The Neath is a beautiful and terrifying world. For me, getting to explore another massive portion of it has made every cent spent on this game worth it. I've even gone on to also back Failbetter Game's next installment, Sunless Skies.
If you like a good fantasy world with heavy Lovecraftian atmosphere and absurd yet consistent lore, and can also bear the trial and error necessitated for a roguelike, if you like stories and peeling back the lawless mystery of night, I would highly recommend this game. And even if you don't, come so that you can feel unduly satisfied when your rodentine nation finally triumphs over those damn invaders!

A game of Banished sets you up with a couple of outcast settlers and a seemingly simple task: survive. Instead of monsters or rival settlements, however, the foes in this game are harsh winters and scarce resources. As you set up a village, assign tasks, build buildings and manage what little you have, until the weather turns against you, you prepare for a slow experience.
Everything in Banished is as connected as it is finely tuned. A failure to set up one more farm and staffing it, might result in a severe food shortage. That will only become prevalent three winters later though, at which point it's obviously too late to save your village from a wave of deaths. Those will drag you down in other areas, since nobody is staffing the mines anymore, and so on. To combat this, you will need to develop a sense for what exactly is needed at any given point and what you can afford to neglect at the moment. Different crop types have different properities in growth time and cold resistance and the difference between 3 quarry workers and 4 is already immense in terms of output. The amount of detail to keep in mind is surprisingly thorough.
As such, Banished has a weird difficulty spike. It will come across as DarkSouls-level frustrating in your first few villages. However, once you have enough familiarity with the mechanics or a natural talent for procurement chains, the game becomes too easy for you. If you are a fan of the Anno series, pick this up at full price, for you shall receive what you crave in your games. If you're not, but are still interested, maybe wait for a sale, because I can't guarantee that you won't overpay.

There are so many "rapturous" reviews for this game, that I decided to write my own, not so ecstatic. I agree that this game has amazingly elaborated world and plot. Elaborated thus much, that the game itself is only 1% or 2% of this world. But this is not an encyclopaedia, this is a game! And the cornerstone here is gameplay. And here some problems occur. 1) Overall level design is nice but very monotonous. All levels look almost the same. 2) Only 2 types of foes: splicers and big daddies. And you encounter them all during first 30-40 minutes of the game. On the following levels developers simply increase HP of those foes instead of adding new ones. 3) There are a lot of additions in comparison to regular FPS games, such as plasmids, different ammo types, ability to hack things, ability to craft, but all of them are useless or boring. Plasmids do not play significant role at all, you can easily finish the game without using them, even on the hardest difficulty. Only one different ammo type that I used was electric buck. Hacking became boring after 4 or 5 hacked things. Craft is almost useless because there is only one useful thing that you can craft - auto hack tool. So if estimate this game as book/encyclopaedia then my score would be 10/10. But if estimate this game as a GAME then my score would be 6/10.

I'm pretty neutral about this game overall. I enjoy Telltale games. I love Batman. While not unfun, this game was lacking on a few fronts.
Pros:
- A twist on the story we all know; not the same old same old. Was a very fresh perspective on a very old franchise. (probably worth playing for that alone)
- A less emotionally constipated take on Batman
- Literally the best penguin costume to date in any media, in my opinion.
- Batcat. Sure he's a playboy, but who isn't a sucker for Batman and Catwoman's complex relationship?
- I did have fun.
Cons:
- Some of the voice options seemed out of character to the point I wanted to restart levels for tripping on "bad" options. From the first moment Bruce snarked at all of his guests that "his wine was worth more than they are" I realized I'd have to be careful which choice I made. (and not in a meaningful way).
- Production quality; high end machine on latest Nvidia drivers, it locked up once and had framerate stuttering issues in multiple places. The transitions between scenes were clunky and obvious at times. Not up to par with previous Telltale titles, but it is playable. Not enough instances to not play it, just very distracting when they crop up.
???:
- Bruce looks uncannily like Archer from the TV show of the same name and it's a little hard to not be distracted by it. Minor detail but still. Weird.
