I love Tropico and have done since my first experience as El Presidente in the original (i love it so much that i rebought 1-4 on steam). For a long time all I ever played were city building games, and I will say that the Tropico series are my favourites. While yes Simcity (the old ones) and even the new Cities Skylines are enjoyable, I usually get bored of the city I'm building after a while with the whole zoning, waiting for people to come to the city and build house/shops/industry build some services then repeat. The Anno series steps it up with you building each building, production chains and the occasional quest making it more engaging for me. Tropico gives me that but it also brings a fantastic humour to my megalomania experience (sorry in advance if I over use humour/funny etc, but it's true) that has me laughing out loud every time I play it and after nearly 300 hours of play I'm still not bored.
In this latest instalment the humour that has kept me endlessly amused in previous games is still fantastic (I wish we could all have a Penultimo in our lives). The building models are done with great detail, the colours and textures of my island paradise are amazing. I sometimes like to zoom the camera right in and tilt it so it's like you standing at street level and watch the occasional sunset/rise.
I used to feel that I never really had enough time lording over my adoring subjects (benevolently lording, most of the time anyway), especially in sandbox with games 3 and 4, but with the eras setup in this latest instalment I’m in El Presidente heaven. The addition of the colonial time is really nice, when declaring independence I always say 'let the redcoats come, I ain't paying the crown anything' (I'm actually British before anyone says anything). And the era specific random quests have fantastic humour in their delivery. There's one quest during the world wars era where La resistance needs messenger animals, the result of each animal tried - pigs are too tasty and become bacon before reaching their destination, still make me laugh every time.
I know there have been a lot of disagreements over the whole DLC thing, I have to admit with other games I've thought they were a bit of a rip off, but with Topico's I've been really quite please. For £2.50 the small single mission ones have kept me entertained for at least a weekend on each play, the 2 £14.99 new campaign ones at least a couple, so I see them as good value (I have played them all more than once). The new random 'side quests' that accompany the DLC's are just as funny as those in the vanilla game and playing through the main campaign again with them popping up can drastically change how things play out. I failed a mission during my 10th play through of the main campaign after the addition of the Mad World and Espionage DLC's, due to a revolt caused by my overuse of banish/kill of crime lords and enemy spies. It was hilarious. So I have bought them all and I probably will continue to buy anymore that come out - if anyone from Kalypso is reading this I loved Pirate Cove, so if you wouldn't mind doing a piratey DLC. As Lulu say's everything is better with pirates!
The one thing I will say I don't like and that's the complete reduction in advisors/representatives. I miss Miss Pineapple and her love of spanking (her little guest appearance visiting the fish people in one of the new side quests from the Waterborne DLC was a nice addition). Where's El Diablo telling me to stop letting the riffraff in. And while I love Lulu's radio show, Sunny and Penultimo's banter in 4 was just as fun (maybe they could do a guest spot). What happened to the other nations diplomats? Sometimes I could do with the 30,000 instead of the promised camel
I’ve would definitely recommend Tropico 5 to anyone who likes city building games and I hope that Kalypso will continue to bring us more life as El Presidente

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
The second "Ace Patrol" game, "Pacific Skies" is a turn-based strategy (TBS) game that is small in scope, simple, yet very engaging and nice to pick up and play for a bit. There really aren't that many historical air combat TBS games out there, so it is hard to compare it to anything else. It feels a bit like a smartphone-port, yet the controls work well so I cannot really say that this is a drawback in itself. The game IS casual, so do not expect it to have overly much complexity to it. The core of the game is assigning different maneuvers to your pilot(s), trying to put them in the best position to shoot down the enemy. As you progress, you unlock new maneuvers and gain new planes and improvements.
Pro:
*Simple, engaging pick-up-and-play gameplay.
*Both sides are balanced the same.
*Has a certain charm to its style.
Con:
*Not that much depth to it.
Summary:
A fun little TBS game that will cater to your desire for a casual TBS experience, Ace Patrol: Pacific Skies is worth its pricetag so long as you do not expect anything with too much depth and complexity to it. 6/10 - Recommended.

I can't recommend it.
The truth is, the minute to minute gameplay of this game is boring as hell. You watch an extremely slow moving ship crawl through empty waters for the majority of your experience. The combat is uninteresting when it does happen, consisting of turning and waiting for cooldowns. When you die (which you will, repeatedly) you get to have the honor of doing the exact same quests over and over each time, with the long lulls of boring boat driving that make up the majority of play time. The beginning economy in the game only makes sense in that you're intended to die, and then balance it out by carrying 50% of your proceeds on through your heirs- literally, the game makes you replay itself to get anywhere.
That's not say this game is all bad. The music is great, the atmosphere is great, the graphics/art design from the detailed locations are great. The interesting story arcs (it is a lot of reading), when you can actually GET to them tend to be interesting and engaging... But then you'll just have to repeat them anyways when your character dies. The issue is that the gameplay itself is simply not fun, and just time-consuming. And then having to repeat that EXACT SAME GAMEPLAY, is just punishment and time-wasting. The experience would have been better as an audiobook or a visual novel.
If you're looking for this type of game, I would recommend Darkwood way more- the pacing, and utilization of map randomization this game so desperately lacks can be found there, and permadeath does not mean literally repeating the same thing over and over at the start of each game.
This game has potential, but unless the gameplay gets revamped, it's better suited to a different medium than being a game.

Project Zomboid, even at it's current stage of development, is probably THE best zombie suvival game out. No question.
Other games like DayZ and The Dead Linger don't even come close. (Even though they're also really early in development). Even with Project Zomboid's recent updates that add multiplayer, it's impossible for it to turn into the deathmatch with zombies as a back drop like DayZ. The zombies are actually a huge threat in Project Zomboid, which is really the best thing about it. You fear them, because one bite, even one little scratch will eventually kill you. A horde that happens to pass through could chase you out of the safehouse you worked for many real-life hours to fortify and stock full of gear and supples.
The survival elements are really deep, despite not being anywear near finsihed, and the problems it does have I won't nit pick about because of that reason. Of course there are some problems. Nothing major, and I'm pretty sure they'll add it in due time but hygenie should be an element in the game, and it should effect happiness/saddness. And you should be able to watch TV or play games for entertainment (as long as the power is on, and use batteries for portable games).
The only real issues I have with the game is the overall graphics, and the fact they took out NPCs that were in ealier versions of the game, I know they're going to come back but it really made me sad that they did that. The blood splatters look great, but that's wear my praise for the graphics end. I don't like how the game looks, they're should be something there that gives the game a darker tone, because the spirtes and graphics look a bit cartoonish in my opinion. I think some special effects should be added to make the game look more pretty, like fog/fancy lighting/etc. That doesn't make me love the game any less, but it would increase the immersion to me.

Hey there!
Sunless Sea is a very unique, extraordinary game, that has great potential but wasted a lot of that with the severe negative factors that interrupt the great narrative. The game has a nice atmosphere, graphics are not amazing but I think they fit the setting very well - and the story-telling is the absolute highlight! You discover this great mysterious world and you have to think about pretty much every decision - but instead of building on top of that, the game forces you to stop exploring and put too much effort into basic maintenance of your ship.
It's the constant pressure to go grab food, fuel and manage your fear that is the big turn-off for me. A lot of players are going to say now "this is part of the difficulty" but for me it's not. It's making the experience boring and monotonous, additionally it absolutely ruins the atmosphere and stories. I don't mind the difficulty itself, I loved games like FTL exactly for that.

Limbo is a platformer with a beautifully simple and eerie atmosphere. The puzzles are challenging but fair, as checkpoints are frequent and never respawn you very far from where you died.
Death is a huge part of the game, so the easy respawns are a huge boon. Actually, the numerous ways you are able to die in this game are part of its charm. You can be skewered, sliced, shot, squished, drowned and break your legs, and its all so freakin cute at times. Often death animations frustrate me and I wish I could skip them, but they are part of this game's charm.
Even more though, is how the game ends. Normally in puzzle games, you can hardly imagine where the game will end and it always seems so far away, but Limbo's ending just... fit. At the end of one of the most intense segments of physics puzzles, when you would expect any other game to just keep going, this one ends in one of the most spectacular and rewarding ways I've ever seen. You feel like you've earned your rest from the grueling deaths of  the previous 4 or so hours.
This game will frustrate you perhaps. It may gross you out. It may terrify you. But the ending takes all that pain and just releases it right when you expect to break. See it for yourself.

So, finally I have Outlast, playing after 3 years of release, and I'm actually glad that its still one of the best horror survival I got for a reasonable price. Ok wait, its not purely 100% horror, but its got some really dark corners and you will lose your sanity when someone like that big guy Chris Walker chases you and you frantically try to find a hiding spot.
Mind it though, Outlast doesn't have spirits and ghosts and all that stuff. From that context, I find this game quite real, considering that there have been crazy asylums in the past. But, I think the best part I liked are the puzzles and the stealth element to it. You need to avoid those lunatics as quickly as possible without making a sound and also ensure that they get trapped for a couple of seconds for you to dash out and escape the madness. Your memory too will be tested, as you need to remember the exact route when trying to escape a lunatic. Some instances will require you to make split second decisions when being chased by a real fast monster. The chases are very adrenaline filled, rarely seen in a walking simulator. 5/5 !
Graphics are AAA and even after 3 years, very well made. Sound design is just awesome. There's always something lurking in the darkness, so keep your ears and if possible, eyes open too!

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #54 - Edge of Space
You'll get an immediate sense of the quirky writing in Edge of Space as you start by having a conversation with a talking shark.  There isn't that much of a story to tell, just that your spaceship crashed and now you are stranded on a planet.  The writing is definitely tongue-in-cheek.
I liked how the game began, and appreciated that it wasn't too difficult to begin with.  Although I do wish they had explained some things a little better.  The game includes a "tutorial video" that I felt was kind of a shortcut, as opposed to just better integrating a tutorial into the game.  Still, the first set of quests you get involve gathering various components to then craft into items, which is a pretty major part of the gameplay.
I wish the controls were better.  I found mining to be frustrating at times.  You use a mining pick that you aim with your mouse.  But the aim is weird at times.  I kept wanting to just point my mouse cursor at a block to mine.  But the aim is actually based on the position of your cursor relative to a point on your body in order to determine direction.  This means sometimes, even when your mouse cursor is on a block, the aim is actually causing the laser to hit a different block.  It's a minor annoyance but mining is such a major part of the gameplay that it definitely adds up.
If you've played Terraria, then you'll pretty much know exactly what to expect here.  It's pretty hard not to consider this game a knock off.  There are some minor differences with crafting, like the way you can use different items to fill a recipe.  But as a whole the gameplay feels extremely familiar.   I don't hold it against Edge of Space for being a knock off, but when you're borrowing from another game, you should at least make some notable improvements.  And it really doesn't feel that way.  And when you add the fact that Terraria is cheaper ($14.99 vs. $9.99 regular prices), I really can't recommend this game unless you've just played Terraria to death and want to scratch that itch with a different game.

The shortest and least substantial expansion pack to the original Half-Life, Blue Shift puts you in the role of Barney Calhoun, a security officer at Black Mesa on the day of the Black Mesa incident. As with Opposing Force and Decay, this game was developed by Gearbox using assets from the original Half-Life. Blue Shift is by far the shortest of the four campaigns, beatable between 2.5-5 hours depending on the difficulty and your experience with first-person shooters.
This game's initial presentation is very good, but its short traversal and occasionally awkward puzzles put a "damper" on things. There are lots of homages to things that happen in Half-Life, Decay, and Opposing Force. The first chapter is really immersive and is a pretty good setup for the rest of the campaign. Unfortunately, Calhoun is relegated to doing the most mundane stuff in the facility, and it really feels like his story is the least important of the four.
****SPOILERS AHEAD****
Because of the game's brevity, it has to compress things greatly, which sometimes works to the detriment of the game. The difficulty escalates much more quickly than in any of the other campaigns. The second chapter is probably the best, but figuring out what Gearbox was thinking with two of the puzzles (i.e., the weird machines you manipulate vertically and going down an obscured ladder to a completely different area) are hard for me to understand why they were chosen. The third chapter introduces marines and this is where things really get hairy. Unlike every other HL game in my experience, the marines in Blue Shift seem to spam the MP5's grenades the most. It feels artificially difficult because the grenades are very damaging and hard to see coming to dodge.
Also in the third chapter, there is a bit of an escort mission, which is exceedingly annoying because the guy decides to stop following you because he says he's tired. Sometimes this happens after he says he'll follow you and not take a single step. Other times he'll just rush ahead of you, which is also annoying when he gets in harm's way. One of the funniest experiences I think most people have had with him is him saying he won't go another step when he's right in front of the security door that he's been ♥♥♥♥♥ing about getting to.
Anyway, after that chapter, you get sent to the alien homeworld and there's a mess of convoluted mazes. This was also the chapter that I discovered Gearbox's proclivity for constantly placing headcrabs right around 90-degree corners in order for them to almost always get a hit on you just because you couldn't see it coming. I thought this was also pretty cheap. There might be multiple ways to get to the destination but I can foresee people getting confused and frustrated with the random organization of everything. Do you take the left path or the right path? It's a lot of trial and error, I think, and I guess I just got lucky. There's also a really annoying platforming section where you have to basically save on every platform. But once you get past that, there's a kind of extended waterfall section that actually feels like it could belong in the original Half-Life. It's certainly better than the factory in Interloper. This is also where you'll encounter almost all of the enemies that Gordon dealt with on Xen, except far, far fewer. After aligning the machinery on Xen, there's again a bit of a head-scratching moment to figure out where to go. You just jump on some crumbled rocks to reach an upper area, d!ck around for a bit (which feels unnecessary), and then find an arbitrary portal back home.
The fifth chapter is the longest and in my opinion the most annoying. You have to find a power cell (battery) in a lower section of Black Mesa. Unfortunately things aren't as intuitive as they should be. For instance, you have to use a barrel as a conduit for a broken wire connected to some dynamite and an explosive lever. You also have to lower the coolant levels just to move some barrels, then raise the coolant levels to jump on the barrels to cross to the other side. But the worst offense (and this is the worst part of the entire game) is figuring out the one extremely random hidden button that raises a bridge to cross to a section you probably didn't even see. This is where the game's lack of explanation drove me batsh!t insane. Anyway, once you figure that all out, you charge the battery and send it back.
The last chapter is pretty easy, you just have to open the damping fields to let the scientists through, then open them for yourself and go through. This is supposed to be tough because of the military guys, but if you know where they're coming from, you can plant a mine and take them out easily.
This game isn't really all that long but it's decent for what it is. There are definitely some moments that are good but probably an equal number of moments that hit with a considerable clunk. It definitely doesn't have the gravitas of the other HL games and some of its puzzles are more annoying than anything. By far the aliens and military spawn point placement in Blue Shift feels the most d!ckish of all the games. But if you can handle those minor annoyances, it's fun to play. But if you're debating between this and Half-Life or Opposing Force, this should be the lowest on your list because it has the least content and feels less substantial (although Calhoun gets the best ending, in my opinion).
P.S. I know it says I have only six minutes in the game. I beat it having "changed game" after having started Opposing Force.

Been in development for years now, Project Zomboid is coming together nicely. A visual style akin the first XCOM game, its simple graphics conceal a devilishly fun and pulse pounding game. Its Sandbox nature, mixed with its emphasis on crafting for survival, creates a game you can easily get lost in and will find your mind wandering back to again and again, contemplating your next moves, where necessary resources could be found, and eventually how far you will ge tbefore you die and start over, with plenty of lessons learned. The addition of multiplayer into the game will certainly be a great addition, and hopefully it won't take it to the DayZ level of Murder For Beans and Laughs. I've died hundreds of times in this game and it doesnt get old, it just makes me more dertermined to prove the opening game message wrong, "This is NOT the story of how I die!"
Now some cons of the game. The complexity of the crafting system and the lack of an actual manual that can help you, can be kind of off putting at first and as this is still in Alpha, there are bugs, crashes and frustrating lack of optimization for the UI and other ncore aspects of the game that need to be completed before a 1.0 launch, but it is still amazing even for an Alpha stage game. The developers are actually putting a ton of content and fixes into the game at a really good pace, so you knwo this isnt one of those cut and run Greenlight projects. Project Zomboid has been around for years and filled a gap in the once barren world of Sandbox, Crafting Zombie Apocalypse Simulators that have become prevelant of late. I recommened picking up this title now, or if you don't want to purchase it til its closer to development than keep it close to the top of your wishlist as this will be a game to get in the future. Think of this as the Minecraft for Sanbox, Zombie Apocalypse  Survival that has always been at the back of your mind, but havent been able to play.

This game is for people who:
-enjoy storybased gameplay
-don't mind a good amount of reading
-are capable of applying lessons learned from game-ending mistakes to a new playthrough
-can cope with losing hours and hours of hard work after dying
The backstory for this game and the world-building are impeccable.  It doesn't outright tell you what is going on, rather you are thrown into a world and expected to surmise the rest based on context.  Though the gameplay is completely different, there is a bit of Dark Souls imbued into the heart and soul of this game.  The things left unsaid are what generate intrigue for the player.
There is a learning curve to this game, it takes several failures to get a handle on what you should be doing, but I think after that point the game really opens up and becomes addictive.  Similar to Don't Starve, you can achieve a lot throughout the game, you can have many items and be able to cover all your needs effectively, but if you die you are dead and you aren't getting any of it back (for the most part).  This game has high potential for rage quitting.
If you like Don't Starve, Darkest Dungeon, Dark Souls--any of the games that reward you for learning from your mistakes--check out Sunless Sea.

You know at first theres a lot to like about this game. As time goes on though, you realize how much of a giant ♥♥♥♥ you the game is. Sure you discover some new places, smuggle a few souls, some sunshine, yada yada yad and you're feeling real good and then you realize after hours of work that you're probably in the red after repairs, fuel, and supplies. You die over, and over, and over, and over again. It's designed to be frustrating and tedious and the developers have openly admitted and are proud of this. in their words, they want playing the game to be so miserable and filled with failure that anytime you had the slightest bit of good fortune it would be amplified by it's contrast to the♥♥♥♥♥♥taste in your mouth. The only way anyone had success in the game without spending literally a hundred hours making peanut profits was by farming certain trade and smuggling routes, but the developers nerfed them all.

I don't like not liking games. Even in the worst games I have found something to them, something I could like and The Beginners Guide took that one thing (the early experiences) and ruined them. As you can guess this is walking simulator in possibly the strictest form. I don't know whether the story is true but if so then I might actually dislike this more...
Spoilers Ahead:
Story

The narrative itself is dull and feels like an emo teen's diary. There is Coda who keeps wanting to make prison games and games about loneliness and Davey (The Narrator) wants to try and stop Coda's depression as he perceives it. Davey shares his games and tries to bring Coda more positive reinforcement by fans but instead of appreciating Davey's effort to help him, Coda just shuts himself more off from the world. Depression Quest has a better presentation of depression and that was a♥♥♥♥♥♥show of galactic proportions. Coda in the end is a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥by not only refusing to explain to Davey his emotions but also to then blame his depression on Davey when he tries to fix it. But wait, Davey then blames himself and ends up with him degrading himself to the point where he likely is becoming depressed and it seems just so stupid to not either make it adamant that the prison game obsession is unhealthy and that Coda needs help or just let him fall. I should really stop before it gets too enraging to describe.
Experience
The early experiences are well done and convey their meaning really well, especially the house tidying one but the further on this gets, the more lacklustre and repetitive they become. You can only beat a depressed horse so much before people think there needs to be a major intervention and it shows. 45 minutes in I felt bored as the same concepts kept coming up and you were constantly beaten over the head with 'Oh No! Coda's depressed what should I do?' without an answer. That is more a story aspect but in a walking simulator, the experience relies on the story and penetrates throughout.
Format
This is not a game in any from. There is no fail state and would have been exactly the same as a movie. The interactions were gimmicks at best and didn't overall effect anything. If all the projects were actually made as projects, then I feel this shouldn't be a paid product. You might argue enough is changed to be classed as fair use but it still feels wrong to monetize off someone else's work when they didn't want it to be shared and when they feel so vulnerable about it being shown. If Davey wanted to get his personal message across to Coda, then he would have made it free.
Overall
It's a walking simulator with a dull story (a la emo teen) and lacks intrigue. It works and runs well but it's an hour and twenty minutes I want back. Score is good however seldom used. Don't waste your time and if I hadn't got this in a Humble Bundle, I would definitely have returned it and played Fahrenheit instead.

Ace Patrol Pacific Skies is basically the exact same game as Ace Patrol (which was set in WW1) moved to WW2 Pacific Theater where you play the Japanese side or the American side.
The game is best described as a turn-based air combat where you move planes from hex to hex, where the "attitude" and "altitude" of the plane, as well as the skill of the pilot, determines what moves you can make. If you are low, you can't use a power dive (drop several levels of altitude) or "falling leaf" (drop several levels of altitude and face a specific direction), for example, or if you were in a left turn, you can't immediately switch to a sharp right turn (unless you learned "roll" manuevers). This is harder to explain than to see for yourself by watching the videos.
You control 2 or 4 planes and corresponding pilots. As pilots make "kills" they gain experience that can be translated to better power moves. So it's not good if you let one pilot do all the killing... Share the bounty.
In a bit of ahistorical equality, there are female pilots (fortunately, you can turn that off).
Try not to let your pilots get shot down. They can be kept prisoner or end up in hospital for several missions. The planes themselves can also be damaged and repairs are not instantaneous.
Typically you have about 6 missions per "year" and there's a big mission at the end. and 4 years in a campaign. You are scored based on how much damage you caused, did you complete your objective (such as taking out a ground target), vs. how much damage did you suffer.
If you like Ace Patrol, Pacific Skies is the same game with faster planes.

This is my first stealth survival horror game. Sound and graphics are superb. Game control is good, you don't need joystick on PC. As it's a stealth game, you can only run or hide from enemy, no combat. There are many dark areas so you often need to rely on your camcorder's nightvision which is limited by the battery. The story is decent although the final chapter is kinda let down. I have problem with surrounding characters identification, they never introduce themselves for sure but the main character can figure out their names better than me. Basically you need to pay big attention to the camcorder's notes and documents you found, as well as the surrounding characters conversation to understand who is who. Make sure you always turn on the camcorder to prevent you missing the notes. But some characters are probably still unclear even until you completed the game, you would end up reading the wikia later probably.
The scare factor is ok, the scare is mostly come from the tension being found out and chased by the villain besides the typical jump scares in horror game. I kinda dislike the idea of lot of harmless or neutral NPC in the game, I think the game atmosphere would be more scarier if it has more sense of desolateness. But my big complaint from this game is it has very low replay value. There is only one ending, no unlockable secret stuffs. You probably would only replay the game for collecting all Notes and Documents, or if you feel challenged you can try Insane mode which is not really rewarding at all IMO. I don't remember how long for me to finish the game on first play, I think it's around 10-13 hours, so I consider the game length to be medium, but other people might consider it short. There is also a Whistleblower DLC, if you like the game's story, you certainly have to play the DLC as it completes the story of the game.
Personally I'm quite satisfied with the game and would like to see Outlast 2, hopefully it will be much better. If the low replay value bugs you, you might want to get the game when it's on sale.

While Ebony Spire: Heresy isn't what you'd call a deep game, it's an excellent casual title for people who enjoy retro dungeon crawlers but don't necessarily have the time to commit to an epic like Ultima Underworld or Eye of the Beholder.
It's a simple matter of clearing your way through 10 random levels as one of three character classes, and powering yourself up by picking up increasingly potent weapons and spells as you go.
The enemies can and will use the same objects around the level as you can, which can lead to some lethal encounters as a slime monster arms itself with the daggers dropped by the lizardman you just killed and stabs you in the back with them.
All in all, it's a fun time-killer for busy adventures, and although it lacks polish, it has enough charm to get away with its rough edges.
It'd be handy if the in-game help mentioned that you can press T to throw things, because that's great fun.
Oh, and the Linux support is greatly appreciated.
(Full disclosure: I was gifted this game by a Twitter acquaintance who ran a lottery for a copy in order to support the dev. But I'd been eyeing it up anyway.)

Upfront: I was gifted this game by a friend who wanted to support the dev because we both read the post-mortem about the fellow quitting his job with only enough money to survive for four months. We felt sorry for him, so I agreed to play and review this. I expected that I would love this roguelike, because it's one of my favorite game genres.
... But the sad truth of the matter is, this game just isn't very good.
It's a roguelike dungeoncrawler in the old, old style. Think of Nethack, or Brogue, or any classic ASCII game. Despite this game's graphical style, that's what you're playing: you're @, you have a few weapons, skills, and potions to your name, and that's about it. While this game controls with WASD and QE to turn, everything else is the archaic style: ? for commands, M for the map, P to pick things up, O to open doors, I for inventory. It's simple, it's straightforward, I honestly don't mind this! Once I figured out what I had to do, playing this game is easy. You bump attack enemies, or cast spells at them through spellbooks and scrolls in your inventory, and so on.
Here's my first set of problem with the game: there are a few typos in item-descriptions. Not a good sign. Second, if you're a spell-caster or rogue who relies on throwing weapons or pistols, to use these attacks, you have to open up the inventory and select the item to use it every single time you want to attack. There isn't a hotkey. It adds a slight delay to every attack, which is just... not good. I know this sounds nitpicky, but the lack of polish hurts, especially when it continues into the rest of the game.
So the gameplay. Roam around a dungeon map in standard dungeon-crawler design, killing enemies, finding new gear, ascending to harder and harder floors. Straightforward, again, but... the dungeon tileset never changes. I made it up to floor seven and it was the exact same gray walls. The only difference were the monsters. And this hurts, especially because you can find portals that take you to optional areas with absolutely charming level design - towns, snowy forests, a pirate ship - all of these creative, fun places are... optional. While you should visit them to get the good gear in there, if you opt not to, you're stuck with the same boring dungeon. (And there are no traps or puzzles or anything. Just randomized stair placement, randomized portal placement, and lots of wooden crates that sometimes have loot in them.)
Which leaves you with the monsters. They have fun sprites! ... They vary in fun levels. In the first level, if you start as the berserker class (there are three classes, essentially warrior, rogue, and mage with fancy names) - once you remember to put on your equipment, because you don't start with anything equipped - you're going to tear through everything. You'll meet a bunch of priests who throw daggers at you and do no damage. All of the monsters in this game love to throw items around - bombs, potions, swords - I've had health potions thrown at me, to no effect. Which is puzzling, but okay! There are other monsters - squiddy priests who cast meteor spells at you, pugilists who throw bombs / try to attack you, etc. A good variety, and most of them have ranged attacks you need to account for. So far so good, right? Varied enemies with interesting designs and attacks are good, right?
...The balance is extremely weird. If you're a berserker, nothing does any damage to you until level 3 or 4, where they start doing 10+ damage per attack. When you have 50hp (give or take). And then the next level jumps up to 20 damage, and more. So you go from overpowered to maybe balanced to suddenly drowning in lethal enemies, and healing - healing potions drop, but not reliably. You don't regenerate unless you find an enchanted axe, and it only heals 0.1 hp every few turns. So you're starving for HP until you find a spellbook of healing, which provides unlimited healing - 10 hp a turn, whenever you can cast it.
So how are you supposed to survive? By using the thrown items and pistols and spells to pick off enemies from a distance. This is what the other classes are built around, as they don't come with the overpowered axe and armor. They're far more fragile, can't do any damage without thrown items or spells, and... it's what you're supposed to do. Play like a coward.
...Which is your standard roguelike, but... it feels so generic and off. The typos, the clunky controls, the boring level design with the optional interesting areas, the way difficulty goes from 0 to 100 without much inbetween, and the sheer lack of hook in playing... (there is little to no sound design, and visual effects are servicable but not really good.)
I can't recommend this game. There's not enough depth or variety in how you can interact with enemies, the level design is bad, and it just feels like it needed more. The sheer fact that I'm struggling to convince myself to boot it back up for another few rounds. Not good.

I've bought the game to support its creator after I've read his post-mortem on Gamasutra. The game looked nice: a love letter to the old MS-DOS dungeon crawlers, with mazes to explore, monsters to kill and loot to gather. It turned out to be even a greater throwback to old times then I expected: the game made me remember how awful the interfaces were back then, and how user-unfriendly a game can be. The game doesn't utilize mouse -- instead there's a key for everything: O to open the door, P to pick up an item, I to go into your inventory, T to throw a weapon. Instructions page are barebones too, so the game provides a double journey of discovery: one as you explore the dungeons, the other as you explore the interface, trying to understand how the hell it's supposed to work. I gave up and dropped the game when I accidentaly pressed Esc in the wrong time and found out that the same button is used to exit the inventory and to drop the game and exit to the main menu. This almost made me shed a tear of nostalgia: yes, the MS-DOS games of old times were exactly this frustrating.
Thumbs up to help the game's creator to pay his mortgage.

To compare this game to the glory that is DF would be an insult, and in truth this game is closer to SimCity than to DF. But this is still a much better attempt than other games.
This game actually feels complete, but is suffering from a few glaring problems.
The first is population control. As there is no combat, your main death source is old age. This requires you to balance a population of adults and children to replace them. The main problem is the game feels the need to fill all vacant houses. Too many houses and you'll have a village of singles who don't make children. Too few houses and the children grow up to live with their parents, with the same result. Once you get the town hall this is managed easily, but if you don't understand it can ruin your experience fast.
The second is control of population. The gathering of the lands resource nodes are all held under one job: labourer. These poor people also have to haul goods to stockpiles and to building sites. You can control this somewhat by raising the priority of an area, but I still feel like this game would have been improved greatly by splitting this generic workforce. You also can't restrict your population from doing certain tasks, like "You don't haul wood, you don't haul stone, you don't haul anything just stand there and wait to do your job!".
The third is expansion. The games funnest moments are in the beginning, when you're laying the blueprints of your meager town and watching it all come to life. You might fail a few times and learn from your mistakes, but once you got it you got it. Expanding your population after that point, especially if you're trying to reach 900, is too repetitive. You're just building your town all over again in another part of the map; lather, rinse, repeat. The best case scenario a tornado comes and wipes out half the map; worse case scenario a fire starts and sets you back a year. Achievements here are not as much a test of skill as they are a test of patience.
I got this game for $5 though, and I can recommend it at that price. All in all, it's a solid game that could benefit from some polish and more end-game content. For full price, I would try looking at other games.

The Arkham games nailed the experience of using Batman's abilities and methods. Telltale, on the other hand, nail the experience of BEING Batman/Bruce Wayne: the responsibilities, the consequences, the emotions. The writers at Telltale understand that the Bruce Wayne persona is just as important as the Batman one, and make you feel the difficulty of maintaining that double life.
I felt incredibly invested in the characters and events of BTTS, perhaps even more so than in any other powerful character-driven experience (it even beats Mass Effect for me in that regard). Your choices -- both in dialogue and in actions -- will affect how the story unfolds and how characters develop over the course of the series. I was also very impressed with the creativity and boldness with which Telltale reimagined established Batman lore; for example, Oswald Cobblepot (the Penguin) becomes a slim, suave, ideologically-motivated terrorist, as opposed to the short, deformed, bird-obsessed crime boss we're used to. That's just the tip of the iceberg -- get ready for some twists that shake the foundations of Bruce's world and what he stands for.
The writing is supported by a fantastic voice cast, with particularly strong performances by Troy Baker as Batman/Bruce and Laura Bailey as Catwoman/Selina. The music is also great -- especially the main theme -- and really adds to the atmosphere and drama.
Conversations (full of choices and dialogue options) make up the bulk of the gameplay. The rest is limited point-and-click exploration, including some rather enjoyable crime scene analysis, and QTE combat without much player choice (Rocksteady already perfected Batman combat, so if you want that, play Arkham). All in all it plays like an interactive graphic novel or episode of The Animated Series.
Visually it's something of a mixed bag. The art direction is great, especially the character designs, and I love the comic book style of the cel shading. But the animations are often clunky, and background images are sometimes quite low-resolution.
The sequel series, Batman: The Enemy Within, is already three episodes in, and thus far is even better than the original. Your save carries over between games, so there's all the more reason to play Series 1.
All in all, I think this may be my favourite Batman experience in any medium, and I strongly recommend this game to any Batman fan, and to anyone who enjoys a character-, story- and choice-driven experience.

Game design is one of those things that, when done really well, goes almost unnoticed. Sadly, this is the one area where Edge of Space really fails to deliver. The art isn't bad, the worlds are imaginative, and some aspects of gameplay are actually very fun! Tearing through rock with a high-powered mining lazer feels great. Unfortunately, these high points are all brought down by clumsily implemented features that are frustrating and poorly explained. A lot of things nagged at me during the 12-or-so hours I spent trying to enjoy Edge of Space, but I'll focus on the worst: dungeons.
At a certain point in the game, progression through the tech-tree is halted by materials that can only be obtained from a dungeon. No problem! Except the dungeons are awful. The freedom of your jetpack and mining laser are stripped from you, and you're forced to clumsily hop along through some kind of half-baked platformer full of dark, confusing, repetitive rooms. Exploring the rest of the dungeon after going down a dead-end branch involves slowly backtracking through rooms that are even harder to navigate in reverse. It's so tedious that it's easier to just die so that you can start again from the top. The drop-rate for those materials you need is abysmal to boot. Just terrible all-around.

Blue Shift was the last game to take place during the same time frame of the Black Mesa incident. This time you portray Barney Calhoun, the same security guard who aided Gordon Freeman & Colporal Adrien Shepard during their survival of the Black Mesa incident. The game start off the same way as the original Half-Life game did within the monerail tram except Barney takes a different tram that show cases locations not shown in Half Life original or Opposing Force. After playing this game you get the idea of how massive the lab facility is. Anyways Barney is an everyday security guard who is about to part take his duty at Black Mesa, upon entering an elevator with a couple scientists, the power goes out and the elevator decends to the lower basement level at a high speed. Upon awakening, Barney wasn't sure how he survived the impact of the elevator fall, but soon he finds out that the lab facility is infested with hidious aliens that want Barney for dead. Upon scavenging armor and weapons, Barney must use his wit and what his training lessons taught him in order to escape Black Mesa in one piece. The scenario is the same as the original & Opposing Force games, except focused on a different character who embarks in different locations of the Black Mesa facility. The game play is similar along with the same minor flaws featured in the other games. Because Barney wears regular swat armor, he can not use the HEV units to regain armor strength instead he must obtain new armor in order to replace the old worn out armor. The enemies are the same and the weapons are the same as the ones used by Freeman & Shepard, but a much different experience. The length of the game is shorter but if you enjoyed playing the previous games, then this game is worth your time as it expands on what happened during the Black Mesa incident along with brief cameos of Freeman & the mysterious G-Man. Highly recommended for die hard Half-Life fans.

Amazing game. Me and my friends played this game on the PS2 endlessly, particularly the stunt mini-games, which are still hilarious. Now I bought this off Steam and I have no regrets. Because I'm not only reliving memories, but also that I can't find today's equivalent of this game (unless you consider Next Car Game: Wreckfest, also made by Bugbear). It's better than many racing games today. It's truly a one-of-a-kind. A good visual novel with survival elements, but tiring after a while. Sunless Sea is a very slow game. It's slow to start, slow to progress and a damned hard slog to get even close to completing. In fact, the only thing not slow is your fuel consumption, which you'll watch happily tick away as your hope fades. And make no mistake, this is a punishing game. You will die over and over and over again, often in the most mundane of ways. Just narrowly escaped a frigate? Too bad! You've run out of fuel in the process. And to see al, that hard work building up your captain only to lose it all is heartbreaking. Especially since it takes many hours to finally start to etch out a living.
So why recommend the game? Because for those first 10 hours or so you'll feel like you're getting better. And it's a great feeling; exploring the map, making the right choices, fighting back against enemies. The game will give you your money's worth, that's for sure.
But just remember that the Zee always wins. And it'll take you in the end. But by the time you realise how deep you are it'll be too late...

'Morphopolis' is a casual 'hidden object game'. As is common in these games, there are some puzzles to be solved, too. The game consists of 5 levels which will take you 25 minutes each on average, mostly depending on how fast you solve the puzzles. The insect you control moves slowly, so this game is not for the impatient.
Gameplay consists of you clicking on large objects (large insects or plants) to see if they need completion (e.g. missing legs or petals). If they do, you'll see an icon of what type of item you need to collect and how many of those you need to collect. Next, you'll be looking for these items and when you have them, click on the large insect or plant again to complete it and advance through the game. Also, when you click on the insect you control, it'll er... do something that can open 'containers' like berries or closed flowers.
None of this is explained in the game. There is some sort of a tutorial but it just points you at the object you need to click on next, without explaining what's happening. Especially the last part I mentioned about clicking on your avatar was something they should have explained. It took me a while to figure it out, I was about to forfait when I accidentally clicked on my avatar near a berry.
The graphics are nice enough but not breathtaking as some people would have you believe. Maybe I expected more simply
a lot of people talk about how stunning the graphics are, could be. Also, during the first level I saw green flashes across half the screen from time to time. I run Windows 7. When looking for a solution for this, I stumbled upon a lot of complaints that the game is suffering from extreme screen flickering when running it in Windows 10, rendering the game unplayable for them. Luckily, the flashing stopped for me after the first level. So there are some technical issues with the game for some people.
The background music is very nice and relaxing. It fits the game's atmosphere completely.
There are no options whatsoever, not for graphics or sound or anything.
'Morphopolis' has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 just for running the game.
The Steam Achievements are most basic and 100% unmissable. I know it's not easy to come up with original achievements for a hidden object game but it can be done. One quick example would be a well-hidden object in each level that you need to find for an optional achievement. The puzzles are certainly a missed opportunity for some optional achievements. One example could be to finish one or more of the puzzles in less than a specified number of moves.
If you like hidden object games that include some puzzling, you'll love this game, although you may find it way too short. If you like puzzle games and/or point & click adventure games but aren't crazy about hidden object games, like I am, give Morphopolis a try anyway. It's short enough, the objects you need to find aren't that well hidden (it's not a pixel hunt at all!) and you really can't go wrong at this price, can you?

Let's get one thing out of the way quickly: if you do not like reading, and if you want instant gratification, you will not like this game at all.
Some parts of the game are randomly generated, and you do lose most of your progress when you die, but personally I would recommend sticking with just one character, as going through the same story events multiple times is rather tiring.
This is not an FTL with some Lovecraftian horror sprinkled on top.
You play as a Zee-captain. Why Zee and not Sea? Because the Zee is an impossibly big underwater lake in a dystopian, steampunk alternate reality. You start in a sunken version of London, ready to discover the old gods that inhabit the place (...or do they?), the lost and not-so-lost civilizations and their unique story.
During the first few hours, I have to say that I got really bored with the game. The ship moved extremely slowly and was pathetically weak. To make any sort of progress you need money. To earn money, at first you need to explore and report back to Fallen London. Remember when I said the ship was slow? Yeah, the constant back and forth was rather tedious. Plus, the monetary rewards were unsatisfactory. To get a good ship you need at least 6k echoes...most Port Reports would give you 40-50. You do the math.
Clearly, that was not the best way. The best way is trading. But you wouldn't know that by just playing the game on your own...
As soon as I got my first good ship, things changed for the better.
My advice to really enjoy this game is simple: read a few articles before playing. They might slightly spoil some events, but trust me, it is absolutely necessary, at least for the start.
The main shortcoming of the game is the lack of efficient information: there is no easily accessible quest log, no main database where you can see the market prices or where each character is. You have to either remember, check the cryptic ingame explanations or open external resources. I know that it adds a bit of mystery, but first and foremost, it's a game, and the immersion cannot be detrimental to the user experience.
Now, I'm bashing this game a lot, but my review is positive, and here's why: the atmosphere and the writing are basically second to none. As you sail the dark Zee, you will encounter madness, horror, love and intrigue. You will swap Zee-stories that you got from killing giant crabs for Extraordinary Implications, which will then form Searing Enigmas. Those are the true resources of the game: stories.
The stories your Zee-Captain comes across, the ones wonderfully written by the creators, and the ones the player makes up in their head. Your choices will have long-term consequences, and the in-house story engine is made in such a way that you never truly know what will happen next until you experience it.
There is combat in this game, but to be honest there's not much to be said about it, you just look at things and wait until your weapons load. The ships are not very nimble, which makes maneuvering hard. I have the fastest ship with the best engine burning permanently at 100%, but that speed, to an external observer, would likely look like the speed of the basic first boat a player would get in other such games.
In a game like Sunless Sea, the actual graphical and tecnical aspects are not the main attraction, but they do exist, so I will rate them. The graphics are serviceable, the art is good, especially when it comes to the cities. They are vibrant and colorful, but the character portraits are a bit...off. There aren't many animations, but they too do their job. The music is fantastic, it immediately brings Zee-life and adventuring to mind.
I know the devs are making Sunless Skies, and it looks like many of this game's issues are getting fixed, so that's obviously a strong point in their favor. Listening to feedback can make or break sequels.
This has been a long review because Sunless Sea is a long and complex game. To summarize, despite its many faults, if you have the patience for it, Sunless Sea will provide a unique dark story experience that rivals those of Inkle games.

A fantastic title that reminds me highly of Fantasy Flight Games' X-Wing Miniatures series, Pacific Skies is a turn based strategy game focused on WW2 air combat in the Pacific. Each side takes turns performing various maneuvers with a handful of aircraft from both the American and Japanese Army/Navy. Most missions are simple, ranging from one on one ace combat, reconnaisance, bombing and zepplin attacks.
Pilots add another layer of strategy as they level up with successful kills. Each level allows the player to choose from three different sets of maneuvers for that specific pilot. Should the player keep damage levels above 50% in a scenario they will gain a part unlock to attach to a plane. This comes in the form of accuracy, damage, speed and maneuverability upgrades.
All in all, a wonderful game with high replayability. The only difference I have noticed between this and the first Ace Patrol is purely graphical, slightly faster plane speeds and higher damage ratios. Recommended at any price!

This game has truly been a treat.  I must admit, it was quite taxing as far as time and patience, so if you have neither, then be warned.  This is a game that truly does reward perserverence, as I personally didn't have a captain who truly dived into the arcane depths that this incredibly rich world had to offer until my 6th captain.  Admittedly, I had made plenty of idiotic mistakes that years of playing punishing games should have tought me otherwise; but I had not truly understood how exactly hardcore this game was until I had gotten about 10 hours in.
There were more than a few times where I moaned and groaned about having to take the same path for trading because it was profitable, if only marginally, just because it was safe, due to the fact that the Zee is undeniable dangerous.  There are perils at absolutely every corner, and if you don't play your cards right, you shall face certain death. You may feel that a lot of your deaths are unfitting, unfair, or downright dirty.  In all honesty, there are only a few times where I would say that luck played into it.  Granted, there are percentages abound for your success throughout this game.   But there are few times that where, in retrospect, my death wasn't something I was asking for.
I was greedy.
I wanted it all.
After all, I am the hero of this tale of tales, aren't I?
Aren't I?
No.
That is what the game tells you, over and over again.  You are not the hero you seek to be.
You are merely a Captain, amongst the Lovecraftian horrors of the Unterzee.
Do you honestly think you are a match for a beast that could besiege mountains?
Hah.
Alas, when you continue upon your journey, and find yourself in the deeper inworkings of the imaginations of the folks at Failbetter, you appreciate the pure imagination of this world that they have built.
There is just so much that this game does right story wise, I simply wish there was a way I could share my joy at discovering the mercurial horrors that eat away at sanity that this game so lovelingly portrays.
I admit, this game does suffer from tedium.
But by golly, there is a beautiful epic hidden beneath it all.
My goodness, is it amazing.
If you have patience, and time, please, give this game a gander.
There is something within all of this bothersome chore of trading that is by far one of the most compelling things I have personally witnessed.

Overall, I recommend it. It's a fun strategy game that can be played either in short bursts on over a long period of time(1+ Hours). In many ways it improves upon the original Ace Patrol, such as more modern planes, new maneuvers, better plane customization, and more detailed maps. But in they totally ruined the feeling of choice the first Ace Patrol had, where you can choose what types of missions you wanted to do, where you did the mission types you liked and avoided the ones you didn't, except for when you were desperate for points to win that Defense/Offense and that mission type you didn't like had bonus points that period.
In both Ace Patrols a campaign consists of alternating between offense and defense, with each offense/defense having 5 battles. Each battle you got to pick between 1-3(1 being the final battle) different mission types. So the whole offense/defense you got to choose your favorites.
In Pacific Skies(this game), It's still a Campaign with 5 alternating Offenses/Defenses and 5 Battles each, but now you can pick your mission type. It just randomly picks one, which BLOWS.
Being able to pick my favorites, or picking my disliked types when I wanted variety was my favorite part. Since enemy Squadrons would rotate pilots between battles, so if the current battle had pilots you didn't like, you can choose a more defensive mission type. But that's gone in this game.
And for some ungodly reason, they removed the full screen option. It was more convenience than anything else, but I see no good reason to remove it since Pacific Skies is basically a retexture of the first game.
Anyway, as a final comment: Unless you hate the planes in the first game or love the planes in this game, just get the fist Ace Patrol, it's better. Though this game is still good too, I guess.

Ebony Spire is a grid-based RPG in the old-school style, but with a twist:  It's designed to be played during a lunch hour or a coffee break.
Imagine you're waiting for something, an email to come through, a bus, or the bath to finish filling... You want to play something, but are fed up with the bland score-chasers like Bejewelled and Temple-Run which get the adrenaline and endorphines flowing using blingy sounds, and bright graphics.  What you want is something you can quickly dive into, but gives you a little bit more cerebral gameplay.
I'm not talking of "Mastermind" level cerebral.  I'm talking about stats and armour and weapons, levels and monsters, like an RPG, but all condensed down into a short 20 minute run!  All the usual elements are there, character classes, a levelling mechanism (albeit a little hidden), weapons, armour, guns, spells... But stripped down so there's only a few of each, so you don't have to spend ages agonizing over which to use.  Also, there's no weapon degredation, so no need to horde either.   Just check to see if stuff's better than what you have, and if so, drop your old stuff, pick up the new stuff, and go squish things!
If anyone's managed to make a better short-play RPG game, I've yet to find it.   Bearded Giant have made an homage to all the old grid-based RPGs like Eye of the Beholder, or Dungeon Master, but slimmed it down into a really fast, enjoyable, easy-to-pick-up experience.  It scratches an itch, but doesn't require a Baldur's Gate amount of time to play through... you can start/stop it at any time, and it's turn-based, so if you need to put the laptop down to pour your hot water into the teacup, just do it,  the game'll wait for you to come back... Genius!
The complete game can be run end-to-end in under 10 minutes.  Of course, how you fare against the big boss at the end will depend on how you spent those 10 minutes... If you hacked and slashed, you'll be okay. If you spent them just running around and looking at the great old-school pixelly texture maps, meh, you'll have had a nice time, but I don't think you'll do so well :)    So, slip on those +4 leather gauntlets, pick up that +32 Longsword, and go get 'em dungeoneer!

Train Valley is a fun casual puzzle game. The screenshots and Steam tags may give you the impression that it's a management sim/tycoon game, but this is not really the case.
The core gameplay is fun enough. You build tracks to connect the various stations and then try to get each train to the right destination by manipulating the railroad switches. During each level new stations will keep popping up, forcing you to expand your rail network.
Your main goal in each level is simply to avoid going bankrupt (this is pretty easy for the most part). Additionally, each level has three bonus objectives that provide extra challenges. Some levels also have special trains arriving from outside the map. All in all there's enough variety to keep things interesting for a single playthrough.
My main issue with the game is the fairly high level of randomness. For the most part this is not really a problem as the game is pretty easy anyway, but in the later levels bad luck can really mess you up. This is not really something I enjoy in a puzzle game.
Overall I found Train Valley a pretty enjoyable experience. I'd recommend it to anyone who likes light puzzle games.
The good:
- Fun puzzle gameplay
- Rather relaxing experience
The bad:
- Too many random elements
- Building tracks is somewhat imprecise
- Some of the later levels get rather micromanagement heavy

Morphopolis is a hidden-object/mini-puzzle game. What makes it special is its insect theme: you guide this bug throughout various stages of its life-cycle transformations!
The game has beautiful hand drawn graphics, fluent animation and relaxing/atmospheric/ambient musical overlay. What mostly frustrated me is that often you don't know what you're supposed to do in the mini-puzzles, or that there's more screens accessible during the hidden objects "quests". The Hint button does not help there...
In overall, I recommend Morphopolis, much more so for its ultra competitive price: 0.99€ (I got it on discount, for 0.24€!).

A classic that I've never played before it's steam release and I'm here to say it's still worthy of most the praise it gets.
I'll keep it short.
GOOD
+Story is fantastic. Many hours of gameplay for a single player game. Even has replay value.
+The FPS elements are great. Using different guns and abilities to take out your enemies doesn't get stale.
+The RPG elements aren't perfect but can really change the way you play, especially when you start upgrading.
+ Even though through most of game the tension is high and it can be downright scary at times, it was never grotesque or resorted to jumpscares to shock you.
+ Difficulty modes. The game might be a bit overwhelming at first but is actually rather easy when you get used to it. But being able to increase the difficulty on subsequent playthroughs solves that problem.
+ Though the visuals might have aged somewhat, I got totally emersed in them.
NOT SO GOOD
- Controls aren't optimal and is part of the overwhelming start. Switching weapons, powers and ammo doesn't get smooth until you learn to just deal with it.
- The Hacking minigame, like in most other games, is too boring and occurs way too frequently. Almost every camera and turret in the game needs to be either hacked or destroyed to progress. And since conserving ammo is quite a big deal, hacking is the best choice but also the most boring one.
-Though survival and conserving your ammo are elements of the game, expect to blaze through on easier difficulties after you get used to the enemies and such. (Big Daddies are Big Babies, no really)
- The final araes of the game take a looong time. This might be a good thing to some, but it feels stretched and a little disjointed from the rest of the game. Making the ending overall a bit weak compared to all you've done to get there.
So step right up and get yourself a ticket to Rapture, because this game is totally worth playing! Especially if you've become a fan of the Bioshock series because of it's more recent installments!

While it might not look like it but Train Valley is one of the best puzzle games that I have played in quite a while.
What makes Train Valley stand out is that while it is pretty simplistic it is still challenging. All you do in the game is build tracks and guide the trains towards their destination. The fun comes from creating the routes and juggling multiple trains at the same time while trying to keep them from crashing into one another and running out of money. Train Valley does a great job of being a relaxing game that still challenges you.
I would classify Train Valley as an easy to play but hard to master game. It is not that hard to beat the levels in Train Valley but it becomes quite hard to 100% some of the later levels so there is quite a bit of challenge if you want it. Length wise the game includes 24 levels and should take at least six to eight hours to complete. I found Train Valley enjoyable enought though that I actually wanted to try and complete as many of the additional objectives as I could which can add quite a bit of time to the game.
If you are looking for a train simulation game or don't really like puzzle games, Train Valley is not going to be for you. If the game's premise sounds interesting though I think you will really enjoy Train Valley.

This game has truly been a treat.  I must admit, it was quite taxing as far as time and patience, so if you have neither, then be warned.  This is a game that truly does reward perserverence, as I personally didn't have a captain who truly dived into the arcane depths that this incredibly rich world had to offer until my 6th captain.  Admittedly, I had made plenty of idiotic mistakes that years of playing punishing games should have tought me otherwise; but I had not truly understood how exactly hardcore this game was until I had gotten about 10 hours in.
There were more than a few times where I moaned and groaned about having to take the same path for trading because it was profitable, if only marginally, just because it was safe, due to the fact that the Zee is undeniable dangerous.  There are perils at absolutely every corner, and if you don't play your cards right, you shall face certain death. You may feel that a lot of your deaths are unfitting, unfair, or downright dirty.  In all honesty, there are only a few times where I would say that luck played into it.  Granted, there are percentages abound for your success throughout this game.   But there are few times that where, in retrospect, my death wasn't something I was asking for.
I was greedy.
I wanted it all.
After all, I am the hero of this tale of tales, aren't I?
Aren't I?
No.
That is what the game tells you, over and over again.  You are not the hero you seek to be.
You are merely a Captain, amongst the Lovecraftian horrors of the Unterzee.
Do you honestly think you are a match for a beast that could besiege mountains?
Hah.
Alas, when you continue upon your journey, and find yourself in the deeper inworkings of the imaginations of the folks at Failbetter, you appreciate the pure imagination of this world that they have built.
There is just so much that this game does right story wise, I simply wish there was a way I could share my joy at discovering the mercurial horrors that eat away at sanity that this game so lovelingly portrays.
I admit, this game does suffer from tedium.
But by golly, there is a beautiful epic hidden beneath it all.
My goodness, is it amazing.
If you have patience, and time, please, give this game a gander.
There is something within all of this bothersome chore of trading that is by far one of the most compelling things I have personally witnessed.

I can't think of more than a handful of games on the market right now that give you more enjoyment per dollar than Project Zomboid--and every single one of those games has been award-winning.
Project Zomboid does something that Zombie games have yet to really try and tackle so far: an accurate simulation of a zombie apocalypse. Most Zombie games really fall short in one area or another when it comes to this idea and many simple eschew realism altogether for the sake of fun gameplay. However, in Project Zomboid the realism works in the player's favor. You can generally guarantee that anything you would imagine is possible in real life is pretty much possible in Zomboid (with the appropriate consequences for bad choices, i.e. setting off a burglary alarm near a horde of zombies). This gives the player a large amount of freedom when it comes to strategy, planning, and execution of whatever task you need to do next. It makes for a very immersive, compelling, and replayable experience. You're usually not thinking, "lemme find the best gun to destroy all these zombies!" In Project Zomboid you have to be thinking, "if I fire a gun, every zombie for miles is going to hear it and come running!"
This is just one example of what makes PZ so compelling. By offering gameplay centered around risk vs. reward and a consistent set of balanced benefits and consequences for actions, the player is challenged AND feels rewarded for their accomplishments.
The game can also be tuned to fit exactly your liking. Do you like The Walking Dead zombies more than Dawn of the Dead zombies? There are options to set up your game for that. Perhaps you prefer Reavers from Firefly or I Am Legend zombies? You can have those too. On top of the standard in-game options to customize your experience, significant mod tools and community-built mods are available to create exactly the experience you want.
I could go on and on about other things that makes this game great. I will offer one word of caveat: this is an Early Access alpha-build. It is not feature complete, there is more content to come and you are not buying a bug-free or content-finished game. If you are fine with that (and I am, I've spent dozens of hours on this game already, I played it before it was ever on Steam and it is a ton of fun even only being about 90% finished), you will be glad you spent your money to help The Indie Stone. They are building a wonderful product and are certainly deserving of your hard-earned cash.

Throwing items at enemies it’s nothing new, but what about enemies throwing things at you? It would be terrifying and exciting, right? This is the big highlight of
, a dungeon crawler with kleptomaniac enemies who can use the same items as the player. Yep, this includes casting spells, using scrolls and drinking potions. Think twice before throwing that giant axe on someone – they can, and
, throw back in your face.
The game is turn based and grid based, but instead of having a whole party to control, you control a single character, like on most roguelikes. And as a roguelike, it has permanent death to shake things up (but you can turn it off if you wish), so take your time to think and strategize the best solution for each encounter. In total there are 20 levels – 10 regular levels and 10 portal levels, and more than 100 items with stats variations (blessed, enchanted, cursed, etc). The portal levels almost always have unique items that will really make a difference when you face boss fights, so don’t skip these levels – even if some of them are harder than normal, the reward you will get for taking the risk is worth it. Items and items positioning are always random, adding a lot to the replay value, and also, there's a mode with
, which make Ebony Spire a game you can literally play forever.
The controls are exclusive for the keyboard, like some classic dungeon crawlers that inspired this game, and they’re very intuitive and easy to use (
for basic movement,
for turning around,
to pick up or drop items,
to throw items,
to open doors,
to access the log,
to view inventory,
to trigger or use an item,
to view/examine your surroundings,
to check affinity levels and modifiers,
to view the map and
to favorite an item or weapon). The sound effects are simple, but very well done – you will know when there’s some enemy attacking you from behind just by listening to the attack or throw sound – and the soundtrack, composed by ambient sounds, adds to the suspenseful atmosphere. Don’t let the screenshots fool you – the graphics are very well done, with detailed sprites, and certainly looks way better ingame than in a screenshot.
It’s also worth mentioning that the game is available under the
and has
integration. This means that the code is easily accessible and you can mod it as you want, so feel free to change things in the game, add new levels, create puzzles or even use your own assets to create your own game.
Developed by
, a
indie studio,
will certainly please you if you like dungeon crawlers and roguelikes. It’s worth mentioning that there’s more content to come in future updates and the developer is very dedicated, passionate about his project and open to suggestions (I was a beta tester and many of my suggestions for improvement were included in the game). If you don’t fear a challenge, join the community, choose your class, grab all loot and throw them at your enemies. Oh, and watch your back – these kleptomaniac monsters will throw everything they can at you – don’t say I didn’t warned you!

First, this is a better game with the Mega Mod, or Colonial Charter mod. Those teams have been refining this game for years and while I think it's important to review the product being sold, to do a review of a three year old game and not mention there are numerous teams working on it with assistance from the original desiger would be an oversight.
The game as released is often misuderstood. It is unique in scope, design, and execution, and does not rely on the tropes and mechanisms typical of the genre. There are some elements that are not ideal, of course (the interface is a new experience with a learning curve and it did not need to be). But the curve is not odious or insurmountable. Learn and use the various status monitors and hotkeys and everything becomes much easier.
Describing this as a "city-building strategy game" is a hideous disservice and bluntly incorrect. This is a game of life and death and moment to moment necessity.
At it's core it is a tribe simulator and has no relationship to anything Sim. It is that rare game that rewards patience, diligence, and forward thinking. If you read a review that demonstrates gameplay of less than 20 hours you are reading the thoughts of a person does not have an understanding of Banished. You are dealing with lifetimes. You will fail several times before you grasp the mechanisms at work in this world. There are moments when the whole thing will come crashing down and you will be scrambling like mad just to keep enough of your people alive to keep the town from dying out completely.
It's deep and non-simple, but once you "get it" there is a lot to love about Banished. Commit to a little work as you enter. As with anything rewarding, effort and error are required. From this player's perspective after many many hours the payoff is 100% worth it. And for the record... I HATED this game when I initially bought it. It just won me over. If there is a better endorsment I cannot think of it.

Flatout 2 has the same developer and publisher as the first game; and yet, somehow, they've managed to make it feel like a cheap Flatout ripoff.
The innovative damage and driving system of the first game is gone, replaced with arcade style physics instead. Missing as well, is unlocking the entire tier of cars in one go, rather having to unlock individual cars as you compete, entirely precluding you from being able to save up for the car you want, and carry it through the tier with you, as with the previous game. Vehicle upgrades are also severely limited when compared to the first game as well, with only one tier for each upgrade, and many upgrades from the previous game being entirely absent. All the vehicles more or less handle the same, despite this game having differences between FWD, 4WD, and RWD cars, with weight and strength not coming into play at all with the exception of during derby events.
Level design makes no logical sense, with entire structures appearing and disappearing with track layouts that are supposed to be in the same location. All the tracks feel as though they were designed as race tracks first, and the copy and pasted into the game's various locals, rather than designed from the ground up to suit that location. As a result, all of the tracks feel more or less the same, with different scenery adorning each one, rather than different and unique challenging locations.
Gone as well is the previous game's unique soundtrack, replaced with generic pop and rock music. While I have nothing against the songs themselves, they take away from the "country and backwoods" feel of a derby-style racing game, and replace it with something that feels like it belongs in Need For Speed: Underground.
All and all, I cannot recommend this game. It is held aloft almost entirely on the success of its predecessor, but with about half the production budget. I recommend buying the first game, and forgetting this travesty ever existed.

The Long Dark is a sandbox survival game, still in development, but not lacking in content. There isnt a story mode as I am writing this, but there will be soon. Cons:
Some in game objects are notably low-resolution compared to everything else.
Certain resources are very finite, and limit the ability to survive for long periods of time.
If youre up for a complicated and very challenging survival experience, this game is perfect.
