Train Valley is a surprisingly good title for not a whole lot of money. You just need to have the right expectations.
This is no ecosim, it's a light puzzler with trains. Your goal is to connect the different train yards, of which more will pop up during any given scenario (always in the same place, but at possibly different times each time you retry the level, i.e. upper right instead of lower left and vice versa). Your only tool are tracks and demolition. This is complicated by the terrain and already present tiles with buildings, etc. on them, which makes construction a lot more expensive if you want/need to go through instead of around. After that it's "simply" a matter of sending out trains to the correct stations by manipulation of the railroad switches and avoiding crashes. Easier said than done sometimes.
Trains will "spawn" after a set amount of time (indicated in the bottom right) and automatically leave the station if all stations have spawned trains already (i.e. you were either sleeping or you spawned extra trains and couldn't get them out in time). This can have dire consequences. The longer a train waits and travels the more of its monetary value it will lose. Since the game deducts a yearly fee (and the year goes by very quickly) you can end up bankrupt thus forfeiting the level completely, which means restarting from the very beginning, since there are no check points nor is manual saving a thing.
Add to that 3 different bonus goals (fixed) for each level (spawn x additional trains, earn x amount of money, don't let a train go to the wrong station, don't press pause, etc.) and the game can become quite hectic, despite the availability of a pause feature. It is still easy to misjudge a train's speed though and send out the next too early, so they crash. The switches get out of hand in later levels, so mistakes are easily made, especially since any train going over a switch that does not have to be changed automatically aligns it as well, which can spell trouble for the following train if you're not on your guard.
Crashes are pretty bad most of the time since they not only mean the train and money is lost forever, but you also have to rebuild the tracks, meaning even more money is lost. You could easily go bankrupt until the next train reaches its destination. However, you can stop a train and even turn it around at almost any given time, but of course this has other negative effects like loss of money and time.
If you like a challenge or want to speed things up, you can do so by up to 4 times the regular speed (2x and 4x speed). Do not press the pause button and see if you can survive ;)
The DLC "Germany" adds a new chapter to Europe, America, Russia and Japan, complete with new trains, new hazards and new music. Every region in the game features its own soundtrack and some levels have interesting hazards to play around with, for example unstoppable speed trains, or even bombing runs. Well worth it in my opinion.

If you didn't know, BioShock is claimed to be one of the most revolutionary FPS's games of all time, and that statement has plently of truth to it. It exceeds in almost all areas, but no gem is without its flaws. Unfortunately for BioShock, these flaws can be quite noticeable when you come across to them. DO NOT let that discourage you from playing this game though; it's an experience you don't want to miss.
In terms of presentation, BioShock fails to unimpress. The view of the underwater city of Rapture will amaze you when it emerges on your screen, and the steampunk art style is very unique, while being consistent throughout the game. Voice acting is perfect without a doubt, and characters such as Ryan Andrew and Sander Cohen will leave a lasting impression long after you finish the game. Sound design is extremly well-done as well: the whale-like moans from the hulking Big Daddies are very creepy, and the game only uses music for atmospheric reasons, adding an extra layer of immersion that makes the game quite screepy, but never outright scary (which is not what the game is trying to do).
The story is the main highlight of BioShock, and presents themes and ideologies that are very applicable to reality, mainly the view of objectivism. Plot twists and unforgetable characters will make the experience a memorable ones, and each audio-diary will flesh out the world of Rapture, especially in events following up to the game. As for the main protagonist Jack, he's the typical silent playable character that every shooter seems to have, but his background information makes him quite interesting. Despite this, the story is damned near perfect, even if it feels ever-so rushed after the games huge revelation and twist.
I could end the review here, as the story is something that alone should be able to sell this game instantly, no strings attached. However, how does BioShock sell as an FPS? The game features an arsenal of weapons from a flamethrower to a machine gun, and are all quite standard. The sense of conserving ammo that the game has at first is very intense, however later on you will have more money than you even need, so that feeling is somewhat lost. Gunplay feels slightly "floaty" (can't really get my finger on what it is), and later on becomes quite inneffective against enemies that suddenly have increased durability from earlier in the game. Speaking of enemies, you'll encounter Splicer's, humans which are addicted to this substance called ADAM, which grants them superpowers but makes them mentally unstable. Some will teleport around you, while others will have a box of grenades to utilize instead. But most significant of all are the Big Daddies.
These hulking beasts present a real challenge, but are neutral if not dealt with. Why? They guard Little Sisters. which are key to the games plot and whether you get a good or bad ending. These altered girls harvest ADAM from dead corpses (and have a creepy sense of innocence to them), and you have the option to either save them or harvest them. Saving leads to the good ending but you get less ADAM, and harvesting them leads to the bad ending but you get more ADAM (and a combination leads to the sad ending). Actually combating the Big Daddies leads to a great deal of planning, and you'll have to acknowledge that you wont come out of the fight without a few scars.
Going backwards, do you recall how I noted how guns became less useful as the game progresses? Well, that is because of Plasmids, which are basically superpowers like shooting flames, bolts of electricity, or even a swarm of bees! These are incredibly fun to use. een though you have to switch to your Plasmids and use them independantly from your weapons, making combat feel slightly clunky. The game also presents you with many RPG features, such as a hacking minigame (meh), weapon/plasmid upgrades, shops, ammo types, and plenty of nooks and cranies to add to it all. Overall combat is slightly outdated by todays standards (no sprint or ADS, if such a thing would bother you), but is still incredibly fun regardless.
BioShock is a prime example of how video games are art, and is one you should not overlook. Even where it missteps in gameplay, it's story and presentation are grand throughout, and provide a unique experience you will not forget and will come back to again and again. There is no denying that BioShock is a game that will stand the test of time, and I would give it a 9/10 (If it was story alone than 11/10, it's that good).
So, would you kindly get it?

Following are the diary logs found on the deck of an abandoned ship:
As I gaze out upon the empty Sea, I feel a tang of blight. Something pulls me away from the lights and safety of London and out towards empty void.
I feel myself dragged, as though Storm were pulling me towards my fate, be it riches or death. I follow in the footsteps of my Father, like his Father before him. We sail, we seek. We shall not be content by the light of a hearth. We need the blackness of the Sea, lit only by lantern for but a few yards out before disappearing in to oblivion.
With a heavy heart I gathered up a crew of odd fellows. We even found a cat! And off we set towards the nothing.
Days pass. Our terror of what might lurk just below the surface is rising. One of the crew had disappeared while on watch, no one even heard a splash.
Times began to get hard. We had to eat the cat. It was stringy and bland, but it sufficed.
Lights! Lights appeared everywhere. What remained of the crew rejoiced! For the first time in a long while they felt hope, something to distract them from the bleak and bitter despair that clouded their days and haunted their nights.
The lights were a trap. Three more men are gone. We are down to two now, myself and a mysterious chef who keeps eyeing me as though he were thinking something horrendous.
I fought off an attack by the chef today. He came at me with a knife, a gleam of insanity in his eyes. He had been cursed. It was with great sadness and regret that I had to throw him overboard to appease the Gods. Now it is just me. All alone. All alone...no one else...
Just me...
Just me...
A sound! I have been hiding a closet for days, hoping the nightmares would leave, but they stay. I find myself chasing shadows, jumping at sounds in the dark and worse. Food is beginning to run out. Perhaps the water will go first and the insanity will take me before the hunger.
Today I had supper with the Queen! It was a grand event! She showed up, quite unexpectedly, with a nice fancy feast for the two of us. She told me that she would make sure that I make it to my home. Oh, to see her go was so sad.
...
I may have finally gone insane. I can no longer trust my own senses. Today, I was certain I saw something beneath the water. It looked like the chef that I had sacrificed to Storm. He was following me. Mocking me. Waiting for me to die.
...
Today I made friends with a Beetle. His name is Steve. I had to eat him. I think he may have been toxic. My eyes have not been the same since...Wait...There seems to be something floating just off the bow of the ship...I think I can reach...

{Spoilers and fanboi rants in this review, read as you please}
As a long standing Batman fan, I can see why a lot of people were biffed at this. I personally enjoyed it, it was a great treat and the usual TellTale formula of excerpts saying somebody just reacted to what you said and the acute anxiety of seeing that. Course many of those prompts in most telltale games doesn't mean much, but still it adds to the ride.
I'll try to keep this as spoiler free as possible, the game isn't bad to start. It's quite good, the story, the character development, the thing I noticed that was different from most Batman incarnations, is that Batman is really green at points. Like Year One Batman green, and I tried to play it off like that in some story points as it feels, with many other reviews addressing the fact, that you're just constantly thrown into one predicament after another, while Batman most of the time plays one step ahead of the villian he's after--which fits the cowl perfectly as it plays into fearing Batman rather than having him fall into your plans once he figures them out and prepares accordingly. This as said, does a 180 at that fact since most of the time you're responding to most things that are entirely out of your control.
And despite that, I still liked this Batman. I think the thing that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the fans, which I could kind of feel at points, is that they humanised batman. You will feel like you're dealing with a million different things and see Bruce/Batman show it as well, while I'm used to the more Stoic, cold, calculating Batman. This Batman shows a lot of emotion you don't often find, you either have the snarky batman, the cold Batman I just mentioned, or this Batman, who's human and makes a lot of mistakes that leave you to either appreciate what Telltale had to work with in their usual formula of doing things, or leave you biffed on something that didn't exactly follow the guidelines. I'm a little bit of both--again the game ain't bad I reccomend you play it if you're a fan, or if you're just like me and you've either burned through the walking dead and came out scorched, or unfortunately finished the Wolf Among Us and are clinging to what really sells a telltale game 'cause good Jesus that game was near-perfect. This one however? Well, we'll get more into that.
I would say, that I've been spoiled with the stoic, cold batman, the batman we see in the Arkham series and everywhere else, and I love that. However, seeing a Batman that can be manipulated, that can be a condescending jerk, a batman in a sense that doesn't think twelve steps ahead, and is more flawed than the original with a lot more Bruce facetime--is a totally different feeling than what I was used to. I think that was the big thing in this game that detracted from a more Batman oriented game, as it tries to follow a balance you want to walk in this game, highlighting whether you want to save Bruce's face against all the shenanigans a billionaire philanthropist falls into, or if you wanted to highlight Batman as the shining beacon of Gotham against all the shenigans a billionaire philanthropist has to deal with. And a lot of the time in this game is placed on Bruce, with batman almost bridging the gap into the next problem that, Bruce, has to face with Batman almost being a tool of his to use. There's also a lot of interesting developments they've did with Bruce Wayne's legacy, that I feel were handled right in the context of this game, the ol' batman predicament of whether he can uphold the honor of batman when he looks at himself.
I must say though, Harvey Dent in this game, has probably the best character development I've seen for him. And despite the new batman feel you have, that could either turn you off, or have you wondering at the very least (or enjoying--to each their own amirite?) it's a good game. The only thing I have to say that I truly didn't like, which could be fixed if they use him right, is the Joker. He feels a little too...calm for the Joker. Yet Telltale has taken a lot of freedom in using characters outside the status quo, and I like that, they're trying something different rather than allowing the rhythm to bleed through every character in them following their archetype, this game doesn't do that and has leeway on characters and how they're utilized and built through the story. It's a breath of fresh air, but one that can also taste stale to others. In the end, the dialogue felt good, despite most of it not holding any weight in the story (as per telltale tradition) some points of the game force you to choose between what event to take on, but looking back on how the story progressed I don't believe it would have had any major impact. Looking back on said storytelling there were some things that weren't explained, things that were just thrown at batman, or for him to walk in on, but overall it concluded very nicely.
Out of my rating system--Great/Good/Bad style; were Great meaning it's a timeless classic that is amazing and whatever flaws it has eventually evolved into charm; good meaning it's a good game that has it's flaws but is still playable, engaging and fun; and bad meaning you won't find much enjoyment out of it and/or it's just too disappointing and/or boring to follow through on--I feel it's a good game in the end. It has it's flaws that can turn you off or on, has it's points that don't make sense or don't feel "batmany" and points where I felt like even if I didn't push the action prompts I still would've kicked♥♥♥♥♥and survived, it's still fun and engaging in the end, if just for the story alone. Quite good, as everyone including the villian, had their motivations and loose ties eventually connected while Batman had to survive it all.
{Sidenote} The game does have some technical issues, such as scenes stuttering, frozen characters, sometimes the models will be seen standing until the scene corrects itself, and even with my 980ti build, at parts it felt like the game was crying and my card didn't know how to baby it. Overall though, it didn't get annoying, and didn't persist onto important parts, it mainly only happened during transitions, other than that everything else ran quite smoothly.

Sunless Sea is a text-based adventure through the cavern in which Victorian London now resides, having fallen from the surface in the years prior to the start of the game.
Firstly, if you are not a fan of slow-paced games, step away. In no way have I found this game tedious (being a fan of both the action-packed and slow-paced genres), however if you are looking for a game where you sail around and fight/loot galleys and merchant ships such as AC4: Black Flag, then this is not the game you are looking for.
I personally have not found any objectively negative things about the game (save for 1 which I'll address later), so I'll simply list out the notable features as opposed to doing a Pro/Con list.
NOTABLE FEATURES
- Permanent Top-down perspective. You will always be looking on from the above, just as it maintains in the trailer
- Most of the gameplay consists of reading and making choices. Yes, you sail around and you can fight various creatures, however to real meat of the game lies in the rich story which you can develop at your own leisure, and in your own way. There are various decisions that are permanent and have lasting effects on your story, making this game in a very real way a living choose your own adventure game.
- 2 modes of gameplay. You can save whenever you want on merciful (I think that's what it's called), or you can do a hardcore run where you only autosave at ports and permadeath is enabled (though there is a way to pass on certain items after death).
- If you're going to buy this game, I wholeheartedly recommend the Zubmariner DLC expansion. It adds a bunch of new ports and with them, certain stories, and it adds more zee-beasts and a whole new layer to the existing map. An important thing to note about this though, is that you must undertake a quest to be able to use the Zubmarine by going to certain places and doing certain things. I have no reservations with this, however others have demonstrated distate for this prerequisite.
- There is no fast-travel, and going as fast as possible from one place to another not only misses one of the points of the game but may also be potentially harmful.
- On the one occassion in which the game did happen to hit an objective fault (my autosave got corrupted somehow and I had to contact support), I lodged a ticket on Failbetter games' website and I was met with speedy and friendly instruction on how to fix the issue. I was able to restore the save, return everything to normal, and continue playing.
- You will probably die. Quite a few times. It can be frustrating at first, especially on your first captain when you most likely don't know where to go or what to do, but eventually you'll be able to roll with the punches and get a steady lineage going, and death will be a mere inconvenience.
- There is some amount of inventory juggling that takes place, especially on certain missions/storylines, but I've found that it doesn't take away from the experience much, especially once you familiarize yourself with each type of item and its importance/use.
- Terror is very important, and the game does a great job of building up a haunting atmosphere that leaves a lasting impact upon the player.
- Many events are based on skill-checks, being left up to RNG to determine the outcome of certain options, though many of them entail at least somewhat the possible outcomes of each action.
Tl;dr
Sunless Sea is a slow-paced, story-based, atmospheric experience set in the hostile underground cavern of the Neath, and what it lacks in action, it more than makes up for in enthralling stories and a riveting journey. If you're a fan of story-rich games, this is a must buy. If you prefer action-packed shooters, maybe give it a pass, unless you really want to try something new.
If you're going to buy the game, the Zubmariner expansion pack has a lot to offer, so I'd wholeheartedly recommend it along with the base game itself.

Sunless Sea is a game that focusses on immersive, atmospheric gameplay, set in a dark fantasy / victorian gothic world. Everything about the previous sentence is something I just love and can't get enough of. Graphicly this game is just wonderful (eventhough it doesn't support resolutions over 1080p) and the sounds really work towards a very immersive game with a great setting.  It reminds me of H.P. Lovecraft and specifically of boardgames based around his novels. Some of the artwork seems as if it would fit in nicely in Call of Cthulhu or Arkham Horror. Even some gameplay elements work towards this comparison (the cards / feats you gather while on sea).
But other than that, the gameplay is just... not that good. Even plain bad at places. The game seems to focus on atmosphere and narrative, rather than on providing a fun experience.
You start up the game, get no explanation on anything, and are immediatly slapped in the face with several walls of text (even an entire manual) to read in game. Nothing is narrated or otherwise visual, we're talking text (with hyperlinks) here. These walls of text are filled with in-game terms you haven't heard of before this moment: Veils, Echo's, Terror, ... Yet you are expected to know what it's about right away. We're also not talking about simple English here. We're talking specific in-game terms and we're talking advanced vocabulary. (I'm a non-native, though very proficient, English speaker and I had to google words.) Turns out reading these walls of text comes in handy, but is not important in any way. Greeeaaat.
After this, I had to to "create a character", which is to be understood as "pick between several options and categories of which you don't know what's what". Woopteedoo. Consequently, you're dropped in the big mean world without as much as a direction what to do and where to go.
In one way, that's kind of the point: You can do whatever you damn well please.
In another way, that's kind of a shame: Minor guidance (atleast in the first few bits of the game) would be a great boon.
You get some pop-ups to the left and the right of the screen. Some you can click, some you can't. You get some more walls of text. Some you'll read, some you'll respond to with "f-- it". And that's it: Go about and be merry.
I played, figuring out the game as I went, and found it to be... lacking. You sail around on your boat, you discover stuff, you're rewarded fragments (took me a google to find out that's Zee-speak for 'XP'), occassionally you dock, you click some pop-ups, get some more pop-ups and you sail around some more. This repeats itself. (Sometimes interrupted by convoluted combat or random occurances.) Add to this that the game is excruciatingly slow and that you're in a constant struggle with the limitations of your inventory... Urgh.
I googled a guide with some beginner's tips and found that, in short, the above is mostly all that's to it. Sure, you get some semblance of quests (sail from A to B, pick-up X and drop off Y) and there's a trading system and whatnot. But the point of it all is: Sail around, gather money (called "echo's", by the way), get rich and retire. That's it. Apart from the setting, I'm not sure I find this appealing at all. (Come to think about it, the setting is the only reason why I bought the game in the first place.)

In order to prosper in an underworld ridden with darkness would require immense perseverance and great tenacity, both from the captain and his/her/its ship. A wonderfully eerie world to explore, with many bizarre and otherworldly locations to discover in the wide, dark unforgiving zee. Meeting strange, yet memorable characters from places far off. Men made from clay, people in bandage, people with faces of squid. SQUID ! Gothic atmospheric game at its best. The writing and exploration sells.
However, no game is free from criticism nor flaws. A key component of games in general is the challenge. Challenges both motivates and puts off those who dared to face them. Large learning curve that is very difficult to get out of when supplies are low and safety is far and few between, with hostile ships and beasts lurking near ports, making it a hassle to get in and out of places without a few dents on the newly repaired ship. It would be a miracle to see my ship's engine not going up in flames (for the 5th time) trying to evade enemies that would make a quick snack from me and my crew. But let's not forget the game's major selling point is its difficulty and death is an opportunity for leaning from the mistakes made that resulted in my swift demise.
Combat is in my opinion, a primary component of the game,but lacks every aspect of the thrills of danger when you are met with a predictable AI and often a minuscule reward for fighting tough enemies. Not much variation in enemy types or the means to end their miserable existence. Even the best gun that money can buy from the bazaar cannot satiate my hunger for blood of creatures that swam in my way. It is very capable of leave corpses and debris in my wake, albeit in a dull and tedious manner. Avoid combat as much as humanly (and humanely) possible, as the risk-reward does not worth the cost of ship repair, and to repeat myself, the reward gained from a defeated enemy does not worth the risk and the danger I have put myself through. A good rule of thumb is to assume everything that floats in the zee is hostile. Even the islands. Turn your lights off if you spot a ship armed to the teeth. Darkness is both the bane of your existence and your ally. Evasion is highly recommended for every threat, even the smallest like pirate ships and crabs.
To conclude, a very atmospheric game set in a bizarre world where death is imminent, but serves as a mild inconvenience. Combat is lacking, but sufficient. The untold horrors awaits in the darkness is what keeps me up at night (playing). Would continue playing regardless of my standings with the game and highly recommend buying if the game is on sale.

Red Orchestra 2 is a thrilling and exciting game. Not because you can jump into a group of enemies and gun them down, but because you know that every shot counts.
I have had countless of cases where I had spotted an enemy, which on his part, was looking right at me. I quickly try to get into cover and aim down my sights, but it's too late: the last thing I see is a white glare coming from his rifle and half a second later I drop dead on the floor.
These examples are what makes this game special. Tripwire has aimed for a realistic experience in which you feel humbled by your lack of power to change the tide of battle on your own. Only teamwork and good coordination can bring you to victory. You actually feel like you're working towards a goal every time you capture a house, a street or an other strategical important objective, and that's what makes this game special and really enjoyable.
TL;DR -> Realistic, team-focussed, slow pased but above all thrilling game!

I put almost 700 hours into this small game, considering I got the game in sale for $9 few years ago, that's quite good deal however about 600 of these hours went into heavily modified version of banished known as Colonial Charter.
I am not going to write elaborate review as the game is over 3 year old and there's already 20k of them.
Banished as stand alone game is really nice looking time sink with relaxing music for maybe about 20 - 50 hours more if you are trying to get all all achievements. Game start roughly and if you don't know how to play it's quite possible you will lose everything really fast. This also scares few of my friends from playing but the moment you learn game everything becomes really easy and only challenge are RNG disasters that can be turned off such as tornados, disease, fire or orchard infestation.
There's many guides and banished wikia contains calculator for optimal field, orchard, graveyard or pasture size turning the game into relaxing simulation instead of challenge.
*You can only earn achievements in unmoded version.
This is where I put most of my hours.
Currently the best mods you can get is
. Don't look in the workshop instead, google their site for instruction and direct download. I heard The North is really nice mod but I didn't had time to check it out.
I admit I feel like even with Adam & Eve - which is supposedly hardest start, starting just with 2 people, buildings in CC makes everything easier than original. Some might think of it as negative but honestly I think it just turn banished into sim city builder with many production chains and nicer visuals thanks to the variety and decoration CC brings.
CC + Megamod adds many new maps, buildings, decorations, animals, plans and so on that it expand the game many times over. The decorations and customized sets such as docks make it worth alone.
If you are looking for more simulation and less survival I would recommend starting with already modded game.

Performance - Game starts to hang out at +10 speed when your population start to hit certain number of people.
In my case it's around 800 to 1200, then I slow game to +5 or +2. However in these large half map covering cities that speed is almost impossible to work on as everything takes ages to finish on lower speed when you are trying to maitain and grow city with population so big.
I noticed this speed isn't much related to your computer setup as it's to the game. For example I can run FF14 or HotS basically any other game next to banished and there's no lag no delay in them and there's no effect on Banished either.
In the end, I do recommended the game modded or not. Both offer quite different experience.
One for a few hours of challenge in I think graphically pleasing builder and other for many hours of simulation.

I hesitated buying this game and this is the first time I buy an "Early Access" game. After reading the reviews I decided to take the risk and get it: I don't regret it. There is something beautiful about this game: it is entertaining and haunting. It is tough but enjoyable.
In my last adventure I survived for 17 days in the Voyager difficulty, I went through two maps, through almost impossible paths and difficult days. On the last day I managed to get several good items and I had a routine that could make me survive for a long time.
On the last day I went to a forest nearby to put a snare, I left the house without medicines because it was a short trip anyway... as I arrived to the right place I saw a wolf eating a rabbit. The wolf saw me and went after me, I tried to make it go away by using a flare. I was too slow and the wolf too fast, he attacked me. I survived but I was badly wounded and without medicines, I was bleeding. I tried to return to my place but a storm suddenly appeared and I lost my way, I was sure that I was quite close, maybe passing another hill I would find home. My health began to drop at a fast rate and I knew that I wouldn't make it. I wandered and wandered and I saw a dark figure in the snow: It was the wolf that attacked me and now it was dead because of the wounds of our fight, I smiled because he died before me, I didn't give him the pleasure of killing me first.
As I reached my final moments I stood besides the dead wolf, I looked to the beautiful scenery around me one last time and prepared my bedroll, I decided to finish the adventure this way. I slept and died.
I love this game.

In order to prosper in an underworld ridden with darkness would require immense perseverance and great tenacity, both from the captain and his/her/its ship. A wonderfully eerie world to explore, with many bizarre and otherworldly locations to discover in the wide, dark unforgiving zee. Meeting strange, yet memorable characters from places far off. Men made from clay, people in bandage, people with faces of squid. SQUID ! Gothic atmospheric game at its best. The writing and exploration sells.
However, no game is free from criticism nor flaws. A key component of games in general is the challenge. Challenges both motivates and puts off those who dared to face them. Large learning curve that is very difficult to get out of when supplies are low and safety is far and few between, with hostile ships and beasts lurking near ports, making it a hassle to get in and out of places without a few dents on the newly repaired ship. It would be a miracle to see my ship's engine not going up in flames (for the 5th time) trying to evade enemies that would make a quick snack from me and my crew. But let's not forget the game's major selling point is its difficulty and death is an opportunity for leaning from the mistakes made that resulted in my swift demise.
Combat is in my opinion, a primary component of the game,but lacks every aspect of the thrills of danger when you are met with a predictable AI and often a minuscule reward for fighting tough enemies. Not much variation in enemy types or the means to end their miserable existence. Even the best gun that money can buy from the bazaar cannot satiate my hunger for blood of creatures that swam in my way. It is very capable of leave corpses and debris in my wake, albeit in a dull and tedious manner. Avoid combat as much as humanly (and humanely) possible, as the risk-reward does not worth the cost of ship repair, and to repeat myself, the reward gained from a defeated enemy does not worth the risk and the danger I have put myself through. A good rule of thumb is to assume everything that floats in the zee is hostile. Even the islands. Turn your lights off if you spot a ship armed to the teeth. Darkness is both the bane of your existence and your ally. Evasion is highly recommended for every threat, even the smallest like pirate ships and crabs.
To conclude, a very atmospheric game set in a bizarre world where death is imminent, but serves as a mild inconvenience. Combat is lacking, but sufficient. The untold horrors awaits in the darkness is what keeps me up at night (playing). Would continue playing regardless of my standings with the game and highly recommend buying if the game is on sale.

Alright, i think the time has come to write a review for this game. I started playing the game on 4th or 5th of june and Steam says that the game ran for over 432 hours. I didn't actually play for all these hours, but i still played A LOT. I have played this game for about 25 days, which means that it ran for 17+ hours on average every day. With that amount of time you can safely say that i am a hardcore gamer and enjoyed it most of the time. I also recently became a volunteer as a translator for Digital Leisure, which is the company that created this game. For a long time i was not sure if i give this game a positive or a negative review, but after the Blackjack tournament that happened last weekend i finally made my decision, but more to this later.
Four Kings Casino and Slots is a casino simulation. A virtual casino where you create an avatar and play popular casino games like Blackjack, Slots, Craps, Video Poker and others. In every game, except Poker, there is a house edge like in a real casino. So, if you like gambling and losing your chips most of the time then this game could get you somewhat addicted.
The game was fully released out of early access on june the 1st with many bugs, errors and easy ways for people to cheat. Especially within about the first 1-2 weeks the game was plagued by cheaters and bugs. They definitely released this game too early and after almost a month now it still feels like you are playing a beta/early access version. I still don't understand why they did that.
It is free to play, so how are they making their money? First there is a shop where you can buy cosmetic items like clothes for your avatar and then you can buy chips with real money.
As a new player you get 10k chips to play with, which sounds good at the beginning, but it is not a lot. You can lose them quickly if you are not careful enough. Especially for Poker players it can be painful, because the buy-in at a Poker table is 5k. So, if you lose two Poker games then you are already broke. There are some ways how you can get free chips and i will list them for you:
-Every 15 minutes you can pick up 250 free chips at the chip station.
-Once per day you can play at the free Poker table and only the winner can get 5k. There is only 1 free Poker table in the room, so you will have to wait and sometimes be fast, because there are many players waiting.
-Every now and then there is also a free Bingo game and depending on the number of players you can win some chips. With the maximum of 40 players it is 10k if i remember correctly, but good luck winning one of these.
-5 daily tasks where you get 200 chips for completing each one of them and an additional 600 if you complete them all. Most of them are very easy like using an emote, playing at the free Poker table or dancing in the nightclub.
-5 weekly tasks. You get 2k for completing each one of them and right now i don't remember how much you can get when you complete them all. Some of them are ridiculous like earning 1000 RP at Keno or Slots. Don't even try if you don't have many chips.
I mentioned RP and this is like a second currency in the game that allows you to buy items in the shops like clothes. You mostly earn RP by winning chips and if you earn enough within a month you can get vip status for a month, which gives you some benefits. You earn RP depending on how many chips you bet/win. There are leaderboards for every game and there is a global leaderboard that are based on the RP you earn. Players who buy chips for money have a big advantage to get to the top of the leaderboards - they are kind of pay to win since these players can max bet all the time and don't have to worry about losing the chips.
There were many errors and bugs. Some of them have been more or less fixed and some games have been improved, but there are still enough that it's annoying to some degree. If you run a casino then functionality is the most important thing. In Four Kings Casino and Slots you can lose chips to bugs and this is kind of ridiculous, because there are people who pay money for their chips. Tables can glitch and become unplayable, players get kicked off tables, game crashes, disconnects and people lose some chips when things like that happen. It also happened to me that one time i didn't receive the chips for completing the daily tasks. You can request chip refunds through the bug report system in the game and most of the time they will give you back your lost chips, but not always. It happened at least twice to me that i can definitely remember where they just didn't refund the chips that i lost although i made these bug reports. Again, especially painful for the players who spent money for their chips. Within the first 2 or 3 weeks the game often felt like a chip refund simulator and not a casino simulation. It is better now, but you can still lose chips to bugs, make a chip refund request through the bug report tool and not receive the chips that you lost. I would not recommend spending money in that game unless you really don't care. If you go to a real casino they don't just kick you off the table for no reason and keep your chips.
So, there was a Blackjack tournament last weekend and i saved up enough chips to play. First, Digital Leisure posted wrong information about the tournament on the Steam discussion board where they always post their information about the tournaments. For example, they wrote that the tournament would be split into segments of 2 hours each and there was also a overall leaderboard. In reality these segments were just 1 hour each. After 3 or 4 hours of the tournament running they restarted the server to make some fixes. Great timing, isn't it? Unfortunately and to my anger these "fixes" still didn't help to prevent some bugs happening. For example, if you played to the end of a 1 hour segment and let the extra time fully run out your score did not count, but if you stood up a few seconds earlier your score did count. They didn't tell us anything about that before.
On the second day of the tournament i had to experience it myself where i made a score that was enough for overall 3rd place, but it didn't count because the timer fully ran out. I had a pretty high score already at 3rd place, but this one was only good enough for place 5 at the end. It also happened to other players and we made a post about it on the discussion board. A Digital Leisure employee responded in that thread and said that we should make screenshots next time. Are you kidding me? It was not our fault, it was a fault on their side. He also said that the score of ALL players in this thread would be corrected and they did, but not with mine. There was a player who had a higher score than i previously had and he posted after me. He got his score corrected, but i didn't get my score corrected. When i mentioned that they forgot me he only said that it wouldn't affect MY payout and still didn't correct my score. What a joke since before that he posted that the payouts would also be corrected by the team. At the end i only ended up at rank 5 instead of rank 3 on the overall tournament leaderboard. Their game bug cost me 2 places and a better payout.
On the final day of the tournament i had 2 really, really good runs that had great potential to make the best score and reach rank 1 in the whole tournament. In one of these runs i had it for sure. My luck and my earnings were crazy this time. I was almost alone in a room sitting at an empty table to play as many hands as possible. I knew it. I saw my score, i saw the time that i had left and suddenly in the middle of these 2 runs the game disconnected me. Very strange that it exactly happened in these 2 runs. I knew what i was doing. I won about 10+ of 48 of the 1 hour tournament segments and made some 2nd and 3rd places. I barely slept this weekend, tried so hard and didn't make it to #1, because of game errors. Unbelievable and ridiculous.

Awesome game! Worth 'almost' every minute. Why?
Story - 7/10 - This game is story-rich! Well, half-story-rich. Set in an underwater abandoned city created by a visionary, Andrew Ryan, you'll need to find out the mysteries that this city is hiding and what happened to her, with the help of some guns, supernatural powers and 'radio friends'. But after one of the biggest plots in video game history, you'll get a big let down with the ending. Still, you'll be remembering the game for its awesome first half and not for the ridiculous final boss fight and ending.
Gameplay - 9/10 - The gameplay is not that pratical when changing from guns to super-powers (especially if you're a beginner) and the guns don't feel powerful, you'll be ending up using the wrench more times than fire power. But those are the only cons here. You got tons of customization to do: collect and choose your preferred physical, engineering and combat abilities; upgrade your powers and weapons; collect and craft special ammo for your guns and more. The research camera is also a pretty good gadget: use it to take pictures of your enemies to learn more about them and get bonus damage when attacking them. The Vita-Chamber can be a bit boring, making you pratically invincible (but you can disable them in the options), but the hacking is a fun little minigame that never gets old!
Graphics and atmosphere - 10/10 - The graphics and atmosphere combine so well together, creating the underwater abandoned city that you had in mind. Wheter it's that time you find the shotgun while Splincers sneak up on you, or the dark corners and Spider Splincers crawling up on the ceiling, or simply the sound of a Big Daddy walking with his Little Sister by his side, you never know when will someone appear and try to kill you.
Conclusion: This is an awesome 'classic' by now. Worth every penny. If you like a good FPS with a rich story, atmosphere and memorable moments, then this is a game for you!

Stylized, nature-based visuals are accompanied by soothing music. This another indy puzzle game, this time involving point and click discovery that results in short collection missions. The collection of certain items triggers mini games which are visual, memory and manipulation puzzles with insect- and plant-based themes.
Mini games are varied and some are MUCH harder than others. There's a lot of matching and picture manipulation.
Even though I am recommending this game - the art style is interesting, the music is pleasant, and the minimal story line is noce - there are a few drawbacks.
1) Because this is a wordless game, sometimes your objectives are really hard to figure out. The help recharges after a certain amount of time to give you hints, but if you're not currently in the part of the map where the help hint will show, it just gives you an "error" sound.
2) Because the art is so stylized and items in the enviroment can look different from different angles, sometimes it's unclear whether an item is one of the kind you should be collecting. Insect parts, in particular are very hard to distinguish from the background foliage. This could very well be intentional, but at times I found it very frustrating, and I'm a fan of jigsaw puzzles and "what's different about these two pictures" type puzzles.
3) The ending is extremely abrupt and I found this kind of disappointing. You following along with the adventures of this little creature through 5 levels and then BAM. It's just done.
Having said that, it's a good way to poke at puzzles for several hours and was challenging enough to keep my interest for a one-sitting game. Little in the way of replay, but I got it on sale, so I feel I got my money's worth.

Ultimately disappointing
I was a big fan of Tropico 3 and 4. This one is still playable, but just doesn't feel like it has the depth of the previous titles. Some of the additions I liked and thought were interesting changes, such as:
- You know have a ruling dynasty and you gain new family members as you go, with different abilities and bonuses
- You have different eras that you move through and different building available in each era. There is also a constitution with options in each area. This is how you control things like open or closed borders, conscription vs high quality military etc.
However, things I didn't like:
- It seems much harder to really get a picture of how your society is going. Little things like : previously in a school you could see all the students and click on them, now you just get '5/10 students' and you can't drill down on them. You can't seem to get a list of your whole population by education level, only the unemployed people. You can't see an individual persons needs anymore, just their ratings. It's harder to watch or track a single person. You can see thoughts, but not what they are currently doing, whereas they used to tell you they were going to the doctor, or to get food. You can't see how many people are using a garage or railway station. Lots of small features like this that they have removed make it really hard to diagnose problems, like whether people are able to commute effectively, or have enough services around them.
- Because of the above, when things go wrong, you often have no idea why. Why is the happiness rating high but my approval rating low? Why do I have so many of every type of entertainment building but the entertainment happiness is still low? Why do I have lots of teamsters but my factories are full on un picked-up goods? It's often hard to tell if it is something you are doing wrong, inconsistencies in the game or bugs. Why do I have so many homeless people who won't move into the housing I have built that is in a good location and appropriate for their wealth level? Why do I still have people listed as 'broke' when I have the social security edict turned on. Why is there a group protesting against my government, but when I click on them many have 85+ approval rating and happiness? What are they upset about? No idea.
All of that being said, the game is still fairly easy to complete, but for those like me that like to not just finish the mission but build the ultimate society in the process, it is so frustrating seeing things like a low approval rating due to homelessness when I have dozens of houses standing empty and other similar things. I ended up giving up because I just wasn't enjoying it any more.
For anyone new to the franchise, go and play 3 or 4, they are awesome.

Morphopolis is a refreshing and relaxing experience, and truly a STUNNING visual masterpiece.
Not really difficult, the game can be completed in less than two hours. Short, for sure, however still a good experience, and worth its price especially since it doesn't costs much.
There are two types of gameplay in Morphopolis. The first is a point-n'click, where you explore the wonderful backgrounds looking for whatever can be useful. You'll soon have a to-gather list of differents items to use on a particular thing (a bigger bug than yours, a flower...) which will either open you a new path or open a puzzle minigame.
These puzzles are the second part of Morphopolis and are as various as a visual memory game, an audio memory game, a "classic" puzzle, a mix-n'-match logical puzzle, and so on.
There are two puzzles per level, and five levels in total.
The moving system could have been more intuitive and will make you grunt sometimes (by example when you want to go somewhere and end on another panel), but is finally no big deal.
The only really annoying thing is that the game doesn't allows you to save your progression while you're in a level, forcing you to restart from scratch the next time.
Not the game of the year, but a nicely breath of fresh air.
Just avoid it if even 2D bugs make you feel uneasy.

This is a great game. Yes, that's a very assertive opening statement. But it is true.
This is a very well built feudal-style city building game.
You have food needs (great variety), fuel needs (for heat in the winter), shelter needs (houses, communal buildings, shacks), etc.
You also have the passage of time, which is very well executed here. You have the four seasons adequately simulated; the age factor on your citizens; the ammount of resources consumed varies with gender and age...
In a general manner, this is a very well put toghether game. It feels solid all around.
Games this title bears resemblance with: Caesar (yeah, the old ones); Age of Empires 3 (graphical-wise); Patrician (resouce management); Port Royale (advancement mechanics) and the Anno series (how buildings behave and work and how you go about the usage of space, even though this lacks the modular approach used in 2070, for example).
The graphics are quite all right (doesn't look terrible from any angle and has some sweet spots like water and sun rays), even though things can get a little choppy performance wise when you start to have a lot going on (i run an old Phenom II quad-core on a 16gb DDR3 rig, GTX960 4gb).
The controls are quite easily memorized and you have hotkeys for most of the important stuff. You can build and manage time using only your keyboard, which is two of the main aspects of the game. This makes for a satisfying control experience.
This is a genuine city builder, since your only goal is to maintain your village in existence, keeping it well supplied of everything (there's a lot you gotta account for) and making wise usage of space. I like. I like it a lot.
Overall score: 9/10.

Just like the first Ace Patrol, "Pacific Skies" is a casual strategy game. You get to play as either US Navy, US Air-force, Japanese Navy or Japanese Air-force, and fly on missions against the other side. The point in the game is to use tactical airplane maneuvers to your advantage and shoot down the enemy airplanes.
Unlike what I expected from a game with Sid Meier's name on its title, both games on the series are quite easy to learn. Having that said, they do get really challenging on the harder difficulty levels. A part of the fun is, you can change the difficulty level while playing, and practically choose the difficulty level of each and every mission. The thing is - the points you get for completing a mission depend on the difficulty level, so for anyone trying to compete for a place on the leaderboards and for some of the achievements, playing on a high difficulty level is a key.
As far as graphics, music and sound effects are concerned, Pacific Skies doesn't offer much beyond the original Ace Patrol. There's nothing fancy or extraordinary regarding those aspects of the game. The gameplay, however, is a lot of fun. I recommend this game to anyone who's into airplanes and strategy.

My first instinct is to put a NO on recommending this game. That's because it's so often infuriating.
The racing here is all about physics and destruction. You can crash into the scenery and your fellow racers, resulting in detailed and wild destruction.
This is what makes the game both fun and frustrating. More often than not, finishing in first place is a matter of blind luck, thanks to all the scattered debris all over the tracks. I mean ALL over everywhere. The slightest bump will send you careening off into the side of the track. Same if you get bumped by a fellow racer.
That's basically my only gripe with the game. Otherwise it's tons of fun. The damage model on the cars and environment is pretty great (I know, I was just complaining about them!) The career mode is nice and simple, varied, with a great selection of tracks and game modes and cars.
Each car can also be upgraded in various ways. You could focus on speed and just go for the finish. You could focus on strength and make your car a high powered ram rod, disabling the competition.
There's also the stunt levels where the already-filmsy realism is flung out through the windshield, just like your driver will be, flying into bowling pins or a velcro wall for points. Very silly, very difficult (at least for me), very fun.

English:
I believe it is important to tell those interested in buying this game that, although it is a very good game, is not exactly a train simulator.
If you exchange the stations for water records, the tracks for pipes and the trains for water, the game operation would remain exactly the same (!), so, it´s a puzzle that uses the "skin" of trains . In the end, you don´t do nothing but have to come up with a way to take the trains (replaceable by any other object) from point "A" to "B" point.
The criticism is because I bought the game having in mind something like the old Railroad Tycoon II, and there is absolutely nothing of his features here.
There is no management of the trains. You indicates your ways and just take care of the break.
The connection of the tracks is simple, limiting creativity in creating lines (intersections) more complex.
There is no freedom to choose which trains to use, which loads carry loads, which station is more important to get that load, and so on .... it is a puzzle where you connect points. A very good and even challenging at times, but a puzzle. Not a simulator.
Likes puzzles, go ahead.
Expect something more than a puzzle ... better pass or run the risk in a very good sale.

PROS:
Progression
-I appreciate the progression in this game, it's not something where you get to end-game gear in one day. I still haven't got to the end-game yet, in fact, I barely even started. According to my character, I have learned less than 10% of everything you can learn in the game.
Progression Part 2
-This may seem grindy, but Edge of Space made this slow progression curve actually fun. They broke up the progression in a way where there's branches you pick, like armor crafting, weapon crafting, base construction and even pet creation, and there's 15 tiers of progression in each branch, each successing tier costing more knowledge points. Everything gives you knowledge points to spend to progress further, and the deeper you dig into the planet, the more points you earn.
NPC's and Crafting Stations
-There's NPC's that hand out quests, which keep you busy, some requiring harder to achieve materials than others. And on top of these NPC's, there's a large amount of crafting stations, requiring you to have some kind of base. There's also command centers, which provide power to nearby devices which require power. It's a neat system I don't see in too many games.
CONS:
(Let's be honest here, no game is perfect. So, let's get to the chase, and say the things I've noticed and dislike about this game. Also, keep in mind that everything I have said is my opinion)
Textures
-Quite a few items in the game share the same texture, like Soft Chitin and Penguin Explosives. These 2 items are very different, but they look exactly the same, and it's a little annoying. This is one example of items sharing the same texture, and there are a few more instances.
Multiplayer
-Multiplayer is a bit janky. When me and my friend played on a server I hosted, we noticed you can have only 1 of each Quest NPC in the world, and command centers (They provide power), cannot be placed anywhere near each other. So, what I'm saying is you and your friend have to share a base, or your friend has to live far away, and one of you has to walk all the way to the other player's base to talk to the NPC's. Also, the quests are independent, but at least the dungeons you can go to are publicly accesible which slighly makes up for this. But all in all, I was far ahead of my friend, and had all the quest NPC's, which ruined his experience a little bit, because we were independently progressing.
All in all, this game has more pros than cons in my opinion, and makes for a great game. If you don't feel comfortable paying $14.99, then wait for a sale. I got this game for only $4.99 around Christmas, and trust me, if you think this game isn't worth $15, then it most certainly is worth $5, because this game has potential for hours of enjoyment!

So, The Beginner's Guide... It's an interesting short story with slight interactivity... But for me, I just don't think it clicked. I can get that this game isn't for everyone, I can get that this game is more about telling a story about its developer more than anything else, and I get that it has a few decent messages that mainly boil down to things like: not being too hard on yourself, not overworking yourself, and not relying on validation from others to survive. But even if I was in almost identical shoes to the developer himself, I would still have some issues with this story/game.
Firstly, the whole fiction with Coda being friends with Davey, the developer of the game. It is kind of flimsy, and that make it kind of hard to really believe that the story was "true." Maybe that was kind of intentional, I don't know. The story isn't very long in of itself, with the game lasting 1 hour and a half if you speed through it, to maybe a little over 2 if you stop and smell the roses. You don't get a whole lot of time to really soak in either of the characters, and for me, I felt very detached from both (Especially since *Somewhat spoilers* the narrator (The developer) just trails off and leaves you to wander through some more corridors for the end of the game). It was probably suppsed to be a moment of revelation and introspection for the narrator, but I didn't have any weight in any of it, I just got to look at some decent scenery.
In The Stanley Parable, even people who don't usually enjoy non-action/non-puzzle/non-real-goal games can enjoy it. The Stanley Parable gives a multitude of options, choices, and paths to take, many of which lead to different endings to the story, making the game interesting, enjoyable, and replayable. The Beginner's Guide on the other hand, is almost entirely a string of hallways/corridors with occasional minor instances    of being able to enjoy something other than the narrators monologuing. There were only a very small handfull of times where doing something other than walking the straight path would give you unique dialogue from the narrator, though none of these choices end up changing anything and you must continue forward. Is this game simply supposed to be less, er, overall entertaining? Is it supposed to be a shallow and ultimately almost pointless little short story through a fictional scenario of events that allude to what was going on in the developers life? Maybe, and it's fine to make what you want and sell it, I just don't know if I feel that this is really even worth putting up there next to Stanley Parable, and every other game for sale on Steam.
Think about it. Steam is the platform where every average gamer goes to buy their Call of Duties and Grand Theft Auto's. This games story is very limited, not to mention it can be very hard to relate to if you aren't somebody who has developed multiple games already and who struggles with anxiety and depression. I struggle with anxiety and depression. I aspire to be a game developer, with a couple of small simple Game Maker projects under my belt, with a multitude of prototype projects sitting in a folder half finished. In the end, I almost felt no connection to the story at all. Maybe this was because I don't wish to focus on art games, whereas this developer obviously wants to. I want to focus on goal oriented games, action, puzzle, maybe even story. But the story presented here had very little weight on me, maybe this is just because of my preference in games. Don't get me wrong, I loved The Stanley Parable, and i don't need every game to be loud action, or clever puzzles. It's just that this game hit so very light in almost every aspect that I personally can not reccomend it.
To recap: I believe there was one puzzle, and once you figure it out that's it. There are no branching paths, not every game needs some, but this game lacks in almost everything. The few chances for dialogue at most only occasionally give you some different flavor text, they all lead to the same goal. It is 1.5 to 2 hours long in total. It has a very specific type of story, that I imagine plenty of people may not be able to relate to.
It's fine to charge money for games obviously. The Stanley Parable is definitely worth at least $10. But is this game worth it's asking price? (The fiction in this game even leads to more questions of why this would be a payed product in the first place, and doesn't resolve any of them) The original Stanley Parable was a free mod for Half Life 2. This is only 1.5 times bigger than that really (Just a use of rhetoric, not an actual measure). I would want to say that the game is good in helping the player realise and deal with any depression/anxiety/social issues, but in my opinion it is not. It strings you along and for a while, and almost keeps a steady ember, but by the end (Which comes quickly) the story just fades out and leaves the player with nothing but a few simple ideas to think over. Ideas that somebody can find in many other things in many various ways besides a short, pretentious, meandering short story adventure.
In my opinion, a story like this could have been done better. How? I'm not 100% sure. If this was in the form of a movie, I would still have felt the same. You can say that maybe this game was just for him (The dev.) but then why is it a purchaseable product on Steam? You can say that all my qualms with the game were *meant* to be there, that they all meant something that I just completely missed, and maybe they did.
If I make a game that I sell on Steam, and all that is in this game is an hours worth of painting a brick wall in a set pattern with no depth, no complexity, no choice, no options, just a pre-planned path that you can paint this wall on... Would it be unfair for some people to end up disliking the game? Especially if before this limited wall-painting game, I developed and sold a game where you not only painted brick walls, but you broke out of the bounds of wall painting, you forged your own path with the paintbrush, and you explored many walls with many types of paint. Would it not be jarring to make a transtition like this? Or would it all be fine because I, the developer, was going through some issues so I decided to sell a dull, shallow wall painting game on Steam instead of one-upping (Or at least equalling) my previous venture?
If you greatly enjoyed it, that is good. If it helped you realise some issues, maybe even help towards fixing them, even better. But for *me*, this game did not do these things. It held my hand through a lightly decorated hallway, tried to tell me a story, drifted off about halfway through and then let go and ran off while I continued towards the exit. Perhaps I just am not the typical case when it comes to similar anxieties and depressions.

A 'hidden object' game blended with minor lateral thinking puzzles, Morphopolis is best summarised as a scavenger hunt within a living painting of the micro-scale insect world.  The interface is minimalistic--there is no options menu of which to speak and only a couple of pointing fingers at the very beginning will provide hints to start you on your way.  Perhaps in an effort to compel the player to savour the environment and explore it, objectives are kept vague and unintuitive, often discovered simply by frantically clicking all over the place until some unremarkable object triggers another collection quest.  It is not a failure--this hands-off approach of function and clear paths of progression does accomplish the task of encouraging exploration, but the developer was a little too loose with it.
Despite these minor flaws, the music and art style are soothing and most of the puzzles, once discovered are simple enough to lend to that same tranquil atmosphere, and each challenge is varied enough to be equally as challenging as rewarding to complete.
If you enjoy hidden object games, you may enjoy Morphopolis as a quick snack, but you'll quickly complete it and find yourself searching for more filling meals afterward.  Morphopolis is right for the price, given that it provides two or three hours of gameplay, and may be plucked for less than a dollar during most Steam sales, so I do recommend it if environmental and casual puzzles or scavenger hunts interest you.

This game is the FPS for the WWII history buff.  While any videogame is always going to be  a pale shadow of the horros and stress of battle, RO2/RS gets a lot of things right and because of this, it feels less like a game and more like a serious look at WWII infantry combat.
The graphics aren't groundbreaking, but they are atmospheric and just work well for the subject matter.  The sounds of weapons and explosions are well done, and the voice acting is good.  The maps are well done and provide good opportunities to different avenues of approach and defense.
The attention to detail on the weapons is outstanding.   Machinegun barrels overheat, magazines hold the right number of rounds, and bullet drop  and variable damage are modelled, if not authentically, then with enough detail to make them feel authentic.   One minute you're impressed with the firepower of your M1 Carbine, the next you'll be cursing at how little damage it delivers compared to a Garand or BAR.
The gameplay rewards the application of basic tactical knowledge and the team that works together best will prevail.  This game demands some thought as well as quick reactions, each team member has to make a contribution in order to prevail.  You can play as a lone wolf, but the game shines when a group performs as a team.
The downside?  If you are expecting the same run and gun tactics that make you a hero in other shooters to carry the day here, you might be dissapointed.  The learning curve isn't steep, but it's unforgiving for the new player who is likey going to be a fish out of water until he learns to work with his team.  There's some nice user provided maps that see little online use.  Some features that require teamwork, like the Japanese banzai charge, see little use because it's just damn hard to coordinate, even with, or because of, voice chat.  Yeah, there's jerks online, but there's some great gamers out there, too.  The single player component is an afterthought.
With all those negatives considered, the historical attention to detail coupled with tactical, team based gameplay make RO2/RS a must have for those with an interest in the subject matter.

Turn-based lite strategy game about WW2 fighter planes. The premise is really interesting and I think the game mechanics are nicely executed. The planes each have a different feel, and the game does a good job of modeling "energy fighting" (e.g. trading altitude for speed and vice versa) and roll/turn rates (a P40 will roll left/right within a hex; a Zero doesn't roll so good but can sustain a turn to 120 degrees, etc.)
Beyond that... it's a good thing this game is just $5 because it is woefully under-polished, especially for a Sid Meier title. The missions are very repetitive (180 are claimed, but they're really a variation on four or five missions with different enemy planes in them), the animations are clunky, and there are endless small boneheaded things that will annoy you.
It's very good for a tablet game, but I can't give it my full recommendation.

Sid Meier's Ace Patrol: Pacific Skies is the sequel to Sid Meier's Ace Patrol. This is not a carbon copy, however, and more was done than simply swapping models and textures.
So what's different? Primarily the setting, although quite a few game mechanics have been changed.
As the name suggests, the game takes place in the pacific theatre of war. The only nations involved are the Empire of Japan and the United States of America. Unfortunately, this reduces the overall choice the player has, since they basically get the option of choosing Army or Navy for either nation. At least each branch has their own planes, so you'll only see a F6F Hellcat when playing the US Navy or a P38 Lightning when playing the US Army.
I have to admit, it's somewhat disappointing the only two options are the USA and Japan. Granted, that's to be expected given the location the game takes place in, but I enjoyed having four different nations to play in Ace Patrol. I can understand the decision to take this route, as the war in Europe would've looked even more like a rehash of Ace Patrol. Even so, the multi-national feel of the first game held more appeal for me.
Like the first Ace Patrol, you have four pilots. They can earn promotions, gain abilities, get callsigns (which give them a unique trait, such as becoming immune to anti-aircraft fire), become injured or captured by the enemy. There's also two new options available: you can make all pilots male or have both male and female (like the first Ace Patrol), and you can allow pilots to die.
Unlike the first Ace Patrol, abilities are no longer tied to the pilot himself. Instead, these abilities are installed on the aircraft. That means each new aircraft you get has no upgrades, even if the plane itself is better in numerous categories. Fortunately, you can switch back and forth between all planes, so if you liked an older plane more than the newest one, you can fly that.
One reason the ability to switch between planes is important because, unlike the first Ace Patrol, aircraft damage isn't repaired after every mission. Instead, damage persists until the campaign is over (admittedly, campaigns are only four missions each, so they don't take much time to complete) and then your plane is fully repaired.
The only exception is the "Grease Monkey" callsign, which lets that pilot repair their plane in small increments after each mission. Callsigns are presented after shooting down seven enemy planes; however, which four callsigns you have to choose from (for each pilot) is selected at random, so you might not see "Grease Monkey" appear or all four pilots could be offered it.
Another change is that you no longer get to select which mission you fly. In the first Ace Patrol, you could choose between three missions (sometimes only one was available, but in those missions the entire squadron flew), but in Pacific Skies, the mission is given to you. As each campaign consists of four missions, you could easily end up flying the same type of mission four times in a row.
The game's graphics are no better (but no worse) than Ace Patrol, except for one area: the pilots themselves. This may be a personal preference, but I preferred the way the pilots look in Ace Patrol. In Pacific Skies, they look like deformed bobble-head dolls. Even more confusing is when pilots gain rank, their emblems or pins don't change, they just gain extra pieces of flight gear. Gain a rank and you'll get goggles, for instance. Sometimes medals don't even show up, despite the fact you were told that pilot was awarded one as well.
Would I recommend Pacific Skies? Only if you really liked Ace Patrol and you've got a strong interest in World War II, particularly the pacific theatre. I don't think Pacific Skies is as "fun" as the original Ace Patrol, but I've always had a stronger interest in World War I than World War II, so perhaps that's my own personal bias getting in the way.

It's more of a "meh". Not bad enough to mark it as "Not recommended", but also far from impressive, and worse of all, quite far from being completely worthy of having "Sid Meier" in its title. When I think of "Sid Meier" games, I think of intricate, comprehensive games that come with challenging learning curves and huge levels of complexity. Ace Patrol: Pacific Skies is far from that: it's small and rather simplistic.
The graphics are really messy at points. Don't expect it to look good. The plane models are the only graphic part I enjoyed.
It can get quite complex, challenging and captivating if you play it on higher difficulty levels. Anyway, the complexity is not given by the number of plane models, skills or upgrades, but mostly by the number of movement possibilities. This can also make it get boring after a while.
Still, you can have a lot of fun with it, especially if you like playing the more-chilled turn-based strategy games or if you're into history or fighter planes. It's a Sid Meier title after all, so it's worth having, especially if you can get it on a discount.

Train Valley has a simple premise. Bring Trains from one Station to another. But what the game makes out of this relatively simple premise is astonish.
Why? Let me explain!
It all starts slow. Two Stations. One Train. The Interface is very intuitive and you will understand every function in absolutely no time. Of course the first mission is also a tutorial, so you will have no problem to get into the game mechanics.
The game offers four chapters with six missions each. Also every mission has 3 “Expert goals” you can try to fulfill. These will change the way you play the mission, what is a motivation to play it again and reach them. But the final goal in every mission is the same. Get every Train that will spawn to their desired station without going bankrupt.
Bankrupt? Yes! Every train as a certain value assigned. As longer as the train needs to reach its destination it loses value over time till it is at $0.
After the first two missions the difficult raises pretty quickly, but the Missions are never getting unfair. You will have the motivation to try it again and never have the feeling that you lost because the mission design was unfair.
I had no crash in my whole play time or any stutters. The game ran smooth at any given moment.
-Motivating Gameplay
-Good tutorials
-It’s very easy to get into the game
-Motivating extra goals in each mission
-Two game modes. Classic and Freeplay
-Difficult raises pretty fast
-The final mission goal is always the same
I found this game only because Steam suggested it to me, and I am really glad about it. Train Valley really took me by surprise. At any time I was motivated to beat the actuall mission and reach as many bonus goals as I could. And when I failed I could see why I did. The price it okay for what you get. Even if you just play through it without playing for the Expert Goals you will need some hours till you beat the final mission.
Even if you never played such a game, like I did, I can still recommend this to you if the screenshots and the trailer appeal to you.
