I don't normally review games, but Project Zomboid is an exceptional game. Even in it's early stages, the amount of things do to  in order to survive is incredible. It pay attention to things most games miss like the power or water cutting off. The Dev's are very vocal on the forums and are quick to respond to bugs etc. They are friendly and easy to approach if you have an idea or question. The multiplayer, even at this stage is incredibly fun as a group of you work together to try and salvage tins of food and make a stand in the bleak apocalypse. Get this game and get your friends to get it too.
EDIT
Since my last review this game has come along leaps and bounds. The aiming system has had an overhaul, making the shooting on the game more sensible and feeling right for the kind of game it is. The stamina system has been implemented so you can no longer run cross map without even breaking a sweat. Now you have to decided whether you have the energy to take those 10 zombies blocking your way, or try to get past them. The medical system has been implemented, meaning even climbing through a broken window could leave you injured. The variety of injuries and appropriate treatments has added an extra depth to the game, which is always welcome. Falling from heights now causes fractures, limiting movement speed until a splint is on the wound and a few days of rest have passed. (Hope you have a lot of skill books to pass the time!)
The erosion feature means that after a certain time has passed, the world will change. Roots and weeds will sprout through the highway, football fields will start to grow small trees, and the buildings you loot will become cracked and weatherworn. Combine this with an ever expanding map, new skills for survival such as Trapping, Foraging and a way to preserve certain foods, and the much anticipated NPC's (no ETA's!)
In short, this game remains one of the best I have played in a very long time, and i have spent many many more hours than my steam profile shows. Whenever the chance arises, i buy a copy of this game for my friends and they get immediately sucked into the game. Buy a copy, or buy a 4 pack, dish a few out to your friends, and try to start a colony in the apocalypse that is Project Zomboid.
EDIT 2 - As much as I love this game, I cannot recommend anyone to buy it. While the devs have spoke about NPC's in the past, and claimed that the engine could not handle vehicles, it seems players are able to get the content out quicker. There is a great Survivor Mod out there, and now the devs are working on vehicles, as that was added as a mod too. There is a lot of work going on in the background, or so we are told each week on the mondoid update. But even that seems to be the same "(x) has been touching up parts of (y), while (z) is working on something in the background."
To clarify, I really enjoy the game, I have bought it for myself and friends in the past. Im hoping when animations finally make it through the gate, it will bring more players in, and the same with NPC's. Then maybe the game can get a much needed combat overhaul. If you go on most servers, the chat is filled with people trying to be edgy or badass about how they killed someone. The ranged combat in this game is terrible. But in its current state, as much as I enjoy the game, I wouldnt recommend anyone to purchase it. If you already own the game, but havent played for a long while, pick it back up and see what's changed. But if you were thinking of buying it, hold off for now.

You'd expect to find this game in a Natural History museum, attracting kids like they were flies to its sticky touchscreen.
The parents are happy that they have a free moment to themselves as their children get absorbed in educational software.
The kids know that they're not going to learn anything. They get frustrated with the terrible touchscreen controls but they keep playing because there is nothing better to do in the museum.
You might have seen the "point and click" tag, but Morphopolis is actually a hidden object game. You are an insect and you wander around 2D backdrops looking for specific objects to unlock the next search.
These can be either plants, eggs or - quite interestingly - dismembered insect parts.
The BGM, which can be described as ambient-easy-listening, might feel relaxing to some although it felt a bit dull to me, not to mention that the game has some annoying jingles everytime you complete a riddle (just like the sound jingle from the edusoft at the museum!).
The art style is beautiful, some luxuriously detailed 2D backdrops of nature, vegetation, and insects. The problem is you have to wander back and forth between those screens repeatedly each level...and because you are slow it gets tedious.
The game also throws 1 or 2 random one-screen puzzles each level. Those range from okay to very boring.
So far it's pretty much a mixed bag, but this is where the recommendation stops.
This is a lazy mobile port. Terribly lazy. The control scheme is just criminal. It's beyond awful.
You might have noticed the "point and click" tag but Morphopolis is actually a "point and drag" or should i say a "drag and drag".
The only way to move your insect is to drag the mouse across the screen. Constantly. You don't just click where you want it to go, you don't use WASD, you just drag, and drag and draaaaaaag. Each 15 minute level is 14 minutes of your finger solidly pressed against the left mouse button.
Did I mention the insect moves at 2 kilometers per millenium? Or that the pathing is pretty fiddly?
Not only can you instantly feel that the game is made for a touchscreen,
For one of the puzzles, I had to resort to google - not to find a solution, but just to figure out how the damn controls work!
I cannot recommend this game, for its carpal tunnel syndrome inducing control scheme. Save it for the kids at the museum, and go find your insect murder mystery fun some place else.

Half-Life: Blue Shift feels like a bit of a disappointment after the amazing job Gearbox did with Opposing Force, however it is still a fun game and well worth playing if you like the Half-Life games.
The main problem with Blue Shift is its length. It only takes about 3 hours to complete which is disappointing considering how Opposing Force was around 8 hours long. It also isn't as unique or original as Opposing Force was.
However despite its flaws the experience is still a fun one. Seeing how Barney Calhoun escaped Black Mesa is interesting if you have played Half-Life 2. Gordon Freeman can be spotted throughout the game which ties it quite nicely with the original. There are some really great puzzle sections as well which really require you to think. The gameplay is very good just like in the other Half-Life games.
Overall, a great game let down mainly by its short length. Worth playing if you are a fan of the franchise.

I've played the 'Big Alpha' with a friend, and I've also seen some reviews before writting mine. I have to say that I really liked tha game and I'm planning on buying it, however since it's only an alpha you can get a taste of the basic general experience, but (I hope I'm right when I say this) that's not all the content the game will have:
1 - On the opening cutscene you get at the beginning of every level (as a hunter) the hunters' lockers appear with their names on them, and some of the names are blurred which maybe could mean more classes for hunter in the future. And I imagine there will be more monsters as well, even with the kraken being OP as it is, it was fun to diversify the experience.
2 - The gameplay may be quite repetitive due to lack of content (keeping in mind it's an alpha and it's not supposed to have all the content right away), but it sure isn't always the same, because the matches are played against a player controlled monster every player will have their abilities and strategies to survive, evolve and kill the hunters.
3 - I would assume that new maps will be available later on, maybe a kind of rainforest planet to make things more colourful and have lots of places to hide as a monsters, or to place/hide traps as a hunter. However the maps available on the alpha where very nice and somewhat diverse to me, I often found myself wanting to play on a map that had a swap area different from the rocky hills I was in, just to find out it was the same map. Yes, I thought the maps would be bigger, but again, after playing on them for a while I still think they are quite big, at least big enough to allow the match to be a good length in my opinion (around 15 - 20 minutes).
4 - I said that I played the alpha with a friend, and it was pretty fun to do it, in a few matches we played around with the different classes (and the monster when we weren't in a party) and found the one(s) we liked the most, with their weak and strong points as well as their skills unique for each class. I have to say I was quite disapointed when I wasn't able to play a match as a monster because I was in a party (I understand that people could exploit this to level up quickly), but I think there should be at least a custom match that didn't give any EXP or rewards just so I could play with, let's say, four friends playing as a hunter while I'm a monster taunting or theathening (as a joke obviously) them in voice chat.
5 - The game is $60 right now, and I would not pay that for the game I played, which just to remind everyone was only an alpha, but it's the standard launch price for retail games, and I expect that by the launch date, the game will have more features (and honestly, a better menu interface). As I said before I didn't buy the game just yet, but I'm planning on buying it, however I will also wait for more content reveals or sneak-peaks to be sure before buying it.
That was a pretty extensive review compared to the ones a usually make, but I thought that I had to say that, and I hope I didn't forget anything important.

Purchased this on a whim in the Christmas sale. I like turn based hex games, I like the history of the Pacific Air War. Sounded like it might be worth a look and it certainly was. Basically a boardgame where the computer controls your opponent and handles all the dice rolls for you - if that is your thing, this is an enjoyable board game for you. You can upgrade your aircraft and pilots if you are succesful in battle. The game consists of many small rounds, so this is also a great game for when you have just a few minutes to spare - do a mission and save the next for later. Multiple skill levels allow you to have relatively easy to quite tricky missions to achieve. I've spent far more time playing this than I ever expected to!

Really interesting game, specially the DLC.
I played it 2 years ago: i binged the whole game in one night, and i was blown away. Today i decided to give it another go. I didn´t have the same amount of joy, but it still felt like a solid experience.
It plays a lot with surprise, tension, and putting you in situations where you feel in hazard, so that the first run is amazing, but once you know what is going to happen/where is the exit that tension is gone. Every game could fall into this problem, but this one specially because there is a lot of scripted events.
Really good visuals, music and controls. Be aware that this is not an action title, so you have to hide and run through the game, while finding keys/switches to keep moving forward in the story.
Horror-wise, the game is really creepy, and uses jump scares mixed with bait environments, and a linear sequence of events, so that you can roam around a place, but not get lost or backtrack to places you have already visited.
The 'thing' about this game that stood out of other titles is that you are carrying a videocamera, that you have to use in some segments where there is no light, using the night vision mode, in the style of the last segment of the horror movie [Rec].
I ENCOURAGE you to play the DLC of this game, because, in my opinion, packs a better story and enemies than the main campaign. There are 'bosses' in the game, as in unique characters that are hunting you along the way, and in this regard, the DLC IS SUPERB.
The game got a bad rep thanks to the amount of Letsplayers that exploited the title for it's shock factor on youtube. It is a lot more than a jumpscare or a walking simulator title, and one if not the best horror game in years. I know it cannot compete with classics of the genre, but it is a SOLID title, specially the DLC. It should be included by default, and arranged as a two path adventure.

Quick Review:
Edge of space is quite a relaxing game. It obviously lacks of fun and ecxiting things to do but it has its simple charm of just simplistic things to do, I'm sure you'll have a good time if you don't compare to terraria and starbound. (unless you hate these 2D kind of games... why would you even consider buying this if thats the case....)
Long Review:
Lets start with describing what its missing and what needs to change. CONS:
First of all, as everyone would say about this game, is that its various inventory and crafting "pop ups" are complete rubbish. They need to change all of these because has it is for now, you have to press around 7 different keys to open 7 different things that literaly take up ALL you screen. And btw it also doesn't pause the game so you'll be sure to be killed if you don't pay attention. So all this inventory bussiness needs to be sorted out.
You'll also have a hard time getting used to this weird new crafting mechanic they use. Even though it isn't the worst, it sure is quite different... I personally don't mind it because it forces you to go out of your base and mine and kill stuff for experience. You then spend this experience on different types of weapons or armor. Tbh the armor and weapons they have at the moment are quite boring. There is nothing special about them so you'll end up just picking what does more damage and what benifits you the most. They will need to make each weapon type more special and more ecxiting.
Finally the envirnment is also quite dull. A lot of what this game lacks of is just fun and cool stuff to do, to craft and to explore. There are some locations to fight and conquer, but there's nothing "special" about them...
So now that we've discussed the cons here are some of the PRONS:
This game has this ability to really start you offvery easily with barely any enemies to attack you at the beggining but has you go further down, the enemies only get stronger and thougher with chaging backgrounds as well. Not many games allow you to start off like this like this game does, and it really helps just to work out what you are supposed to be doing (cause thats quite hard at the begining).
For the reason above, this means that this is quite a relaxing game. It has a wonderfull soundtrack to it which really had an impact on me the first time. I really managed to fully relax and enjoy the game with this wonderfull soundtrack.
I also think the mining in this game is great. You are able to last as long as you want (usually) just peacefully minning away without some great powerful monster sneaking up on you. (lol I'm getting tired of writting so I'm ending here)
I think that since this game is now out of early access, it isn't getting as many updates anymore so I wouldn't get it if you will be expecting more of this game for the future (although I could be wrong). I would say to buy this if you are looking for something out of the oridnary and isn't trying to follow the same foot steps that terraria has left so give it a try (when it isn't as expensive as it is wight now because it definitely isn't worth that much money, basically get it on a sale if you are bored, k bye im done here...)

Placing a piece of track is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ thus making the higher speeds near impossible to play on. However, if you can get past the finicky track placement then you're in for something real, darn good.
Train Valley is essentially a management simulator. You're placing tracks, trying to get "blue train" from point "A" to point "B"; all while trying to complete other, level specific objectives (which are OPTIONAL). If you do manage to complete the level specific objectives, then you'll gain 3 stars. Yes, it's one of those games... This is actually one of the games' biggest advantages though, at least it is for me. I like trying to get all the OPTIONAL stars. I like trying to perfect each level to the best of my ability. So all in all, I think this is a great management sim. It's also very accesible/casual, so that's nice to people who are new to this type of game (like me).
So yeah, if any of that sounds interesting to you then you'll most likely enjoy this game. Just be warned that the track placement is not good, but it's not enough to break the game.

The game is great. This game has a lot of tracks to race on, and a lot of fun obstacles to fight through with your opponents!
It's not only racing, there are also special games modes, for example, you have to jump out of a fast moving car and try to go the highest. This makes the game more fun.
The physics in the game are OK, it feels realistic to drive the cars, and ramming your opponents look awesome! But, be careful when driving fast, because even the tiniest objects, like sticks and rocks, can just bring your car to a wheelie and then crash, allowing your opponents to pass you.
There are a variety of cars to choose from, within 3 categories; derby, race and street. The cars are upgradable which is cool, but you cannot customize your car.
The soundtrack for this game is epic! There are amazing tracks featuring Alkaline Trio and Yellow card etc. I think you'll enjoy the music, and old, classic racing game soundtracks sound great.
You might not like this game if you just want to race, because in this game, you will need to crash other cars as well, to get nitrous.
I really enjoy this game! And it's at a cheap price, so even better! This game is so recommended for fans of Burnout, like myself, and other car-crash and other action games.

The Long Dark is easily the best indie survival game I've ever played. Hinterland Studios has made an amazing game, both in reference to the artistic masterpiece which it is and the groundbreaking gameplay. It's nice to visit an apocalypse in which the threat isn't the supernatural or the future tide of war, but rather the thing which has challenged human kind from the start and far before: Mother Nature, in all her wretched glory.
The use of the simple color palette of the dark wilderness to create beatiful landscapes and drab - but still beautiful and colorful - human creations is complemented only by the immesurable unique artistic stylization, appearing as though every single thing were painted to life by the unprepared. You. You are unprepared.
The game sends you directly into a random location whenever you begin anew, leaving you with only your memory to guide you among the snow and ice.
Food is scarce, and weapons even more so. Only by exploring the dead human ruins of Canada will you live to see tomorrow.
You must keep vigilant of your own condition and your surroundings. Water is near at all times, trapped in the cold snow. Food can be found in human-created cans or within the animals. The cold can be fended off by the means of fire, clothes, the buildings of humans, or a hole in the ground. Sleep can be found anywhere at anytime.
Though, if done with nature, you may find that you will fade into...
The Long Dark.

Just finished my second playthrough and O lord did it end dramatically.
So on my first playthrough, I spawned in the trapper cabin WITH the rifle. I got super lucky. Bad thing is, I was still a complete and total noob, so I died within a few days.
Second playthrough lasted 20 days. I was stacked. I had traveled across all of the major areas, trekked tons of kilometers, and finally made a home for myself in the trapper cabin. Had a bow, and was curing saplings to make a few more arrows. Things were good.
One thing though: I was running out of food, and I had no usable arrows to go hunt. I made tons of mistakes along the road, of course. Didn't gather food when I could have. Basically ignored the urgency of my situation. But one of my major goals in the last expedition I had was to find the rifle.
So I knew it wasn't in the cabin where I settled down, so I went to the hydro dam to go see if it was there. After having a couple of encounters with the wolf and getting lost in the ice canyons below, I finally made my way out of the front entrance of the dam again. Was making my way home when-- oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have no food.
I made my way to the big cabin by the lake, not remembering if I had left food there last time I searched it. Nope.
Went to a lakeside cabin, beginning to starve. No luck there.
Searched 3 of the fishing spots, no food there either. Tried fishing for a bit, had no luck and was severely hungry. Almost dead.
In my last moments, as I stumbled across the ice in a blizzard, looking for a shelter or at least a tiny morself of food, I find a cabin. And a body. AND A RIFLE. And a candy bar.
Ate the candy bar. Food is okay now, but I'm about to die of exhaustion. Stumble inside after 6 tries, being blown back by the intense blizzard. Go to sleep. Wake up, starving again. Can't see anything because of my condition.
I decided to go out peacefully, sleeping. Although it wasn't peaceful, as my rage about finding the rifle before death was still all-consuming.
Never have I experienced more tension and excitement and rage at a game, and still loved it afterwards.
10/10 would find rifle before tragic death again.
TL;DR: Buy the game. It's worth it.

I bought The Long Dark on one of Steam's sales a little while back having never heard of the game.  The concept sounded interesting, and from the reviews others had posted, all the elements appeared to mesh well together.  Going in with no expectations other than some very, very postiive reviews I sat back and welcomed the wild ride that is The Long Dark.
The game is really what you decide to make out of it.  Do you want to survive by methodically raiding each house in a little abandonded town and leaving only  when you've run out of food?  Or do you want to risk several cold nights with only your fragile fire and sleeping bag in order to explore the wide open beautifully harsh landscape?  You can choose to kill wildlife, but with that choice comes the cost of ammunition and other needed supplies for survival.
Every choice you make feels your own and can have severe cosqeunces.  Wandering out at night in a blizzard across a frozen lake with only my lantern and a can of beans was not the best choice.  However my biggest mistake was picking a fight with a bear.  You learn from these mistakes and you learn the general location of key points of interest, but the world is always changing, will you change to adapt?
I will continue to invest many hours in the sandbox mode, but eagerly await the release of the full game featuring an episodic story mode.  Good luck, and happy survival.

Project Zomboid is pretty much your typical zombie survival game.
First of all, any fans of being a Bandit in Dayz. This game is not for you.
Now that's out of the way Project Zombiod is a 2D zombie survival game. Its simple you wake up in a house in a large town split into two districts. You search around the houses cupboards, draws and even the fridge for supply's. Now you go to the window and see that their are many other house's around you probabaly containing even more loot. You open your front door and look out and see no sigh of trouble. You walk over to the house and find that the front door is locked. You walk around the side and open the window. You enter the house and start to look around. You manage to find yourself a new crowbar to use as a weapon. You also use a plastic bag to help you hold more food. You walk up the stairs and see a Zombie jump out at you. You beat it to death but notice that your character is now worried and frightened. You walk back to your house but as you open the front door a zombie sneaks up from behind and attacks you. You spin around, pull out your crowbar and beat it to death.
You walk inside than treat yourself to a nice cold TV Dinner. 15 minutes later you get sick and die. Because you didnt cook the food.
That was my first 20 Minutes in project zomboid and it made an impression. Sure its a simple survival zombie game but its felt real. The scaverging is where the games best moments are. Breaking into houses and carfully moving from room to room, collecting bed sheets to put on the windows as curtains back home so Zombies arn't attracted to the light.
The game plays like any basic 2D game. Just move and click. You have two menus which display your inventory and whats around you. It is very basic in that way. But its how your character is and feels that works well. If you get attacked by a zombie your player will become panicked and won't be as accurate with his hits. Or if your at your base waiting around or reading about new skills your chacter will become bored which can lead to the charcter being un-happy. The weapons are basic. You just swing your bat in the direction and the target and it will hit it. Or if you have a gun its pre much auto-lock. No skill is required you just look,shoot and you hit your target. Their are no cars in the game so your always walking which can become repative and boring. The game is fair from realistc but feels real in a way that you always find stuff in places where you would expect stuff to be. Unlike in Dayz where you find stuff lying on the floor. Here you look in draws,shelfs and fridges to find loot. I love entering new houses or areas not knowing what is going to be there.
The game isn't extremly easy. If you find yourself in a horde of zombies, to put it nicely. You're ♥♥♥♥ed. Zombies are a threat even though they can be taken down by one shot at times with a gun, zombies will hear this shot and close in on you. Once me and my friend were trying to loot a bank, we ran into the parking lot to find a horde of zombies waiting for us. We panicked smashed the window and jumped inside. I lost sight of my friend as 4 zombies that were already in the building closed in on me. I freaked out, pulled out my pistol and shot all 4. Worst decison of my life. Now zombies were flodding in, smashing windows  and breaking down the door's. As I had now discoverd my friend had left me for dead. I ran upstairs and tried to find a new way out and had no luck. As I tried to open a window to see if I could climb out. Zombies snuck up behind me and started attacking me. Already injuired I was dead in seconds. The game isn't easy seeing that zombies are easily attracted to noise and you can only see a small distance where your chacter is facing. The game can be hard on your own. But play it right or with friends and you will grasp it.
Now eventually you will find yourself sellting down and buliding a base. Base building consits of two things, Physical Bulding and Farming. You can build walls to fortify your house and make a large farming area that you have to fertilise and water. It's basic but it works. Farming is also a great idea because eventually all water and power supply stops. So you cant keep your food in the fridge or drink water from the tap.
Once you have a base I can find the game can begin to get repatative and boring. Eventually I found myself repeating the same thing. Going out and scaving as much as I can than bring it home. With the occasional farm. That is where the game really lacks. It get's boring. Their's no big multipalyer too. Sure you can join  populated severs but its just a cluster-♥♥♥♥. In the single player theirs no AI, no objectives, no events or anything like that. I wish their was the occasional moment when you run into a gang of AI and have a all out war. Or find other bases to break into or raid. Or maybe make a town and have AI work in it. All this can be added and I wish it will. Im sure AI will be added at some point with other features because right now after a while the game gets boring. But that is a matter of hours in. You can always start a new life fresh on your own or with friends and do it all again.
The music in the game is great I have to say.
THE VERDICT:
Pros:
-Zombie AI works great
-Scavaging is fun
- Looks fresh and new
-Good fun with friends
-Feels real but not too real
-Base building
Cons:
-Not a whole lot to it
-Gets repeative after a while
-No AI makes the only threat zombies
-Big severs don't work
RATING: 8/10

Having played "Half-Life" and "Half-Life: Opposing Force," I was ready to complete the set and play "Half-Life: Blue Force." When I played it, It felt a bit lacking, but it still managed to have charm. It still maintains what made the other two games work, in terms of it's story and it's engagement.
You play as one of the "red shirts" (or as in this case, blue shirts), aka, a Security Guard, Barney Calhoun. He's one of the lowly security guards in the Black Mesa compound who, surprisingly, proves more badass than most of his own coworkers. Again, for the same reason I enjoyed playing as Gordon Freeman in HL and as Adrian Shepherd in HL:OF, Barney is a character that can get very immersive, owing to his silence. And you never lose control of him in the game, keeping you firmly in his POV.
Most of what I have to say about this game has already been said in my other reviews of HL and HL:OF, so I won't go into too much detail. I liked the continuous level design, giving the feel of exploration, and enough of a story that will keep you invested in the game. I also liked how this game used armor instead of a powered suit, making it easier to maintain by just findining more armor, preventing you from slowing down too much.
But therein lies the problem. Whereas "Opposing Force" had plenty of new stuff, this game feels lacking. You only get a few of the weapons from the first game, and this game is much shorter compared to the first game. I feel this game fell short of it's predecessor by not trying anything new to expand upon the story and setting. I am glad though that there isn't as much platforming as the original, like in HL:OF, which did the same. But the one thing that saved it for me was how they made you feel more involved in the plot, near the climax of the game. But overall, I feel this game could have been so much more.
While this expansion didn't have what "Opposing Force" has to offer, it still manages to work fine on it's own, and it's not terrible. It's enough to keep you invested, but it's kind of a letdown after a good game and a good expansion pack. But if I had to play it again, I'd play it again, soundly.

I've played the 'Big Alpha' with a friend, and I've also seen some reviews before writting mine. I have to say that I really liked tha game and I'm planning on buying it, however since it's only an alpha you can get a taste of the basic general experience, but (I hope I'm right when I say this) that's not all the content the game will have:
1 - On the opening cutscene you get at the beginning of every level (as a hunter) the hunters' lockers appear with their names on them, and some of the names are blurred which maybe could mean more classes for hunter in the future. And I imagine there will be more monsters as well, even with the kraken being OP as it is, it was fun to diversify the experience.
2 - The gameplay may be quite repetitive due to lack of content (keeping in mind it's an alpha and it's not supposed to have all the content right away), but it sure isn't always the same, because the matches are played against a player controlled monster every player will have their abilities and strategies to survive, evolve and kill the hunters.
3 - I would assume that new maps will be available later on, maybe a kind of rainforest planet to make things more colourful and have lots of places to hide as a monsters, or to place/hide traps as a hunter. However the maps available on the alpha where very nice and somewhat diverse to me, I often found myself wanting to play on a map that had a swap area different from the rocky hills I was in, just to find out it was the same map. Yes, I thought the maps would be bigger, but again, after playing on them for a while I still think they are quite big, at least big enough to allow the match to be a good length in my opinion (around 15 - 20 minutes).
4 - I said that I played the alpha with a friend, and it was pretty fun to do it, in a few matches we played around with the different classes (and the monster when we weren't in a party) and found the one(s) we liked the most, with their weak and strong points as well as their skills unique for each class. I have to say I was quite disapointed when I wasn't able to play a match as a monster because I was in a party (I understand that people could exploit this to level up quickly), but I think there should be at least a custom match that didn't give any EXP or rewards just so I could play with, let's say, four friends playing as a hunter while I'm a monster taunting or theathening (as a joke obviously) them in voice chat.
5 - The game is $60 right now, and I would not pay that for the game I played, which just to remind everyone was only an alpha, but it's the standard launch price for retail games, and I expect that by the launch date, the game will have more features (and honestly, a better menu interface). As I said before I didn't buy the game just yet, but I'm planning on buying it, however I will also wait for more content reveals or sneak-peaks to be sure before buying it.
That was a pretty extensive review compared to the ones a usually make, but I thought that I had to say that, and I hope I didn't forget anything important.

Like with Ace Patrol, I also get asked the same question with this one 'is it worth getting?' so lets do this review.
Short answer really, Is yes if you liked Ace Patrol but want something more with a little punch. It comes with most of the other features of the previous game (randomised pilots you can name that can earn RPG traits and manauvers through experince whilst fighting randomised missions between 1-4 AI pilots using hex combat in a turn based system) and it is especially worth it after playing Ace Patrol.
Pacific Skies takes place the era of warfare where planes have shifted over to faster engines and single wings. Thus the turn based combat is slightly deadlier and quicker than in the prequal game but the aim is still the same (get on their six cover your own). The art assets of course are very very different and much more varied. Both the two American and Japanese factions do dog fighting over land and sea and there are a few new twists added (Instead of Offensives it is now eight famous WW2 battles of the campaign with six missions each to do) like a mission to shoot down a pilot or towers to save one of your crashed pilots from a POW camp. Plane customisation has improved, you can now paint five different part of your squadrons plans with a varied amount of WW2 flight insignia.
While like Ace Patrol there are a few minor once in a blue moon issues with the tiles (I had a mission where an enemy pilot just few into a tile and vanished from the game, assumed crashed) it played a straight up solid indie title like previous game. So in total and in my genuide opinion getting this and the older WW1 themed brother together during a sale will entertaining you for a solid 22 hours in total for a first run on each game.

Really interesting game, specially the DLC.
I played it 2 years ago: i binged the whole game in one night, and i was blown away. Today i decided to give it another go. I didn´t have the same amount of joy, but it still felt like a solid experience.
It plays a lot with surprise, tension, and putting you in situations where you feel in hazard, so that the first run is amazing, but once you know what is going to happen/where is the exit that tension is gone. Every game could fall into this problem, but this one specially because there is a lot of scripted events.
Really good visuals, music and controls. Be aware that this is not an action title, so you have to hide and run through the game, while finding keys/switches to keep moving forward in the story.
Horror-wise, the game is really creepy, and uses jump scares mixed with bait environments, and a linear sequence of events, so that you can roam around a place, but not get lost or backtrack to places you have already visited.
The 'thing' about this game that stood out of other titles is that you are carrying a videocamera, that you have to use in some segments where there is no light, using the night vision mode, in the style of the last segment of the horror movie [Rec].
I ENCOURAGE you to play the DLC of this game, because, in my opinion, packs a better story and enemies than the main campaign. There are 'bosses' in the game, as in unique characters that are hunting you along the way, and in this regard, the DLC IS SUPERB.
The game got a bad rep thanks to the amount of Letsplayers that exploited the title for it's shock factor on youtube. It is a lot more than a jumpscare or a walking simulator title, and one if not the best horror game in years. I know it cannot compete with classics of the genre, but it is a SOLID title, specially the DLC. It should be included by default, and arranged as a two path adventure.

The game is great. This game has a lot of tracks to race on, and a lot of fun obstacles to fight through with your opponents!
It's not only racing, there are also special games modes, for example, you have to jump out of a fast moving car and try to go the highest. This makes the game more fun.
The physics in the game are OK, it feels realistic to drive the cars, and ramming your opponents look awesome! But, be careful when driving fast, because even the tiniest objects, like sticks and rocks, can just bring your car to a wheelie and then crash, allowing your opponents to pass you.
There are a variety of cars to choose from, within 3 categories; derby, race and street. The cars are upgradable which is cool, but you cannot customize your car.
The soundtrack for this game is epic! There are amazing tracks featuring Alkaline Trio and Yellow card etc. I think you'll enjoy the music, and old, classic racing game soundtracks sound great.
You might not like this game if you just want to race, because in this game, you will need to crash other cars as well, to get nitrous.
I really enjoy this game! And it's at a cheap price, so even better! This game is so recommended for fans of Burnout, like myself, and other car-crash and other action games.

Got this when they had it up for free, promoting their next game, and I'm really glad I did. The artistic/visual appeal is enormous; it's delightfully eerie, but not actually "scary," IMHO. Despite being a two-dimensional puzzle platformer, it doesn't feel flat, the way platformers often do. The fore/background decoration is very well done, and really gives a sense of depth.
The gameplay also doesn't stagnate, mostly because each chapter gradually introduces some bonkers new obstacle to get past, and the physics are fun. Puzzles are interesting and challenging without being utterly rage inducing, and balance timing with simple logic. (Sometimes at the same time. Those are extra fun.) The controls also handle well and feel very fluid.
All in all, a great game. I deeply enjoyed it.

Keep in mind that this is a game about micromanaging trains, not a strategy/"tycoon" game. This game is quite fun, but quite short of you don't like completing all the challenges in the game.
I picked this game up during a Steam sale for €7.00 including DLC. I would say that it was worth that money, but I am not sure if I would recommend it at full price (€12.50).
Pros:
- The core mechanics, laying rails and directing trains, are easy to understand and work reasonably well
- The theming is great
- The levels are designed well, making it a challenge to find the optimal layout of tracks to complete all challenges
- The game is not incredibly difficult. The 6 levels added by the DLC are somewhat harder than the 24 in the base game. The ability to pause the game makes it a lot less stressful too.
Cons:
- The music is repetitive, and while soothing it just annoyed me after a while.
- Rail junctions work... weird. Rail junctions are blocked when a train is on top of them. However, the game also blocks rail junctions on adjecent rails, or even crossing rails.
- The challenges get stale after a bit. The challenges for Germany have some more fun ones in them, such as blowing up 5 trains.
- The sandbox mode is completely broken, with train stations not showing up at all. Besides that, it's not all that fun without a clear goal or even money to worry about.
- Even after completing every challenge, and completing every other achievement, I only built about 9000 train tracks towards the "build 10.000 train tracks" achievement. Luckily the game counts train tracks built just before restarting a level, so building a lot of useless tracks on a level with high starting money solves that problem, but "grinding building train tracks" is not fun nor won't it give me a sense of achieving something on reaching it.

I waited a long time to review this game, mainly because I don't like or want to contribute to negative reviews.

Fast forward 2-3 years and there is a lot of development, a lot of change, and a game that has been finished. There were many character wipes and world wipes along the way = That was to be expected. I bought it on pre-order before early access, and played for about 6-8 months through early access, so a few save wipes isn't a huge deal.
However, I think another user said it best " I think the negative reviews are born mostly out of frustration with how long the game took to get from early access to release."
Here we are three years later with a game that is no longer in Early Access but still has clunky controls and somewhat of a grind feel. However - it has come a long way, and if you came  here NOT expecting to grind in order to craft and survive, I don't know what you were expecting.

This game is proceeding along a similar path, but a  year or so ago they introduced a Tutorial stage at the beginning of the game. Instead of the tutorial level - the game now appears to have something else, that exists more as a dialogue feature that I won't spoil.
I"ll keep checking in on the updates as they come along.

This is THE most realistic zombie survival game that I have ever played. I haven't played much of this game, but every single moment was memorable. The last time I played I had pretty much scavenged an entire trailer park, picking the whole place clean, and took the stuff back to an old motel where I had been holed up in for a few days. I made sure to board up all the windows and after I put all the stuff away I walked over to turn off all of the lights inside the motel room because it was getting dark and zeds are attracted ti the light, thats when I noticed that the lights were already off and I came to the shocking realization that the power must have gone out, and I knew that it wasn't just the power in the motel that had gone out but more than likely all the power in the entire city was probably out. I knew that the food I had been keeping in the fridge would probably spoil soon, but their was pretty much nothing I could do about that, luckily I had stockpiled dozens of cans of food so I'd be okay for a week or two at least. I was about to go to bed when suddenly I could hear gunshots in the distance, so the relatively quiet neighborhood that I had set up my base in was now swarming with the undead, I could see hoards of them passing by as I peeked out of an upstairs window......

By the way if you're running Windows 7 and you're encountering problems with launching the game or having no in-game audio, just go to
and look for the fix there.
kikoneko in particular posted a helpful fix that helped me launch the game with sound (running windows 7 and had trouble launching Bioshock with audio)
Pasting the specific fix here that worked for me if you don't feel like reading through the entire thread:
The game crashed until I applied the -nosound fix, but then in-game sound was absent. Compatibility mode Windows XP SP 2 fixed it for me. Neither Vista, Vista SP 1 or Vista SP2 or 'run as' admin helped. My only sound device in CP>sound>Playback tab is NVIDIA HD Audio from graphics card (>hdmi>A/V Receiver). Never installed onboard.
Edit: after doing this the game settings reset to default, and changing the game resolution in the game crashed it, so I went to Default.ini file in the Steam game folder and changed this bit:
[WinDrv.WindowsClient]
WindowedViewportX=1920
WindowedViewportY=1080
FullscreenViewportX=1920
FullscreenViewportY=1080
Now it all works.

My first few characters died horrible deaths from hypothermia, dysentery, and wolf induced wounds.
The one that made it past the initial learning curve thrived. I set up a base camp in an abandoned cabin near the entrance to a lake, made it a place to stockpile supplies. The frozen corpse upstairs didn’t help the atmosphere, but it was as close to home as possible. Seven days past while scavenging the lake and surrounding area. Firewood was running low and I needed to find a few tree saplings to craft a bow and arrow. After all, the rifle I found only had a few rounds that wouldn’t last forever. So off I went in the morning, following a frozen river in hopes of stumbling on to small trees. As the day marched on, a deer galloped out of the forest and stopped a hundred feet away. There was plenty of meat left in the cabin so no reason to waste a precious bullet. Besides, a wolf was pacing back and forth just in view; a rifle round could mean the difference between life and death. Having spotted the dear but not my character, the wolf changed course. It growled and sprinted forward. The deer fled in terror. I had no idea wolfs could attack other wildlife – this entire event was unexpected, and the catalyst for a worst night for my character had yet to encounter.
Realizing the wolf would likely catch the deer and kill it, I sprinted after them both. Letting the wolf do my dirty work and expending a single rifle round for double the meat was just too good an opportunity to ignore. As I crested the first hill, I saw the wolf crouched over and feasting on the deer. Its back was turned; it hadn’t yet noticed me. Crouching to reduce noise, I approached closer from the wolf’s blind spot until there was no chance of missing a head shot. The rifle sights lined up, and with a crack that echoed through the valley the wolf dropped. Eager to survey my kills before they froze, I ran to them. There is 29 pounds of meat, two guts, and one hide from the deer along with 17 pounds of meat, two guts, and one hide from the wolf – a very good haul. However, it took more than five hours to harvest. By this time, my character is hungry, thirsty, tired, and very cold. Thirst, hunger, and energy I can fix; I never leave the cabin without 2000 calories of food, a gallon of water, and several tins of coffee. Cold is the real enemy here, and now I am too encumbered to walk quickly. There’s still a few hours left in the day so I can take the time to make a fire and warm up. I can even cook some of this meat so I don’t waste the heat. While building the campfire, I hear a growl. Another wolf has found me and is approaching, ready to attack. The fire keeps it at bay for now it seems, even while I’m in the process of building it. If the fire fails to start, I know the wolf will attack me. Luckily, the fire ignites and the wolf stays on the boundary. Stupid animal, I still have ammunition for my rifle. It’s an easy kill shot. There’s no leaving behind the meat, so I stoke the fire and harvest the second wolf. Night is coming – it’s time to head back to the cabin.
I barely make it a quarter of the way before energy levels become an issue again. The coffee has worn off and I’m cold again. It’s a long trek back and I’m holding twice my carry capacity, a capacity which is fading the more tired and hungry I become. Visibility has also reduced so it’s time to call it and spend the night under the stars. Except this was supposed to be a day trip; I left the heavy bedroll in the cabin. How unfortunate. More coffee it is. I build a fire and warm a single cup of the caffeinated beverage before the wind picks and rudely extinguishes my source of heat. Little did I know this was the start of a blizzard that would rage deep into the night.
The campfire no longer an option and any guiding torch I could make wishful thinking, I move in the direction I think the train tracks are in. I can’t be sure which way I’m heading as visibility has dropped to nothing as the snowy wind reached deafening speeds. A lucky press of hot keys reminds me I have a storm lantern! Lighting it eagerly, I press on. I’m grateful for the increased light and warmth, but it isn’t enough to guide me or save me from hypothermia. Train tracks emerge from the dark; I was correct about the direction of travel. Now which way to go? Picking a direction that feels like a path to the cabin, I continue. Another wolf appears from the tree line but I’m too slow to run and too slow to change back to the rifle. We fight, ending with the wolf receiving a hunting knife to the sternum and me losing my boots. It yelps and slinks off, but I can’t risk going after it to harvest its meat. At this point, it might be best to drop what I have to move faster anyway. The train track fall away under piles of snow, this obscures them from view. I think an indent in the rock walls looks like where I should turn to reach the cabin.
Except all I find is more rock wall. My character is dying from cold, hunger, and sleep deprivation. I’ve lost all bearings in the blizzard and no longer know which way the train tracks are, which way the cabin is, or even where I just came from. The wind is raging on, making a campfire impossible. The fuel in the lantern is fading. This is the end. This is how my character dies. I, outside the game, am breathing heavily and panicking with legitimate anxiety, fear, and readiness to give into the elements despite permanent death. This is the moment I realized The Long Dark is something special worth playing. A game that evokes this level of emotion and draws you back in time and again is rare. One that accomplishes it in so little time over the course of a single event is even rarer.
This story does have a happy ending. I stopped next to another rock wall and discovered it was positioned in such a way that it blocked the wind. This allowed me to build a fire, which in turn allowed me to warm up, heat up coffee, cook meat, and melt water. I waited out the blizzard there and made it back to the cabin where my character still survives.
EDIT: Died on day 12 after bleeding out from a wolf bite. I didn’t have any bandages and didn’t realize you could make some from cloth.

Amazing game! A must have! Unique genre!
It feels totally awesome to play both as a monster or as a trooper. The 4v1 mode is unique, you have the thrill of the hunt, you get the fear of being caught too soon. Eventually when ready, it counts a lot where you get into the last fight. Terrain can be used for great advantage. Also, personal skill is at high value here. This is one of the very best games i have played this year.
it is a 4 FPS vs 1 3rd Person RPG/PvP game that takes place in a huge arena filled with prehistorical like animals that Goliath can feed on. Some of these animals will drop perks (faster movement speed, faster climbing, faster feeding, more damage) If Goliath is chased away from his pray before he can eat to gain the perk, the soldiers also can tap to take this perk for them. There are 4 main abilities as Goliath each of them with 3 different levels of upgrade. A level 3 Goliath can max 3 of these 4 abilities. 1st is Rock Throw, second is a Leap Attack, 3rd is a Fire Breath attack that damages soldiers over time (DOT), and 4th is a Charge. Also you have a melee normal attack. All these abilities have a cooldown. In the arena, the possibilities are endless, sometimes you find a single soldier that got away from his team, sometimes you get ambushed before you could evolve or while you are evolving, you can hide or you can give away your position by stepping in a bird's nest - you have total freedom to try anything you want to try. After evolving to 3rd level you are now able to destroy the power relay of the troopers and be sure that they will defend it.
Troopers: 4 specialities: Assault, Trapper, Medic and Suport. Everyone of these has 4 abilities and everyone of them counts when being used properly, plus the ability to fly using a Jet Pack. In order to fight Goliath, you have to deploy the arena shield so it won't be able to get away. Now you are in a World of Warcraft type of boss fight where one of the players is healing one is shielding the attacked player, one is using crowd control abilities (tranquilizer, harpoon). Damage is done by direct attacks, the shooting, land mines, air strike with rockets (this one is most powerful and should be used when Goliath is succesfully trapped and slowed, or when he is attacking the Power Relay) You have a limited time to revive your fallen team mates. This can be a game changer. I have lost fights as Goliath trying to prevent team from reviving their medic and also won some because they were trying desperately to revive the fallen trooper. The reviving is limited and i think one player can only be revived 3 times in a row. Goliaths can also getaway and replenish shields by eating wild life. Also the perks gained after evolving can be a game changer. Let's say you manage to get away with low HP (red bar almost depleted) and you find a wild beast with a perk that allows your HP to regenerate. You can get back into the fight you have almost lost and change the outcome of the fight.
During loading screens you can see on a minimap the trajectories of everyone on the map, this can be a way to learn new things and new tactics.
To conclude:
This game has the potential to become one of the most powerful titles in eSports competitions. It is like DOTA + Natural Selection (without the RTS factor)
I give it a 10+/10.

Morphopolis sets you in an arty world, above and underground, where you'll take control of different kinds of insects over the course of five stages. Essentially, this is an object finder and puzzles game. During the course of the game you'll come across particular creatures and plants populating the beautifully stylized art work and consistent backdrops. You lead your character, or bug that is, through a terrain of sticks, leaves and otherwise organic world to find hidden objects and to solve puzzles. This in turn enables you to progress to the succeeding stages. The surreal and picturesque environments are well complimented by a soothing soundtrack and the game itself is just very immersive and enjoyable.
While the puzzles are not frustratingly difficult to solve and the hidden objects not obscenely obscured, it is a casual puzzle game for fans of the artistic type.

An unnecessarily overly-complex game with barely any gameplay.
Where to begin? To start with, do you know how occasionally a fantasy world with switch up the names of races to try and seem unique? You know, like "Elves" will become "Torak'thell" or something. Now imagine that, except it's literally every word in the game. You have things that you can work out, like the "Zea" is the sea, but then you have "Iron, Pages, Mirrors" and "Hearts". From what I could work out, this is "Strength, Intelligence, Cunning" and "Will". It doesn't matter, though, since I have no clue what these affect other then your percentage to succeed in certain rolls. Your experience is "Fragments" and your level-ups are "Secrets".
That brings me to the out-of-ship sections, where you'll be thrust into one of those old choose-your-own adventure games from 2005. Except you can't pick anything, since you need four different alchemical items to speak to a beggar or something. Why they don't just get rid of the options you can't pick, or at least put them at the end of the list, I don't know.
As for fairness, the combat is dead-simple. You and the enemy basically chase each other for the entire battle, trying to keep each other in your sights so you can hit them. However, this is pretty pointless, since you'll get a cask of wine if it's a ship that sells for 10 gold (Or whatever you call money in this), or you'll get one supply as a reward. This doesn't matter, though, since you likely spent a lot more in that battle, since both your hunger and your fuel decrease at a rapid rate.
This would be fine, if you could actually get enough money to restock, but as it stands the only way I've found to get money is to get reports from harbours. This doesn't matter, though, since you'll  be able to sail to about four, which'll spend about 8 resources and 5 fuel, then when you return you'll be given fifty bucks, which'll let you restock 4 resources. I'm sure there's some amazing other way to get cash, but for the life of me I can't work it out. There's occasionally passengers that say "I want to go to Berzetien's throat", but they never tell you WHERE it is, which is incredibly annoying on a giant map with no landmarks except for "Slightly blue-er water"
TL:DR: Go buy FTL: Faster Than Light if you want a game similar to this that actually does it right.

An extremely sedate and relaxed game that dives us into a surreal Victorian Gothic underworld (Sea? Zee? Hm.) The amount of content and story exposition is as deep as the universe we sail in, and while it never quite reaches the profound darkness it proclaims to possess (The maturity, themes, and breadth of content and style reminded me of a Young Adults Horror) it still has a magical air and calming nature to it that encompasses both a satisfying game loop, and devilishly twisty stories.
Overall: 4/5, Recommended at asking price.
Pros:
*Polished, engaging game loop is satisfying to play for hours without boring you out.
*Lineage system of continuing your campaign is crazy cool, especially when the game recommends it. You'll see.
*Interesting combat mechanics that have just enough twists or variations to be fun.
*Profound atmosphere and polish to the lore and worldbuilding. Some of the most careful attention to internal accuracy or in-universe sharing of tropes/continuity I've seen.
*Quite long, lots of branching paths, very replayable depending on your style.
Cons:
*Not as dark, Lovecraftian, contemplative or even plain old scary as reviews -- and it -- want you to believe. Struck me very young adult-esque at times, with that accessible and safe diction and delivery of the story.
*Early game is an absolute menace if you don't study up. Can disavow interest from impatient newcomers.
*Without the DLC it absolutely lacks in the mid game department, but has a satisfying conclusion spread after, regardless.
I'm going to abandon explaining the in-game fluff and explanations for both the technology and literal meaning of devices. Boats will be boats, islands will be islands. If I tried to explain that your boat was technically already underwater, but not really--yeah, no firstcomers to this review would know what I'm talking about.
So, Sunless Sea. You sail from island to island, shore to shore, in a bit of a choose your own adventure rogue-like. (God I hate that term.) There are enemies to combat along the way that range from pitiful loot sources to nightmarish bosses, and the complexity and meat of the game is centered around the world of Fallen London (established in a F2P browser game apparently forever ago.)
Each island, ship, outpost, notable landmark or random event will have a story to it. Quest chains of various sizes that embellish more of the rich lore to you, as well as to upgrade your ship, weapons, crew, and relations with people. Your crew also has quests for you. Multiple offices from multiple towns do, too. Each spiraling thread reminds me of the cause/effect found in modern AAA role playing games these days, but done in a much more succinct and satisfying way.
To achieve all these events you don't need to only explore. You collect various sub-resources that essentially act as keys to doing certain things. To loosely explain, you have a universal currency for purchasing stuff. A sub currency to be secretive or have espionage in missions. One for combat encounters. One for society/politics. Etc.
This inherently is awesome for replaying. Sessions can be shorter than an hour or longer than ten if you want, or live. The best part is that the universe constructs itself around your attempts and often times, encourages you to die. It has a lineage system that is not worth omitting from this review. If you die, you become a new captain. You can continue on the rumored quest of your predecessor, or do your own thing. You may also have a kid, raise them however you want throughout the story, and then play as them when you die. How awesome is that? The story will build itself, and react, to this element.
My closing paragraph will be discussing my prior point about the feel of the story. While it is rife with insanity, suicide, crew death or cosmic horror and some shocking societal messages, it never feels... dark. The world feels calm, safe, sedate and unfocused. Some crazy stuff is going on, but it doesn't want you or the characters to feel that way. This universe is normal, this is their lives, this is stuff they see every day. Perhaps the writing matches this mood, but the game -- for all its self promotion -- never once invoked dread or fear, and only played it safe enough to keep me engaged in the otherwise fascinating lore it presents.

Hunt or be Hunted 4 VS 1 at its best!
Thats the name of the game in Evolve. 4 Hunters each with a unique class (assault,Trapper,medic and support) try to Hunt down and Kill a Monster before it trys to EVOLVE! and turn the tydes and make the Hunters the hunted.
Each Class has a role to play in finding and defeating  the monster.  At the time of the Alpha there were only 8 hunters, 2 monsters and 3 maps)
The assault class is the damage dealer in the group and keep the monsters attention. I Mainly played this class.
The Trapper classes job is to track down the monster and Trap it with  harppons to slow the monster down and they have a mobile arena that forces the monster to fight the hunters.
The Support class can use a wide array of diffrent items depending on the character you pick. You might have a missle bonbarment designator, an item that shealds players from damage and an invisability modual that clokes all allies so they can  flee from the monster.
The medic class is there to heal up teammates with their medic guns. They also have tranqulizers to slow down the monsters Movments. I did not get a chance to play much as the medic during the alpha so I dont know all they can do.
Then we have a STAR of the whole game the MONSTER! The person playing the monster has three tasks. In the early start of the match the monsters main objective is to put as much distance between them and the hunters and feed on the wild life and Gain Armor and EVOLVE to your next 2 stages before taking the fight to the Hunters because the monster is at a disadvantage early on at stage one of there evolution and can be killed quite fast. Stage two evens the playing feald you are no longer at a disadvantage to the hunters your and even match for them and at stage three your the hunters worst nightmare dealing Massive amounts of damge! You also have an optional objective to destoy a relay station designated on the map but you can only destroy it when your fully evolved. When you first start as the monster you have 3 points to spend in 4 diffrent skills to help you aginst the hunters you can put all or points is one skill or spend them on multiple ones. You gain 3 more points to spend at stage 2 and 3 more when your fully evolved at stage 3.
(During the alpha there were only 2 monsters avaliabe the goliath a giant power house that throws rocks and breaths fire and the Kraken the flying cephalopod that shoots lighting bolts and land mines that follows the huntes and exploed on contact)
The full relase of the game will have 12 hunters, 3 monsers and 12 maps.
From what i have played its very polished even in alpha, I am excited to play more when the game is finished.

I was a rookie pilot just getting my wings on a mission to shoot down enemy Japanese planes. My maneuvers were weak and so was my aim. I shot down a few but was lost a little later behind enemy lines. Next up came my partner who seemed to fair better but unlucky for him he was terrible too. One by one what was once a total of four slowly became none after failed missions over and over till we were all lost behind enemy lines with no way of escape.  This is the sad story of our our lost soldiers of war.
Ace Patrol: Pacific Skies is a casual strategy hex-grid style game. You control four total pilots which you maneuver around the board trying to take out the enemies. When you start you have a very limited choice of movements. Over time you earn upgrades and better planes to help you out against tougher and tougher enemies. You are scored on each mission on how well you perform. The more you get hit or if you lose a pilot your points drop.
There is a total of eight areas with 4 missions to each one. You will fly around at Pearl Harbor, Midway, Okinawa, and a few other locations on the pacific. You can still fail a mission and move on to the next one. You'll just end up with a lower overall score.
Pacific Skies is not a bad game and you can get it for fairly cheap. It also comes from the great Sid Meier who has a fantastic game making record. So if you enjoy a little challenge, WWII history, or Sid Meier games I recommend you try this game out.

Caution:  This game has several bugs and performance issues that may affect your enjoyment of the game.  I encountered a bug that broke a conversation early on in my playthrough that forced me to start over.  The game may freeze and stutter at the start of cutscenes (which take up a fair chunk of the game).  Whether or not you decide to use the Cloud to save your games, do not change this setting after you start or you may find your save file overwritten (I discovered this the hard way).  If any of this is a deal-breaker, do not buy the game.
However...
If you are not dissuaded by these issues, the game itself is good.  Despite all the problems I encountered, I still had a lot of fun. Take on the dual personas of Bruce Wayne and Batman and shape how the denizens of Gotham perceive (both of) you.  This series offers a new and unique interpretation of many familiar characters of the Batman mythos.  The writing and voice acting are great, and you will be presented with several difficult choices with no clear, "right" answer.  The decisions you make can be imported into Season 2, which, as of the time of writing, is two episodes in and great.
TL;DR If you like Batman and you like Telltale and don't mind bugs and performance issues, pick it up.  Choices carry over to Season 2 (which runs a lot better).

Third city:
Go to Steam Workshop and find the newest verison of Colonial Charter.
You just added a whole lotta depth to the game. Have fun exploring all the new ressources and professions.

I hate to put it so crassly, but Medusa's Labyrinth does seem to be a take on Amnesia: The Dark Descent only in ancient Greece. There are notes to pick up leading down a rabbit hole of otherworldly terror, a limited-use light source to make those dark corridors even more threatening, and of course a monster whose very sight distorts your vision in abject horror.
Where this game bucks its predecessor's formula is in the inclusion of a bow. These monsters can be killed, but an imprecise shot still means certain death. You are both the hunter and the hunted.
With the constant game of cat and mouse forcing the player to listen carefully for noises in the poorly lit passages of some catacomb, it seemed a shame Medusa's Labyrinth still felt the need to lean on horror cliches. The pounding music employed around stressful moments seemed like an unnecessary hold over of Amnesia's sanity mechanic. The incidental music was, however, more forgivable than the tired tactic of jump scares. There was no need for jump scares in a situation that garners so much tension on its own.
Medusa's Labyrinth is rough in both design and execution, but as the store page points out, this is only a small part of the game that was planned. It should be taken more as a demo or a teaser and on that count it succeeds. If another chapter is ever released – and it does seem like that's the plan – I'd play it based on the recommendation this installment provides alone.

On top of that, when you are forced into a position where you get chased because of rail roading, the chase is too... Frantic. You don't have time to take literally two seconds to look left and right at the junction and decide which direction to run.
Which ends up boiling down to this: You spawn and immediately grab the batteries under the bed (you already knew they were there), you run down the hall, you turn left because you know right is a dead end. You open the door into the locker room, but don't try to hide in the lockers because you already know you are guarenteed to get caught. You run to the far end of the room where there is another door. You open the door and die. A 'monster' was waiting there. Maybe you're suppose to try to jump out of the windows? You spawn and immediately grab the batteries...

The Long Dark is easily the best indie survival game I've ever played. Hinterland Studios has made an amazing game, both in reference to the artistic masterpiece which it is and the groundbreaking gameplay. It's nice to visit an apocalypse in which the threat isn't the supernatural or the future tide of war, but rather the thing which has challenged human kind from the start and far before: Mother Nature, in all her wretched glory.
The use of the simple color palette of the dark wilderness to create beatiful landscapes and drab - but still beautiful and colorful - human creations is complemented only by the immesurable unique artistic stylization, appearing as though every single thing were painted to life by the unprepared. You. You are unprepared.
The game sends you directly into a random location whenever you begin anew, leaving you with only your memory to guide you among the snow and ice.
Food is scarce, and weapons even more so. Only by exploring the dead human ruins of Canada will you live to see tomorrow.
You must keep vigilant of your own condition and your surroundings. Water is near at all times, trapped in the cold snow. Food can be found in human-created cans or within the animals. The cold can be fended off by the means of fire, clothes, the buildings of humans, or a hole in the ground. Sleep can be found anywhere at anytime.
Though, if done with nature, you may find that you will fade into...
The Long Dark.

Just finished my second playthrough and O lord did it end dramatically.
So on my first playthrough, I spawned in the trapper cabin WITH the rifle. I got super lucky. Bad thing is, I was still a complete and total noob, so I died within a few days.
Second playthrough lasted 20 days. I was stacked. I had traveled across all of the major areas, trekked tons of kilometers, and finally made a home for myself in the trapper cabin. Had a bow, and was curing saplings to make a few more arrows. Things were good.
One thing though: I was running out of food, and I had no usable arrows to go hunt. I made tons of mistakes along the road, of course. Didn't gather food when I could have. Basically ignored the urgency of my situation. But one of my major goals in the last expedition I had was to find the rifle.
So I knew it wasn't in the cabin where I settled down, so I went to the hydro dam to go see if it was there. After having a couple of encounters with the wolf and getting lost in the ice canyons below, I finally made my way out of the front entrance of the dam again. Was making my way home when-- oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have no food.
I made my way to the big cabin by the lake, not remembering if I had left food there last time I searched it. Nope.
Went to a lakeside cabin, beginning to starve. No luck there.
Searched 3 of the fishing spots, no food there either. Tried fishing for a bit, had no luck and was severely hungry. Almost dead.
In my last moments, as I stumbled across the ice in a blizzard, looking for a shelter or at least a tiny morself of food, I find a cabin. And a body. AND A RIFLE. And a candy bar.
Ate the candy bar. Food is okay now, but I'm about to die of exhaustion. Stumble inside after 6 tries, being blown back by the intense blizzard. Go to sleep. Wake up, starving again. Can't see anything because of my condition.
I decided to go out peacefully, sleeping. Although it wasn't peaceful, as my rage about finding the rifle before death was still all-consuming.
Never have I experienced more tension and excitement and rage at a game, and still loved it afterwards.
10/10 would find rifle before tragic death again.
TL;DR: Buy the game. It's worth it.

I bought The Long Dark on one of Steam's sales a little while back having never heard of the game.  The concept sounded interesting, and from the reviews others had posted, all the elements appeared to mesh well together.  Going in with no expectations other than some very, very postiive reviews I sat back and welcomed the wild ride that is The Long Dark.
The game is really what you decide to make out of it.  Do you want to survive by methodically raiding each house in a little abandonded town and leaving only  when you've run out of food?  Or do you want to risk several cold nights with only your fragile fire and sleeping bag in order to explore the wide open beautifully harsh landscape?  You can choose to kill wildlife, but with that choice comes the cost of ammunition and other needed supplies for survival.
Every choice you make feels your own and can have severe cosqeunces.  Wandering out at night in a blizzard across a frozen lake with only my lantern and a can of beans was not the best choice.  However my biggest mistake was picking a fight with a bear.  You learn from these mistakes and you learn the general location of key points of interest, but the world is always changing, will you change to adapt?
I will continue to invest many hours in the sandbox mode, but eagerly await the release of the full game featuring an episodic story mode.  Good luck, and happy survival.

Easily now one of my favorite games of 2017.
Story:
You play as Cuphead and/or Mugman if you want to play with someone else, two brothers who end up getting into deep water as they go to a casino to have a little fun, unfortunately for them they take it too far and end up challenging the devil, they obviously lose but luckily they have a way out of this if they can collect the souls of the devil's other debtors instead of their own. So begins the journey.
Gameplay:
As most know by now, the gameplay is a simple run n' gun experience that is heavily focused on boss fights, the challenge comes from the bosses themselves, and let me tell you, it does not matter what experience you have in this genre, you will die quite a few times to each boss, as they have multiple phases, no health bar so you don't know how long each phase will take. To top it off, you only have 3 hits throughout each boss, so make sure to recognize each attack pattern, these bosses will kick your harder than what a basketball players wife recieves.
There are two modes of difficulty which is Simple and Regular, does not matter, both are tough as nails.
There are also a few segments in the game where you will do normal run n gun to get to the end of the level, these phases have coins in which you can give to Porkrinds emporium to upgrade your attacks and charms to aid you through the experience.
As for everything else, music is amazing, animation is superb. All of it made from handscratch and actual talent of drawing. Everything is beautiful, colorful, and vibrant from what you will expect in a 1930s cartoon.
If you guys love a challenge, look no further!
Highly recommend this great game!

A perfect crossover between Pipe Dream and Flight Control HD.
You layout rails to bring a constant flow of trains to their designated stations. Very easy concept but gets hectic as more stations spawn around the map and the train numbers increase.
Each train you deliver will increase your money to build more tracks, and pay the taxes each year (which is very short in game time!). Trains lose worth fast, so don't deliver them fast and you risk going bankrupt.
You can also launch extra trains at a random location for a fee. Gamble on this option to increase your cash, but abuse it and you'll end up overloading your network which is certain to lead to disaster, or to fun!
Once you have multiple trains running between stations you'll need to micromanage switches and stop your trains if necessary (losing precious money) to avoid accidents which will always make your trains blow up violently; I think it must be explosives that you are delivering.
You can play the levels in a variety of styles. Spend loads of cash to build a huge rail network which can support loads of trains running at the same time. Or play it stingy and try to see how many trains you manage to circulate back and forth on a single narrow piece of track. Both methods have their risks and rewards.
Some of the later maps have special features, such as high speed trains that you cant control or stop, adding to the excitement.
The campaign is not extremely long, but you have sandbox levels at the end of each stage, and stamp challenges on each level also increase replayability. This can make some easy levels very challenging, for example play the level without using pause, without stopping any train, and launch 10 additional trains.
The game runs smooth and seamlesly performance wise, and hardly has any bugs. There are 4 (5 with DLC) countries which all have a pleasant and unique visual style, and the trains have some nice variety from around the world. You can see that the devs like their trains, even though this is a puzzle game, not a tycoon one.
Also the game still receives attention from the devs, patches, and DLC. At the really honest price tag this is sold I can not do anything but recommend Train Valley to everyone!
