it is a 4 FPS vs 1 3rd Person RPG/PvP game that takes place in a huge arena filled with prehistorical like animals that Goliath can feed on. Some of these animals will drop perks (faster movement speed, faster climbing, faster feeding, more damage) If Goliath is chased away from his pray before he can eat to gain the perk, the soldiers also can tap to take this perk for them. There are 4 main abilities as Goliath each of them with 3 different levels of upgrade. A level 3 Goliath can max 3 of these 4 abilities. 1st is Rock Throw, second is a Leap Attack, 3rd is a Fire Breath attack that damages soldiers over time (DOT), and 4th is a Charge. Also you have a melee normal attack. All these abilities have a cooldown. In the arena, the possibilities are endless, sometimes you find a single soldier that got away from his team, sometimes you get ambushed before you could evolve or while you are evolving, you can hide or you can give away your position by stepping in a bird's nest - you have total freedom to try anything you want to try. After evolving to 3rd level you are now able to destroy the power relay of the troopers and be sure that they will defend it.
Troopers: 4 specialities: Assault, Trapper, Medic and Suport. Everyone of these has 4 abilities and everyone of them counts when being used properly, plus the ability to fly using a Jet Pack. In order to fight Goliath, you have to deploy the arena shield so it won't be able to get away. Now you are in a World of Warcraft type of boss fight where one of the players is healing one is shielding the attacked player, one is using crowd control abilities (tranquilizer, harpoon). Damage is done by direct attacks, the shooting, land mines, air strike with rockets (this one is most powerful and should be used when Goliath is succesfully trapped and slowed, or when he is attacking the Power Relay) You have a limited time to revive your fallen team mates. This can be a game changer. I have lost fights as Goliath trying to prevent team from reviving their medic and also won some because they were trying desperately to revive the fallen trooper. The reviving is limited and i think one player can only be revived 3 times in a row. Goliaths can also getaway and replenish shields by eating wild life. Also the perks gained after evolving can be a game changer. Let's say you manage to get away with low HP (red bar almost depleted) and you find a wild beast with a perk that allows your HP to regenerate. You can get back into the fight you have almost lost and change the outcome of the fight.
During loading screens you can see on a minimap the trajectories of everyone on the map, this can be a way to learn new things and new tactics.
To conclude:
This game has the potential to become one of the most powerful titles in eSports competitions. It is like DOTA + Natural Selection (without the RTS factor)

In a way, this is a sort of real-time puzzle game, not unlike Tetris. You lay a finite amount of track, attempt to make the best use of the limited space to deliver the most trains in the shortest time, and revise your track configuration as necessary.
The satisfaction of finding the right configuration is hard to describe. Let me put it this way: If you're the type of person who likes optimizing processes, such that an unexpectedly high workload can still be managed with nothing going wrong, you will find much to like in this game.
It is a heuristics development and revision game where learning the optimal layout for each situation is half the fun, and the other half is guiding trains through that layout with nothing exploding.
Though it usually has little bearing on gameplay, I should also say that this game uses locations and times from history rarely seen in videogames, especially the DLC.

(This is an review of an Alpha Build and should in no way be juged as a Full release)
Hunt or be Hunted 4 VS 1 at its best!
Thats the name of the game in Evolve. 4 Hunters each with a unique class (assault,Trapper,medic and support) try to Hunt down and Kill a Monster before it trys to EVOLVE! and turn the tydes and make the Hunters the hunted.
Each Class has a role to play in finding and defeating  the monster.  At the time of the Alpha there were only 8 hunters, 2 monsters and 3 maps)
The assault class is the damage dealer in the group and keep the monsters attention. I Mainly played this class.
The Trapper classes job is to track down the monster and Trap it with  harppons to slow the monster down and they have a mobile arena that forces the monster to fight the hunters.
The Support class can use a wide array of diffrent items depending on the character you pick. You might have a missle bonbarment designator, an item that shealds players from damage and an invisability modual that clokes all allies so they can  flee from the monster.
The medic class is there to heal up teammates with their medic guns. They also have tranqulizers to slow down the monsters Movments. I did not get a chance to play much as the medic during the alpha so I dont know all they can do.
Then we have a STAR of the whole game the MONSTER! The person playing the monster has three tasks. In the early start of the match the monsters main objective is to put as much distance between them and the hunters and feed on the wild life and Gain Armor and EVOLVE to your next 2 stages before taking the fight to the Hunters because the monster is at a disadvantage early on at stage one of there evolution and can be killed quite fast. Stage two evens the playing feald you are no longer at a disadvantage to the hunters your and even match for them and at stage three your the hunters worst nightmare dealing Massive amounts of damge! You also have an optional objective to destoy a relay station designated on the map but you can only destroy it when your fully evolved. When you first start as the monster you have 3 points to spend in 4 diffrent skills to help you aginst the hunters you can put all or points is one skill or spend them on multiple ones. You gain 3 more points to spend at stage 2 and 3 more when your fully evolved at stage 3.
(During the alpha there were only 2 monsters avaliabe the goliath a giant power house that throws rocks and breaths fire and the Kraken the flying cephalopod that shoots lighting bolts and land mines that follows the huntes and exploed on contact)
The full relase of the game will have 12 hunters, 3 monsers and 12 maps.
From what i have played its very polished even in alpha, I am excited to play more when the game is finished.

Before reading, remember that there are going to be some spoilers ahead.
The way that
presents itself is a bit misleading.
It starts as a guide in how to make game levels, but the focus is not about the levels themselves.  The levels are really a way to present its story.  The story revolves around Davey the narrator’s experience playing the projects created by a programmer simply called Coda.  For those that do not know, Coda is a term that means the end of a song or story.  The fact that a mystery person called that instead of a normal name or a typical screen name lets everybody know that the person is not a real person.  The thing that makes this name even more out of place is that all the projects have a start, but they never have any ending.
As for the various projects, they feel more like random chaos.  As the story progresses, the narrator presents a star base where the player has a gun but no enemies, a stage without an audience, and a house with nonstop housecleaning.  There is even one where the user is supposed to do the game while blind without any audio clue.  Even for incomplete projects, they feel like multiple people instead of a single person created them.
What brings all the random projects together is the final one.  During that project, everything is for keeping the user, the narrator specifically, from reaching the end.  This includes a door that is impossible to open from the front side.  Through hacks, the narrator allows the viewer to continue.  After progressing a little further, several messages show how Coda really about everything Davey done.  He then admits the entire collection is simply to get Coda attention to apologize and to get back to making games again.  He even goes so far as to say his real e-mail in order to try getting Coda to talk again.  However, since Coda is not a real person, the e-mail is for us to send feedback to Davey instead—something that he hopes that many people do.
Is it worth 10 dollars for a visual story that last a little more than an hour?  Personally, I do not think so.  However, if you do find an opportunity to see the story, it might be worth the time to see it.  It could give something to think about afterwards.  For those not interested in the story, the evolution of the game does act as a beginner's guide.  For inspiring game designers, it could even teach how to make games.

First of all, since this is a tease/demo and not a fully fledged game it will be treated as one. Thus this review is gonna be much more favorable to this experience than a normal review would be.
Okay, Medusa's Labyrinth is a survival horror game set in the catacombs of a temple in Ancient Greece. I have to give props to Guru Games on this one. This is a very original and well-thought setting for a horror game.
So the gameplay. Medusa's library starts off pretty well. The amazing sound-effects, the whole aesthetic and the moment you start descending into the catacombs, it was spot on and loved every second of it. I also liked the music in the game. I find it pretty fitting. Graphics were also fine and did their job well.
The documents are a nice touch, as you can learn about the origins of the Medusa (at least i think it was Medusa, maybe i'm wrong, i dunno. It was a nice touch none the less) Also, a small detail that i really liked is that the breath of the character becomes faster and louder when seeing an enemy get close.
However, the game has it's fair share of negatives.
The game later on when things get tense and enemies show up, becomes kinda repetitive and loses the charm it had during the beginning. The enemies are one-shot, they dont change at all during the whole gameplay, thus you gonna see the same model everytime. The catacombs remain the same design during the whole experience not changing one bit. The map is linear, meaning that the whole concept of a labyrith is thrown out of the window and also the whole torches think is pretty much useless since you can pass the whole game without lights because even without them you can faintly see where you are going.
In the end the whole experience becomes kind of a mixed bug. Guru games clearly have some talent and passion in game developing. Like i said, the aesthetic was there and again, the sound-effects were spot on but the negatives throw a shadow over the good aspects of the game.
I would love to see the Medusa project finished. With polishing, more diverse gameplay and more time and budget i believe this can become a great horror game. At the time being, this is good but unfinished. It deserves however a recommendation, because i did have fun in this game, it had a strong horror factor and it is a good teaser.

Well this was underwhelming. I'll vote the game down. Why? Because if one buys the Anthology, he won't care about this at all. But if someone checks the individual games, maybe gets a little look into the game, and I hope that can understand this. To be really short: game is too short, quite shallow, less guns, less varied environments - nowhere as good as HL or Opposing Forces.
HL Blue Shift currently stands at 90% positive reviews, while HL and Opposing Forces if I remember well has 96% and 95%  positives, and I have to agree with the trend - the game was fine, but not even as good as HL (This is my third, final review of the anthology - in my book Opposing Forces > Half-Life > Blue Shift, simply based amount the fun I had while playing)
The game features a really awesome physics based puzzle (barrels in coolant), had a fun part shooting gas cannisters' top to make them shoot at a door, and a barrel-detonator puzzle  which is really questionable in my opinion.
Otherwise this game feels like a well-written, longer trailer for Half-Life. Alien contact's majority are headcrabs, there are maybe two Alien Grunts and Masters - the enemy variety could have been better from the gameplay aspect - the lack of stronger enemies really felt like the protagonist is away from the bigger happenings, making him feel like an underdog.

is a very rare type of game subgenre within the horror genre that the developer wanted to convey. It is not that it is scary by any means, but through a very vivid and creepy soundtrack, the environment becomes an enthralling trudging through Greek mythology. Yes, the game is very short and can be completed within one sitting at around thirty minutes depending on skill. However, if you want to take in the environment, read all the notes left along the way, which are divided into parts, until the whole story invested into Greek culture is explained, it can take around one hour. While I do not expect this game to rise in popularity on the charts of top free-to-play games, I would recommend this game for anyone who has a very thorough and loving appreciation for Greek mythology and ancient civilizations, especially Roman civilization.
One of the primary features of
that stands out is its immersive sound design. It is as if you can hear the groans, coughing, and sickness among the people that came before, and although you never encounter human characters in the game nor does the story ever reveal if they died somehow by later discovering Medusa, the notes we find along the way depict a traveler’s thoughts. In fact, the traveler’s mother and father who sent this girl named Aloyna to the temple to become an oracle- one who is a person of wisdom as either a priest or priestess for whom advice and counsel was always sought because they were supposed to be the wisest of all people when it came to knowledge of the natural world. We see more of this theme of oracles that occurs readily in Plato’s famous book Euthyphro, which depicts the dialogue of events and people in Socrates life right before his trial took place. This was when Socrates was seventy years old in the year 399 BCE (cf. p.47,
, Reeve & Miller).
Miletus condemned Socrates in the trial based of impiety. It was not just the distinction between pious and impious acts of moral ethics that was the topic of discussion during Socrates time, but a discussion that ran rampant in the idea that Euthyphro, who was a wise scribe at the time, was believed to have corrupted the youth. He despised anyone who may have taught a philosophy that was seen by the community as deceptive and not something that was taught to them. This is interesting because in Greek culture, much like a priest in monism is ordained for their teachings, oracles must affirm in polytheism that any individual’s teachings are regulatory in the bounds not of opinion but of human interest.  On the other hand, in
, there is not much story, except for the sections of notes we can piece together to at least presume what has happened to those who came before in the temple. It seems, that some people were held captive and taken as prisoners down in Medusa’s liar and they only have a limited time to make it out before the doors will be shut for good and they will be trapped in a underground hell of catacombs and tunnel sections.

I have stayed away from this game for a while due to its low ratings, but decided to buy it during the christmas sale. I wanted to play it for myself to see how it was. Here are my thoughts from just an hour and a half of playtime.
Pros:
+ Has something like a main quest line
+ Has mini events that appear on the planet, with objectives
+ Has a crafting system with trees that look like they have a reasonable amount of items
+ Has an npc with a bunch of dialogue, uncommon for this genre
+ Has a strange (but interesting) artstyle that reminds me of AVwW, but a little different
+ Some of the equipment looks well drawn, and very nice as future outfits
Cons:
- Crafting system requires large amounts of materials to make mundane or low tier objects
- Enemies and destructibles drop lots of loot and it feels like my inventory is weighed down with junk just a few minutes into the game
- The tiered system for items/crafting isn't intuitive or sensible (other than weapons/tools named "Mk. 1", "Mk.2", etc.)
- The tiers locking you out of building or crafting some items feel arbitrary despite being in an already arbitrary game setting
- Mining the necessary materials for the beginning quests or items is very slow, boring, and repetitive; it's so unengaging that it feels like busy work
- Mining laterally is A PAIN at times because the laser eminates from your upper chest and you can't mine a straight line below or above that level due to that constraint - you have to mine extra blocks to get line of sight for your laser (which technically makes sense, but this isn't real life and an arbitration could be made here, even just letting us CROUCH would fix half of the problem)
- Moving the character is clunky, you stop on a dime and using the jetpack arrests upward movement to begin a slow acceleration upward (but using the jetpack to slow your fall does very little to slow you unless you were already falling at a slow speed)
- The npc with dialogue is annoying, makes annoying sounds each time you respond to it, and doesn't help you with the early game much other than telling you what the tutorial pane (accessed with the U key) does.
- Several parts of the game are very arbitrary, like being magically unable to mine in an event area until you complete the event (but then able to mine with no problem afterward)
Conclusion: The game almost has the barebones of a sandbox crafting adventure game, with what looks like a reasonable amount of content added in. But content doesn't make a game, it only adds to it. The base gameplay, the platforming, the item collection and crafting, just feels bad. It does not feel finished. It feels like a prototype with extra content.

My first few characters died horrible deaths from hypothermia, dysentery, and wolf induced wounds.
The one that made it past the initial learning curve thrived. I set up a base camp in an abandoned cabin near the entrance to a lake, made it a place to stockpile supplies. The frozen corpse upstairs didn’t help the atmosphere, but it was as close to home as possible. Seven days past while scavenging the lake and surrounding area. Firewood was running low and I needed to find a few tree saplings to craft a bow and arrow. After all, the rifle I found only had a few rounds that wouldn’t last forever. So off I went in the morning, following a frozen river in hopes of stumbling on to small trees. As the day marched on, a deer galloped out of the forest and stopped a hundred feet away. There was plenty of meat left in the cabin so no reason to waste a precious bullet. Besides, a wolf was pacing back and forth just in view; a rifle round could mean the difference between life and death. Having spotted the dear but not my character, the wolf changed course. It growled and sprinted forward. The deer fled in terror. I had no idea wolfs could attack other wildlife – this entire event was unexpected, and the catalyst for a worst night for my character had yet to encounter.
Realizing the wolf would likely catch the deer and kill it, I sprinted after them both. Letting the wolf do my dirty work and expending a single rifle round for double the meat was just too good an opportunity to ignore. As I crested the first hill, I saw the wolf crouched over and feasting on the deer. Its back was turned; it hadn’t yet noticed me. Crouching to reduce noise, I approached closer from the wolf’s blind spot until there was no chance of missing a head shot. The rifle sights lined up, and with a crack that echoed through the valley the wolf dropped. Eager to survey my kills before they froze, I ran to them. There is 29 pounds of meat, two guts, and one hide from the deer along with 17 pounds of meat, two guts, and one hide from the wolf – a very good haul. However, it took more than five hours to harvest. By this time, my character is hungry, thirsty, tired, and very cold. Thirst, hunger, and energy I can fix; I never leave the cabin without 2000 calories of food, a gallon of water, and several tins of coffee. Cold is the real enemy here, and now I am too encumbered to walk quickly. There’s still a few hours left in the day so I can take the time to make a fire and warm up. I can even cook some of this meat so I don’t waste the heat. While building the campfire, I hear a growl. Another wolf has found me and is approaching, ready to attack. The fire keeps it at bay for now it seems, even while I’m in the process of building it. If the fire fails to start, I know the wolf will attack me. Luckily, the fire ignites and the wolf stays on the boundary. Stupid animal, I still have ammunition for my rifle. It’s an easy kill shot. There’s no leaving behind the meat, so I stoke the fire and harvest the second wolf. Night is coming – it’s time to head back to the cabin.
I barely make it a quarter of the way before energy levels become an issue again. The coffee has worn off and I’m cold again. It’s a long trek back and I’m holding twice my carry capacity, a capacity which is fading the more tired and hungry I become. Visibility has also reduced so it’s time to call it and spend the night under the stars. Except this was supposed to be a day trip; I left the heavy bedroll in the cabin. How unfortunate. More coffee it is. I build a fire and warm a single cup of the caffeinated beverage before the wind picks and rudely extinguishes my source of heat. Little did I know this was the start of a blizzard that would rage deep into the night.
The campfire no longer an option and any guiding torch I could make wishful thinking, I move in the direction I think the train tracks are in. I can’t be sure which way I’m heading as visibility has dropped to nothing as the snowy wind reached deafening speeds. A lucky press of hot keys reminds me I have a storm lantern! Lighting it eagerly, I press on. I’m grateful for the increased light and warmth, but it isn’t enough to guide me or save me from hypothermia. Train tracks emerge from the dark; I was correct about the direction of travel. Now which way to go? Picking a direction that feels like a path to the cabin, I continue. Another wolf appears from the tree line but I’m too slow to run and too slow to change back to the rifle. We fight, ending with the wolf receiving a hunting knife to the sternum and me losing my boots. It yelps and slinks off, but I can’t risk going after it to harvest its meat. At this point, it might be best to drop what I have to move faster anyway. The train track fall away under piles of snow, this obscures them from view. I think an indent in the rock walls looks like where I should turn to reach the cabin.
Except all I find is more rock wall. My character is dying from cold, hunger, and sleep deprivation. I’ve lost all bearings in the blizzard and no longer know which way the train tracks are, which way the cabin is, or even where I just came from. The wind is raging on, making a campfire impossible. The fuel in the lantern is fading. This is the end. This is how my character dies. I, outside the game, am breathing heavily and panicking with legitimate anxiety, fear, and readiness to give into the elements despite permanent death. This is the moment I realized The Long Dark is something special worth playing. A game that evokes this level of emotion and draws you back in time and again is rare. One that accomplishes it in so little time over the course of a single event is even rarer.
This story does have a happy ending. I stopped next to another rock wall and discovered it was positioned in such a way that it blocked the wind. This allowed me to build a fire, which in turn allowed me to warm up, heat up coffee, cook meat, and melt water. I waited out the blizzard there and made it back to the cabin where my character still survives.
EDIT: Died on day 12 after bleeding out from a wolf bite. I didn’t have any bandages and didn’t realize you could make some from cloth.

When I initially bought the game a few years back, it was very barebones. It had one region and was initially, a very difficult game. What hooked me in was how the devs were approaching it and how much I enjoyed just walking around in the beautiful environment that they have made. The game started to get fun once I played it more.
The gameplay in The Long Dark is unique among other survival games i have played before it. It always is challenging and I can never know quite what to expect when I leave my shelter in the morning. The weather is something you need to worry about at all times, as more than an hour outside in a snow-storm can kill you. The crafting system is interesting, letting you collect resources and use them to craft such items as: clothing, weapons, medical supplies, equipment, and much more. The game challenges you and has regions for all different types of players from the casual people who just want to look at the scenery, to hardcore survival fanatics who want to be forced into situations where choosing the wrong path can mean certain death.
If there was something the devs should pride themselves in, its that this game has beautiful scenery and audio. The subtle sounds of deer running in the distance, to the terrifying howls of wolves, to your character commenting on their immediate surroundings. The art style is gorgeous and is very unique, making it feel amazingly realistic, without destroying your computer. The sounds of yourself walking, echoing through the desolate forests and abandoned buildings give you an amazing appreciation for games that take time and care into giving you an amazing feel not just gameplay.
This game is, simply put, the greatest early access game I have ever played. The game captivates me with its stunning visuals and terrifies me with its audio and enemies. The feeling of loneliness is overpowering and finding that one item you have been searching for for so long makes you feel amazing inside. Survival is the name of the game and it holds up its listing in that genre like no other. The game challenges you and rewards you constantly, making it never a boring time playing through. Everything I love in video games put into 1.

Bioshock, the game that became and instant classic. The beautiful set design, character design, research, and thought that went into this game made it a solid argument for video games being art.
The game is based on Ayn Rand's novel Atlas which was a fictional representation of her personal philosphy. She believed that if a person worked for something then it should be theirs. She believed the government had no right to tax of you of your hard earned cash to pay for people who didn't or couldn't work. That government and religion had no place dictating science, art, and industry. That religion and oppressive governments were corrupt and holding us back. She believed that we could only be a great society if everyone worked hard together to create a new society where the individual rights ruled. While this all sounds good on paper, how would it actually work in real life? People are rarely the saints Rand's philosophy would need you to be to work.
This is where Bioshock comes in. Andrew Ryan believed strongly in Rand's philophy and so set about creating a new nation away from the world's corrupt influinces. In the 1930's he began building a city, Rapture, under the Atlantic Ocean. Once finished he invited the world's greatest scientists, artists, and businessmen to join him in Rapture. Things seemed to be going fine for a while but a society with no limits or review process on scientific discovery,  the harmfulness of products being sold, or safety net for the poor and disenfranchised is a ticking time bomb.
The seething anger of the lower classes explode when a product called Adam is put on the market. This new scientific discovery can rewrite your dna to give you superpowers, change your looks, your gender, or even your race. But it has a cancer like effect on the mind and body, driving it's users insane the more they use it. War breaks out.
The game then starts with a man named Jack on an airplane that promptly crashes right at the surface entrence to Rapture. Jack has to fight his way through the city, battling the insane and twisted denizens, to try and find a way back to the surface. Along the way he has no choice but to use Adam to survive. You have access to several superpowers such as throwing fire, hypnotizing your enemies into fighting for you, freezing into blocks of ice, controling cameras and turrets, etc.
Along the way you will be faced with moral choices and a growing inability to recognize friend from foe.
I highly reccomend this game. The story line is dark and full of twists, the scenery is beautiful and tragic, and the voice acting is top notch.

I absolutely love this game. It's a must if you like puzzles. I played it through in one sitting.
The game is a bit slow to start with, but after clicking around a bit, it's pretty easy to figure out the overall goals. You move through one insect body to the next (in each stage),

Just point and click/drag. Sometimes your bug will have a

Simple, ambient instrumental melodies. I wish there was a soundtrack for the game.

Disclosure: I bought this game due to a recommendation by a friend, P. Johnston, rather than my personal interest. I did not receive the game for free.
There is no plot that I’m aware of, but due to this being a puzzle game, I have not included it against the overall score.
You flip over red or blue cards to reveal pictures. Let’s say you’re on the red team. If you match your own cards, red, you damage yourself. If you match the opponent’s cards, blue, you damage them instead. Unlike a match-3 game, there is a much higher ratio of skill to RNG.
At the end of the day, you as a human player are not going to beat a
in a memory game. Though there are sliders for difficulty, it feels a bit contrived. I did not try the online functionality for the following reasons.
The animations are really slow. This is a problem between the synergy of gameplay and graphics. In an attempt to spice up the graphical presentation of the game, long animations slow down the flow of gameplay. Any time you flip a tile or do damage, you’re waiting for about one to two seconds for anything else to happen. This pacing is
slow for a puzzle fanatic.
This is a generous score that considers the newness of the developer and the genre of the game — puzzle. Puzzle tiles need to be clean and easy to recognize. Avatars, not participating in actual gameplay, should have at least some memorable characteristics. Though I can appreciate the tidy, uniform tiles/icons used in matching, there’s absolutely nothing memorable or special about the tiles/icons used.
I believe the tiles/icons are all dangerous things, like lightning, fire, Molotov cocktails, etc. Some of them are a little more abstract like snowflakes, hammers, or buzzsaws. There were a few tiles/icons that I couldn’t identify. There’s one that reminds me of a holy trinity or celtic knot shape, but less ornate. It’s harder to remember because I’m not even sure what to call it. That’s a very small complaint.
As for the avatars, I’ll give points for them being animated, but I’ve seen better from F2P flash games. Not interesting or unique, despite being the mascots for the game.
Wildly uninspiring. Both music and sound effects are not memorable.
If I wanted to crush young children with my memory skills or get owned by a computer, I’d go to Neopets.
Has a bit of polish to it, but lacks the heart or addictive nature of a flash game.
I have more hope for a second game, if there is one.

Morphopolis, a simple yet intriguing game. A pathway made to learn the morphology of the small creatures living in unseen ground. Playing a tiny creature gathering and evolving to the next stage. It is an abstract except realistic concept of evolution.
You are first invited by the artistic style of visual artwork as you soon immerse into the world of insects. The visual layout is painted into 2-Dimensional layers which creates the 3-Dimensional atmosphere and depth. The colours are all earthy and saturated which emphasises the textural tone of the visual design. The creator really has brought out the artistic feel and paintings to life.
The controls are fairly simply and all movement is controlled by a simple mouse clicks. The character moves by holding down the mouse as the character moves towards it. This development of movement is a really nice touch towards the essence of the lower level world. However I do have to complain that there is no quicker movement. Travelling back screens if you missed pieces is very tedious as you are trapped in the sluggish movement of your creature, but at least it does give some reason on how these bugs move. That they travel at their own pace and shouldn’t be rushed. Controlling movement around objects and towards areas can be fiddly as the direction is not always accurate when you want to turn above and right except it just goes straight up. At least it has a unique style of movement and is a patient game as you find the items.
All in All Morphopolis is a really nice Puzzle Game!

Cons: There are a few cons, and they are mostly inherent to the genre. Like most survival games, you will die often in the beginning. Survival depends on learning lots of idiosyncratic tricks. Retreading the same ground which you have covered many times before is boring. Fear of being bored again is not really the ideal motivator. It would have been nice if the same inventiveness which went into creating the world also went into your character. Unfortunately, your character is kept vague. This not in order to have a universal protagonist who will appeal to everybody, because you choose a gender and a backstory. It's just that none of that matters, and very little character development occurs after that point. Even when livechanging events occur to your character, like having your organs converted into crystal or falling in love with a mysterious character, it doesn't affect your gameplay.

I don't play tower defence games anymore, because I have this game instead. If you don't see the appeal to tower defence at all, this game is not for you. If you've got the tower defence itch, this game will scratch it until it bleeds.
This game doesn't have an undo button, so push your luck too far and it's game over. I know why that would put some people off, but it works for this game.
Why is this better than tower defence? In any good tower defence game, getting good at it means learning how the towers work and how each enemy type works. Once you've figured that out, there's not much left to learn or do.
With this game, the trains behave the same way (at different speeds) and the track laying rules are intuitive. Will you overpopulate your grid with trains to build up money, or will you play it safer with collissions, but risk facing bankruptcy? Can you time them perfectly so they almost hit but don't? What is the best configuration for the tracks? Is it worth paying extra to demolish your way through a shortcut? These dilemmas you get to face from game 1, without having to remember what does what.
There is only one change I would make to this game if I were the developer, and that is this: When the game is paused, I want to still be able to see which trains are going full speed and which trains have only started moving. As a father, I love a game that I can pause and come back to after a nappy change, but I often forget which trains are going full speed and which are not by the time I return.

I've been looking for something to scratch the Transport / Railroad Tycoon itch for a while now, and although there are some potentially promising games on the horizon, it seemed like there were no good examples in the genre at the moment.
And then I stumbled upon Train Valley, which, within a few minutes of playing confirms that the above is true - this isn't a tycoon game.  What it is, is a puzzle game - and once you get a few levels in, it's fiendish.  It conjurs up the correct mix of raising a smile when things go to plan, and swearing at your screen when you get overwhelmed and the inevitable happens - and trains crash.
The premise is simple; you are given a grid and two coloured stations on each map, and you drag lines from one to the other, avoiding or bulldozing (at a cost) your way through buildings and trees, some of which are randomly placed whilst some are always in the same place.  Trains will spawn in the stations with a colour indicating that they want you to direct them to the other station, you click to launch the train and it makes its way down the track and you get paid when it arrives - each train has a value which ticks down from the moment it spawns to the moment it arrives at the destination.  The complexity comes in as the map progresses.  New stations will spawn on the map - in predetermined positions but in a random order, and begin to spawn trains all eager to go somewhere else.  You will lay more tracks, launch trains, and use the track switches to try and avoid a catastrophe.  Fortunately you can stop and reverse trains, but this doesn't always help if you're not keeping a good watch out - only one train can occupy a station, so it will launch itself if a second one is about to spawn.
The difficultly ramps up; early maps serve to teach you the basics and later ones cram stations in awkward places with choke points to force trains onto the same pieces of track.  When things go well, it's great - but sometimes, you just can't avoid an explosion.
Back to my search for a tycoon game - even though this clearly isn't one, the art style and simple way of laying track would lend itself very well to a more in depth strategy game which, if I were the developer, I'd seriously consider.

-Good destructive fun
-Much more content than FlatOut 1 with Race and Street mode, with lots of new Events.
-There are too many forks/alternate routes that lead to manufactured collisions compared to FlatOut 1.
-The destruction overall is much more manufactured than FlatOut 1. Most of the time you can either choose to jump, which will lead to a crash, or you can drive to the side which either has obstacles/a pipe on the floor which will make you spin. That's not a lot of fun and can get pretty frustrating.
-College Rock soundtrack isn't really to my taste.
-There are some small audio bugs such as glitched engine noise, no engine noise and tinny sound quality (especially in tunnels), and visual bugs such as clipping.
- Tracks just have way too much clutter on them. In FlatOut 1 most of the clutter came from tyres from tyre walls, in FlatOut 2 you have all kinds of clutter that obscure the view of the track. Most of the clutter also has 'weight' which means that if you drive into it then you'll collide with it instead of just driving over it or through it. This normally wouldn't be so bad, but because there is so much clutter it usually covers the width of the track so you have no choice but to collide into it. Driving in 1st person mode it can get very tricky when this clutter attaches itself to the bonnet of the car, obscuring your entire view and making you have to change camera. That's just poor design.
The game has partial controller support with the racing being fine with the gamepad but the menus are only navigational with a keyboard.
Overall it's not a bad game, if you haven't played FlatOut 1. FlatOut 2 has more content, but I much preferred the track design and organic destruction of FlatOut 1.

My priority for games goes in this order: Atmosphere > music + visuals > gameplay.
While I appreciate a challenge I prefer to simply get lost in a great atmosphere. I'm also not into multiplayer gaming. I like my adventures solo. THE LONG DARK is  everything I've always dreamed of for an atmospheric single-player adventure-survival game. Seriously, the atmosphere in this game is incredible. I don't normally like scavenging and crafting either, but this game actually makes you care about your survival so you'll do whatever it takes. This is an emotionally involving game that makes you care. You can see the love and thought that the developers have put into crafting this unique and involving experience.
PROS
+ Incredible atmosphere
+ It makes you care about your survival
+ It makes you want to explore
+ Beautiful scenery
+ Subtle use of music
+ Day / Night cycle
+ Brilliant weather effects
+ Compelling Scavenging and crafting
CONS
- No jump (it just feels weird not being able to jump over little things)
- 99% of indoor environments are disconnected from outdoor (e.g. 'loading')
- Loading time between major outdoor areas too (it reminds me I'm playing a game)
- Inventory management is slightly annoying
- A bit of scenery pop-up (could just be my crusty video card)
- No storymode (yet)
SUMMARY
Personally, this is everything I've always wanted from a survival game. It's got an incredible atmosphere and it makes me care about my survival. I really look forward to seeing how this develops.

Day 2, I was pretty geared up.  I had a rifle, and some food, however I had run out of water. I decided to trek out in the morning, as I was quite parched. I came upon a derailed train and spotted a wolf beside it, and I quickly thought to myself, "If I engage this wolf, will my rifle be enough?" He engaged me first, and he ran at me snarling, I fired off a shot and, "oh what a surprise, I missed!" He tackles me into the snowbank, I fight for my life, and eventually I win and throw him away. He began running but I wasn't having any of that. He tore my jacket wide open and sprained my ankle, why would I let him escape? I began chasing him, but he was ready. In retaliation for me chasing him he turned around and began counter-charging. Ofcourse I had my rifle ready this time, yet I barely managed to graze him, he went down! I started cutting him open, good eats tonight! However my conditions are worsening. I'm freezing, my ankles are broken, and I'm still thirsty. I begin running for about 10 seconds until I spot a small overhang. (7% Condition Overall Now) I put the last of my twigs together, and just barely managed to create a fire. I sat by the fire cooking my fish. As I'm about to eat the delightful lake trout, I hear something coming up behind me! I stumble backwards into my fire, and fall to the ground. (2% Condition!) I can barely see now, life is fading away...
On the other side of the fire, a wolf stares at me. With a last moment memory, I pulled out a flare. "Flares can be used to scare away animals" as said in their descriptions; so I light this sucker up, and with my last breaths I throw it at the wolf. Success, he runs! I feel so achieved but so broken, and I know I have to find shelter. I begin sprinting, (Crawling on the ground fast at this rate.) It's so blurry, I can't see! Where should I go? I follow the tracks, but too my demise, they were the last things I ever saw...
AMAZING GAME, I was genuinely scared by that wolf at the fire, the immersion is unreal.

Story
You are Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist who hears that illegal activity is happening in Mount Massive Asylum and you enter the asylum to investigate. Miles gets trapped in the asylum and your goal is to escape. It's basic but the game has memorable moments and characters. You get to learn about characters like Chris Walker and The Walrider through the games documents, which are the game's collectibles.
Gameplay
The gameplay is quite simple, but very fun. You use a camcorder to record events in the asylum and you use your night vision to see in the dark. But you can't use night vision all of the time becuase you have a limited amount of batteries. As for combat, there is none, all you can do is run and hide. The lack of combat does not make this game boring at all, in fact, it just makes it more intense and horrifying.
Graphics and Atmosphere
Graphics don't make a game better or worse, but Outlast does have solid graphics and a great atmosphere. The atmosphere in Outlast changes as you explore many different locations in the asylum. But there's not a single location where you feel safe. You might be walking through a fully lit hallway, but that jumpscare is still more than likely going to get you.
Overall
Outlast takes 4-5 hours to complete. That may seem short for a $20 game, but you can get it on sale for under $10 and it's most definitely worth the price. In general, Outlast is a great horror game and it's worth at least one playthrough.
I loved it and I highly recommend it.

The Long Dark was my favorite game for a while, but I found myself falling out of love with it. The landscape is gorgeous and exploring the world for the first time was a great experience, but long-term survival is where the game falls short. I'm hoping that they'll rebalance some things so that the game is more realistic in some aspects, but right now it seems a bit ridiculous.
Pros:
+Beautiful landscape
+The map is laid out really well for spacing between points of interest
+There are a lot of ways to get food and supplies, so you aren't forced into a grind
Cons:
-The animals are super dumb. If you scare one, it will run straight ahead wherever it's facing and bounce like a pinball everywhere, even straight through you.
-The thirst meter is poorly paced. You need to drink every 7-8 hours or you will become dehydrated, meaning that you can't get a full night's sleep without beginning to die.
-Some easy tasks take way longer than they should. Drinking a couple ounces of water takes several minutes. Opening a can takes like 15 minutes. It wastes daylight.
-Spoilage is a big problem. At one point you will have much more food than you need and there's no way to preserve it. Then you can take a gamble for food poisoning on food that's going bad or just leave it. Soda cans and sealed crackers don't spoil in a week, come on.
-Important tools have no viable alternative in the late game. If you run out of whetstones, you're pretty much dead since the homemade knife is much worse and can't be sharpened.
The early game is really fun, gathering important tools and exploring the land. The late game is terrible, since there's no real objective other than surviving and important resources will run out and can't be replaced. 5/10.
Enjoying this so much now, even though it's a WIP. Can't wait for bugs to be ironed out and a few other things implemented so we can enjoy this with a bunch of friends on multiplayer too!

Sunless Sea is a game with an amazing sountrack, beautiful art design, and some of the best writing that has ever graced video games. That being said, it's not for everyone. The pacing can be rather slow at the early to midgame, and there are some rather odd balance issues. Combat is relatively weak but works well enough. Going into this game, you should be going in mainly for the, again, absolutely phenomenal story and the incredible world that Failbetter has managed to create. Those buying this game out of a "roguelike" perception or those looking for a fast-paced, action-filled game, I would encourage to look elsewhere.
To expand on the roguelike comment, Sunless Sea is hard. Very hard. Unless you do one of two things: learn through experience (once you know general locations and where you can buy fuel/supplies or the optimal ways to finish important storylines, like the last curator, the game becomes much easier) or using the wiki to accomplish the same goal. I highly recommend the former (and that's not to be elitist - I'm a wiki addict and it made the game much easier for me) for at least a few runs, consulting the wiki if you truly need help.
All in all, I strongly recommend Sunless Sea for its fantastic writing, incredibly varied environments, and beautiful soundtrack, but not quite for its gameplay.

In fact should you in any way try to give a similar origin story to an original character it would be considered a lazy move and the author a hack. We've all seen it in movies, read in comics, watched in cartoons, basically Batman is a beloved hero by many but his origin story is not something you want to see for the
. Nonetheless, Telltale manages to put a nice, modern spin to it which keeps the material fresh enough for the player to be invested in.
I'm gonna start off by saying, that the episodes played out beautifully and if the game was a movie I'd have to say that the cinematography and direction were brilliant. The game's story is more focused and cohesive and goes from place to place seamlessly while at the same time keeping the player on the edge of their seat.
Without going into too many spoilers, it's always refreshing to see/play Batman series which are clearly divergent from that cartoon/comic feel. Batman feels real, like these events could actually happen in a realistic scenario, regardless of how truly far-fetched they might appear. Villains retain their comic book looks while at the same time show more depth into their personalities and motives for their actions. Their relationship with Batman goes beyond a cartoony one-dimensional thought bubble, "I'm gonna get ya Batsy!", and instead flows outward into creating doubts even inside your own head "I would probably hate Batman too if I was Two-face/Penguin/etc.".
It humanizes the villain and such an approach I believe is the strongest when trying to relate with a story. There's no black & white morality code yet at the same time you don't live on a constant dubious greyscale world which is also equally uninspiring and sophomoric for the player/viewer. Actions have consequences, convictions are challenged, paths are recalculated and so on. I will note however on the aspect of the
when it comes to Telltale games. That is too say that some events cannot be differentiated too much regardless of your choices but from what I've seen/played, despite the inevitability of such a modicum, there's plenty of room to have fun with what you say/do as Batman.
Telltale managed to make an already tiring origin story intriguing enough. Sure there's some bad dialogue here and there, some awkward moments between characters but the spirit of the the game never strays too far from other titles you've come to known and love like
and
. And while it might not have the humor from TFTB or the emotional weight of TWD, there's some pretty good story and characters in Batman.
The quick time events are improved and dare I say are
less unforgiving than before. Not that there was anything inherently hard in the past, but now even if your reflexes are a bit slower, there's a bit of leeway until you press the correct prompt. The 'investigation' mode and the action sequence battles were also pleasant surprises which I'd love to see in any future Telltale games.
But it wouldn't be the 'new' Telltale games without some technical issues. I had a couple of crashes during my playthrough, the loading times when you enter the game are atrocious (because the game checks Every.Single.Time for DLC even though I had the full game installed), cloud saving takes forever and there's even some micro-stuttering between chapters per episode. These issues have become a worrying trend when it comes to new Telltale games and while they might not be draining from the experience that much, they have become unfortunately a sore spot and a deterrent for normal pricing buys.
To sum up, if you're a Telltale fan then I see no reason to skip this. Batman fans will also enjoy this deviation from the standard origin story and a new twist on classic characters like Penguin, Two-face, Catwoman and Joker. However because the game still has some minor technical issues and because of its shorter length than previous Telltale titles, I'd recommend getting this game on a sale. I got this for about $5 and for that amount of money I was thoroughly entertained. With the ongoing release of the episodes for the second season, I'm hopeful we'll see less of the technical issues and more of the good storytelling that Telltale has brought us over the years.

So I decided to go out on a limb and board the Hype Train to FNAF-ville, after trying to stay as far away from it as possible.
Having said that, I haven't even paid for this game; somebody who owns it library-shares with me, so if anything I'm more of a stowaway if anything.
So far, recent releases have been tech prototypes, new engines, and AAA releases with slightly moister skin textures than the last iteration in the♥♥♥♥♥♥of Duty and Battle♥♥♥♥ series, so the break to Indie Horror was a nice one. This game dumps you in a security office in a corrupted chucky-cheese of sorts, where Fred and his rather♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of mates drank one too many Carlsbergs and decided their newfound anger was to be taken out on yours truly. Your task is to defend yourself using a camera which covers your entire field of view while being checked (because gameplay, I suppose) and some gravity defying doors, which lock
when you run out of power. Personally, I'd rather have the door stay shut when I run out of power, and being crowbarred out in the morning. I don't see anything wrong with a filing-cabinet barricade either, in all honesty.
As mentioned earlier, you also have to keep an eye on your power, because Fazbear's Fez Restaurant appears to be run by scratty pickpocketers who love saving money so much, they dich the power grid for on-site batteries. If you run out of power, you die. If you are inept with your camera usage and gravity-defying door closing, you die. The gameplay is okay, most certaintly difficult, but it leaves a lot to be desired. A stack of planks, some nails and a hammer would be appreciated at times.
Possibly my favourite feature about this game is the fact that if you get too tensed up by this game's rather unsettling environment, you can just mash ESC and bail straight out to your pre-prepared fluffy kitten pictures you have ready on your desktop. Being the nerd who gets picked on myself, as well as being a socially awkward nobhead, I kind of wish I had one in real life, to bail out of awkard situations. If that was a thing, I could just pull out a keyboard, mash ESC, then sprout a jetpack and fly into the sun next time I drop my M&Ms in the shopping centre, which would be nice.
Do I like Five Night's at Freddy's? The atmosphere drives me nuts to a point where I often have to stop playing, but I can't help but not only wander why the difficulty curve is so steep, but to also wander why the security officer hasn't just bought a gun into work, or just flat-out quit his job yet.

Ok, let's get over the misconception first: No matter what the dumb user defined tags say, this is not a sim. This is an active puzzle game, that just happens to involve trains.

Personally I love the fact that there's a speed function that lets me play fast and just pause when I need to, it makes for a super great challenge (until they put in no pausing as a stamp requirement in the new DLC that made me sad).
I personally experienced no crashes of any sort, only in the DLC did I have a bit of a bug where the main menu wouldn't pop up if I hit escape, which was basically just a trifling annoyance.
To sum it up: I love finding little unknown games like this which I end up enjoying way more than I ever thought I would, and I'm highly looking forward to future DLC!

Then, right before any other game ever would have begun to spam random cart puzzles to fill space, you get off the cart and continue with a new mechanic.
The art was pretty, the chapters were short and concise, the save mechanic is genius, and it doesn't overstay it's welcome. Too many games today are way to long just to validate ridiculous prices.
LIMBO is a game that game designers need to learn from.

I love this game. It's one of my all-time favorites. It's a little slow to start, since  death comes so easily, your starting ship and engine are slow and money is tight in the beginning, but the writing and quests are so dark and wonderful and the journeys can be harrowing which makes completing them all the more satisfying.
It has a ton of replay value because there's no way to finish all the quests with one captain (some end the game). Unexpected things happen and something you've planned on is no longer an option (like an officer that is now changed and you've promised to kill him if so...which kinda wrecks the future you'd planned for him). I like that this game surprises me. I like that I never know whether a decision was the right one until after I've learned the consequences. And there are so often consequences! I like that places change as the story progresses, even when it's a devastating change. The great thing that you don't realize the first time you make an unfortunate decision and wish you had a save, is that with your next captain, you can try to get a different outcome. I think of the lineage as one big game, rather than their own discrete ones.
That's the thing to remember at the beginning: If you succeed with one captain, you can make life for later captains easier by storing away heirlooms in your study. This means you really only have to struggle with the first captain and get through the initial grind for money once if you make a will and have a scion and are reasonably careful. I died a lot in the beginning  before I got the hang of it.
One thing I get as soon as I can afford it is the avid suppressor so my engine doesn't explode at full power. That plus eventually a good engine and Maybe's Daughter allows you to sail around at a reasonable speed without repercussions (except losing a slot, but for me it's worth it). The other thing I wish I knew when I started is to do the surface run to Naples as soon as you get a bigger ship. Yes, I've seen people who say stay with the small ships. I don't care about optimizing. I like to use the ponderous merchant ship with tons of space until I upgrade to fight.  I hate inventory management and that takes care of it. You have to be careful on surface runs to keep an eye on crew and fuel, but supplies are cheap and it's a good way to keep funded.
If Failbetter keeps putting out games and DLC like this, I will buy every one. I have hundreds of hours spent on this game and it has been well worth the money I spent.

Where do I begin? This game started out as average. I was intrigued and curious but it seemed pretty basic at first. As time went on the plot thickened, the enemies got more twisted and much harder to beat, and the visuals... the visuals including the atmosphere and the map design were AMAZING. You'll find dozens of rooms that lead to nothing but loot and dead bodies. It made for an awesome, non-linear feel. I found myself exploring and deviating from the path. Seriously this game became an instant favorite about halfway through. I played on the hardest settings, and with that in mind...
PROS:
-Good customization and upgrades between weapons and abilities
-Intensely-crafted plot
-Really fun combat
-INSANE map design
-Beautifull attention to detail on the maps
-Really good voice acting
-Very tedious detaiuls to explore and appreciate
-Unique style and graphics
-Had a very unique storyline that didn't seem cliche
-Ragdoll physics
-Intricate mechanics like electricity in water, spreading of fire, hacking robotics, etc...
-Cool ending
-Really interesting concepts and parallels to society that made the game so much deeper
-Smart relationship to other characters and even other enemies (like the Big Daddy's who are neutral usually until you need to kill them).
-Overall SUPER immersive. I felt like I was in the 1960's with the clothing, music styles, fonts, posters, etc...
CONS:
-Without uber good hacking abilities, hacking is impossible (literally) sometimes later on in the game. Not even challenging, literally impossible in some hack attempts. Good thing hacking is optional.
-The security bots (flying ones especially) are so damn annoying to hack, fight, etc... they felt overpowered sometimes.
-The final boss seemed a bit too easy. With full health packs I was able to beat him first try but it still was a close fight.
-It became too easy to run out of ammo. No, I wouldnt miss all my shots and that led me to need more ammo., Ammo is just plain scarce unless you buy it or get lucky and find it. Thing is, I spent all my money on health and plasmid hypos. In other words, it's a hard balance to make and during tough gun battles it's frustrating. I ended up going to my wrench (only melee weapon and it has unlimited ammo) to fix this and ended up loving the wrench so I guess it's bitter sweet.
Not going to lie, a lot of the "cons" I listed are opinionated and aren't flaws of the game. I sincerely loved this title and can't wait to move on to the next ones. 10/10 for Bioshock.

I keep trying to figure out why I dislike Sunless Sea, in spite of it being a mechanically sound game. Obvious time and effort was put into the game, and it shines on many fronts, not least of which is the intriguing world to discover. The game is low on graphics, but high on decision making, which suits its narrative focus: in Sunless Sea, your biggest payoffs come from finishing small story pieces, or storylets, encouraging risk-taking and striving towards unlocking pieces and options that require some prerequisite you don't start with.
Then I realize the problem: the narrative.
As I mentioned, the game is low on graphics. Whenever you're having a choose-your-own adventure, its rare you even get a picture of what's happening. This doesn't bother me; some of my favorite games are primarily driven by text with graphics there to serve the action. The problem I have is with the prose. Instead of describing what you're looking at in plain text, the writers seem to take gleeful pride in describing the FEELING of what you're looking at. This would make sense if the player knew the world like the characters do, but for those of us who haven’t played Fallen London, I don’t know when the game is being flowery with its metephors, or literal
For example, there’s a place called the Iron Republic (Hell's Outpost in the world of Sunless Sea) where physics don't work how they should. But the writing never SAYS "In the Iron Republic, physics are messed up and don't work" they say instead "The Devils offer emancipation, and in doing so, emancipation from the laws of reality." Even simple sentences often need decryption because the rather fascinating world of Sunless Sea is also quite foreign, and there’s little to ground your understanding of the world upon.
In this sense, Sunless Sea can be annoying. It’s a shame, because a free-roaming, sailing horror game where the mechanics are focused on story instead of fighting or trade is a great concept. I just wish the writers could literally describe things to me, stead of leaving me wondering if they’re being literal, or hyperbolic.
I’d recommend this game only to those who have a very large vocabulary, and a patience for rougelikes.

After playing "The Walking Dead" by Telltale games I was excited when I learned that they have made a Batman game in the same style. I have been a childhood fan of Batman and so was immediately roped in to play this game, and it didn't dissapoint.
The game is played from a story point of view with your interactions in the form of dialogues and decision making with some quick time events thrown in for combat purpose. The game offers you also the choice to tackle some of the situations as either Bruce Wayne or Batman which was really interesting. You are also faced with certain moral dilemmas when approaching criminals and allies and it really shows the pressures of being in Bruce Wayne's shoes as you try to balance both sides of his life.
The graphics are presented in DC Comics book style and I liked the art and presentation. Also, most of the small and big characters are from the Batman universe and I really liked their own versions being played in the story by the developers as opposed to the ones followed in the comics and movies. If you play you will know what I am talking about. The Episodes were approximately an hour or two in length and the pacing was good. One minor complaint was the main villain in the story which I did not find that engaging but I still enjoyed it and I know it can be improved upon in the second game. The soundtrack and music is just awesome and is a mix between the theme of Danny Elfman and Hans Zimmer. The story itself feels a mix between the Tim Burton movies and the Nolan Trilogy.
I did not encounter any crashes or performance issues with the game. I read on the forums that the game is notorius to FPS drops and other crashing issues but thankfully I did not face them. Maybe the game has been patched and fixed by the developers so its safe to give it a try again for people who were previously having issues.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you are a fan of Batman and its universe as a whole. It has some interesting deviations from the main story and it feels fresh to see a different take on the story as compared to the ones we have seen in movies and comics.
Also, one of your favourite villains has a small cameo in this game, setting him up for the second part (We all know who that is :) )  Buy it or get it on a sale.

Story
You are Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist who hears that illegal activity is happening in Mount Massive Asylum and you enter the asylum to investigate. Miles gets trapped in the asylum and your goal is to escape. It's basic but the game has memorable moments and characters. You get to learn about characters like Chris Walker and The Walrider through the games documents, which are the game's collectibles.
Gameplay
The gameplay is quite simple, but very fun. You use a camcorder to record events in the asylum and you use your night vision to see in the dark. But you can't use night vision all of the time becuase you have a limited amount of batteries. As for combat, there is none, all you can do is run and hide. The lack of combat does not make this game boring at all, in fact, it just makes it more intense and horrifying.
Graphics and Atmosphere
Graphics don't make a game better or worse, but Outlast does have solid graphics and a great atmosphere. The atmosphere in Outlast changes as you explore many different locations in the asylum. But there's not a single location where you feel safe. You might be walking through a fully lit hallway, but that jumpscare is still more than likely going to get you.
Overall
Outlast takes 4-5 hours to complete. That may seem short for a $20 game, but you can get it on sale for under $10 and it's most definitely worth the price. In general, Outlast is a great horror game and it's worth at least one playthrough.
I loved it and I highly recommend it.

Even though Steam says I have not a lot of hours played for this game don't be fooled! I have played this game long before I even joined Steam and all I can say is that FlatOut 2 is one of the best derby games out there.
Pros:
- Great Soundtrack: In my opinion, the majority of the soundtrack is epic that'll put you right in the racing mood.
- Replay Value: No joke, this game has so much variety it'll take a long long time before you'll get bored. From races to derby matches to even stunts, it seems endless. For example, you may have a Single Player race in the forest lands. Well there are 3 maps of forest or so to chose from. This applies to everything in Single Races, like racing in the city or racing on a track.
- It's Hilarious: If you crash your car at a certain angle your driver ejects out as a ragdoll. It's just hilarious. The stunts involve ragdolls as well, which makes the stunt aspect challenging as you can move your ragdoll in the air- or give it a little 'nudge' to go farther or higher.
- Handling: The steering isn't too hard. Playing with the keyboard isn't too difficult to manage. if you get used to it, you can go off with a victory without using a gamepad.
- "Realistic": In moderation, of course. You can lose a wheel and driving the car becomes more challenging. If you use a 'street' car in the forest the handling won't be so easy. Pieces fly off your car, doors fall off, windows break, muffles unhinge, it's a joy ride if you love crashes!
Cons:
- Since the world on the race track is practically destroyable in every way some things can cost you a first place finish. For example, if a fence falls apart and finds its way on the road it can interact with your car differently than say.. some tires! The fence can slow you down as your car hits it compared to the tires just bouncing off. Some ramps are sudden and it can toss you all over into the car or into a wall. But it's all for the fun of it really, crashing is a part of the whole game.
- Some Racers have an advantage over you: this is quite an interesting thing in the game. If you were to go into a derby with clunky cars, Frank Malcov will be, most likely, the last one standing because of the heavy car he uses. However, in a race, he won't come near first because of the disadvantage of having a big heavy car. Each car is different and so is every driver. This isn't so much of a con but something to be aware of!
This game is the best for games that involve crashing. It's fun to crash into others, it's fun to demolish everything because everything is practically demolish-able! For the price, it's something I would get for sure.
UPDATE: After all these years, the game is still better than so many games that came out after it.

Where do I begin? This game started out as average. I was intrigued and curious but it seemed pretty basic at first. As time went on the plot thickened, the enemies got more twisted and much harder to beat, and the visuals... the visuals including the atmosphere and the map design were AMAZING. You'll find dozens of rooms that lead to nothing but loot and dead bodies. It made for an awesome, non-linear feel. I found myself exploring and deviating from the path. Seriously this game became an instant favorite about halfway through. I played on the hardest settings, and with that in mind...
PROS:
-Good customization and upgrades between weapons and abilities
-Intensely-crafted plot
-Really fun combat
-INSANE map design
-Beautifull attention to detail on the maps
-Really good voice acting
-Very tedious detaiuls to explore and appreciate
-Unique style and graphics
-Had a very unique storyline that didn't seem cliche
-Ragdoll physics
-Intricate mechanics like electricity in water, spreading of fire, hacking robotics, etc...
-Cool ending
-Really interesting concepts and parallels to society that made the game so much deeper
-Smart relationship to other characters and even other enemies (like the Big Daddy's who are neutral usually until you need to kill them).
-Overall SUPER immersive. I felt like I was in the 1960's with the clothing, music styles, fonts, posters, etc...
CONS:
-Without uber good hacking abilities, hacking is impossible (literally) sometimes later on in the game. Not even challenging, literally impossible in some hack attempts. Good thing hacking is optional.
-The security bots (flying ones especially) are so damn annoying to hack, fight, etc... they felt overpowered sometimes.
-The final boss seemed a bit too easy. With full health packs I was able to beat him first try but it still was a close fight.
-It became too easy to run out of ammo. No, I wouldnt miss all my shots and that led me to need more ammo., Ammo is just plain scarce unless you buy it or get lucky and find it. Thing is, I spent all my money on health and plasmid hypos. In other words, it's a hard balance to make and during tough gun battles it's frustrating. I ended up going to my wrench (only melee weapon and it has unlimited ammo) to fix this and ended up loving the wrench so I guess it's bitter sweet.
Not going to lie, a lot of the "cons" I listed are opinionated and aren't flaws of the game. I sincerely loved this title and can't wait to move on to the next ones. 10/10 for Bioshock.

However, the AI in this game is bad. In SP, you get to be the commander to direct your troops to certain spots. Sometimes they listen, but most of the time they don't (often occurs in small enclosed areas). Their cover positions aren't really good, and yet they defy orders. Another thing to note is optimisation. This game stutters too much. I've played many missions where the game just lags out of nowhere. I tried turning off all background programs and even tried on a newly formatted PC, but to no avail. I'm not sure why but when I play other AAA games like Metro franchise, the game doesn't lag.

i5-4570
8GB RAM
AMD R9 290
Windows 7 (with the latest updates)
...

Cuphead has very spotty level design; issues like on one of the first bosses in world 2, whose second stage has certain enemies who can spawn on top of the character with no telegraph. This leads to situations where whole portions of the screen are basically "danger zones," especially if you're playing for A+ grades where getting hit once means you need to restart. This isn't an issue in EVERY level, but when it is an issue it'll bother you for a good long time till you beat that boss/level.
2) The developer's chose graphic consistency over graphic utility;
One of Cuphead's biggest draws is its one-of-a-kind artstyle. The gameplay is tailored to play around the artstyle, but in certain situations the gameplay takes a backseat to this. An egregious example is a boss where the level is scrolling with the player jumping from platform to platform during the level. The platforms, when spawned, are obscured by the boss so you can't see them for a good quarter of the screen. These should be brought to the front of the screen instead of the back. This is a more conscious decision than the con above.
Overall, Cuphead is a very good game though. Aside from those two cons I provided above, I have nothing else negative to say about the game. I'd rate it a solid 8/10, games like this are very few and far between; this is a game that you'll definitely want to share with your friends.

I keep trying to figure out why I dislike Sunless Sea, in spite of it being a mechanically sound game. Obvious time and effort was put into the game, and it shines on many fronts, not least of which is the intriguing world to discover. The game is low on graphics, but high on decision making, which suits its narrative focus: in Sunless Sea, your biggest payoffs come from finishing small story pieces, or storylets, encouraging risk-taking and striving towards unlocking pieces and options that require some prerequisite you don't start with.
Then I realize the problem: the narrative.
As I mentioned, the game is low on graphics. Whenever you're having a choose-your-own adventure, its rare you even get a picture of what's happening. This doesn't bother me; some of my favorite games are primarily driven by text with graphics there to serve the action. The problem I have is with the prose. Instead of describing what you're looking at in plain text, the writers seem to take gleeful pride in describing the FEELING of what you're looking at. This would make sense if the player knew the world like the characters do, but for those of us who haven’t played Fallen London, I don’t know when the game is being flowery with its metephors, or literal
For example, there’s a place called the Iron Republic (Hell's Outpost in the world of Sunless Sea) where physics don't work how they should. But the writing never SAYS "In the Iron Republic, physics are messed up and don't work" they say instead "The Devils offer emancipation, and in doing so, emancipation from the laws of reality." Even simple sentences often need decryption because the rather fascinating world of Sunless Sea is also quite foreign, and there’s little to ground your understanding of the world upon.
In this sense, Sunless Sea can be annoying. It’s a shame, because a free-roaming, sailing horror game where the mechanics are focused on story instead of fighting or trade is a great concept. I just wish the writers could literally describe things to me, stead of leaving me wondering if they’re being literal, or hyperbolic.
I’d recommend this game only to those who have a very large vocabulary, and a patience for rougelikes.
