I am a sucker for survival games, but with the oversaturated market it gets tough to find a good one that presents a challenge. The Long Dark, abbreviated herein as "TLD," is one of the exceptional ones.
Survival is the name of the game here. You have a backpack with a fairly large capacity, and clothes that won't keep you alive for long. Much like "The Forest," TLD requires you to find sticks, branches and fuel to craft fires and new items. Unlike most survival games, you may see the world as somewhat familiar to you - at least, it was to me. If you have experience with survival/adventure games, you will love this game, and coming from other atmospheric games, TLD is the ideal survival game for me.
This game is easy. This game is hard. This game is everything in between. Each "region" of the world that you play in has its own difficulty; some have prebuilt shelters for you to keep warm, and others are nothing but desolate wilderness. You can find yourself stranded on a frozen lake, or sipping coffee in the log house. The more you play, the easier you will find the game in general to be, regardless of the difficulty of the region you begin in. For instance, it took two playthrough attempts for me to realize that for some odd reason, the water in toilets is considered potable. Huh. Sleep is key in this game; oversleep and you will burn too many calories, but undersleep and your health will decline. If you are skilled at balancing different aspects of a character, such as hunger v. sickness and agility v. pack size, you will have no trouble with starting on at least a moderately difficult region.
This game is, in one word: atmospheric. From the calming to somewhat-creepy background audio to the smoothness of the main character's voice, the audio in this game is absolutely fantastic. I would highly advise you to wear your best set of headphones/earphones when playing this game, as you will notice a difference.
As for the graphics, well, I'm simply amazed at the simplicity yet the spectacular attention to detail in this game. I actually purchased this game solely for the visual quality, and after playing I knew that it was the right choice. Surprisingly, this game is made with UNITY. Yes, you read that right -- Unity. From screenshots, most might say that it looks like a Source 2 engine game. In that regard, I feel like the devs did a great job pushing Unity to its limits to make this game.
One of my personal favorite areas in the game to explore is the forest house by the Coastal Highway and Log Yard area. It's very home-y, and although I was definitely creeped out when I first went upstairs and came across a corpse, it's one of the more calm locations in the region. Outside of shelters, one of the very unique aspects is something that usually goes unnoticed: footprints. I love the fact that your footprints stay in the snow, and maybe it's just me, but I feel that it definitely adds a lot to the game with just one added detail. I have not noticed yet whether the footprints will stay for a certain time duration or if it is based on basically a graphical asset limit, such as 100 or 150.
Speaking of Unity, let's talk about one of its downfalls: performance. I play this game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 860M card, and I do get a steady 60fps. However, at some points textures glitch out and frames drop. My GPU/CPU are not throttling, which leads me to believe it could just be a bug or the result of Unity's poor optimization. It's definitely not the developers' fault. My system does run hot when playing, much hotter than while playing titles such as CS:GO and Saints Row 3/4, but at a similar temperature as when I run Metro 2033/Last Light Redux. If you have at least a 700 series card and proper cooling and ventilation, you'll have no issues.
At this stage of the game's development, I feel that it warrants a price tag of maybe $15 instead of $20. Having played it and seen fairly fast development progress, this IS an early access game that you do want to cash in on because, as many other Early Access games, the price will go up.
TLD is glorious in its appearance, unforgiving in its challenges, and sensory magic at heart. Don't miss out.
Be sure to check out any of my other reviews on my profile, and please upvote if this helped you, I hope it did! Thanks for reading!

The Lovecraftian atmosphere is very well created. The thrill of running away from huge monsters is bolstered by the painfully slow moving ships you command.
You need to master the management of food, fuel, money and crew, while trying to overcome events and obstacles and certain shady individuals, with your wits or strength. This involves one-time-chance dice roll, which can affect the rest of your captain's life. But again, he/she will die and you will start afresh, but this time knowing what to bring to the encounter.
All in all, a very well planned and presented Lovecraftian game, for those who are willing to read copious amounts of text and enjoy the thrill of commanding a ship which moves slower than an aground starfish.

Telltale games have really been interactive novels since Jurassic Park and Walking Dead.  However, this does not mean that their games are not interesting to play or fun to play.  With Batman, I found myself playing a comic book and getting to choose what happened next.  In this game, there are moments where you can choose which locations to go next during an emergency.  Both locations require your aid, but only one can be chosen.  This is similar to Walking Dead where you had to choose which character to help from a zombie attack, meaning one character was most likely going to die while another saved.  This is very similar here for Batman.
I did find that my quicktime event abilities didn't do much to help.  There were times where I completely missed pressing a button or doing a motion, yet Batman seemed to be able to deal with it on his own.  This was strange and did not make me feel as a part of the game as other Telltale games offered in the past.  I hope they go back to every action having an effect, rather than just pivotal choices having an effect.  Even if it means me dying and having to try again, I'm willing to allow death and restarting from a checkpoint, than not successfully getting a combo correct and still moving forward int he story.  While the story is king here in this game, I feel this gets me out of the immersive gameplay that it should be.
The storyline is wonderful, I love meeting characters we all know so well and seeing how Bruce/Batman met them or first interacted with them.  It definitely pays homage to the comic books, but at the same time brings in a new story that really shines.  Definitely one not to miss if you enjoy Batman or Telltale games.  Highly recommended.

Back into the fray with another Telltale game. I'd say giving it a year long break since my last game, that being Michonne, is probably about right when it comes to their formulaic approach not wearing out [too] much. To cut the long intro short it's time for Batman - The Telltale Series.
It is interesting to see a Batman media that simultaneously glosses over his origin story, told and re-told so many times already, and yet makes its own version of said story so integral to the entire premise. What do I mean by that? Well, keeping this spoiler-free let's just say that Telltale has their own spin on what Batman's parents were up to in cahoots with the local criminal boss and blatantly corrupt major. This comes back to bite Bruce Wayne in the behind seeing as consequences of those decisions endured. Get it? Actual present story you're dealing with ranges from the local major candidacy run, with everyone's favorite two-faced coin tosser being a central figure, some cat burglary happening about and no Batman game would be complete without a green haired fan favorite who, much to my own surprise, ends up relegated into a cameo more or less. Now that I think about it Telltale really put their own mark on the game with the way they handled established characters and even some you wouldn't expect. The likes of Vicki Vale, for example.
There's your story or as much as I can divulge of it. Seeing this is a Telltale game you can see there's plenty of “we're winging it from episode to episode” but in my opinion this is probably one of better examples of tighter storytelling versus something like The Wolf Among Us which, despite its qualities, really suffered from pull-push writing and constant lack of focus. Batman actually has a solid story to tell and you can see threads of overall narrative in every episode with a healthy sprinkling of characters advancing their plans over the course of multiple episodes. This is kinda where we tie into my first big problem with the game – it's all so very low scale and production for about first two episodes or so until the meat of the story kicks in. While this benefits from them becoming more fleshed out in the process, you're basically interacting with the same half dozen characters or so and, looking at it from the final standpoint, game really blows through everything it has to offer during those episodes.
As far as tackling the characters goes... they're your Batman cast. You'll be seeing most of the favorites befitting a relatively small-time criminal story which sadly means your more specialist antagonists like Mr. Freeze and others are out of the picture. Game is quite dedicated to keeping it grounded with plot points like police force corruption, hostile company takeover and old friend from Bruce's youth returning until the last episode when it goes into overdrive with action. I can't really add anything new here because characters largely play it straight with their established personalities. Game's highlight is still its character interaction and there are some particularly effective scenes, like for example when Batman and Catwoman have a very real existential crisis moment wondering if it's all worth it or Bruce and Harvey with their BFF interactions. I liked it and it felt like real people interacting more than once.
Adding anything about Telltale's games mechanics might be redundant at this point seeing how dead set they are on being adventures-lite, but Batman actually has few surprises in his toolbet in that department. Is it it perfect? No way, but I rather liked the clear cut between more diplomatic Bruce approach and aggressive Batman style. Game offers you the choice on who will take the lead on couple of occasions to predictable results where former gets to talk his way through situations while latter is more along the lines of planning out his takedowns. Problem here is talking your way through problems is how Telltale games play while Batman's action/deduction approach feels either clumsy because the engine can't handle proper action so it's QTE central with awkward stop-and-go between segments or game stops to a halt so you can “solve puzzles” aka connect two obvious clues in sequence and then wait for the game to explain it to you. In short, it's familiar and action segments from Michonne are now greatly expanded upon in order to make for bulk of Batman's action.
Technically you can tell devs absolutely put in effort to upgrade the visuals from what I would classify as their last-gen games, but why couldn't performance be the priority? It still chugs when transitioning between scenes and odd shader flickering isn't uncommon when even I managed to notice it. That hand drawn edge filter around the edges also has its odd moments when looking at the screen from a distance, but looks much better up-close when you can appreciate it without dithering and aliasing detracting from overall presentation. All I can say is I guess I was lucky to not experience many problems people seem to be reporting on the forum.
So what to say in conclusion? You've seen the recommendation and despite having some, mainly technical, issues I liked this one as well. I've given up on choices actually mattering in these games so I won't hold it as a negative against Batman which admittedly has some different outcomes, for example how Harvey Dent situation plays out. I walked away satisfied in no small part thanks to moody soundtrack and a satisfying finale that actually managed to have a fight that wasn't godawful.

I got this game when it was available for free, and I was pretty happy and impressed with it (I've noticed that many games temporarily offered for free are subpar or mediocre). It should also be noted that I have not played the Broforce game, so this was my first experience with the game variant.
If you like casual, arcade-style, 2D sidescrolling action in the vein of Metal Slug (minus any usable vehicles or weapon upgrades/switching), lots of destruction and gore, and/or the Expendables movie, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very good - the environmental destruction (voxel-style) is absolutely fantastic. I enjoy just shooting my grenade launcher at enemies and watching them run around, eventually blowing up a small radius of the area around them. The music and sounds are also great and add to the atmosphere of general mayhem and destruction. The narrator's voice is quite funny and sounds like a stereotypical  "bro" suffering from excess-testosterone.
The controls are very simple, and the game plays well with either a controller of mouse+keyboard. I switched the keybindings to allow mouse use (default is keyboard only), and I find it much easier with that setup. There is no tutorial - you are thrown immediately into the game, however, familiarizing yourself with the game is quick and painless, so this isn't a problem. The learning curve is very minimal - just shoot enemies, free captives, avoid all enemy projectiles (you die in one hit, and also from environmental hazards like heavy objects falling on top of you).
When you play, you must make it to the end of the level, where you will raise an American flag - this will signal a helicopter evac. Once you jump onto the heli's ladder, the level will end and you will be shown you how many people you've killed, the amount of time it took to complete the stage, and how many more rescues you require to get the next unlock (more characters). You rescue captives by destroying their cages and moving through them (this also grants an extra life). Once you have more characters, you will also switch to a random ally every time you free a captive.
You start off with one character and one life, so if you die you must restart the stage from the beginning. By the end of the first stage, you will have unlocked a second character to use. As you unlock more characters, you will switch to a random one every time you die (so long as you have lives remaining). American flags are raised as checkpoints if you pass through them, however, it is recommended you keep an eye out for these because it is possible to miss them - the voxel-style destruction means you can take many different routes.
The random character selection whenever you die adds to the surprise and helps keep the game slightly unpredictable, however, I would have liked to at least be able to select the character I will enter the stage as. Each character has a regular attack, melee attack, and "special," which is usually a powerful move with medium-to-large area of effect.
Overall, the game is pretty easy, and each level is short - providing a nice time filler if you only want to play for a few minutes. The game is a lot more fun if you are playing local multiplayer. For a free game, it is much higher quality than the type of games that make the norm.
If you are interested in 2D shoot-em-ups with lots of environmental destruction and gore, check this game out.

I am utterly shocked that this game has received such high reviews.   This is a point and click with a different sort of artsy backdrop of bugs and plants.  The artistry is nice, but it really stops there.  I really tried to like this game and even completed it, hoping for some redeeming value.  getting the bug to move from screen to screen was tedious, having to go back to old screens to collect items you weren't allowed to collect originally (even knowing it would be necessary later), and having to figure out what you were to do on each screen became monotonous. And the bug was SLOW.  getting the puzzles to start was also slow (the lightening bugs, for example).  There was a good 15 second delay.  Does not seem like much in the scheme of things, but just sit there waiting to understand what the game is doing, and it seems like an eternity.
By the end of the game, when I wasn't sure what was next, my thought was, "it had better not make me go through all of the screens on this level to collect the water drops.  If it does, its over!"  It did not, thankfully, but that did not make the game any more fun.
There is no guide, except a little question mark in the upper right corner to "help" you when you are stuck.  But, it does not always help you.  It ONLY helps when looking for a collectable item and it is on the page you are on, otherwise it gongs.  If there is another step (a branch, for instance) it does not help you find it.  Time was wasted on trying to figure out what the many puzzles wanted.  Once I understood them, it was fine, but it was not intuitive.
My final though was, "did I really spend money on this game?"  I bought it on sale, but, that does not make me any happier.  I buy most of my games based on the very positive ratings they receive.  I would not pay money for this game unless I were a point and click collector.  There are plenty of other point and clicks (even free) that are much more enjoyable.  The two hours I lost on the game were not enjoyable ones.

It's not a game. It's an experience, and it can be an emotional one if you let it. Stop reading these reviews, and decide. Do you want to spend a few hours on an experience, are you willing to let yourself care, or would you rather just move on to a game?
I will say it'll be best experienced going in naive and open, with no foreknwoledge of what's to come. In the spirit of that, stop reading.
On a more personal note, it's a story I relate to. As things progress, I started to resent some of the things done by the narrator, without really understanding why. The "Press Enter" moments - I didn't, on a few of them, because I disagreed with the idea, fundamentally. "Stop doing that," I found myself thinking. It made me uncomfortable. I think I knew why.
The dialog choices were difficult, because I let myself care about them. I knew they likely didn't matter, but it's not a game, it's an experience, so I cared. In retrospect, the things I selected seemed to say more about me than the game. Upon realizing that, I went with it, and that just drew me in further. I was expecting it all to be some grand test, some shockingly clever personality quiz, and the thought excited me. Ironic how close and how far we can be..
Will I play it again? Probably not. It was difficult to live through, in a way, and in another way, I'm pretty sure I got all I could out of playing it. Maybe just once more, to really pay attention, to see what I missed. To perhaps find answers to the unanswered..
Will I watch someone else play? Absolutely. Probably anyone who will let me watch.
Is the price worth it? I generally set a $1/hr rate on a game, to decide its merit in a recommendation. This came closer to $5/hr for my playthrough, and I spent a lot of time looking around. As someone who enjoys experiences, and the 'deep dive' into the psyche, here's how I look at it now. If I was offered a full or partial refund, I'd decline. It was an experience I want to have paid for.

This isn’t a game in the same way a piece of postmodern performance art can’t be labeled as theater per se, but in a strange way, it could just as well be called one.
While the concept and its core dilemma paints a clear picture of just what is going on through the eyes and the mind of the developer, and believe me, I understand those dilemmas very well, doing what I do for a living, I can say that these pressing issues, those dark looming clouds are imaginary, we give out the meaning, and not the other way around, we put the walls in our prisons, we define the boundaries of our possibilities by sheer ignorance of what we really are and what we can actually accomplish as a species.
We are told what to do and think, we are told what is good, what must be expected of us, what is the proper and the improper way to do, feel and believe, but in truth, reality is non-descript until we give it meaning, we choose either unconscious or conscious or by sheer stupidity to swallow and regurgitate things and experiences that we instinctively know are not doing us any good, we have been sick for so long, that we have begun to believe and accept that being ill IS the way we have to be, and to consider any other alternative is out of the question, the hard part, the almost impossible truth is, that all it takes to get better is just wanting and making an effort to do so, it takes the same amount of energy to feel good than it takes to feel bad, it’s just that no one dares, no one believes, and we rather just drown in the proverbial half empty half full glass of water.
The ideas behind this work, to me, just places more nails on the same non issues, in the same imaginary coffin, we choose to be miserable over being free…

Although this is a great shooter, I still have my reservations of recommending this game (Single Player).
It is realistic. It provides you with a real war experience that it is fun yet challenging. The graphics is quite nice (for a 2011 game).
However, the AI in this game is bad. In SP, you get to be the commander to direct your troops to certain spots. Sometimes they listen, but most of the time they don't (often occurs in small enclosed areas). Their cover positions aren't really good, and yet they defy orders. The upside is that this not only applies to your ally; the enemies at some missions are pretty stupid. Yet this will result in you getting stuck at one mission as your checkpoints get overwhelmed easily.
Another thing to note is optimisation. This game stutters too much. I've played many missions where the game just lags out of nowhere. I tried turning off all background programs and even tried on a newly formatted PC, but to no avail. I'm not sure why but when I play other AAA games like Metro franchise, the game doesn't lag.
My specs are:
i5-4570
8GB RAM
AMD R9 290
Windows 7 (with the latest updates)
...
*other not-so-related-to-lags parts*
...
Key bindings can be quite a problem. I don't blame the dev because there are too many commands (for realism). BUT those tutorials that teach you how to operate tanks and use commands? LONG RVW: At last (I say "at last" as if I've just started playing; I've been playing ROHoS for a few years now and actually have about 550 hrs that were wiped for some reason when the game was divided into multiplayer and single-player versions.... So I have in reality around 1600 hrs in not counting close to 1000 in campaign...) a game wherein your enemies, ya know, they DIE when (unlike SOO many FPS's in the sad world today) you shoot them center chest with a MEASLY 7.62x54mm round easily capable of penetrating 12mm of steel on any given day. After a half hour or so of bullet-sponging it on CoD, ROHoS is sweet relief and a breath of realism (as much 'realism' as can be in a video game anyway...) CoD drives me nuts with "damage fall-off", REALLY? A hot-loaded .338 Lapua round loses 75% of its power at 60m??? What crack-pot idiot came up with this garbage?? Oh well enough ranting as I'm obviously not rating a CoD game here...   So, a review about gameplay:

PROS: 1. Bullet/Shell ballistics are spot on. Projectile travel time, elevations and ballistic effects are something lacking in most FPS games. (If it only had a windage-effect it would be perfect)

2. (More of a continuation of #1) The vitality of the characters. Cut enough arteries/veins or a shot through the chest and he's gone (with rifles at least, the realism of the ballistic trauma is nice; sometimes a 7.62x25mm round won't cause enough trauma for a clean kill unless the shot is perfect and within range.
3. Tank Realism: The tanks aren't perfect (see CONS) but are still very well simulated. You don't shoot it right; it won't be destroyed. The tanks don't simply have hit-points. Everything from the tracks to the FRIKKIN gunsight can be damaged/destroyed. Even the co-ax MG can be knocked out. And, handled correctly (play the tutorial dummies) and the tanks are a joy to use. They are complex and you have to be on your mental toes to use them. But once you're used to the way they work you can -as they say- go to town with it.
4. A Wide Variety of Maps. The map content is huge and still growing. Every possible map type can be found. Large, small, flat, hilly, open, forested and everything in between. If you play on a rotation server (or a vote/campaign server that's not full of noob CoD'ers voting to play the same map over and over) you will never get map-bored.
5. A Fairly Simple and Pragmatic Level-up System. No 'points' to spend. No micro-trans. You simply unlock weapons as you gain kills and combat experience- The idea, I think is that veterans often had access to (or knew how to "acquire") more advanced or newly issued weapons as they came in for field testing etc. And also being allowed to use an "Enemy Class" isn't in my opinion a far-fetched idea. I'd think that a man who'd somehow survived 8 or 10 weeks in Stalingrad likely had learned to collect and use enemy weaponry on a day-to-day basis- Therefore I think the level-up system is at least semi-realistic/pragmatic.
6. Realistic Objectives. "Territory" (hereafter abbreviated "TE") is the primary game mode. In TE your platoon has to capture and hold a certain number of 'objectives' in order to win the battle. These objectives are based wholly or partly on actual areas that the Soviet and German commanders had selected as strongpoints during the Battle of Stalingrad. In other words: The objectives are not a "ring of light" that you have to pile up in waiting to be mown down.They're -for the most part- real buildings, bridgeheads, forrests, trenchlines and so forth that were actually fought over during the battle in WWII.
CONS: 1. Poor/Unresponsive AI. The AI troops ('bots') often get 'stuck'. They ignore enemies on the flanks most of the time. They ignore commander orders 40-60% of the time. Bots can be in a dead run and hip-fire from 60m and hit you in the head... EVERY time. They also seem to have no friendly (or enemy for that matter) line-of-fire detection. They will run directly in front of a FRIENDLY MG as it is firing for example. They also run headlong into both friendly and enemy artillery fire and will walk right up to a friendly satchel charge that's clearly seconds from detonating (i.e. placed on an enemy tank). Lastly they can see through walls, trees, grass and just about anything. They'll detect and kill you even when it's obvious that no human- in real life or a video game- would ever know where you were.
2. MG's are a little "over-balanced" if you will. The barrel on an MG-34 heats up much more quickly than in real life. It's over-regulated and hurts realism. I've been firing weapons since I could walk... And firing 40 rounds even in just a few seconds will not overheat a barrel to the point of bursting... And why the heaven can you not get a full combat load of ammo at the ammo dumps??? You get one belt/mag and that's it! Again a comparrison with Ostfront: On there you can sit at an ammo dump for a few seconds and get not only your full load but sit a few more seconds and you can get even more. Why would a man go all the way to an ammo dump and only get one mag? Besides with EVERY OTHER WEAPON you get a standard combat load at the ammo dump. Makes absolutely no sense. At least your squadmates can resupply you if you're an MG'er...
3. Artillery Fire has a long 'cool-off' and cannot be adjusted. Again, I know this was probably done for "balance" but war is anything BUT balanced. Once artillery is requested it cannot be adjusted/corrected at all (they could at least let you adjust it ONCE per barage...) Also if for some reason the request is canceled the ARTY must go through the entire cool-off period before it can be used again; even if you canceled it before it actually started firing. Put simply, the Artillery needs a little more work. Other than the Katyusha rockets (which actually did take several minutes to re-load) the cool-off really makes artillery an emergency measure that's held to the last second. The ARTY on RO Ostfront had limited ammunition (on average 7 barages worth) instead of a cool-down timer. I wish they'd put that on ROHoS instead of the timer.
4. Bullet Penetration is "off kilter". This one is beyond understanding. You can kill an enemy through a brick or concrete wall but not sheet metal and small trees... I know it seems like a small issue, but it aggravates me; and everyone that I've talked to about it agrees that it needs a lot of work.
5. Tripwire will not DEBUG the darned thing. A grenade won't go through a 2 foot wide window. Invisible walls are everywhere, I fall through the game world every 10 minutes and half the places you should be able to deploy an MG cannot be used.... FIX IT PLEASE. It's not the most buggy shooter I've played, but it needs a lot more work.
6. The tanks are great, but.... They get stuck on things that they should easily run over. and I get tired of seeing "can't switch seats while someone else is moving" when NOT A SOUL is switching seats anywhere. And sometimes for no reason the tank will just start easing forward as if left unattended in neutral while you're trying to use the main gun or co-ax MG... And the engine gets damaged from being shot in the gun mantlet????
Despite it all ROHoS is the absolute most realistic FPS I have ever seen. I recommend it to anyone tired of pupming 30 unrealistic rounds into an unrealistic character only to be shot dead by him once your mag is empty. Give it a chance, it's well worth it. Also I hope soon a more modern combat game with the same level of realism will be produced. Maybe a Red Orchestra: Korea. Not enough respect is given to the the brave men and women who fought and died there. Whether you agree with the why's and what's of the war or not, the brave souls who fought it should not be forgotten.

BioShock is a fun game with an interesting story, but it crashed or hung frequently on my Windows 8.1 system with a GeForce GTX 750 Ti GPU, so I had to keep replaying portions of the game from previous saves, which was NOT fun. I recommend treating BioShock as though it is from Bethesda Softworks and saving OFTEN.
• If you find a new item, SAVE.
• If you reach a new area, SAVE.
• If something notable happens in the story, SAVE.
• If you are about to do something that may trigger an event, such as starting a machine, SAVE.
• If you hear a family member, housemate, or friend speak, laugh, or yawn, SAVE.
• If you hear an animal meow, purr, bark, whistle, bleat, bray, neigh, whinny, or hiss, SAVE.
• If you hear a windchime outside, SAVE.
• If you feel thirsty, SAVE.

This might be one of the most calming Rouglikes I have ever played. The challenge of the game is primarily in resource management and figuring out the best risk:reward ratio. Naval battles can be avoided and are easy with the right weaponry and tactics, but one wrong judgement in supply needs means you can end up stuck in the middle of the ocean with no fuel and a crew eating each other. It's not a good game for when you need action, but it's a great game to play after a hard day of work.
The story plays out like a very boat-centric choose-your-own-adventure book written by Lovecraft. This can leave events feeling a bit disjointed, but it mixes well with it's odd narrative. The game forces you to re-learn how the world works if you want to get far, but isn't a random mess with no tangible connections. And because the game changes events on islands based on how long you have been playing, you feel like you are learning something new about the world each time you pull into a port.
I'd reccomend keeping notes as you play in order to keep up with the game's complex trade routes and to make subsequent playthroughs easier. The only thing that changes between playthroughs is island placement, so a good book of notes can help you know where you should be and when in order to achieve your goals.

I'd survived for weeks. I had a home-base set up in an abandoned gas station next to a frozen lake. I was using the garage as an area to store meat and cure hides. I had a ton of tools foraged and had managed to find a hunting rifle. In one outing, I found a bear on the frozen lake. I shot it 3 times from afar, which seemingly did nothing. I got closer to see if it was a glitch. It wasn't. The bear stood up, charged and began mauling me. I survived the attack by one point of health, but lost consciousness. I awoke freezing to death and bleeding out on the icy lake. My controls were barely able to guide my body to a nearby fishing hut, which I kept falling over and out of every time I tried to stand. I was barely able to make a fire in the potbelly stove to keep from freezing to death. I took meds and slept on and off for three days, nursing myself back to health. Eventually I got my strength back and returned to the lake where I'd dropped my rifle during the attack. Laying next to it was the dead grizzly, having stayed alive after 3 gunshots just long enough to maul the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. After that, I was pretty attached to that save game. After all, if you die, that is IT . Eventually, weeks later, I was running low on food and came down with food poisoning from expired canned peaches. I had to march to a second location where I'd stored more food. I got there and was getting steadily worse, when I found that I had no antibiotics stored to cure myself. Rest and water helped, but I'd exhausted the backup food supply and I was barely able to walk as it was. I went outside to look for firewood, but I'd been indoors for so long that my "hours of daylight/darkness" counter had gone to "???". I stepped out into the black of night during a hellacious blizzard. There was zero visibility and I couldn't even find the door to get back inside. I thought my time might be up. Seconds later, I heard the growling of wolves in the pitch black. I never even saw them attack me..... I do miss that save game. The saddest part was the post-game stats screen, which displayed "Number of times attacked by wolves: 56" right above "Number of wolf attacks successfully fought off: 55"

FlatOut 2 came out just 2 years after its predecessor and was released in June 2006. That would make it around the time when I actually first played the game with my friends. Man, the game was good. Recently I have decided to try it out again, and to my surprise the game still rocks!
FlatOut 2 is by far the best racing game of it's kind that I have played. Long time has passed since the release, but everything about the game still seems really good from graphics to gameplay. Unfortunately there's no online but LAN via other software is possible. Do not fret though, single player is extremely fun. The AI is scripted very well. By the end of 2-3 cups you will understand how every individual AI drives. They don't always want to win now, some of them want to crash others players cars. It does not mean that it will always be you though. So expect some random stuff happen to you during the game. Never under estimate the opponent.
The  soundtrack just blew my mind. I do like the type of music that this game has, but to think that I know almost all of the songs in the game just makes it so much better. This game has lots of big names  like Rob Zombie, Wolfmother and .... Nickleback. But what's more important is that the car engine sound like a boss, the noise is so sexy, sometimes I just lower the music volume.
It been almost 9 years now, but the graphics will not hurt your eye, in fact this game probably eclipsed a ton of racing games which came out around the same time. Car details are very good, both brand new and half destroyed. The maps look just awesome, textures still look good to this day. Human ragdolls are a bit on the downside again, but you do not tend to fly out as often anymore. Overall, I am extremely happy about the graphics and how they are still so good even eight years after.
What else is important about the racing game for PC players, a game that was also realsead on consoles? The answer is controls. Finally, I played a game, where you can easily steer just by using your arrows on the keyboard. Game is very playable without a joystick. It also feels that the developers made it easier to control cars in the first place.
By now your thinking that there must be something bad about the game. Well, I am going to tell you that there are non big things that will off put you. There are minor things about interacting with physical objects, but that's about it guys, this game is almost perfect!
Replayabilty is massive, once you discover the LAN.
To conclude, this game deserves the price. If there's no sale then just buy it. You will not regret it. The game is so good, you will end up driving at least for the next 5 hours before taking a break.

If you love City Building Games then I highly and most certainly recommend this game for sure. It is by far the most interesting and tedious city builder there is to date which covers a lot of ground to keep you busy and reeled in for hours on end.
There are only two major complaints I still have about this game - read why below.
1 - The Multiplayer was horrible at first and because of that the game got a really bad wrap from the get go so players stopped playing it online due to the issues it originally had. On a positive note most of those problems were fixed and it does work very well online now. However, due to that bad start it may be hard to play it online unless you go to the community or get a friend to join you.
2 - One of my biggest problems that I have always had with this game with each of it's following game sequences is that the buildings are way too repetitive as in all of the building types are the exact same. So once you get further into the game you'll notice that you have lots of areas with houses and buildings but they all look exactly alike with absolutely no variance whatsoever. I have repeatedly complained to them about this in every series and nothing has been done and I doubt now that it will ever change either unless a ton of people start to do the same. One thing though that does make it a little better is the different building types and the added buildings from the dlc but still if you have a bunch of houses and similar buildings you will notice that and it may become an annoyance. If you can look past that then you'll enjoy it! On top of that the Eras also do help aid with that in changing the look of several types of buildings after upgrades have occurred from advancing in time but many do not such as housing unfortunately.
Anyhow though, aside from those two issues it is still an epic game and I definitely think it's worth the price in full but if you'd rather wait for a sale then I would certainly recommend grabbing it for sure to say the least!

This is a fun little train game.  It's economics are exceedingly simple as is the user interface.
The basic game play is simple.  Lay track, control swiches, send trains to the right stations, don't run trains into each other or off the track.
The challenges, however, can be very difficult.  You may be required to earn a specific minimum amount of money while getting all your dispatches perfect, and doing so will require you to schedule extra trains that you can only just barely get enough routed, while trying to make sure you're switches are all lined up so the trains don't run into each other and end up on the right track.
Some reviewers have said the game is short.  This is true- there are only 24 scenarios and no scenario takes more than an hour.  However, the harder scenarios have great replay value and frankly will take many attempts to master anyway.
For enthusiasts of games like Railroad Tycoon (and I am a HUGE fan myself), this takes train management down several notches to the level of operating your own home layout - which quite frankly is something I've no doubt many people have been longing for because for all the wonderfullness of Railroad Tycoon, what it is NOT is a train dispatcher simulation.  Train Valley is.
Pros:
- Simple interface, simple economics
- You run trains, not companies
- Scenario complexity is just the right level of hard
- Feels like a home train layout vs. a national railroad model
Cons:
- UI needs refinement
- A little cutesy looking
- Feels like a home train layout vs. a national railroad model (yes this could be a pro OR con)
Overall?  4 stars with potential.

This isn’t a game in the same way a piece of postmodern performance art can’t be labeled as theater per se, but in a strange way, it could just as well be called one.
While the concept and its core dilemma paints a clear picture of just what is going on through the eyes and the mind of the developer, and believe me, I understand those dilemmas very well, doing what I do for a living, I can say that these pressing issues, those dark looming clouds are imaginary, we give out the meaning, and not the other way around, we put the walls in our prisons, we define the boundaries of our possibilities by sheer ignorance of what we really are and what we can actually accomplish as a species.
We are told what to do and think, we are told what is good, what must be expected of us, what is the proper and the improper way to do, feel and believe, but in truth, reality is non-descript until we give it meaning, we choose either unconscious or conscious or by sheer stupidity to swallow and regurgitate things and experiences that we instinctively know are not doing us any good, we have been sick for so long, that we have begun to believe and accept that being ill IS the way we have to be, and to consider any other alternative is out of the question, the hard part, the almost impossible truth is, that all it takes to get better is just wanting and making an effort to do so, it takes the same amount of energy to feel good than it takes to feel bad, it’s just that no one dares, no one believes, and we rather just drown in the proverbial half empty half full glass of water.
The ideas behind this work, to me, just places more nails on the same non issues, in the same imaginary coffin, we choose to be miserable over being free…
Oh and don’t get me wrong, I love walking sims, but this one is just biting its own tail, over and over and over in circles, when it could just will those prison bars away.

The Beginner's Guide is less a game and more an interactive documentary. You play through the unique but seemingly unfinished games that someone has created, as an acquaintance of the creator walks you through their perception of the mindset of the creator during those periods. This is an introspective story that pulls you in right from the beginning and doesn't let go. The message is relatable, the environments are immersive, and the voice acting is perfect. I felt a really surprising range of emotions throughout this, and I'm sure that a lot of you out there will be able to experience those too.
I played through in 90 minutes from beginning to end, and paid $1 for it as a part of the most recent humble bundle. It was easily worth the money. This obviously isn't something you're going to be playing every day (as a linear story with one ending) but I can definitely see myself coming back to this game in the future to experience this again.

LONG RVW: At last (I say "at last" as if I've just started playing; I've been playing ROHoS for a few years now and actually have about 550 hrs that were wiped for some reason when the game was divided into multiplayer and single-player versions.... So I have in reality around 1600 hrs in not counting close to 1000 in campaign...) a game wherein your enemies, ya know, they DIE when (unlike SOO many FPS's in the sad world today) you shoot them center chest with a MEASLY 7.62x54mm round easily capable of penetrating 12mm of steel on any given day. After a half hour or so of bullet-sponging it on CoD, ROHoS is sweet relief and a breath of realism (as much 'realism' as can be in a video game anyway...) CoD drives me nuts with "damage fall-off", REALLY? A hot-loaded .338 Lapua round loses 75% of its power at 60m??? What crack-pot idiot came up with this garbage?? Oh well enough ranting as I'm obviously not rating a CoD game here...   So, a review about gameplay:

PROS: 1. Bullet/Shell ballistics are spot on. Projectile travel time, elevations and ballistic effects are something lacking in most FPS games. (If it only had a windage-effect it would be perfect)

2. (More of a continuation of #1) The vitality of the characters. Cut enough arteries/veins or a shot through the chest and he's gone (with rifles at least, the realism of the ballistic trauma is nice; sometimes a 7.62x25mm round won't cause enough trauma for a clean kill unless the shot is perfect and within range.
3. Tank Realism: The tanks aren't perfect (see CONS) but are still very well simulated. You don't shoot it right; it won't be destroyed. The tanks don't simply have hit-points. Everything from the tracks to the FRIKKIN gunsight can be damaged/destroyed. Even the co-ax MG can be knocked out. And, handled correctly (play the tutorial dummies) and the tanks are a joy to use. They are complex and you have to be on your mental toes to use them. But once you're used to the way they work you can -as they say- go to town with it.
4. A Wide Variety of Maps. The map content is huge and still growing. Every possible map type can be found. Large, small, flat, hilly, open, forested and everything in between. If you play on a rotation server (or a vote/campaign server that's not full of noob CoD'ers voting to play the same map over and over) you will never get map-bored.
5. A Fairly Simple and Pragmatic Level-up System. No 'points' to spend. No micro-trans. You simply unlock weapons as you gain kills and combat experience- The idea, I think is that veterans often had access to (or knew how to "acquire") more advanced or newly issued weapons as they came in for field testing etc. And also being allowed to use an "Enemy Class" isn't in my opinion a far-fetched idea. I'd think that a man who'd somehow survived 8 or 10 weeks in Stalingrad likely had learned to collect and use enemy weaponry on a day-to-day basis- Therefore I think the level-up system is at least semi-realistic/pragmatic.
6. Realistic Objectives. "Territory" (hereafter abbreviated "TE") is the primary game mode. In TE your platoon has to capture and hold a certain number of 'objectives' in order to win the battle. These objectives are based wholly or partly on actual areas that the Soviet and German commanders had selected as strongpoints during the Battle of Stalingrad. In other words: The objectives are not a "ring of light" that you have to pile up in waiting to be mown down.They're -for the most part- real buildings, bridgeheads, forrests, trenchlines and so forth that were actually fought over during the battle in WWII.
CONS: 1. Poor/Unresponsive AI. The AI troops ('bots') often get 'stuck'. They ignore enemies on the flanks most of the time. They ignore commander orders 40-60% of the time. Bots can be in a dead run and hip-fire from 60m and hit you in the head... EVERY time. They also seem to have no friendly (or enemy for that matter) line-of-fire detection. They will run directly in front of a FRIENDLY MG as it is firing for example. They also run headlong into both friendly and enemy artillery fire and will walk right up to a friendly satchel charge that's clearly seconds from detonating (i.e. placed on an enemy tank). Lastly they can see through walls, trees, grass and just about anything. They'll detect and kill you even when it's obvious that no human- in real life or a video game- would ever know where you were.
2. MG's are a little "over-balanced" if you will. The barrel on an MG-34 heats up much more quickly than in real life. It's over-regulated and hurts realism. I've been firing weapons since I could walk... And firing 40 rounds even in just a few seconds will not overheat a barrel to the point of bursting... And why the heaven can you not get a full combat load of ammo at the ammo dumps??? You get one belt/mag and that's it! Again a comparrison with Ostfront: On there you can sit at an ammo dump for a few seconds and get not only your full load but sit a few more seconds and you can get even more. Why would a man go all the way to an ammo dump and only get one mag? Besides with EVERY OTHER WEAPON you get a standard combat load at the ammo dump. Makes absolutely no sense. At least your squadmates can resupply you if you're an MG'er...
3. Artillery Fire has a long 'cool-off' and cannot be adjusted. Again, I know this was probably done for "balance" but war is anything BUT balanced. Once artillery is requested it cannot be adjusted/corrected at all (they could at least let you adjust it ONCE per barage...) Also if for some reason the request is canceled the ARTY must go through the entire cool-off period before it can be used again; even if you canceled it before it actually started firing. Put simply, the Artillery needs a little more work. Other than the Katyusha rockets (which actually did take several minutes to re-load) the cool-off really makes artillery an emergency measure that's held to the last second. The ARTY on RO Ostfront had limited ammunition (on average 7 barages worth) instead of a cool-down timer. I wish they'd put that on ROHoS instead of the timer.
4. Bullet Penetration is "off kilter". This one is beyond understanding. You can kill an enemy through a brick or concrete wall but not sheet metal and small trees... I know it seems like a small issue, but it aggravates me; and everyone that I've talked to about it agrees that it needs a lot of work.
5. Tripwire will not DEBUG the darned thing. A grenade won't go through a 2 foot wide window. Invisible walls are everywhere, I fall through the game world every 10 minutes and half the places you should be able to deploy an MG cannot be used.... FIX IT PLEASE. It's not the most buggy shooter I've played, but it needs a lot more work.
6. The tanks are great, but.... They get stuck on things that they should easily run over. and I get tired of seeing "can't switch seats while someone else is moving" when NOT A SOUL is switching seats anywhere. And sometimes for no reason the tank will just start easing forward as if left unattended in neutral while you're trying to use the main gun or co-ax MG... And the engine gets damaged from being shot in the gun mantlet????
Despite it all ROHoS is the absolute most realistic FPS I have ever seen. I recommend it to anyone tired of pupming 30 unrealistic rounds into an unrealistic character only to be shot dead by him once your mag is empty. Give it a chance, it's well worth it. Also I hope soon a more modern combat game with the same level of realism will be produced. Maybe a Red Orchestra: Korea. Not enough respect is given to the the brave men and women who fought and died there. Whether you agree with the why's and what's of the war or not, the brave souls who fought it should not be forgotten.

So first off, let's just say I don't particularly like this game. And when I say that I don't like this game, I mean that I really don't like this game.
I got this game on release day, installed it on release day, played around 2 hours on release day. It was a weird experience to say the least. I think that pretty much everyone who picked up this game on release day was expecting something that was literarily just "terraria in space". This game is anything but that. From a terraria perspective, the characters are a weird size, seeming just too big. The game is similar to starbound with the way you mine and build things, but starbound just feels more complete. The game has a weird graphics style that just doesn't quite complete. It seems a bit rough around the edges. I am not saying that no one could love it, just that I can't.
If you own Terraria and want a similar experience, then get Starbound. "But I already have Starbound" you say? Wait for an update to Terraria and then you will be right.
If you own Startbound and want a similar experience, then get Terraria. "But I already have Terraria" you say? Wait for an update to Starbound and then you will be right.
I cannot recommend this game for the simple reason of there are already games out there that do everything this game does but better; want a great 2D building/exploring/sandbox experience? Get Terraria. Want a great 2D space building/exploring/sandbox experience that isn't quite complete, but still great?. Get Starbound. Want some weird space thing? Get Defy Gravity.
P.S. Just as a warning for this game, there are save wipes
P.P.S. I have also played this game since release day, enough to find form valid arguments about this game.

I'd survived for weeks. I had a home-base set up in an abandoned gas station next to a frozen lake. I was using the garage as an area to store meat and cure hides. I had a ton of tools foraged and had managed to find a hunting rifle. In one outing, I found a bear on the frozen lake. I shot it 3 times from afar, which seemingly did nothing. I got closer to see if it was a glitch. It wasn't. The bear stood up, charged and began mauling me. I survived the attack by one point of health, but lost consciousness. I awoke freezing to death and bleeding out on the icy lake. My controls were barely able to guide my body to a nearby fishing hut, which I kept falling over and out of every time I tried to stand. I was barely able to make a fire in the potbelly stove to keep from freezing to death. I took meds and slept on and off for three days, nursing myself back to health. Eventually I got my strength back and returned to the lake where I'd dropped my rifle during the attack. Laying next to it was the dead grizzly, having stayed alive after 3 gunshots just long enough to maul the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. After that, I was pretty attached to that save game. After all, if you die, that is IT . Eventually, weeks later, I was running low on food and came down with food poisoning from expired canned peaches. I had to march to a second location where I'd stored more food. I got there and was getting steadily worse, when I found that I had no antibiotics stored to cure myself. Rest and water helped, but I'd exhausted the backup food supply and I was barely able to walk as it was. I went outside to look for firewood, but I'd been indoors for so long that my "hours of daylight/darkness" counter had gone to "???". I stepped out into the black of night during a hellacious blizzard. There was zero visibility and I couldn't even find the door to get back inside. I thought my time might be up. Seconds later, I heard the growling of wolves in the pitch black. I never even saw them attack me..... I do miss that save game. The saddest part was the post-game stats screen, which displayed "Number of times attacked by wolves: 56" right above "Number of wolf attacks successfully fought off: 55"

If you love City Building Games then I highly and most certainly recommend this game for sure. It is by far the most interesting and tedious city builder there is to date which covers a lot of ground to keep you busy and reeled in for hours on end.
There are only two major complaints I still have about this game - read why below.
1 - The Multiplayer was horrible at first and because of that the game got a really bad wrap from the get go so players stopped playing it online due to the issues it originally had. On a positive note most of those problems were fixed and it does work very well online now. However, due to that bad start it may be hard to play it online unless you go to the community or get a friend to join you.
2 - One of my biggest problems that I have always had with this game with each of it's following game sequences is that the buildings are way too repetitive as in all of the building types are the exact same. So once you get further into the game you'll notice that you have lots of areas with houses and buildings but they all look exactly alike with absolutely no variance whatsoever. I have repeatedly complained to them about this in every series and nothing has been done and I doubt now that it will ever change either unless a ton of people start to do the same. One thing though that does make it a little better is the different building types and the added buildings from the dlc but still if you have a bunch of houses and similar buildings you will notice that and it may become an annoyance. If you can look past that then you'll enjoy it! On top of that the Eras also do help aid with that in changing the look of several types of buildings after upgrades have occurred from advancing in time but many do not such as housing unfortunately.
Anyhow though, aside from those two issues it is still an epic game and I definitely think it's worth the price in full but if you'd rather wait for a sale then I would certainly recommend grabbing it for sure to say the least!

I wrote here some silly jokes before but now it's time to get serious.
Sunless Sea is a story based survival/horror game. Game will change with the decisions you made and with the time you spent in Unterzee. Most of the stories in this game are gorgeous with rich story-writing and the atmosphere of the places astonishing. However, game has some serious problems about being "survival" game.
First of all, Sunless Sea's first principal utterly wrong: Game expects from you dying a lot and restart the whole game with same stories with same results and yes, when you die or succeed an ambition your's new captain playthrough will be mostly same except some improved stats or money. I don't know what were developers thinking when they put this mechanic but I know most of the players not going to like to play that way espically the ones who played 50 hours on single captain like me. It's like playing a fps game with different gun but always in same map.
Second thing that is frustrating trade mechanics in this game are useless, selling a product from london to other places will only give you 1 or 2 echo per unit and this will not even repay your fuel cost. The only ways to make decent money in this game following stories which give you trinkets for selling Alarming Scholar or going illegal and selling sunligth or souls. I believe trade is wasted opportunity in this game.
Although game is cruel, it is never warning you about real dangers of Unterzee: Tutorial book given in the beginnig only teach you some basic things which anyone can learn after short time.  I highly sure most people rage quitted when they killed from Mt. Nomad in Chapel of Lights at the beginning of their game. Most captain's first travels are real horror of Sunless Sea.
Less but not last it is very odd this game doesn't have any language choice except English. Story based game like this must be multiple language choice or people may can not understand stories properly and believe me, some sentences in this texts are really hard to understand but I think it's not a bad thing because these sentences are the ones who make stories interesting.
My big recommendation: Play in Merciful Mode. Take a save beginning of the game, take saves before critical points in stories, load last save when you unexpectedly died, load last save when you saw a story end which ended your captain's career. Discover all the stories with one captain and fell the beatiues of stories without fear of death. I admit this will kill horror function of the game but if your reason to play discover all stories like me then you should play in that way.
Sunless Sea is good but not great game, give it a try if you are interested.

The story is OK at the most. The surprising turns consist of
. At least one of these revelations is really shocking; it's cool how the writers ignored some of the canons. Also, I don't know if they'll have any relevant impact on season 2 (probably not). Overall, I think Telltale could be more ambitious and really make the story oscillate wildly depending on the choices made.

I've removed my previous review because it is no longer valid.  I reviewed the game with Monster Edition purchased and shortly before the game was launched with beta then afterwards.  I put about 50 hours into the Stage 1 game and then another 40 odd hours into Stage 2.  To put it bluntly, TRS has done an amazing job of a F2P port.  See below.
The game costs nothign.  Literally nothing as of 8/6/16.  You can download the game and play for ABSOLUTELY free.  There are no strings attached.  You get to play the hunters and monster in rotation, but it's still FREE.  Not one cent you have to pay for anything.  This is a huge draw to the new player whom wants to get their feet wet in this glorious game.  Yes, I said glorious because the game is such.  It's something you don't see very often and other companies are now copying what TRS has developed with Evolve Stage 2.
Previously, the games were very much slower.  When I say slower, I mean upwards of around 15 to 30 minutes per match at least.  Nobody wanted to play Trapper since they were tasked with placing a dome around the monster and if the Trapper died, then the dome would be brought down.  It's very easy for the monster to focus down one specific hunter even at the cost of their armor and some of their health.  Now?  Any hunter can dome.  This major change has brought games from a 15 to 30 minute duration to a 5 to 15 minute duration and that's being very forgiving.  The games are now such a length where people (myself included) can have a vested interest in the game and keep playing round after round if time permits.
Finding the monster used to be huge pain in the butt.  I'm serious about that.  It was possible for the monster to evade the hunters without ever being spoted until stage 3 when the monster is pummeling the power relay.  It's easier now since the Trapper can use satellite beacon and get a general location of the monster.  TRS has made the game possible for Hunters and Monsters to play rapidly if they choose to do so.  A 30 minute investment game only to lose is EXTREMELY frustrating and you don't feel that when losing or even winning 5 to 10 minutes into the match.
The game is faster, more challenging when fighting and I absolutely love it.  If you're reading this and are on the fence about the game then give it a shot and decide for yourself.  Seriously, the game is free.  FREE, no strings attached.  Even if you don't have all the hunters or monsters and are playing 100% free then you still have a decent fighting chance.  The game is designed to give you that chance.

The very first thing you should know about this game is that it is
a business simulation! This is no Railroad Tycoon or Industry Giant. It is more of a micro management focused virtual model railway. If that sounds strange and unconventional to you you might want to check out the free demo first.
The gameplay consists only marginally of financial management and largely of creating track layouts and manual train guidance. The challenge comes from creating connections between set stations and handling an ever growing amount of railway traffic that will put your planning skills to the test. With the help of 3 different game speeds and a pause button at your disposal you can decide yourself how reflex heavy each level will be.
This game is best played in short bursts since each level can be finished within minutes. Yet it maintains a decently high level of replayability, especially for players that like to maximize their efficiency and want to perfect track layouts for optimal capacity.
The level design is appealing and varied with an almost toy-like aesthetic. And the music is appropriately soothing and up-beat. Though it might get repetetive if you decide to 'binge' the game and finish it in one sitting.
Depending on your personal aim in terms of perfection and Highscores that may take you between 5 and 20 hours.
Overall you can expect a very pleasent experience for a rather low price tag.

I want to preface this review with the fact that while I do not recommend
that does
mean that I want to discourage its developers from continuing with their projects or even one day returning to this sort of project in future. I also understand that this was meant as but a tiny slice of what the devs wanted to accomplish with more time, funds, etc.
So what is
? Well, it sees the player filling the shoes (or, more appropriately, sandals) of a Grecian delving into the labyrinthine catacombs beneath Greece.
I detected what I believed to be very definite influences of Frictional Games'
series, as well as
in
, which isn't necessarily a complaint: if you want to go first-person horror, Frictional Games are one of the kings of the genre and looking to their games for guidance is a fantastic starting point. However, the question that arose while playing this was, "What does this game do differently than those games?" The answer, sadly, being, "Not that much, really." Even in this limited glimpse into what the devs envisioned, it just sort of felt like
, using the same sort of effects, same sort of gameplay (though without Frictional Games' "push and pull" control system), and the same sort of scares.
That's not to say there aren't good ideas here: the setting is a fantastic place to set a horror game, as I can't think of a single [i[horror[/i] game set in Ancient Greece. It's an untapped well and there is a lot of excellent material for use there. I also think that Guru Games did a very nice job on environments and should
be commended for their sound design: early on in the game I was genuinely starting to get nervous, based on the sound design alone. As far as story goes, I would have been interested to see how things turned out.
That being said, I think it is fortuitous that this did not get a full release. If this sounds harsh, it is not intended to be: I think that Guru Games has a great setting and some excellent ideas here but it is in its gameplay that
is the weakest. Had they spent the time to flesh the game out fully and release it, I fear it would have been more of the same: walking slowly through hallways, avoiding one-hit kill monsters, all the lights go out, spooky noises, etc. The setting is incredibly unique but the gameplay is very much something that has been done many times and is risking becoming quite stale.
Admittedly, this is an oddly in-depth review for a half an hour, free-to-play demo of a game that might never be but my hope is that such a critique will aid Guru Games in growing and learning. There is definite potential here but, as it stands, the gameplay would need some polish for me to feel like I could recommend more of it.

I have played this game quite a bit, and while fun I do think that it suffers from some major issues.
First, the games are stacked into the casino's favor WAY more than a normal casino.  I know it sounds like I'm just being idiotic, but I started testing a few things in the game.  First, when playing slots you almost never hit bonuses. Once in 200 spins or so seems to be the average.  If you've ever been to a real casino, you know bonuses are a lot more common.  In fact the payout on the slot machines is ridiculous.  You can expect to lose 75% of the money you put into the slot machine over about 10 spins.  Slots are money losers, I know, but 75% over 10 spins, nine out of ten times? Come on.  Yes you can go on win streaks, but its as though when the game feels you have built up enough using a Martingale system (doubling your bet after you lose), it will make sure you keep losing.  You can go up to max bet and lose, which is normal using that system.  But to continue losing 10 more bets after that?
Not convinced?  Blackjack.  I counted the number of cards between yellow cards.  Instead of the standard 6 decks.. there is 4.5.. not 4, not 5.. but 4.5.  So which cards are extra and who gets which? Go ahead, try it.  You can bet 15 times in a row using basic blackjack strat and not win a single round.  Meanwhile the dealer will pull 14, or 16.. and they will get just enough to beat you.
Why?  Well, the problem is the whole pay-to-play structure.  While it would take a lengthy amount of time to lose your chips making minimum bets, you will never make VIP.  VIP allows you to play Baccarat (not available on the normal floor), as well as play higher stakes games, and a few other perks. You earn VIP status through earning Reward Points.  You earn Reward Points for winning bets.  The higher the bet, the more reward points you are eligible for.  It takes a lot of grinding. Edge of Space takes dedication to be appreciated. I recomment this game because I've grown to enjoy it after about 2 months of intensive in-game experimentation, but it was a winding road with a dull beginning.
The biggest flaw with EoS is its glaringly lacking help menus. This is a significant flaw because the opportunities offered by the game far outweigh the amount of helpful information about the different tools and installations you can craft. This can lead to extended periods of aimless mining and construction that can feel pointless and frustratingly anti-climactic (I've been surprised quite often at how little I could accomplish during long hours of continuous play because of a lack of clear objectives).
That being said, I've grown to enjoy Edge of Space very much. Here's a bit of context: you are dropped on a foreign planet after a spaceship crash and evacuation. Your codex (the help menus) is obviously incomplete and written very much like the entries in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: unfocused and essentially devoid of any useful information beyond vague hints at a distant purpose. As the player, it is your job to extrapolate meaning -and ultimately results- from what little help and guidance you are offered by your interplanetary employer.
Edge of Space plays very much like the old NES and SNES Metroid games, with the added elements of terraforming and crafting. The bottom line is that once you've "figured out" the basics, the game works. Very well.
So, provided you're willing to tolerate fuzzy objectives and the occasional quirks, you should enjoy Edge of Space for what it is: a wacky, competely over-the-top sandbox with a lot of potential and a ton of fun! And laser sharks!
FREE TIP: Keep digging deeper. And when you think you've gone deep enough, keep going. Edge of Space offers a BIG world!

By far the greatest game I've played on steam... AND its still an early access, which means it can only get better. I adore this game: the atmosphere, the art, the chill I get when staying up the play the game till early hours of the morning. I don't think I can recommend it enough. The body heat mechanics and weather work perfectly in sync and I haven't run into any problems yet. This game can get tense. I remember gripping my keyboard as I urged my character to go forward. It was before I reached the coastal highway and I had no food and no wood. In game I was close to freezing to death as irl I sipped at a warm mug of tea, close to tears, since I had down so well so far. And then it happened. I saw a shadow of a trailer through the blinding blizzard and I can assure you, I've never been happier. I found enough food and wood (for heat and water) to hole up in that little safe haven for 10 days waiting for that raging blizzard to calm down enough to continue. But my god was that blizzard beautiful. Deadly, sure, but gorgeous. The world fell dark and for the first time in the game, I felt extremely alone. What if I saw a bear? What happened to everyone? Why am I alone? Those questions circled in my mind. But when there wasn't a blizzard and the setting or rising sun set a golden glow on the world, I felt at home. Peacefully happy and it aww at how this game was developed. Haunting questions didn't circulate my mind this time, instead I mused what other gorgeous weather phenomenons I'd experience. I go to this game all the time: when I want to have a break from my hectic life, when I have free time, when I want the tense survival experience of being alone in already isolated world. This is the only steam game I have ever deemed good enough for me to a review on, the only steam game I'd pay way more than it's worth for, and the only steam game I keep coming back to without ever getting bored. Please get this amazing game and start your own beauifully tense experience.

Do you prefer to move with the speed of a wounded snail?
Do you like huge areas with nothing but green void?
Do you hate in-game music?
Do you enjoy reading about exploration as much as actually exploring?
If yes, you will LOVE sunless sea! Go for it, man!
For the rest of us...
The trailers are very misleading.
It looks like you can explore stuff, fight monsters, get loot,
craft, build, recruit cool characters, be a pirate, and all bells
and whistles.
Sure. It s all there.
In text form.
All that stuff about "eating your crew" and "exploring" - yeah, it all
takes place on game menus, popups, dialogue boxes, charts and windows.
Your "crew" is just a number on your screen, like your fuel or "pages".
They have no names, no background, not even pictures! So when you eat them
it s like "you used 1 unit of fuel". You can recruite more serious ones, but
even those just boost your stats.
The exploration is the same.
Your ship is pretty much just a map marker that you move PAINLESSLY
SLOWLY on a huge green map filled with labels, so yeah, you are actually
moving on the "world map" only. When you reach a port all that happens
is that a window pops up and you can talk and "explore" in that window.
How do you explore a new town, dungeon, or location?
By clicking dialogue options, of course.
They are full of exciting new vocabulary for you, "mirrors", "veil",
"echo", "heart" and like two dozen more vague and ambigious new terms
that actually mean a hell lot of different stats, variables, numbers,
currencies, values that you have to keep track of. It s like doing
math in Chinese...
In this game most of the time you will be treading through huge
areas of green nothing in total silence (no music! good job!),
just to collect a few gold and maybe buy a better gun after like 15 return trips.
Boredom.
Silence.
Futility.
Then a sudden and unfair death and you can go and start over again.
Conclusion:
Sunless sea is like a book that has been made into a browser game
or a smartphone app.
If you love READING fantasy books and looking for casual click-and-choose
fun, then you might like this game.
If you are looking for some cool steampunk gothic action try grim dawn
or...well, anything else but sunless sea.
(btw i always play offline so my game time is not accurate)

The very first thing you should know about this game is that it is
a business simulation! This is no Railroad Tycoon or Industry Giant. It is more of a micro management focused virtual model railway. If that sounds strange and unconventional to you you might want to check out the free demo first.
The gameplay consists only marginally of financial management and largely of creating track layouts and manual train guidance. The challenge comes from creating connections between set stations and handling an ever growing amount of railway traffic that will put your planning skills to the test. With the help of 3 different game speeds and a pause button at your disposal you can decide yourself how reflex heavy each level will be.
This game is best played in short bursts since each level can be finished within minutes. Yet it maintains a decently high level of replayability, especially for players that like to maximize their efficiency and want to perfect track layouts for optimal capacity.
The level design is appealing and varied with an almost toy-like aesthetic. And the music is appropriately soothing and up-beat. Though it might get repetetive if you decide to 'binge' the game and finish it in one sitting.
Depending on your personal aim in terms of perfection and Highscores that may take you between 5 and 20 hours.
Overall you can expect a very pleasent experience for a rather low price tag.

Not sure if you've ever played "Sid Meier's Railroads" but it's a much more simplified version of that (and that game was fairly simple to begin with!). Someone also compared it to "Lionel's(?) Train Town" which is also a fair comparison to make!
To start with, it's not a tycoon game so don't be fooled by the images if they look like a Railroad Tycoon. The game is more focused on being a puzzle game based around trains. I'm sure if you've played Railroad Tycoon or the like you've had to overcome complicated junctions or network improvements the puzzles tend to focus on that skill - placing stations in awkward places.
Every so often the game will general a train which will be at one of the stations (there's a gauge timer thing at the bottom right of the screen so you can see when the next train will generate) - you can also call on addional trains to create additional revenue. The train will be assigned a colour and you have to create a route via the switches/junctions you've made in your solution to get the train to it's destination. Laying track and destroying objects costs money and, along with a tax you have to pay, your balance can deplete quickly - going below 0 results in bankrupcy and you lose the game.
There are four different regions progressing in difficulty. Difficulty in this game is present through awkwardly placed stations, objects to either neogotiate around or destroy and build over at an addition cost (depends on what you destroy for cost) and the challenges present in each level (spend x money, don't let trains go to the wrong stations, etc) create some replayability.
This is a fun puzzler and the trains were just a bonus (well, at least for me anyway).

Finally, a well designed walk around casino for PC. Remember Ceasars Palace? That was a good game made 15 years ago and there hasn't been something similar until now. The Four Kings is a huge casino and you can walk up to any table/machine and play it. 10/10
You start with 10k chips and can purchase 400k for $20. If you're smart, that 400k will last an extremely long time even with max bets. For a free game, the 10k can last you a long time. That's a pretty incredible deal. Don't like it? Stop playing, or decide to spend $20 for the largest package of chips. The avatars are cheap and you can earn quite a few perks at the poker and blackjack tables for free. $20 out of the gate is very fair.
There's tons of selection of games. Multiplayer makes this game awesome. You can sit down at a blackjack, craps, poker, roulette, war and money wheel and even bingo with real people. First person table view is excellent. Tired of playing? Go for a walk and sit down on a couch, eat some lunch, and come back. There's also a VIP area and many shops to buy things for your avatar. Call your friends up and play poker together with other people online.
Yes, this game requires major computer resources as people are saying, so if you can't handle it turn them to low in the settings.
