, which in this game is the creation of your first captain choosing their past and essentially selecting the main quest that you will spend the majority of the game working your way towards its completion. The atmosphere is wonderfully captured and centres around a dystopian Fallen London that is situated underground and surrounded by the unterzee, a vast underground ocean of loneliness with your only real companion being the menace and mayhem you will regularly encounter along the way.
The story is captivating, and it sucked me as I mentioned from ‘hello’, combine this with an excellent music score and the combination creates a perfect storm in which to engage the player. And engage it did, the first 30 hours I spent trundling around in my less than perfect starting ship the Ligeia-class Steamer, going from port to port scraping together what echoes (gold) I could to either upgrade my lodgings back in London, or purchase crucial components for my ship and crew to make the trundling less difficult.
As the game advises dying is something you should get used to, so at around 45 hours I was horribly mauled by a flock of Blue Prophets (Parrots), I sank to the bottom and my first captain had indeed died. At this point the whole death thing kicks off and you are forced to make some choices for your next captain, which I aptly named after my son.
And off I go again, only this time I have the deck mounted gun handed down from my last captain (thanks Dad!), 50% of some their stats and their charter (map), also I managed to buy an apartment. Great! At this point I have great anticipation of what lies ahead, after all death is supposed to be such a part of this game that I assumed things would really start to unfold from here… But sadly this is where Sunless Sea begins to sink to the bottom of the unterzee, slowly, slowly sinking.
The game is suffering from a bit of an identity crisis, it doesn’t quite know what it wants to be, is it a roguelike, or is it an RPG? To me at this point I’m quite unaware. But I think it’s just an interactive novel.
As I venture out I realise that the gun that I’ve inherited and the minor stat increases are a complete pittance, and not only that but I have to do everything all over again, the world is mostly completely unchanged and seems unaware of any the events of my previous captain. This is my first disappointment as I realise all the grinding of quests and endless port reports I did, now all need to be done again. Everything.
So I start to think completion, and focus on the main quests then I have my next realisation, the extent to which I am required to fetch and carry, grind port reports and all of the like just to stay alive is then multiplied by the enormity of the requirements to meet any victory conditions, doubly multiplied by how mind numbingly slow the game is. Add to this that the excellent story writing now starts to become your enemy, and taking any risks as the game encourages you too, becomes a bit of a fools act, doing an event on your first time that ends up killing a number of your crew, then requires you to trundle back to London at a lesser speed than the mind numbingly slow speed from before. And if I were to die like the game advises, just so I could go back and do the story again for a second time just to get it right the next time does not feel roguelike, it feels kind of pointless.
I did complete the game and felt some sense of satisfaction, overcoming the odds and all that, but there were so many completely frustrating moments when the story and the juggling act of fuel, supplies and terror all combines and conspires to completely undermine the satisfaction, sense of fun, or believability of the game. Combine this with, and despite what the fans will say, the fact that questline missions are excessively grindy to the point of utter frustration. There is a good game within Sunless Sea, but it becomes so obscured at times that it becomes hard to recognise for all the reasons mentioned.
Beyond all this this the journal is very poor, I would often lose information amongst the log book, information that is important is never presented very well. The combat system although satisfying to begin with, you quickly figure out that it has no real tactics.
I enjoyed my first 40 hrs, hated the next 40, and didn’t mind the last 6 or so as I completed the main questline, but I was already over the story by this point. The Zubmariner content made things much more bearable mid to late game, without it I think I would have lost all interest and closed the book on Sunless Sea.
Based on this whilst the game is entertaining, there is just too many negative moments that ruin the fun, and after all that’s what we’re here for, playing a game should be fun at a basic level and not feel at all like a chore, so I can’t really recommend it.

TL;DR
A spin-off of the browser based text adventure Fallen London, Sunless Sea is a Lovecraftian flavored top-down roguelike that takes place in a vast, beautiful, terrible underground cavern, the Neath. You are a captain of a steamship, cast upon the Unterzee by fates unknown. Smuggle goods, endear yourself to rulers, fight living mountains, find your father's bones, eat your crew, write an epic, find love, build a legacy. But a word from the wise? Mind the devils.
Follow us here
Steamship Discord:
Steamship Steam group:
Pros
Cons
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The gameplay is overall very simple and easy to understand. Combat takes place in the from of ship battles and encounters with sea monsters, and while it can be challenging and tricky to master in the beginning it is usually avoidable.
Sunless Sea has many stories. In the beginning you choose your win conditions, which could be considered your overall plot for that captain, and smaller stories can be found as you play. These change between captains as well; one who visits Venderbright might find different events than those who came before.
Characters the player encounters in passing are overall very interesting, spiced with many peculiarities and adjoining stories. The player collects officers for their crew, which provide perks and buffs as well as their own personal questlines.
The graphics are minimal, but what there is is very polished. The style is all one could expect from such a dark game, capturing well the dank, anxious environment one might expect from an underground ocean.
Sunless Sea is overall a captivating game. Though it suffers from a clunky UI and poor organization, there is much to discover by those who muscle past.

This is a Rogue Lite game, with a lot of adventures, plenty of stories and choices that have consequences, unfortunately one of the features of this genre is that you have no idea what anything does, so yeah googling everything is kinda important before making decisions, the tutorial doesn't really help that much, you will die, and that is also a feature of the game and of the genre itself, after you die you will pick another capitain and that capitain will have an easier start, you can choose what aspects of your previous capitain will pass over - or at least a portion of it - so it's not exactly a go back to zero start, it does give you some quickstart options if you died at the 'zee' (sea).
I really do like the game and have already spent over 25 hours in it, lost a couple of capitains, and almost lost my current one to birds, yeah one thing that you will learn very quickly is don't mess with monsters and animals at the zee, because they will F you up, pirates are very easy to deal with though, so you can farm them for resources and even money (or echos as they call it in game)
So besides 'zee' monsters and pirates, what else is trying to kill you? Everything,  even the zee itself (sea) is trying to kill you. The game has a terror mechanic, and every second you spend on the open zee you will be accumulating terror points, as you pass certain thresholds (which are not explained in the game at all by the way), you will start to get nightmares as well as ocasionally losing your sailors and you die if you lose all of them, those nightmares can increase terror, or reduce depending on how lucky you are or which choice you went with, if you pass the 90 points of terror, the music will change to a very dramatic and horrific song that is to no doubt scare the hell out of the player and make him/her seek refuge in a port quickly, the longer you spend over 90 points of terror the higher the chances of very bad events to happen, some pretty mild like losing a sailor here or there, but some events can quite literally kill you straight up, it will give you a almost impossible RNG choice, and you will die if you don't get extremely lucky in the dice, which needless to say if you add some insta death mechanic like that to an already confusing and not very well explained terror mechanic,  makes for some pretty infuriating deaths in the game.
But again, death is not the end is just the begining of something new.
The game does give you some ways of making sure that your next capitain will have a very good start, when you can write your own will and even leave him/her with a fantastic treasure that you will be able to use to get a quick start and not have to do the boring grinding that you most likely will have to do it at the begining.
Other than getting killed at the zee there are also chances of getting killed in ports base on your choices, again keep in mind that being curious will increase your chances of death, while not being curious will certantly kill you from lack of progress and lack of resources, so you need to strike a balance somewhere along those lines.
So besides trying to avoid death, what is the purpose of the game? You choose, the game gives you victory states at the begining of your career, and you can pick between several victory conditions, and you can change those victory conditions later in the game if you feel like trying to do something different with your capitain, or you can just explore and try to just follow some of the many adventures and plotlines in the game, because there are many that don't seen to be that related to any of the victory conditions, and there is a lot of mystery that you can try to shine a light on through out the game (and that has its own risks of death attached to it so keep that in mind).
And since death is a major aspect of the game the replayability is obviously also important, and just like other games in the genre the map is somewhat random, so ports are not always in the same spot, which keeps the exploration part of the game fresh in each playthrough which is nice.
It's a very fun game, great writing with some good sense of humor here in there, quite terrifying in some places and as i said, a lot of mystery to be solved, if you choose to do that, and that is another thing that the game does very well you have a lot of choices.
It does have problems though, my biggest issue has to do with the bugs, the game is very well polished for the most part, but some bugs are present and they do tend to irritate me, especially since this game is also a survival game where you have to manage resources and you need to at any possible moment reduce terror somehow, and one of the most reliable ways of getting a big chunk of terror out of your head, is to go back to london after some time, unfortunately though this is where a glitch can happen, depending on your current missions, someone might imediatelly open up a conversation with you when you reach london, which i believe can cause the window that is supposed to allow you to reduce you terror back to 50, doesn't popup anymore which makes you unable to reduce your terro from the 90s. There are other ways of reducing terror though but they tend to cost resource or echoes (coin).  And again the way that the terror mechanic works is basically like a clock, everytime you leave port you are on a clock, you can not spent too much time at the zee or you risk literally getting killed by your own nightmares, or by your own crew in some situations (again RNG goes crazy by the time you reach terror level 90).
Anyway, there is also a glitch that involves combat, if you engage in combat with a ship/monster and right as you destroy the ship/monster another enemy engages you, the game will glitch and you will be unable to fire back at your enemy, the only way to solve this as far as i know is to run as fast as you can until the combat mode can disengage and you can engage back on again.
Anyway but after 25 hours in, those bugs are not really that problematic, they are annoying but they don't happen at a frequent enough basis to ruin the fun of the game.
Overall the game is fantastic, even for someone like me. A lot of people compared this game to FTL and i think they are correct, but for me this games does something that FTL didn't which is to make me care about the characters and the story, that is the main focus of the game, and it accomplishes that objective very well, the story is very well written and the character are all very interesting and intriguing some ways, so even though i didn't like FTL, this game did enough things different to make me enjoy the hell out of this game. So i definitely recommend, it's a very fun game.

I won't even discuss the graphics or mechanics of this game. I think they suck, but I guess some people would be into it. But  it just fails horribly in the simplest things. Some things that gave me headache even with my small playtime:
- Citizen ai is horrible and absollutely opaque. If I designate an area for resource gathering half of the people will start gathering them from the farthest end. If I designate several areas I can be 100% sure that they will start not from the closest one 20 meters away, but from that small piece I marked 100 meters away. There is no clue what exactly labourers will do, good luck if you marked both stone and wood, but really need only 20 of each at first to start construction. They will be gathered absolutely randomly. If builders can't continue with construction, they will just silently go and do something else, leaving me wondering why no one bothers to build the trading post. Or maybe they just don't want to do it, I have no clue.
- Spent a lot of time building the trading post. If I produce lots of fish and I can stockpile fish on the trading post, then I can trade fish for tools, rigth? Wrong! After all that construction and waiting for the trader it turns out that fish has 0 value. 0! I can't sell it and I can't buy it! Why can I put it in the trading post in the first place? Didn't check other resources, but I'm sure some of them will have the same problem.
- Absolutely no clue how your resources will be distributed and processed. How much of that wood I gather will go into tools? Firewood? Construction? No clue. Whoever manages to grab it first will use it first. Speaking of grabbing first, I had 2 people starve to death with hundreds of food produced simply because 4 houses snatched all food for themselves. They had several hundreds of food stockpiled while the new house stood with empty larder for years, until the people there starved.
- Time flow is absolutely untransparent. I guess that sun-rain-snow effects are meant to specify the change of seasons and don't have any other effect, but it makes no sense when several years fly by in a couple of realtime minutes, meanwhile people can go hungry or cold - for many months what looks in game, and nothing happens to them. Then they just die. Without warning.
- If deer want to cross the river, they just walk on water.
- No indication at all what resources are gathered. I have a foresters' hut and 3 people working there. Why do I have no logs? Are they snatched by woodcutter? Are they not produced? Should I make more foresters? Place their hut in a different place? No ♥♥♥♥ing clue. It's the start of the game, mind you, about 15 people total and only the basic buildings.
- If people can walk in whatever direction they please, then why can I construct buildings only on the global rectangular grid and build roads only along its cells? With those stupid 90 degree angles people never walk along roads unless they have no other path or it's a straight line path. Why do I bother building roads at all?
- I have fishing docks (separated enough) and hunter's lodge, more than half of population is working there. Why do I constantly get shortage of food and my barn is empty? Am I doing something wrong? Am I doing everything right but the notification system is wrong? No clue.
I could go on. Overall this game is worth neither your money nor your time, it's too basic and broken even for a basic indy city builder. I have no clue why would anyone play this instead of much better games on the market.

TLDR: The art alone is worth the price of this game (especially on sale), but don't expect to be blown away by the gameplay.
----------------------
Long review:
First off let me say that I love puzzle games, and I'm always a sucker for an artistic or atmospheric game, even if the gameplay is trivial. I was ready to love this game. Unfortunately it has some serious shortcomings that prohibit me from loving it.
The art is amazing, we all agree on that. The artists spent a lot of time on it, and it's obvious that the whole team had a great idea for a game. The bad part is the controls. They are so bad. Like why, WHY can't I just use WASD to control the bug? Click and hold is terrible. Even if it's designed for touch screen, that is still a terrible way to move around. Frequently (the whole time) I would be clicking for an item, and accidentally move to the adjacent frame. Which you can't cancel, you have to wait for the animation, then go back to where you were. Super annoying.
Also getting around the environment is not very intuitive, and it's not always clear that there are pathways to other areas. This could be considered a pro if you're into exploration, but the controls are so slow and annoying that it isn't fun at all to explore. Then many of the puzzles suffer from♥♥♥♥♥♥controls as well. The last puzzle was infuriating, and would have been pretty easy with proper controls.
Which leads into another downfall... poor puzzle design. Some were good. The moth mosaic was very satisfying, and I would absolutely play a game consisting solely of that puzzle. Others were just straight up annoying or felt like busy work.
In any case, this game is cheap, and it was worth it to me to support the devs with less money than I would give to a homeless person, even if it was for the art alone. I had some fun in the short amount of time it took me to beat it. I look forward to what they come up with in the future, and I hope that they manage the gameplay a little better for future projects.

Despite what you may think looking at the store page, this is more of a straight-up railroading puzzle game and less of a management sim, although it does a decent job of simulating a rail network. It's quite a good game too: fun, challenging and pretty to boot.
However, I have to say that Train Valley reminds me of an older train puzzle game, one near and dear to my heart:
, developed in 2000 by Dynamix. Whereas that game focused on completing missions and solving puzzles, in Train Valley your main goal is to simply survive until the end of a level without going bankrupt, although completing side goals earns you stamps of recognition.
Train Valley has players reenact a more realistic depiction of railroading history - although it's mainly in the background - all the while attempting to stay afloat and expand to meet the needs of industry. Players take the role of a trainmaster, which means sending and routing trains to their intended destination.
TrainTown has you manually hauling freight such as ore to smelters, hamburgers to grills, or numbers to multiplication equations. It plays its Lionel model train aesthetic to the hilt and is definitely "wackier", if you're into that sort of thing. Controlling multiple locomotives at the same time is only really needed in the later levels; although it's possible in every level, you'll usually only need to control one train at a time in the early game.
In TrainTown,
crash fails a level, and some of those levels were as complex as any you may find in Train Valley. I mean, if the first set of levels was intended for elementary school kids, the last set was probably meant for college sophomores. I feel comfortable in saying TrainTown is harder, but oh so satisfying to play as well.
I know this is a recommendation for Train Valley, which I absolutely recommend for puzzle and train fans, but if you like it I'd say you should give TrainTown a shot too. It's more or less abandonware at this point anyway, no harm in trying it.

However, Limbo fell short in:
- Pacing in the later levels felt rushed and the game ends before you even know it
- Certain puzzles are almost impossible to figure out until you have tried everything and explored every corners of the map
- Sometimes certain mechanics are hard to figure out (such as the glow worm) without much explanation
- The latter levels became too reliant on dexterity and timing, and abandoned some creativity thinking, turning into more and more Super Meat Boy
- Half of the puzzles requires you to die at least once before you can figure it out
Overall, my rating for this game is an 8/10

Half-Life: Blue Shift
Short but sweet
After the success of Opposing Force, Gearbox decided to make another expansion pack for Valves critically acclaimed fps, Half-Life.
When aliens from Xen are teleported to his work place at Black Mesa, security guard Barney Calhoun must cut his shift short and try to escape the alien infested base, as well as fighting off the HECU marines who are tasked with neutralising the situation by killing all lifeforms in the facility.
Like Half-Life, the game explains where you need to go, what you need to do and why, however trying to wrap your head around the backstory of the Half-Life universe proves to be a difficult task. This expansion pack brings us to new areas of Black Mesa, unseen in previous games and there are a few Gordon Freeman cameos throughout.
What made Opposing Forces’ gameplay so much fun and memorable was the fact that Gearbox introduced new weapons and enemies. Unfortunately, in Blue Shift, all the weapons and enemies were recycled from Half-Life. Dr Rosenberg’s companionship was a new gameplay aspect introduced in Blue shift. Unlike other scientist in Half-Life, who only have 4 character models, Dr Rosenberg has distinctive facial features and is an essential character who makes multiple appearances throughout the game. As well as this new feature, you can look forward to the return of fun but difficult puzzles and awesome shootouts against aliens and soldiers.
Like Opposing Force, the graphics in this game have dated significantly since 2001. It is still enjoyable none the less however for those gamers who play the new shiny 1080p games, then this may be a struggle for you. Like all Half-Life games, a lot of thought has gone into the level design especially in the old areas of Black Mesa, where the equipment, hallways and signs have new textures. Notable were the health and HEV suit chargers, as there was an obvious change in their design to suit the old run down areas of the facility.
This game was a short but sweet expansion pack, only taking me 4 hours to complete. Like Opposing Force, there were no new “stand-out” soundtracks, those from Half-Life were once again recycled. However, it was fun to see the Lambda incident through the eyes of Barney Calhoun. Venturing into the old areas of Black Mesa was a unique experience, the gameplay was solid and it was interesting working with Dr Rosenberg as this companionship had not been done yet in a Half-Life game.
7/10

游戏讲诉了关于一个男孩进入Limbo的世界寻找姐姐的故事。画风比较压抑，死亡在游戏中是家常便饭，不过能令玩家不会因为死亡产生挫败感，则是这款游戏的精髓所在。小男孩在森林里醒过来，发现他身处在LIMBO地狱的边缘，这是一个黑白的世界，四周一片漆黑寂静，只有小男孩的双眼发出白色光芒。第一眼看见画面，模糊雾气和斑驳杂讯的效果，多半会使玩家感到沉重郁闷；游戏中没有播放任何背景音乐，偶尔冒出的风声、脚步声和机械运转声更衬托出不寻常的静默感。正因为这股不寻常的气氛，激起你探索的欲望：这是什么地方？小男孩在这里做什么？往前走也许会发现什么？游戏运用独特的黑白美学和音效表现营造出这股阴郁的气氛，少了这股气氛，《LIMBO》就不会那么引人入胜。
它看似宁静如水、波澜不惊，却又隐隐透露着令人窒息的绝望与恐惧。黑白、虚实、生死，强烈的反差带来的是深层的思考，每个人都会有自己不同的解读。果由心生，相由缘见，本作所呈现的，就是你所相信的那个世界和故事。

I've tried to enjoy this game through its many iterations and complete changes. In it's current (release) state, the game is tolerable, but lacking in many respects still, the largest being actually fun. I only play games of this sort multiplayer, so the experience may be different for playing solo.
The mining tool is my biggest gripe. It fires in a line, that is based on an unusual place on your character, making getting at specific tiles difficult, and hard to aim at anything but straight up/down/left/right. The mining tool is INCREDIBLY slow compared to other games such as Terraria or Starbound. In the latest incarnation, they added new mining tools that slowly (at about half-speed) dig out the tiles around the tile it's hitting, but generally this doesn't help much because it's slower and you can't generally dig in a way to take much advantage of it.
Then there is dealing with the plants of the world, which require a saw of some sort to gather. This is even slower than the mining tool, you just sit and wait and wait for it. And finally get your 2 protovine or whatnot. Good luck finding any seeds!
And then creating much of anything requires so many resources, but you have a tiny inventory and finding storage is time consuming. And though it is an interesting idea to have tiers of what sort of item something is (eg, "Inorganic - Mineral - Radioactive - Uranium"), when you need to build something that just needs a mineral, it should just say "Uranium" or similar names... but it has the entire long list for Uranium, making it hard to tell exactly what it is you need without really long names for things.
And the world itself is just a bunch of skylands, with occasional larger ones tossed in there for actual "ground", except that when you get lower, you have another giant gap of space before getting to the next "tier" of skyland below you. You generally find out about that after having walked off a cliff of your "ground" near the beginning of the game, because it is very abrupt: "Just walking along, oh there's a little hill, let's hop down... no, there's no bottom. NO! Oh, I'm dead again..."
The game USED to have an entire tutorial, teaching you how to use the interface, move around, use the laser pick, etc. but the release version removed all of that in favor of a talking shark that just tells you to get it things... without any details on how to do much of anything. I'm glad I already knew how to switch between foreground and background tile mining/placement from the previous tutorial, because I probably would have gone nuts trying to figure it out.
There are now side missions that take you to your own personal instance that are not multiplayer at that point... there are random NPCs to get that don't do much (a couple give you ok-ish rewards for doing tasks)... there are various weapons, but most require ammo that is frustrating to get.
All of this and, while playing, you still have no idea what you're actually doing. The premise seems to be something about terraforming, but to what end?

This review originally written on May 21, 2012 on GameFAQs
"The weakest of the Half-Life games, but more Half-Life is always good."
This is a standalone expansion of the original Half-Life, and the second and final expansion. I recommend everyone plays this first after Half-Life and before Opposing Force for various reasons I will explain. The ratings and my feelings of this expansion are gauged in relation to the first Half-Life.
STORY: 9/10
You play as Barney Calhoun, security guard. You are actually the security guard you see banging on the door at the very beginning of Half-Life, pretty cool how it's all linked. You experience the events of the resonance cascade but at different parts of the facility. Your main goal is to escape with the scientists. The story actually isn't bad, but it ends kind of abruptly and feels like there should have been a little more.
GRAPHICS: 9/10
These are the same graphics as the original Half-Life which is both good and bad. The good part is it all looks the same and this expansion came with an HD pack for all the original Half-Life games. The bad part is that when this game came out in 2001 the graphics were starting to look dated even for the time. This isn't a big deal to me as I enjoy the graphics (with the HD pack).
SOUND: 9/10
The sound is the same as Half-Life. Not changing the alien sounds is fine, but I would've liked some new voices for the guards and scientists. Although there is a new voice for a certain scientist, that's it.
WEAPONS: 8/10
The weapon system works the same as Half-Life but you get a fewer selection of weapons to play with and no new ones. This is very disappointing.
ENEMIES: 9/10
You see a return of nearly all of the enemies from Half-Life, but that's it. There is nothing new which is again disappointing.
LEVEL DESIGN: 10/10
This is the only part where this game lives up to Half-Life. The level design is very similar and the few puzzles and situations where you must figure out what to do are very fun. And you get to revisit my favorite level!
LENGTH AND REPLAYABILITY
This game is extremely short, clocking in at 2 hours, 2 and a half if you play on hard and take your time like I did. Still, it is fun to play as Barney and re-experiencing the levels in a future playthrough is certainly viable.
FINAL SCORE: 9/10
The game is good and well made, but rushed and without any real new content. You should play this before Opposing Force because if you play it after you will be disappointed expecting this to at least be on the level of content of Opposing Force. If you liked Half-Life, this is still a must play.

A spin-off of the browser based text adventure Fallen London, Sunless Sea is a Lovecraftian flavored top-down roguelike that takes place in a vast, beautiful, terrible underground cavern, the Neath. You are a captain of a steamship, cast upon the Unterzee by fates unknown. Smuggle goods, endear yourself to rulers, fight living mountains, find your father's bones, eat your crew, write an epic, find love, build a legacy. But a word from the wise? Mind the devils.

The gameplay is overall very simple and easy to understand. Combat takes place in the from of ship battles and encounters with sea monsters, and while it can be challenging and tricky to master in the beginning it is usually avoidable.
Sunless Sea has many stories. In the beginning you choose your win conditions, which could be considered your overall plot for that captain, and smaller stories can be found as you play. These change between captains as well; one who visits Venderbright might find different events than those who came before.
Characters the player encounters in passing are overall very interesting, spiced with many peculiarities and adjoining stories. The player collects officers for their crew, which provide perks and buffs as well as their own personal questlines.
The graphics are minimal, but what there is is very polished. The style is all one could expect from such a dark game, capturing well the dank, anxious environment one might expect from an underground ocean.
Sunless Sea is overall a captivating game. Though it suffers from a clunky UI and poor organization, there is much to discover by those who muscle past.

Cuphead is a great game. Not a perfect one, but a really really great one.
Controls feel tight, but you might want to rebind some of the key maps to something that feels more comfortable (personally, I had to move the dash to spacebar so that my hand wasn't splayed so awkwardly on the keyboard). Honestly, the core gameplay itself is very well polished and top-tier.
Cuphead suffers from two issues:
1) Level design could be better;
Cuphead has very spotty level design; issues like on one of the first bosses in world 2, whose second stage has certain enemies who can spawn on top of the character with no telegraph. This leads to situations where whole portions of the screen are basically "danger zones," especially if you're playing for A+ grades where getting hit once means you need to restart. This isn't an issue in EVERY level, but when it is an issue it'll bother you for a good long time till you beat that boss/level.
2) The developer's chose graphic consistency over graphic utility;
One of Cuphead's biggest draws is its one-of-a-kind artstyle. The gameplay is tailored to play around the artstyle, but in certain situations the gameplay takes a backseat to this. An egregious example is a boss where the level is scrolling with the player jumping from platform to platform during the level. The platforms, when spawned, are obscured by the boss so you can't see them for a good quarter of the screen. These should be brought to the front of the screen instead of the back. This is a more conscious decision than the con above.
Overall, Cuphead is a very good game though. Aside from those two cons I provided above, I have nothing else negative to say about the game. I'd rate it a solid 8/10, games like this are very few and far between; this is a game that you'll definitely want to share with your friends.

This is a Rogue Lite game, with a lot of adventures, plenty of stories and choices that have consequences, unfortunately one of the features of this genre is that you have no idea what anything does, so yeah googling everything is kinda important before making decisions, the tutorial doesn't really help that much, you will die, and that is also a feature of the game and of the genre itself, after you die you will pick another capitain and that capitain will have an easier start, you can choose what aspects of your previous capitain will pass over - or at least a portion of it - so it's not exactly a go back to zero start, it does give you some quickstart options if you died at the 'zee' (sea).
I really do like the game and have already spent over 25 hours in it, lost a couple of capitains, and almost lost my current one to birds, yeah one thing that you will learn very quickly is don't mess with monsters and animals at the zee, because they will F you up, pirates are very easy to deal with though, so you can farm them for resources and even money (or echos as they call it in game)
So besides 'zee' monsters and pirates, what else is trying to kill you? Everything,  even the zee itself (sea) is trying to kill you. The game has a terror mechanic, and every second you spend on the open zee you will be accumulating terror points, as you pass certain thresholds (which are not explained in the game at all by the way), you will start to get nightmares as well as ocasionally losing your sailors and you die if you lose all of them, those nightmares can increase terror, or reduce depending on how lucky you are or which choice you went with, if you pass the 90 points of terror, the music will change to a very dramatic and horrific song that is to no doubt scare the hell out of the player and make him/her seek refuge in a port quickly, the longer you spend over 90 points of terror the higher the chances of very bad events to happen, some pretty mild like losing a sailor here or there, but some events can quite literally kill you straight up, it will give you a almost impossible RNG choice, and you will die if you don't get extremely lucky in the dice, which needless to say if you add some insta death mechanic like that to an already confusing and not very well explained terror mechanic,  makes for some pretty infuriating deaths in the game.
But again, death is not the end is just the begining of something new.
The game does give you some ways of making sure that your next capitain will have a very good start, when you can write your own will and even leave him/her with a fantastic treasure that you will be able to use to get a quick start and not have to do the boring grinding that you most likely will have to do it at the begining.
Other than getting killed at the zee there are also chances of getting killed in ports base on your choices, again keep in mind that being curious will increase your chances of death, while not being curious will certantly kill you from lack of progress and lack of resources, so you need to strike a balance somewhere along those lines.
So besides trying to avoid death, what is the purpose of the game? You choose, the game gives you victory states at the begining of your career, and you can pick between several victory conditions, and you can change those victory conditions later in the game if you feel like trying to do something different with your capitain, or you can just explore and try to just follow some of the many adventures and plotlines in the game, because there are many that don't seen to be that related to any of the victory conditions, and there is a lot of mystery that you can try to shine a light on through out the game (and that has its own risks of death attached to it so keep that in mind).
And since death is a major aspect of the game the replayability is obviously also important, and just like other games in the genre the map is somewhat random, so ports are not always in the same spot, which keeps the exploration part of the game fresh in each playthrough which is nice.
It's a very fun game, great writing with some good sense of humor here in there, quite terrifying in some places and as i said, a lot of mystery to be solved, if you choose to do that, and that is another thing that the game does very well you have a lot of choices.
It does have problems though, my biggest issue has to do with the bugs, the game is very well polished for the most part, but some bugs are present and they do tend to irritate me, especially since this game is also a survival game where you have to manage resources and you need to at any possible moment reduce terror somehow, and one of the most reliable ways of getting a big chunk of terror out of your head, is to go back to london after some time, unfortunately though this is where a glitch can happen, depending on your current missions, someone might imediatelly open up a conversation with you when you reach london, which i believe can cause the window that is supposed to allow you to reduce you terror back to 50, doesn't popup anymore which makes you unable to reduce your terro from the 90s. There are other ways of reducing terror though but they tend to cost resource or echoes (coin).  And again the way that the terror mechanic works is basically like a clock, everytime you leave port you are on a clock, you can not spent too much time at the zee or you risk literally getting killed by your own nightmares, or by your own crew in some situations (again RNG goes crazy by the time you reach terror level 90).
Anyway, there is also a glitch that involves combat, if you engage in combat with a ship/monster and right as you destroy the ship/monster another enemy engages you, the game will glitch and you will be unable to fire back at your enemy, the only way to solve this as far as i know is to run as fast as you can until the combat mode can disengage and you can engage back on again.
Anyway but after 25 hours in, those bugs are not really that problematic, they are annoying but they don't happen at a frequent enough basis to ruin the fun of the game.
Overall the game is fantastic, even for someone like me. A lot of people compared this game to FTL and i think they are correct, but for me this games does something that FTL didn't which is to make me care about the characters and the story, that is the main focus of the game, and it accomplishes that objective very well, the story is very well written and the character are all very interesting and intriguing some ways, so even though i didn't like FTL, this game did enough things different to make me enjoy the hell out of this game. So i definitely recommend, it's a very fun game.

I don’t want to give too much away by writing all the spoilers in a review, so I’ll try not to give anything away. This story-rich, atmospheric, and ultimately horrifying rogue-like has completely surpassed my expectations. I purchased this on a whim, expecting a poorly-built Kickstarter game, but I was hooked for ages (haven’t played for a while as my save corrupted).
Sunless Sea starts you off as a citizen in Fallen London in the 1800s, in a world where London has fallen into a large underground cavern hosting a huge underground ocean, aptly named the Unterzee. You become a zee-captain, and take off in your zee-ship with your zailors to conquer zee-lands and fight off zee-beasts. Lots of Zs. ZZZs (sleeping) is something you won’t be experiencing playing this game, though. It’ll keep you hooked. Just… one… more… port…
This game is incredibly difficult on your first run, so unless you make frequent checks to the wiki, you’ll find your captains dying a lot. But don’t worry: that’s part of the game. It’s an intended feature for you to die. Crazy, right? So yeah, if you decide to pick up this game, don’t be too surprised if your ship sinks within the first 20 minutes. Just keep going. A really nicely designed legacy system makes all that dying (kind of) worth it.
The combat, despite being simple, is challenging and engaging, as you have to fight with different styles when attacking different types of foe, whether it be a monstrous oversized crab, a moving iceberg, or some ruthless pirates, the combat is challenging. However, as soon as you learn the attack pattern, enemies become a piece of cake.
Gameplay wise, this game isn’t too spectacular, but it definitely has its perks. Managing your crew’s hunger, fear statistic, and your ships fuel is a delicate balance, and you really have to think about how you play this game, and how to interact with the story. Other than at zee, this game is text-based, with lots of long stories and choices to choose from. If you don’t like reading, this game probably isn’t for you.
The map is massive, and even if you have the biggest ship with the strongest engine, it will take you a while of sailing through a zee of dark nothingness (accompanied by an awesome, eerie soundtrack) to go all the way across. There are a lot of ports to explore, and the islands change positions slightly with each new captain, so it doesn’t get stale.
The music is absolutely superb. It matches with your current in-game position status and really makes the whole game more immersive. If your crew’s “terror” statistic gets too high, the music ramps up, with shrieking violins and thumping drums to get your heart racing. If you are near the Khanate, the game will play a groovy track. The whole game experience is intensified with the brilliant music choice and composition.
The lore and story is amazing. Incredibly well-written and super detailed. That’s all I have to say.
So yeah, for 19 dollars or 14 pounds, this game can be yours. And SUNLESS SEA is definitely worth checking out, as it’ll provide you with many hours of intense, sweat-breaking, heart-pounding zailing.

I was a huge fan of Fallen London and recently started playing it again. When I heard that they'd released a game on Steam I went for it immediately because I figured that it would have to be amazing. Unfortunately... not quite.
Pros:
-Interesting concept: Fallen London is a great universe and expanding it too the zee holds some fascinating possibilities
-Gender options: As a nonbinary person, I have always loved Fallen London's approach to gender
-Story: What I actually saw of the story seems pretty cool
Cons:
-Slow mechanics: The boat just moves so slowly. It takes forever to get anywhere.
-Combat: Every time I had to enter combat I was just annoyed. All I wanted was to advance the story, explore, etc. but I had to deal with some monster in a combat system that was downright frustrating.
-Focus on strategy: Coming into this as a fan of the universe, I was surprised by the heavy focus on strategy. It isn't my thing at all and made it hard for me to focus on the story.
-Text? Not text?: It tried to continue the text-based fashion of Fallen London, but then added in non-text mechanics that just didn't mesh well together for me.
All in all, I think that this is a great game for someone other than me. The focus on strategy and combat was too frustrating and the gameplay was too slow for my tastes. I wish that I could play $20 for unlimited actions in Fallen London instead. I'd still recommend that people try this out if it sounds like their things, but it isn't mine.

Published by: Dan Walters
Developed by: Dan Walters, Ceri Williams
Genre: Hidden Object, Point & Click, Puzzle
Release Date: August 14, 2014
Time to complete: 90 minutes
Find hidden objects in this beautiful bug-inspired artistic puzzle game.
Morphopolis is a really cute bug-themed point and click puzzle game with a relaxing and atmospheric soundtrack. You play as various bugs as you solve puzzles and find hidden objects to progress to the next chapter. The game is very slow-moving, which was frustrating at times as you have to do a lot of back and forth movement between the different sections to find all the objects. The game doesn’t give any instructions, so you have to work it out for yourself. That’s not really an issue as the game is very straightforward, however there were some points where I wasn’t entirely sure how to proceed and thus spent a lot of time slowly moving from place to place, trying to work out where to go.
There is no save function, so if you don’t complete a chapter (there are 5), you have to start it over. This wouldn’t be an issue for me if the movement wasn’t so incredibly slow. The chapters aren’t particularly long though, so it’s not so bad (though, a save feature would be a nice addition).
The hidden object component isn’t particularly difficult, but the few puzzles scattered throughout the game do increase in difficulty as the game goes on, the last puzzle being quite a brain teaser. It took me roughly 90 minutes to complete the whole game, but your play time will likely be significantly less than mine if you’re good at puzzles (evidently, I’m pretty average at them!). Only a mouse is needed to play Morphopolis, so the controls add to the simplicity of the game.
It’s no secret I’m drawn in by ’pretty’ games, and that was a major component in my decision to purchase Morphopolis. All of the art and animation within the game is completely hand-drawn with beautiful, vibrant colours, and is very pleasant to look at (unless of course you’re not a fan of creepy crawlies).
Simple, serene and effective; the soundtrack is largely what makes this game so relaxing, with simple instrumentals coupled with sounds from nature.
Because it’s a puzzler, once you’ve worked the puzzles out the first time, there’s probably no real point playing it again.
All the achievements in Morphopolis can be obtained simply by playing through the game. An easy 100%!
Because of the enjoyable few hours of gameplay Morphopolis gave me, I would definitely recommend it (especially on sale, I picked this one up for only 50 cents and it seems to go on sale frequently). It provides just enough challenge to keep it interesting, and the simplicity makes it a great choice for all age groups.

Train Valley, a quirky little title that got a surprising amount of press attention considering this is the publisher’s first game. Are we really that starved for train management styled games that anything that resembles one needs to be checked out? The answer is probably yes. The genre has been forever dominated by Open Train Tycoon, Train Tycoon Deluxe and the like for the past 20 years. Entries into the genre are far and few between, often lacking in quality. Here’s the thing, Train Valley isn’t a management game in the traditional sense. Not by a long shot. This is more of a puzzle game where the single objective is to figure out how to solve the level without running out of cash and subsequently going bankrupt. Everything else is a secondary concern.
On the surface, it looks like a simple micromanagement game and it is but there’s some mechanics woven in to make the experience more interesting. All you’ll be doing is deploying trains, building track and managing switches. During the level, trains need to be deployed and delivered to their destination station as soon as possible for a couple of reasons: each train has a money value, that’s rewarded to the player upon completion, which slowly deteriorates over time. Additionally, trains will launch automatically from the station after a certain amount of time. The only warning you’ll get is a five second notification before they launch. So, you need to make sure that stations are regularly deploying trains to prevent any accidents from occurring. This is made more complicated by the levels themselves which will spawn additional stations which need to be connected to the rest of the line and increasingly faster trains. Furthermore, there’s an in-game annual tax that you have to make sure to have money for. So, avoid being greedy or risk losing the level. Finally, as time passes, buildings will crop up over time that you may need to maneuver around or destroy (costing a lot of money).
There are four chapters in total that are centered around a particular nation (or group of nations) that create the overall theme for each level and the trains you’ll see. This includes Europe, the United States, Russia and Japan. Over the course of each chapter, the levels will transition from the early 1830s to the modern age of 2020 while featuring a certain time era for that nation in the level. This changes what the trains look like as well. In terms of how it affects mechanics, the changing of time will increase the length of the trains and make them faster. For each chapter, there’s five challenge levels and one score attack level. Each challenge level also comes with the option to continue the level forever once you’ve finished it. For each level, there’s three optional goals you can try to shoot for and you don’t have to get all of them in one go. These goals can range from never wrecking a train, to gaining a certain amount of money to not allowing a train arrive at the wrong destination. They can be challenging to acquire, especially the gaining X amount of money, and may require several redos. I recommend trying to finish one of them during a level because they’ll add challenge to the levels and give them their own personality. It would have been nice if the achievements you had already completed were marked as such but it’s not a big deal. The score attack level is the culmination of the entire chapter. It plays the entire time period for the nation in one go from 1800s to 2000s while also doubling the in-game speed. This can be very tricky to deal with as it means taxes come twice as fast even though your trains stay at the same speed. Good luck on the Japan level, it’s brutally difficult.
Settings for Train Valley are decent, if limited. Video settings only include two sliders for resolutions and quality. You’ll probably run the quality at “fantastic” unless you’re trying to run this off a toaster. Resolution choices seem pretty good and it maxes out at the monitor’s resolution. The game has a cheap 3D look to it so it’s not like there’s any options missing. Fullscreen on/off and colorblind mode are included as well. There’s only two sound slider options for effects and music. You’ll probably end up turning music off quickly because it is quite awful. That definitely could have used some more work. Rebindable keys with secondary buttons are here for every control as well. The game also supports multiple languages.
I’ve been looking for a lighter train management experience like Train Valley for some time and their timing was lucky. The game looks cheap both mechanically and visually but it’s got a surprising amount of depth to keep the player engaged throughout the four chapters. Their asking price is right on the money in my opinion. Biggest issues I have with Train Valley are the music and sandbox mode. The music is awful, repetitive and not fun to listen to. The sandbox mode basically gives you unlimited resources to do whatever you want but there’s not a lot of flexibility to do anything crazy, so I don’t think you’ll use it much. For a bit of micromanagement fun to play every now and again, Train Valley works and plays well. The four chapters are challenging enough that you won’t blitz right through them and playing for the achievements will give you even more playtime. An enjoyable, if light, indie game.

Limbo is a physics based puzzle platformer, but a first glance at it casts a message as a game full of grim and creepy images. This isn’t a horror game at all as this game is focused on platforming and solving physics puzzles, but Limbo has a distinctly dark atmosphere that suits the style and theme when playing through.
There isn’t too much in terms of story. A boy wakes up in a forest, and as the game description states, tries to find his sister. There is no dialogue at all in the game, as the only things that expand on this story are the various interactions with other people and creatures as you keep moving forward in each level. The story does get resolved later on, though that is something that will be revealed along the way as the game continues.
As a platformer game, the boy that you control doesn’t have much in terms of abilities. All the boy can do is walk, jump, and perform actions on other objects. As the game progresses, new level objects come in to play with different game mechanics to utilize. In the beginning, most puzzles tend to be simple platforming challenges. Later on, more difficult physics puzzles start to appear, requiring some puzzle solving compared to the easy solutions in the beginning. Toward the end, the puzzles are much harder and more involved, also requiring some good timing as well. Throughout the game, trial and error is a core aspect of solving the puzzles. You can definitely get away by being observant and thinking about each puzzle logically, but the harder puzzles require jumping into hazards to see what things do or to get a clue on how to solve the puzzle. The difficulty starts out quite easy, and becomes quite tough near the end of the game that the puzzles require some thought and coordination. Limbo’s simple platforming gameplay gives way for the interesting and well crafted physics puzzles, which require some deaths to successfully complete each puzzle.
The art style for Limbo is one of the biggest motivators for the general tone of the game. The entire game is done like a black and white movie, complete with some film grain and blur to enhance the effect. The 2D design of the world though is quite beautiful in a way, with black silhouettes against gray shaded backgrounds. There is plenty of detail with the background scenery having softer blurred designs while the game objects sport hard, yet rounded shapes. This black and white style does heighten the creepy nature of the game a bit, evoking a feeling like watching old horror movies.
The grim, grisly nature of Limbo is evident throughout the game, with many things hiding until they pop out to kill the boy. Early deaths are quite gory and violent, with the boy being dismembered or mauled in several ways. These things work well with the black and white style by simplifying details while still capturing the harshness of the world. These bloody deaths actually happen less later in the game, as more focus shifts on to the puzzles set in a more isolated man made environment. Overall, the dark style of the game works well with the art style for a creepy and bleak world.
Keeping in tune with the dark themes of the game, there are no distinct songs in Limbo. Instead, the game uses an ambient soundtrack that heightens the mood and conveys game information. The sounds of each environment sets the backdrop and the tone, while subtle changes in the music sends a message of what is happening in the game. In addition to the ambient soundtrack adding so much in terms of tone and gameplay, the sound design is very well done. The sounds for the hazards sound distinct from the music which helps players recognize obstacles, while the sounds for deaths sound quite gruesome. With the ambient music and well designed sounds, the eerie atmosphere of the game is heighted more as each action unfolds.
With heavy dark and grim tones, Limbo delivers some fun and somewhat challenging puzzle platforming wrapped up with a unique style. Each of the various aspects of the game work together to deliver this kind of foreboding atmosphere. As the game’s style is draws you in, the gameplay smoothly runs through the world with difficulty arising later on. Limbo works as a great experience of a game, both in the style it achieves, and the puzzle platforming gameplay that offers some good challenge with its crafty levels.

9/10. This is my first time playing a Telltale game, and I enjoyed it a fair bit. I would recommend it to many players, albeit with a few caveats: this is primarily a story-driven experience, with relatively minimal gameplay; and, the violence is surprisingly graphic. If you are looking for something challenging or family-friendly, look elsewhere.
So, this is basically a movie with quicktime events. You have to react fast sometimes, but there is no repetitive button mashing. There are puzzles...kind of...but they are very easy. As a fan of puzzle games, I was a little disappointed at this. However, it's an understandable design choice, since they obviously wanted to keep the story moving at a good pace.
There are five episodes, which took me a total of about 8 hours to complete. The story arc is mostly predetermined, but you still have lots of choices. They seem to only affect things in small ways, but they were still fun and engaging for me.  There were a few events that frustrated me, but sometimes that made things more interesting. I suspect the game would not stand up well to repeated playthroughs, because you will know what's coming.
I found the visual style to be very appealing. It's 3D, but with seemingly hand-drawn textures, and that's a style that seems especially well suited for comic-book characters. Most of the game is beautiful to look at. The way they render human eyes is a bit cloudy, as if they all have cataracts, and I did find that distracting sometimes. There were a couple of minor graphical glitches, but nothing that impeded the gameplay.
The writing is pretty good, with several compelling characters. There were many tense and exciting moments. The overall plot was just okay - a bit implausible at times, but that's fine. Suspending disbelief for a Batman game is par for the course. The dialogue was the part that impressed me the most; almost every conversation seemed to flow pretty well despite all the branching choices, and there were some snappy lines to boot. The voice acting is quite good, too.
Overall I recommend this pretty highly. It made me want to try out some other Telltale games, too. Enjoy!

Holy hell, this game is an unforgiving mass of brutal fun.  Without burying you in details, I will say, if you are a casual gamer who wants to play this game on its easy mode, where you can save any time you like and reload the saves if you mess up, I am sure there is something rewarding to be found for you.  However, I feel so much is lost of the meat of this game if the risk of permadeath is taken off the table.  Your decisions no longer feel like they carry any weight.  You care nothing for blind exploration, because death is no longer around *every* corner.   I would highly recommend playing this game on its default diffculty, by *not* manually saving.  In my opinion, you will ruin the experience for yourself.
My only minor complaint with this game has been stated many other times (and is apparently going to be included in their next game), is that the text that you get throughout the game does *not* appear on your screen as it shows in the trailer.  That was actually a huge selling point for me, and many others, because the immersion it offered seemed incredible.  Instead you are updated with text in the bottom left of your screen in your little journal page, that also pops up with regular updates of other boring information.  This really detracted from the overall experience for me.
That being said, phenomenal game, and I look forward to Sunless Skies.

This review is not just about Sunless Sea (SS from here on), but compares it to games similar to SS. The games I have in mind are the Avernum and Geneforge series, Neo Scavenger, FTL: Faster than Light, and Patrician 3.  If you like SS, I'd say there's about a 50-70% chance you'll like those games, and vice versa--they share a lot of common elements. So let's go over some of the elements these games have in common.
1.  Atmosphere: Of all the games I've named here, Sunless Sea is the darkest.  The color palette is mostly oceanic gray, black, blue, and green. SS features starvation, rats, a city where humans are wrapped in bandages and sent to die, large crabs, jellyfish and sea monsters, and rather freaky and Lovecraftian stuff. Compare to FTL: a futuristic, spacey feel, slick steel starships, and war, but probably lighter overall than it is dark. Neo Scavenger has some humans transformed into dogmen, cannibalism, and is set in a post-apocalyptic near-future with bits of advanced technology. In the Avernum series you spend a fair amount of time underground, fighting rats, bats and goblins and drinking mushroom ale, but then also spend time up on the surface, fighting giants, Nephilim, troglodytes, and other similar creatures. And like SS, Patrician 3 is a sea-focused game, centered on business strategy and ship trade in the North and Baltic Seas in the 1200-1400's.
2.  Combat: In SS combat is real-time. At first combat was painful for me, but with more familiarity it's ok. You take direct control of your ship, maneuvering to shoot at the enemy, while watching your ship's hull strength and possibly running from battle.  You can buy upgrades for your ship weapons, improve stats for fighting and questing, hire crew to further improve your abilities, and even purchase new ships. FTL is closest: improve your spaceship and the abilities of its crew; there's a huge selection of weaponry available; and combat is nominally real-time, but as in SS you can pause the game when you need to, though you can't target ship systems in SS. In Avernum, Geneforge, and Neo Scavenger, combat is on the ground, focuses on fighting between individuals or groups of individuals, and is all turn-based--opposed to real-time combat in SS.  And in Patrician 3, combat is real-time, and just as in SS depends on steering your ship correctly and getting shots off at the right time.
3. Difficulty/rogueness: In roguelikes Neo Scavenger and FTL, people have long complained about the high difficulty.  Early on you die often, and well into the game there's a good chance of dying. (In my most recent game of Neo Scavenger, I was several hours in and my character was doing quite well and had quite a bit of good equipment, so I felt prepared.  Then I got into a random fight; on my first turn of combat, I hid my character from enemy ranged attacks. I never got a second turn in the fight--I was dead almost immediately, and never saw what killed me.  It felt very arbitrary and I haven't picked it up since.)
SS is similar.  As with FTL and Neo Scavenger, you may find that luck just is not with you. In SS I repeatedly found my ship running lower and lower on money, fuel, supplies, and hull strength; engines going from Slow to CRAWL after the “boost” fried the ship; then one last fight to finish me off. What doesn't kill you in SS, FTL, or Neo Scavenger, often will not make you stronger... it just further depletes your resources, until down the road something else will have an easier time finishing the job. And once you're dead, you can't reload your game--you have to start a new character. Brutal! Geneforge, Avernum, and Patrician 3 have none of this--save and reload to your heart's content.
But I'd contend that SS might be the best of the whole bunch in this regard. Yes, you'll die, and you'll need to start a new character. But in SS your new character can inherit a portion of the money, items, stats, or even ship crew from previous characters; once far enough, new characters can even inherit the old character's home. So there are definitely still consequences to your actions, unlike so many games where you can just reload if something goes wrong; but the consequences aren't quite as punishing as in some roguelikes. New characters benefit from the accomplishments of previous characters, so you don't have to start from scratch each time. (And you can even choose to play in a "Forgiving" mode in SS, which I think actually DOES allow you to reload if you die.)
4.  Story/adventuring: I didn't get too far into SS, so I can't say just how much of a main plot there is, but it's clear there are a lots of people to meet, locations to explore, quests, decisions to make that will put you on one side of the law or other other, and so on. This is true of FTL as well; Neo Scavenger, in comparison, seems much more focused on your character going it solo, crafting and scavenging items that will help you survive (a lot like Minecraft actually), with trade and character interactions playing little or no role (at least in the earlier parts of the game). But SS actually feels closest to Geneforge and Avernum as far as sidequests and discovery of interesting places and people and items goes.  But the Geneforge and Avernum games have very large and intricate plots. I got the feeling that SS is more open-ended--lots of small things going on, but maybe not so much of a cohesive plot.  Having only gotten 9 hours in, I can't say for sure. In any case, all these games will require a fair amount of reading to get through: the narrative is especially important in SS, Geneforge, and Avernum.
5.  Money-making and strategy: Having skimmed some guides for SS, trading ultimately seems to be the single most important element of the game--the primary way you have to make money, much like Patrician 3, though quests can take a large role. And here's something I haven't seen before: you can sell STORIES!
Combat mostly isn't worth it early on; you'll have to do a lot of trade runs to get ahead. You might WANT to spend your time meeting lots of interesting people, blowing up sea monsters, and seeking out novelties. But your food, fuel, and hull plating are too limited early on to do much of this. So your real goal at the start is to find the items, locations, and quests for buying/selling profitable items.
Perhaps this is where we come to the real question, of whether you want to play SS: do you like lots of trading, interspersed with many minutes of travel and running from most fights? If not, you'll probably want to find a different game to play. Or find some online guides to give you a good boost.
(Forgot to mention: Transcendence, a free roguelike set in space; heavy emphasis on combat and exploration, and less on trading; a lot thinner on narrative, characters, and story; and about 75% similarity to SS.)
EDIT: I recently discovered Assassin's Creed: Black Flag. If you like SS, I think there's a good chance you'll like Black Flag. It's brighter, more combat-driven, and less character-driven, but there's tons to explore with your ship.

Separating Eggs:
Cold eggs separate more easily than those at room temperature because the whites hold together better.
separating egg yolk and egg whiteTo separate an egg: Crack the egg and hold the shell halves over a bowl. Transfer the yolk back and forth between the halves, letting the white drop into the bowl. Do not cut the yolk (whites containing any yolk will not beat properly). Transfer the yolk to another bowl.
The tiniest bit of fat or egg yolk will wreck a meringue, as fat interferes with the formation of good foam. When separating eggs, if a speck of egg yolk falls into the egg whites, lift it out with an empty eggshell half. Do not try to fish it out with your fingers; the oil on your skin will prevent the egg whites from expanding.
Avoid letting your fingers touch the areas that will come in contact with the egg whites. That way, you'll avoid leaving oils from your hands on the utensils you just washed.
Room Temperature: After separating, bring egg whites to room temperature to ensure volume when beating (as warmer eggs whip faster than cold eggs). Egg whites right out of the refrigerator will not whip well. The ideal temperature to whip a common meringue is room temperature, about 70 degrees F. (21 degrees C.). Usually 30 minutes is adequate to obtain room temperature.
A beaten egg white can foam to 6 to 8 times its original volume if the egg whites have been at room temperature for 30 minutes before beating.
Bowls and Utensils:
Copper, stainless-steel, or glass bowls work best for making meringues. Avoid using plastic bowls for whipping egg whites as they can often harbor traces of grease or fat, which prevents the whites from getting stiff. Whichever type of bowl you use, be sure it is spotlessly clean. Make sure that all your utensils are immaculately clean, completely grease-free, and completely dry. Meringues are very sensitive and they don't like any moisture.
Place the egg whites into a large, tall bowl and set your mixer to medium-high speed.
NOTE: I would not hand beat a meringues (too much work). Beating or whisking causes the protein in the egg whites to unfold, forming films that trap the air bubbles, and the sugar stiffens the foam. As the mixing time increases, the bubbles become smaller and more numerous; this increases the volume and makes a more-stable structure.
Adding Sugar:
Do not add sugar before whipping the egg whites. Adding sugar at the beginning can double the time you have to whip the egg whites to get a foam. Add the sugar at the very end when the whites have formed soft peaks.
I like to use superfine sugar when making meringue because it dissolves faster than table sugar. When beating egg whites and the recipe calls for sugar, Gradually add the sugar, a few spoonfuls at a time and beating the whole time.
As a general rule, add a total of 1/4 cup of granulated or superfine sugar for each egg white. Do not make meringues that have less than 2 tablespoons of sugar per egg white. If you use any less, the foam will not set and the meringue will shrink. To tell if the sugar is dissolved when you are beating egg whites for meringues, rub a bit of the foam between your fingers. If it feels gritty, the sugar is not dissolved, so keep beating for a few minutes. It should feel completely smooth when the sugar is dissolved.
By varying the amount of sugar in the final mix, you control how hard or soft the final meringue will be:
For soft peaks - Place egg whites in a clean glass or metal bowl (not plastic), and beat with an electric mixer on medium speed or with a rotary beater until egg whites form peaks with tips that curl over when the beaters are lifted. For stiff peaks, continue beating egg whites on high speed until they form peaks with tips that stand straight when the beaters are lifted.
For stiff peaks - Continue beating egg whites on high speed until they form peaks with tips that stand straight when the beaters are lifted. Once you start a making whipped egg whites, continue it straight through and finish it off. Do not stop halfway to take a break. The meringue is done when it is not runny and when you can hold a spoonful of it upside down and none of it drops off. Also when you swirl a spoon through it and the swirls hold their shape indefinitely.
Using Meringue:
Make the meringue first - then prepare the filling (such as pie filling).
Place meringue on the piping-hot filling to begin cooking the bottom of the meringue. The residual heat carried by the filling cooks the base of the meringue ever so slightly, making it less prone to leaking or shrinking. Make sure the meringue completely covers the hot filling right up to the edge of the crust. This helps the bottom of the meringue cook and stick to the filling so it will not slide off the when it is cut. Use a small spoon or spatula to make high peaks and decorative swirls in the meringue before baking.
Baking Meringue:
Meringues will become more done if you bake them at a lower temperature for a longer time. Bake the meringue at 325 degrees F. for 20 to 30 minutes or until a cooking thermometer registers 160 degrees F. Remember a hot filling is important
Cutting Meringue:
To cut baked meringue into serving pieces, use a knife dipped in cold water.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

First off the bat, let me say that if you are considering a city builder like SC4/5 or CitiesXXL, GET THIS INSTEAD. It is much more fun, has more options and play value, and has the added element of humor (with alternatives being rather deadpan). In addition to that, it's much easier, so a great choice if you are new to the city builder genre and looking to learn. To this end, it also has GREAT tutorials, making it a snap to learn and get playing. It offers both "campaign" mode with guided missions, and "sandbox" mode with endless play where you choose the parameters. It also has the added play element of how corrupt to be, whereas in similar games you are apparently the Angel Mayor.
Furthermore, it has excellent DLC at reasonable prices, but plays just fine without that (unlike a couple games I could name). It is better than equivalent city builders in almost every way, the one notable exception being Cities: Skylines. If you were planning to get that, go right ahead.

This is also one of the only games I really pressured my close friends into playing, as one of those "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ you have to play this!" kind of things.
