Before I get into the review here's the basics of how the review will work. There are normally 10 categories
that I use when reviewing a game. Those ten categories are Fun, Creativity, Challenge, Graphics, Music, Cinematics,
Story, Content, Controls, Gameplay. Each Category will be rated 1 through 10 with a maximum score out of 100.
So let's get started on the review.
Train Valley is an Indie, Simulation, Strategy game published by Flazm and developed by  Alexey Davydov, Sergey Dvoynikov, and Timofey Shargorodskiy, and was released on September 16th of 2015.
Category 1: FUN (10 out of 10).
After playing about 40 minutes of the game I have found that the game is actually quite entertaining to me. While I'm not normally a puzzle gamer this game did catch my eye as I do have quite an interest in trains in general.
Category 2: Creativity (10 out of 10).
In this Category my perspective is that mostly for train based games, I've normally found simulation or strategy types without a puzzle element. Now while I'm sure that there are other puzzle genre train games out there, this is the only one that I have come across in these early days of my gaming channel. I'm sure that I'll be finding more out there.
Category 3: Challenge (10 out of 10).
In the beginning of the game, as to be expected, there was no challenge at all. At first I thought the challenge aspect wasn't going to really build up but by the fourth level, I found that I was just lying to myself. Things got quite interesting in fact. Now, I only made it the first 5 levels before I started becoming flustered and gave up.
Category 4: Graphics (10 out of 10).
The Graphics in this game seem to me to be a bit child-like cartoonish, but in all honesty I also feel that being a family friendly game, it was meant to be done in this fashion. My framerates while both generally playing and recording this video stayed steady between 29 and 30 frames per second for me while utilizing an MSI R7 250 2gb pci-e video card with the resolution set at 1920 by 1080, with the fullscreen option ticked and quality settings put at recommended (which I believe were at the highest quality settings.) It was easy enough to see everything with my vision problems and the textures were quite decent for the style given.
Category 5: Audio (06 out of 10).
There's really not much to be said about the music in the game other than it seems to be one looped track throughout what I've played. If the music changes in the game, I've not been made aware of it as of yet. That being said, the music seems to be slightly upbeat and wasn't overtaxing on my ears; however, I do tire of the same thing on a constant basis when it comes to instrumental music. I'd prefer variety and would have liked to seen more tracks during my gameplay. The sounds effects however were lovely and I was able to distinguish what I was listening to based on the effects of the actions taken. The sound effects is basically what is saved this category.
Category 6: Cinematics (05 out of 10).
The only cinematics that I've experienced is at the beginning of the game and between the levels where the portfolio book opens and the levels get stamped. Now, while a lot of others would not call it cinematics but more along the lines of animations which would end up in graphics, I felt as if putting it here would be the best choice. That being said, I felt as if they could've used a bit of work by actually making the animations into a more lively cinematic by adding an arm coming from the screen and a hand actually opening the portfolio. I would have also like to have seen some sort of cutscenes either animted or filmed to help fit the story line.

Category 7: Story (08 out of 10).
While there is a Story Mode to the game I've not really witnessed the story, but based on several reviews I've read including those from Steam Users and well known reviewers the Story is pretty good. I didn't have the time to fully delve into the Story itself, I've rated this Category based on many many reviews both positve and negative.

Category 8: Content (08 out of 10).
With 15 different trains and 18 different cars I was quite happy in the beginning with what was available. While I didn't get to witness all of the trains or cars personally during my short playtime, I was quite happy with the levels 'release' of train types based on level and time and am quite positive that as the Story unfolds any player will love experiencing each type. I would also love to see future releases of content with more cars and engines and maybe even some sort of expansion pack or update that allows more freedom. I would even like to see turntables and signals added into the game to give a bit more realism in stopping or turning the train around. Maybe even an option to also choose an engine type when selecting an early train. But all in all, I'm satisfied with what is available now.

Category 9: Controls (10 out of 10).
First let me just say that I love the controls in this game; and one of the things I like most is that you can map the controls to your liking. Control mappings are Switch mode, Build mode, Demolish mode, Scheduling additional trains, Pausing, Speed settings and even the Menu. You also have the capability of inverting the zoom functionality as well as adjusting the scroll speeds to your liking. The mouse movements were very fluid and I was able to hit switches with ease as well as getting the trains to stop and reverse with great ease. With all the games I've played, I never could stand having to put the mouse in a very small precise locations in order to toggle something and that includes train as well as aviation simulators. I was quite pleased with how well the controls were made.

Category 10: Gameplay (10 out of 10).
The gameplay itself was quite easy to understand from the beginning and the small video tutorials that popped up were a huge help. For being some one who's easily distracted, I was able to keep focues while playing lest I wreck everything and destroy the world. I also loved the fact that if you didn't acknowledge a train within a certain timeframe that they would depart anyhow, and if you aren't paying a lick of attention, there's no telling where that train could end up. As the cities grew I was fascinated by each building popping up as trains arrived, as if the city was growing. As the game continues and I progressed the levels I became more and more interested in the game.
Overall Rating: So when all is said and done, I'm giving Train Valley an overall rating of 87 out of 100. I was quite pleased with everything and looking forward to playing this game a lot in the future as a wonderful way to either pass time or test my logic when I'm feeling quite... illogical.
Thanks for reading my review and I hope it helped in your decision regarding the purchase of this game. Remember, there is a Demo if you'd like to try before you buy and experience it for yourself.

You start out with a couple of train stations popping up with a train or two, they're waiting for you to lay down some tracks so they can be on their way, safe and sound, for now, to their final destination.
As you progress more train stations will pop up here or there and that's when it starts to get interesting, trains are flying this way and that, tracks need to be layed then switched at the right junctions so you're heading to the correct station, meanwhile another train is coming at it head on. soon you'll have up to 10 trains running at the same time and you'll be looking at your elegant and efficient track layout with a smile just as a train you forgot about explodes after another head on.
With a spare half hr or so to kill i'll happily have a go of each level again, it can also be hard to drag yourself away once started.

Train Valley is a real time puzzle-strategy game based on trains and railroads. The player connects train stations and makes sure trains reach their correct destination by changing switches on the railroad he/she build himself/herself.
The game has a nice simplistic menu that is shaped as a stockbook (book that is used by stamp collectors). Every Postage stamp in it is a level of the game. There are 20 levels total. The game has two game modes. One of them is classic mode which consist of levels that has a time and money limit, and also have optional objectives. The other mode is sandbox. As the name suggests, there are no restrictions and limits. Also in this mode, the player decides stations’ spawn time and when a train is scheduled from a station. At the beginning, all levels except the first one is locked. New levels are opened by beating the previous level. To play sandbox version of a level, the player needs to beat the same level in classic mode.
First level is a tutorial level that shows basics of the game. Although it shows the most important parts of the game with nice message boxes, other parts are only mentioned in small bubbles that can be easily missed. Luckily, game is very simple and can be learned in a few games. That said, it would be nice to have a better tutorial.
A level starts with two stations. Player is given some money to build railroads. After that trains start to be scheduled. When such train is scheduled, an icon appears on the station it is in. Then player starts the train by simply clicking it. That said, it is not possible to make a train wait forever. After an unknown time, it starts to count down from 5 and moves when the countdown reaches zero. As time passes, more stations are spawned making the game and railroad network more complicated. That said, it will never be too complicated as a tycoon but has its challenges of its own.
Origin and destination of a train is handled very nicely in the game. It is color coded. Every train and station has a color on it. And the purpose is to make a train reach the station with the same color. When the train reaches its destination, the player gets the money. Amount of money is determined at the time of the spawn of a train. After that it will start decreasing even if the train is still in the starting station.
This game is not a detailed tycoon game. It is designed as a puzzle-strategy game. The main purpose of the game in a level is not to bankrupt, but in this game, “bankrupt” means “negative money”. There are no loans, no maintenance cost, no economy. The player earns money by making a train reach its correct destination. After that he/she uses the money to build railroads to connect newly spawned stations. Every game year, a constant tax is debited from the money. There are only two ways the player’s money goes below zero; tax and train crash. As soon as the player’s money is negative, he/she loses. This mechanic is the games strategy part.
The puzzle part is more interesting. Because the actual puzzle is built by the player without him/her realizing. After connecting a few stations with railroads, railroads become a (simple) maze with switches left and right. More stations mean more railroads with more switches. It is never possible to create a network without switches because of either landscape or money constraints. Towards the end of a level, the player keeps clicking switches to send the trains to correct road and prevent crashes. This is the most fun part of the game.
Sounds in the game is nice and relaxing but it would be better to have a few different sound tracks.
Total game length is a bit short. There are 20 levels but if the player doesn’t care about optional objectives, then they will end quickly.
All menus and tabs are cleverly put together in a clear and simple manner.
Because it is simple and lacks ambition, it is fit to be played just to relax.
Don’t have many levels.

A simple but surprisingly addictive little game about model trains and railways.
There are two main components to this game: Setting up an efficient railway between given stations on the map, and directing as many trains to their destinations as possible.
Each train is worth a set amount of money that decreases with time, so the quicker you get it to its destination, the more money you get. As the game goes on, you'll have to juggle more and more trains with different lengths and speeds.
Beyond earning money, each level has specific objectives which will require different approaches to beat. (like don't stop any trains, don't destroy tracks or buildings, launch a number of extra trains and so on)
The demo version covers most of what the game has to offer, so I recommend you start with that.

I'm not a fan of racing games, but FlatOut 2 is one of my favourite games ever. Here's why I love it:
- The graphics might be outdated for some, but I'm still in love with the sunsets in some of the tracks.
- I'm pretty sure, you've seen better physics since this game came out, but boy, is it fun to run over a bench in the park at full throttle, rocketing inthrough the air, while spinning like the devil's wheel and landing in first place, smashing someone else's car to pieces.
- Lots of people ♥♥♥♥♥ about the rock music chosen for the game, but they can go and buy another goddamn racing game, because all of them are the same with techno, hip-hop and rap music. Finally a game that is an exception. Okay, I might be a bit biased, because if you look into my mp3 player you'll find most of the bands that have gotten into this game. Some examples: Rise Against, Rob Zombie, Fall Out Boy, Yellowcard, Papa Roach, Audioslave and yes, Nickelback (but none of the cheesy songs), among others.
- Yes, most of the maps return in the game, but they'll be different in playstyle because you'll have a different car as well as your opponents. Where you could speed up earlier and smash into something, later on in the game, you'll probably have to avoid, because the races get faster and the cars less durable. I know every map by heart and still cannot stop playing this game.
- I did not care much about the mini-games, where you have to smash your driver out of the car through the window, but that's just me, it was still really funny with some friends gathered around.
- I promise, you won't find any other racing game in which smashing into an opponents car is as satisfying as in this one. You can see the damage you've done, and if you want to, you can destroy  any opponent's car, so they don't get much points during the racing events. Count your points, win the first three races of the event and spend the last race wrecking all the other racers (you'll get to like some of the AI racers, and you'll grow to hate others, I for one hate Sofia Martinez with a burning passion :P ). Oh, and did I mention you get money for the destruction you cause?
So, if you are bored to death by all the neon and hip-hop filled games in which you cannot damage your car, this one's for you! Try it, buy it, love it! :)

A unique setting coupled with fantastic writing and challenging gameplay makes Sunless Sea a special gem. As a retired veteran of Fallen London I was excited to return to the incredible mythos the creators had wrought, and I was not disappointed.
Some describe this game as Lovecraftian, but I disagree. In Lovecraft's work there was usually a feeling of hopelessness and despair, but in Sunless Sea hope, humor, and the ability to  destroy the lightless horrors that plague you make it a rewarding game.
It is true the game is difficult and punishing if you try to fight things out of your league. I lost three captains and ten hours before figuring out how to reliably make money, but the intrigue was worth it.
If you don't want to risk the permadeath there is a save option that can be enabled, but in my experience the fear of losing most of your progress makes you actually consider if you want to risk your ship and crew for a glimmer of gold instead of recklessly shooting everything.

You will die. So much. Why will you die? Cold and wolves. You will only be able to punch the wolves, even after acquiring a hunting knife, or a hatchet, both of which are much more effective weapons. If by some miracle you manage to survive the wolves, you will then freeze to death. Why will you freeze to death? Because you don't have enough fabric to make new clothes. Where can you get fabric? Certainly not from one of the many beds throughout the game, outfitted with a full set of sheets, blankets, and comforters. After you die of cold because you couldn't replace your default sweater and jeans with the plush comforter and fleece blanket staring you in the face, I guarantee that you will also press Esc, exit to desktop and promptly uninstall game.

Perfect little game worth the money. One of the few games I can see trying to do all the achievements . If my time log is right, I 'beat' this in 18 hours, but I can see the challenge of getting most of the remaining achievements worth another 10 or 20 hours alone. I wish it would have overlaid another level of challenge on each level with some kind of star ranking based on money earned or some other metric. Instead, it general gives you three objectives, so 'beating' a level 'completely' is meeting the three objectives, which is often very challenging. But it would add even more replayability if it set an income level for a bronze, silver, and gold medal, or a three-star rating, for example.
The game feels like someone boiled down a Railroad Tycoon game until the concentrated essense that was left fit on one screen and took maybe 20 or 30 minutes at the very most to complete. Most of the good stuff is present, but it's compressed and highly concentrated into a challenging packet of fun, minus any of the tedious or slow-moving aspects.
It's worth the money at $10 USD.  If it's on sale, grab it.

I have not played this game in about a year, so I decided too re-install it, and look at it, as well as the reviews... and I see nothing has changed. It's still the confusing heap of garbage it was a year ago. The dev's seem to have abandoned this game. The game still feels like it's in an Alpha stage. It's choppy, the sprites are glitchy at times, and the amount of work you need to do to be able to get anything, it's outrageously difficult.
I had been an avid Minecraft and Terraria player, having LAN parties with my friends. We had beaten Minecraft, and had beaten all the regular bosses in Terraria. Then, one of them found this game. It looked cool, so we bought the game, and ran it. 5-7 hours in, and we still have the basic tools. None of us could figure out how to upgrade them, or get new tools! All the crafting involved electrical gates the technicians use!! We ended up abandoning the game, and never spoke of it again.
So, unless you're a senior technician that knows electrical gates by heart, don't waste the $15 on this game.
On another note: Terraria is about 250 mb. Edge of Space of a little over 2 Gb. Terraria has hours upon hours, upon hours of gameplay, with lots of replayability, and an active online community. Edge of Space has very little content, very little to no online presence, and actually very hard to set-up a server for. Hmm, I wonder what the better choice is....
If you don't know what Terraria is, and just found this game by surprise, get Terraria.
---EDIT---
So, another year has passed, and my friends decide to check this game out again. From what I've seen, and remember of this game, it has defintely changed, for the better. The crafting is easier to understand, the leveling up system, albeit a bit demanding and stops gameplay, is pretty interesting. The gunplay is great, the mining system could use a bit of work, and the UI is still pretty bad with my only issue being that every individual thing, such as inventory, crafting, skills, etc., requires a different button to press in order for that specific menu to come up(how hard could it have been for it to just open up with one button, and have different tabs for everything?).
Me and my friends played this for about 5 hours straight, and we all said that it is definitely fun. Though there are still issues, the game is in a playable state. But... I don't think mutch will change in the future, unless these developers are secretly working on this without giving updates, as the last form of any game update was last year(April 28th 2015, if I remember correctly), while the last time a dev spoke about the game(on steam at least), was 2 months ago(April 25th). The post said that they were sorry for being silent about the game, and that logistical issues came about, and that they would get back to the playerbase and explain what was happening. Well, it's been 2 months. Where's the explanation?
tl;dr
In the state this game is in currently, I still wouldn't recommend this to anyone. Unless you have a group of friends to play with, know how to portforward(because Hamachi doesn't work), and have some extra money laying around, then don't buy this game. It still seems like the developers have abandon this game, or don't have a whole lot of motivation for it.
I would still rather play Terraria.

Those who are willing to put in the time to explore the world of Edge of space will find a colossal amount of content just waiting to be discovered and enjoyed. The sheer variety of weapons, deployables, pets, mounts, materials, dungeons, bosses etc is impressive, and although there are some obvious similarities to Terraria for instance, it is in fact a very different game. I would definitely recommend trying to find someone else who you can play with though, as it does enhance the experience a lot.
There is a sort of tutorial in the form of a friendly laser shark who asks you to do a few short quests to get you used to the basic mechanics of the game, but the rest is mostly left up to you to figure out, (there are instructions on how to do everything if you dig in the menu) and so a degree of effort is required in order to get into the real meat of the content. Once you do however, you'll realise just how much there is to do and discover.
Edge of space is very colourful and is graphically the equivalent of eating too many packets of Skittles in one sitting, the pallette is well chosen and easy on the eye, the art style is great, and everything stands out. Some players have complained about the lighting system but personally I haven't had any problems with it.
The music is great, very relaxing and suits the mood well. The best thing however is the splendidly warped sense of humour that the developers obviously have and that comes across not only in the design of the world but in many of the descriptions and explanations that are there to be read if you take the time (and I recommend that you do)
Gameplay is a lot of fun and some of the weapons in particular are extremely satisfying to use. I know I have only just started to scratch the surface but already I am enjoying flying around on a net full of jellyfish with a small glowing fox creature following me around and helping to light my journey into the planet's extensive cave systems.
In summary, if you like randomly generated 2D exploration games with crazy amounts of content and are willing to put in the time and effort required to get through the initial learning stages, then you will get very good value from Edge of space, even more if you can find someone else to team up with.

Morphopolis is a stunningly beautiful point and click/hidden object game. Now I usually have some dislike towards hidden object games, but the style presented within Morphopolis makes up for that.
There really is no story in Morphopolis. You are an insect who goes through several metamorphic changes. However Morphopolis should not be played for the story. It should be played for the atmosphere. Adding to the very colourful and fantastical world is the soundtrack. Now even though the soundtrack is not quite remarkable or rememberable, it does add to the atmosphere.
As with many puzzle games, the learning curve is important. The puzzles within Morphopolis are common throughout the genre. Thus, being common, they are fairly easy, with the last one being the most difficult. That is great for the learning curve, however Morphopolis does not have any creative or new puzzles, which are always welcome in a point and click game. Another flaw is that you move incredibly slowly throughout the level, and if you miss something and have to back track it becomes tedious.
With all that being said, Morphopolis is a colourful world on a bare bones hidden object/point and click game. If you want a casual and bright experience, I would pick up Morphopolis on sale as part of the Art Appreciation Pack.

I started playing this game last year. My friends have since moved on. They want to play RTS games and Mechwarrior Online.
But I am still fighting in the white sand and burning heat of Peleliu. I will always be fighting there. Trying to save Bill, that sniper who thought he could outfox a knee mortar. Trying to finally kill Hideki, that wily Japanese officer with a samurai sword who -- I swear on my life and all game mechanics -- becomes stronger and more resistant to gunfire the very moment that sword leaves its sheath.
Like they all say, this game is extrememly underrated. If you have ever played scenario paintball, this is just about the closest thing to it that you will find at a keyboard. For that matter, it is as close to realistic combat as I have ever heard any veteran attest to.
The scariest part may be that eventually, you get used to the PTSD-inducing moments, like that time when your best new foxhole buddies became lifeless sacks of flesh from a mortar hit. You become hardened. You watch newbies crest the ridge and laugh darkly -- you know that they will not live long enough to learn about proper cover. In fact, this game has a constant struggle with newbies that is strangely similar to things you read about in Band of Brothers. Half of your team hates them, and knows that they will just be body bags that drag the assault down The other half of your team just wants to help them, to mentor them, to make sure that they don't walk into a Japanses position with the naive notion that it's not booby-trapped to high heaven with grenades.
I have become a force of nature with the BAR. I have virtually no weapon upgrades on anything else but my BAR resembles a SOCOM-tweaked assault rifle covered in Christmas lights. Not really, but it does have a bipod. Once our team was bogged down trying to assault a warehouse, and I knew my moment had come. I charged up a ladder, through a mess of smoke -- and found myself in the midst of 8 Japanese soldiers, all firing outside. Not a one of them had seen me.
This was it, I was about to be the savior of the entire team. I aimed and let fly. Soldiers perished. Chaos reigned. One of the Japanese even killed his comrade in the midst of the confusion. When the smoke cleared, I was wounded. But the warehouse was taken.
The wise Japanese commander subsequently dropped a naval artillery strike directly onto the left side of my face. My corpse landed on a spike protecting a bunker, several dozen meters away.
Would become meat popsicle again. 10/10.

I will recommend this game despite it's shortcomings.
TL;DR
Frustrated with Tropico 4's poor economy design? Find yourself at home here. More of an economy simulator rather than a political simulator. Llarge portion of the political aspect cut or dumbed down, economical aspect expanded upon. Lots of DLC. The graphics are a large improvement over Tropico 4, A step forward in some directions and a step back in others.
A few gripes I have about the game:
- Your island will most of the time look like a Soviet Era industrial city due to the lack of building variety, as all buildings of the same type have no little to no variation between them, forcing you to have row upon row of identical houses and factories. The strict grid system contributes to this fact.
- While Tropico 4 had a large pool of representatives for all factions/countries, this game basically only has 3. That's two people representing half the factions each, and one person representing all the foreign countries. I really miss the variety of characters, as it all added to the political satire as they were mostly based on real life people.
- Rebels will appear regardless of approval rating (Highest I've gotten is 98% but still faced constant guerilla attacks on my distant mines and farms)
-  DLC!!! As of now there is nearly $50 worth of DLC for a game thats $40. I know Kalypso is money hungry but this is ridiculous.
- Penultimo's new voice :(
I enjoy particularily:
- Traffic jams can finally be avoided by proper planning and management. Teamsters also have a huge improvement
- It is a lot harder to win elections and this actually now requires effort
- Combat has been hugely improved
- Multiplayer is a huge plus, I love co-op games!
- The budget system vs salary system removes a lot of micromanagement, although I wish that constitution options would give you a choice of which to use (Free market = Budget, Planned Economy = salary).
- In the campaign mode you use the same two islands (alternate between missions) throughout the campaign, meaning it does not reset your island after each mission like in Tropico 4. Encourages long-term planning
There are a lot more minor things I enjoy, and a lot more minor things that annoy me.
Overall it's still a fun game, although it does make me go back to Tropico 4 every now and then.

These paths are incredibly difficult to pick out so you just end up pushing your avatar in a direction to see if he can go that way or not. When the game inevitably asks you to back track you end up waiting a painful amount of time for what is little more than a screen change. In a baffling choice of design there is even a delay on the "collection" of items as they slowly move across the screen to your 'counter' before they are registered and allow progression.
I know an awful lot of fuss has been made over the artwork of the game but I think it fails. When still every screen is a painting and certainly striking. However as an interactive medium there are hardly any subtle pointers of where you can go. Why can you climb here and not there? Because the game says so and thats it. Being able to find out where you are allowed to go let alone where you should go is simply a case of trial and error for the most part.

Outlast is indeed a visually appealing game with decent sound effects, lighting and design however it’s not enough to veil the many its many flaws.  As anyone knows horror, it’s a very hard medium to get right and this game didn’t go all the way for me in terms of what makes horror so fascinating.  Sure it contains violence, nudity and profanity like a typical horror movie, but what’s lacking is the originality, the risks in playing with taboos subjects, connecting with the protagonist(s) and see how far they’re willing to go make it to the end.  I’ve played this game four times (twice for the main game and twice for the DLC) to filly analyze the game, collect all the goodies and fully immerse myself into it to the point that I can even talk about it.  That being said, the game suffers from repetitious puzzles that utilizes little to no thought at all, the AI is extremely predictable and stupid to the point where once you understand how they’re program, they come less threatening, and wish I knew more about the characters I’m playing I can remotely care for them or even allow them to make choices that’ll change the outcome of the story.
Overall, the game feels incomplete and truly wished they step it up in their upcoming game and take risks.  Even though I may have selected not recommend, I actually wanted to select both because people have to play this game to really know why I critique it the way I do because of its setting. Also while playing the game I felt like I was riding an intricate escalator with twists, turns, ascend, descend, go backwards and forwards, but ultimately it’s just one path I’m forced to ride on with a few stops on the way to the end or what others say a “walking simulator” with jump scares like some small time fair ride.  Anyways, the lists below are my thoughts on the game, so I hope they’re helpful and illuminate why I think this game is holding back.  Here they are:

Note: I write this as someone who loves story-driven games, and couldn't care less about an FPS.  I played through Bioshock on easy difficulty, not caring a whit about the combat or combat mechanics.  If you want those reviewed; look elsewhere.
I played through Bioshock with a feeling of awe and wonder.  The world was beautiful and beatifully realized.  It was creepy and ugly and dysutopian in all the right places... and yet, the Art Deco art and architecture, the music and voice overs coming and going as you make your way through the city... the setting was incredible.  The background--essentially an Ayn Rand-esque utopia that's descended into madness and chaos--is interesting as well.
The plot was solid, if not horribly original.  I'll admit that while I recognized that not everything added up, I didn't see the big twist coming.  That being said, I found the ending extremely satisfying.  Unlike so many games (and other media), the endings pull no punches.  If you've set up a good end, you get a very good end.  If you set up a bad end, you get a very bad end.  None of this post-hoc analysis, "leave it open to player interpretation" nonsense.  You make choices; those choices matter.
So I can't speak to FPS fans.  But if you like story-driven games, set in interesting environments, then I cannot possibly recomend Bioshock highly enough.

Train Valley is a nice game if you like trains and micro managing switches.
Because this is 100% what this game is about.
Also it has a demo, which is rare enough.
The tutorial and the demo (which include the tuto + 2 levels) already shows you 100% of the gameplay.
Bear in mind that all other levels are just "more of the same".
So you goal is to build a railway (with switches all over the place) so that trains of a given color (there is a proper color-blind mode but all trains and stations have symbols, in addition to the color) reaches the stations of the matching color as fast as possible without bumping in other trains and without runing out of money.
The longer it take a train to reach a station, the fewer money it earns you.
Laying tracks cost money, with a penalty when you destroy something that already exist (house/tree).
Each year passing by also cost you a maintenance fee.
Each levels have three optionnal objectives, the real one is just no to run out of money.
Completing the objectives by the end of the level (which have a predetermined duration) will earn you stamps.
Even if it is easy not to run out of money, earning all the stamps is quite challenging. and will require you to restart some missions multiple times.
The game has 24 missions, divided in 4 seasons which only slighly change the looks of the levels (they are themed Europe, USA, Russia and Japon).
All levels are of the same size : super tiny, which is challenging and frustrating at the same time...
I wish there were bigger levels.
So feel free to test the demo, if you are not like "I want more of this" by the end of it, the game is not for you.
Otherwise, it will occupy about 10+ hours of your time.

This game's visuals are absolutely stunning, it is so pleasing to look at.
GamePlay:
Story Mode:
Story Mode is very good to start with, mainly because it houses the tutorial for basic mechanics and some other complex mechanics. After you get past the town of Milton how ever, it gets a bit tedious considering there are a ton of fetch quests in the mystery lake section but it isn't completely awful. It's just tedious, you also get an option to start from a checkpoint if you die in story mode which isn't present in survival. Story mode is far more hand holdy and feels linear at some points, but it's story is actually very engaging and fun to go through.
Survival Mode:
You have 4 difficulties to choose from in survival mode they all change the game in a signifigant way. This is accomplished by changing the spawns of almost everything in the game, making food scarce and hostile wildlife far more inhospitibale and common. This game's survival aspects are very well rounded and realistic aswell, it leaves no stone unturned when it comes to that. A thing new players get trouble with the game is when it comes to gear and supply management, it is very common to get either very little gear or too much gear to know what to do with, you have to invest time into thinking of strategies and locations to go to in order to thrive. If you aren't looking for the harsh survival difficulties this game offers, than the "Pilgrim" setting allows for nice exploration with it's beautiful landscapes. You still have to eat and find bare necessities, but you won't be attacked by any animals what so ever. Either way, this game feels very relaxing on the easier difficulty, it's more focused on exloration and wandering than it is battling the elements and nature. I have a few problems though.
Problems:
If you aren't very familar with survival techniques and have basic objectives in the harder difficulties, you're often going to be lost on what to do and how to survive. It has happened to me a lot in this game so I suggest you get some knowledge on basic survival tips. Also, it's extremely easy to get lost if you're wandering a lot; mapping out the terrain is a bit problematic consdering you only map out so little. The weapon choice is kind of sparse as well, you don't get many ranged choices in the game which is both good and bad. There are 3 ranged weapons that are currently available in this game, they all are decent but it would be nice to have something like a higher caliber hunting rifle. Otherwise the ranged weapons are fine, just needs a little more choices.
(this is something minor): There's no jumping in this game, it can make it hard to traverse land sometimes because of it, but most of the time you just have to get a running start to get over something small.
Conclusion:
Overall, for 40$ this game is alright. It could use some more content, but overall, it has a lot of good things about it. I give it a 8/10 because I enjoy it. It's very atmoshperic and if you're willing to give this game sometime, very engaging.

I started playing this game last year. My friends have since moved on. They want to play RTS games and Mechwarrior Online.
But I am still fighting in the white sand and burning heat of Peleliu. I will always be fighting there. Trying to save Bill, that sniper who thought he could outfox a knee mortar. Trying to finally kill Hideki, that wily Japanese officer with a samurai sword who -- I swear on my life and all game mechanics -- becomes stronger and more resistant to gunfire the very moment that sword leaves its sheath.
Like they all say, this game is extrememly underrated. If you have ever played scenario paintball, this is just about the closest thing to it that you will find at a keyboard. For that matter, it is as close to realistic combat as I have ever heard any veteran attest to.
The scariest part may be that eventually, you get used to the PTSD-inducing moments, like that time when your best new foxhole buddies became lifeless sacks of flesh from a mortar hit. You become hardened. You watch newbies crest the ridge and laugh darkly -- you know that they will not live long enough to learn about proper cover. In fact, this game has a constant struggle with newbies that is strangely similar to things you read about in Band of Brothers. Half of your team hates them, and knows that they will just be body bags that drag the assault down The other half of your team just wants to help them, to mentor them, to make sure that they don't walk into a Japanses position with the naive notion that it's not booby-trapped to high heaven with grenades.
I have become a force of nature with the BAR. I have virtually no weapon upgrades on anything else but my BAR resembles a SOCOM-tweaked assault rifle covered in Christmas lights. Not really, but it does have a bipod. Once our team was bogged down trying to assault a warehouse, and I knew my moment had come. I charged up a ladder, through a mess of smoke -- and found myself in the midst of 8 Japanese soldiers, all firing outside. Not a one of them had seen me.
This was it, I was about to be the savior of the entire team. I aimed and let fly. Soldiers perished. Chaos reigned. One of the Japanese even killed his comrade in the midst of the confusion. When the smoke cleared, I was wounded. But the warehouse was taken.
The wise Japanese commander subsequently dropped a naval artillery strike directly onto the left side of my face. My corpse landed on a spike protecting a bunker, several dozen meters away.

My most memorable moment in this game was probably when my friend and I went ahead and decided to learn how to drive a tank in the midst of battle.
When we spawned in, our tank crew went as follows: My friend as the driver, me as the person manning the tank's actual gun, and a random person operating the machine gun. Our crash-course, self-led tutorial basically consisted of my friend driving in circles because he could hardly see anything out of the driver's slit; me not being able to shoot the gun properly because the tank was constantly moving, resulting in tank shells being fired haphazardly around; and the machine gunner, who knew what he was doing, yelling at us and calling us incompetent idiots. I proceeded to accidentally pop my head out through the tank's top, only to instantaneously be shot. My dead body slumped back into the tank cockpit and awkardly jostled there as everything in the tank was suddenly painted with my blood. I can imagine Russian soldiers peeping out of their foxholes, only to comically spectate a German tank spin around, firing randomly and carelessly.
Later in the siege, our commander called in artillery on friendly positions and we lost.
I think they actually kill employees to record the game's death screams. Red Orchestra 2 can easily be named 'PTSD Simulator 1942.'
Seriously, though. This game is great. Easily one of the best World War II shooters I've ever played. Shots kill you instantly (If you're lucky enough to survive a bullet, you usually just sit in sadness as you listen to your character scream or cry to death as they bleed out), the carnage feels authentic and the atmosphere is truly war-like. The developers really harped on realism, and I can say they nicely achieved it.
That's not to mention the soundtrack is proud and patriotic, while at the same time solemn and depressing.
The only problems I can think of is the game are its graphics-intensive nature, so you need a decent computer to run it, and the game is so structured around teamwork that an incompetent team can really rain on your gameplay experience (Or boost it, depending on the scenario).

So, lets address the elephant in the room. Yes, this is another city building game, a distant relative of Sim-u-know-what. Surfing thru the ages gives you a new challenge, particularly because you need to carefully reshape your city every now and then as the main campaign progresses.
One of the issues I had at first is that the game forces you to jump between two islands, giving a false sense of “choosing”. You pick first knowing next to nothing about the resources available at the start, but then the game forces you to alternate between them making sometimes a really hard time, specially if you created a “military powerhouse” for some mission, and then pushed back to turn it into a “tourist heaven”.
Having said that, whatever you are required to do, always think you may need to revisit your island, so make it as self-sustainable as possible. If you sacrifice population growth, happiness or food production for some short term objective, you may have a nightmare to deal with in the later episodes.
Oh, the freaking military troops.. that is really annoying how they spread and head to the enemy's objectives instead of attacking the incoming troops.. man! How many battles lost because only a single troop faced 3 enemy squadrons while the other 4 where zipping mojitos at the gold mine or the farm “waiting” for the enemy to reach them. For the invasion times, try to built towers and army thingys close to the shore.
Now for the good side:
Loved the political puns, especially Penultimo quotes. Was kind weird hearing the same sentences once you're throw back in time and some technologies have to be “re-invented” though, if he is a time traveler as you are, why to repeat those? (ok ok, nitpicking here).

Note: I write this as someone who loves story-driven games, and couldn't care less about an FPS.  I played through Bioshock on easy difficulty, not caring a whit about the combat or combat mechanics.  If you want those reviewed; look elsewhere.
I played through Bioshock with a feeling of awe and wonder.  The world was beautiful and beatifully realized.  It was creepy and ugly and dysutopian in all the right places... and yet, the Art Deco art and architecture, the music and voice overs coming and going as you make your way through the city... the setting was incredible.  The background--essentially an Ayn Rand-esque utopia that's descended into madness and chaos--is interesting as well.
The plot was solid, if not horribly original.  I'll admit that while I recognized that not everything added up, I didn't see the big twist coming.  That being said, I found the ending extremely satisfying.  Unlike so many games (and other media), the endings pull no punches.  If you've set up a good end, you get a very good end.  If you set up a bad end, you get a very bad end.  None of this post-hoc analysis, "leave it open to player interpretation" nonsense.  You make choices; those choices matter.
So I can't speak to FPS fans.  But if you like story-driven games, set in interesting environments, then I cannot possibly recomend Bioshock highly enough.

Batman - The Telltale Series is an adventure game following the telltale adventure game style with quick time events and time-constrained choices. It is a Batman game, but it isn't set in any well-known Batman universe (Nolan-verse, Arkham-verse, DC comics, DC movies, etc...). Simply put this Batman game set in an alternate universe (similar to the Elseworld series)
The game is mainly based on quick time events which i think doesn't suit well to a Batman game, especially after seeing possibly the best Batman series so far, the Arkham series. Besides, the plot changes a VERY CRITICAL part of Batman's backstory which doesn't go well with the classical motivation of Bruce Wayne/Batman. I think this change didn't work at all and made Batman much, much less than who he is in more classical incarnations. Also, the plotline is extremely convoluted. The game tries to put as many Batman characters to a single game most of them lack depth. The game is much more about Bruce Wayne than Batman, which might have been an interesting idea but I believe the personification of Bruce Wayne is not done quite good so this focus on Bruce Wayne doesn't seem to work in the context of this game.
Also, technically there are many choices you, as the player, can take. However, 99% of these choices do not affect the main storyline at all instead only affect very simple things which makes this "Story tailors itself based on your choices" focus of the game completely moot. Action sequences are extremely simple. So, the game is not challenging at all (which maybe a good thing depending on you preferences.)
Pros:
- Polished game with very good voice acting.
- If you like interactive movies, then it is an enjoyable game.
Cons:
- The game is basically an interactive movie instead of an actual game. Most choices you take have little to no effect on the actual story. You can practically choose whatever you want in any dialog option and beside simple things the outcome of the game will always be the same.
- Depiction of Batman here is a huge let down. Batman is generally not in control in many situation and doesn't have the iconic grimness and stoicness of the character.
- The story is very convoluted and the change in the back story of Batman doesn't work at all.

WINTER IS COMING
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
One month ago my plane failed and I parachuted out. Landing in a cold forest during daylight I was able to find shelter in an abandoned shack near a frozen lake. Fortunately for me there were a few granola bars and a can of soda on a shelf so I was able to sustain myself for a day on that.
The next day leaving the shack, I found a few more nearby with some more supplies. I felt lucky even though I was always cold. All I had to keep me warm was a fleece coat, jeans, and some tennis shoes (in addition to my long johns).
Making my may around the lake I found what seemed to be an abandoned rental office for the shacks around the lake. I decided to live here until someone came by to tell me I couldn't.
Over the days I ate cattails and melted snow to make water and stayed nourished for a bit but knew I would need to find food so I set off outdoors to explore the nearby forest.  Wandering for a few hours I came upon a trapper's shack and found a rabbit snare inside so gathered it up. There was a box of tea there so I took that too, even though I don't normally drink tea, and left the shack to rush back "home" to the camp rental office as soon as I could because a storm had kicked up and I could barely see 10 feet in front of me.
I got lost.
All there were was trees around and the temperature had dropped dangerously low.
I could barely feel my feet as I wandered around...looking for a way I knew.
I had gathered some sticks while on the way to the trapper's cabin and now looked for a place safe from the icy wind to build a small fire because I was so cold I couldn't feel anything and my vision was going fuzzy.
I got a fire going and heated up the tea. I drank it and felt a little bit better though still very cold. God must have been talking to me when I left the Camp Office because on a whim I'd brought the storm lantern on the counter there with me so lit it and walked on...
I could barely see 10 feet in front of me because it was dark and the blizzard blocked all view.  Just a little in front I could make out trees...nothing but trees.  I wandered lost and I felt terror. I was already freezing and I knew If I could not find shelter the blizzard would turn me into a human ice cube.
I walked along and could physically hear my heart pounding. All I could see were some trees and the wind blown snow all around the air in front of me ... nothing but misty snow...
I thought, "I'm going to die out here. No one will see me ever again."
And then I saw something... a faint silhouette of a cabin.
"Home."
OH my God....LUCK!!!!!!
I ran towards the cabin and threw open the door.... heart pounding.
Alll of me was freezing but I knew that I would be okay
I went upstairs to the bed and slept completely clothed.
I made it though another day.
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

I had this game on my wishlist for awhile as it seemed to have been unanimously praised. When it was offered for free on Steam 6/21 and 6/22, I was eager to try it out. I was ultimately very disappointed with the game. Several times during my playthrough, I commented to friends that had I purchased

+ The graphic style is unique and the developers succeeded in creating an atmosphere that makes the player feel isolated and uncertain. It reminded me a bit of how
used the noir graphics. From an aesthetic standpoint,
is a treat. The game runs at a constant 60FPS (locked) at 1080p.
+ The game length (about 3-4 hours on a first playthrough) is just about right. I didn't really want to play it any more than this (more on this below).
+ The checkpoint system is generous. Given the instant-death, trial-and-error nature of the puzzles, it is necessary.

- The trial-and-error nature of the puzzles is more frustrating than it is motivating. Successfully overcoming the objectives doesn't feel rewarding and oftentimes the solutions can only be discovered by dying repeatedly. Cheap deaths occur regularly, often from unavoidable hazards intentionally obscured by the shadows.
seems to go for the "gotcha" and it ranges from irritating to frustrating. There is one particular puzzle (about 2/3rds through) where the game provides a paradigm to follow and then a second later rips the carpet out from under the player by shifting it so that the same action results in instant death. It isn't clever. I enjoy games that challenge me to think, and failing in games like
or
felt fair and motivated me to try again.
left me wanting to press on simply so I could get through the game. After 3-4 hours, I had enough.
- Movement feels floaty. The best comparison I could make would be
as that also features wonky platorming, but
is worse. For a game that oftentimes requires precise timing/jumping, character movement is oftentimes sluggish.
- The game lacks any graphics options and in general the settings are extremely bare-bones. Before playing through
I thought this was at worst an oversight, at best an attempt by the developer to emphasize the experience rather than having the user worry about tweaking framerates and texture levels. After playing, I am inclined to think this was a conscious decision done not in the spirit of emphasizing a certain aesthetic but rather to scold the player for daring to want to adjust or customize the experience to their liking. Maybe that's unfair, but given the "gotcha" moments experienced in the puzzles, it combined with the lack of options to give me that sort of feeling.
Had I paid for this game, I would have refunded it. Given that it was offered free for a limited time, all I lost was my time.

NOTE: This is a review I wrote for an Australian computer and technology forum, figured I would post it on here as well, as I think extremely highly of this game. This review isn't exactly written in the style of your standard steam reviews, but it outlines some of the gameplay mechanics and other things in that game make it one of the more enjoyable titles around at the moment, due in part to the multiplayer that is now part of the game.
Over the last several years, I've eagerly been watching this game grow and evolve, once in a while I would download the latest build and test it out. Everything was very promising. Here I had a game that offered a True Zombie Apocalypse "Simulator", a game where there is no real goal other than to survive, this was well before games like Day Z started popping up too.
Project Zomboid is much different however, first of all the game uses an isometric viewing angle, secondly it tries to "simulate" everything. From cooking, to building to reading books. There are literally hundreds of different items in the game, majority of them have a use. Canned soup can be consumed, but only if you have a can opener, access to a fire or stove and a pot to cook it in. Books can be read to increase your skills in things like fishing, carpentry or farming. All of this takes "time" to do. Your character can be affected by dozens of different things, go out in the rain, you get wet, stay wet for too long, you can get sick. If you're wet, you can change your clothes or dry off with a towel. If you get sick, you can find painkillers and other meds to help you get over it. Get scared by too many zombies and cant find any survivors and your character can start to become panicky and depressed. This is just scratching the surface of what can be done in the game though.
The world is persistent, this means you can barricade houses, as long as you have a hammer, nails and some planks, you can cover open windows with sheets so the Zs cant see you inside. Weapons can be repaired with things like Duct Tape or glue, weapons can be modified (not sure how many at this stage have mods) ie. getting a baseball bat and hammering some nails to make it a "nailed baseball bat". You can build doors, doorframes, walls, floors, stairs etc. and essentially build your own fortress, or connect several houses together with wooden walls being used as passageways, so you are safe from the Zs when going between houses.
The Zs themselves are quite cool as well, if you play Sandbox or multiplayer mode, you are able to change several different things about the zombies to make them easier or harder, this allows you to customise the Zs to be similar to the ones from your favourite movies (fast, slow, blind/deaf etc) Zombies also give chase, depending on their memory settings, you can lose them just by getting a certain distance away, or you may have to lead them on a merry chase through houses and the bush to make them lose your scent and successfully escape.
Combat is fairly standard, however it works great is very satisfying if you get your timing right. There are guns in the game, but majority of the time you will opt for melee weapons, guns will attract zombies, to the point where you can inadvertently attract a horde of 30+ zombies. It makes for some great gameplay and very tense moments.
On top of all of this, the game now has multiplayer, at the moment it is join by IP only, so no proper server browser, but once you make/find a server to play in, you will find that the world is persistent, items don't respawn, neither do zombies, zombies will often wander around and may eventually occupying an area that you have previously cleared, but overall this means you can essentially clear out an area and be safe from Zombie Hordes, as they won't respawn once you kill them.
This all comes together to create the most enjoyable Co-op experience I have had in as long as I can remember. For $15 on steam, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you still love zombie games, you may find that despite how the game is presented (look at it on the steam store, first reaction is usually that it graphically looks quite dated) it is one of the most feature rich and amazing Zombie Survival games on the market.
There is far more that I could list about this great game, but I suggest if it sounds interesting enough from my explanation above, take the plunge and see how you like it. There is also a demo available  which is still quite indicative of what you can expect should you decide to purchase the full game.
Seriously guys, get on it.

After putting more hours into the game I thought I'd do a more thought-out review than the previous:
Evolve is a 4 vs 1 coop game from Turtle Rock who previously made Left 4 Dead which I liked immensely when it came out. This makes it hard not to compare the two games to each other and to Killing Floor somewhat.
In essence Evolve feels like a mod to Left 4 Dead where the four survivors (Hunters) look for and hunt down the player controlled tank (Monster).
The core gameplay is interesting although I fast found it to be also quite shallow and monotonous.  The monster and the hunters are looking to kill each other. The monster has three levels, the first being the weakest. The hunters in turn have to be fast to find the monster before it can get stronger. The monster needs to hide long enough to be able to level up.
It's a neat concept I suppose but the Hunt game mode doesn't go much further than that. The matches can go from two to twenty something minutes but they're usually quite short. Most of the time is spent going over the map trying to find the monster. There are different classes but there's little you can do to adapt your playstyle to them outside of the fights. Everyone just runs around looking for the monsters.  In any case you wait.
This wouldn't be bad if you didn't have to wait so much outside of the game too. This is one of the big problems with the game. You wait to launch the game and get to the menus, you wait for the matchmaking to find players, you wait for the players to load and sync, you wait for the map to load, you wait for people to select their loadouts, you wait for the game to start and you wait to go back to the lobby once the game ends. This is not including the connectivity issues a lot of people are having with not finding any players for 20 minutes.
Loading times for the levels aren't bad  either but having to go through this barrage of loading screens every time takes it's toll.
Another complaint is that the game is wildly unbalanced due to the player leveling system that is in place meaning those who've played longer have better gear with better stats, more class loadouts and better perks.
The monster players especially can unlock themselves this Cthulhu looking creature that can wipe out the entire team on level 1 if they choose to have faster cooldowns and max their lightning skill before the game starts.
The leveling system feels like a cheap way to give the player a sense of progression. You have an edge on lower level players but leveling doesnt' much change the way you play the game. This wasn't an issue in Killing Floor where you do have levels but gaining levels makes it possible for you to pass harder versions of the same levels. And getting through a level with a harder difficulty is what felt satisfying. Same thing in L4D although it didn't have a leveling system. In Evolve the existence of a leveling system doesn't feel justified in it's current iteration.
Talking a bit more about the balance. The maps can some times have different weather effects to them such as there being lowered visibility due to rain or snow. This could be an interesting way to make the game harder for the hunters if they're up against a low level monsters. Currently the weather effects seem to come at random.
Another mild issue I had is that when you play as the hunters there isn't any real sense of dread as the hunters themselves don't seem too fearful of the monsters. This could've been intentional but it doesn't fit the Predator vibe the team seemed to be going for and otherwise did a good job at. Instead I felt much more vulnerable playing as the base monster. In that sense the game is more similiar to The Most Dangerous Game than Predator which is in no way bad, just different from what I imagined the game would be like.
In alpha there is also a common bug that makes parts of the hub disappear so you're unable to tell if you should flee or not. It makes for some really cheap losses.
Evolve is an okay game based on the alpha but not worth the asking price for the presumed amount of content the game will have. I suppose it can be a good time waster for a few hours a day but I don't see it as having much long lasting appeal as it doesn't really Evolve anywhere. *snicker*

Well, after finishing the game once and playing most of the previous Telltale Games/Series, i am actually sad to give this a thumbs down.
Pros:
- Nice story with somewhat "new" character origins and design, especially concerning the Waynes
- Some semi-individuality by taking on issues as Batman or Bruce Wayne
- "Link"-concept for "detective work" and planning takedowns
Cons:
- Graphics/ Optimization
- Story (compared to other TT-Games: Less dramatic and intruiging, no real humour), though the above mentioned "fresh take" on the franchise, still stands as a pro.
- Much too short chapters (compared to other TTGs). Feels like artificially stretched out to make it to 5, instead of just 3 chapters.
- Link-System feels sometimes pointless, like stuffed out to increase game time (there was a kidnapping, you know who kidnapped whom, so why bother reconstructingthe kidnapping without any additional nfo out of it).
- A bit too soft on the violence: Neither Batman nor the villains REALLY go to the lengths, that press/police attribute to them. (very personal opinion;) Though the rating clearly isn´t for "children" and there are sometimes "More violent" options that make Gordon angry.
- Some rather shallow characters
Graphics:
So first of all, there were previous, less known, comic book adaptions by TTG (Telltale Games), and the Comic-style graphics fit the material very well. SO WHY change it in the most well known COMIC franchise TTG took on so far? He´s a (THE) comic book character, so who needs "fancy" lighting and semi-3D-textures?!
The next thing is, that these textures look simply ♥♥♥♥♥♥ when displayed in low settings, whereas the previous TTG-titles looked still fine on LOW.
The OPTIMIZATION was criticised a lot in other places - rightly so.
One point is, that they are not "recommended [to play] with Intel integrated graphics". But when i use my Geforce 940M, i still can´t go above medium level graphics without delays/lags/stuttering, which makes QTEs nearly impossible.
THEN i use my INTEL graphics and guess what, i can basically take the graphics to the same level as with my Geforce? WTF? So in the end i save energy by using my integrated graphics, but cant show the slightly better graphics anyway. "Cut scenes" seem to stutter (especially at the beginning) independently of graphics processor or settings.
Also after playing the  game half through it did "hang itself" and didn´t display afterwards. Onl ythe symbol in the taskbar was visible. After all the questions i found a helpful answer/FIX: Configure start-options (in library: right click, properties...) to "-windowed". Doesn´t show it windowed now, but full screen then, yey. AS ADMINISTRATOR also helps, the often mentioned "comaptibility settings" did SHT.
(playing on Win 10 notebook, i5-5200u, Geforce 940M, 8GB RAM)
Story/Characters:
As i said, the story takes a nice fresh swing at the Batman lore, altering some of the more stiff realations in the universe, like the bigger role of Vicky Vale, the background of the Waynes or the age of the Penguin.
But i really missed the "highs" of previous TTG-Titles. The stories usually have been much more intruiging with characters that basically had to be built up from scratch, since (most) players didnt know them beforehand. TWD had a really dramatic and intruiging (overuse, sorry) story with choices that really made you feel uneasy. Tales from the Borderlands had a lot of humour besides the interesting story. Wolf among us was a great thriller with the right portion of gore to make the universe come alive.
In BATMAN it seems they just said "it´s Batman, people know it, they will buy it". The Penguin, as pointed out in other reviews, is interchangable and shallow. While two-face and others are introduced and used somewhat more "believable".
And as mentioned above, the story already feels stretched out, but is still too short compared to the above mentioned TTGs.
I´m glad i got it on sale/in a bundle. That´s how i would buy the 2nd part too, because it´s BATMAN and some interesting characters are about to show up. But i hope the sequel improves the issues mentioned, maybe even GOES BACK in graphics.

Though this is a fine addition to the original Half-Life series, it is the weakest installation from my experience. Its gameplay is solid; however its weakness lies with the enemy and weapon verity. For the majority of the game, you are fighting Vortigaunts and soldiers. You are primarily armed with a revolver, pistol, shotgun, automatic rifle, a bazooka for tough enemies, some explosives, and the trusty crowbar in hand.  Barney, the protagonist of this game, is not as well equipped as his counterparts, Gordon and Adrian. For that reason, he doesn’t fight that many strong enemies like Alien Grunts or even encounter the Black Ops. This expansion is also short; it only took me about two hours to complete it in a single run.  However, I enjoyed the level design a bit more because it eliminated a lot of awkward platforming which plagued Half-Life. It also doesn’t have an awkward final boss like the Nihilanth to round the game off which actively tried to break the flow of the game.
Overall, after playing Half-Life, I believe this game is a weaker experience, but it has aged better than Half-Life in terms of level design. If you enjoy old school FPS games or want to familiarize yourself with them, you can’t go wrong with Half-Life: Blue Shift.

Terrifying game. It took me weeks to get through it, because I could only play it for about 11 minutes at a time before I would just close the game screaming 'F*** that!'. If the goal of buying this game is to experience the kind of terror that makes your lower spine tingle, mission accomplished.
My friends all thought I was being a wuss, complaining day after day that this game was scaring me. Then I Steam streamed my next attempt while they watched. After that it went from 'whats wrong with you?!' to 'whats wrong with this game?!' One of them even closed the stream before I wussed out. Absolutely horrifying.
However, while being a great horror game, it has very little replay value. Once you are no longer lost, know when/where the jump scares occur, etc, the fear factor dissolves completely. Great game, but know going in that you won't be playing it for years to come. It will likely just be the one time through.
Would recommend, assuming you enjoy the kind of stress that causes heart attacks, and are unsatisfied with the lack of poo in your pants.

As I give a thumbs up for my review, I think to myself, "What kind of person are you?"
You know when you are playing a horror game or watching a horror movie and everything tells you that the situation is not good and it is not going to get any better and that you will save yourself some scarring if you turn it off? Yet, you keep playing or watching, submitting yourself to any horror that will be thrown at you, BECAUSE YOU JUST HAVE TO KNOW HOW IT ENDS.
That is my relationship with Outlast. I don't know if I would even call this game scary, but I do know that I would call it horrific and tension-filled. I feel like this game already has enough reviews to cover the pros and cons, so here are just some thoughts on how this game affected me.
It was a brilliant, tense, horrific experience and the thought to turn the game off never entered my mind. The idea of investigating a mental hospital for its questionable ethics is fairly typical adventure/survival horror material. However, I felt that Outlast was very fresh and original in its delivery. I've never played anything quite like it, and honestly I hope I don't play many more like this.
I loved the familiar territory of the adventure aspects of this game. Exploring and discovering the secrets of the hospital via notes and documents is always a treat. Luckily, not the entire game is running from people who want to kill you. Actually, it was refreshing to find the mental patient who wanted to help, in his own way, of course. The atmosphere reminded me of wonderful games like Amnesia, where you are in almost constant peril and there is no way to fight back.
Now, maybe I am a little sheltered but after playing Amnesia, Dead Space, and the Silent Hill series, I thought I could face what Outlast had to offer. For a while I could. Raving lunatics wandering halls, bodies everywhere, psychos chasing you - standard fare. But then the DLC Whistleblower unleashed a level of horror that I hope I never see again. His name is The Groom. A fair warning for those who love horror games, what The Groom does may test your gore threshold.
Mechanic wise, I found that the game ran very smoothly and looked great. The constant need to have your camera out added an edge that I haven't felt since Fatal Frame.
So do I recommend this game? Yes. Did I find it fun? That is debatable. I couldn't stop playing. Not because it was necessarily fun, but because I had to believe that putting the poor protagonists through all this was worth it. In the end, I think it was, and I am glad that I played it.

To summarise this real quick: Sunless Sea is a browser game manifested in a game engine with some sloppy mechanics. It has wonderful, haunting writing that makes you think the whole story takes place in a fevered dream - there are many cool quests and stories which are accompanied by many nasty decisions on player part. You really feel like you're struggling to make a living, giving many illicit and horrid opportunities a go just to pull yourself out of the gutter, while holding dearly to the little scraps of sanity you still have left after the last voyage.
But it comes with a major drawback - the pacing and gameplay outside the story part are kind of bad. Battle mechanics are sloppy and there's a few tricks you can (and should) abuse in order to stay ahead of your foes. There's lots of downtime where you don't do anything at all, just traveling mindlessly through the vast and deep zea for hours of real time. The grind you have to go through to earn anything and repeat it again on your next playthrough doesn't really give you satisfying rewards.
DLC solves some of the problems with the zea travel by introducing new exploration mechanics and littering map with more spots of interests and ports, new traderouts, but the main hustle of going port to port and gnawing lack of cargospace are still there.
I would recommend getting it together with DLC and be prepared to read A LOT OF TEXT; it's a game that requires big chunks of time and attention, and if you show it a lot of love it might respond. Otherwise, you should probably stay away.

It's not quite as rare as you might think for a game to have mechanics that aren't actually fun when looked at by themselves, but when viewed as part of the overall game as a whole, serve to define the experience and make the game what it is.  There's no light without shadow.
With that in mind, we turn to Sunless Sea, a game in which you spend very long stretches of time gliding through the darkness, doing nothing of consequence, waiting to make port and read more story stuff.  I'm not the first to argue that the boredom induced by these journeys is actually beneficial to the pacing and feel of the game.  You might be motivated to make decisions that go against your own personal morality, purely so that you have something interesting to read.  This is one of the game's most interesting themes, in my opinion, and conveys the experience of being underway on a long voyage away from the sight of land pretty well.  There's a mystery to the sea, even one with sun shining down on it, a sense that the rules of society and reality don't quite apply with the same force out there.  In allowing the player to become bored, in making you long to see port again, the game puts you in the shoes of your character extremely well.
When you make port, you can participate in story events that largely consist of reading some of the finest writing I've seen in a game in many years.  Occasionally, you make dice rolls based on your skill numbers.  Where Sunless Sea far surpasses Fallen London, the game and universe from which it springs, is in its eschewing of repetitive skill-building stories in favor of building skills with a simple one or two line conversation with your ship's officers.  There is also far less filler in Sunless Sea than in Fallen London, far fewer stories where the player is barred from entry for silly reasons like not being a donator or for having skills or reputations that are too low.  In Sunless Sea, your only barriers to entry are your resources: the supplies and fuel to make it to where you're going and back, and the will and patience to wait out the journey.  Every story is interesting and precious, and there are an awful lot of them.
The game's overall tone and aesthetic draws heavily from cosmic horror, with a smattering of sea stories and sailorly superstitions.  It's a compelling mix, and not without its lighter moments, such as Pigmote Isle, where rats and guinea pigs struggle for dominance.  Personally, I'm a big fan of the way Hell is interpreted in this game: the Iron Republic, where the laws of nature don't apply.  Cannibalism is of course a major theme, befitting any horror story about seafaring folk, limited resources, and desperation in the dark unknown.
The combat is an afterthought, as are the ship upgrading mechanics, and so too the roguelike elements.  The way the game handles succession between players makes zero sense (why do your kids relive the same stories?).  This is a game where you learn the mechanics only so much as to serve your goal of going out to sea again, one more time, looking for another story.  Don't let monsters and death distract you from your search.
The expansion, Zubmariner, adds a huge amount of new content, meaning of course, yet more stories.  Being able to dive underwater and explore down there essentially doubles the amount of stuff to find and read, and if you intend to pick the game up, I also recommend getting the DLC as soon as you decide this is the sort of game you're into.
