A very generous friend gifted this game to me, and I was excited to try it because I enjoy “meta” games, and the premise interested me. My gameplay experience left me feeling somewhat ambivalent.
If you like games that focus on creative design, thought-provoking narratives, walking simulators, and being told a story, then you will probably enjoy this game. Be advised, if you are looking for something similar to The Stanley Parable, you will NOT find that here. This is literally a walking simulator that tells you a story for approximately 1.5 hours. Also, while I normally try not to mention price, I do not feel that the current $10.99 CAD is justified – perhaps half or even 75% of that amount would be more appropriate. Where I live, that is about the same cost for a movie ticket, but after playing, I would personally wait until this one hit the discount day (cheap Tuesdays). Hopefully you were able to snag this on the recent Humble Bundle (HB Indie Bundle 17).
One thing I’d like to add before continuing – many of the reviews you will read paint this game as being “pretentious,” however, I feel that this is not the case. Although the ending felt awkward to me, it was still very powerful.
The aesthetics are decent and standard of your old-school Counter-Strike-era titles (the games showcased were all created using the Source engine). Beginner’s Guide is narrated by Davey Wreden, the mastermind behind The Stanley Parable (both the original Half-Life 2 mod and standalone game), who does an excellent job of drawing in your attention and interest. The narrative is the product you are purchasing – it has heavy “meta” themes and offers insight into game design as a form of artful expression (which I agree with). This recurring theme is given to you very, very well – there was a specific part where I realized I was being judgmental based only on information given by the narrator. When I caught myself, I felt good and bad at the same time (like when you first realize that character POVs in books like Game of Thrones are not always reliable).
Controls are very simple – the game is purely storytelling placed on top of a walking simulator. There are no puzzles or a difficulty since everything is linear.
Gameplay consists – you guessed it – of you walking around, exploring different levels of varying games while Davey tells you a story. For me, there was one part that I found rather cringe-y, but I can see how that specific scene would be powerful to others. The game is peppered nicely with intelligent lines that dig into your humanity (ex: “maybe he just liked. . .”), and anyone who enjoys creative design for anything – not just games – should enjoy this story.
Overall, if you do not mind the price (or get it on a discount), I think exploring Beginner’s Guide is worth your time. Approach it with an open mind and really think about the story. Something I enjoyed seeing is the amount of fan theories that have been proposed since this game was released. Davey’s legacy of making people think continues after The Stanley Parable with Beginner’s Guide.
If you like storytelling and the art of creative design, then you should definitely give this game a try.

Browsing Steam late one evening in December 2013, I was looking for a different zombie game to play. I found Project Zomboid. After watching the trailer, I was intrigued but cautious. The game was pretty fun as it was and the idea of watching it grow was appealing but prior to PZ, I’d only ever played finished articles or free demos/betas, mostly on console. I was aware I could be left disappointed if development stopped before I was satisfied but decided £10 was a sacrifice I willing to make.
It’s now October 2017, almost 4 years since I made my purchase. The game is still in early access. Do I feel my investment was worthwhile? Absolutely. For me, even without being complete, PZ has numerous qualities and a certain charm that every other zombie game lacks. The isometric viewpoint is something I immediately fell in love with and feel it makes PZ more immersive than it’s 3D cousins. It doesn’t rely on realistic gory textures/graphics to convey a tense and bleak atmosphere.
The aim of the game, survive for as long as possible in the zombie apocalypse.  It’s not about killing as many zombies as possible (you can if you’d like) but more about the burden of everyday survival and the decisions you make to delay your inevitable death.
To begin, create a character and choose a profession. Each profession has various XP modifiers for different skills, ranging from Agility type skills like Sprinting or Sneaking, Survivalist skills like Fishing, Trapping and Foraging, or Crafting skills like Carpentry, Cooking or Farming, plus numerous others. You also have positive and negative traits you can take that give you other boosts or buffs. Once you spawn, you get to explore and survive in a HUGE open world full of food, weapons, medicine…but also zombies. Barricade and fortify an existing building to make it your safe house, or go into the woods and build your own, live like a nomad. Play on your own or with a friend coop, or online multiplayer, it’s entirely up to you.
There are no crazy special zombies that explode, are big tank like brutes or spit goop at you. Just classic Romero shamblers. Individually, they are not a threat but in numbers, they can be devastating. It only takes one bite, one momentary lapse in judgment to end hours of effort. No remedies or potions to stop/delay you turning (Zombrex & Antizin, I’m looking at you). Get too blasé, fail to spot that bathroom zombie and get bitten, you’re done! Just like in the movies.
Much of the game is moddable, especially if you play Sandbox mode that allows adjusting of practically anything you want. Zombie population, speed, strength, cognition, memory, decomposition.  How the infection transmits and its reanimation time. Day length and what season you start in. The time before water/electricity shut off or food spoils. The list goes on and on. Project Zomboid is all about tailoring the zombie apocalypse to suit you.
Project Zomboid also has an excellent community. The Indie Stone released Mapping Tools to allow you to create your own maps to survive in. In times between updates when I’m not playing the game as much, I’m recreating my hometown so I can eventually live out what I’d do in an actual zombie apocalypse. I’ve even started to learn Java and Lua in an effort to mod other aspects of the game in the future. Community members on The Indie Stone forums have been especially helpful in starting this process.
I accept the development speed as been slower than I’d like but the people who are most disappointed at this pace are the developers themselves. They are a small team, only 4 full time programmers I believe and a handful of other people part time. It’s their first game as a studio, creating an engine from scratch. When development started, programs like Unity didn’t exist. They have enormous ambition and won't settle for mediocre, even if it means development is slower than expected. TIS admit they’ve made mistakes along the way, but people are allowed to make mistakes. It's what helps us grow in life.
I know I've made the right choice buying Project Zomboid. It's what I've always been looking for in a zombie game and will continue to enjoy watching The Indie Stone’s vision come to fruition, regardless of how long it takes.

is a survival city building simulator. In charge of a caravan of settlers looking to eke out a living in the wilderness, establish a village where you must cater to the needs of every inhabitants, surviving the odds of the seasons from generation to generation.
: This is a very different take on an economy-based city builder. Each individual member of your community is put to the test. You must hunt, fish, and gather resources for food, clothing, firewood and building material, perhaps surviving long enough to grow your own crops or trade for livestock you hope will multiply. Population must be balanced: while children spend years being little more than additional mouths to feed, they are crucial to replenishing your workforce as your existing population grows older. You will come to depend on each inhabitant's individual contribution, but disaster might strike and see all your efforts washed away when half your population starves because a single crop goes bad, or dies of cold when you run out of firewood in the middle of winter, or loose all your investment in your livestock that dies from a disease. Unless you play in easy mode, you WILL fail, often, and the challenge lies in learning from your mistakes as you undertake the challenge of another town. Beyond being a game, this experience puts a lot of perspective on how early settlers of the western world tried, and often failed, to create a life for themselves.
: The game lacks variety, and while I understand the realism of its setting doesn't open it to much variety, the lack of a currency-based economy holds you back from successfully growing into a thriving city, meaning you'll always be nothing more than a village, big or small. That same lack of variety also makes the game somewhat repetitive from one playthrough to another, as you have a very limited amount of building types or sizes for each role. The weather effect washes the colors out of the game, and you spend your playthrough in this bleak atmosphere void of any optimism, even when successful.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
certainly gets my recommendation, but it's meant for a specific, even niche, crowd. You don't get the thrill of sprawling a city like you would in a game like
, but I suppose that's precisely what makes it different. Give it a try, who knows how many hours you'll spend on it.

The game's free so I can't really complain too much. Plus in the end I did enjoy myself, so if you want 30 minutes of some creepy Greek crypts go ahead and give this a look.
PROS:
- An eerie atmosphere that totally sucks you in.
- Fantastic sound design.
- Great pacing.
- The environment is really unique and interesting to explore.
MIDDLE GROUND:
- Definitely needs to be expanded upon.
CONS:
- Terrible enemy AI that spoils the game's scares.
- The bow and arrow feels useless.
- Medusa ain't even in the game.
SCORE: 7/10

Train Valley is a casual game where you must lay tracks to connect multiple stations to each other, and route trains without crashes or delays with the goal of sending trains to the correct station marked by a coloured flag.  It's not a tycoon or serious transport management sim and there is no cargo or passenger quota to manage.  It's more a strategy/puzzle type of game that challenges you to meet a set of goals before time or money run out.
It's silly in a fun way as the difficulty ramps up and you find yourself frantically clicking switches in the hope of avoiding crashes or wrongly-routed trains.  Some trains are faster and longer than others and it soon becomes manic.  Don't even think of trying a delaying tactic!  Keep a train waiting long enough and it will release itself whether you're ready or not!  The tutorial is somewhat scant but the game is intuitive to play with a simple interface.  You are not automatically thrown out of the game if you suffer a collision (luckily) though your profits take a hit and you'll probably need to do some track repairs.  You are given a set of objectives to meet for each location - of increasing difficulty with a greater number of stations to be served.
Quite honestly, not much.  At first, it feels a bit TOO casual (ie Facebook style) but as the difficulty and number of stations ramp up, the game becomes a real challenge of strategy and timing.  The graphics are somewhat muddy and aliased (no in-game options to correct this).   Station colours can be a bit obscured by train flags at times when there are a lot of things going on, and a couple of colours are a little too similar which adds unnecessarily to the level of difficulty (for example: the orange and yellow station colours look very similar).  These are all minor gripes however, and don't detract from the fun of the game.
Train Valley is no 'Sid Meier' or other type of management or tycoon sim, but it's a fun and addictive little game easily worth its low price.  Recommended!

A very generous friend gifted this game to me, and I was excited to try it because I enjoy “meta” games, and the premise interested me. My gameplay experience left me feeling somewhat ambivalent.
If you like games that focus on creative design, thought-provoking narratives, walking simulators, and being told a story, then you will probably enjoy this game. Be advised, if you are looking for something similar to The Stanley Parable, you will NOT find that here. This is literally a walking simulator that tells you a story for approximately 1.5 hours. Also, while I normally try not to mention price, I do not feel that the current $10.99 CAD is justified – perhaps half or even 75% of that amount would be more appropriate. Where I live, that is about the same cost for a movie ticket, but after playing, I would personally wait until this one hit the discount day (cheap Tuesdays). Hopefully you were able to snag this on the recent Humble Bundle (HB Indie Bundle 17).
One thing I’d like to add before continuing – many of the reviews you will read paint this game as being “pretentious,” however, I feel that this is not the case. Although the ending felt awkward to me, it was still very powerful.
The aesthetics are decent and standard of your old-school Counter-Strike-era titles (the games showcased were all created using the Source engine). Beginner’s Guide is narrated by Davey Wreden, the mastermind behind The Stanley Parable (both the original Half-Life 2 mod and standalone game), who does an excellent job of drawing in your attention and interest. The narrative is the product you are purchasing – it has heavy “meta” themes and offers insight into game design as a form of artful expression (which I agree with). This recurring theme is given to you very, very well – there was a specific part where I realized I was being judgmental based only on information given by the narrator. When I caught myself, I felt good and bad at the same time (like when you first realize that character POVs in books like Game of Thrones are not always reliable).
Controls are very simple – the game is purely storytelling placed on top of a walking simulator. There are no puzzles or a difficulty since everything is linear.
Gameplay consists – you guessed it – of you walking around, exploring different levels of varying games while Davey tells you a story. For me, there was one part that I found rather cringe-y, but I can see how that specific scene would be powerful to others. The game is peppered nicely with intelligent lines that dig into your humanity (ex: “maybe he just liked. . .”), and anyone who enjoys creative design for anything – not just games – should enjoy this story.
Overall, if you do not mind the price (or get it on a discount), I think exploring Beginner’s Guide is worth your time. Approach it with an open mind and really think about the story. Something I enjoyed seeing is the amount of fan theories that have been proposed since this game was released. Davey’s legacy of making people think continues after The Stanley Parable with Beginner’s Guide.
If you like storytelling and the art of creative design, then you should definitely give this game a try.
Recommend!

I'm finally at a point to where I feel like I can leave a fair review for this game.
I'll start with the day one scenario. You load into a world based on a few different spawn points. The weather will be random upon loading in, so depending on a little RNG - you might find yourself in a very bad situation. However, this is a good thing, this lets you know very quickly what your goals are in this game. You have to stay alive.
The game doesn't hold your hand for the most part, and you have to be able to think on your feet, and make life and death decisions on a daily basis. You're contending with the weather, hunger, thirst, and your overall "health" - which can change based on injury and various other ailments.
The only RNG I have really seen in the game is when it comes to weather, loot placement; which loot does NOT respawn in game, so you must use it wisely/strategically, and things that require a skill - such as lighting a fire, or repairing an object. The more you do a skill based task, the more skill you gain in doing so, much like real life. This is perfect because it means that you won't die simply due to RNG.
There is plenty of content to see in game, especially with the added maps (for free!). The free maps they added also allow you to transition from one map to the next, you're free to go back and forth as you please. This gives you the ability to setup a base in one map, then move to a whole other map once you feel like you've depleted the resources on your first map. And there is a sense of wanting to keep your survivor alive for as long as possible. Death is permanent, and when it does happen, it's very upsetting - but it also leaves you retracing your steps that led up to it. You learn from your deaths, and you learn what mistakes to not repeat.
I haven't experienced any game breaking bugs, and only a few minor crashes (2 in nearly 20hrs of play time). I have to recommend this game because it has everything; solid mechanics, good loot, nice graphics, minimal bugs, tons of content, and it's actually a survival game.
I'm going to end this review with a little comparison if you will. The issue I have with other games in my library is that they market themselves as survival games, when in fact they are open world sandbox games with a couple survival mechanics thrown in. This game isn't about building fancy houses, it's literally about staying alive. You're not going to be crafting guns out of soda cans and a few nuts and bolts laying around. You won't be taming dinosaurs, or fighting cannibals with an Emergency Hatchet. You will be moving from location to location trying to gather enough supplies to keep you alive for another day.
The balance is very fair, and there is a lot of realism to the game. Yes, it's still just a game at the end of the day, so they had to account for that with some elements of game-play (otherwise no one would survive a week), but for the most part they kept it as realistic as possible.
If you're looking for a solid survival game, that focuses on actually surving - then I don't think you'll find a better game. If you're tired of "survival" games where you're stuck crafting up a tech tree, constantly building bases, and walking around with no purpose, then this is the game for you.
TL;DR
Solid mechanics.
No RNG deaths.
Several maps that all connect in game.
True sense of survival.
Highly recommended if you're looking for a real survival game.
Excellent, fun, absorbing game.

It's a challenging game with a couple twists on what calls itself a "shooter". The RPG elements are well-known, "plasmids" which give superpowers and the ability to upgrade weapons and craft items.
The game is buggy and has design flaws.
Critisisms:
-EVE which powers plasmids, runs out very quickly, and ammo is sparse, so you might be down to a wrench to smack super-soldiers with. "EVE Saver" doesn't help much.
-Objects like turrets and cameras can be hacked, but sometimes the hack is impossible geometrically, which is very frustrating, especially considering the punishment to hacking: you get zapped and damaged and/or alarms set off and robots attack you for a full minute, which is a bit too long.
-The game is a bit long, with a lot of running around the same areas over and over again.
-The plotline is very complicated, even granting that it's meant to be so.
-Targetting: the targetting system for NPCs is very flawed. Allies will only attack an enemy after they've been attacked by you (which ruins the point of an ally), or they've already attacked you.
-Buggy: there are interface bugs which can become very frustrating, for example, every time you get a new plasmid, the slots are mixed up, so in fast-paced combat, you can easily fire the wrong plasmid and die as a result. When you assign a new plasmid, it offsets others and mixes the slots. FIX: cycle through each slot, placing a dummy plasmid in a slot, then the appropriate one for each slot sequentially, this usually places them in the right spot.
Good parts:
-Low penalty for death: you revive at half life, half EVE to a nearby Vita station, within which you cannot be attacked. So how challenging this game is is diffused by dying not being a huge set-back.
-Challenging: enemies move unnaturally and turrets will kill you very quickly. A bit of critisism in that the turrets seem to kill you way faster than others.
-Good storyline: the narritive is interesting and suspenceful, while overly complicated. Some big moments in the plot are a bit unsatisfying, but arguably for narritive reason.
Minor things:
-Gatherer's Gardens and Gene Banks need to be one thing, expecially with the bug of slotting, where if you buy and slot a new plasmid it screws the hotkeys up until you can find a gene bank.
-RESCUE THE GIRLS, DON'T HARVEST.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second of two standalone expansions that Gearbox developed for Half-Life. Like Opposing Force, you won't be playing as Gordon Freeman in this one. Instead, you'll be seeing the Black Mesa Incident from the point of view of Barney Calhoun, a security guard who you may already know if you played Half-Life 2 first.
The thing to know about Blue Shift is that aside from having its own campaign, it adds absolutely nothing. No new weapons, in fact less than either of the previous iterations. No new enemies, again less than Opposing Force. You don't even get a new boss fight. On top of all that, it's short, only three hours (or less).
The one thing Blue Shift adds is the High Definition pack, which overhauls (some) models and textures and can be applied to both Half-Life and Opposing Force. It does a decent job of bringing Half-Life's looks up to standards (for 2001), but some dislike the changes it makes to certain things unnecessarily. Some say it changes the feel of Half-Life. I wouldn't go that far, although there was literally no reason to change the MP5 to an M16. Some might like it, some might not.
Seems like I'm pretty hard on Blue Shift, and it's true, when it was released a lot of people hated it. Having said all that, Blue Shift isn't bad, per se. It's basically just more Half-Life. One thing, I don't know if this was just me, but one of the interesting things about Blue Shift is that while Hard Mode in Half-Life meant that you were never going to have enough health, Blue Shift's hard mode seems to extend that to ammo. That means that until you start fighting marines later in the game, it almost feels like a survival horror game. This is very enjoyable, and adds a difference of feel from Shephard or Freeman as playable characters.
Blue Shift isn't bad, it just isn't much. I wouldn't say it's worth buying on its own, but if you buy it with the Anthology pack, it's a decent extra.

Plane crashed in the Canadian wilderness.  It was snowing pretty bad and I was getting cold.   Saw a lookout tower on the hill.  Climbed up and got inside.  Was really hoping to find a hatchet, but nope, nothing there.   Got warm and then left.  Found some train tracks which led to a house.  Nice big house that I could've stayed in for a while, but there was no hatchet.  Decided to keep looking.  Found some ice huts and went fishing.  Caught 3 fish.   A bear must have smelt my fish because he started wandering around the hut.   Bear got bored and left.
Headed back to train tracks and walked.  Got chased by a wolf.  Climbed on top of a fallen train car.  Wolf walked away, but another showed up.  Had to wait for it to get bored and leave.
Kept walking and found a dam.  Entered into it and it was dark as night.  I heard something moving.  Another wolf.  I got into a corner and put a lantern in front of me.  The wolf came in, but got scared of the light.  I hear it go downstairs and then yelp and everything goes quiet.  I go to sleep.
Wake up next day and and find dead wolf at bottom of the stairs.  Guess he tripped and broke his neck.  I don't know.  I explore and and get supplies and try to warm up a bit.  In hind sight I should've take the time to repair my clothes.  I exit the lower part of the dam only to find a blizzard and I'm locked out.  I rush down the hill where, of course, there is a wolf waiting for me.  I run.  Not sure what happened, but the wolf fell over and died.  Maybe it was too cold?
Found a cave where I could warm up a bit, but I was running low on food.  Couldn't really get the warmth/rest i wanted.  Exited into some high winds.
Found an ice fishing shack down the road a bit. Did I mention I now have hypothermia? Tried to get some wood, but I was tired and almost falling asleep gathering it.  Fired up the stove and slept for 3 hours before I ran out of firewood and nearly out of food.  Time to go exploring.
Found a park bench with a hatchet!  Yes!  But incredibly tired and its starting to get dark.  Walk down the road and my vision is getting blurry.  Storm starts up again and I can't see very well, plus I'm about to fall asleep and I'm freezing and can hear my heart pounding as if I'm about to die.  Decided to try to light a fire, outside, during a blizzard, in the middle of the road.  I get it started and start to warm a bit.  I decided to try to sleep for an hour, but I can't because its too cold.  I walk to the fire to add some wood and I fall over and land on top of it and burned to death.
TL;DR   Went to Canada, got hypothermia and burned to death.

Well, if you like the call of arcade driving coupled with skating on very thin ice, then fallout 2 is the game for you.
Dated by todays standards, this driving game still hits the grade through the insane use of its own game physics. While other games have you concentrating on the perfect cornering speed, flatout 2 has you holding on for dear life just to stay on the track. If it wasnt bad enough that the AI are hell bent on killing you it seems the scenery is in on act too so be warned every laps a white knuckle affair. To fuel this further the game has some weird trates like for instance making you a magnet to every piece of crap on the track including enemy AI from time to time or instant slowing down in certain one on one clashes.
The graphics is what you would expect for its age so polished reflections gleeming off the hood of your ride arent on the menu but with a game hellbent at keeping you off the track, besides the begininng of any race your hardly likely to care let alone notice after the first hour.
The AI is unbalanced which you will notice through their use of what appears as an inexhaustable supply of nitros
and IF THAT WASNT BAD ENOUGH, theirs seems to work better than yours too.
Choice of ride varies although the game really calls for a balance of speed and strength and heaven help the player that chooses the top ride (street events unlockable car) for a dirt track (seriously funny affair to be tried).
You also get mini stunt games further abusing the physics as you rag doll your driver from one event to the next and in some cases quite literally.

All in all i had as much fun with it this time as i did when it first came out and although not the most challenging game in terms of events is definitely worth the purchase in a steam sale if you fancy a cheap laugh.

After extensive playing of Edge of Space since the release I decided to rewrite my review.
Pros:
Sci-fi setting with a good intro video explaining why you are on a planet that’s hostile and heck bent on killing you.
I love the sci-fi graphics, and the look of the broken planet landscape.
Excellent array of items to craft, in fact, the list is HUGE, including three different sets of armor (each with their own upgrade tree), all kinds of different weapon types, and a lot of other things that give my love of farming resources, and collecting new, interesting bits and pieces, a lot of reasons to feel content.
A very large selection of base building decorations, workstations, defenses, etc. And yes, the advanced items require extensive farming and playing the game to gather enough resources to make, which some might feel is grindy, but I feel motivates me to keep exploring and mining for “a few more minutes” and then turns out to be two-three hours of game time I didn’t even know slipped by when I glance at the clock.
I’ve heard a lot of negatives about the user interface, but personally I see nothing wrong with it, and you can see it demonstrated in action via screen-shots, youtube videos, and streams, so it’s not like the developers are trying to hide something… If it doesn’t interfere with my game-play and fun, I don’t see how it’s a problem.
Lots of biomes, and mobbies, and some good humorous moments.
Tons of new areas to explore, and lots to keep you busy.
Developers that are getting the kinks worked out as fast as possible, and they are very active and responsive in the forums begging those with issues to send them logs so they can fix any issues for everybody else.
I’ve put a ton of time in and I am thoroughly enjoying myself, because I find the game both extensive and challenging.
I myself haven’t crashed even once, and though I experience lag here and there it only happens for me after playing for several hours straight. My computer is an Asus Rog Gaming Laptop, win 10, and I have an nvidia card.
The mini patches since 1.0 hit have improved the game a lot, in my opinion.
Active Devs that really want this game to succeed and are willing to do whatever it takes — though they get knocked around a lot by players that seem unwilling to give them time to hear and fix any issues that might be present…
Cons:
The Lead Dev has said the game was designed more for multiplayer, so mobs tend to spawn in waves that can overwhelm a single playing character… After reading that bit of info, I was sad, because I look at these games as something I wish to spend a lot of time with soloing. Like in Terraria when I played with a friend he wanted to kill this boss, and that boss, and I wanted to just find resources. I never played with anyone again, though once I got to Moon Lord I lost interest, because I realized that fight wasn’t balanced for single player at all (my opinion).
EOS needs some patches to iron out the kinks, and I bet my life SO WILL Terraria Otherworld when it’s released. Even Terraria has had at least a half dozen mini patches since 1.3 hit, and I don’t see anyone knocking Terraria for it… And Starbound will continue to see many updates and patches before and after its 1.0 version hits… Whenever that might happen — sooner than later, me hopes!
Players rush to leave negative feedback, rather than logging the problem and helping the Devs get a handle on it. They have asked and asked for player input via logs, but some grumpy, unhelpful players would rather sink their chance at sales than help get the game working perfectly for everyone.
The game is extensive and resource gathering takes a long, long time. And some ingredients are very hard to find and farm — like Penguin parts and even Headhunter parts, and though I love to farm resources, even I wish these dropped more often…
Sometimes things feel unfair, unbalanced, such as weapon upgrades that don’t do much to make you feel like the mobbies are being hurt… I swear there was a penguin laughing at me at a Penguin Rave — it was hysterical, this little penguin dancing at a Rave as I’m shooting him, pew pew for half a minute…
It seems New Players find the beginning confusing, and perhaps because the game is so extensive more time should have been put into a longer, more engaging tutorial, with an option to skip it for more advanced players…
Final thoughts:
Personally I’m enjoying my time in the game, and though I have a large library, it keeps pulling me back with that one more node feeling, and I wake up excited to play and find new areas and new upgrades, etc. Some might not like gathering, farming games, and if the game is balanced around MP, I think MP should have been a bigger priority, as I believe a lot of complaints have stemmed from the MP community, AND I feel us solo players might not find the game as satisfying in the later stages, if the game really cannot be completed single player (which I’ve no idea if it can or cannot, but I’m hoping!!!)

Sunless Sea is a game in which you, a starting zea captain, zail the Sea Where the Sun Doesn't Shine, discovering the scary but intriguing lovecraftian world of Sunless sea. Sunless sea is most likely one of the most intriguing games that I have ever played. The world and the writing are just so alluring and well made, and the few but well placed pictures support the narrative greatly. The world isn't ruined by showing too much; the game allows you to imagine the far-away places that you have heard on your travels. On the other hand the game's combat system isn't bad but it certainly isn't very good. It can get pretty boring when you understand its flaws and start to abuse them. Other than that, the game packs a very deep feeling of unknown and distress when you zail the Sunless Sea for the first times. I also like how the game punishes you for making mistakes. At zea, you have many resources to pay attention to and balance out, and if you fail at that you'll die. Furthermore, there are many hazards roaming the zea that prove to be dangerous adversaries for the inexperienced. The Fallen London isn't the only cradle of civilization in Sunless Sea; there are many more ports and mystical places to explore, such as the London's eternal rival, the Khanate and the bountiful but dangerous lands of the  Elder continent.
If you are looking for a review rating, I'd give this game a 9/10, since the writing and narrative just make up for the most of the flaws of Sunless Sea. Happy zailing, captains.

TL;DR: Game effectively abandoned, used to have potential but developers failed to adapt to criticisms and appear to have dropped the project. Starbound offers better exploration and a proper story (albeit super linear) while Terraria offers more interesting combat and a more rewarding grind (even though I don't care for grind myself).
Some history:
Game offered some cool features when it came out. Felt like Terraria on space steroids. However it quickly became apparent that the developers were missing some pieces to the puzzle for creating the whole game experience, as they were experimenting with different formulas that became more and more restrictive and further from the initial impression I got when I first played. The same thing happened with Starbound, they took a really free and open world with exploration and turned it into a linear progression system which people do. not. want. in this genre. Oxygen Not Included seems to have a much better formula (I watched my friend play it yesterday and it was fun even to watch).
I was initially strongly attracted to Edge of Space because it offered much better movement and maneuvering than Terraria, which is honestly a fairly grindy endeavor to play through with fresh characters. Top that off with a tech system that doesn't require exploring dozens of worlds like Starbound and I felt like I had a winner. HOWEVER the base building was not thought out much beyond "like Terraria" and I don't recall enjoying combat at any point. The atmosphere was pretty cool though, I do wish it had the support it deserved and I still feel like there is a good game buried in here. It WAS fun for the first few hours I played!

I tried Sunless Sea on a free weekend. And I'm glad that I tried it.
I've played Fallen London (which is the companion browser-based game), and I've played other Rogue-Likes (NetHack, FTL). Rogue-Likes have never really appealed to me, but I wondered if Sunless Sea might pull me in thanks to the storytelling.
It didn't.
The stories are interesting, and so is the artwork. It's a very compelling game, but not one that I enjoyed playing. Even the short time that I played it was very trying.
What bothered me the most, however, was the UI. I have a 15.6" display, running at FHD. I couldn't quite get the size of the fonts or windows right, so that it was readable, but didn't cover up the game window, and still looked good.
I think I'll stick to playing big, dumb games, with big dumb graphics that hit me with "fun" right out the door. As nice as Sunless Sea is, I can't muster the patience to play it on my short playing squirts.

Being a great supporter of Red Orchestra Ostfront, and Red Orchestra: Combined Arms (mod) I was very hyped about RO:HOS. How could Tripwire go wrong, now with an even better budget. Well, much to my dismay they f*cked it up.
Now, I cannot recomment this game at its current state, and likely the state that will remain from now on. Tripwire has failed us with the so called realism of this game. Instead they adopted a Call of Duty faster pace combat with level ups and mixed it with a touch of realistic creativity.
First, your run speed. Its very fast! you have no problems getting around. The sense of weight is missing. No sound that even slightly indicates you are carrying a load of any sort. Again, this is completely apart from the RO1 scheme. where running and gunning often meant certain death, and sprinting was only available for a short brief of which would affect your over all acuracy. (yeah in RO2, being winded no longer affects your ability to aim! yeah REALISM ISNT IT?!)
Combat fatigue; IN Ro1 there was a great sense of self preservation. BUllets whizzed by with a sharp snap and your vision would become blurry. Machinegunners doing their job.
In RO2, well.. this is somewhat missing. The System has been succeeded by a colorblind supression. You visions doubles and you cant see♥♥♥♥♥♥ the bullets snap are muted and feinted.  You no longer fear bullets and you dont care about taking  cover. you just find it annoying.
Graphics, this area I can give Tripwire a break. It looks fairly good. You cringe at some of the scenery that is obviously 2d Like some background, and every now and then objects you get in contact with such as  trees. really. 2D trees (in 2015! WTF!?). Metals look rusted, leather looks... leathery, snow looks like a white carpet. Its a hit and miss in the graphics department but overall it looks good. specially the weapon animation and design.
Community. Alot of people still play so you will have no problems finding a server with players to shoot at. The problem isnt population. Its diversity. There are hardly any community created maps in circulation. Not that they arent making them, but as many Admins claim; whenever they get a custom map into circulation it  crashes the servers. This has led to mostly official maps only in the server browser. They are not well made and they get old fast. Sorry Tripwire, but what evere happened to the amazing map design of your previous games? really.
Sound. aye... this is where the game suffers the most. your foot steps sound like a 5 year walking. Gun shots sound weak  and arent loud. Do not expect BF4 style of gunshots. Explosions are extremely muted. WTF? Tank engines sound like lawnmowers and the scout biplanes.. well they sound. TERRIBLE! while the sound department is lacking at least Tripwire was generous enough to add german and russian voices the game characters (after so much feedback from the community about Germans and Russians speaking accented english)
Gameplay. Prepare your♥♥♥♥♥♥for the meat grinder of your life. most matches are about defending or attacking. because the speed of characters and vulnerability to bullets it makes the gameplay a little too straight forward and fast. In turn, the attacking team ussually rushes and the defending team mowes them down. rinse and repeat. This created a lack of tactical gameplay with little strategy to go about. teamwork is not as essential as it was in Red Orchestra: Ostfront. im sorry to say and I have to agree that most of us Veterans to the series are disappointed by this lackluster.
Thats not to say that this game offers some fun now and then, but the reason that alot of us RO veterans dislike Ro2 is because all the broken promises, sound quality, gameplay mechanics and maps. what kind of people like this game? hard to say. I'd say those who like a cross between Call Of Duty and Arma II. theres some realism, but it was obviously not in Tripwires plan to fully complement it as it was in previous RO games.
Cannot recomend to the Fast paced Call of Duty players and not to the Realism seekers of Arma III.

I had my doubts whether Cuphead would've been the kind of game that revolved largely around its style, but it quickly became clear that the devs really know what makes for an engaging and high-quality boss fight.
So much thought was put into the bosses, consistently! The patterns are almost all of the time reasonable due to careful timing and clear audiovisual telegraphing, but damn...the amount of creativity crammed into these fights is second to none:
1) Aesthetically beautiful battles, but also how the team ran with an theme and made a given boss attacks (or the way the fight unfolds) feel cohesive.
2) Finding the time to cram in all kinds of gags or referential nods throughout the whole thing without it interrupting the flow of the fight or without relying on the same gimmicks.
3) Fights feel fresh from beginning to end.
Cuphead is a legitimately impressive game. Adding the run & gun stages and the sublime 30's jazz soundtrack is just the icing on the cake.
Couldn't recommend it enough: "MUST HAVE" game.

Watching trailers and the gameplay of others allows me to say that this seems like a good game. However my personal experience of playing it does not allow me to say that it is. Now before I list the issues I have I will say that it could very well just be my copy. So don't judge the game just by this review. And I may as well say that it is not an issue with my computer as it is highly capable of playing this game flawlessly.
We'll start with the controls. Straight away there doesn't seem to be a way to allocate key bindings. While fine for some it does mean that you cannot customize it to fit your own personal play style. This also extends to a controller. While the controller does work (well sometimes but I'll get to that) there is actually no way of showing what buttons does what on the title screen like it does for the keyboard. So for someone using a controller the entire game at the start is simply a trial and error experiment. Resulting in the occasional loss of arrows.
And then sometimes the buttons on the controller don't do what they are supposed. e.g, Often taking several attempts to knock an arrow. This is a very frustrating factor.
There is also a major sound bug. 9/10 times I start the game, there is no sound and I have to quit out and keep trying until the sound decides it wants to be a thing. Adjusting the various volume sliders in the options menu has zero effect.
What hurts my progress the most though is, no matter what the graphics settings, I can not spend more than 10 minutes maximum in game before it crashes. And when you already have to re-open it several times just for the sound to work, it quickly becomes more effort than it is worth to play it. As stated in the beggining it is not an issue with the computer as it can run, very smoothly, games that require far higher specs. Plus as stated it crashes regardless of graphical settings so that is not a factor.
So from my experience it is just totally buggy and basically unplayable. Which is a shame as I liked the idea of this game and really wanted to give it a go. I would like to say that there is a very high chance that it is not the game's fault in a general view. More, I believe, I just ended up with a really broken and buggy copy. Considering the game is free, it's not a cause of anger, as there is no waste of money. It just is a dissapointment that I can't experience it fully.
So while I would like to recommend this game (based upon the trailers and the gameplay of others) I unfortunatly have to go by my own personal playing experience and say that I do not recommend it.

The Long Dark an amazing game which some how creates the perfect combination of growing bleak despair mingled with courageous hope. From the very get go I found myself fighting against the harsh unforgiving elements of nature. I had to do my best to survive from snow blinding blizzards blasting against my body quickly robbing it of what warmth it was maintaining as I sought shelter. What a feeling of salvation and relief as I with exhausted body and wracked mind suddenly came across a cabin in the distance.
Surviving in this world where a global natural disaster has occured is unrelenting brutality yet very rewarding when one comes across something precious such as food to keep ones daily calorie count high enough to stay healthy. Using tools and utensils can make the difference between salvaging all the meat possible from a frozen deer using an an axe or getting less meat out of it using other tools and downright impossible bare handed if more than 50% frozen.
Gathering wood for fires to stay warm is a must as I had to weigh the benefits of picking up smalls sticks of wood or take the time to break down some branches into smaller pieces which meant being exposed to the heat draining health damaging freezing cold for a longer period. Stay out in the cold long enough and it will sap ones strength making movement harder as well as slower reducing my chances of getting back to a place of shelter.
I have to constantly balance what I have making sure not to use up all my current supplies too fast or else risk not having things like fire wood to use when a fierce blizzard makes it impossible to step outside to gather more.
The voiced female and male characters are done splendidly with intensely beliveable execution of their lines making me feel empathy and compassion for what they are going through pushing me to do my best to make them survive. When my characters died from the many dangers of The Long Dark such as freezing to death due to hyperthermia, starving to death from lack of food and water,being ripped apart by starving wolves or a protective grizzly bear, bleeding to death from untended wounds, infection, illness, exhaustion from lack of sleep etc I truly felt their loss as the grim death screen in shocking red letters appeared in all its finality.
Graphics and audio come together like some grand convergence of Feng Shui energies to create a stunning haunting vast visceral vibrant living world. A world where howling winds are heard as I struggle to stay warm in a cabin while salvaging what supplies I can from it as neon blue beams of light shine in from windows informing me night is approaching with its bitter cold kiss. A world where the pitter patter of feet startles me in surprise as I think a wolf is about to pounce on me only to turn and find out its a small rabbit or deer racing by sometimes with a wolf hot on their heels. A world where waking up in the pitch black dark of early morning gives a sense of intense isolation where i desire to see the light of a beautiful sunrise as quickly as possible if just to inspire me with the thought I survived to begin a new day. A world where the howling of distant wolves gives me a feeling of dread of possibly being their next meal and sadness that they struggle as I do.
Game mechanics totally deliver with just enough realism to keep things fun and tense but not tedious and tiring. Calories have to be watched to keep things in the healthy count of 2000 with each food type giving a certain amount of calories.
Wood can be gathered from the wilderness or broken down from furniture to use for fires along with books,news papers. Some wood allows fire to burn for longer periods of time. When attacked by animals I may suffer from wounds which can lead to infection or death from loss of blood etc. A misstep traveling on a hilly area may cause me a broken ankle thus slowing down my movement which can mean the difference between life and death especially if already suffering from exhaustion and hyperthermia. Avoiding dehydration can be done by drinking beverages or melting snow which in turn needs to be boiled to be safe to drink. Water purification tablets can also be used to avoid getting sick.Cooking and drinking tea promotes rest and healing.
Hyperthermia once gotten I had to stay inside for a day or two avoiding the blistering numbing cold until I was well enough to go for a supply run, hunting for food etc. This of course meant making sure I had enough food and wood during this time not to mention combustible items like matches and fuel to start a fire and cook. This is but a small look at all the many wonderful survival game mechanics The Long Dark has.
THE LONG DARK a glistening diamond of a game which will satisfy like no other game while making one appreciate the friendships, comforts and joys of life.

I find this to be a very entertaining game, although frustrating at times.  I have now spent several hours playing and would recommend this game to others.  That said, there are a few things which I would like to see added to the game.
First, although the monetary value of each train tends to tell you something about the length of the train, I would like to be able to see a profile for each train before I release it from its station.  If I were to design the profile I would provide information regarding the total length of the train in number of cars.  Further, I would like to know the top speed of the locomotive so as to compare the top speeds of every locomotive currently waiting to be released from a station.  Added to that, it appears that most of the trains have the same top speed, despite the number of cars being pulled by the locomotive.  I know that there are a couple of different locomotives, but I do not know when a different locomotive is hitched to a load.  If the locomotive is random, I would like the profile to list its top speed under different loads.
Second, it appears that trains are ready to leave random stations at random times.  If this is indeed random, I would like a queue added which tells me in which order the waiting trains were introduced so as to help me decide which trains should be released in which order.  Further, trains do not stack in their railyards, so two trains cannot be waiting to be released at one time.  Instead, if another train is about to be added to a station, you receive a sudden five second warning and the first train is automatically relased.  If trains can only sit waiting to be released for a designated period of time, I would like to see a timer added into the queue so I know how much time is left before a train automatically disembarks.
If, however, trains are not random and a schedule truly does exist, I would like to have access to this schedule so I know when a train will be ready to leave a station, and where it needs to go.  It could even be the case that a single train could be required to visit multiple stations as opposed to a single station.
I believe that these additions could both simplify and introduce difficulty as more planning is possible and required.

I'm finally at a point to where I feel like I can leave a fair review for this game.
I'll start with the day one scenario. You load into a world based on a few different spawn points. The weather will be random upon loading in, so depending on a little RNG - you might find yourself in a very bad situation. However, this is a good thing, this lets you know very quickly what your goals are in this game. You have to stay alive.
The game doesn't hold your hand for the most part, and you have to be able to think on your feet, and make life and death decisions on a daily basis. You're contending with the weather, hunger, thirst, and your overall "health" - which can change based on injury and various other ailments.
The only RNG I have really seen in the game is when it comes to weather, loot placement; which loot does NOT respawn in game, so you must use it wisely/strategically, and things that require a skill - such as lighting a fire, or repairing an object. The more you do a skill based task, the more skill you gain in doing so, much like real life. This is perfect because it means that you won't die simply due to RNG.
There is plenty of content to see in game, especially with the added maps (for free!). The free maps they added also allow you to transition from one map to the next, you're free to go back and forth as you please. This gives you the ability to setup a base in one map, then move to a whole other map once you feel like you've depleted the resources on your first map. And there is a sense of wanting to keep your survivor alive for as long as possible. Death is permanent, and when it does happen, it's very upsetting - but it also leaves you retracing your steps that led up to it. You learn from your deaths, and you learn what mistakes to not repeat.
I haven't experienced any game breaking bugs, and only a few minor crashes (2 in nearly 20hrs of play time). I have to recommend this game because it has everything; solid mechanics, good loot, nice graphics, minimal bugs, tons of content, and it's actually a survival game.
I'm going to end this review with a little comparison if you will. The issue I have with other games in my library is that they market themselves as survival games, when in fact they are open world sandbox games with a couple survival mechanics thrown in. This game isn't about building fancy houses, it's literally about staying alive. You're not going to be crafting guns out of soda cans and a few nuts and bolts laying around. You won't be taming dinosaurs, or fighting cannibals with an Emergency Hatchet. You will be moving from location to location trying to gather enough supplies to keep you alive for another day.
The balance is very fair, and there is a lot of realism to the game. Yes, it's still just a game at the end of the day, so they had to account for that with some elements of game-play (otherwise no one would survive a week), but for the most part they kept it as realistic as possible.
If you're looking for a solid survival game, that focuses on actually surving - then I don't think you'll find a better game. If you're tired of "survival" games where you're stuck crafting up a tech tree, constantly building bases, and walking around with no purpose, then this is the game for you.
TL;DR
Solid mechanics.
No RNG deaths.
Several maps that all connect in game.
True sense of survival.
Highly recommended if you're looking for a real survival game.

Yeah, when this game was in EA it was a little rough around the edges, but it was still a game, which I can say is more than most can say at this point, but it's out and 1.0. Does it still have a few rough spots? Sure, but what game doesn't on initial release, but they are working hard on it, to fix what is going on, and are very connected with the community giving us regular updates on whats up.
The game is built around the idea of exploration, terraforming and expansion. Each of which is handled very well.
The experience system that has been added in replacing the old way of researching is MUCH better and a welcome addition, as is all the UI cleanup that has been done.
One thing I love about this game is there is nothing you pick up that is completely worthless (except building structure tiles if you don't plan to build with them). You can use Dirt, Stone, Biomass, jelly, shark stuff, to make guns, armor, jetpacks, tools and ammo.
The Game is deep, and has more content in it than I will ever have time to discover, but for those of you whom have enjoyed Terraria, Starbound and Crea this is a welcome addition to the collection.
Like I said, it's not a perfect game, but it still a heck of a lot of fun, I'd give it a 8/10.
(Also be very warry of the negative reviews, most were done while it was in EA and a lot has changed since then, or many have been posted since it went live, but they have 0.0 hours of play time since it has.)

Being a great supporter of Red Orchestra Ostfront, and Red Orchestra: Combined Arms (mod) I was very hyped about RO:HOS. How could Tripwire go wrong, now with an even better budget. Well, much to my dismay they f*cked it up.
Now, I cannot recomment this game at its current state, and likely the state that will remain from now on. Tripwire has failed us with the so called realism of this game. Instead they adopted a Call of Duty faster pace combat with level ups and mixed it with a touch of realistic creativity.
First, your run speed. Its very fast! you have no problems getting around. The sense of weight is missing. No sound that even slightly indicates you are carrying a load of any sort. Again, this is completely apart from the RO1 scheme. where running and gunning often meant certain death, and sprinting was only available for a short brief of which would affect your over all acuracy. (yeah in RO2, being winded no longer affects your ability to aim! yeah REALISM ISNT IT?!)
Combat fatigue; IN Ro1 there was a great sense of self preservation. BUllets whizzed by with a sharp snap and your vision would become blurry. Machinegunners doing their job.
In RO2, well.. this is somewhat missing. The System has been succeeded by a colorblind supression. You visions doubles and you cant see♥♥♥♥♥♥ the bullets snap are muted and feinted.  You no longer fear bullets and you dont care about taking  cover. you just find it annoying.
Graphics, this area I can give Tripwire a break. It looks fairly good. You cringe at some of the scenery that is obviously 2d Like some background, and every now and then objects you get in contact with such as  trees. really. 2D trees (in 2015! WTF!?). Metals look rusted, leather looks... leathery, snow looks like a white carpet. Its a hit and miss in the graphics department but overall it looks good. specially the weapon animation and design.
Community. Alot of people still play so you will have no problems finding a server with players to shoot at. The problem isnt population. Its diversity. There are hardly any community created maps in circulation. Not that they arent making them, but as many Admins claim; whenever they get a custom map into circulation it  crashes the servers. This has led to mostly official maps only in the server browser. They are not well made and they get old fast. Sorry Tripwire, but what evere happened to the amazing map design of your previous games? really.
Sound. aye... this is where the game suffers the most. your foot steps sound like a 5 year walking. Gun shots sound weak  and arent loud. Do not expect BF4 style of gunshots. Explosions are extremely muted. WTF? Tank engines sound like lawnmowers and the scout biplanes.. well they sound. TERRIBLE! while the sound department is lacking at least Tripwire was generous enough to add german and russian voices the game characters (after so much feedback from the community about Germans and Russians speaking accented english)
Gameplay. Prepare your♥♥♥♥♥♥for the meat grinder of your life. most matches are about defending or attacking. because the speed of characters and vulnerability to bullets it makes the gameplay a little too straight forward and fast. In turn, the attacking team ussually rushes and the defending team mowes them down. rinse and repeat. This created a lack of tactical gameplay with little strategy to go about. teamwork is not as essential as it was in Red Orchestra: Ostfront. im sorry to say and I have to agree that most of us Veterans to the series are disappointed by this lackluster.
Thats not to say that this game offers some fun now and then, but the reason that alot of us RO veterans dislike Ro2 is because all the broken promises, sound quality, gameplay mechanics and maps. what kind of people like this game? hard to say. I'd say those who like a cross between Call Of Duty and Arma II. theres some realism, but it was obviously not in Tripwires plan to fully complement it as it was in previous RO games.
Cannot recomend to the Fast paced Call of Duty players and not to the Realism seekers of Arma III.

Cuphead is a great game. Not a perfect one, but a really really great one.
Controls feel tight, but you might want to rebind some of the key maps to something that feels more comfortable (personally, I had to move the dash to spacebar so that my hand wasn't splayed so awkwardly on the keyboard). Honestly, the core gameplay itself is very well polished and top-tier.
Cuphead suffers from two issues:
1) Level design could be better;
Cuphead has very spotty level design; issues like on one of the first bosses in world 2, whose second stage has certain enemies who can spawn on top of the character with no telegraph. This leads to situations where whole portions of the screen are basically "danger zones," especially if you're playing for A+ grades where getting hit once means you need to restart. This isn't an issue in EVERY level, but when it is an issue it'll bother you for a good long time till you beat that boss/level.
2) The developer's chose graphic consistency over graphic utility;
One of Cuphead's biggest draws is its one-of-a-kind artstyle. The gameplay is tailored to play around the artstyle, but in certain situations the gameplay takes a backseat to this. An egregious example is a boss where the level is scrolling with the player jumping from platform to platform during the level. The platforms, when spawned, are obscured by the boss so you can't see them for a good quarter of the screen. These should be brought to the front of the screen instead of the back. This is a more conscious decision than the con above.
Overall, Cuphead is a very good game though. Aside from those two cons I provided above, I have nothing else negative to say about the game. I'd rate it a solid 8/10, games like this are very few and far between; this is a game that you'll definitely want to share with your friends.

Though I regard myself as an AVG fan, this is the first modern telltale game Ive ever played. I have totally no idea what this genre has evolved into in the last decade. To get myself started, I picked this one despite its rather mediocre reputation, because I don't wanna have a very high expectation of a critical-acclaimed game like Life is Strange or Wolf among Us and then only to feel disappointed after playing it. Though far from perfection, the game really impressed me.
Character 9/10: Character building has always been what distinguishes Telltale Games and Lucas Arts productions from other AVG games on the market. They do extremely well in this game, especially the villains. The Lady Arkham, Penguin, and Harvey/Two-face really impressed me. But my favorite goes to a "side role" — the Joker. Though he only appears in two scenes, that combination of extreme calmness and insanity portraits the character right out of comics. This is the Joker we seldom see but it is really convincing.
Story 8/10: No spoiler man, rest assured. I grab this game partly because Ive always been a batman fan. After finishing the game, I tried to recall the main plot, only to find the scene having the deepest impression on me is
. The story is rather cliched in my opinion. Of course there are turning points, but nothing much that can really give you a surprise. Compared to the adventures of batman in movies and comics, this one in the game a little bit lackluster. But taking into consideration this is rather a pre-sequel to the seasons to come, it is acceptable.
Graphics 7/10: Just the common TTG style. I have no objection to it but I don't think it appeals to everyone.
Art 7/10: The Catwoman and Joker are superb. Bruce, Al, and Harvey are good. Others are meh. Just personal opinion.
Audio performance 10/10: Brilliant. Cinematic performance.
Gameplay 4/10: You don't buy this game to "play" it right? What adds to the poor gameplay is the fact many choices you make in the game don’t actually have much influence.
Optimization 2/10: This is where I hate most about the game. Run on low graphic quality with Nvidia 980m and the graphic card is often overloaded. Too many lags and glitches during the game.
Catwoman 12/10
For me this game is all about the question on the first line of this review. Who do we really wanna be beneath the mask, Bruce or Batman? The game lets you choose to attend occasions as Bruce or Batman many times, which underscores the topic. Borne with wealth, fame, and his parents death, shall Bruce take on the family's legacy, good and evil, or shake off the burdens of the past and just be the vigilante in the darkness? In former Batman works we take this for granted but this game let us experience the price Bruce has paid to become who he is.
Overall 7.5/10 Must-buy for Batman fans,  especially if you wanna try the second season(looks much better). For other better grab this on discount. The playthrough takes around 10 hrs, a little bit short for the full price.

Outlast is a virtual experience where the story's fabrications induce suspense, haunting horrors, and jump scares. Although, the direction in which the story develops, followed by simple repetitive objectives undermines the greatness this horror game has to offer.
During my 6-hour walkthrough of the main game, the majority of the time, I was screaming or quietly panicking at what could be around the corner, just waiting for me. Whether it was the pure gore, lore-rich journals and notes, or the insane patients within the asylum looking to kill me. Outlast stays true to the horror genre, and like the game’s protagonist, keeps me wanting to find the exit from this insane world the game creates. Furthermore, with fine details such as the bloody footprints your character leaves and being able to see your own body, help with the illusion that you are in the game. However, about 4 hours into the game, or 3 chapters of the story, a majority of devices used to trick the player into feeling directly involved lose this effect. A key component that causes the player to disassociate with Outlast’s story are the continuous story objectives. Whether it be turning valves or finding a key, these objectives bog down the momentum of the player’s escape and make the game feel like a forced tour of the Mount Massive Asylum. Lastly, Outlast’s decision to focus in on the sci-fi components of the lore and ending of the story, creates a confusing and subpar explanation to why the experimentation within the asylum occur.
Despite the elements that underwhelm story development and gameplay, Outlast does a great job at being a horror game. So if you’re looking for something to scare ya, and are not too worried about the game’s story, Outlast is a good game to play.

I find this to be a very entertaining game, although frustrating at times.  I have now spent several hours playing and would recommend this game to others.  That said, there are a few things which I would like to see added to the game.
First, although the monetary value of each train tends to tell you something about the length of the train, I would like to be able to see a profile for each train before I release it from its station.  If I were to design the profile I would provide information regarding the total length of the train in number of cars.  Further, I would like to know the top speed of the locomotive so as to compare the top speeds of every locomotive currently waiting to be released from a station.  Added to that, it appears that most of the trains have the same top speed, despite the number of cars being pulled by the locomotive.  I know that there are a couple of different locomotives, but I do not know when a different locomotive is hitched to a load.  If the locomotive is random, I would like the profile to list its top speed under different loads.
Second, it appears that trains are ready to leave random stations at random times.  If this is indeed random, I would like a queue added which tells me in which order the waiting trains were introduced so as to help me decide which trains should be released in which order.  Further, trains do not stack in their railyards, so two trains cannot be waiting to be released at one time.  Instead, if another train is about to be added to a station, you receive a sudden five second warning and the first train is automatically relased.  If trains can only sit waiting to be released for a designated period of time, I would like to see a timer added into the queue so I know how much time is left before a train automatically disembarks.
If, however, trains are not random and a schedule truly does exist, I would like to have access to this schedule so I know when a train will be ready to leave a station, and where it needs to go.  It could even be the case that a single train could be required to visit multiple stations as opposed to a single station.
I believe that these additions could both simplify and introduce difficulty as more planning is possible and required.

This game took lots of inspiration from Terraria. Developers analyzed flawlesly what is the best about Terraria - the open, proceduraly generated world, great combat system, pixeled but detailed graphics, massive crafting, home building, interesting and very different bosses, etc, and with expert precision took it all out.
The combat system is bad, your greatest enemy are not the very few mobs, but aiming system, reloading and limited energy. The game is far from polished, it looks like beta+, not full release. Graphics are relatively nice and detailed, but for some reason look worse then Terraria. Crafting is on one hand better - you don't search wiki for recipes, but that is the only plus it has. World generation is strange,  on one hand looks completely unnatural, on the other is hard to navigate and the way jetpack is implemented is not helping you. There is no real need to build your home - at best you create long flat terrain to place your factories at.
I could continue, but enough is enough. I Can't recommend this game. Maybe, maybe in a year, if they fix the bugs, mobs, world generation and combat, it will be interesting game. Of course, such complete overhaul is very unlikely.

We've all had that conversation sitting around with friends. "I will survive the zombie apocalypse, I know this with absolute certainty."
Project Zomboid hears your confident boast, and then laughs manically as it smashes your preconceved notions of survival. In recent years we've been treated to a swell of zombie mania. From Dawn of the Dead to Left for Dead, from Walking Dead on print to AMC's terrible adaptation, we seem to have a surplus of zombies in film, TV, print, and games.
The problem with most zombie themed games is they are all a bit narrow in scope. You get some guns, maybe board up a window or two, and shoot for infinity. Project Zomboid takes it to the next level.
You begin life standing in a home with nothing but the clothes on your back and from here you are turned loose on the game's MASSIVE open world. And for a 2D isometric game, the world has a surprising ammount of depth. Time passes, seasons change, incliment weather can even give you a cold. As of the current build (26) there are not yet NPC's so you are utterly alone. No quests, no missions, just you and your plan. And the ammount of freedom is surprising. You want to find some guns and go Rambo? Have at it! Want to stockpile resourses and see how long you can lay low? Give it a shot. You want to build a massive sniper tower to stockpile resourses and go Rambo on zombies from the safety of the third floor bird's nest? Yes you can.
The game is very difficult, as the develepors seem to be striving for realism, but they've also included a sandbox mode if you aim for a more arcade style. There is also "Last Stand" which has two modes, one where you face a constant onslaught and another that is similar to Call of Duty's  Zombies. If you don't feel like remaining in the confines of the rules, the game already has a budding modders community (which the Devs fully support and encourage) and cheating is extremely easy. And you will be tempted to cheat as you can contract the zombie virus, a fatal infection with no cure (in vanilla.)
The game open to many playstyles, multiplayer is being open tested now, I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes sandbox crafting games or zombies.

When this game came out I read a bunch of reviews that said it was Tropico 4 all over again and passed on it as a result.
Boy, was I wrong.
TL;DR at the bottom
Tropico 5 takes everyone's favorite role of "El Presidente" and adds a bunch of fancy new features that really round out the Tropico expereince and take it to the next level.
First off, we have a technology component where Libraries and other buildings help you "discover" new buildings, technology and constituional options.
Secondly, you have a Constitution; which provides a choice between Global perks / mods that affect how you run your Island.
Third, is the concept of "Eras", where we begin in the Colonial Era and Gradually progress into Modern Times.
All in all, what this does is create distinct stages of evolution for your island so you truly feel that your island "changes with the times".
Combined with this new evolutionary aspect is the concept of the Family in the Regime; your leader will have children who all have different personalities. At every election you can ask a Regime member to run in the election in lieu of your original Leader. They can be sent on missions and kidnapped, assassinated or disowned.  They have personalities which you can "upgrade" with money from your Swiss Bank Account to make them more effective as managers as as Regime members.
Also new is the aspect of "managers" where the people running each building can bring a minor perk that you can assign to whichever of your buildings you choose.
All this is wrapped in the same familiar "Tropico" packaging that fans of the series know and love.
So, Long Story Short, though I am glad I grabbed this on sale for $10, this game is MILES more than Tropico 4 was and any fan of the series should pick it up.

I bought this game because I enjoy building train layouts, liked the original Railroad Tycoon way back in the early 90s, and like optimization puzzles.  That's good, because this game hits all those likes of mine to some degree, and I love it for that.
What you do:  you build tracks between stations, and dispatch trains that the game randomly builds (or, you can summon your own in addition to the random ones).  Each scenario is a bit different--goals for specific scenarios don't vary within the scenario, but placement of stations and obstacles do to a degree.  In general, goals are of the variety:  don't crash trains, build X amount of track, make X amount of money, manually summon X amount of trains.  These sound simple, but the land area of each scenario is small and you need to make efficient rail networks in that small space without going bankrupt.
Additional stations appear as the game progresses, so you have to modify your rail network on the fly.  This isn't a surprise after your first scenario, but they are also placed somewhat randomly in a random order, meaning you have to think on the fly.  Thankfully, the game does include a pause button and you should make use of it often.  You direct the trains as you go, throwing switches to put trains on specific paths.  Screw up switching even once, and you may be restarting the scenario if it's a bad enough miss.  :)
Good:  engaging play, certainly not a piece of cake, but not impossible either.  Graphics are clean and perfect for this kind of game.  Music and sounds work well and fit the game.  Bugs are pretty much non-existent.
Meh:  keyboard shortcuts appear to be unlabeled nor identified, and not changeable.  Some of them can wreak havoc with your game.  No ability to save in mid level, and scenarios aren't super quick.
Bad:  Scenarios often have razor thing win margins.  This is not unusual for optimization puzzle games, but can be frustrating if you've never played one before.  So, perhaps this isn't a "bad" thing, as I'd sure not want this changed.  Still, it comes as a warning--not so much to stay away from the game, but don't give up on it too quickly.
Overall:  Highly recommended for those who like optimizing things for fun, designing rail networks in confined spaces, and choo choo trains.  Easily frustrated by puzzles?  Probably not for you.

Very enjoyable railroad building game, with attentive developers willing to listen to the players on possible improvements.
The latest update helped to alleviate the bankruptcy issue, leaving the challenges of actually running the trains and building the tracks the focal point.  Beware! Some trains schedule themselves for departure, and you have to be ready to  handle them, or suffer the consequences.
The overarching victory condition on all levels is to survive. The bullets shown on the right of the screen are optional, and none of them need to be achieved in order to advance to the next level. Those optional bullets are very challenging, and add replayability to the game.
The actual laying of the tracks and placing of the switches is very easy. Faster trains become available as you progress through the level you are playing, but watch out for older, slower trains as they are NOT retired, but continue to function, adding additional challenge to the level.
The graphics are nice and functional. Same for the trains.
This is one of those games where you'll want to play until you beat the current level, and can't wait to conquer the next.
Definitely worth the price of admission.

Element number 2, You should feel isolated an example would be how you're trapped in a asylum and your main goal is to escape. Element number 4, A good Horror game should have uncertainty like you being unsure of what's gonna happen when you open a door. Element number 5, It should have a Lingering fear something to stay with you even after you stop playing or finish it, Like a scary movie about spiders would give you a fear of spiders after you watch it. To begin with, it's drag-able track, that automatically links up or creates crossings by itself. Then you run trains, and where you can afford or have space to, extra trains.
However, TV is not without issues.
1. bankruptcy is common. 3K of tax annually cripples you if you've been building a lot or had a bad year for revenue.
2. Beware the optionals - achieving them is harder than it looks.
3. Russia is incredibly hard to conquer. Get some practice in.
